This paper presents a variational based approach to fusing hyperspectral and
multispectral images.

The fusion process is formulated as an inverse problem
whose solution is the target image assumed to live in a much lower dimensional
subspace.

A sparse regularization term is carefully designed, relying on a
decomposition of the scene on a set of dictionaries.

The dictionary atoms and
the corresponding supports of active coding coefficients are learned from the
observed images.

Then, conditionally on these dictionaries and supports, the
fusion problem is solved via alternating optimization with respect to the
target image (using the alternating direction method of multipliers) and the
coding coefficients.

Simulation results demonstrate the efficiency of the
proposed algorithm when compared with the state-of-the-art fusion methods.

Notions of simulation, among other uses, provide a computationally tractable
and sound (but not necessarily complete) proof method for language inclusion.

They have been comprehensively studied by Lynch and Vaandrager for
nondeterministic and timed systems; for B\"{u}chi automata the notion of fair
simulation has been introduced by Henzinger, Kupferman and Rajamani.

We
contribute to a generalization of fair simulation in two different directions:
one for nondeterministic tree automata previously studied by Bomhard; and the
other for probabilistic word automata with finite state spaces, both under the
B\"{u}chi acceptance condition.

The former nondeterministic definition is
formulated in terms of systems of fixed-point equations, hence is readily
translated to parity games and is then amenable to Jurdzi\'{n}ski's algorithm;
the latter probabilistic definition bears a strong ranking-function flavor.

These two different-looking definitions are derived from one source, namely our
coalgebraic modeling of B\"{u}chi automata.

Based on these coalgebraic
observations, we also prove their soundness: a simulation indeed witnesses
language inclusion.

Let s_q(n) denote the base q sum of digits function, which for n<x, is
centered around (q-1)/2 log_q x. In Drmota, Mauduit and Rivat's 2009 paper,
they look at sum of digits of prime numbers, and provide asymptotics for the
size of the set {p<x, p prime : s_q(p)=alpha(q-1)log_q x} where alpha lies in a
tight range around 1/2.

In this paper, we examine the tails of this
distribution, and provide the lower bound |{p < x, p prime :
s_q(p)>alpha(q-1)log_q x}| >>x^{2(1-alpha)}e^{-c(log x)^{1/2+epsilon}} for
1/2<alpha<0.7375.

To attain this lower bound, we note that the multinomial
distribution is sharply peaked, and apply results regarding primes in short
intervals.

This proves that there are infinitely many primes with more than
twice as many ones than zeros in their binary expansion.
A gapped repeat (respectively, palindrome) occurring in a word $

w$ is a
factor $uvu$ (respectively, $u^Rvu$) of $w$. In such a repeat (palindrome) $u$
is called the arm of the repeat (respectively, palindrome), while $v$ is called
the gap.

We show how to compute efficiently, for every position $i$ of the word
$w$, the longest gapped repeat and palindrome occurring at that position,
provided that the length of the gap is subject to various types of
restrictions.

That is, that for each position $i$ we compute the longest prefix
$u$ of $w[i..n]$ such that $uv$ (respectively, $u^Rv$) is a suffix of
$w[1..i-1]$ (defining thus a gapped repeat $uvu$ -- respectively, palindrome
$u^Rvu$), and the length of $v$ is subject to the aforementioned restrictions.

We present a fully relativistic calculation of the observed galaxy number
counts in the linear regime.

We show that besides the density fluctuations and
redshift-space distortions, various relativistic effects contribute to
observations at large scales.

These effects all have the same physical origin:
they result from the fact that our coordinate system, namely the galaxy
redshift and the incoming photons' direction, is distorted by inhomogeneities
in our universe.

We then discuss the impact of the relativistic effects on the
angular power spectrum and on the two-point correlation function in
configuration space.

We show that the latter is very well adapted to isolate
the relativistic effects since it naturally makes use of the symmetries of the
different contributions.

In particular, we discuss how the Doppler effect and
the gravitational redshift distortions can be isolated by looking for a dipole
in the cross-correlation function between a bright and a faint population of
galaxies.

We investigate the computational power and unified resource use of hybrid
quantum-classical computations, such as teleportation and measurement-based
computing.

We introduce a physically causal and local graphical calculus for
quantum information theory, which enables high-level intuitive reasoning about
quantum information processes.

The graphical calculus defines a local
information flow in a computation which satisfies conditions for physical
causality.

We show how quantum and classical processing units can now be
formally integrated, and give an analysis of the joint resources used in a
typical measurement-based computation.

Finally, we discuss how this picture may
be used to give a high-level unified model for hybrid quantum computing.

Boolean operations of geometric models is an essential issue in computational
geometry.

In this paper, we develop a simple and robust approach to perform
Boolean operations on closed and open triangulated surfaces.

Our method mainly
has two stages: (1) We firstly find out candidate intersected-triangles pairs
based on Octree and then compute the inter-section lines for all pairs of
triangles with parallel algorithm; (2) We form closed or open
intersection-loops, sub-surfaces and sub-blocks quite robustly only according
to the cleared and updated topology of meshes while without coordinate
computations for geometric enti-ties.

A novel technique instead of
inside/outside classification is also proposed to distinguish the resulting
union, subtraction and intersection.

Several examples have been given to
illus-trate the effectiveness of our approach.

We compute the relative-order-v^4 contribution to gluon fragmentation into
quarkonium in the 3S1 color-singlet channel, using the nonrelativistic QCD
(NRQCD) factorization approach.

The QCD fragmentation process contains infrared
divergences that produce single and double poles in epsilon in 4-2epsilon
dimensions.

We devise subtractions that isolate the pole contributions, which
ultimately are absorbed into long-distance NRQCD matrix elements in the NRQCD
matching procedure.

The matching procedure involves two-loop renormalizations
of the NRQCD operators.

The subtractions are integrated over the phase space
analytically in 4-2epsilon dimensions, and the remainder is integrated over the
phase-space numerically.

We find that the order-v^4 contribution is enhanced
relative to the order-v^0 contribution.

However, the order-v^4 contribution is
not important numerically at the current level of precision of
quarkonium-hadroproduction phenomenology.

We also estimate the contribution to
hadroproduction from gluon fragmentation into quarkonium in the 3PJ color-octet
channel and find that it is significant in comparison to the complete
next-to-leading-order-in-alpha_s contribution in that channel.

This document is an introduction to the use of the point-centered quarter
method.

It briefly outlines its history, its methodology, and some of the
practical issues (and modifications) that inevitably arise with its use in the
field.

Additionally this paper shows how data collected using point-centered
quarter method sampling may be used to determine importance values of different
species of trees and describes and derives several methods of estimating plant
density and corresponding confidence intervals.

New to this version is a revision of Appendix D which now includes R Shiny
Apps to carry out many of these calculations.

References to data sets in the
previous version that are no longer publicly available have been removed.

These
have been replaced with examples and exercises which demonstrate the use of the

In this work, we propose an adaptive spectral element algorithm for solving
nonlinear optimal control problems.

The method employs orthogonal collocation
at the shifted Gegenbauer-Gauss points combined with very accurate and stable
numerical quadratures to fully discretize the multiple-phase integral form of
the optimal control problem.

The proposed algorithm relies on exploiting the
underlying smoothness properties of the solutions for computing approximate
solutions efficiently.

In particular, the method brackets discontinuities and
"points of nonsmoothness" through a novel local adaptive algorithm, which
achieves a desired accuracy on the discrete dynamical system equations by
adjusting both the mesh size and the degree of the approximating polynomials.

A
rigorous error analysis of the developed numerical quadratures is presented.

Finally, the efficiency of the proposed method is demonstrated on three test
examples from the open literature.

A polynomial skew product of C^2 is a map of the form f(z,w) = (p(z),
q(z,w)), where p and q are polynomials, such that f is regular of degree d >=
2.

For polynomial maps of C, hyperbolicity is equivalent to the condition that
the closure of the postcritical set is disjoint from the Julia set; further,
critical points either iterate to an attracting cycle or infinity.

For
polynomial skew products, Jonsson (Math.

Ann., 1999) established that f is
Axiom A if and only if the closure of the postcritical set is disjoint from the
right analog of the Julia set.

Here we present the analogous conclusion:
critical orbits either escape to infinity or accumulate on an attracting set.

In addition, we construct new examples of Axiom A maps demonstrating various
postcritical behaviors.

We build on recent works on Stein's method for functions of multivariate
normal random variables to derive bounds for the rate of convergence of some
asymptotically chi-square distributed statistics.

We obtain some general bounds
and establish some simple sufficient conditions for convergence rates of order
$n^{-1}$ for smooth test functions.

These general bounds are applied to
Friedman's statistic for comparing $r$ treatments across $n$ trials and the
family of power divergence statistics for goodness-of-fit across $n$ trials and
$r$ classifications, with index parameter $\lambda\in\mathbb{R}$ (Pearson's
statistic corresponds to $\lambda=1$).

We obtain a $O(n^{-1})$ bound for the
rate of convergence of Friedman's statistic for any number of treatments
$r\geq2$. We also obtain a $O(n^{-1})$ bound on the rate of convergence of the
power divergence statistics for any $r\geq2$ when $\lambda$ is a positive
integer or any real number greater than 5.

We conjecture that the $O(n^{-1})$
rate holds for any $\lambda\in\mathbb{R}$.
It was predicted by Tewari [Phys. Rev. Lett.

{\bf 100}, 027001 (2008)] that a
teleportationlike electron transfer phenomenon is one of the novel consequences
of the existence of Majorana fermion, because of the inherently nonlocal
nature.

In this work we consider a concrete realization and measurement scheme
for this interesting behavior, based on a setup consisting of a pair of quantum
dots which are tunnel-coupled to a semiconductor nanowire and are jointly
measured by two point-contact detectors.

We analyze the teleportation dynamics
in the presence of measurement backaction and discuss how the teleportation
events can be identified from the current trajectories of strong response
detectors.

The Efficient Market Hypothesis (EMH) is widely accepted to hold true under
certain assumptions.

One of its implications is that the prediction of stock
prices at least in the short run cannot outperform the random walk model.

Yet,
recently many studies stressing the psychological and social dimension of
financial behavior have challenged the validity of the EMH.

Towards this aim,
over the last few years, internet-based communication platforms and search
engines have been used to extract early indicators of social and economic
trends.

Here, we used Twitter's social networking platform to model and
forecast the EUR/USD exchange rate in a high-frequency intradaily trading
scale.

Using time series and trading simulations analysis, we provide some
evidence that the information provided in social microblogging platforms such
as Twitter can in certain cases enhance the forecasting efficiency regarding
the very short (intradaily) forex.
Twitter is one of the most prominent Online Social Networks.

It covers a
significant part of the online worldwide population~20% and has impressive
growth rates.

The social graph of Twitter has been the subject of numerous
studies since it can reveal the intrinsic properties of large and complex
online communities.

Despite the plethora of these studies, there is a limited
cover on the properties of the social graph while they evolve over time.

Moreover, due to the extreme size of this social network (millions of nodes,
billions of edges), there is a small subset of possible graph properties that
can be efficiently measured in a reasonable timescale.

In this paper we propose
a sampling framework that allows the estimation of graph properties on large
social networks.

We apply this framework to a subset of Twitter's social
network that has 13.2 million users, 8.3 billion edges and covers the complete
Twitter timeline (from April 2006 to January 2015).

We derive estimation on the
time evolution of 24 graph properties many of which have never been measured on
large social networks.

We further discuss how these estimations shed more light
on the inner structure and growth dynamics of Twitter's social network.

The ability to detect change-points in a dynamic network or a time series of
graphs is an increasingly important task in many applications of the emerging
discipline of graph signal processing.

This paper formulates change-point
detection as a hypothesis testing problem in terms of a generative latent
position model, focusing on the special case of the Stochastic Block Model time
series.

We analyze two classes of scan statistics, based on distinct underlying
locality statistics presented in the literature.

Our main contribution is the
derivation of the limiting distributions and power characteristics of the
competing scan statistics.

Performance is compared theoretically, on synthetic
data, and on the Enron email corpus.

We demonstrate that both statistics are
admissible in one simple setting, while one of the statistics is inadmissible a
second setting.

The aim of this paper to draw attention to several aspects of the algebraic
dependence in algebras.

The article starts with discussions of the algebraic
dependence problem in commutative algebras.

Then the Burchnall-Chaundy
construction for proving algebraic dependence and obtaining the corresponding
algebraic curves for commuting differential operators in the Heisenberg algebra
is reviewed.

Next some old and new results on algebraic dependence of commuting
q-difference operators and elements in q-deformed Heisenberg algebras are
reviewed.

The main ideas and essence of two proofs of this are reviewed and
compared.
One is the algorithmic dimension growth existence proof.

The other is
the recent proof extending the Burchnall-Chaundy approach from differential
operators and the Heisenberg algebra to the q-deformed Heisenberg algebra,
showing that the Burchnall-Chaundy eliminant construction indeed provides
annihilating curves for commuting elements in the q-deformed Heisenberg
algebras for q not a root of unity.

Recently, Landau, Reid and Yershov provided a novel solution to the problem
of redistricting.

Instead of trying to ensure fairness by restricting the shape
of the possible maps or by assigning the power to draw the map to nonbiased
entities, the solution ensures fairness by balancing competing interests
against each other.

This kind of solution is an example of what are known as
"fair division" solutions---

such solutions involve the preferences of all
parties and are accompanied by rigorous guarantees of a specified well-defined
notion of fairness.

In this expository article, we give an introduction to the
ideas of fair division in the context of this redistricting solution.

Through
examples and discussion we clarify how fair division methods can play an
important role in a realistic redistricting solution by introducing an
interactive step that incorporates a certain kind of fairness that can be used
in concert with, and not a substitute for, other necessary or desired criteria
for a good redistricting solution.

In a k-linear triangulated category (where k is a field) we show that the
existence of Auslander-Reiten triangles implies that objects are determined, up
to shift, by knowing dimensions of homomorphisms between them.

In most cases
the objects themselves are distinguished by this information, a conclusion
which was also reached under slightly different hypotheses in a theorem of
Jensen, Su and Zimmermann.

The approach is to consider bilinear forms on
Grothendieck groups which are analogous to the Green ring of a finite group.

We specialize to the category of perfect complexes for a self-injective
algebra, for which the Auslander-Reiten quiver has a known shape.

We
characterize the position in the quiver of many kinds of perfect complexes,
including those of lengths 1, 2 and 3, rigid complexes and truncated projective
resolutions.

We describe completely the quiver components which contain
projective modules.

We obtain relationships between the homology of complexes
at different places in the quiver, deducing that every self-injective algebra
of radical length at least 3 has indecomposable perfect complexes with
arbitrarily large homology in any given degree.

We find also that homology
stabilizes away from the rim of the quiver.

We show that when the algebra is
symmetric, one of the forms considered earlier is Hermitian, and this allows us
to compute its values knowing them only on objects on the rim of the quiver.

Additive deformations of bialgebras in the sense of Wirth are deformations of
the multiplication map of the bialgebra fulfilling a compatibility condition
with the coalgebra structure and a continuity condition.

Two problems
concerning additive deformations are considered.

With a deformation theory a
cohomology theory should be developed.

Here a variant of the Hochschild
cohomology is used.

The main result in the first partad of this paper is the
characterization of the trivial deformations, i.e. deformations generated by a
coboundary.

Starting with a Hopf algebra, one would expect the deformed
multiplications to have some analogue of the antipode, which we call deformed
antipodes.

We prove, that deformed antipodes always exist, explore their
properties, give a formula to calculate them given the deformation and the
antipode of the original Hopf algebra and show in the cocommutative case, that
each deformation splits into a trivial part and into a part with constant
antipodes.

This paper maps the national UK web presence on the basis of an analysis of
the .uk domain from 1996 to 2010.

It reviews previous attempts to use web
archives to understand national web domains and describes the dataset.

Next, it
presents an analysis of the .uk domain, including the overall number of links
in the archive and changes in the link density of different second-level
domains over time.

We then explore changes over time within a particular
second-level domain, the academic subdomain .ac.uk, and compare linking
practices with variables, including institutional affiliation, league table
ranking, and geographic location.

We do not detect institutional affiliation
affecting linking practices and find only partial evidence of league table
ranking affecting network centrality, but find a clear inverse relationship
between the density of links and the geographical distance between
universities.

This echoes prior findings regarding offline academic activity,
which allows us to argue that real-world factors like geography continue to
shape academic relationships even in the Internet age.

We conclude with
directions for future uses of web archive resources in this emerging area of
research.

We investigate the impact of coulomb screening on primordial nucleosynthesis
in a universe having scale factor that evolves linearly with time.

Coulomb
screening affects primordial nucleosynthesis via enhancement of thermonuclear
reaction rates.

This enhancement is determined by the solving Poisson equation
within the context of mean field theory (under appropriate conditions during
the primordial nucleosynthesis).

Using these results, we claim that the mean
field estimates of coulomb screening hardly affect the predicted element
abundances and nucleosynthesis parameters$, \{\eta_9,\xi_e\}$. The deviations
from mean field estimates are also studied in detail by boosting genuine
screening results with the screening parameter ($\omega_s$).

These deviations
show negligible effect on the element abundances and on nucleosynthesis
parameters.

This work thus rules out the coulomb screening effects on
primordial nucleosynthesis in slow evolving models and confirms that
constraints in ref.[7] on nucleosynthesis parameters remain unaltered.

Now that so much of collective action takes place online, web-generated data
can further understanding of the mechanics of Internet-based mobilisation.

This
trace data offers social science researchers the potential for new forms of
analysis, using real-time transactional data based on entire populations,
rather than sample-based surveys of what people think they did or might do.

This paper uses a `big data' approach to track the growth of over 8,000
petitions to the UK Government on the No. 10 Downing Street website for two
years, analysing the rate of growth per day and testing the hypothesis that the
distribution of daily change will be leptokurtic (rather than normal) as
previous research on agenda setting would suggest.

This hypothesis is
confirmed, suggesting that Internet-based mobilisation is characterized by
tipping points (or punctuated equilibria) and explaining some of the volatility
in online collective action.

We find also that most successful petitions grow
quickly and that the number of signatures a petition receives on its first day
is a significant factor in explaining the overall number of signatures a
petition receives during its lifetime.

These findings have implications for the
strategies of those initiating petitions and the design of web sites with the
aim of maximising citizen engagement with policy issues.

Recently, there has been focus on penalized log-likelihood covariance
estimation for sparse inverse covariance (precision) matrices.

The penalty is
responsible for inducing sparsity, and a very common choice is the convex $l_1$
norm.

However, the best estimator performance is not always achieved with this
penalty.

The most natural sparsity promoting "norm" is the non-convex $l_0$
penalty but its lack of convexity has deterred its use in sparse maximum
likelihood estimation.

In this paper we consider non-convex $l_0$ penalized
log-likelihood inverse covariance estimation and present a novel cyclic descent
algorithm for its optimization.

Convergence to a local minimizer is proved,
which is highly non-trivial, and we demonstrate via simulations the reduced
bias and superior quality of the $l_0$ penalty as compared to the $l_1$
penalty.

Broadcast MIMO techniques can significantly increase the throughput in the
downlink of cellular networks, at the price of channel state information (CSI)
feedback from the mobiles, sent over the uplink.

Thus, it creates a mechanism
that can tradeoff some uplink capacity for increased downlink capacity.

In this
work we quantify this tradeoff and study the exchange ratio between the
feedback rate (over the uplink) and the downlink rate.

We study both finite and
infinite networks, and show that for high enough (but finite) SNR, the uplink
rate can be exchanged for increased downlink rate with a favorable exchange
ratio.

This exchange ratio is an increasing function of the channel coherence
time, and a decreasing function of the number of measured base stations.

We
also show that devoting a constant fraction of the uplink to CSI feedback can
increase the downlink multiplexing gain continuously from 0 to 1, in finite
networks.

On the other hand, in infinite networks (with infinite connectivity)
our bounds can only show doubly logarithmic scaling of the rate with SNR.

The
presented results prove that the adaptation of the feedback rate can control
the balance between the uplink and downlink rates.

This capability is very
important in modern cellular networks, where the operators need to respond to
continuously changing user demands.

This paper introduces a class of mixed-effects models for joint modeling of
spatially correlated intensity variation and warping variation in 2D images.

Spatially correlated intensity variation and warp variation are modeled as
random effects, resulting in a nonlinear mixed-effects model that enables
simultaneous estimation of template and model parameters by optimization of the
likelihood function.

We propose an algorithm for fitting the model which
alternates estimation of variance parameters and image registration.

This
approach avoids the potential estimation bias in the template estimate that
arises when treating registration as a preprocessing step.

We apply the model
to datasets of facial images and 2D brain magnetic resonance images to
illustrate the simultaneous estimation and prediction of intensity and warp
effects.
> Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being used in medical imaging to improve diagnostic accuracy, reduce workload, and improve patient care.
However, the use of AI in medical imaging raises ethical, legal, and social issues that must be addressed to ensure the safe and effective use of AI in healthcare.
In this paper, we present the results of a consensus-building process that involved a multidisciplinary group of experts in AI, ethics, law, and medicine.
The goal of the process was to develop a set of guiding principles and consensus recommendations for trustworthy AI in future medical imaging.
The process involved a series of workshops and online discussions, during which the experts identified key ethical, legal, and social issues related to the use of AI in medical imaging.
The experts then developed a set of guiding principles and consensus recommendations for trustworthy AI in future medical imaging.
The guiding principles and consensus recommendations cover a wide range of issues, including transparency, accountability, fairness, privacy, and security.

The principles and recommendations are intended to provide a framework for the development and use of AI in medical imaging, and to ensure that AI is used in a way that is safe, effective, and ethical.
The results of the consensus-building process are presented in this paper, along with a discussion of the implications for the development and use of AI in medical imaging.
The paper also highlights the need for continued research and collaboration to ensure that AI is used in a way that is safe, effective, and ethical.

We present a novel approach to interactive segmentation that is based on a novel edge-guided flow model.
Our model is trained on a large dataset of images with segmentation masks, and is able to predict a flow field that can be used to segment new images.
The flow field is guided by the edges in the image, which allows the model to capture the structure of the image and produce accurate segmentations.
Our model is trained using a novel loss function that is based on the edge-guided flow model.
The loss function is designed to encourage the model to produce a flow field that is consistent with the edges in the image.
We evaluate our model on a number of benchmark datasets, and show that it is able to produce accurate segmentations.
We also show that our model is able to produce segmentations that are more accurate than those produced by other state-of-the-art methods.

In this paper, we propose a semi-supervised contrastive learning framework for label-efficient medical image segmentation.
The proposed framework consists of two components: a semi-supervised contrastive learning module and a segmentation module.
The semi-supervised contrastive learning module is designed to learn discriminative representations from unlabeled data, while the segmentation module is used to perform segmentation on labeled data.
The two modules are trained jointly in an end-to-end manner.
Experimental results on two public datasets demonstrate that the proposed framework can achieve state-of-the-art performance with significantly fewer labeled data.

The method uses a deep neural network to learn a mapping between the image and the description, and then applies a series of progressive refinement steps to improve the accuracy of the segmentation.

The results show that the proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art methods on several benchmark datasets, and demonstrates the potential of cross-modal learning for improving the performance of computer vision tasks.
Food image segmentation is a crucial task in the field of computer vision with numerous applications in areas such as robotics, agriculture, and e-commerce.
Despite the recent progress in this field, there is a lack of benchmark datasets and standardized evaluation metrics to compare the performance of different methods.
In this paper, we present a large-scale benchmark for food image segmentation that includes a diverse set of images and evaluation metrics.
Our benchmark dataset consists of over 8,000 images of various food items, annotated with segmentation masks.
We also propose a set of evaluation metrics, including intersection over union (IoU), precision, recall, and F1-score, to assess the performance of different methods.
We evaluate several state-of-the-art methods on our benchmark dataset and provide a comprehensive comparison of their performance.
Our results show that our benchmark dataset and evaluation metrics can be used to compare and evaluate the performance of different food image segmentation methods in a standardized manner.
Bayesian logistic shape models (BLSMs) are a powerful tool for image segmentation tasks, particularly in cases where the shapes of the objects of interest are complex and difficult to model.
In this paper, we present a novel approach to BLSM inference that is specifically designed for cochlea image segmentation.
Our method uses a combination of prior knowledge about the shape of the cochlea and Bayesian inference to estimate the parameters of the BLSM.
We evaluate our method on a dataset of cochlea images and show that it outperforms other state-of-the-art methods for cochlea segmentation.
Our approach has the potential to be applied to other image segmentation tasks where the shapes of the objects of interest are complex and difficult to model.
The paper presents a novel approach to active contours and image segmentation using a generalized asymmetric dual-front model.
The proposed model extends the traditional symmetric dual-front model by introducing asymmetry in the fronts, which allows for more flexible and efficient segmentation.
The model also incorporates a novel regularization term that improves the stability and robustness of the segmentation process.

The effectiveness of the proposed model is demonstrated through extensive experiments on various image segmentation tasks, and the results show that it outperforms the traditional symmetric dual-front model and other state-of-the-art methods.

Overall, the paper provides a significant contribution to the field of active contours and image segmentation by introducing a new and effective approach that can handle a wide range of image segmentation tasks.
The paper "Rethinking BiSeNet For Real-time Semantic Segmentation" presents a novel approach to real-time semantic segmentation using the BiSeNet architecture.
The proposed method addresses the challenges of real-time performance and accuracy by introducing a new attention mechanism that focuses on the most relevant regions of the input image.
Additionally, the paper introduces a new loss function that encourages the model to focus on the most important regions of the image during training.
The results show that the proposed method outperforms the original BiSeNet architecture in terms of both accuracy and real-time performance.
The paper concludes by discussing the potential applications of the proposed method in real-world scenarios such as autonomous vehicles and medical imaging.
The paper presents GENESIS-V2, a novel method for inferring unordered object representations without iterative refinement.
The method is based on a generative model that learns to map input features to a latent space where objects can be represented as a set of unordered features.
The model is trained using a combination of supervised and unsupervised learning techniques, and is able to learn representations that are robust to variations in object appearance and pose.
The paper demonstrates the effectiveness of the method on several benchmark datasets, and shows that it outperforms previous methods for unordered object representation learning.
Semantic segmentation is a critical task in computer vision that involves assigning a label to each pixel in an image.
Generative models have shown promising results in this task, but they often require large amounts of labeled data for training.
In this paper, we propose a semi-supervised learning approach for semantic segmentation using generative models.
Our approach leverages a combination of labeled and unlabeled data to learn a generative model that can accurately segment images.
We also demonstrate strong out-of-domain generalization capabilities of our model, which is trained on a source domain and tested on a target domain with different image styles and structures.
Our results show that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of both accuracy and generalization ability.
Ensemble learning is a powerful technique that combines the predictions of multiple models to improve the accuracy and robustness of the final output.
In this paper, we propose an ensemble learning approach for polyp localisation that utilizes classifier prediction confidence and comprehensive learning particle swarm optimisation (CLPSO).
The proposed approach first trains multiple classifiers on the training data and then uses their predictions to generate a set of confidence maps.
These confidence maps are then used as inputs to the CLPSO algorithm, which optimizes the parameters of a polyp localisation model.
The proposed approach is evaluated on the publicly available Kaggle dataset and shows significant improvements in accuracy and robustness compared to state-of-the-art methods.
Pneumothorax is a common medical condition that can be life-threatening if not diagnosed and treated promptly.
Early detection and diagnosis of pneumothorax is crucial for effective treatment and patient outcomes.
In this study, we propose a deep learning-based image segmentation model to predict pneumothorax from chest X-ray images.
Our model uses a combination of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and fully connected networks (FCNs) to segment pneumothorax from chest X-ray images.
We trained our model on a large dataset of chest X-ray images and evaluated its performance on a separate test set.
Our results show that our model achieves high accuracy in predicting pneumothorax from chest X-ray images, with an accuracy of 95%.
Our model can be used as a tool to assist radiologists in the diagnosis of pneumothorax, and can potentially improve patient outcomes by enabling earlier detection and treatment.

The abstract for the academic paper titled "FANet: A Feedback Attention Network for Improved Biomedical Image Segmentation" is as follows:

Biomedical image segmentation is a critical task in various medical applications, including disease diagnosis, treatment planning, and drug discovery.
Deep learning-based methods have shown promising results in recent years, but they often suffer from overfitting and lack of interpretability.
To address these challenges, we propose a novel feedback attention network (FANet) for improved biomedical image segmentation.
FANet incorporates a feedback mechanism that allows the network to learn from its own predictions and refine the segmentation results.
Additionally, we introduce an attention mechanism that enables the network to focus on the most relevant regions of the image during segmentation.
We evaluate FANet on several benchmark datasets and demonstrate its effectiveness in improving segmentation accuracy and reducing overfitting.
Our results show that FANet outperforms state-of-the-art methods and provides interpretable segmentation results.
Self-guided and cross-guided learning for few-shot segmentation is a novel approach to training deep learning models for image segmentation tasks with limited labeled data.
In this paper, we propose a self-guided learning method that utilizes unlabeled data to improve the performance of a pre-trained model on a few-shot segmentation task.
We also introduce a cross-guided learning method that combines self-guided learning with cross-modal learning to further improve the performance of the model.

Our experiments show that both methods outperform state-of-the-art methods on several benchmark datasets, and that the cross-guided learning method achieves state-of-the-art performance on some tasks.
In this paper, we present a novel approach for learning to segment objects from scribbles using multi-scale adversarial attention gates.

Our method leverages the power of adversarial training to learn a mapping between scribbles and segmentation masks, while simultaneously incorporating multi-scale attention gates to capture the spatial relationships between the scribbles and the objects they represent.
We evaluate our method on several benchmark datasets and demonstrate state-of-the-art performance in segmenting objects from scribbles.
Our approach provides a new way to leverage the information contained in scribbles to improve the accuracy of object segmentation tasks.
In this paper, we present a novel approach to segmenting fluorescence microscopy images using deep neural networks.
Our method involves training a deep convolutional neural network (CNN) to learn meta-structures that can be used to segment images at multiple scales.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on a variety of fluorescence microscopy images, including those of cells, tissues, and organisms.
Our results show that our method is able to achieve state-of-the-art performance on these tasks, and that it is able to generalize well to new images and scales.

Overall, our work represents a significant advancement in the field of fluorescence microscopy image segmentation, and has important implications for a wide range of applications in biology and medicine.

Abstract:

Medical image segmentation is a crucial task in the field of healthcare, with applications ranging from diagnosis to treatment planning.
Despite the availability of various supervised and unsupervised methods, achieving accurate and robust segmentation results remains a challenge.
In this paper, we propose a novel unsupervised medical image segmentation approach based on contrastive registration.
Our method leverages the spatial and intensity differences between two input images to generate a contrastive registration field, which is then used to guide the segmentation process.
We evaluate our approach on a publicly available dataset and demonstrate its effectiveness in comparison to state-of-the-art methods.
Our results show that our approach achieves competitive performance with significantly less computational resources, making it a promising tool for clinical use.
In this paper, we present a novel approach for learning food portion sizes from monocular images using cross-domain feature adaptation.
Our method leverages the strengths of multiple feature domains, including color, texture, and shape, to improve the accuracy of portion estimation.
We first extract features from multiple domains and then adapt them to the target domain using a cross-domain adaptation algorithm.
We then combine the adapted features to estimate the portion size.
We evaluate our method on a dataset of food images and show that it outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of accuracy and robustness.
Our approach has the potential to be used in a variety of applications, including food labeling, portion control, and meal planning.
The paper presents FedDG, a novel approach to medical image segmentation that leverages federated learning to improve domain generalization.
The proposed method utilizes episodic learning in continuous frequency space to enable the model to learn from multiple tasks simultaneously, leading to improved performance on unseen tasks.
The paper demonstrates the effectiveness of FedDG on several medical image segmentation tasks, including brain tumor segmentation and lung lesion segmentation.
The results show that FedDG outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving significant improvements in domain generalization.
Overall, the paper provides a valuable contribution to the field of medical image segmentation, offering a new approach to improve the performance of deep learning models on unseen tasks.
Semi-supervised medical image segmentation is a challenging task that requires the use of limited labeled data and a large amount of unlabeled data.
In this paper, we propose a novel approach to semi-supervised medical image segmentation that utilizes dual-task consistency to improve the performance of the model.
Our approach involves training a deep neural network to perform two related tasks simultaneously, namely image segmentation and image classification.
By enforcing consistency between the two tasks, we can improve the accuracy of the image segmentation task using limited labeled data.
We evaluate our approach on several benchmark datasets and demonstrate significant improvements in segmentation accuracy compared to state-of-the-art methods.
Our approach has the potential to improve the efficiency and accuracy of medical image segmentation, which can have important implications for clinical decision-making and patient outcomes.

The abstract for the academic paper titled "Unsupervised Domain Adaptation Network with Category-Centric Prototype Aligner for Biomedical Image Segmentation" is as follows:

In this paper, we propose an unsupervised domain adaptation network with a category-centric prototype aligner for biomedical image segmentation.

Our method leverages the inherent category-level structure of the source and target domains to align the category-centric prototypes and transfer the knowledge from the source domain to the target domain.
We evaluate our method on two benchmark datasets and demonstrate its effectiveness in improving the performance of existing methods without requiring any labeled data in the target domain.
Our results show that our method outperforms existing methods by a significant margin, demonstrating its potential for clinical translation.
Medical image segmentation is a crucial task in the field of healthcare, with applications ranging from disease diagnosis to treatment planning.
However, obtaining high-quality annotated data for training deep learning models can be time-consuming and expensive.
In this paper, we review recent deep network models for medical image segmentation that can operate with limited supervision.
These models leverage various techniques such as transfer learning, semi-supervised learning, and unsupervised learning to improve performance with limited labeled data.
We discuss the advantages and limitations of each approach and provide a comprehensive overview of the state-of-the-art in this field.

The Environmental Microorganism Image Dataset (EMIDS) is a widely used dataset for multiple image analysis tasks related to environmental microorganisms.

The fifth version of EMIDS (EMIDS-5) includes a larger number of images and more diverse types of microorganisms, making it an ideal resource for researchers and practitioners in the field of environmental microbiology.
In this paper, we present the details of EMIDS-5, including the image acquisition process, data preprocessing, and annotation procedures.
We also discuss the various image analysis tasks that can be performed using EMIDS-5, such as classification, segmentation, and object detection.
Finally, we provide an overview of the available tools and resources for working with EMIDS-5, including software packages and databases.

Overall, EMIDS-5 is a valuable resource for researchers and practitioners working on a wide range of environmental microbiology projects, and we believe it will greatly contribute to the advancement of the field.
Saliency-Aware Class-Agnostic Food Image Segmentation is an innovative approach to image segmentation that focuses on identifying salient regions in food images.
This technique is class-agnostic, meaning it can identify any type of food in an image, regardless of its class.
The paper presents a novel method for segmenting food images that uses saliency maps to identify the most important regions of the image.
The saliency map is then used to segment the image into regions, with each region representing a different type of food.
The results of the study show that the proposed method is highly accurate and can be used to segment food images with high precision.
The paper concludes by discussing the potential applications of this technique in areas such as food safety, nutrition, and marketing.
Image segmentation is a crucial task in computer vision and has numerous applications in various domains.
However, the accuracy of image segmentation models can be affected by label corruption, which occurs when the ground truth labels are incorrect or incomplete.
In this paper, we propose Co-Seg, an image segmentation framework that addresses label corruption by leveraging multiple sources of information.
Specifically, Co-Seg combines image-level and object-level supervision to improve the accuracy of image segmentation models.
We evaluate Co-Seg on several benchmark datasets and demonstrate its effectiveness in reducing label corruption and improving the performance of image segmentation models.
Our results show that Co-Seg outperforms state-of-the-art methods and sets a new benchmark for image segmentation under label corruption.
Medical image segmentation is a critical task in the field of healthcare, with applications ranging from diagnosis to treatment planning.
However, the performance of segmentation models can be limited by the availability of labeled training data, which is often scarce and expensive to obtain.
In this paper, we propose a novel approach to knowledge transfer for medical image segmentation that is network-agnostic, meaning it can be applied to any deep learning-based segmentation model.
Our approach involves leveraging a pre-trained model on a large dataset to transfer knowledge to a target model on a smaller dataset, without requiring any additional labeled data.

We evaluate our approach on several benchmark datasets and demonstrate significant improvements in segmentation performance compared to state-of-the-art methods that do not utilize knowledge transfer.

Our results suggest that knowledge transfer is a powerful technique for improving the performance of medical image segmentation models, and that our approach can be easily applied to a wide range of segmentation models and datasets.
Nonparametric clustering for image segmentation is a powerful technique used to group pixels in an image based on their similarity.
This method does not require any assumptions about the underlying distribution of the data, making it more flexible than parametric methods.
In this paper, we review several nonparametric clustering algorithms that have been applied to image segmentation, including k-means, hierarchical clustering, and density-based clustering.
We also discuss the challenges and limitations of these methods, and propose some new approaches to improve their performance.
Our results show that nonparametric clustering can achieve accurate and robust segmentation of images, even in the presence of noise and complex structures.
Overall, this paper provides a comprehensive overview of nonparametric clustering for image segmentation and its applications in various fields.
The paper presents a novel approach for semantic segmentation of point clouds using boundary-aware geometric encoding.
The proposed method leverages the geometric information of point clouds to encode the boundaries of objects in the scene, which is then used to segment the point cloud into different regions.

The boundary-aware geometric encoding is achieved by using a combination of geometric features such as normals, curvature, and distance maps to capture the shape and structure of the objects in the scene.
The segmentation is then performed using a deep neural network that is trained on the encoded point cloud.
The proposed method is evaluated on several benchmark datasets and shows significant improvements in segmentation accuracy compared to state-of-the-art methods.
The paper presents a novel approach for unsupervised domain adaptation on hip joint bone segmentation using intra- and cross-modality semantic consistency.
The proposed method leverages the inherent consistency between different modalities to improve the performance of the model on unseen data.

The approach involves first learning a joint representation of the input modalities using a deep neural network, and then enforcing semantic consistency between the joint representation and the individual modalities.
The method is evaluated on a large dataset of hip joint bone segmentation and shows significant improvements in performance compared to state-of-the-art methods.
The results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach for unsupervised domain adaptation on hip joint bone segmentation.
The abstract for the academic paper titled "CAKES: Channel-wise Automatic Kernel Shrinking for Efficient 3D Networks" is as follows:
In this paper, we propose a novel method called CAKES (Channel-wise Automatic Kernel Shrinking) for efficient 3D convolutional neural networks (CNNs).
The proposed method automatically shrinks the kernel size of each channel in the 3D convolutional layers, which significantly reduces the computational cost and memory usage of the network.
The shrinking process is performed in a channel-wise manner, which allows the network to adapt to different input sizes and channel dimensions.

We demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method on several benchmark datasets, including the MRI-Net and the 3D U-Net, and show that it can achieve state-of-the-art performance with significantly reduced computational cost.
Medical image segmentation is a crucial task in the field of healthcare, which involves identifying and separating different regions of interest within an image.
However, traditional methods often require large amounts of labeled data and are computationally expensive.
In this paper, we propose a novel approach to few-shot medical image segmentation using a global correlation network with discriminative embedding.

Our method leverages a global correlation network to capture the spatial relationships between different regions within an image, and a discriminative embedding to learn a compact and informative representation of the image.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on several benchmark datasets, achieving state-of-the-art performance with significantly fewer training examples.
Our work has important implications for improving the efficiency and accuracy of medical image segmentation, which can ultimately lead to better patient outcomes.
In this paper, we propose a novel active contour segmentation model for infrared images with intensity inhomogeneity.
The proposed model utilizes multiple features, including intensity, texture, and shape, to improve the segmentation accuracy.
The model is based on the active contour method, which iteratively evolves the contour boundaries to minimize the energy functional.
The energy functional is defined as a weighted sum of the intensity, texture, and shape features, where the weights are learned using a neural network.
The proposed model is trained on a dataset of infrared images with intensity inhomogeneity and evaluated on a separate test set.
The results show that the proposed model outperforms the state-of-the-art methods in terms of segmentation accuracy and robustness to intensity inhomogeneity.
In this paper, we propose a novel bidirectional recurrent neural network (RNN) architecture for few shot learning of 3D medical image segmentation.
Our approach leverages the inherent temporal structure of medical images to learn a compact representation of the image data, which can be used to segment new images with minimal training.
We evaluate our method on a benchmark dataset of 3D medical images and demonstrate significant improvements in segmentation accuracy compared to state-of-the-art methods.
Our approach has the potential to revolutionize the field of medical image segmentation by enabling faster and more efficient diagnosis and treatment planning.
The paper presents a novel deep learning model, w-Net, for medical image segmentation.
The model utilizes dual supervision, multi-dimensional attention, and cascade multi-scale convolution to improve the accuracy and efficiency of image segmentation.
The dual supervision technique combines both pixel-level and object-level supervision to enhance the model's ability to segment complex structures in medical images.

The multi-dimensional attention mechanism allows the model to focus on the most relevant regions of the image for segmentation, while the cascade multi-scale convolution enables the model to learn features at multiple scales.
The results show that w-Net outperforms state-of-the-art models on several benchmark datasets, demonstrating its effectiveness in medical image segmentation.

However, traditional image segmentation methods often struggle with handling complex and diverse image data, such as those with multiple modalities or limited labeled data.
In this paper, we propose a novel approach for multimodal and semi-supervised image segmentation that leverages the strengths of different modalities and unsupervised learning techniques.
Our method first disentangles the image into its constituent modalities, then aligns the modalities to a common space, and finally fuses the modalities to produce a segmentation result.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on several benchmark datasets and show that it outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of both accuracy and robustness.
Our work paves the way for more efficient and accurate image segmentation in complex and diverse scenarios.

In this paper, we propose a teacher-student framework for semi-supervised medical image segmentation from mixed supervision.
Our framework leverages a combination of weak and strong supervision to improve the performance of the student model while reducing the amount of labeled data required.
We evaluate our framework on two benchmark datasets and demonstrate significant improvements in segmentation accuracy compared to state-of-the-art methods.
Our results highlight the potential of our framework for improving the efficiency and effectiveness of medical image segmentation tasks.
The abstract for the academic paper titled "HS-ResNet: Hierarchical-Split Block on Convolutional Neural Network" is as follows:
In this paper, we propose a novel hierarchical-split block (HS-block) for convolutional neural networks (CNNs).
The HS-block is designed to improve the efficiency and accuracy of CNNs by splitting the convolutional layers into multiple smaller layers with different filter sizes.
This allows the network to learn more complex features at higher levels of abstraction, while reducing the computational cost of the network.

We demonstrate the effectiveness of the HS-block through experiments on several benchmark datasets, including ImageNet and CIFAR-10, and show that the HS-block outperforms state-of-the-art CNNs in terms of accuracy and efficiency.
In this paper, we present MetaBox+, a novel active learning method for semantic segmentation that utilizes priority maps to guide the selection of regions for labeling.
Our approach is based on the MetaBox algorithm, which uses a combination of region-based and object-based features to identify regions of interest for labeling.
However, MetaBox can be computationally expensive and may not be suitable for large datasets.
To address these limitations, we introduce a new priority map-based approach that reduces the computational complexity of MetaBox while maintaining its effectiveness.
Our approach uses a priority map to identify regions that are most likely to be informative for the model, and then selects these regions for labeling.
We evaluate our approach on several benchmark datasets and demonstrate that it outperforms MetaBox and other state-of-the-art active learning methods.
This paper presents a novel approach for interactive segmentation of patterned images using content-based propagation of user markings.
The proposed method involves the use of a content-based representation of the image to propagate user markings across the entire image.
The content-based representation is generated using a deep learning-based feature extraction algorithm that captures the underlying patterns in the image.
The user markings are then propagated across the image using a graph-based approach that takes into account the spatial relationships between the marked regions.
The proposed method is evaluated on a dataset of patterned images and compared to state-of-the-art methods.
The results show that the proposed method outperforms the existing methods in terms of accuracy and speed.
In this paper, we present a novel approach for learning to segment microscopy images with lazy labels.
Our method utilizes a combination of deep learning and active learning techniques to automatically segment images with minimal human intervention.
We use a convolutional neural network (CNN) to learn the features of the images and a lazy labeling strategy to select the most informative samples for labeling.
Our approach is able to achieve high accuracy with a small number of labeled samples, making it suitable for applications where labeling is time-consuming or expensive.
We evaluate our method on several benchmark datasets and demonstrate its effectiveness in segmenting a variety of microscopy images.
Mask-guided sample selection for Semi-Supervised Instance Segmentation is an approach to improve the performance of semi-supervised instance segmentation models.
The paper proposes a novel method that uses masks to guide the selection of samples for training.
The masks are generated using a pre-trained mask generator and are used to select samples that are most likely to be correctly segmented.

The paper demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed method on several benchmark datasets and shows that it can significantly improve the performance of semi-supervised instance segmentation models.
The paper also discusses the limitations of the proposed method and suggests areas for future research.
The paper presents PC-U Net, a novel deep learning model that simultaneously reconstructs and segments the cardiac walls in 3D from CT data.

The model uses a combination of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and generative adversarial networks (GANs) to learn the complex relationships between the cardiac walls and the surrounding tissue.
The model is trained on a large dataset of CT scans and achieves state-of-the-art performance on both reconstruction and segmentation tasks.
The paper also presents a novel loss function that encourages the model to learn both tasks simultaneously, leading to improved performance and better generalization to new data.
Overall, the paper demonstrates the potential of deep learning for improving the accuracy and efficiency of cardiac wall reconstruction and segmentation from CT data.

This paper presents a novel approach to image segmentation using cellular automata (CA), a type of discrete-time dynamical system.

The proposed method involves defining a set of rules that govern the behavior of cells in a grid, and then iteratively applying these rules to generate segments that represent the objects in the image.
The segments are grown by adding cells that satisfy certain conditions, and the process is repeated until the desired level of detail is achieved.

The effectiveness of the proposed method is demonstrated through experiments on a variety of images, and the results are compared to those obtained using other state-of-the-art segmentation techniques.

The results show that the proposed method is able to accurately segment images with a high degree of precision, and that it is particularly well-suited for images with complex structures and overlapping objects.
Polarimetric Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) image semantic segmentation is a challenging task due to the complex nature of SAR images and the lack of ground truth data.
In this paper, we propose a novel approach for polarimetric SAR image semantic segmentation using 3D discrete wavelet transform (DWT) and Markov random field (MRF).
The proposed method first applies 3D DWT to the polarimetric SAR image to extract the spatial and frequency features.
Then, we use MRF to model the spatial dependencies between pixels and classify the pixels based on their features.
We evaluate the performance of the proposed method on several benchmark datasets and compare it with state-of-the-art methods.
The results show that the proposed method achieves state-of-the-art performance on polarimetric SAR image semantic segmentation.

The abstract for the academic paper titled "Shape-aware Semi-supervised 3D Semantic Segmentation for Medical Images" is as follows:

This paper presents a novel approach to 3D semantic segmentation of medical images using a combination of supervised and unsupervised learning techniques.
The proposed method is designed to take advantage of the inherent spatial relationships between different organs and tissues in medical images, as well as the availability of limited labeled data.
The approach involves first extracting shape features from the input images, which are then used to train a shape-aware model for semi-supervised 3D semantic segmentation.

The model is able to accurately segment organs and tissues in medical images with limited labeled data, and the results are compared to those obtained using traditional supervised learning techniques.

This can be a challenging task, as it requires the ability to recognize and differentiate between objects, patterns, and textures within the image.

In this paper, we present a novel approach to automatic image labelling at the pixel level, using deep learning techniques to train a neural network to accurately predict the label for each pixel in an image.
Our approach involves the use of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to extract features from the image, followed by a fully connected layer to make the final predictions.
We evaluate our approach on a large dataset of images, and demonstrate that it achieves state-of-the-art performance in terms of accuracy and speed.
Our work has important implications for a wide range of applications, including image recognition, object detection, and segmentation.
The paper presents an uncertainty-based human-in-the-loop system for industrial tool wear analysis.
The system combines machine learning algorithms with human expertise to predict tool wear and optimize maintenance schedules.
The system uses a probabilistic approach to estimate tool wear, which allows for uncertainty quantification and decision making under uncertainty.
The human-in-the-loop component allows for real-time feedback and adjustment of the system's predictions.

The system is evaluated on a dataset of industrial tool wear measurements, and the results show that the uncertainty-based approach improves the accuracy of tool wear predictions and reduces maintenance costs.
The paper concludes with a discussion of the potential applications of the system in industrial settings and future directions for research.
Cardiac segmentation is a crucial task in medical imaging analysis, which involves identifying and separating the cardiac structures from the background.
However, manual annotation of cardiac images is time-consuming and prone to errors.
In this paper, we propose a novel approach called Dual-Teacher, which integrates intra-domain and inter-domain teachers for annotation-efficient cardiac segmentation.

The intra-domain teacher is a deep neural network that is trained on a large dataset of cardiac images, while the inter-domain teacher is a pre-trained convolutional neural network (CNN) that has been trained on a large dataset of non-cardiac images.
The Dual-Teacher model uses the intra-domain teacher to learn the cardiac-specific features and the inter-domain teacher to learn the general image features.
We evaluate the performance of the Dual-Teacher model on the publicly available Cardiac Segmentation Challenge (CSC) dataset and compare it with the state-of-the-art methods.
Our results show that the Dual-Teacher model outperforms the existing methods in terms of both accuracy and efficiency.

Hyperbolic geometry provides a natural way to model high-dimensional data, while CNNs are effective at learning spatial hierarchies and features from data.
In this paper, we propose a new architecture for FH-CNNs that leverages the strengths of both hyperbolic geometry and CNNs to achieve state-of-the-art performance on a variety of tasks.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our architecture on several benchmark datasets, including image classification, object detection, and semantic segmentation.
Our results show that FH-CNNs outperform traditional CNNs and other hyperbolic-based architectures, achieving competitive performance with significantly fewer parameters.
Overall, our work represents a significant advancement in the field of deep learning, providing a new and powerful tool for modeling high-dimensional data.
The paper presents a novel approach to robust semantic segmentation in adverse weather conditions using fast video-sequence segmentation.
The proposed method utilizes a combination of deep learning and computer vision techniques to accurately segment objects in videos captured under challenging weather conditions.
The approach involves training a deep neural network on a large dataset of annotated video sequences, which enables the network to learn robust features that are invariant to weather conditions.

The proposed method is evaluated on a benchmark dataset of video sequences captured in adverse weather conditions, and the results demonstrate significant improvements in segmentation accuracy compared to state-of-the-art methods.
The paper concludes by discussing the potential applications of the proposed method in areas such as autonomous vehicles, surveillance systems, and robotics.

Our method leverages the ROI information to guide the inpainting process and improve the quality of the generated supervoxels.
We first extract the ROI information from the input image and use it to guide the inpainting process.

Model theory is a branch of mathematics that studies the relationship between mathematical structures and their properties.
In this paper, we explore the model theory for a compact cardinal, which is a type of infinite cardinal number that has certain properties related to compactness.
We begin by defining the concept of a compact cardinal and its properties.
We then introduce the notion of a model structure on a set of sets, which is a way of organizing sets into a hierarchy based on their properties.
We show that the set of all compact cardinals forms a model structure on the set of all infinite cardinals.
We then explore the relationship between compact cardinals and other types of cardinals, such as regular and uncountable cardinals.
We show that every uncountable cardinal is either compact or has a compact subcardinal.
We also show that every regular cardinal is compact if and only if it is a successor cardinal.
Finally, we discuss some applications of model theory for compact cardinals.
We show that the concept of a compact cardinal can be used to study the behavior of functions on infinite sets, and we give some examples of how this can be applied in practice.

Overall, this paper provides a comprehensive overview of the model theory for compact cardinals, and shows how this area of mathematics can be used to study a wide range of problems in set theory and beyond.
Trace refinement is a technique used in labelled Markov decision processes (LMDPs) to improve the accuracy of the model by refining the transitions between states.
The technique involves iteratively updating the transitions based on the observed data, and then evaluating the resulting model using a trace-based metric.
The paper presents a new trace refinement algorithm that is more efficient and accurate than previous methods.
The algorithm is based on a combination of trace-based and state-based metrics, and uses a gradient descent optimization technique to update the transitions.
The paper also provides a theoretical analysis of the algorithm, and demonstrates its effectiveness through a series of experiments on real-world datasets.

Overall, the paper shows that trace refinement is a powerful tool for improving the accuracy of LMDPs, and that the new algorithm presented in this paper is a significant improvement over previous methods.
The paper "Descent c-Wilf Equivalence" presents a new approach to studying the relationship between different types of algebraic structures.
Specifically, the authors introduce the concept of descent c-Wilf equivalence, which is a generalization of the well-known c-Wilf equivalence.
The authors show that descent c-Wilf equivalence is a powerful tool for understanding the structure of algebraic systems, and they provide several examples to illustrate its applications.

Hyperspectral and multispectral image fusion is a critical task in remote sensing, which aims to combine multiple spectral bands to improve the accuracy and resolution of the resulting image.
In this paper, we propose a novel approach to hyperspectral and multispectral image fusion based on a sparse representation.
Our method first applies a sparse representation to each spectral band to obtain a set of sparse coefficients.
Then, we use these coefficients to reconstruct the original image and fuse the spectral bands.
We evaluate our method on several benchmark datasets and show that it outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of accuracy and computational efficiency.
Our approach has the potential to revolutionize the field of hyperspectral and multispectral image fusion and has numerous applications in remote sensing, agriculture, and environmental monitoring.
This paper presents a coalgebraic approach to fair simulation for nondeterministic and probabilistic Buechi automata.
The proposed approach is based on the concept of fairness, which is a fundamental property of automata theory.
The paper first introduces the concept of fairness in the context of Buechi automata and defines the notion of fair simulation.
Then, it presents a coalgebraic framework for fair simulation, which is based on the concept of coalgebraic semantics.
The paper shows that the proposed framework can be used to simulate nondeterministic and probabilistic Buechi automata in a fair manner.
Finally, the paper presents some examples to illustrate the proposed approach.
The sum of digits of a prime number is a well-known distribution in number theory.
In this paper, we study the tail distribution of this distribution.
Specifically, we derive bounds for the probability that the sum of digits of a prime number is greater than or equal to a certain value.
Our bounds are based on the distribution of the sum of digits of prime numbers and the distribution of the sum of digits of composite numbers.
We also provide some numerical examples to illustrate our results.
Our work has implications for the study of prime numbers and their properties.
The study of longest gapped repeats and palindromes in DNA sequences has important implications for understanding the structure and function of genetic information.
Longest gapped repeats are sequences of DNA that have repeating patterns with gaps between them, while palindromes are sequences that read the same forwards and backwards.
Both of these types of sequences have been found to play important roles in various biological processes, including gene regulation, recombination, and genome stability.
In this paper, we review the current state of research on longest gapped repeats and palindromes, including their identification, characterization, and functional annotation.

We also discuss the computational methods that have been developed to study these sequences, including algorithms for identifying repeats and palindromes, as well as methods for analyzing their properties and interactions with other DNA sequences.

Overall, this paper provides a comprehensive overview of the current research on longest gapped repeats and palindromes, and highlights the importance of these sequences for understanding the structure and function of DNA sequences.
The study of large-scale structure (LSS) in the universe has been a topic of great interest in recent years.
In this paper, we explore the possibility of isolating relativistic effects in LSS.
We use numerical simulations to study the distribution of matter in the universe and the resulting gravitational lensing effects.
We find that relativistic effects can be isolated by studying the distribution of matter in the universe and the resulting gravitational lensing effects.

Specifically, we show that by studying the distribution of matter in the universe and the resulting gravitational lensing effects, we can isolate the effects of dark matter and dark energy on the large-scale structure of the universe.
Our results have important implications for our understanding of the nature of dark matter and dark energy, and for our ability to study the universe in the future.
Hybrid hypercomputing is an emerging field that seeks to unify quantum and classical computation.
This paper presents a comprehensive review of the current state of the art in hybrid hypercomputing, including recent advances in quantum computing, classical computing, and their integration.

The paper presents a novel approach to Boolean operations on triangulated surfaces.

This paper presents a study of the higher-order relativistic corrections to gluon fragmentation into spin-triplet S-wave quarkonium.

The point-centered quarter method is a quantitative analysis technique used to determine the probability of a specific event occurring in a given time period.
This method involves dividing the time period into four equal quarters and calculating the probability of the event occurring in each quarter.
The results are then combined to determine the overall probability of the event occurring.
This method is particularly useful in situations where the event is not evenly distributed throughout the time period.
The paper provides a detailed explanation of the point-centered quarter method and its applications, including examples from various fields such as finance, engineering, and healthcare.
The paper also discusses the limitations and assumptions of the method and provides recommendations for future research.
Overall, the point-centered quarter method is a valuable tool for quantitative analysis and can provide valuable insights into the probability of specific events occurring in a given time period.
The paper presents a novel high-order adaptive Gegenbauer spectral element method for solving nonlinear optimal control problems.

The paper investigates the postcritical sets of polynomial skew products on the complex plane C^2.
Specifically, we consider axiom A polynomial skew products, which are defined by a polynomial of degree d in the first variable and a constant in the second variable.

In this paper, we propose a novel approach for anomaly detection in time series of graphs based on locality statistics.

Algebraic dependence of commuting elements in algebras is a topic of interest in algebraic geometry and commutative algebra.

The existence of Auslander-Reiten triangles is a fundamental result in the study of perfect complexes for self-injective algebras.
