The interpretation of observed spectra of stars in terms of fundamental
stellar properties is a key problem in astrophysics.

For FGK-type stars, the
radiative transfer models are often computed using the assumption of local
thermodynamic equilibrium (LTE).

Its validity is often questionable and needs
to be supported by detailed studies, which build upon the consistent framework
of non-LTE.
In this review, we outline the theory of non-LTE.

The processes
causing departures from LTE are introduced qualitatively by their physical
interpretation, as well as quantitatively by their impact on the models of
stellar spectra and element abundances.

We also compile and analyse the most
recent results from the literature.

In particular, we examine the non-LTE
effects for 24 chemical elements for six late-studied FGK-type stars.

A major open question in the study of synchronization of coupled oscillators
is to find necessary and sufficient condition for a system to synchronize on a
given family of graphs.

This is a difficult question that requires to
understand exactly how the nonlienar interaction between local entities evolves
over the underlying graph.

Another open question is to obtain bounds on the
time complexity of synchronization, which has important practical implications
in clock synchronization algorithms.

We address these questions for
one-parameter family of discrete pulse-coupled inhibitory oscillatorscalled the
$\kappa$-color firefly cellular automata (FCA).

Namely, we show that for
$\kappa\le 6$, recurrence of each oscillator is a necessary and sufficient
condition for synchronization on finite trees, while for $\kappa \ge 7$ this
condition is only necessary.

As a corollary, we show that any non-synchronizing
dynamics for $\kappa\le 6$ on trees decompose into synchronized subtrees
partitioned by `dead' oscillators.

Furthermore, on trees with diameter $d$ and
maximum degree at most $\kappa$, we show that the worst-case number of
iterations until synchronization is of order $O(\kappa d)$ for $\kappa\in
\{3,4,5\}$, $O(\kappa d^{2})$ for $\kappa=6$, and infinity for $\kappa \ge 7$.
Lastly, we report simulation results of FCA on lattices and conjecture that on
a finite square lattice, arbitrary initial configuration is synchronized under
$\kappa$-color FCA if and only if $\kappa=4$.

We discover new hereditary classes of graphs that are minimal (with respect
to set inclusion) of unbounded clique-width.

The new examples include split
permutation graphs and bichain graphs.

Each of these classes is characterised
by a finite list of minimal forbidden induced subgraphs.

These, therefore,
disprove a conjecture due to Daligault, Rao and Thomasse from 2010 claiming
that all such minimal classes must be defined by infinitely many forbidden
induced subgraphs.

In the same paper, Daligault, Rao and Thomasse make another conjecture that
every hereditary class of unbounded clique-width must contain a labelled
infinite antichain.

We show that the two example classes we consider here
satisfy this conjecture.

Indeed, they each contain a canonical labelled
infinite antichain, which leads us to propose a stronger conjecture: that every
hereditary class of graphs that is minimal of unbounded clique-width contains a
canonical labelled infinite antichain.

Kleisli simulation is a categorical notion introduced by Hasuo to verify
finite trace inclusion.

They allow us to give definitions of forward and
backward simulation for various types of systems.

A generic categorical theory
behind Kleisli simulation has been developed and it guarantees the soundness of
those simulations with respect to finite trace semantics.

Moreover, those
simulations can be aided by forward partial execution (FPE)---a categorical
transformation of systems previously introduced by the authors.

In this paper, we give Kleisli simulation a theoretical foundation that
assures its soundness also with respect to infinitary traces.

There, following
Jacobs' work, infinitary trace semantics is characterized as the "largest
homomorphism."

It turns out that soundness of forward simulations is rather
straightforward; that of backward simulation holds too, although it requires
certain additional conditions and its proof is more involved.

We also show that
FPE can be successfully employed in the infinitary trace setting to enhance the
applicability of Kleisli simulations as witnesses of trace inclusion.

Our
framework is parameterized in the monad for branching as well as in the functor
for linear-time behaviors; for the former we mainly use the powerset monad (for
nondeterminism), the sub-Giry monad (for probability), and the lift monad (for
exception).

We establish a Minkowski measurability criterion for a large class of
relative fractal drums (or, in short, RFDs), in Euclidean spaces of arbitrary
dimension in terms of their complex dimensions, which are defined as the poles
of their associated fractal zeta functions.

Relative fractal drums represent a
far-reaching generalization of bounded subsets of Euclidean spaces as well as
of fractal strings studied extensively by the first author and his
collaborators.

In fact, the Minkowski measurability criterion established here
is a generalization of the corresponding one obtained for fractal strings by
the first author and M.\ van Frankenhuijsen.

Similarly as in the case of
fractal strings, the criterion established here is formulated in terms of the
locations of the principal complex dimensions associated with the relative drum
under consideration.

These complex dimensions are defined as poles or, more
generally, singularities of the corresponding distance (or tube) zeta function.

We also reflect on the notion of gauge-Minkowski measurability of RFDs and
establish several results connecting it to the nature and location of the
complex dimensions.

(This is especially useful when the underlying scaling does
not follow a classic power law.)

We illustrate our results and their
applications by means of a number of interesting examples.

In this paper, we propose a novel label propagation based method for saliency
detection.

A key observation is that saliency in an image can be estimated by
propagating the labels extracted from the most certain background and object
regions.

For most natural images, some boundary superpixels serve as the
background labels and the saliency of other superpixels are determined by
ranking their similarities to the boundary labels based on an inner propagation
scheme.

For images of complex scenes, we further deploy a 3-cue-center-biased
objectness measure to pick out and propagate foreground labels.

A
co-transduction algorithm is devised to fuse both boundary and objectness
labels based on an inter propagation scheme.

The compactness criterion decides
whether the incorporation of objectness labels is necessary, thus greatly
enhancing computational efficiency.

Results on five benchmark datasets with
pixel-wise accurate annotations show that the proposed method achieves superior
performance compared with the newest state-of-the-arts in terms of different
evaluation metrics.

We construct two error feedback controllers for robust output tracking and
disturbance rejection of a regular linear system with nonsmooth reference and
disturbance signals.

We show that for sufficiently smooth signals the output
converges to the reference at a rate that depends on the behaviour of the
transfer function of the plant on the imaginary axis.

In addition, we construct
a controller that can be designed to achieve robustness with respect to a given
class of uncertainties in the system, and present a novel controller structure
for output tracking and disturbance rejection without the robustness
requirement.

We also generalize the internal model principle for regular linear
systems with boundary disturbance and for controllers with unbounded input and
output operators.

The construction of controllers is illustrated with an
example where we consider output tracking of a nonsmooth periodic reference
signal for a two-dimensional heat equation with boundary control and
observation, and with periodic disturbances on the boundary.

S-folds are generalizations of orientifolds in type IIB string theory, such
that the geometric identifications are accompanied by non-trivial S-duality
transformations.

They were recently used by Garcia-Etxebarria and Regalado to
provide the first construction of four dimensional N=3 superconformal theories.

In this note, we classify the different variants of these N=3 preserving
S-folds, distinguished by an analog of discrete torsion, using both a direct
analysis of the different torsion classes and the compactification of the
S-folds to three dimensional M-theory backgrounds.

Upon adding D3-branes, these
variants lead to different classes of N=3 superconformal field theories.

We
also analyze the holographic duals of these theories, and in particular clarify
the role of discrete gauge and global symmetries in holography.

In the main part of the paper, certain properties of cohomology groups
associated to the S-folds were conjectured and used.

This arXiv version
includes an appendix written by Kiyonori Gomi in 2023 providing the proofs of
the required properties using the technique of Borel equivariant cohomology,
whose brief review is also provided.

The application of nonlinear transformations to a cyclostationary signal for
the purpose of revealing hidden periodicities has proven to be useful for
applications requiring signal selectivity and noise tolerance.

The fact that
the hidden periodicities, referred to as cyclic moments, are often compressible
in the Fourier domain motivates the use of compressive sensing (CS) as an
efficient acquisition protocol for capturing such signals.

In this work, we
consider the class of Temporal Higher Order Cyclostationary Statistics (THOCS)
estimators when CS is used to acquire the cyclostationary signal assuming
compressible cyclic moments in the Fourier domain.

We develop a theoretical
framework for estimating THOCS using the low-rate nonuniform sampling protocol
from CS and illustrate the performance of this framework using simulated data.

Quantum coherence and quantum correlations lie in the center of quantum
information science, since they both are considered as fundamental reasons for
significant features of quantum mechanics different from classical mechanics.

We present a group of complementary relations for quantum coherence and quantum
correlations; specifically, we focus on thermal discord and conditional
information in scenarios of multiple measurements.

We show that the summation
of quantum coherence quantified in different bases has a lower bound, resulting
from entropic uncertainty relations with multiple measurements.

Similar results
are also obtained for thermal discord and for post-measurement conditional
information with multiple measurements in a multipartite system.

These results
indicate the general applications of the uncertainty principle to various
concepts of quantum information.

We prove lower bounds for energy in the Gaussian core model, in which point
particles interact via a Gaussian potential.

Under the potential function $t
\mapsto e^{-\alpha t^2}$ with $0 < \alpha < 4\pi/e$, we show that no point
configuration in $\mathbf{R}^n$ of density $\rho$ can have energy less than
$(\rho+o(1))(\pi/\alpha)^{n/2}$ as $n \to \infty$ with $\alpha$ and $\rho$
fixed.

This lower bound asymptotically matches the upper bound of $\rho
(\pi/\alpha)^{n/2}$ obtained as the expectation in the Siegel mean value
theorem, and it is attained by random lattices.

The proof is based on the
linear programming bound, and it uses an interpolation construction analogous
to those used for the Beurling-Selberg extremal problem in analytic number
theory.

In the other direction, we prove that the upper bound of $\rho
(\pi/\alpha)^{n/2}$ is no longer asymptotically sharp when $\alpha > \pi e$. As
a consequence of our results, we obtain bounds in $\mathbf{R}^n$ for the
minimal energy under inverse power laws $t \mapsto 1/t^{n+s}$ with $s>0$, and
these bounds are sharp to within a constant factor as $n \to \infty$ with $s$
fixed.

This paper studies the coordinated beamforming (CoBF) design in the
multiple-input single-output interference channel, assuming only channel
distribution information given a priori at the transmitters.

The CoBF design is
formulated as an optimization problem that maximizes a predefined system
utility, e.g., the weighted sum rate or the weighted max-min-fairness (MMF)
rate, subject to constraints on the individual probability of rate outage and
power budget.

While the problem is non-convex and appears difficult to handle
due to the intricate outage probability constraints, so far it is still unknown
if this outage constrained problem is computationally tractable.

To answer
this, we conduct computational complexity analysis of the outage constrained
CoBF problem.

Specifically, we show that the outage constrained CoBF problem
with the weighted sum rate utility is intrinsically difficult, i.e., NP-hard.

Moreover, the outage constrained CoBF problem with the weighted MMF rate
utility is also NP-hard except the case when all the transmitters are equipped
with single antenna.

The presented analysis results confirm that efficient
approximation methods are indispensable to the outage constrained CoBF problem.

We study interacting components and their compatibility with respect to
synchronous and asynchronous composition.

The behavior of components is
formalized by I/O-transition systems.

Synchronous composition is based on
simultaneous execution of shared output and input actions of two components
while asynchronous composition uses unbounded FIFO-buffers for message
transfer.

In both contexts we study compatibility notions based on the idea
that any output issued by one component should be accepted as an input by the
other.

We distinguish between strong and weak versions of compatibility, the
latter allowing the execution of internal actions before a message is accepted.

We consider open systems and study conditions under which (strong/weak)
synchronous compatibility is sufficient and necessary to get (strong/weak)
asynchronous compatibility.

We show that these conditions characterize
half-duplex systems.

Then we focus on the verification of weak asynchronous
compatibility for possibly non half-duplex systems and provide a decidable
criterion that ensures weak asynchronous compatibility.

We investigate
conditions under which this criterion is complete, i.e. if it is not satisfied
then the asynchronous system is not weakly asynchronously compatible.

Finally,
we discuss deadlock-freeness and investigate relationships between
deadlock-freeness in the synchronous and in the asynchronous case.

of multiple binomial sums and that compute recurrence relations for them.

conjunction with geometric simplifications of the integral representations,
this approach behaves well in practice.

The process avoids the computation of
certificates and the problem of the appearance of spurious singularities that
afflicts discrete creative telescoping, both in theory and in practice.

Our approach has been tested on a dataset of liquid samples, and we have shown that it can accurately segment and analyze the samples, as well as identify relationships between the regions.
Overall, our method has the potential to revolutionize the way that liquid samples are analyzed in hospitals and medical labs, by providing a fast and accurate way to automate these tasks.
Medical image segmentation is a critical task in the field of healthcare, with applications ranging from diagnosis to treatment planning.
Deep learning techniques have shown promising results in this task, but achieving high accuracy remains a challenge.
In this paper, we propose a novel approach to multi-label deep supervision for medical image segmentation.
Our approach involves training a deep neural network with multiple labels simultaneously, using a combination of cross-entropy and multi-label loss functions.
We evaluate our approach on several benchmark datasets and demonstrate significant improvements in accuracy compared to state-of-the-art methods.
Our results highlight the importance of multi-label supervision in medical image segmentation and pave the way for future research in this area.

Quantization of Deep Neural Networks for Accurate Edge Computing
Abstract:
Deep neural networks (DNNs) have shown remarkable performance in various applications, including image and speech recognition.
However, the high computational complexity and memory requirements of DNNs make them impractical for edge computing, where resources are limited.
In this paper, we propose a novel quantization technique for DNNs that reduces the precision of weights and activations while maintaining accuracy.

Our technique is based on a combination of pruning and quantization, where we first prune the network to remove unnecessary connections, and then quantize the remaining weights and activations to reduce their precision.
We evaluate our technique on several benchmark datasets and show that it significantly reduces the computational complexity and memory requirements of DNNs while maintaining accuracy.
Our results demonstrate the feasibility of using DNNs for edge computing and pave the way for the development of more efficient and accurate edge computing systems.
This paper presents a novel approach to disease classification and segmentation using self-supervised learning and interpretability-driven sample selection.
The proposed method utilizes a combination of unsupervised and supervised learning techniques to improve the accuracy and interpretability of disease classification and segmentation models.

The self-supervised learning component involves training a model on unlabeled data to learn useful representations of the input data, which can then be used to improve the performance of a supervised learning model.
The interpretability-driven sample selection component involves selecting a subset of the training data that is most informative for improving the interpretability of the model.

The proposed method is applied to the task of classifying and segmenting skin lesions, and the results demonstrate significant improvements in accuracy and interpretability compared to previous methods.
Image segmentation is a crucial task in computer vision that involves dividing an image into meaningful regions.
However, the performance of image segmentation models can be limited when applied to new images that differ significantly from the training data.
To address this issue, we propose a novel approach to image segmentation called constrained domain adaptation.

Our method involves finding a mapping between the source and target domains that preserves the semantic structure of the images while also taking into account the differences in the image distributions.
We achieve this by optimizing a loss function that combines the segmentation loss with a domain adaptation loss.
Our experiments show that our method outperforms state-of-the-art domain adaptation methods on several benchmark datasets, demonstrating the effectiveness of our approach.
Image segmentation is a crucial task in computer vision that involves dividing an image into meaningful regions.
However, the performance of image segmentation models can be limited when the source and target domains have significant differences.
Source-relaxed domain adaptation (SRDA) is a novel approach to address this problem by relaxing the source domain constraints during training.
In this paper, we propose a SRDA framework that leverages the strengths of both source and target domains to improve the performance of image segmentation models.
We evaluate the effectiveness of SRDA on several benchmark datasets and demonstrate that it outperforms state-of-the-art methods.
Our results show that SRDA can significantly improve the performance of image segmentation models in scenarios where the source and target domains have significant differences.
MeanShift++ is a novel algorithm for mode-seeking that is designed to be extremely fast and efficient.
It is based on the MeanShift algorithm, which is a popular method for image segmentation and object tracking.
However, MeanShift++ improves upon the original algorithm by incorporating a new mode-seeking strategy that is more robust and effective.
The key innovation of MeanShift++ is its use of a new mode-seeking strategy that is based on the concept of "extremal mode seeking."
This strategy involves identifying the mode that is most different from the current mode, rather than simply selecting the mode that is closest to the current mode.
This approach has several advantages, including improved convergence and faster convergence rates.
In addition to its mode-seeking strategy, MeanShift++ also incorporates several other improvements over the original MeanShift algorithm.

These include the use of a more accurate estimate of the mode's position, the incorporation of a new smoothing term that reduces noise, and the use of a new initialization strategy that is more robust to initial conditions.
The results of several experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of MeanShift++ in a variety of applications, including image segmentation and object tracking.
In particular, MeanShift++ is shown to be significantly faster and more accurate than the original MeanShift algorithm, making it a valuable tool for researchers and practitioners in these fields.
The paper "Locate then Segment: A Strong Pipeline for Referring Image Segmentation" presents a novel approach to the task of referring image segmentation.

The proposed method involves two stages: first, an object locator is used to identify the object of interest in the image, and then a segmentation model is applied to the region surrounding the object to extract a precise segmentation mask.

The paper demonstrates the effectiveness of this pipeline by comparing it to state-of-the-art methods on several benchmark datasets, and shows that the proposed approach achieves superior performance in many cases.
The paper also discusses some of the challenges and limitations of the proposed method, and suggests some possible directions for future research.
Overall, the paper provides a valuable contribution to the field of computer vision and image segmentation, and is likely to be of interest to researchers and practitioners working in this area.

DCNAS: Densely Connected Neural Architecture Search for Semantic Image Segmentation

In this paper, we present DCNAS, a novel neural architecture search (NAS) method for semantic image segmentation.
Our approach utilizes a densely connected network architecture that enables efficient search and optimization of the network structure.
We propose a novel search space that includes both the number of layers and the number of connections between them, allowing for a more comprehensive search of the network architecture.
Our method is trained using a combination of supervised and unsupervised learning, and we demonstrate its effectiveness on several benchmark datasets.
Our results show that DCNAS outperforms state-of-the-art NAS methods and achieves competitive performance with human-designed networks.
The field of artificial intelligence has seen a rapid growth in recent years, with neural networks being at the forefront of this development.
However, designing effective neural architectures remains a challenging task, requiring extensive experimentation and fine-tuning.
In this paper, we propose a novel approach to learning versatile neural architectures by propagating network codes.
Our method involves encoding the desired architecture as a set of network codes and then propagating these codes through a series of neural networks to generate the final architecture.
This approach allows for the creation of architectures that are optimized for specific tasks, while also being flexible enough to adapt to changing requirements.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method through several experiments, including image classification and natural language processing tasks.
Our results show that our approach is able to generate architectures that outperform traditional methods, while also reducing the time and computational resources required for training.
Overall, our work represents a significant advancement in the field of neural architecture design, providing a powerful tool for developing versatile and effective AI systems.

The field of medical image segmentation has seen significant advancements in recent years, with deep learning techniques such as convolutional neural networks (CNNs) achieving state-of-the-art performance.
However, these methods often require large amounts of labeled data for training, which can be a significant barrier to entry for many applications.
In this paper, we propose a novel location-sensitive local prototype network (LSPN) for few-shot medical image segmentation.
Our approach leverages the spatial relationships between pixels in an image to learn a set of location-sensitive prototypes that can be used to segment new images with limited labeled data.
We evaluate our method on several benchmark datasets and demonstrate that it outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in the few-shot setting.
Our work has important implications for medical image analysis, where labeled data is often scarce and expensive to obtain.
This paper presents a novel approach to multi-modal cardiac image segmentation that utilizes unsupervised adaptation of point-clouds and entropy minimization.
The proposed method is designed to adapt to different modalities and image types, making it applicable to a wide range of cardiac imaging techniques.

The paper demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed method through experiments on various cardiac image datasets, including magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), computed tomography (CT), and ultrasound (US).
The results show that the proposed method achieves high accuracy and robustness in segmenting cardiac structures across different modalities and image types.
Overall, this paper contributes to the development of a versatile and efficient method for multi-modal cardiac image segmentation that can be applied in various clinical settings.

Deep Superpixel Cut for Unsupervised Image Segmentation

In this paper, we present a novel approach for unsupervised image segmentation using deep superpixel cut.
Our method is based on the idea of dividing an image into non-overlapping superpixels and then cutting each superpixel into smaller pixels.
We use a deep neural network to learn the superpixel boundaries and then apply a superpixel cut algorithm to segment the image.
Our approach is unsupervised, meaning that it does not require any labeled data for training.
We evaluate our method on several benchmark datasets and show that it outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of both accuracy and speed.
Our approach is also scalable to large images and can be applied to a wide range of applications, including medical imaging, satellite imagery, and autonomous vehicles.
The Rand Index is a widely used measure of agreement between two classification models.
However, it is often difficult to obtain strong labels for the data, which can limit its usefulness.
In this paper, we propose a new version of the Rand Index that is designed to handle weakly-labeled data.
Specifically, we introduce a new metric called the Weakly-Labeled Rand Index, which is based on the idea of using a combination of strong and weak labels to evaluate the performance of a model.
We show that the Weakly-Labeled Rand Index is more robust to noise in the data than the standard Rand Index, and we provide some examples of how it can be used in practice.
Overall, our work demonstrates the importance of considering weakly-labeled data in the evaluation of classification models, and it provides a useful tool for doing so.
Embryo egg detection is a crucial task in the field of agriculture, as it helps farmers to identify and monitor the growth of their crops.
In this paper, we propose a K-means segmentation-based approach for embryo egg detection using the Lab color space.
The proposed method involves first converting the input image into the Lab color space, which separates the lightness information from the color information.
Then, we apply K-means clustering to the Lab color space to segment the embryo eggs from the background.
The segmented eggs are then classified using a support vector machine (SVM) classifier.
The proposed method was evaluated on a dataset of embryo egg images, and the results showed that it achieved high accuracy and precision in egg detection.
Overall, the proposed method provides a simple and effective solution for embryo egg detection, which can be easily implemented in real-world applications.
Urban expansion is a complex phenomenon that involves various factors such as population growth, economic development, and infrastructure expansion.
Predicting urban expansion accurately is crucial for urban planning and resource allocation.
In this paper, we propose a novel CNN-LSTM-based approach to predict urban expansion.
Our approach combines the strengths of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and long short-term memory (LSTM) networks to capture spatial and temporal patterns in urban expansion data.
We use a CNN to extract features from satellite images of urban areas and an LSTM to model the temporal dependencies in the extracted features.
We evaluate our approach on a dataset of urban expansion in China and show that it outperforms state-of-the-art methods in predicting urban expansion.
Our approach has the potential to revolutionize urban planning and resource allocation by providing accurate predictions of urban expansion.

Semantically Meaningful Class Prototype Learning for One-Shot Image Semantic Segmentation

In this paper, we propose a novel approach for one-shot image semantic segmentation that utilizes semantically meaningful class prototypes to improve the performance of the model.
Our approach is based on the idea that the class prototypes should be learned in a way that captures the semantic meaning of the classes, rather than just their visual appearance.
We achieve this by using a combination of supervised and unsupervised learning techniques, and by incorporating semantic information into the learning process.
Our approach is evaluated on several benchmark datasets, and we show that it outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of both accuracy and speed.
Image compositing is a technique used to combine multiple images to create a single image with improved visual quality.
In this paper, we propose a novel approach to segment surgical tools using image compositing without the need for manual annotations.

Our method involves first identifying the surgical tool of interest in the image and then using image compositing to combine multiple images of the tool to create a more detailed and accurate segmentation.
We evaluate our method on a dataset of surgical images and demonstrate that it outperforms traditional segmentation methods that rely on manual annotations.
Our approach has the potential to significantly improve the accuracy and efficiency of surgical tool segmentation, which can have important implications for medical imaging and surgical planning.
MudrockNet is a deep learning-based approach for semantic segmentation of mudrock scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images.
The proposed method utilizes a convolutional neural network (CNN) to classify each pixel in the image into one of three categories: mudrock, background, or artifact.
The CNN is trained on a large dataset of mudrock SEM images, which are labeled using a combination of human annotation and automated image processing techniques.
The performance of MudrockNet is evaluated on a separate test set of mudrock SEM images, and the results show that the method achieves state-of-the-art performance in mudrock SEM image segmentation.

The proposed method has the potential to improve the accuracy and efficiency of mudrock characterization and analysis, which is important for understanding the properties and behavior of mudrock in geological and engineering applications.
Mask-based data augmentation is a technique used to enhance the performance of semi-supervised semantic segmentation models.
This technique involves generating new training data by applying transformations to the original images and their corresponding masks.
The transformations include random cropping, flipping, and rotation.
The generated images are then used to train the model, along with the original images and masks.
The effectiveness of the technique is evaluated on several benchmark datasets, and the results show that it can significantly improve the performance of the model.
The technique is particularly useful when the amount of labeled data is limited, as it allows the model to learn from a larger amount of data.
Overall, mask-based data augmentation is a valuable tool for improving the performance of semi-supervised semantic segmentation models.
Finger vein recognition is a biometric technology that has gained significant attention in recent years due to its potential for high accuracy and non-invasive nature.
In this paper, we present a novel approach to finger vein recognition using a code generation technique.
Our method involves generating a unique code for each individual based on their finger vein pattern, which is then used to identify the person.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through experiments on a dataset of finger vein images, achieving high accuracy rates and outperforming existing methods.
Our work has important implications for the development of secure and efficient biometric recognition systems.
The paper presents a novel approach for domain adaptation in semantic nighttime image segmentation.
The proposed method utilizes a map-guided curriculum to adapt the model to the target domain, while also incorporating uncertainty-aware evaluation to improve the model's performance.
The map-guided curriculum involves gradually increasing the complexity of the training data, while also incorporating domain-specific features such as streetlights and buildings.
The uncertainty-aware evaluation involves using a combination of uncertainty maps and confidence scores to identify areas of uncertainty in the model's predictions.

The results show that the proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art methods in semantic nighttime image segmentation, particularly in challenging scenarios such as low-light conditions and complex urban scenes.
The paper presents RatLesNetv2, a fully convolutional network (FCN) designed for the segmentation of rodent brain lesions.
The network is trained on a large dataset of rodent brain images with lesions and without lesions, and achieves state-of-the-art performance on the task.
The network architecture includes multiple convolutional layers, pooling layers, and fully connected layers, and utilizes skip connections to improve the flow of information.
The network is trained using a combination of cross-entropy loss and Dice loss, and achieves high accuracy and precision on the task.
The paper also presents a thorough analysis of the network's performance on different lesion types and sizes, and demonstrates the effectiveness of the network in clinical settings.
Overall, RatLesNetv2 represents a significant advancement in the field of rodent brain lesion segmentation and has the potential to greatly improve the accuracy and efficiency of clinical diagnoses.
Histopathology image segmentation is a crucial task in medical diagnosis and treatment planning.
However, obtaining labeled data for training deep learning models is expensive and time-consuming.
In this paper, we propose a novel semi-supervised approach for histopathology image segmentation using unlabeled data.
Our method leverages the inherent spatial and temporal correlations in the images to generate pseudo-labels for the unlabeled data.
We then use these pseudo-labels to train a deep learning model for image segmentation.
Our approach is evaluated on two publicly available datasets and shows promising results, achieving state-of-the-art performance on one of the datasets.
Our method has the potential to significantly reduce the amount of labeled data required for training deep learning models in medical image analysis tasks.
Domain adaptation is a crucial problem in computer vision, particularly in the field of semantic segmentation.
This paper presents a novel approach to domain adaptation for semantic segmentation of aerial images.
The proposed method involves training a deep neural network on a source domain and then fine-tuning it on a target domain.
The fine-tuning process is performed using a combination of domain-specific and domain-invariant features.
The results show that the proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art methods in domain adaptation for semantic segmentation of aerial images.
The paper also provides a thorough analysis of the effectiveness of different features and techniques used in the proposed method.
Overall, this work contributes to the development of more robust and accurate domain adaptation methods for semantic segmentation of aerial images.
In this paper, we propose a novel approach for 3D medical image segmentation called Prior-Guided Local Self-supervised Learning (PGL).
Our method leverages prior knowledge about the structure of the target segment to guide the learning process, while also utilizing self-supervision to improve the accuracy of the segmentation.
We use a combination of prior-guided local contrastive learning and prior-guided local consistency learning to train our model.
Our experiments show that our method outperforms state-of-the-art methods on several benchmark datasets, demonstrating the effectiveness of our approach for 3D medical image segmentation.

The paper "DoDNet: Learning to segment multi-organ and tumors from multiple partially labeled datasets" presents a novel deep learning approach for segmenting multi-organ and tumors from medical images.
The proposed method utilizes a multi-task learning framework to simultaneously segment multiple organs and tumors from multiple partially labeled datasets.
The model is trained using a combination of supervised and unsupervised learning techniques, which allows it to learn from both labeled and unlabeled data.

The results show that the proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art methods on several benchmark datasets, and demonstrates the potential for multi-task learning to improve the performance of medical image segmentation tasks.
The abstract for the academic paper titled "ROAM: Random Layer Mixup for Semi-Supervised Learning in Medical Imaging" is as follows:
In this paper, we propose a novel semi-supervised learning framework called ROAM (Random Layer Mixup) for medical image classification.
The proposed method leverages the power of layer mixup to generate synthetic samples and augment the limited training data.
Specifically, we randomly mix the feature maps of two different images at multiple layers to create new samples.
We then use these synthetic samples to train a deep neural network for medical image classification.
Our experiments demonstrate that ROAM outperforms state-of-the-art methods on several benchmark datasets, including the MIMIC-III and ChestX-ray datasets.
Furthermore, we show that ROAM can effectively handle class imbalance and improve the performance of the model on rare classes.
Overall, our work provides a new and effective approach for semi-supervised learning in medical imaging.
This paper presents a novel approach to segmentation of disease features from medical images using deep learning techniques.
The proposed method combines interpretable and synergistic deep learning techniques to improve the accuracy and reliability of the segmentation results.

The interpretable deep learning technique allows for visual explanation of the segmentation process, while the synergistic deep learning technique leverages the strengths of multiple deep learning models to improve the overall performance.
The proposed method is evaluated on a dataset of medical images and shows significant improvements in segmentation accuracy and reliability compared to state-of-the-art methods.
The accuracy of medical image segmentation is crucial for the diagnosis and treatment of diseases.
However, the performance of segmentation algorithms can be affected by human error in labeling the ground truth.
In this paper, we propose a novel approach to disentangle human error from the ground truth in medical image segmentation.

Our approach involves training a deep neural network to predict the probability of each pixel belonging to a particular segment, and then using this probability to correct the human errors in the ground truth.
We evaluate our approach on several benchmark datasets and demonstrate significant improvements in segmentation accuracy.
Our approach has the potential to improve the reliability of medical image segmentation and aid in the diagnosis and treatment of diseases.

The field of cell membrane segmentation has seen significant advancements in recent years, with the development of new techniques and algorithms that enable the accurate identification and segmentation of cells at ultra-high resolutions.

However, the effectiveness of these methods is often evaluated based on quantitative metrics such as accuracy, precision, and recall, which may not fully capture the human perception of the segmented images.

In this paper, we propose a novel evaluation criterion that takes into account human perception, specifically the ability of the segmented images to accurately represent the underlying biological context.
Our approach involves the use of a human annotation task, where participants are asked to evaluate the segmented images and provide feedback on their accuracy and relevance.

We then use this feedback to calculate a human perception-based evaluation score, which takes into account both the segmentation accuracy and the relevance of the segmented regions to the overall biological context.

Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, showing that human perception-based evaluation criteria can provide a more comprehensive assessment of the quality of cell membrane segmentation methods.

Self-Supervision with Superpixels: Training Few-shot Medical Image Segmentation without Annotation
Abstract:
Medical image segmentation is a crucial task in the field of healthcare, but it requires a large amount of labeled data for training.
However, obtaining annotated data is time-consuming and expensive.
In this paper, we propose a novel approach to train few-shot medical image segmentation models without annotation.
Our approach utilizes self-supervision with superpixels to generate synthetic annotations for training.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on several benchmark datasets, achieving state-of-the-art performance with significantly fewer labeled examples.
Our work has the potential to revolutionize the field of medical image segmentation by enabling the training of models on large-scale datasets with limited annotation resources.
The paper presents a novel approach to image segmentation that leverages cross-modal progressive comprehension to improve the accuracy and robustness of the segmentation results.
The proposed method uses a combination of visual and textual information to generate a more comprehensive understanding of the image content.
The visual information is used to extract features from the image, while the textual information is used to provide contextual information about the image.
The two modalities are then combined using a progressive comprehension model that iteratively refines the segmentation results based on the feedback from both modalities.
The proposed method is evaluated on several benchmark datasets and shows significant improvements in segmentation accuracy and robustness compared to state-of-the-art methods.

The paper "Segmentations-Leak: Membership Inference Attacks and Defenses in Semantic Image Segmentation" presents a novel attack method for inferring sensitive information about individuals or objects within an image through the use of semantic image segmentation models.

The attack is based on the observation that these models often produce segmentation masks that reveal information about the objects within the image, even when the objects are not explicitly labeled in the segmentation output.
The paper demonstrates the effectiveness of this attack method through several experiments and proposes several defenses to mitigate the impact of these attacks.
The paper also discusses the implications of these attacks for privacy and security in image-based systems.
In this paper, we propose a new approach to designing neural networks for games that are equivariant to finite groups.
This allows us to train models that are invariant to certain transformations, which can be useful in a variety of game-related tasks.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through several examples, including image classification and reinforcement learning.
Our results show that our models are able to achieve state-of-the-art performance on these tasks, while also being more robust to certain types of transformations.
Overall, our work represents an important step towards building more robust and generalizable models for games.
The abstract for the academic paper titled "Deep Neural Network for 3D Surface Segmentation based on Contour Tree Hierarchy" would be:
This paper presents a novel deep neural network architecture for 3D surface segmentation based on contour tree hierarchy.
The proposed method utilizes a hierarchical representation of contours to extract features from the surface, which are then fed into a deep neural network for classification.
The contour tree hierarchy is used to group contours based on their similarity and to extract features at different levels of abstraction.
The proposed method is evaluated on several benchmark datasets and shows state-of-the-art performance in terms of accuracy and speed.
The results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method for 3D surface segmentation and its potential for applications in computer vision and robotics.

The abstract for the academic paper titled "Universal Semantic Segmentation for Fisheye Urban Driving Images" is as follows:

This paper presents a novel approach to semantic segmentation for fisheye urban driving images.
The proposed method utilizes a universal model that can be applied to a wide range of semantic segmentation tasks, including object detection, lane detection, and pedestrian detection.
The model is trained on a large dataset of fisheye images and uses a combination of convolutional neural networks and attention mechanisms to achieve high accuracy.

The results show that the proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art methods on several benchmark datasets, and demonstrates the potential for universal semantic segmentation to improve the safety and efficiency of urban driving.
In this paper, we propose a novel deep learning approach for nuclear segmentation in digital pathology images.
Our method utilizes sparse coding to extract relevant features from the input images, followed by a deep decision tree ensemble to classify the nuclei.
The sparse coding step reduces the dimensionality of the input images, making the model more efficient and interpretable.

The deep decision tree ensemble is trained using a combination of supervised and unsupervised learning techniques, which allows the model to learn both the spatial and temporal relationships between the nuclei.
We evaluate our method on a large dataset of digital pathology images and demonstrate that it outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of accuracy and speed.

Our approach has the potential to revolutionize the field of digital pathology by providing a fast and accurate method for nuclear segmentation, which is a critical step in the diagnosis of many diseases.

Scribble-based domain adaptation is a challenging task in computer vision, as it requires the model to learn to map scribbles from one domain to another, where the scribbles are often noisy and ambiguous.
In this paper, we propose a novel approach to scribble-based domain adaptation via co-segmentation.
Our approach leverages the inherent spatial relationships between the source and target domains to learn a mapping function that can effectively map scribbles from one domain to another.
We achieve this by jointly training a segmentation model and a co-segmentation model on the source and target domains.
The co-segmentation model learns to segment both the source and target domains simultaneously, which helps to align the segmentation boundaries between the two domains.
We evaluate our approach on several benchmark datasets and demonstrate that it outperforms state-of-the-art methods in scribble-based domain adaptation.
Image segmentation is a crucial task in various fields such as medical imaging, satellite imaging, and autonomous vehicles.
In this paper, we propose a novel deep learning-based approach for large-scale image segmentation with structured loss.
Our approach utilizes a structured loss function that incorporates both pixel-wise and region-based losses to improve the segmentation accuracy.
We also introduce a novel attention mechanism that enhances the performance of the model by focusing on the most relevant regions in the image.
We evaluate our approach on several benchmark datasets and demonstrate its effectiveness in achieving state-of-the-art performance.
Our results show that our approach outperforms existing methods in terms of accuracy and speed, making it a promising tool for large-scale image segmentation tasks.
The paper presents a novel approach for globally optimal segmentation of mutually interacting surfaces using deep learning.
The proposed method utilizes a graph-based representation of the surfaces and their interactions, and applies a graph convolutional network (GCN) to learn the optimal segmentation.
The GCN is trained using a combination of graph-based and image-based loss functions, which ensure that the segmentation is both accurate and consistent with the surface interactions.
The proposed method is demonstrated on several benchmark datasets, and achieves state-of-the-art performance in terms of both segmentation accuracy and computational efficiency.
In this paper, we present Naive-Student, a novel approach to urban scene segmentation using semi-supervised learning in video sequences.
Our method leverages the inherent temporal structure of video data to improve the performance of semi-supervised segmentation algorithms.
We propose a novel objective function that combines temporal consistency and spatial consistency to optimize the segmentation process.
We also introduce a novel temporal regularization term that encourages the model to maintain consistency across frames.
Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of Naive-Student in urban scene segmentation, achieving state-of-the-art performance on several benchmark datasets.

Autoregressive Unsupervised Image Segmentation is a novel approach to image segmentation that utilizes an autoregressive model to predict the next pixel value in an image based on its previous pixel values.
This method is able to segment images without the need for labeled training data, making it a powerful tool for unsupervised image analysis.
The paper presents a detailed description of the proposed algorithm, including the mathematical model and implementation details.
The effectiveness of the method is demonstrated through experiments on a variety of image datasets, where it is shown to outperform other unsupervised segmentation techniques.
Overall, this work represents a significant advancement in the field of unsupervised image segmentation, providing a new and efficient method for automatically separating objects within images.
Active learning is a popular approach to machine learning that involves selecting the most informative samples to label and train a model.
In the context of image segmentation, active learning can be used to improve the accuracy of the model by selecting the most challenging regions to label.
However, uncertainty estimation is a key component of active learning, as it allows the model to identify the regions that are most uncertain and therefore most likely to benefit from labeling.

In this paper, we explore different approaches to uncertainty estimation in the context of image segmentation, including entropy-based methods, variance-based methods, and deep learning-based methods.
We evaluate the performance of these methods on several benchmark datasets and show that deep learning-based methods generally outperform the other approaches.
We also discuss some of the challenges and limitations of uncertainty estimation in active learning for image segmentation, and suggest some directions for future research.
The abstract for the academic paper titled "Suggestive Annotation of Brain Tumour Images with Gradient-guided Sampling" would be:
This paper presents a novel approach for suggestive annotation of brain tumour images using gradient-guided sampling.

The proposed method utilizes a deep learning model to generate a set of candidate annotations for a given image, and then uses gradient information to select the most informative annotations for further refinement.
The gradient-guided sampling process is iterative, allowing for multiple rounds of refinement until the final annotation is satisfactory.
The proposed method was evaluated on a dataset of brain tumour images, and was found to outperform traditional annotation methods in terms of accuracy and efficiency.
Overall, the results demonstrate the potential of gradient-guided sampling for improving the quality and reliability of brain tumour image annotations.
This paper presents a novel approach for semi-supervised medical image segmentation and domain adaptation that utilizes uncertainty-aware multi-view co-training.
The proposed method leverages the inherent uncertainty in medical images to improve the performance of the segmentation model.
The approach involves training multiple models simultaneously on different views of the same image, with each model learning to specialize in a specific view.
The models are then combined to produce a final segmentation result that is more accurate and robust than any individual model.
The proposed method is evaluated on a dataset of medical images and shows significant improvements in segmentation accuracy compared to state-of-the-art methods.

Additionally, the approach is shown to be effective for domain adaptation, allowing the model to be trained on images from one domain and applied to images from a different domain with minimal additional training.
The abstract for the academic paper titled "Pyramidal Convolution: Rethinking Convolutional Neural Networks for Visual Recognition" would be:
In this paper, we propose a novel approach to convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for visual recognition tasks.
Our method, pyramidal convolution, utilizes a hierarchical structure to learn features at multiple scales, allowing for more efficient and accurate recognition.

We demonstrate the effectiveness of pyramidal convolution through experiments on various benchmark datasets, achieving state-of-the-art performance with significantly fewer parameters than traditional CNN architectures.
Our work provides a new perspective on the design of CNNs, enabling more efficient and accurate visual recognition.
Multi-organ segmentation is a challenging task in medical image analysis, especially when dealing with partially labeled datasets.
In this paper, we propose a novel approach to multi-organ segmentation that leverages multi-scale feature abstraction to improve the accuracy of the segmentation results.
Our approach involves first extracting multi-scale features from the input image, and then using these features to train a deep neural network for multi-organ segmentation.
We also incorporate a novel partially labeled dataset augmentation technique to improve the robustness of the model to variations in the labeling scheme.

Our experiments show that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods on several benchmark datasets, demonstrating the effectiveness of multi-scale feature abstraction and partially labeled dataset augmentation for multi-organ segmentation.
Transfer learning has emerged as a promising approach for medical image segmentation tasks.
This paper presents a critical assessment of transfer learning for medical image segmentation with fully convolutional neural networks (FCNNs).
The paper reviews the literature on transfer learning for medical image segmentation and identifies the key challenges and limitations of this approach.

The paper also presents a comprehensive analysis of the effectiveness of transfer learning for medical image segmentation tasks, including the impact of the choice of pre-trained model, transfer learning strategy, and fine-tuning approach.
