Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have emerged as a powerful tool for this task, achieving state-of-the-art performance on many benchmark datasets.
However, there are still several challenges that need to be addressed in order to improve the robustness and reliability of these models.
In this paper, we propose a novel approach to improve calibration and out-of-distribution detection in medical image segmentation with CNNs.
Our method involves training a multi-task CNN that simultaneously predicts the segmentation mask and a confidence map indicating the uncertainty of the prediction.
We then use this confidence map to perform out-of-distribution detection, identifying regions of the image that are likely to be misclassified by the model.
We also propose a novel calibration technique that uses the confidence map to adjust the predicted probabilities, improving the overall performance of the model.
We evaluate our method on several benchmark datasets, demonstrating significant improvements in calibration and out-of-distribution detection compared to state-of-the-art models.
Our results have important implications for the clinical use of medical image segmentation, highlighting the need for more robust and reliable models in this critical application domain.
The paper presents a new validity index for fuzzy-possibilistic C-means clustering.
The proposed index is based on the concept of fuzzy entropy and is designed to measure the quality of clustering results in fuzzy environments.
The index is derived from the fuzzy entropy of the cluster centers and the fuzzy entropy of the cluster memberships.
The paper demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed index through several experiments and compares it with other validity indices.
The results show that the proposed index provides a more accurate measure of clustering quality in fuzzy environments.

Title: Lake Ice Monitoring with Webcams and Crowd-Sourced Images
Abstract:
Lake ice monitoring is crucial for understanding the impacts of climate change on aquatic ecosystems.
Traditional methods of ice monitoring are time-consuming and expensive, limiting their effectiveness in providing real-time data.
This study proposes a cost-effective and efficient method for lake ice monitoring using webcams and crowd-sourced images.
The study utilized webcams installed on three lakes in Canada to capture images of the ice cover.
The images were then analyzed using computer vision algorithms to determine the extent and thickness of the ice cover.
Additionally, a crowdsourcing platform was developed to allow users to contribute images of the lakes, which were also analyzed using the same algorithms.
The results showed that the webcam-based method was highly accurate in determining the extent and thickness of the ice cover, with an accuracy of 95%.
The crowdsourced images also provided valuable data, with a high level of user engagement and participation.
Overall, this study demonstrates the potential of webcams and crowdsourcing for lake ice monitoring, providing a cost-effective and efficient method for real-time data collection.
The results can be used to inform decision-making and management of aquatic ecosystems, and to better understand the impacts of climate change on these ecosystems.
In this paper, we propose a novel approach for weakly supervised medical image segmentation using adversarial constrained-CNN loss.
Our method leverages the power of adversarial training to improve the performance of weakly supervised segmentation models.
We introduce a new loss function that incorporates adversarial constraints to improve the robustness of the model.
Our approach is trained on a large dataset of medical images with limited annotations, and we demonstrate its effectiveness on several benchmark datasets.
Our results show that our method outperforms state-of-the-art weakly supervised segmentation models, and we provide a detailed analysis of the effectiveness of our approach.
Overall, our work represents a significant advancement in the field of weakly supervised medical image segmentation, and we believe it has important implications for clinical practice.

The field of medical image segmentation has seen significant advancements in recent years, with deep learning techniques playing a crucial role in improving the accuracy and efficiency of image segmentation tasks.
However, the process of designing and training deep neural networks for medical image segmentation can be time-consuming and computationally expensive.
In this paper, we propose a novel coarse-to-fine neural architecture search (C2FNAS) approach for 3D medical image segmentation.
Our approach leverages a combination of coarse-to-fine search strategies and transfer learning techniques to efficiently search for optimal neural architectures for medical image segmentation tasks.
We evaluate our approach on several benchmark datasets and demonstrate its effectiveness in improving the accuracy and efficiency of medical image segmentation tasks.
Our results show that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of both accuracy and computational efficiency.
In this paper, we present a novel adversarial attack method that can fool any model, regardless of its architecture or training data.
Our approach is based on the idea of mimicking the behavior of the model itself, by generating inputs that are similar to the ones it is most likely to output.
We show that this can be done using a simple and efficient algorithm, and that it is effective against a wide range of models and tasks.

Our results demonstrate the importance of understanding the underlying assumptions of machine learning models, and highlight the need for more robust and task-agnostic defenses against adversarial attacks.

C-Flow: Conditional Generative Flow Models for Images and 3D Point Clouds
Abstract:
In this paper, we propose C-Flow, a novel generative flow model that can generate high-quality images and 3D point clouds conditioned on arbitrary input distributions.
C-Flow is based on a conditional generative flow model that learns to map input distributions to output distributions using a sequence of conditionally parameterized transformations.

We demonstrate the effectiveness of C-Flow on image generation tasks, including image inpainting, style transfer, and super-resolution, as well as on 3D point cloud generation tasks, including point cloud completion and point cloud synthesis.
Our experiments show that C-Flow outperforms state-of-the-art generative models on these tasks, achieving state-of-the-art results on several benchmark datasets.
Land cover segmentation is a critical task in remote sensing and environmental science, which involves identifying and classifying different land cover types from satellite imagery.
However, land cover segmentation can be challenging due to variations in image quality, sensor characteristics, and atmospheric conditions.
In this paper, we propose a domain adaptation approach to improve land cover segmentation across multiple satellites.
Our approach involves training a deep neural network on a source domain and then fine-tuning it on a target domain using transfer learning.
We evaluate our approach on several land cover segmentation tasks and demonstrate significant improvements in performance compared to state-of-the-art methods.
Our results show that domain adaptation can effectively overcome the challenges of land cover segmentation across different satellites and provide more accurate and reliable land cover maps.
The paper presents LT-Net, a novel approach for one-shot medical image segmentation that utilizes label transfer by learning reversible voxel-wise correspondence.

The proposed method leverages a pre-trained network to generate a set of correspondences between the source and target images, which are then used to transfer the labels from the source to the target image.
The learned correspondences are reversible, allowing for the transfer of labels in both directions.
The method is evaluated on several benchmark datasets and shows significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods for one-shot medical image segmentation.
Structured output variables are commonly found in various domains such as natural language processing, speech recognition, and computer vision.
Predicting these variables is a challenging task due to the complex and non-linear relationships between the input features and the output variables.
In this paper, we propose StructBoost, a novel boosting method for predicting structured output variables.

StructBoost combines the strengths of existing boosting methods such as AdaBoost, Gradient Boosting, and XGBoost by incorporating structured output variables into the loss function and optimizing the model parameters.
We evaluate StructBoost on several benchmark datasets and demonstrate its effectiveness in predicting structured output variables.
Our results show that StructBoost outperforms existing methods and achieves state-of-the-art performance on several tasks.
The abstract for the academic paper titled "Meta Segmentation Network for Ultra-Resolution Medical Images" is as follows:
In this paper, we propose a novel meta segmentation network for ultra-resolution medical images.
The proposed network is designed to segment medical images at multiple resolutions simultaneously, which can improve the efficiency and accuracy of medical image analysis.
The network consists of a series of meta-segmentation blocks, each of which contains a set of convolutional layers and pooling layers.
The meta-segmentation blocks are connected by a set of meta-connections, which allow the network to learn a hierarchical representation of the input image.

We evaluate the performance of the proposed network on a set of benchmark medical image segmentation tasks and demonstrate that it outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of both accuracy and efficiency.
Reinforced active learning (RAL) is a promising approach to improve the efficiency of image segmentation tasks by leveraging human feedback to guide the learning process.
In this paper, we present a novel RAL framework for image segmentation that utilizes a deep reinforcement learning algorithm to select the most informative samples for labeling by human annotators.
Our approach is based on a multi-objective optimization problem that balances the trade-off between the exploration of the model's uncertainty and the exploitation of the annotator's time.

We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on several benchmark datasets and show that it outperforms state-of-the-art RAL methods in terms of both segmentation accuracy and annotation efficiency.
Our work provides a valuable contribution to the field of active learning and has the potential to significantly improve the performance of image segmentation models in real-world applications.
Clustering based on Point-Set Kernel is an unsupervised machine learning technique used to group similar data points together.
This paper presents a comprehensive review of the clustering algorithms that use point-set kernel functions.
The point-set kernel function maps the high-dimensional data into a lower-dimensional space, where the similarity between data points can be measured easily.
Several point-set kernel functions, including the Gaussian kernel, polynomial kernel, and radial basis function kernel, are discussed in detail.

The performance of these clustering algorithms is evaluated using several benchmark datasets, and the results show that the point-set kernel function-based clustering algorithms outperform traditional clustering algorithms.
Furthermore, this paper also discusses the limitations and future research directions of point-set kernel function-based clustering algorithms.
Neuron boundary segmentation is a crucial step in the analysis of neural circuits, as it enables the identification of individual neurons and their connections.
However, accurately segmenting neuron boundaries in 2D images can be challenging due to the complex and variable shapes of neurons.
In this paper, we propose an efficient method for 2D neuron boundary segmentation that incorporates local topological constraints.
Our approach uses a graph-based representation of the neuron, where each neuron is represented as a graph and the connections between neurons are represented as edges.
We then use a local topological constraint to enforce the connectivity of the graph, which helps to improve the accuracy of the segmentation.
Our method is tested on a dataset of 2D images of neurons, and we demonstrate that it outperforms other state-of-the-art methods in terms of accuracy and efficiency.
Overall, our approach provides a powerful tool for the analysis of neural circuits, enabling researchers to more accurately identify and study individual neurons and their connections.
Medical image segmentation is a crucial task in the field of radiology, which involves identifying and separating different anatomical structures within an image.
However, the accuracy of segmentation can be affected by variations in the observer's perception and interpretation of the image.
In this paper, we propose a novel approach to medical image segmentation that incorporates observer variation-awareness by combining deep learning and surrogate-assisted genetic algorithms.
Our approach involves training a deep learning model on a diverse set of images and using surrogate-assisted genetic algorithms to optimize the model's parameters for each observer.

We evaluate our approach on a dataset of chest X-ray images and demonstrate that it outperforms traditional deep learning-based segmentation methods in terms of accuracy and observer variation-awareness.
Our findings have important implications for improving the reliability and consistency of medical image segmentation, which can ultimately lead to better patient outcomes.
The abstract for the academic paper titled "Unpaired Multi-modal Segmentation via Knowledge Distillation" is as follows:
In this paper, we propose a novel approach for unpaired multi-modal segmentation using knowledge distillation.
Our method leverages the knowledge of a pre-trained model on a source modality to improve the performance of a target model on a target modality.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on several benchmark datasets, achieving state-of-the-art results in some cases.
Our method can be easily applied to various multi-modal segmentation tasks, and it does not require any additional training data or complex architectures.
Overhead image segmentation is a challenging task in computer vision, especially when dealing with complex scenes and occlusions.
In this paper, we propose a novel approach to generalize deep models for overhead image segmentation using Getis-Ord Gi* pooling.
Our method leverages the spatial autocorrelation of the image to improve the performance of deep models on complex scenes.
We evaluate our method on several benchmark datasets and show that it outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of accuracy and speed.
Our approach can be easily integrated into existing deep learning frameworks and can be applied to a wide range of overhead image segmentation tasks.
Deep learning has revolutionized the field of computer vision, enabling accurate object recognition and classification.
However, color constancy errors can significantly impact the performance of deep neural networks, leading to incorrect results.
This paper presents a comprehensive analysis of color constancy errors and their impact on deep learning performance.
We propose a novel approach to address these errors by incorporating color constancy into the training process.
Our approach involves the use of color-corrected images and a modified loss function that accounts for color constancy.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through extensive experiments on various datasets, showing significant improvements in accuracy and robustness.
Our work highlights the importance of addressing color constancy errors in deep learning and provides a valuable contribution to the field.
The paper presents PI-RCNN, an efficient multi-sensor 3D object detector that utilizes a point-based attentive cont-conv fusion module to improve the accuracy and robustness of the detection.
The proposed method is designed to work with multiple sensors, including LiDAR, Radar, and Cameras, to provide a more comprehensive and accurate 3D object detection.
The paper demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed method through extensive experiments on various datasets, including the KITTI, CityScape, and PASCAL VOC datasets.
The results show that PI-RCNN outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of accuracy and speed, making it a valuable tool for real-world applications such as autonomous driving and robotics.
The abstract for the academic paper titled "Thickened 2D Networks for Efficient 3D Medical Image Segmentation" would be:
In this paper, we propose a novel approach for efficient 3D medical image segmentation using thickened 2D networks.

Our method involves training a 2D convolutional neural network (CNN) on 2D slices of the 3D image and then applying a thickening operation to the output of the 2D CNN to obtain a 3D segmentation result.
The thickening operation involves concatenating the output of the 2D CNN with a set of learned 3D filters to create a 3D segmentation map.

We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on several benchmark 3D medical image segmentation datasets and show that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance with significantly fewer parameters and computational resources compared to traditional 3D CNNs.
Image co-segmentation is the process of simultaneously segmenting multiple objects in an image into their respective regions.
This technique is widely used in various applications such as medical imaging, satellite image analysis, and robotics.
This paper presents a comprehensive survey of automatic image co-segmentation methods, including region-based, object-based, and deep learning-based approaches.
The paper discusses the advantages and limitations of each method and provides a comparative analysis of their performance.
Furthermore, the paper highlights the challenges and open issues in the field of image co-segmentation and suggests potential research directions for future work.
Overall, this survey provides a valuable resource for researchers and practitioners interested in automatic image co-segmentation.

The abstract for the academic paper titled "One Network to Segment Them All: A General, Lightweight System for Accurate 3D Medical Image Segmentation" is as follows:

This paper presents a novel deep learning-based system for accurate 3D medical image segmentation.
The proposed system utilizes a single convolutional neural network (CNN) to segment multiple organs and tissues simultaneously, without the need for separate networks for each organ.
The CNN is designed to be lightweight and efficient, with a small number of parameters and a fast training time.
The system is trained on a large dataset of 3D medical images, and achieves state-of-the-art performance on several benchmark tasks.

The proposed approach has the potential to revolutionize the field of medical image segmentation, by providing a general-purpose solution that can be applied to a wide range of imaging modalities and clinical applications.
Domain generalization is a critical challenge in machine learning, as it is essential to enable models to perform well on new, unseen data.
One approach to domain generalization is to learn semantic features that capture the underlying concepts and relationships in the data.
However, existing methods for learning semantic features are often domain-specific and may not generalize well to new domains.
In this paper, we propose a novel approach to domain generalization via model-agnostic learning of semantic features.
Our method learns a set of domain-independent semantic features that can be used to represent data from any domain.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on several benchmark datasets, showing that our method outperforms existing domain-specific methods in terms of domain generalization.
Our work provides a valuable resource for researchers and practitioners seeking to develop more robust and generalizable machine learning models.
This paper presents a novel approach for remote sensed image segmentation using an encoder-decoder based convolutional neural network (CNN) and a fully connected conditional random field (CRF).
The encoder-decoder CNN is used to extract features from the input image, while the fully connected CRF is used to refine the segmentation results.
The proposed approach is trained using a combination of supervised and unsupervised learning techniques, and is evaluated on several benchmark datasets.
The results show that the proposed approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of accuracy and speed.

End-to-End Deep Convolutional Active Contours for Image Segmentation
Abstract:
In this paper, we propose an end-to-end deep convolutional active contours (DCAC) framework for image segmentation.
The proposed framework combines the advantages of deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and active contours to achieve accurate and efficient image segmentation.
The proposed DCAC framework consists of two main components: a deep CNN-based encoder-decoder network for feature extraction and a graph-based active contours model for shape modeling.
The encoder-decoder network learns to extract high-level features from the input image, while the active contours model learns to model the shape of the object in the image.
The two components are integrated in an end-to-end manner to achieve accurate image segmentation.
We evaluate the proposed DCAC framework on several benchmark datasets and demonstrate its effectiveness in achieving state-of-the-art performance.
Overfitting of neural nets under class imbalance is a common problem in image segmentation tasks.
This paper presents an analysis of the causes of overfitting and proposes several improvements to address this issue.
The analysis shows that overfitting occurs when the neural network is biased towards the majority class, leading to poor performance on the minority class.
The paper proposes several techniques to address this issue, including data augmentation, class weighting, and ensemble learning.
The results show that these techniques significantly improve the performance of the neural network on the minority class, while maintaining good performance on the majority class.
The paper concludes that overfitting of neural nets under class imbalance is a common problem in image segmentation tasks, but that there are several effective techniques to address this issue.
Neural style transfer has been shown to be effective in improving image segmentation in various applications.
In this study, we investigate the effectiveness of neural style transfer in improving 3D cardiovascular MR image segmentation on inconsistent data.
We applied neural style transfer to 3D cardiovascular MR images and compared the segmentation results with those obtained using traditional methods.
Our results showed that neural style transfer significantly improved the segmentation accuracy and reduced the segmentation time.
We also found that neural style transfer was effective in handling inconsistent data, which is a common problem in medical imaging.
Our findings suggest that neural style transfer can be a useful tool for improving 3D cardiovascular MR image segmentation on inconsistent data.
Image segmentation is a crucial task in computer vision and image processing.
It involves dividing an image into multiple regions, each representing a distinct object or feature.
One of the most common techniques used for image segmentation is the multi-threshold technique.
However, the traditional multi-threshold technique has several limitations, including the need for manual threshold selection and the inability to handle images with complex backgrounds.
In this paper, we propose a novel image segmentation technique using multi-threshold by histogram sampling.
Our technique involves sampling the histogram of the image to obtain multiple threshold values, which are then used to segment the image into multiple regions.
We evaluate our technique on several benchmark datasets and show that it outperforms the traditional multi-threshold technique in terms of accuracy and speed.
Our technique is also robust to changes in image lighting and can handle images with complex backgrounds.
Medical image segmentation is a crucial task in the field of radiology, which involves separating the relevant information from the background in medical images.
Deep learning-based methods have shown promising results in this task, but they require large amounts of labeled data for training.
In this paper, we explore the possibility of training deep learning-based medical image segmentation using a single manually delineated scan.
We propose a novel approach called extreme augmentation, which involves generating synthetic images by applying various transformations to the original image.
We evaluate the performance of our approach on a dataset of lung CT scans and show that it can achieve state-of-the-art results with significantly fewer labeled images than traditional methods.
Our findings suggest that extreme augmentation can be a valuable tool for training deep learning-based medical image segmentation in resource-constrained settings.
Medical image segmentation is a crucial task in the field of radiology and computer-aided diagnosis.
In this paper, we propose a novel approach to medical image segmentation using a mixed-supervised dual-network architecture.
Our approach combines the advantages of both supervised and unsupervised learning to improve the accuracy and robustness of the segmentation results.
The proposed network consists of two sub-networks, one for supervised and the other for unsupervised learning.
The supervised sub-network is trained on labeled data, while the unsupervised sub-network is trained on unlabeled data.
The outputs of these two sub-networks are then combined using a mixing layer to produce the final segmentation result.
We evaluate our approach on several benchmark datasets and demonstrate its effectiveness in improving the accuracy and robustness of medical image segmentation.
The paper presents a novel method for computing the spatial probability of inclusion inside partial contours for computer vision applications.
The proposed method is based on the concept of spatial probability, which is a measure of the likelihood of an object being included within a given region.
The method involves the use of partial contours, which are contours that are not fully closed, and the computation of the spatial probability of inclusion inside these contours.
The paper demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed method through several computer vision applications, including object detection, segmentation, and tracking.
The results show that the proposed method outperforms existing methods in terms of accuracy and efficiency.
The abstract for the academic paper titled "DDSL:
Deep Differentiable Simplex Layer for Learning Geometric Signals" is as follows:
In this paper, we propose a novel deep differentiable simplex layer (DDSL) for learning geometric signals.
The DDSL is designed to be differentiable, which enables end-to-end training of deep neural networks for geometric signal processing tasks.
The DDSL is based on the simplex layer, which is a widely used non-linear activation function in deep learning.
However, the simplex layer is not differentiable, which makes it difficult to train deep neural networks for geometric signal processing tasks.
We address this issue by introducing a differentiable version of the simplex layer, which is based on the concept of geometric differentiation.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of the DDSL through several experiments, including learning geometric shapes and surfaces from point clouds.
Our results show that the DDSL outperforms existing methods for geometric signal processing tasks.
SkrGAN is a novel unconditional generative adversarial network (GAN) designed for medical image synthesis.
The proposed model leverages a sketching-rendering pipeline to generate high-quality medical images from low-resolution sketches.
The generator consists of two stages: a sketching stage that generates a low-resolution sketch of the target image, and a rendering stage that refines the sketch into a high-resolution image.
The discriminator is designed to distinguish between real and fake images at both stages of the pipeline.

The model is trained using a combination of adversarial loss and perceptual loss, which encourages the generator to produce images that are both visually realistic and consistent with the input sketch.
The results demonstrate that SkrGAN is capable of generating high-quality medical images from low-resolution sketches, with applications in areas such as medical diagnosis and treatment planning.
Medical image segmentation is a crucial task in the field of healthcare, with applications ranging from disease diagnosis to treatment planning.
However, the limited availability of labeled data and the complexity of medical images pose significant challenges for achieving accurate segmentation results.
In this paper, we propose a novel multi-task attention-based semi-supervised learning framework for medical image segmentation.
Our approach leverages the inherent similarities between different medical image segmentation tasks to learn a shared representation that can be fine-tuned for each specific task.
We incorporate attention mechanisms to focus on the most relevant regions of the image for each task, and utilize a semi-supervised learning strategy to leverage both labeled and unlabeled data.
Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, achieving state-of-the-art performance on several benchmark medical image segmentation tasks with limited labeled data.
DeepAtlas is a novel deep learning approach for joint image registration and segmentation.
It utilizes a semi-supervised learning strategy that combines unsupervised and supervised learning techniques.
The unsupervised learning component uses a deep convolutional neural network (CNN) to learn a mapping between the input images and their corresponding deformed versions.
The supervised learning component uses a CNN to learn a mapping between the input images and their corresponding segmentation masks.
The two mappings are learned jointly using a multi-task loss function that combines the registration and segmentation losses.
The proposed approach has been evaluated on several benchmark datasets and has shown state-of-the-art performance in terms of both registration accuracy and segmentation accuracy.
Brain segmentation is a crucial task in medical imaging analysis, which involves dividing the brain into distinct regions of interest (ROIs) based on their anatomical and functional characteristics.
In this paper, we propose an end-to-end recurrent attention network (ETRAN) for brain segmentation from k-space.
The proposed ETRAN is a deep learning model that takes as input the k-space representation of a magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan and outputs a set of segmentation masks for each ROI.
The ETRAN consists of a series of convolutional layers, followed by a recurrent attention mechanism that allows the model to focus on the most relevant regions of the image at each time step.
The attention mechanism is trained end-to-end using a combination of cross-entropy loss and attention loss, which encourages the model to learn the most informative features of the image.
We evaluate the performance of the ETRAN on a publicly available dataset of MRI scans and show that it outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of both accuracy and speed.
Our results demonstrate the potential of ETRAN for clinical applications in brain imaging analysis.
Camera pose estimation is the process of determining the orientation and position of a camera relative to its environment.
This task is crucial in various applications such as robotics, computer vision, and augmented reality.
In recent years, deep learning techniques have shown great promise in solving complex computer vision problems, including camera pose estimation.
This paper provides an introduction to the state-of-the-art methods and techniques used in camera pose estimation with deep learning.
It covers the basics of deep learning, including neural networks, convolutional neural networks, and recurrent neural networks.
It also discusses the different types of camera pose estimation problems, such as 6-DoF pose estimation and multi-view stereo.
The paper reviews the various deep learning-based approaches for camera pose estimation, including supervised learning, unsupervised learning, and reinforcement learning.
Finally, it provides an overview of the challenges and future directions in camera pose estimation with deep learning.
This paper presents a novel deep learning approach for automatic 3D bi-ventricular segmentation of cardiac images.

The proposed method utilizes a multi-task learning framework to simultaneously segment the left and right ventricles, and incorporates shape refinement techniques to improve the accuracy and robustness of the segmentation results.
The proposed approach is trained on a large dataset of cardiac images and achieves state-of-the-art performance on standard benchmarks.
The results demonstrate the potential of deep learning methods for clinical applications in cardiac imaging.
Cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) imaging is a valuable tool for diagnosing and monitoring cardiovascular diseases.
However, the interpretation of CMR images can be challenging due to the complex anatomy of the heart and the presence of artifacts.
In this paper, we propose a novel self-supervised learning approach for cardiac MR image segmentation using anatomical position prediction.
Our method learns to predict the anatomical position of a voxel based on its surrounding voxels, without requiring any manual annotations or external supervision.
We evaluate our method on a large dataset of CMR images and demonstrate that it achieves state-of-the-art performance on the task of cardiac MR image segmentation.
Our approach has the potential to improve the efficiency and accuracy of CMR image analysis, and could be applied to other medical imaging modalities as well.
The abstract for the academic paper titled "A Regularized Convolutional Neural Network for Semantic Image Segmentation" would be as follows:
In this paper, we present a novel regularized convolutional neural network (CNN) for semantic image segmentation.
Our proposed model incorporates L1 and L2 regularization to prevent overfitting and improve the generalization performance of the CNN.
We also introduce a novel attention mechanism that allows the model to focus on the most relevant regions of the input image during training and prediction.
Our experimental results show that our proposed model outperforms state-of-the-art CNNs on several benchmark datasets, achieving state-of-the-art performance on the COCO dataset.
Our work demonstrates the effectiveness of regularization and attention mechanisms in improving the performance of CNNs for semantic image segmentation.
Medical image segmentation is a crucial task in the field of healthcare, with applications ranging from diagnosis to treatment planning.
However, the performance of existing methods is often limited by the lack of labeled data in the target domain.
In this paper, we propose a novel approach to cross-modality domain adaptation for medical image segmentation, which leverages the synergistic relationship between image and feature adaptation.
Specifically, we propose a joint optimization framework that simultaneously adapts the image and feature representations to the target domain, while preserving the consistency between them.
Our approach is based on a deep neural network architecture that consists of a feature extractor, a domain adaptation module, and a segmentation module.
The feature extractor is pre-trained on a large dataset of source images, while the domain adaptation module is designed to learn a mapping between the source and target domains.
The segmentation module is then fine-tuned on the adapted feature representations to produce accurate segmentation results.
We evaluate our approach on several benchmark datasets and demonstrate its effectiveness in improving the performance of existing methods on limited labeled data.
Our results show that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on several tasks, including brain tumor segmentation and lung lesion detection.
Blurry boundary delineation is a common problem in image processing and computer vision tasks.
In this paper, we propose a novel approach to address this problem by leveraging semantic information to guide the learning of encoder features.

Specifically, we use a combination of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and attention mechanisms to learn a semantic-guided encoder that can effectively capture the spatial relationships between pixels and their corresponding semantic labels.
We then use this encoder to learn a blurry boundary delineation model that can accurately segment images with blurry boundaries.
Our approach is evaluated on several benchmark datasets and shows significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods.
Budget-aware Semi-Supervised Semantic and Instance Segmentation is an academic paper that presents a novel approach to semantic and instance segmentation using a semi-supervised learning framework.
The paper proposes a budget-aware algorithm that can efficiently allocate resources to different tasks, allowing for the use of limited labeled data while still achieving high accuracy.
The algorithm utilizes a combination of supervised and unsupervised learning techniques to improve the performance of the model.

The paper also presents a novel method for instance segmentation that utilizes a combination of semantic segmentation and object detection to accurately identify and segment individual objects within an image.

The results of the experiments show that the proposed algorithm outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of accuracy and efficiency, making it a valuable tool for applications where labeled data is limited.
In this paper, we present a novel approach for weakly supervised semantic segmentation using captions as the only source of supervision.
We propose a deep learning model that can automatically extract semantic information from captions and use it to improve the performance of a weakly supervised semantic segmentation model.
Our model is trained on a large dataset of images with captions and achieves state-of-the-art results on several benchmark datasets.
We also analyze the effectiveness of different caption-based features and show that our approach can be easily extended to handle more complex caption structures.
Overall, our work demonstrates the potential of captions as a valuable source of supervision for weakly supervised semantic segmentation.
Nostalgin is a novel approach to extracting 3D city models from historical image data.

The paper presents a deep learning-based method that uses a combination of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and generative adversarial networks (GANs) to generate 3D models of cities from 2D images.
The proposed method is trained on a large dataset of historical images and can generate highly accurate 3D models of cities with complex architectural features.
The paper also presents a novel loss function that is specifically designed for this task, which improves the quality of the generated 3D models.
The results of the experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method and show that it can be used to extract 3D city models from historical image data with high accuracy.
Skin cancer is a major health concern worldwide, and early detection is crucial for successful treatment.
In this paper, we propose a novel deep learning-based approach for skin cancer segmentation and classification using NABLA-N and Inception Recurrent Residual Convolutional Networks (IR-RCNN).
Our approach combines the advantages of both NABLA-N and IR-RCNN to improve the accuracy and efficiency of skin cancer segmentation and classification.
We evaluate our approach on a large dataset of skin lesion images and demonstrate its effectiveness in accurately segmenting and classifying skin lesions.

Our results show that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods in skin cancer segmentation and classification, and we believe it has the potential to revolutionize the field of skin cancer diagnosis.
The purpose of this study is to develop a super resolution convolutional neural network (SRCNN) model for enhancing the resolution of rock micro-computed tomography (micro-CT) images.
The proposed model is trained on a dataset of high-resolution and low-resolution rock micro-CT images using a combination of bicubic interpolation and SRCNN.
The results show that the proposed model is able to significantly enhance the resolution of rock micro-CT images with high accuracy and precision.
The proposed model can be used for various applications in geology, mineralogy, and materials science.
The abstract for the academic paper titled "Cross-Modal Self-Attention Network for Referring Image Segmentation" is as follows:
In this paper, we propose a novel cross-modal self-attention network for referring image segmentation.
The proposed network leverages the strengths of both image and text modalities to improve the performance of image segmentation tasks.
The network uses a self-attention mechanism to learn the relationships between the image and text modalities, and then applies this knowledge to improve the segmentation accuracy.

VisDA: The Visual Domain Adaptation Challenge

Abstract:

In this paper, we present the Visual Domain Adaptation Challenge (VisDA), a large-scale benchmark for evaluating the performance of VDA algorithms.

The challenge consists of a set of tasks that involve adapting images or videos from one visual domain to another, such as adapting images from a summer scene to a winter scene or adapting images from a daytime scene to a nighttime scene.
We also present a set of metrics for evaluating the performance of VDA algorithms, including both quantitative and qualitative metrics.
We hope that the VisDA challenge will provide a standardized and comprehensive evaluation of VDA algorithms, and will help to drive research in this important field.

The clique-width of a graph is a measure of its complexity that captures the size of the largest clique (complete subgraph) that can be induced in the graph.

We also provide algorithms for testing membership in these classes and for computing the clique-width of a graph in these classes.
Our results have applications in various areas of computer science, including algorithm design, database systems, and network analysis.

The paper presents a new approach to studying the measurability of compact sets and relative fractal drums in Euclidean spaces.

In this paper, we present a novel approach to salient object detection in the wild.
Our method combines inner and inter-label propagation to improve the accuracy and robustness of the detection results.

The paper presents a new approach to the design of robust controllers for regular linear systems with infinite-dimensional exosystems.

The paper "S-folds and 4d N=3 superconformal field theories" explores the relationship between S-folds and 4d N=3 superconformal field theories.

This technical report presents a novel approach to compressive temporal higher order cyclostationary (HoC) statistics.
The proposed method utilizes a combination of wavelet transform and HoC statistics to compress time-series data.
The wavelet transform is used to decompose the time-series data into different frequency bands, while HoC statistics are used to estimate the statistical properties of each frequency band.

The results are demonstrated through simulations and real-world examples.
Quantum coherence and quantum correlations are two fundamental concepts in quantum mechanics that have been extensively studied in recent years.
While they are often used interchangeably, they are in fact complementary concepts that are related to each other in a complex way.
In this paper, we explore the complementary relation of quantum coherence and quantum correlations in multiple measurements.

We show that while quantum coherence is related to the degree of interference between different quantum states, quantum correlations are related to the degree of non-locality between different quantum systems.
We also show that the complementary relation between these two concepts can be used to develop new quantum technologies, such as quantum cryptography and quantum computing.
Our results provide a new perspective on the fundamental nature of quantum mechanics and have important implications for the development of future quantum technologies.
The Gaussian core model is a widely used statistical model for high-dimensional data analysis.

It is based on the assumption that the data is generated by a multivariate Gaussian distribution, and it has been used to model a wide range of phenomena, including financial markets, weather patterns, and genetic data.
In this paper, we review the Gaussian core model and its applications in high dimensions.
We discuss the assumptions of the model, the estimation of its parameters, and the interpretation of its results.
We also review recent developments in the field, including the use of nonlinear models and the incorporation of external data.

The paper presents recent results in semileptonic B decays obtained by the BaBar collaboration.

The study of electrical properties of bi-implanted amorphous chalcogenide films is an important area of research in the field of materials science.
These films are used in various applications such as solar cells, photovoltaic devices, and memory devices.
In this paper, we present a comprehensive review of the electrical properties of bi-implanted amorphous chalcogenide films.
We discuss the various factors that affect the electrical properties of these films, such as the composition, thickness, and processing conditions.
We also review the different techniques used to measure the electrical properties of these films, such as capacitance-voltage measurements, current-voltage measurements, and Hall effect measurements.
Finally, we discuss the current state of research in this field and the future directions for further research.
The paper presents a global relaxation result for bistable solutions of gradient systems in one unbounded spatial dimension.

The main result is that under certain conditions, any bistable solution of a gradient system with a smooth potential function and a linear diffusion coefficient converges to a steady state as time goes to infinity.
The proof is based on a combination of the maximum principle and the method of characteristics.
The result is applied to a specific example of a reaction-diffusion equation and numerical simulations are presented to illustrate the behavior of the system.

Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has the potential to revolutionise medical imaging, but also carries the risk of perpetuating and even increasing existing health inequalities.

An international collaboration of experts from diverse fields has come together to consider how to ensure that AI in medical imaging is developed and deployed to maximise the benefits and minimise the harms.

Following a two-stage online consultation, we used a modified Delphi method to achieve consensus on key issues, and we provide here a summary of our discussions and recommendations for future AI development and deployment.
Combining the principles of trustworthy AI with consideration of fairness and equity, we propose a framework to inform the development and deployment of AI in medical imaging.

To ensure the trustworthy and fair use of AI in medical imaging, developers, clinicians and researchers should consider the following: promoting health equality and equity; upholding data privacy and security; maintaining technical performance; supporting clinical performance and decision making; and being responsive to patients and the public.
In this report, we outline a consensus view on the key issues that need to be addressed, and make recommendations for the future development and deployment of AI in medical imaging.
Recent progress in interactive segmentation has primarily focused on extracting object boundaries accurately rather than the entire object region.
While boundary-based methods can achieve better performance, they often require a time-consuming initial segmentation step to generate the boundary predictions.
Moreover, interactions for these methods become complicated as they involve modifying the boundary rather than the entire object region.
In this paper, we present EdgeFlow, a framework for achieving practical interactive segmentation with edge-guided flow.
It leverages a boundary-based approach but removes the initial segmentation step, making the interaction process as intuitive as the recent region-based methods.

Specifically, given a preliminary segmentation result, EdgeFlow directly optimizes the segmentation by introducing a novel edge-guided flow, which can effectively propagate the user's modifications to the entire object region while maintaining the boundary details.
We build a theoretical guarantee for the flow's convergence, and the flow's implementation is efficiently accelerated via graph cuts.
Our method can handle both binary and pixel-wise segmentation with or without explicit edge information.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of EdgeFlow on both benchmark datasets and a new dataset that contains complex object instances and illustrations.
When compared to state-of-the-art methods on the latter, EdgeFlow improves the efficiency of interaction by at least one order of magnitude while maintaining comparable performance.
Recent progress in medical image segmentation has largely been driven by supervised learning, but the availability of large-scale manually annotated datasets remains a bottleneck.
In this paper, we tackle the problem of medical image segmentation with a semi-supervised learning framework that leverages only a small amount of labeled data.
Our approach contrasts an encoder's representations of image patches with different labels, and uses the contrastive loss to regularize the encoder's parameters.

We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach on three public segmentation benchmarks (MRBrain, ISLES, and LiTS), where we achieve competitive performance compared to fully-supervised methods, while using only a fraction of the labeled data.
In particular, on the MRBrain dataset with only 200 labeled images (out of ~1000), our approach achieves a Dice score of 0.8314, outperforming the fully supervised state-of-the-art by ~3%.

Recent progress in segmentation of multiple organs in medical images has resulted in algorithms that are often trained and evaluated on heavily imbalanced datasets, where certain classes may have far fewer training examples than others.
This can lead to overfitting on the majority class and poor performance on the minority classes.
We find that the commonly used class weighting scheme, in which the loss is weighted by the inverse frequency of the class in the training set, may not be sufficient to handle this imbalance.

In this paper, we investigate the use of two other classes of techniques, including (1) sampling strategies that result in more balanced datasets and (2) loss functions that are designed to handle imbalance.
We find that both approaches can significantly improve performance on minority classes, but that they work in different ways and are most effective when used together.
To facilitate future research on multi-organ segmentation, we make our datasets, implementations, and results publicly available.
We present a novel approach for training a 3D seismic fault segmentation model using only a few 2D slice labels.
The model is based on attention mechanisms, which allow it to focus on the most relevant features in the input data.
We show that our approach can achieve high performance on 3D seismic fault segmentation tasks, even when trained with only a small number of 2D slice labels.
Our approach is fast and efficient, and can be used to segment faults in large 3D seismic volumes.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on a public dataset, and show that it outperforms the state-of-the-art in 3D seismic fault segmentation.
Code is available at https://github.com/yzslab/SeisFaultSeg.
Recent works tend to complicate segmentators for better performance, making them inaccessible to low-power platforms like IoT devices, and impractical for real-time applications.
In this work, we aim to simplify semantic segmentation, while maintaining high performance.
We propose Segmenter, a transformer-based segmentation model that is extremely lightweight, fast, and parameter-efficient.

It achieves this with a simple transformer architecture, and an innovative relative positional encoding strategy, which allows the model to easily run on devices with memory or computational constraints.

We conduct extensive experiments on ACDC and Cityscapes datasets, and show that our model achieves 79.3% and 91.3% mIOU on ACDC-Char and Cityscapes-Char, while being up to 22 times faster, and up to 4 times lighter compared to the state-of-the-art.

Recent progress in semantic segmentation mainly focuses on designing models that compile images and their annotations into compact representations, in order to exploit the strong correlations among pixels.
These models however ignore the fact that the annotations themselves contain valuable information, which could be used to improve the segmentation.
In this paper, we follow a different approach, and attempt to exploit the contextual information in the image captions.
We design a simple yet effective approach to mine the contextual information, and integrate it into the recently proposed Mask R-CNN.

Specifically, we propose to use a graph neural network to build a context graph for each word in the caption, and then we compose these context graphs to obtain a global context graph for the whole caption.
Finally, the global context graph is exploited in Mask R-CNN to refine the segmentation results.
We perform comprehensive experiments on the Cityscapes and COCO datasets, and the results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach.

Recent progress in deep learning has advanced referring expression comprehension, i.e., the understanding of sparse referring expressions that refer to objects or regions in images or videos, from image regions identification to pixel-wise segmentation.
However, existing works mainly focus on 2D referring expression comprehension disregarding the inherent 3D structure of the real world.

In this paper, we present a comprehensive multi-modal framework to tackle referring image segmentation, which takes advantages of both referring expressions and geometric constraints, to achieve referring expression comprehension with 3D awareness.
Specifically, we first devise a new geometric constraint that leverages the 3D scene structure to obtain initial segmentations.
Then, we formulate referring expression comprehension as a maximum a posteriori estimation problem that integrates the referring expression predictions and the geometric constraint.
Furthermore, we explore a progressive refinement approach to iteratively refine the segmentation results.
We validate the effectiveness of our method on the ReferItSeg dataset, which is a large-scale dataset for referring image segmentation, and achieve state-of-the-art performance.

This paper explores the connection between few-shot segmentation and contrastive learning.

Given a fixed network fine-tuned on a large dataset, we show that training the network to classify segments in a small number of classes (e.g., 5) is highly ineffective, as the network's capacity to memorize incorrect labels is surprisingly high.
To overcome this, we propose a two-step training approach.
First, we train a global contrastive learning (GCL) model by minimizing the mutual information between segment predictions and labels on the training set.
This is followed by a localization step that iteratively refines the segmentation map within the support regions of each class.
We show that this approach effectively combines the global and local characteristics of few-shot segmentation, improving accuracy by large margins over the state-of-the-art on multiple benchmarks.
Interactive segmentation is an important technique for correcting mispredictions in medical images, but existing methods can be time-consuming and require significant user interaction.
This paper presents a efficient and generic interactive segmentation framework that reduces the amount of user interaction required while maintaining high accuracy.

The framework utilizes a fully-automatic segmentation algorithm as a starting point, and then allows the user to quickly and easily correct any mispredictions using a novel interactive segmentation tool.
The tool enables the user to quickly select the correct segmentation boundary, and the framework then automatically refines the boundary based on the user's input.
The framework is evaluated on a variety of medical image datasets, and results show that it significantly reduces the amount of user interaction required while maintaining high accuracy.
Furthermore, the framework is designed to be generic, and can be easily adapted to segment different anatomical structures in various medical image modalities.
We provide a general framework for constructing prediction sets, i.e., sets that predict the values of an uncertain quantity, with probability 1.
In addition to simplicity and accuracy, our framework controls risk by leveraging the order structure of the variable of interest.
We provide both a distribution-free and a frequentist approach, with the latter enabling formal statistical inference for the prediction set.

We illustrate the approaches through two real data examples: the first concerns the number of tropical cyclones in the Atlantic ocean, and the second the number of Ph.D. graduates in US mathematics departments.
Compared to other prediction sets, ours achieve much better accuracy and smaller expected prediction errors.

Deep learning has recently become popular for sonar image segmentation, but the majority of research has focused on supervised learning approaches that require large amounts of manually labeled training data.
This can be a time-consuming and costly process, particularly for underwater sonar images where manually labeling images is slow and difficult.
In this paper, we present an iterative, unsupervised synthetic aperture sonar image segmentation framework that is both deep and learns from sparse labels.
Our approach uses a U-Net architecture and an iterative self-supervised learning strategy that progressively refines the segmentation results without any user interaction.

We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach on a synthetic aperture sonar dataset and show that our method can achieve high segmentation performance with only a small number of labeled training examples.
Our code and data are available at https://github.com/ARL-RED-Team/idus.
Recent progress in image synthesis through the use of GANs provides a new opportunity for image understanding.

In particular, we show that the image representation learned by GANs can be used to produce state-of-the-art performance on semantic image segmentation, a task that is fundamental to many applications in computer vision.
We achieve this by proposing a new framework that leverages the rich structural information encoded in the generative models of GANs.
Our approach, which we term "Segmentation in Style", combines an adversarial reconstruction loss with a discriminator that performs segmentation.
This framework is applicable to any GAN architecture and we demonstrate its effectiveness on top of StyleGAN2 and CLIP, a recently proposed GAN-based image representation.
Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on the ACDC and Cityscapes segmentation benchmarks without requiring any labeled data for training, but rather only a few images for initialization.
Semantic image segmentation, which aims to assign semantic labels to each pixel in an image, is a fundamental problem in computer vision.
Recent progress in this field is mainly driven by deep learning models, which can leverage large-scale labeled images to learn robust representations.
However, training such models requires a significant amount of labeled data, which is difficult and expensive to obtain.
To overcome this challenge, we propose a novel approach for semantic image segmentation based on double similarity distillation (DSD).
Our method exploits the intrinsic hierarchical structure of segmentation models to effectively reduce the amount of labeled data required for training.

Specifically, we introduce a teacher-student paradigm, where a teacher model is trained on a small amount of labeled data and then used to distill knowledge to a student model trained on a larger dataset.

By leveraging the similarity between the teacher and student models, we can significantly improve the performance of the student model while keeping the amount of labeled data required for training low.
We evaluate our method on the challenging PASCAL VOC 2012 segmentation benchmark, and achieve state-of-the-art performance with only a fraction of the labeled data required by previous approaches.
Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in reducing the amount of labeled data needed for training robust segmentation models.
Our code and models are available at: https://github.com/Cartucho/DSD

Recent advances in supervised learning for medical image segmentation have benefited from large datasets and powerful models, but training data with ground truth segmentations remain scarce for many applications.
In this work, we tackle the issue of limited training data for medical image segmentation by developing a spatial guided self-supervised clustering (SGSC) network.
Our approach leverages the spatial consistency of medical images to learn meaningful representations for segmentation without relying on ground truth segmentations.
We introduce a novel self-supervised loss function that encourages spatial coherence among cluster assignments, and combine it with an attention module to focus on informative regions.

We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on three different medical image segmentation tasks: fetal brain, abdominal aortic aneurysm, and prostate, showing that our approach produces segmentations comparable to state-of-the-art supervised methods while using only unlabeled data.
General image segmentation is a fundamental task in medical imaging, and deep learning methods have demonstrated promising performance.
However, these methods often require large amounts of manually annotated training data, which is difficult to obtain for medical images.

In this paper, we present a new framework for general medical image segmentation that is based on a fully convolutional neural network (FCN) and a novel loss function that is tailored to medical images.
Our framework is designed to be robust to variations in image quality, resolution, and noise, which are common in medical images.
We demonstrate the performance of our method on a publicly available dataset of abdominal computed tomography (CT) scans, and show that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance.
We also show that our method is general and can be applied to other medical image segmentation tasks, such as lung CT segmentation.
Recent studies have demonstrated the potential of deep learning for medical image analysis.
However, these methods usually require a large amount of manually annotated training data, which is difficult to obtain for medical images.
In this paper, we present a semi-supervised learning method for left atrium segmentation in cardiac MR images.
Our method leverages a large amount of unlabeled data and a small amount of manually annotated data to train a deep neural network.

To deal with the class imbalance and the lack of annotated data, we use a mutual consistency training strategy, which ensures that the predictions from the model with semi-supervised labels are similar to the fully supervised labels.
Our method achieves a Dice similarity coefficient of 0.8033 and a Hausdorff distance of 7.35 mm on a public dataset, which outperforms the state-of-the-art fully-supervised method by a large margin.
Furthermore, our method only requires approximately 1/50 of the annotated training data.

Recent advances in deep learning have propelled the development of visual tracking algorithms, enabling the adoption of off-the-shelf deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) as features for correlation filtering-based methods.
However, deep correlation filters still face challenges in handling target appearance variations, occlusions, and out-of-distribution (OOD) samples.

To address these issues, we propose to learn a cell-level convolutional architecture for visual tracking (CHASE), which enables the model to adapt to different kinds of target appearance variations and occlusions.
We first introduce a cell-level correlation filtering framework that operates on cell-generated features for efficient feature representation and localization.
Then, we propose a differentiable neural architecture search (NAS) framework to optimize the cell-level architecture for accurate and robust tracking.

Specifically, we design an innovative search space that explicitly considers the correlations between cells, such that the learned cell-level architecture can effectively capture the target structure and context.
Moreover, to alleviate the OOD issues, we propose a robust tracking framework that can explicitly handle OOD samples via a robust loss function and an OOD detection module.
Experimental results on multiple challenging datasets, including OOD scenarios, demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach against state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods.
We introduce a new weakly-supervised segmentation framework based on the geodesic active contour model (GAC).

Unlike existing methods that use pairwise constraints learned from shape contexts, our approach utilizes a new energy term in the GAC model that favors contours that intersect a given set of extreme points.
We show that the resulting optimization problem can be formulated as a geodesic flow on a Riemannian manifold and propose an efficient algorithm to solve it.

We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach on the challenging task of annotating pixels in densely-packed objects (e.g., cells in tissues) in a weakly-supervised manner, where only the locations of a small subset of pixels inside the objects are given.
In this setting, our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on two benchmark datasets.

K-Net: Towards Unified Image Segmentation

We present a simple, fast, and effective approach to image segmentation that achieves state-of-the-art performance on both integer and pixel-wise labeling.
K-Net learns a linear classifier in a weakly-supervised manner by leveraging the power of conditional random fields and the structure of deep neural networks.
This allows us to use a single network to segment images without needing to choose between the computational efficiency of integer-based methods and the accuracy of pixel-wise labeling methods.
Our approach is fast enough for semi-interactive segmentation, while achieving strong performance on multiple benchmarks.
Code is available at https://github.com/autonomousvision/K-Net.
Recent progress in deep learning has propelled convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to advance the state-of-the-art in image segmentation.
However, CNNs suffer from the lack of effective uncertainty measures, which hinders their applications in reliable and safety-critical environments.
In this paper, we exploit Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) to address this issue, which have shown promising results in producing meaningful uncertainty measures.
Nevertheless, BNNs usually demand a large number of parameters and thus are less compact compared to CNNs.
To overcome this limitation, we propose ComBiNet, a novel BNN architecture that is specifically designed for image segmentation.
It inherits the merits of both CNNs and BNNs, namely high performance and uncertainty estimation, while maintaining a compact architecture.
We validate ComBiNet on multiple public datasets, including MIT-CBCL, NYU-VOC, and Cityscapes.
Results show that our approach achieves promising performance with significant uncertainty estimation, and outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods.
We address the problem of semantic segmentation of very fine resolution urban scene images, where the ground truth pixel-level labels are available.
We propose a bilateral awareness network (BAN) that utilizes a transformer encoder decoder to model the bilateral relations of objects in the scene, while also taking into account the global context.

Our approach is based on the observation that fine-grained object segmentation of very high resolution (VH) urban scene images exhibits a strong bilateral constraint, i.e., the object appearance is influenced by its bilateral context, which we refer to as the object and its spatially-adjacent background.

The BAN effectively captures the bilateral context by introducing a novel bilateral transformer encoder decoder architecture that learns to predict object masks and their corresponding background masks.
It models the bilateral relations of objects with a self-supervised objective that does not require any additional annotation.
We evaluate our approach on the Cityscapes dataset and show that it achieves state-of-the-art performance.
