Recent developments in distributed computing and cluster computing technologies have made it possible to efficiently process huge datasets that cannot be handled by a single computer.
In this paper, we present a framework for efficient processing of large-scale image segmentation problems based on distributed clustering algorithms.
Our approach is based on dividing the input image into smaller regions, and processing each region in parallel on different computers.
We propose a few distributed clustering algorithms that are suitable for image segmentation, and evaluate their performance on a large-scale image segmentation benchmark.
Our experimental results show that the proposed approach can achieve significant speedup compared to a single-computer implementation, while maintaining a high quality of segmentation results.
We present a real-time algorithm for the segmentation of medical images based on a trilateral attention network.
Our approach combines the use of a convolutional neural network (CNN) with a graph-based segmentation algorithm to achieve accurate and efficient segmentation.
The CNN is used to extract features from the medical image, while the graph-based segmentation algorithm uses these features to segment the image.

The trilateral attention network is designed to improve the segmentation accuracy by considering the relationships between the three primary anatomical structures in the image: the tumor, the healthy tissue, and the background.
We evaluate our algorithm on a dataset of head computed tomography (CT) scans and show that it achieves a high degree of accuracy and is able to run in real-time.
Our algorithm has three main components: the CNN, the graph-based segmentation algorithm, and the trilateral attention network.
The CNN is used to extract features from the medical image, including the tumor, healthy tissue, and background.
The graph-based segmentation algorithm uses these features to segment the image, using a shortest-path algorithm to find the boundaries between the tumor and healthy tissue.
The trilateral attention network is designed to improve the segmentation accuracy by considering the relationships between the three primary anatomical structures in the image.
It does this by combining the features from the CNN with the graph-based segmentation algorithm, using attention weights to determine the importance of each feature in the segmentation process.
We evaluate our algorithm on a dataset of head CT scans and show that it achieves a high degree of accuracy, with a mean absolute error of 0.69 mm and a mean relative error of 2.47%.
Our algorithm is also able to run in real-time, with a processing time of 32.5 seconds.
This is faster than other state-of-the-art medical image segmentation algorithms, which typically take several minutes to process a single image.
We propose a new algorithm for real-time stereo matching, which can potentially be used in minimally invasive surgery.
Our algorithm is based on the Bayesian dense inverse searching (BDIS) algorithm, which uses a probabilistic approach to find the best match between two sets of data.
The BDIS algorithm is designed to be efficient and to handle large amounts of data, which makes it well-suited for real-time applications.
We evaluate our algorithm on a set of stereo images from the MICCAI 2012 stereo matching challenge and compare its performance to that of other state-of-the-art algorithms.
Our algorithm achieves competitive results while running at nearly real-time speeds.
Furthermore, we modify the BDIS algorithm to incorporate a smoothness prior, in order to improve its performance on challenging regions of the images.
This modification improves the accuracy of our algorithm, particularly in areas with low contrast and texture.
We believe that our algorithm has the potential to be used in real-time stereo matching applications, such as minimally invasive surgery.
Recent advances in connectomics have yielded high-quality images of neural tissue, but manual analysis still poses a substantial bottleneck.
In this paper, we present RLCorrector, a reinforced proofreading system that assists a user in segmenting connectomics images.
It is common for users to accidentally add or remove pixels from their segmentation, so we train a neural network to correct such errors.
We train our network using a novel loss function that incentivizes it to make corrections resembling human corrections.
We evaluate RLCorrector on both simulated and real world data, and show that it induces significant improvements in segmentation accuracy whilst requiring minimal user interaction.
We introduce Points2Polygons, an approach for training a geometric context-based segmentation model using only weak labels, i.e., point-level labels.
Our model segments images based on the underlying geometric context of the weak labels.
We introduce an encoder-decoder architecture that leverages the geometric consistency of object segments to refine initial predictions.
We train our model using an adversarial loss that encourages the model to produce segmentations with geometric properties similar to the weak labels.
Our method does not require any post-processing steps, such as graph cuts or conditional random fields.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on the Cityscapes and KITTI datasets, where we achieve state-of-the-art performance on the weakly-supervised segmentation task.

Our results show that our approach performs on par with fully-supervised segmentation methods in terms of accuracy, while being more efficient in terms of training time and the amount of labeled data required.
Our main contributions can be summarised as follows:
We propose a new weakly-supervised segmentation approach that utilizes geometric context to segment images without any post-processing steps.
We introduce an encoder-decoder architecture that leverages the geometric consistency of object segments to refine initial predictions.
We train our model using an adversarial loss that encourages the model to produce segmentations with geometric properties similar to the weak labels.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on the Cityscapes and KITTI datasets, where we achieve state-of-the-art performance on the weakly-supervised segmentation task.

We present a view of exact inference in graphs from the degree-4 sum-of-squares hierarchy (SoSH) that yields the currently fastest known algorithms for approximate counting, maximization, and minimization derived from a broad range of probability distributions.

These algorithms have an approximation quality that is rarely worse than existing state-of-the-art algorithms for the corresponding problems, while having the advantage of yielding exact inference results in graphs under the SoSH relaxation.

We present a general recipe for converting any problem in graphs that is solvable by belief propagation (BP) on a factor graph into a problem that can be solved by generalized belief propagation (BP^*) on a factor graph, and show that the resulting algorithm is always an approximation of the original problem with a quality that is rarely worse than previously known algorithms for the corresponding problem.
This recipe enables us to obtain our fast algorithms for approximate counting, maximization, and minimization.
We present experimental results that demonstrate the performance of our algorithms on a set of real-world benchmarks.
In this paper, a method of high-resolution segmentation of tooth root fuzzy edges based on polynomial curve fitting with landmark detection is proposed.
Specially, we establish a coordinate system of dental radiograph via four detected landmark points, and then fit the polynomial curve to the top and bottom of the tooth root.
Next, we segment the tooth root fuzzy edges based on the fitting curves.
The experimental results show that the proposed method can effectively extract the tooth root and its fuzzy edges, and has the advantages of high precision and good stability.
We present a new algorithm for deep active contours that combines the advantages of distance vector flow (DVF) and the recent progress in deep learning.
Our approach uses a convolutional neural network (CNN) to learn a locally controlled distance function in a data-driven manner.
This allows us to modify the behavior of the DVF according to the local characteristics of the image, resulting in a more flexible and accurate algorithm.
We show that our approach can handle a variety of tasks, including image segmentation, object tracking, and pose estimation, and we demonstrate its performance on several challenging datasets.
Our code and models are publicly available at https://github.com/CVMI-Lab/DAC-LCDVF.
Most referring expressions in natural language are grounded in visual or spatial content, such as demonstratives (e.g., “here”, “there”) or spatial prepositions (e.g., “in”, “on”).

Moreover, the successful deployment of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies often hinges on the interpretability of the model outputs, especially in safety-critical domains such as healthcare and autonomous driving.

In this paper, we tackle the referring expression generation (REG) task with a progressive comprehension (PC) approach, where a referring expression is generated by gradually refining an initially vague description of the referent through interaction with a user.
We propose a cross-modal PC framework that can not only reason about the visual and linguistic content together, but also explain how the final referring expression is derived.

We evaluate our method on the ReferIt dataset, and show that our model can generate more accurate referring expressions compared to the state-of-the-art methods while providing interpretable referring segments.

A Large-Scale Benchmark for Food Image Segmentation

Food image segmentation is a fundamental task for enabling smarter tools in culinary applications.
There have been recent advances in the field, but no standardized benchmark is available for the community to compare different approaches.
We introduce a large-scale dataset of 5000 images, each of which is manually segmented into nine semantic classes by human experts.
To the best of our knowledge, this is the largest dataset with pixel-level segmentation for food images.
We further provide a benchmark of five state-of-the-art segmentation methods for this dataset.
The evaluation results show the characteristics of different methods, and provide insights into how to improve segmentation performance.

Overview of the Benchmark

Food segmentation differs from general image segmentation in that the former often requires a fine-grained and per-class segmentation, while the latter usually focuses on global image segmentation into few classes (e.g., foreground vs. background).
Some recent works on food image segmentation usually make an assumption that the food lies in the foreground, and segment the image into two classes: food vs. background.
This assumption may not hold true in some situations.
In this work, we define nine semantic classes, including seven food classes and two background classes.
The seven food classes are "Background", "Appetizer", "Beverage", "Dessert", "Main Course", "Sides", and "Utensils".
The two background classes are "Tabletop" and "Plates".
An example is shown in Figure 1.
We segment each image into these nine classes.
We search for existing food image segmentation datasets.
There are some datasets with ground truth segmentation that are specific to certain cuisines (e.g., cakes, fast food), or specific applications (e.g., plate detection).
However, these datasets are usually small, and thus are not suitable for training and evaluating segmentation models.
There are also some datasets with bounding boxes of food regions, but no pixel-level segmentation.
Since pixel-level segmentation is a prerequisite for many follow-up tasks (e.g., recognition, attribute prediction), we feel that a pixel-level segmentation dataset is more useful to the community.
Our dataset is collected from Flickr with the help of a food image search engine.
We manually segment each image into nine classes.
To provide a fair comparison, we choose five state-of-the-art segmentation methods, including Graph Cuts, GrabCut, Conditional Random Fields (CRF), Expectation-Maximization (EM),
We propose a Bayesian logistic shape model (LSM) for image segmentation based on a latent variable model that we refer to as the conical LSM.
The conical LSM is a variation of the standard LSM in which each class is described by a conical region, thereby allowing for spatial variation in the classification likelihoods.
We propose a practical inference algorithm for the conical LSM based on a reversible jump MCMC algorithm that allows us to borrow strength across images and models.
We apply our method to the segmentation of cochlea images.
Experimentally, we demonstrate that our method yields more accurate segmentations at a lower computational cost than state-of-the-art methods.
We present a new active contour model for image segmentation based on a generalized asymmetric dual-front approach.

In this model, the interface is described by two fronts, one for the exterior and one for the interior of the object, which move simultaneously toward each other or away from each other depending on the local gradient direction.
The front that is inside the evolving contour is always faster than the outside front.
This feature imposes a strong constraint on the contour evolution, resulting in a bias toward the formation of a global contour that is closed and does not leak out of the object boundary.

An important advantage of the proposed method is that it is very fast and easy to implement because it only involves a simple calculation of the gradient of the image and a marching process in the gradient direction.
Experimental results on several segmentation benchmarks show the efficiency of the proposed approach compared with state-of-the-art active contour models.

Recent works usually enhance the performance of semantic segmentation models mainly in two ways: (i) increase the complexity of the model, e.g., designing more powerful CNN architectures, or (ii) utilize more training data.
However, these methods usually lead to a significantly increased computational cost which limits their applications on mobile devices or for real-time applications.
In this work, we try to revisit the BiSeNet, a well-designed lightweight model for semantic segmentation, to make it better suit for real-time applications.

Specifically, we propose a fast and lightweight semantic segmentation architecture by modifying the original BiSeNet in four major ways: (i) we remove the redundant skip connections in the original model to save computational cost, (ii) we introduce an adaptive instance normalization mechanism to adaptively adjust the channel numbers of the outputs of the Atrous Spatial Pyramid (ASP) blocks, (iii) we remove the ASP blocks in the original model and replace them with a single ASP block with a channel number determined by the adaptive instance normalization mechanism, and (iv) we remove the concatenation layers in the original model and directly stack the deep features and the shallow features as input of the final conv layers.
The proposed method is thoroughly evaluated on four popular semantic segmentation benchmarks, i.e., NYUv2, NYUv2-360, Cityscapes and ACDC, and promising results are achieved.

Generative Models are typically trained under strong assumptions: 3D object categories are assumed to have a large number of object instances, and those instances are assumed to be ordered, e.g., sorted by their horizontal pose.
We question these assumptions in the context of arranging object instances in a horizontal strip: How many instances can be recovered, if at all, when there are no ordering constraints?
If ordering is imposed, how much does it help, and how much supervision is required?
We investigate the limits of generative modeling under various supervisory signals, ranging from ordering constraints (e.g., horizontal pose) to no supervision at all.

Our analysis reveals that while fully-supervised models perform well when the number of instances is large, they struggle when the number of instances is small or when the instances are even partially ordered.
In contrast, our proposed method, GENESIS-V2, which does not rely on iterative refinement, performs consistently across all settings, often outperforming the state-of-the-art.
Recent works on semantic segmentation have achieved remarkable performance on standard benchmarks, but most lack the ability to generalize to unseen domains.
In this paper, we investigate the use of generative models, namely Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), for producing more robust feature representations for semantic segmentation.
We propose a semi-supervised approach where a GAN is trained to synthesize training samples in the target domain, and show that this leads to improved performance and robustness.

To effectively utilize the limited labeled data in each target domain, we propose a novel consistency loss that enforces the segmentation model to be robust to variations in the unlabeled images, as well as a domain-adversarial loss that explicitly trains the model to recognize differences between domains.
When tested on the Cityscapes dataset, our approach yields meaningful improvements in segmentation quality and out-of-domain robustness, even with no target-domain labels.

We further demonstrate the generalization capability of our approach on two different datasets: a synthetic dataset rendered from a 3D city model and a real-world dataset captured by an autonomous driving car.
Polyp localisation in Computed Tomography (CT) colonography is a challenging image processing task.
In this paper, we propose a new approach for polyp localisation based on ensemble learning and particle swarm optimisation (PSO).
The ensemble learning is based on classifier prediction confidence, and the PSO is used for comprehensive learning.
The proposed approach is evaluated on a public dataset, and the results show that it outperforms the state-of-the-art approaches.
The proposed approach is also shown to be robust to variations in the input data and the number of classes in the dataset.

Abstract:

Pneumothorax is a common medical condition in which air leaks into the space between a patient's lungs and chest wall.
It can be challenging to identify pneumothorax in medical images, as it can take on many shapes and sizes, and appear near other structures such as the heart and lungs.
In this paper, we present a method for the automatic segmentation of pneumothorax in medical images using deep learning.
Our method uses a U-Net architecture, trained on a large dataset of annotated images, to learn a robust feature representation for pneumothorax segmentation.
We evaluate our method on a separate test set, and show that it outperforms existing methods in terms of accuracy and speed.
Our method has the potential to be a valuable tool for the diagnosis and treatment of pneumothorax, and may also be useful for other medical image segmentation tasks.

Here is a 250-word summary of the paper:

The paper presents a method for the automatic segmentation of pneumothorax, a medical condition in which air leaks into the space between the lungs and the chest wall, in medical images using deep learning.
The goal of the paper is to develop a robust and accurate method for the segmentation of pneumothorax, which can assist in the diagnosis and treatment of the condition.
The method uses a U-Net architecture, which has been successfully used for other medical image segmentation tasks.
The U-Net is trained on a large dataset of annotated images, which helps it to learn a robust feature representation for pneumothorax segmentation.
The annotated images are collected from medical imaging databases and manually annotated by experts in the field.
The U-Net architecture consists of an encoder and decoder network, which are trained together.
The encoder network extracts features from the input images, and the decoder network uses these features to predict the segmentation of the pneumothorax.
The two networks are trained in a supervised manner, with the annotated images used as the training data.
The paper evaluates the method on a separate test set, and shows that it outperforms existing methods in terms of accuracy and speed.
The evaluation is performed by comparing the method to other methods for pneumothorax segmentation, and measuring the accuracy and speed of the predictions.
The paper also shows that the method is generalizable to different types of medical images, and can be used to segment pneumothorax in images from different patients and imaging modalities.

Recent advances in segmentation algorithms have shown that the use of attention mechanisms within convolutional neural networks (CNNs) can improve performance.
In this work, we propose a novel architecture for biomedical image segmentation, called Feedback Attention Network (FANet).
FANet incorporates an attention mechanism that utilizes both bottom-up and top-down attention, whilst also including a feedback loop from the attention module to the encoder.
This unique combination improves performance by focusing on relevant image regions and leveraging global information for disambiguating between similar tissue types.
We evaluate FANet on three publicly available datasets of different modalities (MRI, CT, and histology), in which we achieve state-of-the-art performance.
Code is available at https://github.com/CCRALAB/fanet.
Few-shot segmentation is a challenging problem in which the goal is to segment new classes given only a few training examples.
In this paper, we propose a self-guided learning approach with an adaptive similarity metric learning module to address this problem.
Specifically, we learn a similarity metric adapted to the few-shot segmentation by minimizing the divergence between the predicted and ground truth segmentations.

Furthermore, we explore the connection between the few-shot segmentation and the well-studied image segmentation problem with a large number of labeled images and show that the latter can provide valuable information for the former.
We propose a cross-guided learning approach to exploit the information from the well-studied problem and integrate it into the self-guided learning framework.
The proposed methods are evaluated on the popular Cityscapes and Mapillary Vistas datasets, and the results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approaches.
We present a fully convolutional network that learns to segment objects in images, given only sparse scribbles as input.
The network uses multi-scale adversarial attention gates to aggregate information provided by the scribbles across multiple scales, while focusing on the regions most relevant for segmentation.
We introduce a novel loss function that trains the network to predict object masks directly, without the need for post-processing steps such as graph cuts.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on the public Scribble Reconition Benchmark (SRB), achieving state-of-the-art performance.
Code is available at https://github.com/ankitsharma008/scribble-segmentation.
Deep learning has become a popular method for image segmentation, but it suffers from a lack of understanding.
We propose a novel approach to image segmentation using deep neural networks that learn meta-structures in the input image to aid in segmentation.
Our approach is based on the observation that deep neural networks can learn to detect and utilize subtle patterns in the input image, which can be used for segmentation.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on fluorescence microscopy images, which contain complex and subtle structures that are challenging to segment using traditional methods.
Our results show that our approach can achieve state-of-the-art performance in image segmentation, while providing insights into the decision-making process of the neural network.

Our approach can be useful for segmenting other types of images, such as medical images and satellite images, which often contain complex and subtle structures that are challenging to segment using traditional methods.
Additionally, our approach can be used to understand the decision-making process of deep neural networks, which can help to improve their performance and interpretability.
Recent progress in deep learning has propelled medical image segmentation towards a fully automated pipeline, however, most approaches rely on large amounts of manually annotated training data.
This is especially challenging in the domain of medical imaging, where expert annotation is expensive and time-consuming.
In this paper, we tackle the problem of training a segmentation model from unsupervised learning, i.e., without relying on annotated examples.

Our approach leverages a robust registration algorithm that aligns clinically acquired scans to a baseline atlas, and a contrastive loss that encourages the segmentation model to output consistent segmentations across the aligned images.

We show that our approach is capable of learning representations that are highly transferable to a variety of segmentation tasks, and moreover, that the use of contrastive learning significantly improves generalization performance.

We evaluate our approach on multi-atlas based segmentation and on per-patient segmentation without any atlas, demonstrating state-of-the-art performance on the ISLES 2017 challenge and the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) dataset.
Recent progress in deep learning has led to numerous successful applications, but most of these applications focus on confined datasets and trained models lacking generalization capability.
In this paper, we tackle the problem of learning a deep neural network for food portion estimation with limited training data.

We propose a method to leverage knowledge from a source domain with more training data (e.g., image segmentation) to adapt a pre-trained model to a target domain (i.e., food portion estimation) using few training samples.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on a public food portion estimation dataset, showing consistent performance improvement over the state-of-the-art.
Our code and models are available at https://github.com/AI4FOOD-Foundation/CrossDomainFeatureAdaptation.
Recent progress in medical image segmentation has largely been achieved by leveraging large institutional datasets.

However, such efforts suffer from dataset heterogeneity, inhibiting the generalization of learned models across institutions and resulting in poor performance on datasets outside the training distribution.
In this paper, we propose FedDG, a flexible framework for learning robust segmentors via federated domain generalization (FedDG).
FedDG leverages episodic learning, a technique inspired by human cognitive learning, to model distributions in continuous frequency space.
We demonstrate that our model can learn robust segmentors from only a few institutional contributions, resulting in improved performance on both in-distribution and out-of-distribution datasets.
We showcase the efficacy of our approach on three public medical image segmentation benchmarks, yielding state-of-the-art performance with trained models that are over 200 times smaller.
Code is available at https://github.com/AI4Finance-Foundation/FedDG.

We present a semi-supervised segmentation framework that utilizes the dual-task consistency (DTC) loss, which aligns the hidden representations of a shared encoder across two tasks: image classification and segmentation.

Benefitting from large amounts of unlabeled data and the powerful representations learned by the encoder, our approach shows robust performance on three challenging medical image segmentation tasks: abdominal CT, cardiac MRI, and brain tumor MRI.

In particular, given a single fully-labeled image, our method achieves 42.0%, 56.4%, and 66.4% mean accuracy on the abdominal CT, cardiac MRI, and brain tumor MRI segmentation benchmarks, respectively, significantly outperforming the state-of-the-art.

Recent progress in deep learning greatly advanced biomedical image segmentation, but the trained models are hardly transferable to clinical settings, because the amount of manually annotated clinical data is scarce.

We propose a category-centric prototype aligner to effectively align the source and target distributions in unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA), which is a key challenge in the application of deep learning to biomedical image segmentation.

In the category-centric prototype aligner, we introduce a category-centric loss to align the data distributions of different categories in the source and target domains, and a prototype-centric loss to align the data distribution of prototypes in the source and target domains, and we optimize both of them jointly via a stacked progressive four-layer encoder-decoder network.
In the encoder layer, we utilize a categorize-then-distribute mechanism to obtain category-centric and prototype-centric features.
In the decoder layer, we utilize a category-centric prototype aligner to align the features of different categories and prototypes of the source domain to their counterparts in the target domain.

We evaluate our method on the ISLES challenge 2019 dataset for liver and kidney segmentation, and achieve the best average precision and recall scores among the eight competing methods on both the source and target domains.
Recent advances in deep learning have achieved remarkable performance in medical image segmentation, aiming to provide accurate segmentation results with minimal human effort.
However, fully supervised learning still demands a significant amount of manually labeled training samples, which is difficult to obtain in the medical field due to the expertise and time required.
In this paper, we conduct a comprehensive review of recent deep learning models that address the medical image segmentation task with limited supervision.
We first categorize existing methods into three categories based on the level of supervision they require.
Then, we discuss the deep learning models that have been applied to each category, including fully supervised learning, weakly supervised learning, and unsupervised learning.
We also review the recently emerged few-shot learning approaches that are designed to segment new classes with only a few labeled examples.
Next, we survey the state-of-the-art methods designed for specific medical image segmentation tasks, including neuronal tissue segmentation, tumor segmentation, and cardiac image segmentation.
We also discuss the evaluation metrics commonly used in the field.
Finally, we highlight the advantages and limitations of each approach and point out potential research directions.

EMDS-5 is an ongoing project to create a large-scale dataset of microbial samples, which can be used for training and testing of machine learning algorithms for classification, segmentation, and detection tasks.
The dataset is composed of microscopic images of microorganisms, including bacteria, fungi, and protozoa, as well as samples of non-living objects, such as dust and dirt.

The images are manually annotated with labels at the pixel level, and the dataset is designed to be challenging for machine learning algorithms, with a high level of variability in the appearance of the microorganisms, and a large number of classes and instances.
This paper describes the creation of the EMDS-5 dataset and the challenges associated with its creation, and it presents a set of baseline results for several image analysis tasks.

We hope that the EMDS-5 dataset will be a useful resource for the machine learning and microbiology communities, and will help to advance the state of the art in the analysis of microscopic images of microorganisms.
Recent progress in convolutional neural network (CNN) architecture design has propelled the advancement of semantic segmentation, especially in the context of natural image datasets.

However, the assumption that the training data is abundantly labeled, which is often satisfied in natural image segmentation, does not hold for specialized domains such as food image segmentation, which demands much effort and expense to collect and label.
To overcome the lack of labeled training data, we can utilize the prior knowledge in the form of rules or culinary knowledge to learn a segmentation model.
In this work, we borrow ideas from the recent advancement in the field of salient object detection and propose a saliency-aware class-agnostic segmentation approach for food images.

Specifically, we first utilize a pre-trained CNN as a feature encoder to extract mid-level features and then build a segmentation model that is trained by explicitly incorporating the prior knowledge of food images, which is in the form of a global saliency map.
The global saliency map is learned in a class-agnostic manner, but is tailored to the food domain.
We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach on the public FOOD-101 dataset.
Recent progress in image segmentation has primarily been evaluated on tightly-controlled benchmark datasets, which inevitably skew the distribution of real-world images.
In practice, the performance of these models can degrade significantly given small amounts of label corruption, motivating research on robust methods.
We propose Co-Seg, a simple yet effective framework for image segmentation that is capable of handling label noise.
Co-Seg leverages a pre-trained segmentation model as a soft prior and learns a small classifier to refine the segmentation by aligning with the prior.
We show that this approach is capable of correcting label noise, and also naturally integrates edge information to improve performance on boundary regions.

Co-Seg achieves state-of-the-art performance on the Cityscapes and Mapillary Vistas datasets even without any form of regularization, and is on-par with state-of-the-art methods on the CamVid dataset with a simple regularization technique.

Recent progresses in medical image analysis have been largely driven by large-scale annotation efforts, which however are difficult to replicate for specific domains and hospital settings, especially in surgical imaging.
In this work, we tackle the problem of transferring segmentation knowledge from large-scale annotated images to novel domains, without requiring any explicit pairing or domain-specific training data.
We introduce a new approach to domain adaptation based on a network-agnostic knowledge transfer framework.
Our method operates in the image domain and does not require any pairing between source and target domains, nor any pre-trained models.

We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach on three different intraoperative imaging datasets (cranial ultrasound, laparoscopic and endovascular ultrasound), showing improvements over strong baselines in terms of both segmental and boundary accuracy, as well as a significant reduction of segmentation errors.
Image segmentation is typically approached as a clustering problem, whereby pixels in an image are assigned labels belonging to different clusters, each characterized by a mean color.
In this paper we study the performance of several nonparametric Bayesian models, including Gaussian mixtures and Ising models, for segmenting images using a variational approach.
We derive a new energy function which assigns costs to labeled regions based on how consistent they are with observed data and with a specified labeling structure.
We introduce a new prior on the means of the Gaussian mixtures to encourage natural, visually meaningful segmentations.
Finally, we introduce a new algorithm for tuning the hyperparameters of the segmentation model.
This new approach is fully automatic, and is shown to produce state-of-the-art image segmentations.
We present a novel boundary-aware geometric encoding (BAGE) for efficient and effective semantic segmentation of point clouds.
BAGE utilizes a boundary-aware interpolation strategy to encode geometric information of point clouds into a continuous and dense feature space, where semantic segmentation can be performed.
Specifically, we design a boundary-aware weight function to emphasize the boundary points and grant more reliable predictions on object boundaries.
Furthermore, we propose a distance-weighted voting mechanism to refine the segmentation results and highlight the regions with complex shapes.

To evaluate the performance of BAGE, we conduct extensive experiments on the Semantic3D and S3DIS datasets, and the results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in comparison to the state-of-the-art methods.
Our source code is available at https://github.com/AI4SEG/BAGE.
Recent progress in computer vision has resulted in breakthroughs in well-known datasets such as ImageNet, which however often represent constrained and controlled conditions.

In contrast, medical imaging datasets usually come from different domains (different hospitals, different acquisition modalities, etc.), leading to a data distribution shift and a degradation of the performance of the models.
In this work, we address the problem of domain adaptation on hip joint bone segmentation, with a particular focus on intra-modality and cross-modality inconsistencies.
We propose ICMSC, a simple and effective method that combines an inconsistency-aware loss and a modality-consistent regularization.

We show that our approach is able to adapt effectively both within each individual modality and across different modalities, leading to state-of-the-art performance on a public dataset of hip x-ray images.

Recent works have shown that 3D integration is a promising direction for technology scaling of AI accelerators, but the rapidly increasing computational complexity and large volume of 3D networks pose significant challenges for designing high-performance and area-efficient 3D networks.

In this paper, we propose Cakes, a channel-wise automatic kernel shrinking (CAKES) framework that can effectively reduce the volume of 3D networks while preserving their computational integrity and without requiring any kernel-level modification.
Cakes can be readily applied to any 3D network with minimal effort.

We present an extensive evaluation of Cakes on a wide range of 3D networks, where up to 50% volume reduction is achieved with an average of 29.4% volume reduction, and the overall computational latency is improved by up to 4.35% with an average of 1.77% for the Cake-treated networks compared to their original counterparts.

Few-shot learning aims to reduce the amount of labeled training data required to build a robust model by transferring knowledge from a source task with abundant labeled data to a target task with only a few labeled samples.
In this work, we propose a few-shot learning approach for medical image segmentation problems, which are typically characterized by the scarcity of labeled images.
We exploit a global correlation network as a universal feature encoder for learning robust representations that facilitate the few-shot segmentation.
Specifically, we pre-train the global correlation network on a large dataset of images in an unsupervised manner, and then fine-tune it with a discriminative embedding on a few labeled images.
The proposed method is evaluated on four public abdominal organ segmentation benchmarks, and compared with other few-shot learning methods as well as the state-of-the-art fully-supervised methods.
Our results show that the proposed method achieves promising performance in terms of segmentation accuracy, and is particularly effective for few-shot learning scenarios.
In this paper, we propose a novel active contour model for infrared image segmentation with intensity inhomogeneity.
The proposed method is driven by a set of multi-features, including gradient, gradient magnitude, and curvature.
By introducing a new energy term, the proposed method is capable of adapting to the intensity inhomogeneity of infrared images.
In addition, a novel algorithm is presented to optimize the proposed model.
The proposed method was evaluated on a public infrared image segmentation benchmark, and the experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach.
We present a novel approach for few-shot learning of 3D medical image segmentation based on bidirectional recurrent neural networks (BiRNNs).
Our method utilizes a pre-trained convolutional neural network (CNN) for feature extraction and a BiRNN for learning temporal dependencies between frames in a video.
We introduce a novel few-shot learning framework that combines both global and local information for segmenting 3D medical images.
Our global information is derived from the pre-trained CNN, while our local information is generated by the BiRNN.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on the task of few-shot learning for 3D medical image segmentation.
Our experimental results show that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on the MRI skull stripping dataset and is competitive with other methods on the X-ray chest dataset.
Furthermore, we present an analysis of the impact of different design choices on the performance of our method.
w-Net: A Dual Supervised Medical Image Segmentation Model with Multi-Dimensional Attention and Cascade Multi-Scale Convolutional Neural Network.
In this paper, we propose a novel approach for medical image segmentation based on a deep learning model.
Our method is based on a multi-dimensional attention mechanism and a cascade of multi-scale convolutional layers.
This allows us to capture complex spatial and contextual information in medical images, resulting in accurate and robust segmentation.
We evaluate our method on three different medical image segmentation datasets, and show that it outperforms the state-of-the-art in all cases.
Our method can be generalized to other medical image segmentation tasks, and we believe it will be a valuable tool for medical image analysis.
The proposed method consists of a convolutional neural network (CNN) with a multi-dimensional attention mechanism and a cascade of multi-scale convolutional layers.
The CNN is trained on a large dataset of medical images and their corresponding segmentations.

The multi-dimensional attention mechanism allows the model to focus on different aspects of the input image, while the cascade of multi-scale convolutional layers enables the model to capture complex spatial and contextual information.

The proposed method was evaluated on three different medical image segmentation datasets: the ISBI 2017 Challenge on Mitosis Detection, the Camelyon 2017 Challenge on Breast Cancer Metastasis Detection, and the MedIA 2017 Challenge on Pancreas Tumor Segmentation.
The results show that the proposed method outperforms the state-of-the-art in all cases.
The proposed method has the advantage of being able to handle large and complex datasets, and can be generalized to other medical image segmentation tasks.
It can be used as a stand-alone tool for medical image analysis, or as a pre-processing step for other medical image analysis tasks such as classification or detection.
Recent progress in image segmentation is largely driven by large-scale supervised learning with abundant labeled data.
However, in many real-world applications, obtaining abundant labeled data is difficult, and a supervised learning paradigm is therefore insufficient.
In this paper, we present a new framework that leverages not only labeled data but also other modalities (e.g., unlabeled images and point clouds) for image segmentation.
We disentangle the shared and individual information among different modalities to achieve segmentation by aligning and fusing the disentangled information.
The key challenge lies in the unlabeled images and point clouds, which may contain severe misalignment and large domain gaps.
To handle it, we propose a novel geometric alignment method to establish a coherent feature space across different modalities.
Then, we exploit the geometric structures of the point clouds and the spatial-temporal coherence of videos to propagate the labeled information to multiple modalities for segmentation.
Extensive experiments on public datasets (e.g., SceneNN and NYUR) show the superiority of our approach over the state-of-the-art.
In this paper, we present a teacher-student framework with an attention module for semi-supervised medical image segmentation from mixed supervision.
We train a teacher model using only labeled images, and then use the pre-trained teacher model to generate pseudo labels for unlabeled images.
We propose an attention module to weigh the importance of different information for segmentation.
We optimize the student model with both labeled and pseudo labeled data, and the proposed attention module further improves the segmentation performance.
In addition, we investigate the use of multiple teachers for the purpose of knowledge transfer.
The experimental results on three different public lung segmentation benchmarks, using mixed supervision of CT and MRI scans, show that our method outperforms the state-of-the-art approaches.
HS-ResNet employs a novel hierarchical-split (HS) block that performs well in the computer vision tasks.

In addition, we systematically study the effectiveness of the HS block compared with the state-of-the-art models, in which the HS block is inserted into the pre-trained ResNet models, including ResNet-18, ResNet-34, and ResNet-50.
In the experiment, we evaluate the performance of our proposed models on ImageNet-1k dataset, and the results show that our proposed models achieve state-of-the-art performance.

Recent results on semantic segmentation largely benefited from the use of large datasets and powerful models, such as Encoder-Decoder based models like U-Net or more recent object detection architecture adaptations.
However, acquiring a large amount of labeled data is expensive and time-consuming, especially when only a small amount of initial training data is available.
In this context, active learning appears to be a promising solution.

Nevertheless, most of the state-of-the-art active learning methods for semantic segmentation are based on point-based approaches, which require a dense annotation for each pixel, and often rely on heuristics that may not perform well in many cases.
In this paper, we present MetaBox+, a new region-based active learning approach for semantic segmentation.

MetaBox+ leverages an innovative priority map that is built from both a global and local perspective, and a novel sampling strategy that aims to minimize the risk of missing hard positive and negative examples.
We conduct experiments on a recently introduced dataset, called SceneCrafter, which contains pixel-wise annotations for about 800 images.
We show that our method outperforms the state-of-the-art point-based active learning methods for semantic segmentation.
Interactive image segmentation differs from automatic segmentation in that it allows the user to impose his or her prior knowledge on the segmentation process.
In many real-world applications, the user has specific prior knowledge about the regions of interest in the image and can provide initial segmentations.
Once an initial segmentation is provided, an interactive segmentation algorithm propagates this prior information in order to produce a final segmentation.
The success of the interactive segmentation algorithm depends on the accuracy of the initial segmentation and the robustness of the propagation process.
In this paper, we propose a new interactive image segmentation algorithm that combines advantages of gradient-based and texture-based approaches to segmentation.
In particular, we propagate user markings based on image gradients when the image regions have distinct gradients, and based on image texture when gradients are absent.

Furthermore, to the best of our knowledge, we are the first to address the problem of interactive segmentation of patterned images, i.e., images in which texture is the dominant factor in the scene and for which classical texture-based approaches do not work well.
We demonstrate the robustness of our approach on a database of patterned images.
Recent works have shown that training powerful semantic segmentation models with limited amounts of labeled data is possible by leveraging large amounts of unlabeled data.
However, manually labeling pixels in microscopy images is expensive, and relying on expensive labels for training has so far limited the amount of training data that can be used.

We propose a simple yet effective method for training on limited amounts of manually labeled data by learning to segment images using a small number of "lazy" labels (i.e. labels where only a small subset of pixels within an image are manually annotated).

We show that lazy labels can be used to learn a model that generalizes well to the entire image and evaluate our method on two different microscopy image segmentation benchmarks, achieving state-of-the-art performance.
Recent semi-supervised instance segmentation methods mostly focus on modeling spectral or spatial relationships between pixels in different images through consistency and/or similarity learning.

These methods either treat all pixels within an object as a unit or assign labels independently at each pixel without considering their spatial coherence, which limits their ability to capture complex object structures.
In this paper, we propose a Mask-guided Sample Selection (MSS) approach for training a semi-supervised pixel-level classifier.
Given a pixel of interest, our method selects its class-consistent neighboring pixels as semantic contextual samples through a learned mask.
We pose the learning of the mask as a binary classification problem, where the mask is the decision boundary between the foreground (object) and background (rest of the image).
Specifically, given an initial guess of the mask, we minimize the cross-entropy loss by iteratively refining the mask through gradient descent.
We optimize the mask in a bottom-up fashion, starting from the pixels with the highest response and traversing the areas with the most uncertain labels.
We evaluate MSS on four semi-supervised segmentation benchmarks, achieving state-of-the-art performance.
Current clinical practice for cardiac assessment in patients with congenital heart disease (CHD) is mostly based on 2D evaluations of the cardiac chambers and great vessels.
However, a more comprehensive assessment would additionally analyze the cardiac walls to measure cardiac muscle thickness and evaluate the presence of wall-related CHD.
A standard clinical practice to assess the cardiac walls is to manually segment the cardiac chambers in MIP views and then measure wall thicknesses in a few selected views.
This approach is time-consuming, subjective, and does not provide comprehensive information on the cardiac wall thicknesses.
In this paper, we present a deep learning-based framework for automatic reconstruction and segmentation of the full cardiac walls in 3D from a single CT scan.
Our framework learns to jointly reconstruct the whole cardiac volume and segment the cardiac walls in a fully-supervised learning framework.
We introduce a novel deep learning architecture, namely PC-U net, to address the aforementioned tasks.

The proposed method is evaluated on 20 clinical CT scans (including healthy and pathological cases), and the results show that the PC-U net is capable of reconstructing and segmenting the full cardiac walls with an accuracy that is sufficient for clinical evaluation.
The framework is implemented in clinical routine at our institute since 2019.
A new method for image segmentation via Cellular Automata is presented in this paper.
It is based on a simple yet effective technique for the detection of edges and regions in binary images.
The method is motivated by the observation that edges in binary images often correspond to transitions between regions of different colors or intensities.
The proposed method utilizes this property to partition an image into a set of regions, each of which is characterized by a distinct set of colors or intensities.
The method is simple, efficient, and easy to implement, and it can be used to segment a wide variety of binary images, including those with complex shapes and structures.
The experimental results presented in this paper demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.
In this paper, we propose a new polarimetric SAR image segmentation method based on 3D discrete wavelet transform (DWT) and Markov random field (MRF).
The proposed method extracts texture information from polarimetric SAR images in various scales using 3D DWT.
The MRF is then applied to model the spatial dependence of the segmented images.
The experimental results show that the proposed method achieves better segmentation performance in terms of accuracy and speed, compared to the state-of-the-art methods.
The proposed method is also validated on a polarimetric SAR image dataset from the literature.
Extraction of texture information from polarimetric SAR images is a crucial step for various applications such as object detection, classification, and change detection.
The polarimetric SAR images often contain complex texture information that is challenging to extract using traditional image processing techniques.
In this paper, we propose a new method based on 3D DWT to extract texture information from polarimetric SAR images in various scales.
The 3D DWT is a multi-scale, multi-dimensional image processing technique that has been widely used for image analysis and classification.
The proposed method extracts texture information from polarimetric SAR images in various scales using 3D DWT.
The extracted texture features are then used to train a MRF model that models the spatial dependence of the segmented images.
The MRF model is a probabilistic model that captures the spatial dependence of the segmented images using a set of random variables.
The experimental results show that the proposed method achieves better segmentation performance in terms of accuracy and speed, compared to the state-of-the-art methods.
The proposed method is also validated on a polarimetric SAR image dataset from the literature.
The proposed method offers several advantages over the state-of-the-art methods.
First, the proposed method is able to extract texture information from polarimetric SAR images in various scales using 3D DWT, which allows for more accurate segmentation.
Second, the proposed method is able to model the spatial dependence of the segmented images using MRF, which allows for more robust segmentation.
Third, the proposed method is able to achieve better segmentation performance in terms of accuracy and speed, compared to the state-of-the-art methods.
Deep learning has been demonstrating state-of-the-art performance in various computer vision tasks, including image segmentation.
However, whether deep learning is the best choice for image segmentation remains questionable.

This paper compares deep learning-based image segmentation with other classical image segmentation methods, including edge-based segmentation, region-based segmentation, and hybrid methods, on various metrics.
To perform a fair comparison, the same evaluation metrics and data sets are used for all methods.
The comparison results reveal that deep learning-based methods perform better in terms of accuracy but not in terms of runtime.
Furthermore, the state-of-the-art deep learning-based methods do not outperform classical methods by a large margin, which questions whether deep learning is necessary for image segmentation.
Recent works on 3D semantic segmentation largely focus on natural images, where large-scale training data is readily available.

In contrast, medical images provide critical information for clinical diagnosis, but they pose significant challenges for 3D semantic segmentation due to the scarcity of labeled training data and the uniqueness of anatomical structures' shapes.

In this paper, we present a shape-aware semi-supervised 3D semantic segmentation framework that utilizes the shape information of structures and leverages available unlabeled data from multiple sources for training.
We propose a novel shape-aware loss function that encourages the network to produce segmentations with coherent and meaningful shapes.
Furthermore, we introduce a data augmentation module that synthetically generates additional training samples with anatomical structure shapes from unlabeled data.
We evaluate our method on two public available abdominal CT datasets with limited labeled data and achieve promising results compared to the state-of-the-art.
Recent advances in deep learning have enabled automatic image labelling at superpixel level.
However, most of these methods rely on some prior knowledge about the images such as large amounts of paired superpixel and label annotations or a fixed set of object classes.
In this paper, we present a method for automatic image labelling at pixel level that is completely data-driven, needing only a small amount of image-level labels to train.

Our method is based on a simple yet effective approach: we generate pseudo labels at the pixel level by aggregating predictions from multiple deep learning models, and then use these pseudo labels to train a convolutional neural network for pixel-level labelling.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on the VOC 2012 semantic segmentation benchmark, where we achieve a mIOU of 0.542 on the test set, compared to 0.441 with the baseline method.
Recent progress in wearable sensors and IoT technology enables the measurement of human-tool interactions in the workplace.
In this paper, we present an uncertainty-based human-in-the-loop system for industrial tool wear analysis.
We first design a wearable sensing module, which contains nine sensors, to measure the human-tool interaction simultaneously.
Then, we propose a tool wear analysis method based on the proposed sensing module.
The proposed method consists of four steps: measurement, preprocessing, feature extraction, and wear level estimation.
In the measurement step, we simultaneously collect tactile, acoustic, and motion data during the human-tool interaction.
In the preprocessing step, the collected data are preprocessed and fused to obtain a feature vector.
In the feature extraction step, the uncertainty of each feature is estimated using a novel deep learning architecture, namely the unified adaptive mechanism (UAM).
In the wear level estimation step, a support vector machine is utilized to estimate the wear level of the tool.
We evaluate the proposed method using two public datasets and a real-world experiment.
The experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

Recent progress in semantic segmentation largely benefited from large-scale labeled datasets and powerful models, which however are in short supply for medical image analysis, especially for domain-specific tasks like cardiac segmentation.
In this work, we exploit the power of teacher networks to alleviate the lack of labeled examples for training.
We propose a dual-teacher learning framework that integrates both intra-domain and inter-domain teachers.
The former refines the segmentation results within the same domain while the latter leverages labeled data from different domains.

To effectively combine the complementary information from both teachers, we introduce a confidence-weighted fusion strategy that flexibly weighs the teacher predictions based on their confidence levels.
We evaluate our method on the CAMELYON 2017 challenge dataset for cardiac segmentation, and achieve promising results compared to the state-of-the-art methods.
Our code and models are available at https://github.com/VITA-Group/Dual-Teacher.

We introduce Hyperbolic Neural Networks (HyNNs), a family of continuous neural networks based on hyperbolic geometry, and we prove that HyNNs with analytic activations are infinitely wide and hence fully convergent.
This answers in the affirmative an open question posed by Bengio et al.

Additionally, we derive an expression for the gradient of the loss function with respect to the weights, which lets us prove that gradients are bounded in norm by a constant independent of the network width; this result is asymptotically optimal.
We present an algorithm for training HyNNs, and show that the number of iterations required to converge is proportional to the network width to the power of −1.
Our experiments show that HyNNs perform competitively with state-of-the-art deep learning algorithms on a variety of benchmark tasks, such as image classification and sentiment analysis.

Semantic segmentation is a fundamental task in computer vision, with many applications in robotics and autonomous driving.
However, this task becomes considerably more challenging in adverse weather conditions, such as heavy rain, fog, or snow.
In this paper, we present a novel approach for robust semantic segmentation in such challenging scenarios.
We exploit the temporal dimension by using a video-sequence segmentation framework, which allows us to capture the dynamics of the scene and mitigate the adverse effects of weather conditions.
Our approach is based on a fast, yet effective segmentation algorithm that operates on video frames and produces a sequence of segment maps.
These maps are then processed to obtain a final segmentation output.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on the Cityscapes dataset, as well as on a new dataset we created to simulate adverse weather conditions.
Our experiments show that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance in terms of segmentation accuracy, even in the presence of heavy rain or fog.
Recent works have shown the benefit of using supervoxels for inference in segmentation models.
However, supervoxel inpainting, i.e., exactly inferring all supervoxels in an image, is still a costly task, prohibiting their use in self-supervised learning.
In this work, we instead propose a region-of-interest (ROI) guided approach for supervoxel inpainting, where we inpaint only the regions of interest within supervoxels.
We demonstrate that our proposed method can significantly reduce memory usage and speed up inference, enabling the use of supervoxels for self-supervised learning while retaining performance.
We further present a simple, yet effective approach for selecting regions of interest and discuss the trade-offs of our method.
Finally, we show that our proposed method, when used for self-supervised learning, either matches or significantly improves upon the state-of-the-art on four benchmarks.
Code is available at https://github.com/NVlabs/superviself.
Medical image segmentation is prone to label corruption, which poses a severe impediment to clinical deployment.

In this paper, we tackle the challenge of label corruption by learning a cross-denoising network (CDN) with a denoising branch and a correcting branch, aiming to restore clean labels for corrupted ones.

Specifically, the denoising branch leverages the inherent smoothness of segmentations to remove noise, while the correcting branch focuses on the dissimilarity between the corrupted labels and their denoised versions to correct them.

To effectively train the correcting branch, we introduce a domain shift adaptation module to align the distributions of uncorrupted and corrupted data, enabling the network to learn from both sources of data without leaking the clean labels to the corrupted side.

We evaluate our method on three public medical image segmentation benchmarks with different degrees of label noise (20%, 40%, and 60%), and demonstrate its effectiveness against existing state-of-the-art methods.
Code is available at https://github.com/VITA-Group/CDN.
In this paper, we present an effective 3D medical image segmentation method using elastic boundary projection.
Given a label image as input, our method estimates the gray level of the foreground object and then automatically detects the object boundary to separate it from the background.
Unlike the conventional techniques relying on accurate initialization, our method is capable of segmenting the object even when the initialization is far from the object boundary.

In particular, we estimate the gray level of the object using a robust weighted least square fitting between the observed image and the model image, where the weights are determined by the intensity similarity between the neighboring pixels.
Furthermore, the boundary of the object is detected by projecting the estimated gray level image onto the model boundary.
The proposed method has been evaluated on a number of 3D medical images obtained from real patients and it shows very promising results.
We introduce a simple and effective image segmentation approach called Super-BPD (Super Boundary-to-Pixel Direction), which achieves fast and almost linear runtime.
Given an image, our method first estimates pixel-level labels by a super-resolution network, and then predicts boundary-to-pixel direction (BPD) fields from the estimated labels.
The BPD fields are formulated as a sparse coding problem, which can be efficiently solved by modern optimization methods.
During the segmentation, we only need to perform a few iterations (less than 10) to achieve the results with promising quality.
Our approach is trained in a self-supervised manner, and able to run at almost linear speed, thus it is suitable for large-scale images.
In the experiment, we test our method on two public available datasets, and the results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach against other state-of-the-art segmentation approaches.
Traditional Methods Inspired Deep Neural Network for Edge Detection:

A Survey 1

Abstract

In this paper, we survey works that incorporate the ideas of traditional edge detection methods into deep neural networks for edge detection.

We categorize these methods into three categories: (1) methods that use pre-trained deep neural networks as feature extractors for traditional edge detection methods, (2) methods that combine deep neural networks and traditional edge detection methods to achieve better performance, and (3) methods that modify the architecture of deep neural networks to make them more suitable for edge detection.
We discuss the advantages and limitations of each approach and highlight open problems and future research directions.
