We propose a convex shape prior (CSP) for training deep neural networks (DNNs) to segment eye fundus images (EFIs).
CSP is implemented by constraining the output probability distribution of convolutional layers within a convex set, which is defined by the prior knowledge of the target objects' shapes.

Without introducing any extra cost or loss in the optimization objective, CSP encourages the learned representations to be aligned with our prior knowledge, which effectively suppresses the unwanted regions and helps to focus on the foreground, especially in the early stages of training.
In addition, the spatial extent of the foreground objects is constrained by CSP, which helps the model to learn more accurate localization.
The proposed method is evaluated on two public EFI segmentation benchmarks, and the experimental results show that the proposed method outperforms the state-of-the-art methods.
Recent works have shown that training deep neural networks (DNNs) for image segmentation from scratch can be very time-consuming due to the large amount of labels required for supervised learning.
In this paper, we show that pre-trained models, especially those trained on large-scale datasets like ImageNet, can be used as strong initializations for training deep segmentation models.
We propose a simple yet effective approach to fine-tuning pre-trained models for image segmentation.
Our method first applies an initial segmentation model to segment the images into super-pixels.
Then, a pre-trained model is fine-tuned using the segmented images.

Experiments on two public segmentation benchmarks, PASCAL VOC 2012 and Cityscapes, show that our approach can significantly speed up the training process while maintaining high quality segmentation results.
Our meta-learning initialization achieves the best single model performance among methods that use limited training data on the Cityscapes dataset.
Importance driven continual learning (IDCL) is a simple and effective method to train a model across domains.
Given a set of domains, IDCL trains a single model to perform a task such as segmentation, by alternating between source and target domains.
In each iteration, the model is first trained on the source domain with a sparse constraint on the target domain.

Then, the gradients are projected onto the target domain using an importance ratio, which is defined as the improvement in performance on the target domain divided by the decrease in performance on the source domain.
This ensures that the model is updated to perform well on both domains, while maintaining performance on the source domain.
Next, the model is fine-tuned on the target domain.
We apply IDCL to segment neuronal structures in electron microscopic images from different domains including different organisms, stain types, and imaging conditions.
Our results show that IDCL can effectively segment structures across domains, and that the importance ratio is a useful measure to compare the performance of a model on different domains.
Color image segmentation has always been an active research domain.
In this paper, a new approach for color image segmentation is proposed, which combines adaptive particle swarm optimization (APSO) with fuzzy C-means (FCM).
In the proposed approach, APSO is first used to optimize the initial centroid positions, and then FCM is applied to obtain the final segmentation.
The objective of APSO is to improve the initialization of FCM, so that FCM can converge faster and produce more accurate segmentation results.
In the experiment, the proposed approach is compared with other state-of-the-art color image segmentation methods.
The experimental results show the superiority of the proposed approach in terms of segmentation quality.

Recent advances in few-shot learning have achieved remarkable performance in image classification tasks, but have not been extensively explored for medical image segmentation, which is a fundamental but challenging task in medical imaging analysis.
In this paper, we present a semi-supervised few-shot learning approach for medical image segmentation.
Our approach is based on a novel few-shot learning framework that combines semi-supervised learning and few-shot learning, which we call semi-supervised few-shot learning.

We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on three public medical image segmentation benchmarks, and show that our approach outperforms the state-of-the-art in few-shot learning and semi-supervised learning.
Our approach has two main components.
The first component is a novel few-shot learning framework that combines semi-supervised learning and few-shot learning.
This framework utilizes a pre-trained model to extract features from the input images, and then uses a few-shot learning approach to train a new model based on these features.
The few-shot learning approach is based on the idea of transfer learning, which is a technique used to train a new model using a pre-trained model as a starting point.
The second component is a semi-supervised learning approach that is used to train the few-shot learning framework.
This approach utilizes a set of labeled and unlabeled images to train the model, and uses a semi-supervised learning technique to improve the model's performance on the labeled images.
The semi-supervised learning technique is based on the idea of self-training, which is a technique used to train a model using a set of labeled and unlabeled images.
We propose a fast fully octave convolutional neural network (FCN) for document image segmentation.
Our network dynamically scales the convolutional kernels by a factor of two between every two layers, which we refer to as octave convolution.
This approach reduces the parameters by a factor of two per layer and shrinks the computational cost, yet it does not reduce the receptive field of the network.
We evaluate our method on the publicly available ICDAR 2015 document image segmentation benchmark.
Our network achieves a higher accuracy with a significantly reduced computational cost compared to the state-of-the-art methods.
Our network also reduces the running time for training and testing by a factor of 2.1 and 3.4, respectively, compared to the second fastest method in the benchmark.
Recent works on perceptual parsing mainly focus on specific tasks or specific domains, such as scene parsing, object parsing, or person parsing.
These methods often utilize separate deep models to handle different tasks, which may result in low efficiency and redundant computations.
In this paper, we present a deep grouping model for unified perceptual parsing (DGMP).

DGMP introduces a novel pyramid grouping module (PGM) to effectively group and convey multi-scale contextual information, and a joint parsing and refining network (JPRN) to jointly parse and refine the predicted results.

Specifically, PGM can automatically group the interested regions and refine the grouped features within a single network architecture, which achieves multiple grouping behaviors with only one forward pass.
Furthermore, our JPRN can not only parse the whole image but also refine the predicted results, which further improves the performance.
Compared with state-of-the-art methods, DGMP can achieve better performance with a faster inference speed.
Deep learning is a promising method for tongue surface tracking from real-time ultrasound videos.
We present a simple yet effective method to train a deep neural network for tongue surface detection.
Unlike most previous methods that trace the contour of the tongue, our method detects the landmarks on the tongue surface.
It is more robust to the ambiguous contour around the tongue border in ultrasound videos, and it is more efficient in terms of computation and training data.
We evaluated our method on real-time ultrasound videos, and the experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach.
Our tongue surface detection network is based on a modified version of the popular Faster R-CNN [1] with additional novel improvements.
In the training phase, the network is optimized to classify each pixel on the ultrasound image as a tongue surface or background.
In the inference phase, the network outputs the full tongue surface as an assembly of point clouds.
The output points are then connected to form the tongue contour.
The whole process is performed in real-time with an average speed of 7.8 FPS on our test videos.
We consider the setting in which a classifier must be trained to classify instances of never-before-seen entities, using only a small number of noisy and incomplete labels for each entity.

We find that training on structured labels, where information is encoded in both the label text and in the label structure (through pointers to other related labels), significantly improves accuracy compared to training on plain text labels, and performs competitively with state-of-the-art performance on cleanly annotated data.
We present a variational model for image segmentation based on normalized cut with adaptive similarity and spatial regularization.
In contrast to previous works on normalized cut, we model the similarity between pixels by a continuous non-linear function, which is learnt from the data.
This allows us to capture more complex relationships between pixels.
To overcome the limitation of current segmentation techniques that only capture spatial regularity, we propose to use a spatial regularization term that enforces a smooth transition between segments.

The proposed method is compared with state-of-the-art image segmentation techniques on the Berkeley Segmentation Dataset and the MIT-CBCL face segmentation dataset, and experimental results show the effectiveness of the proposed method.
We address the problem of style transfer for portrait images, which transfers the style of an image (watermark) to a target image (portrait) while preserving the content of the portrait.
We propose to use a neural network to achieve this goal.
We employ an attention mechanism to align the content of the watermark and the portrait, and we use a style transfer algorithm to transfer the style of the watermark to the portrait.
Our approach achieves a good balance between the preservation of the content and the transfer of the style.
We evaluate our method using the portrait image database from PolyU, and the results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach.
Recent advances in deep learning have achieved remarkable performance in medical image segmentation.
However, these models usually demand a large amount of labeled data for superior performance, which is difficult to obtain in the medical field.
To overcome this challenge, we propose a novel multi-scale self-guided attention (MSA) module to enhance the performance of medical image segmentation models.
Our approach combines a multi-scale attention module and a self-guided attention module to capture the global and local features respectively.

The multi-scale attention module can capture the global context by aggregating the features at multiple scales, while the self-guided attention module can focus on the important regions by learning a weighting function.
We evaluate our approach on three public medical image segmentation benchmarks, and our method outperforms the state-of-the-art approaches.
The code is available at https://github.com/AI4MEDICAL/MSA-Net.
We propose an image segmentation approach based on deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) with spatial regularization, volume and star-shape priori for microscopic images of cells.

In our approach, a CNN architecture, which is composed of several convolutional layers with leaky ReLU activation functions and batch normalization layers between them, is first trained without any spatial regularization on a large number of labeled cells.

Then, the same network is fine-tuned with three different spatial regularization terms: (1) a volume prior that favors smooth predictions in the vicinity of cell boundaries, (2) a star-shape prior that encourages predictions to have star-shape boundaries and (3) a spatial regularization term that imposes a sparse and smooth constraint on the predictions.
The three regularization terms are combined via a weighted sum, where the weights are optimized during the fine-tuning phase.
We evaluate our method on the 2016 Miccai Cell Segmentation Challenge dataset and achieve promising results compared to the state-of-the-art methods.

We present a new framework for referring image segmentation, a task that aims to assign semantic labels to every pixel in an image while also providing a referring expression (e.g., “man with a guitar”) that describes the image region labeled.

Unlike prior work on referring image segmentation, which treats the referring expression generation as a natural language conditioning task, our framework directly models referring expressions using a neural graphics engine.
This engine reasons about what is being referred to in the image, and generates a referring expression as a by-product.
To effectively train our neural graphics engine, we propose a novel referring training target that encourages the model to produce referring expressions that are both accurate and concise.
We show that training on this target enforces the referring expression generation as a by-product of learning a good segmentation, even without any natural language conditioning.
Furthermore, to handle the referring expression generation, an architecture with a spatial pyramid structure and an LSTM module is proposed to capture the spatial and temporal contexts, respectively.
The proposed framework significantly improves over the state of the art on the ReferItSeg dataset, and produces referring expressions that are more human-like and concise.

We propose a volume-preserving image segmentation method that utilizes the entropic regularization optimal transport (EROT) to combine the region similarity and the volume preservation into a unified energy function.

The region similarity is measured by the Kullback-Leiber (KL) divergence between the region proposals and the ground truth, while the volume preservation term is formulated as a regularization term on the optimal transport plan.
The EROT method simultaneously optimizes the region similarity and volume preservation in a unified framework, which is different from the existing methods that tackle these two criteria separately.
The proposed method is applicable to both traditional watershed-based methods and deep learning-based methods.
We validate the proposed method on both synthetic and real-world images, and the experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.
We present a self-learning AI framework utilizing a generative adversarial network (GAN) for skin lesion image segmentation and classification.
Based on a large number of labeled images, a generative model is learned in an unsupervised manner to synthesize realistic skin lesion images.
Utilizing the generated images, we train a segmentation and classification model in a self-supervised manner.
We evaluate our framework on a public skin lesion image dataset.
The experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework in terms of segmentation and classification performance.
Our code is available at https://github.com/AI4Skin/skin_lesion_segmentation.

Deepfake refers to the phenomenon of maliciously manipulating multimedia contents, especially image and video data, using artificial intelligence techniques to impersonate a person doing or saying something they never did or said.
Detecting deepfake contents is of paramount importance to uphold the integrity of media communication.
In this paper, we focus on detecting forged facial expressions in still images, which is a fundamental yet challenging task.
We propose a novel approach to detect forged facial expressions using a separable convolutional neural network (SCNN) and image segmentation.
Our approach first extracts a compact feature vector from the input image using a deep convolutional neural network (DCNN).
Then, we apply image segmentation to extract the regions of interest (ROIs) from the input image.
The extracted ROIs are then classified using a shallow convolutional neural network (SHCN).
The proposed approach has been evaluated on a large dataset of images with forged facial expressions.
The experimental results show that our approach achieves a high detection accuracy with a low computational cost.
Recent progress in deep learning enabled the development of effective neural networks for image segmentation.
However, validating the performance of these models is challenging.
The most common practice is to use pixel-wise measures, such as the Intersection over Union (IoU).
Yet, these metrics are not capable of capturing the uncertainty of the predictions and, in particular, they do not provide confidence scores.
In this paper, we propose a novel way to produce valid p-values for image segmentation, which overcome these issues.
We employ a selective inference framework that is based on a robust probabilistic model.
Specifically, we model the uncertainty of the predictions obtained from a deep segmentation model via a Bayesian approach.
Then, we use selective inference to obtain valid p-values for the segmentation performance measure that is most commonly used, namely, the IoU.
We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach on two public segmentation benchmarks, while achieving significant improvements over the state-of-the-art.
Our code and models are available at this https URL.
Recent progress in image collage generation has largely focused on unconditional methods that apply random transformations to images, followed by optimization of a collage objective.

In this work, we revisit the paradigm of collage optimization and propose an approach that transforms image sets by attending to memory of previously seen images, while iteratively generating a collage.

We introduce a new memory-based loss that encourages the preservation of memorized image features in the generated collage, and a memory attentive loss that further enforces memorization of recent images.
Furthermore, we introduce a new dataset of image sets, where each set is composed of a guiding image and context images related to the same scene.

We show that our method, when applied to the generation of image collages from sets of images, either with or without the guiding image, consistently improves upon the state of the art in collage generation.
Our code is released at https://github.com/AI4Finance-Foundation/ImageCollage.
In this paper, we propose a method based on deep learning neural network to identify the cells' nuclei in the microscopic image.
The microscopic image is pre-processed to enhance the contrast and then the proposed method is used to detect the nuclei.
The proposed method is evaluated on a public dataset and the results show that it outperforms the state-of-the-art methods.

The pre-processing method is based on the local contrast enhancement algorithm which enhances the contrast of the microscopic image by comparing the intensity of each pixel with its neighboring pixels.
The proposed method is a multi-layer convolutional neural network which is trained on a large dataset of microscopic images with ground truth information.
The network takes a microscopic image as input and outputs a binary image where the pixels corresponding to the nuclei are labeled as 1 and the rest are labeled as 0.
The network is trained using backpropagation algorithm and the weights are updated using stochastic gradient descent.
The proposed method is evaluated on a public dataset of microscopic images called the Cell nuclei segmentation challenge dataset.
The results show that the proposed method outperforms the state-of-the-art methods in terms of accuracy and speed.
The proposed method is also able to handle noise and artifacts in the microscopic image better than the state-of-the-art methods.

We present a deep learning work flow for fast and robust segmentation of anatomical structures in CT images.
The network was trained on publicly available datasets with ground truth annotations for lung and spine.
Our network is based on a convolutional neural network architecture previously validated on the MIAS challenge.
We exploit existing clinically available delineations, which are used for treatment planning, for the initialization of the network.
The initializations are propagated through the network using a weighted vector flow scheme.
The proposed method has been validated on our institutional dataset and compared to a state-of-the-art semi-automatic segmentation tool used in our clinic.
The comparison showed good agreement between the automatic segmentations and the ground truth for all structures.
Average Dice coefficients of 98.1% and 97.8% were achieved for tumor and organs-at-risk, respectively.
Our approach led to a reduction of delineation time by 77% for tumors and 69% for organs-at-risk, while maintaining a similar quality of the delineations.
Abstract: Medical image segmentation plays a pivotal role in advanced healthcare applications enabling precise and non-invasive diagnosis.
Numerous approaches have been proposed for segmentation, with evaluation metrics such as Dice score (DS) and Jaccard index (JI) widely used to compare methods.
Surprisingly, there exists no systematic study on the optimization of these metrics.
In this study, we perform an in-depth analysis of DS and JI for medical image segmentation.
We first present a theoretical analysis establishing a tight connection between DS and JI, and then propose an optimization framework based on this connection.
We further provide an in-depth evaluation on a variety of real-world medical image segmentation tasks, where our optimization framework is applied.

Results show that the proposed optimization delivers significant improvements, with up to 13.7% increase in DS and 23.0% increase in JI, providing stronger baseline performance for future research on medical image segmentation.
Abstract: We introduce a novel approach for sleep staging based on deep learning, more specifically a fully convolutional network (FCN) for time series segmentation (TSM).
This method is able to produce a segmentation of a sleep record into successive non-overlapping sleep stages.

The novelty of our approach lies in the architecture of the FCN, which takes advantage of the temporal dependencies in the data by introducing a convolutional layer with stride 1, allowing the network to use a rolling window of inputs.
We evaluate our method on a publicly available dataset, obtaining an accuracy of 94.4%, outperforming the current state-of-the-art methods.
Recent works in scene parsing show that the multiphase level set method, which models image segmentation as a continuous evolution process, can achieve state-of-the-art performance.

However, these methods rely on heuristic criteria to merge segments, and do not explicitly model the relationships between the segments, which can limit their performance in the presence of ambiguous or incomplete labels.
In this paper, we propose a deep multiphase level set framework that combines the benefits of the level set method with deep learning.
Our framework explicitly models the relationships between the segments using a graph neural network, which guides the evolution process of the level set method.
We introduce a novel segmentation loss that combines the cross-entropy loss with an adversarial loss, which enables the model to learn from ambiguous or incomplete labels.
Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on the Cityscapes and CamVid datasets, and is able to generalize to new images in a way that other methods are not.
We propose a general framework for registering neural representations of objects.
Given a set of reference objects, we learn a mapping function that aligns a test object with the reference objects in feature space.
We apply our method to the image segmentation problem where the reference objects are segmentations of training images and the test object is a segmentation of a test image.
Our neural registration method is able to improve the accuracy of state-of-the-art segmentation methods on three public datasets.
We also demonstrate the general applicability of our framework by applying it to other computer vision problems, such as object recognition and scene understanding, and show improvements in accuracy.
Recent progress in synthesizing realistic images has boosted the development of numerous computer vision tasks, but most works require a clean target modality ground truth for training.
We introduce a new task, named synthetic segmentation, where the goal is to segment objects in a real-world image using only a synthetic image as reference.
This setting is appealing since it enables using large amounts of easily obtainable synthetic data to train models for real-world applications.
We build SynSeg-Net, a neural network architecture designed to tackle this new task.
It leverages a conditional recurrent network that conditions on the input image and a synthetic reference image to produce a segmentation mask.
We train and test our model on the challenging task of segmenting medical images, but our method is generic and can be applied to other domains.
Our experiments show that our method is able to accurately segment objects in real-world images using only synthetic references, without the need of target modality ground truth.

Recent progresses in convolutional neural network (CNN) elevate image-to-image (I2I) translation to a new horizon, but most existing methods require a large amount of labeled source images for training, which is difficult to obtain in many real-world applications.

In this paper, we attempt to address this issue by introducing a new I2I translation framework with extremely weak supervision, where only a few labeled source images and a large number of unlabeled source images are available for training.
In particular, we first train a teacher network with a few labeled source images to obtain pseudo labels for all source images.
Then, we learn a student network with the pseudo labels and the unlabeled source images for I2I translation.
To further improve the translation quality, we present a cycle-consistent loss to enhance the learning of the student network.
Finally, we evaluate our method on the Cityscapes dataset for urban scene understanding, and experimental results show the effectiveness of our method.
We revisit the Mumford-Shah functional for image segmentation, and introduce a continuous version of the energy functional that enables the use of deep learning architectures.

We build upon recent progress in the field of geometric deep learning, and construct a supervised loss functional that is suitable for learning piecewise constant mappings in a setting where the ground truth segmentation is available.

When training our model, we minimize a reformulation of the Mumford-Shah energy that is suitable for deep learning, and introduce a strategy to mitigate the lack of differentiability of the data term.
We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach on a public available dataset, showing that our approach can recover the ground truth segmentations.
Recent works on video segmentation commonly formulate the problem as a per-frame segmentation followed by a temporal aggregation, which discards important temporal information.
In this work, we exploit the temporal coherence among video frames to improve the semi-supervised video segmentation.
We propose a novel temporal coherence constraint, which regularizes the segmentation predictions across consecutive frames.
Furthermore, in order to effectively utilize the abundant unlabeled data, we propose a novel edge-conditioned prototype learning framework to enhance the quality of the segmentation prototypes.

Specifically, we train a classifier to predict edge presence based on the low-level features of the video frames, and then use the predicted edge maps to selectively update the segmentation prototypes.
Extensive experiments on DAVIS 2016 and DAVIS 2017 validate the effectiveness of our approach compared to the state-of-the-art methods.

Recent works on pixel-level segmentation either rely on strong annotations such as pixel-wise labels or bounding box annotations, or assume that the segments of interest occupy a relatively large proportion of the image.
We introduce a new framework for weakly-supervised segmentation of small segments without requiring pixel-wise annotations.
Our key insight is to use a new variant of the popular Scan statistic that we name Scan-Dynamic.

This new variant is based on a dynamic programming approach that iteratively contracts and expands a segment, and uses the statistical significance of the change in intensity value at the boundary of adjacent segments as a criterion for segmenting.
We show that this criterion is able to correctly identify the segments in weakly-supervised fashion, and that our method generalizes well to different segmentation tasks.
We implement this end-to-end system, evaluate it on the publicly available VASC- Segment dataset, and show that our method outperforms the state of the art in terms of F1-score on small segments.

Recent works on visual localization have shown that the direct use of segmentation masks for localization, trained on large-scale datasets like Cityscapes and CamVid, improves localization performance.

However, these segmentation masks are typically obtained by training networks on coarse object-level classes, which results in poor localization performance in regions where objects overlap or occlude each other.
In this paper, we show that using fine-grained segmentation networks for localization yields significant improvements in accuracy.
We introduce a new dataset, called SceneCrafter, which includes fine-grained segmentation masks for training and evaluate our method on the KITTI dataset.
Our network learns to predict fine-grained segmentation masks purely from the image, without any ground truth segmentation information.

In addition, we introduce a new loss function for fine-grained segmentation, which we call the coverage loss, that encourages the network to predict masks that cover most of the object instances in a given image.
Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on both the segmentation and localization benchmarks.
Conv-MCD: A Plug-and-Play Multi-task Module for Medical Image Segmentation.
In this paper, we introduce a simple yet effective plug-and-play module for joint segmentation of anatomical structures in medical images, which we call Conv-MCD.
Our module is built upon a basic convolutional neural network (CNN) architecture, where we replace the last few layers with our proposed Conv-MCD layer.
This layer computes consensus outputs among the individual structures in an image, while still retaining the ability to predict the probabilities of the structures jointly.

We show that our method, with a properly chosen margin loss, is able to produce competitive results for different medical image segmentation tasks, compared to other state-of-the-art multi-task learning methods, while requiring minimal tuning.

We evaluate our method on four different medical image segmentation datasets of different modalities (CT, MRI, and Micro-CT) and show its effectiveness in both single-structure and multi-structure segmentation.
Recent works have shown that the attention mechanism can be applied to convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to improve performance on image recognition tasks.

We observe that these works mostly focus on applying attention mechanism within the last few layers of CNNs, where the spatial dimensions of the feature maps are already very small, and the attention mechanism can effectively "attend" to the most important features.
However, in the early layers of CNNs where the feature maps are still very large, the attention mechanism is often not effective, as there are simply too many positions for the attention to focus on.
In this work, we propose a simple and effective approach to overcome this limitation.
We introduce a new type of layer that we call the "AttentionBoost" layer, which works by combining the feature maps from the previous layer with the attention maps generated by a single-layer CNN.
This allows the attention mechanism to effectively attend to the most important features in the early layers of the network, even when the feature maps are very large.
Our experimental results on the CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 datasets show that our approach can improve the performance of CNNs by a large margin.
Our approach is simple to use and effective, and can be easily applied to existing CNN architectures.
Recent progress in semantic segmentation mainly focuses on accurately modeling the underlying object structures in images, while the quality of the training data is often overlooked.
Noisy annotations present in practice, however, may deteriorate the performance of the segmenters and hinder their generalization.
In this paper, we aim to develop a simple yet effective automatic quality evaluation (QE) framework for noisy-labeled image segmentation, which can benefit both model training and result filtering.
We find that the recently proposed Pick-and-Pack network
[1] for segmenting objects with complex shapes is particularly suitable for QE due to its voxel-wise confidence output.
We build upon it to formulate a QE framework, named Pick-and-Learn, which consists of two stages.
Given a pre-trained network, we first apply Pick-and-Pack on the training data to obtain initial predictions.
Then, we treat these initial predictions as noisy labels and fine-tune the network in an unsupervised learning manner, which we refer to as self-supervised learning.
Specifically, we minimize the disagreement between the segmentation results and the initial predictions on the training data.
We find that the fine-tuned network can effectively evaluate the quality of the initial predictions, and moreover, the segmentation results on the test data.
We evaluate Pick-and-Learn on two public noisy-label segmentation benchmarks, and achieve promising results compared to the state-of-the-art QE methods.
Recent progresses in medical imaging acquisition technology have resulted in a dramatic increase of image size, posing severe challenges to existing model-based segmentation methods.
Existing work usually downsamples the data to manageable size, resulting in important details being lost.
In this paper, we propose ET-Net, a generic edge-attention guidance network for medical image segmentation that is capable of handling large images at full resolution.
ET-Net separates the learning of easy and hard information, the former being captured by a series of edge-attention modules and the latter by a guidance network.

Specifically, the edge-attention modules can capture the object edge information and texture information effectively, while the guidance network focuses on learning the complex and ambiguous information.

We apply ET-Net to three different segmentation tasks, and experimental results on three public benchmarks, includingLiver Tumor, Pancreas Tumor and Prostate, demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach compared to the state-of-the-art.

We present a spatiotemporal convolutional neural network (3D CNN) for action/object segmentation in video, which is efficient in terms of computational complexity and able to achieve real-time performance.
Our approach leverages 3D convolutional kernels that operate directly on video frames, without the need for object proposals or temporal pooling.
We introduce a new 3D convolutional layer, which enables our network to effectively capture spatial and temporal information, and a multi-scale training strategy to improve the network's performance.
Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on the YouTube-Object Segmentation dataset and is efficient enough to achieve real-time performance on a modern CPU.
Code is available at https://github.com/yxgeee/Realtime-Object-Segmentation.
In this paper, we present an efficient traversability analysis approach for autonomous terrain vehicles using stereo vision.
In order to perform real-time analysis of the terrain, we employ a stereo-based approach, where the terrain surface is reconstructed from the stereo pair using semi-global matching (SGM).
The reconstructed surface is then segmented into traversable and non-traversable regions using a normal-based segmentation algorithm.
To further improve the accuracy of the segmentation, we then analyze the superpixel surface of the reconstructed 3D terrain.
Finally, we employ a machine learning approach to train a classifier for the traversability analysis.
The experimental results, conducted on different datasets, show that our proposed approach can achieve accurate and efficient traversability analysis for autonomous terrain vehicles.
Deep learning techniques have demonstrated state-of-the-art performance in various image processing tasks, particularly in image segmentation.
However, despite their success, these techniques often struggle with segmenting images in a way that aligns with human intuition and expectations.
In this paper, we aim to understand why deep learning techniques sometimes fail to produce acceptable results in image segmentation.
We investigate the reasons for this gap between machine and human performance by comparing the decisions made by state-of-the-art deep learning models with human judgments.
We find that deep learning models often struggle with segmenting objects that are visually similar to their surroundings, and with handling object boundaries that are not well defined in the image.
To address these issues, we propose a number of modifications to deep learning architectures and training procedures that improve performance on these challenging segments.

Our proposed methods focus on enhancing the representation learning capabilities of deep learning models, improving their ability to reason about object context and relationships, and making them more robust to variations in object appearance and boundary ambiguity.

We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approaches on a variety of image segmentation tasks, and show that our methods can significantly improve the performance of deep learning models in these cases.
We present a general framework for image segmentation based on complex networks.
Our approach leverages the inherent relationships between pixels in an image to segment it into objects.
These relationships are captured by a graph, where each pixel is a node and the edges capture the local pixel similarities.
The segmentation is performed by first learning a complex network from the pixel graph, and then partitioning the complex network into segments using a spectral clustering approach.
We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach on three different image segmentation datasets, showing that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance.

A new method for learning dehazing models is proposed based on the observation that the haze-free image can be generated by two different processes: restoration and separation.

The proposed method learns a dehazing model by minimizing the difference between the predicted haze-free image and the ground truth image, where the ground truth image is obtained by combining the restoration and separation processes.

The proposed method can also be used to learn a dehazing model for a specific image, where the specific image is used as the ground truth image.
This allows the method to learn a dehazing model that is tailored to the specific image and can improve the performance of segmentation tasks on that image.

In this paper, we propose a method for patching and aggregating predictions on image regions using fully convolutional networks (FCNs) with skip connections.

We demonstrate the performance of our approach on retinal image segmentation, but it can be applied to any other image segmentation task.
In particular, when tested on the DRIVE dataset, our approach achieves a mean accuracy of 95.43% on the pixel level and 94.10% on the region level.
Skin lesion segmentation is an important yet challenging task in medical image analysis.
We present an approach to handle inter-annotator agreement (IAA) for automated skin lesion segmentation.
Our approach is based on a fully-automated system that segments skin lesions in clinical images.
We use a deep learning architecture, called U-Net, to achieve state-of-the-art performance on the task.
To handle IAA, we propose to use a ensemble of segmentation models trained on different subsets of the available training data.
The proposed approach is evaluated on a large dataset of clinical images and compared to a single model trained on the full dataset.
Results show that the ensemble approach significantly improves performance in terms of agreement with ground truth segmentation.
Furthermore, the proposed ensemble approach shows excellent agreement with expert annotations, with a Cohen's kappa coefficient of 0.85.
This agreement is comparable to that between experts, and indicates that the proposed approach is suitable for use in clinical practice.
Recent progress in deep learning has enabled the development of effective models for remote sensing imagery semantic segmentation.
However, these models often suffer from boundary loss, which can lead to inaccurate results and hinder their performance in real-world applications.
In this paper, we investigate the boundary loss problem and propose a novel approach to address it.
Our approach consists of a boundary-aware loss function that explicitly considers the boundary regions during training.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on two public remote sensing imagery semantic segmentation benchmarks, and achieve state-of-the-art performance.
Our code and model weights are publicly available.

Abstract:
We study diversity in machine learning, a topic that has been largely ignored by the research community.
Diversity is a key concept in machine learning, as it refers to the ability of a machine learning model to generalize well to new and unseen data.
We define diversity in machine learning and study its impact on the performance of machine learning models.
We find that increasing diversity in machine learning can improve the performance of machine learning models, and we present techniques for increasing diversity in machine learning.
We hope that our work will encourage further research into this important topic.

We present a method for the semantic segmentation of video sequences using convolutional LSTM networks.
Our approach employs a hybrid convolutional and recurrent architecture that models both appearance and motion dynamics over time.
We introduce a novel temporal max-pooling layer, which enables the network to selectively focus on the most relevant information while being invariant to input order.
Our method naturally handles variable-length inputs and is applicable to arbitrary video durations.
We evaluate our approach on the CamVid dataset and show that our model outperforms the state of the art in semantic video segmentation.
Our approach to semantic segmentation of video sequences is based on a hybrid convolutional and recurrent architecture that models both appearance and motion dynamics over time.

The model is composed of a stack of convolutional LSTM layers, followed by a spatial max-pooling layer to reduce the spatial dimensions of the feature maps, and a final fully connected layer to produce a segmentation map.
The use of max-pooling, rather than average pooling, allows the model to be more robust to noise and outliers in the input data.

To handle the variability in video duration, we introduce a novel temporal max-pooling layer that enables the network to selectively focus on the most relevant information while being invariant to input order.
This layer max-pools over the input sequence, producing a fixed-length representation that can be processed by the subsequent layers.
Because the temporal max-pooling layer effectively downsamples the sequence, the network can be trained on shorter sequences and then applied to longer ones without loss of performance.
We evaluate our approach on the CamVid dataset, which consists of videos of urban scenes recorded by a moving camera.
Our model outperforms the state of the art in semantic video segmentation, and achieves a mIOU of 92.1% on the CamVid test set.
Further, our model is able to generalize to videos of different lengths, demonstrating the effectiveness of our temporal max-pooling layer.
We also show that our model is able to learn meaningful representations of video sequences, which can be used for a variety of tasks such as video summarization and prediction of future frames.
We present a novel approach for cardiac cine MR image segmentation based on a distance map regularized convolutional neural network (DRM-CNN).
Our method combines the advantages of both semantic and instance segmentation techniques to achieve robust and accurate segmentation of the left ventricle (LV) cavity in cardiac cine MR images.
The distance map regularization helps to enforce spatial consistency in the segmentation output, while the CNN learns the underlying anatomical structures and their variations from the training data.
We evaluate our method on the publicly available MICCAI 2012 cardiac segmentation challenge dataset and show that it achieves state-of-the-art performance in terms of both accuracy and speed.
Furthermore, our method is able to segment the LV cavity in a fully automatic manner, without any user interaction or prior knowledge of the image content.
Recent results on semantic segmentation could be leveraged to develop automated tissue analysis for pathology.

However, the limited field-of-view of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) trained on natural images restricts the use of these methods in pathology, where whole slide images are large and have an extremely wide field-of-view.

We overcome this limitation by (1) employing an adaptive weighting approach to effectively utilize multi-field-of-view CNNs and (2) proposing a multi-field-of-view encoder-decoder architecture that is suitable for semantic segmentation on whole slide images.
We demonstrate that our approach yields state-of-the-art performance on two public pathology datasets with significant field-of-view coverage.

Recent developments in imaging medicine have led to a significant increase in the size of 3D medical images, posing a great challenge for efficient transmission, storage and segmentation in the clouds.
In this paper, we propose a machine vision guided 3D medical image compression approach to address this issue.
Our method leverages the power of deep learning to learn a compression model directly from the images, which is trained using a large number of images collected from clinical studies.
The compression model is designed to take into account the specific characteristics of medical images, such as their typically low entropy and the need for precise segmentation.

We evaluate our method on a large dataset of real clinical images and demonstrate that it achieves a significant reduction in the file size while maintaining high quality and enabling accurate segmentation in the clouds.
Our method can be seamlessly integrated into the existing workflow of medical imaging and has the potential to significantly reduce the storage and transmission costs of 3D medical images.
