Auto-DeepLab: Hierarchical Neural Architecture Search for

Semantic Image Segmentation

Abstract:

Semantic image segmentation, which aims to assign semantic labels to every pixel in an image, is a fundamental task in computer vision.
Recently, hierarchical architectures have demonstrated promising performance for the task.
However, designing such architectures manually is highly challenging.

In this work, we present a learnable hierarchical architecture search framework, named as Auto-DeepLab, which aims to automatically find a hierarchical architecture with promising performance for semantic image segmentation.
Specifically, we first introduce a hierarchical architecture search space, which is learned from a set of pre-trained models.
Then, a genetic algorithm is employed to search for the best architecture within the search space.
Finally, the discovered architecture is fine-tuned for semantic image segmentation on the Cityscapes dataset, and the results demonstrate the effectiveness of our method.
We propose an image generation model that generates vehicle images based on rough sketches of the vehicle and its surroundings.
In the training process, we use a unit of rectangular patches to simulate the rough sketches.
We also propose an adaptive loss function that assigns different weights to the well-drawn and poorly-drawn patches according to the style strength of the input sketch.
This model shows promising results in generating vehicle images that suit the surroundings.
Abnormal brain anatomy, such as congenital anomalies, may have an impact on the cerebral blood circulation, in particular, the DSC perfusion MR measurements.
In this paper, we present a method to correct for the effect of abnormal anatomy.
The method is based on the CUSUM filter, which has been successfully used for noise filtering in MR images.
The CUSUM filter is applied to the DSC perfusion MR head scans to improve the segmentation of the brain.

The method has been tested on a patient with congenital anomaly, and the results show that the CUSUM filter can improve the brain segmentation in DSC perfusion MR head scans with abnormal brain anatomy.
The procedure of the CUSUM filter for brain segmentation on DSC perfusion MR head scans is as follows.
First, the DSC perfusion MR head scan is obtained from the patient.
The CUSUM filter is then applied to the DSC perfusion MR head scan to improve the segmentation of the brain.
The CUSUM filter is designed to remove the noise and artifacts in the DSC perfusion MR head scan, and to enhance the edges and contours of the brain.
The resulting image is then segmented using a standard brain segmentation algorithm.
The segmented image is then compared to the original DSC perfusion MR head scan, and the differences between the two images are used to improve the segmentation of the brain.
We present an efficient, fully-automated and interactive system for segmenting medical images through deep learning.
Our system is based on fully convolutional neural networks (FCN), which enable efficient inference on entire slides with high throughput.

Unlike existing FCN-based approaches, which rely on pre-defined network architectures and training protocols, we introduce an adaptive architecture that dynamically varies across tiles within each slide.
This allows our system to achieve better segmentation performance by leveraging local information, and results in better utilization of computational resources during inference.
We employ a tile-based processing paradigm that can effectively utilize modern GPU memory, and show that our method achieves real-time performance on slides with sizes up to 512^2 pixels.
In a user study, we show that our interactive segmentation method achieves higher accuracy and faster performance compared to a state-of-the-art automated method.
We open source our code.

We propose a novel, deep learning-based approach to segment multiple objects in 3D that are defined on multiple surfaces (i.e., cartilage, bone, and meniscus) from knee magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans taken over time (4D).
This approach is designed to address the challenges associated with the complex and variable appearance of these objects across patients and time.
We introduce a cost function that is trained using a supervised learning approach on a small set of manually segmented training images.

The cost function is designed to segment all objects on all surfaces and is composed of a series of independently trained deep neural networks that operate on different image slices and different objects.

We apply our method to segmentation of cartilage, bone, and meniscus across ten surfaces (i.e., the inner and outer cartilage and bone layers of the femur and tibia) from the Osteoarthritis Initiative, a public-access dataset of knee MRI scans.
We compare our method to a state-of-the-art, manual segmentation approach and find that our method is both faster and more accurate.
We present a hybrid approach to left atrium segmentation in cardiac MR images.
Our method combines global shape modeling, which we derive using a mixture model (MM) of left atrium shapes, and local intensity modeling, represented by a deep convolutional autoencoder (AA).
Intensity features are extracted from the autoencoder's encoder layer and combined with the MM-based shape prior.
We introduce an energy function that combines the global shape prior with the local intensity prior in a data-driven manner.
We optimize the energy function using graph cuts.

The proposed method was validated on 100 synthetic and 55 clinical MR images and compared to 16 state-of-the-art methods on the MICCAI 2018 Challenge on Mitral Valve and Left Atrium Segmentation and Labeling (MVLA).
Our method achieved second place in the segmentation track and fourth place in the labeling track.
We present HyperDense-Net, a densely connected Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) for multi-modal image segmentation.
It leverages recent advances in CNN architecture design to achieve state-of-the-art performance on the 2015 Multi-Modal Brain Tumor Segmentation (BraTS) Challenge.

A novel feature of our approach is its use of a densely connected CNN architecture, whereby each layer in the network is connected to every other layer, rather than just the immediately preceding layer.
This allows the network to learn complex, hierarchical representations of the input data, which proved critical for performance on the BraTS 2015 dataset.
We evaluate our approach on the BraTS 2015 validation and test datasets and achieve a weighted intersection over union (IoU) of 0.8314 and 0.7981, respectively, ranking first in the challenge.
Code and models are available at https://github.com/HyperDense-Net/HyperDense-Net.
We present an approach for dense 3D visual mapping of indoor scenes.
We aim at building a compact 3D model of the environment that replaces the original photometric and geometric texture with a simplified yet semantically coherent one.
In this way, our model is able to capture the intrinsic organization and structure of the scene, producing a coherent and recognizable 3D map.
To achieve this, we start by learning an overcomplete dictionary of atoms via sparse coding, i.e., finding the best low-dimensional representation of the training data.
Atoms are synthesized by combining a set of pre-defined 3D geometric primitives that are learned from the dataset.
In order to enforce semantic coherence, we then optimize the dictionary atoms to conform to the scene structure, leveraging on a dense 3D reconstruction of the environment.
The final 3D map is obtained by densely projecting the optimized atoms onto the scene surfaces.
In order to evaluate the performance of our approach, we compare it to other state-of-the-art methods on two public benchmarks, and analyze the statistical properties of the learned dictionaries.
Brain MRI segmentation is a fundamental step in clinical MRI analysis.
However, manual segmentation is tedious and time consuming, while automatic segmentation is challenging due to the large variation in brain morphology and image quality.
In this paper, we present a rule-based hybrid approach for brain MRI segmentation that integrates both automatic and manual segmentation methods.
Our approach combines the advantages of both methods to achieve accurate and efficient segmentation.
In particular, we use a rule-based approach to automatically segment the brain, and we use a manual segmentation method to refine the automatic segmentation results.
The automatic segmentation is based on a set of rules that use brain morphology and image quality to determine the segmentation.
The manual segmentation is based on a set of editing tools that allow the user to refine the automatic segmentation results.
We evaluated our approach on a dataset of 20 MRI scans, and our results show that our approach is accurate and efficient.
Our approach achieved an average segmentation accuracy of 92%, and our average editing time was 6 minutes per scan.
We present a novel framework for learning to segment neurons in 3D electron microscopy images.
Our approach is based on a metric graph learned by a convolutional neural network (CNN) from synthetic training images.
During training, the CNN is taught to generate simulated images from a metric graph, which encapsulates the spatial relationships between neurons.
Given a new image, our method estimates a metric graph that captures the local geometric structure of neuron branches.
This graph is then searched to find the optimal segmentation.
We show that the proposed approach is effective in segmenting neurons, even in challenging cases where other state-of-the-art methods fail.
Our code and models are available at https://github.com/shenwanz/EM-Segmentation-Metric-Graph.
We present a deep learning framework for joint shape learning and segmentation of medical images.
Our method leverages a minimalistic deep network architecture that is low-cost in memory and computational requirements, making it suitable for clinical deployment.
We introduce a novel shape prior encoded into the network via a shape-conditioned loss function that promotes consistent object boundaries across image slices.
Furthermore, our method combines expert-labeled and self-supervised shape priors into a single framework to overcome the limited availability of expert-labeled training data.
We demonstrate the efficacy of our method on the problem of left-atrium segmentation from cardiac MR images.
In comparison to related methods, our approach achieves a significantly higher segmentation quality while maintaining a low computational cost.
Code is available at https://github.com/Radiology-ICU/ShapeSeg.
Recent advances in deep neural networks have achieved significant performance in biomedical image segmentation.
However, these models are data-hungry and require a large amount of labeled examples for training, which are difficult to obtain in the biomedical field due to the high cost of expert annotation.

In this paper, we propose a universal decoding method, called Cascade Decoder, for training data-efficient segmentation models that can be applied to any image domain with only a few annotated examples.

Cascade Decoder first utilizes a set of pre-trained decoders to extract features from the input image, and then learns a new decoder to refine the predictions based on the segmented images and their annotations.
By cascading the decoders in a coarse-to-fine fashion, our method can effectively leverage both the global and local information in the image to achieve segmentation.

We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on three different image segmentation tasks: tumor cell segmentation from confocal images, neuron segmentation from electron microscopic images, and white matter fiber tract segmentation from T1-weighted MRI images, with only 10%, 4% and 0.5% of the images in the training set, respectively.
Our method achieves comparable performance to the state-of-the-art while using only a fraction of the labeled data.
We explore the use of retrained off-the-shelf (OTS) deep neural networks for image segmentation in iris recognition.
We train two segmentation networks, a U-Net and a Mask R-CNN, from scratch to segment iris images.
Then we retrain both networks with ImageNet pre-trained weights.
We use the segmented images to localize the iris and then recognize the iris using a pre-trained deep neural network.
Our method achieves an accuracy of 97.53% on CASIA-Iris-VI database with SIFT as the feature extractor.
In this paper, we propose a novel holistic decomposition convolution (HDC) for effective semantic segmentation of 3D MR images.
Our approach is designed to explicitly exploit the structural information of MR images via a novel convolution operation that we refer to as holistic decomposition convolution.
Specifically, we decompose the 3D MR image into a set of 2D patches, and then we apply a convolution operation to the patches while maintaining the spatial structure of the original image.

Our experiments on the CamVid and Cityscapes datasets show that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance in 3D MR image semantic segmentation, outperforming other approaches in both accuracy and efficiency.
Recent progress in interactive segmentation largely focuses on proposing sophisticated interfaces to enable users to generate precise seeds for the subsequent segmentation.
However, it remains a challenging task for non-professional users to design effective seeds.
In this paper, we present SwipeCut, a novel interactive segmentation method that actively utilizes diversified seed proposals to ease the burden on users.

Given a sparse initialization, our method iteratively refines the segmentation results by densely sampling a set of candidate seeds from the proposal pool and propagating them using a learned diffusion model.
Specifically, we generate a collection of seed proposals via a simple yet effective kerneling method that combines a segmentation mask with appearance and geometry features.
At each iteration, we select a subset of proposals to guide the diffusion process and encourage exploration of diverse regions by explicitly modeling the proposal diversity.
Furthermore, we present an adaptive refinement module to improve the quality of the candidate seeds, making them more applicable for the subsequent segmentation.
Our method significantly outperforms the state-of-the-art on the interactive segmentation benchmark, even when the number of iterations is limited to only a few.

We present a fast computation of the matrix-vector products involving the graph Laplacian of fully connected networks by combining two techniques: the Non-Uniform FFT (NFFT) for graph signals and Krylov methods for linear systems.
The NFFT allows us to express the graph Laplacian in terms of a discrete convolution operator on the frequency domain, for which efficient matrix-vector products can be performed via FFT.
The method relies on the choice of a suitable basis for the vector space of graph signals; we propose to use the basis of Krylov subspace methods for linear systems as this basis.

We show that if the network is sparse (has a low density of edges), the proposed method is faster than the standard convolution technique, while being of the same order of magnitude when the network is dense.
We finally discuss the potential of our method for solving sparse inverse problems on graphs.
We present an approach for exclusive independent probability (EIP) estimation from intensively sampled imagery data.

Our specific application is brain region segmentation from IsoIntense infant brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), where the goal is to accurately estimate the joint probability of labeled regions given the image, while ensuring that the estimated probabilities are mutually exclusive and independent.

Our key insight is that densely connected fully convolutional neural networks (FC-DNNs), with a suitable architecture and training scheme, can perform EIP estimation, as measured by the Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC).
We achieve this by modifying a recent state-of-the-art FC-DNN architecture to estimate eight brain regions in infant brain MRI.
We train our network using a recently proposed consistency loss, which enforces explicitly the EIP property during training.
We show that our approach compares favorably with state-of-the-art methods, while providing explicit probabilities for each class, which can be used for assessing the uncertainty of the segmentation.
Brain tumor segmentation and classification is a crucial task in medical imaging analysis to diagnose and treat brain tumors.
We propose an ensemble of 3D U-Nets (3D UNets) to segment and classify brain tumors on magnetic resonance (MR) images.
Our method segments the tumor into three classes: tumor core, tumor mantle, and healthy tissue.
The ensemble combines the outputs of multiple 3D U-Nets, each trained on a different slice of the MR image.
The ensemble approach enables the network to utilize information from multiple slices, improving performance compared to a single 3D U-Net.
In addition, we propose a new radiomic feature for overall survival (OS) prediction based on the tumor segmentation.
This feature utilizes the information of the tumor core and tumor mantle to calculate the tumor volume and tumor doubling time.
The proposed feature shows promising results on the OS prediction task.
We present a simple and efficient foreground clustering approach for joint segmentation and localization of objects in videos and images.
Our method leverages the prior knowledge of object geometry and motion to achieve robust and accurate results.
Given a set of initial segmentations, our approach iteratively refines the segmentations and localization by clustering the foreground regions in a joint spatial-temporal space.
We introduce a novel distance measure that considers both the spatial and temporal coherence of the pixels.
This allows us to efficiently handle objects that exhibit complex shapes, appearances, and motions.

We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on a variety of challenging video and image sequences, and show that our method compares favorably to the state-of-the-art in terms of accuracy and efficiency.
Abstract: Medical image segmentation plays a crucial role in the computer aided diagnosis and treatment.
In this paper, we propose a hybrid deep learning network called RA-UNet to extract liver and tumor in CT scans.
The proposed network consists of a U-Net based architecture integrated with attention mechanism and relevance aggregation (RA) module.
The RA module is designed to capture the global and local information and it can be trained end-to-end jointly with the U-Net.
We evaluate our method on two public available CT scan datasets: LiTS and Tumor Segmentation Challenge (TSC) 2018.
The experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in terms of precision, recall and F1-score.
Furthermore, a comprehensive comparison between our method and other state-of-the-art methods on LiTS is presented.
Our code and models are available at: https://github.com/RuiChen16/RA-UNet.
We present a fast graph-cut based optimization method for dense deformable registration of volume images.
Our method is built upon a unified framework that optimally integrates motion estimation, interpolation, and gradient-based optimization.
We utilize a B-spline kernel with a learned shape-dependent grid to achieve both flexibility and efficiency.
Furthermore, we propose a new dense deformation vector field (DDF) initialization strategy that is suitable for 3D volumes.
Our method can efficiently handle large datasets, such as cardiac images with approximately 10000 volumes, with a registration speed of about 1.4 seconds per volume.
We validate our method on the recently released Cardiac Atlas, showing improved accuracy over the state-of-the-art.
Code is available at: https://github.com/VitalCore/DDF-Registration.

Recent advances in medical imaging technology have resulted in a vast amount of labeled medical images from different domains, posing challenges for traditional medical image analysis approaches that are designed to specific domains.
In this paper, we present a novel unsupervised domain adaptation framework for medical image segmentation.
It selectively adapts the source domain (e.g., CT) to the target domain (e.g., MRI) by leveraging the structural similarity between the domains and the similarity in the annotations of the images.
Specifically, we propose to optimize an objective function that minimizes the segmentation error on the target domain while keeping the structural similarity between the source and target domains.
The proposed method is evaluated on four different public available abdominal organ segmentation datasets (CT and MRI) with different sizes.
The experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method compared to the state-of-the-art approaches.
We present a fully convolutional two-stream fusion network (TCN) for real-time interactive image segmentation.
The TCN is designed to leverage the benefits of both feed-forward and recurrent neural networks while avoiding their limitations.
Our network is composed of two streams: a feed-forward convolutional neural network (CNN) stream and a recurrent convolutional neural network (RCNN) stream.
The CNN stream provides initial segmentation results, which are refined by the RCNN stream in a coarse-to-fine fashion.
The two streams are combined at the feature level using a concatenation layer, which allows the network to leverage the strengths of both streams and improve the segmentation performance.
We evaluate the TCN on the interactive image segmentation benchmark ISBI 2017 and achieve competitive results with state-of-the-art methods.
Our network is implemented using the TensorFlow library and can run in real-time on a modern GPU.
Code is available at: https://github.com/yzslzz/TCN.
In this paper, we present an effective cloud detection and segmentation algorithm for satellite imagery based on a gradient-based approach.
Our algorithm utilizes the gradient information of the input image to detect and segment clouds, and is capable of handling both bright and dark clouds.
We apply our algorithm to the PERSIANN-CCS dataset, which consists of satellite images labeled with ground truth information, and evaluate its performance against the current state-of-the-art method.
Our results show that our algorithm significantly improves the cloud detection and segmentation performance, resulting in an F1-score of 0.8519 and a precision of 0.8279.
Our algorithm consists of three main steps: gradient computation, gradient-based filtering, and post-processing.
The gradient computation step calculates the gradient information of the input image, which is then used in the gradient-based filtering step to detect and segment clouds.
The post-processing step refines the cloud segments and removes small false positives.
We evaluate our algorithm using the PERSIANN-CCS dataset, which consists of satellite images labeled with ground truth information about the presence and location of clouds.
Our results show that our algorithm achieves an F1-score of 0.8519 and a precision of 0.8279, outperforming the current state-of-the-art method.
Our work demonstrates the effectiveness of using a gradient-based approach for cloud detection and segmentation in satellite imagery.
By utilizing the gradient information of the input image, our algorithm is able to detect and segment clouds with high accuracy and efficiency.

We believe that our algorithm has the potential to improve the performance of cloud detection and segmentation in satellite imagery, and can be applied to a wide range of applications such as cloud monitoring, weather forecasting, and environmental analysis.
We address the problem of 3D segmentation of objects with highly unbalanced object sizes in the context of point clouds.
We introduce a new loss function, the exponential logarithmic loss, which compensates for the errors made by the model in predicting the sizes of the objects.
We show that our method improves the performance of state-of-the-art methods for 3D segmentation on the ScanNet and S3DIS datasets, which contain a large variety of object sizes.
Our code and models are available at https://github.com/autonomousvision/logloss.
In this paper, we present a time series graph cut image segmentation scheme for liver tumors.

Our method combines the advantages of both the level set method and the graph cut method, and it is designed to handle the challenges of liver tumor segmentation in dynamic contrast enhanced CT (DCE-CT) images.
The scheme is based on a region-based segmentation approach that utilizes a graph cut algorithm to optimize the segmentation results.
The input to the graph cut algorithm is a time series of images, where each image is obtained by enhancing the contrast of the DCE-CT image using a different parameterization of the diffusion kernel.

Our method has been evaluated on a public dataset containing DCE-CT images of liver tumors, and the experimental results show that our method can accurately segment the tumors while handling well the challenges of intensity variations and noise.

Abstract: Image segmentation is a fundamental step in medical image analysis, and it is particularly challenging for liver tumor segmentation in DCE-CT images due to the intensity variations and noise.
In this paper, we present a time series graph cut image segmentation scheme that combines the advantages of both the level set method and the graph cut method.
Our scheme is designed to handle the challenges of liver tumor segmentation in DCE-CT images, and it has been evaluated on a public dataset containing DCE-CT images of liver tumors.
The experimental results show that our method can accurately segment the tumors while handling well the challenges of intensity variations and noise.
The proposed method has the potential to improve the accuracy of liver tumor segmentation in clinical practice, which may lead to better diagnosis and treatment of liver tumors.

YouTube-VOS: A Large-Scale Video Object Segmentation Benchmark\
Abstract: \
We introduce YouTube-VOS, a large-scale video object segmentation benchmark consisting of over 5.4 million video clips and more than 600 object classes.
The dataset is collected from YouTube and contains a diverse range of objects, scenes, and motions.
It is designed to be challenging and representative of real-world video understanding tasks.
The benchmark includes a training and validation split, and we provide baseline results using state-of-the-art object detection and instance segmentation methods.
We believe YouTube-VOS will be a useful resource for the research community working on video object segmentation and other video understanding tasks.
We address the problem of recognizing iris images with a database of iris images obtained in visible light using a smartphone camera.
We show that the use of this type of camera, which acquires images in natural light, can be an alternative to near-infrared cameras, reducing the cost of iris recognition systems.
Initially, we extract the iris region and eliminate the eyelids and eyelashes in order to have only the iris for recognition.
Subsequently, we propose to use the Local Binary Pattern (LBP) histogram as a feature for recognition.
First, we divide the iris into several zones, and for each zone, we compute the LBP histogram.
Then, we use Fisher's linear discriminant analysis (FLDA) to reduce the dimensionality of the feature vector and classify the samples.

We use two well-known iris databases, namely the iris database of the Institute of Automation of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (CASIA) and the iris database of the University of Notre Dame (UND), to evaluate our proposal.
In order to assess its performance, we conduct a comparison with other recent works that have used these databases.

In summary, the proposed method is a fast and efficient iris recognition system, which is capable of detecting and recognizing the iris even when the input images present eyelids and/or eyelashes, in addition to being robust to occlusions, illuminations, and resolutions.
In this paper, we present an approach for the segmentation of microscopy data for the purpose of identifying and locating nuclei in breast tissue images.

We utilize a combination of techniques including image enhancement, thresholding, and morphological operations as preprocessing steps, with the primary segmentation approach utilizing a variant of the watershed transform.
The watershed transform, initialized using gradient vector flow, is applied to the enhanced image, and then refined using a gradient-based approach.
The resulting segmentation is evaluated using both manual and automated measures.
The automated measure utilizes a graph cut based approach to evaluate the segmentation in a similar manner to the ground truth annotation.
Results of the segmentation are presented, as are comparisons to other approaches.
The code and data related to this paper are available at: https://github.com/midn8-sfa/nuclei_segmentation.
Recent works have shown that segmentation models benefit from explicit representation of semantic concepts in the form of concept modules.
However, existing concept modules are constructed manually, which limits their generalization and scalability.
In this paper, we propose a new framework called Concept Mask, which automatically discovers concept modules from raw image pixels without any human annotation.

Specifically, we formulate the concept module discovery problem as a non-parametric binary classification problem, where each class corresponds to whether a certain region contains a specific concept.
We utilize a diffusion model with an adaptive context to classify whether each pixel belongs to a given concept, and further employ an attention module to refine the predictions.
Furthermore, we propose a novel online training strategy to optimize the model parameters towards accurate concept segmentation.
Our method achieves top performance on the Cityscapes and COCO-Instance segmentation datasets, and our discovered concept modules are visually consistent with the ground truth.
We present a 3D coarse-to-fine framework for volumetric medical image segmentation.

Our method leverages a fully convolutional neural network (FCN) that is trained in a coarse-to-fine fashion, where the network produces an initial segmentation that is subsequently refined through iterative application of the network.
We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach on the task of abdominal organ segmentation from T1-weighted MR images.

In our experiments, we observe that our approach, when compared to a single-stage FCN, reduces the misclassification rate by up to 47.4% and decreases the mean distance to ground truth by up to 30.2%.
We show that the proposed approach yields segmentations of greater accuracy and detail and allows for precise localization of abdominal organs.
Recent developments in MRI acquisition enable the acquisition of multiple contrasts confounding the manual delineation of the thalamus.
We propose a method to segment the thalamus in MRI volumes acquired with diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) and magnetization transfer (MT) weighted imaging.
Our approach is based on a multi-atlas segmentation framework leveraging the structural and the functional information available in those two contrasts.

We used 50 manually annotated atlases built from synthetic brains generated with Diffusion Toolkit (DITK), and two atlases built from real MRI datasets to obtain an initial segmentation of the thalamus.
Then, to combine the information provided by the atlases, we defined a cost function that quantifies the disagreement between the predicted segmentations and the ground truth labels in the atlases.
We used a greedy algorithm to obtain the final segmentation where the cost is minimized.
The proposed method is evaluated on a dataset of 20 subjects (10 healthy controls and 10 Parkinson's disease patients) with encouraging results.
Abstract: UNet++ is an architecture extension of U-Net, using nested U-Net buildings for medical picture segmentation.
By nesting U-Net models, we are able to make the most of the multi-scale characteristic throughout the total image without losing representation ability on any scale.
In UNet++, the input image is first processed by a series of nested U-Net blocks, followed by global pooling and a fully connected layer for segmentation.
The nested U-Net blocks effectively capture multi-scale context information without increasing the number of parameters or the computational complexity.

We evaluate UNet++ on 3 publicly available medical picture segmentation benchmarks, and our model achieves state-of-the-art performance in 2 out of 3 datasets without any data augmentation or transfer learning.
The code and models are available at https://github.com/uo0v/UNet-Plus-Plus.
Automated iris recognition has been successfully used in many applications, but it typically relies on live iris images taken under controlled conditions.
Post-mortem iris images, taken after death, present additional challenges that require new techniques for segmentation and recognition.
In this paper, we propose a data-driven approach for the segmentation of post-mortem iris images.
Our approach is based on a convolutional neural network (CNN) that has been trained on a large dataset of post-mortem iris images.
The CNN learns to predict pixel-level segmentation labels for each input image, resulting in a binary mask that highlights the iris region.
We evaluate our approach on a new publicly available dataset of post-mortem iris images and show that it achieves a high degree of accuracy compared to the state-of-the-art.
Our approach is designed to address the specific challenges of post-mortem iris imaging, which include iris collapse, pupil misalignment, and image noise.
To handle these challenges, we propose to use a two-stage approach.
In the first stage, we use a CNN to predict a coarse segmentation mask, which is then used to refine the segmentation in the second stage.
The refined segmentation mask is then used to extract the iris region from the image.
We evaluate our approach on a new publicly available dataset of post-mortem iris images, which we make available to the research community.
Our results show that our approach achieves a high degree of accuracy compared to the state-of-the-art.
We also perform a comprehensive analysis of our approach and show that it is effective in handling the challenges of post-mortem iris imaging.
Our work is a step towards developing a fully automated system for the segmentation and recognition of post-mortem iris images.

Such a system could potentially be used for identification purposes in situations where live iris images are not available, such as in mass disaster scenarios or when identifying remains in forensic investigations.
We introduce a new class of layer-specific function norms for deep networks, which are inspired by classical regularization methods such as weight decay and dropout.

These function norms are defined as the sum of the absolute values of the gradients of the activation functions with respect to the inputs, and they act as a regularizer by penalizing large activation functions.
We show that our function norms lead to improved generalization performance compared to the commonly used weight decay and dropout regularization methods.

We present a novel optimization algorithm that minimizes a upper-confidence bound (UCB) objective that includes our function norms, and demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on a variety of deep learning tasks, including image classification and object detection.
This paper proposes a fully-automatic method for myocardial segmentation of contrast echocardiography sequences.
The method is based on random forests, using a shape model constructed with a dictionary of myocardial shapes.
The shape model is used to produce an initial segmentation, which is then refined by a random forest to produce a final segmentation.
The method was evaluated on a database of 25 contrast echocardiography sequences, and produced segmentations that were compared to manual segmentations produced by an experienced observer.

The method achieved a mean distance of 11.4 pixels between the automatically segmented and manually segmented myocardiums, and 96.2% of the automatically segmented myocardiums were within 15 pixels of the manually segmented myocardiums.

The method also achieved a mean distance of 8.7 pixels between the automatically segmented and manually segmented left ventricles, and 96.6% of the automatically segmented left ventricles were within 15 pixels of the manually segmented left ventricles.
The results show that the method is able to produce accurate segmentations of the myocardium and left ventricle in contrast echocardiography sequences.

We present a method for real-time prediction of segmentation quality while the network is training.
Given a set of training images, we train a student-teacher network with an auxiliary segmentation branch whose sole purpose is to predict segmentation quality.
Since the teacher network is defined in terms of the student network, the two networks can be trained jointly in an end-to-end fashion.
During training, the predicted quality metric provides reinforcement signal to guide the training process of the student network and it could be used to protect the regions of interest.
In the test phase, the segmentation quality predictor can be used for active learning and selective sampling.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on the Cityscapes dataset.

We present a concurrent spatial and channel squeeze & excitation (CSSE) module for fully convolutional networks that concurrently performs channel-wise and spatial squeeze and excitation operations as a single layer, allowing for efficient network designs that achieve better performance and robustness compared to conventional architectures.
The proposed CSSE module is composed of a spatial squeeze path and a channel squeeze path, which perform orthogonal transformations to capture different kinds of important features.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed module through extensive experiments on four benchmark datasets: CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, SVHN, and ImageNet.

The proposed CSSE module achieves state-of-the-art performance on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and SVHN, and improves over the state-of-the-art ResNet-50 model by 1.7% on ImageNet, surpassing the performance of many complex architectural variations.
Today's contextual bandit algorithms operate under the assumption that the context features are directly observable.

However, in many real-world applications such as fraud detection or customer journey analysis, the contextual features are not directly observable, and we can only observe their aggregates (e.g., sum, count, average) over a sliding window of recent observations.
In this paper, we close this gap by proposing a new algorithmic framework called CFCM: Segmentation via Coarse to Fine Context Memory.
CFCM maintains a context memory to store recent observations and dynamically adjusts the context window size based on the underlying distribution.
It then uses a segmentation algorithm to recover the fine-grained context features from the aggregated features stored in the context memory.

We show that the proposed CFCM can achieve optimal contextual bandit performance (i.e., Bayes-optimal prediction and O(1)/O(1/e) regret) under certain mild conditions, and experimental results on real-world datasets demonstrate its efficacy and efficiency.
We present a fully-automatic deep learning approach to 3D shape segmentation, and demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on the ShapeNet part segmentation benchmark.
Our approach is based on a fully convolutional network (FCN) that processes the input shape directly without requiring a voxelization or surface reconstruction step.
To handle the variability and ambiguity of 3D shapes, we propose a novel FCN architecture that is capable of learning context-aware representations from multiple input viewpoints.
We evaluate our method on the ShapeNet part segmentation benchmark, and show that our approach outperforms the state-of-the-art on both the part segmentation and chamfer distance metrics.
Our source code and trained models are available at https://github.com/sshaoshuai/3D-Shape-Segmentation-FCN.
Deep learning-based models for medical image segmentation are typically evaluated on the entire image slab, irrespective of the anatomical region of interest.
In this work, we draw analogy from attention mechanisms in natural language processing to develop a method for automatically learning to attend to the region of interest (ROI).
We propose an attention u-net architecture that learns a map of attention weights for each input slice to selectively attend to the region of interest while ignoring the background.
We demonstrate the efficacy on pancreas segmentation in CT volumes from the NIH Pancreas Phantom and Pancreas Divisibility Challenge.
Our method improves upon the baseline u-net model (FROC: 0.83 vs 0.81) and reduces the run-time by approximately 55%.
Recent progress in deep learning has led to significant advances in medical image segmentation.
However, fully automated segmentation algorithms still face challenges in dealing with anatomical variation, lesion appearance, and similar tissue structures.
While manual segmentation by domain experts is accurate and robust, it can be tedious, time-consuming, and suffers from intra- and inter-user variability.
There has been a growing interest in interactive segmentation techniques that seek to combine the strengths of both fully automated and manual segmentation methods.
In this paper, we propose a novel approach for interactive medical image segmentation that combines point-based interaction and sequential patch learning.
Our method enables the user to quickly highlight points on the image to define an initial segmentation boundary.
These user-defined points are then used to generate a initial segmentation mask, which is subsequently refined using a sequential patch learning algorithm.
The patch learning algorithm utilizes a deep learning model to predict pixel-level labels for each patch within the mask, and iteratively updates the mask based on the predicted labels.

We evaluate our method on a public dataset of abdominal CT scans and demonstrate that our approach achieves substantial improvement in segmentation accuracy compared to existing interactive segmentation methods.
This paper describes the Matlab implementation of a machine vision algorithm for the evaluation of ballast degradation using image processing techniques.
The algorithm was developed as a part of a larger project on ballast degradation evaluation and was implemented using the Matlab programming language.
The implementation was done by first developing a set of image processing techniques that could be used to extract the necessary information from a series of images of ballast degradation.
These techniques included methods for image enhancement, feature extraction, and image segmentation.
Once the image processing techniques had been developed, they were then combined into a single algorithm that could be used to evaluate ballast degradation.
The algorithm was implemented using a set of Matlab functions that were developed specifically for this purpose.
The functions were designed to be easy to use and modular, so that they could be easily modified or extended in the future.
The implementation was tested on a set of images of ballast degradation and was found to be effective in evaluating the degradation.
The algorithm was able to extract the necessary information from the images and provide a measure of the degradation.
The results of the testing were consistent with the expected results and demonstrated the effectiveness of the algorithm.
We present an unsupervised image segmentation approach specifically designed for pathological whole-slide images (WSIs).
Given a WSI, our goal is to segment the image into regions corresponding to tumor and healthy tissue.
We employ a recently proposed representation learning approach, spherical k-means (SKM), to learn a low-dimensional feature representation for WSIs.
Our approach is unsupervised, meaning it does not require labeled data for training.
We demonstrate the performance of our approach on WSIs from a public dataset, the CAMELYON17 challenge dataset, which contains 16 cases (slides) with a total of 1,421 tiles.
Our approach achieves a mean tile F1-score of 0.5139, which is comparable to recent supervised approaches that rely on labeled data.
We also perform a detailed analysis of the proposed approach to understand its behavior and identify areas for improvement.
We present an approach for training deep learning models for multi-organ segmentation.
Our method utilizes sample selection based on the relaxed upper confident bound (RUCB) algorithm.
Given a limited number of training samples, we aim to select a subset that covers the distribution of all classes well, in order to reduce the model's generalization error.
We show that our approach can achieve better performance compared to existing methods, such as cross-validation and random sampling, in terms of average precision and intersection over union.
Our method is particularly useful for the training of deep learning models in medical imaging, where the available training data is often limited.
We present an approach for surgical instrument segmentation in intra-operative images that leverages a generative model of the deformable surgical instrument appearance, learned from synthetic data.
Given a query image, the model predicts instrument appearances that explain the image pixel intensities.
These predictions are used to induce a region proposal network that computes an initial segmentation.

We introduce a novel overlap-based metric that compares segmentations with the ground truth, and use it to produce a final segmentation by iteratively fusing proposals in a process internally akin to watershed.
We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach on a new publicly available dataset of intra-operative images.
Segmentation of anatomical structures in 3D MR images is a crucial step towards automated analysis of these images.
We present an adaptive strategy for superpixel-based region growing to segment 3D MR images.
In this approach, 3D MR images are first transformed into a stack of 2D images using orthogonal plane slices.
Each 2D slice is segmented by employing a simple and efficient superpixel-based region growing algorithm.

To handle the anatomical variation in the size of structures across different patients, we propose an adaptive strategy that estimates the optimal superpixel size by analyzing the gradient distribution of the 2D slices.

The proposed adaptive strategy enables the algorithm to produce significantly more accurate segmentations compared to fixed-size superpixel approaches, while maintaining a practical computational complexity.
The segmented 2D slices are then combined to generate a 3D segmentation of the anatomical structure of interest.
The proposed method has been evaluated on manually annotated MR images of the knee joint, lower lumbar spine, and femur.
The results show that the proposed method is capable of producing accurate segmentations of the different anatomical structures within these images.
Active contour models have been widely used in image segmentation due to their simplicity and efficiency.
However, existing active contour models assume that the image to be segmented possesses homogeneity and smoothness in the intensity values of the image pixels.
Such assumptions are not valid for many real world images where intensity inhomogeneities and discontinuities exist.
In this paper, we propose a new active contour model, which we refer to as the Inhomogeneity Estimated by Orthogonal Primary Functions (IEOPF) model, to overcome this limitation.
In the IEOPF model, the inhomogeneities in the image are estimated by using a set of orthogonal primary functions.
The primary functions are optimized to minimize the cost function in the active contour model.
The use of orthogonal primary functions enables us to decouple the optimization of the inhomogeneity estimate and the active contour model.
The IEOPF model is capable of effectively handling intensity inhomogeneities and discontinuities in the image and significantly improving the segmentation accuracy.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through experiments on synthetic and real world images.
Knee joint magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is important in the study of osteoarthritis as it is a noninvasive procedure.
However, the manual segmentation of the knee joint MRI is tedious and time-consuming.
In this paper, we present a survey on computer-aided knee joint MRI segmentation methods.
We first introduce the problem and present the commonly used knee joint MRI datasets.
Then, we survey the state-of-the-art segmentation methods.
We also present an evaluation of these methods using two datasets.
The results show that the performance of these methods is far from satisfactory.
We then discuss the reasons and suggest possible improvements.

An Iterative Spanning Forest Framework for Superpixel Segmentation

Abstract
We present an effective image segmentation approach based on an iterative algorithm that combines the benefits of spectral clustering and greedy region-growing strategies.

In each iteration, our algorithm iteratively constructs an optimal spanning forest using a graph-based segmentation, and then improves it by performing a spectral clustering that reduces the number of segments.
In this way, we obtain a sequence of segmentations, where the segmentation obtained in each iteration is an optimal spanning forest in the sense that every region of the image is connected.

Our framework is extremely fast, and it is able to produce very good segmentations for a large number of images, outperforming state-of-the-art algorithms in terms of objective evaluation metrics as well as visual inspection.

The design includes a VGG11 encoder, pre-trained on ImageNet, that is modified for semi-supervised segmentation.

We present a new approach to semantic segmentation, a process that aims to assign semantic labels to each pixel in an input image.
Our method is based on a convolutional neural network (CNN) with multiple soft cost functions.
These cost functions are designed to encourage consistent predictions across neighboring pixels, as this is often a strong cue for object boundaries in images.
Furthermore, we introduce a new type of layer, which we term the "highly fused convolutional layer," that combines the responses of multiple filters in a single layer.
This has the effect of making our network more resilient to noise and other sources of error.
We evaluate our method on the public Cityscapes dataset and achieve a competitive result, with a mean accuracy of 82.1%.
Semantic image segmentation has gained increasing attention, as it alleviates the manual effort required for pixel-level labeling by automatically assigning a class label to each pixel in an image.

Most existing works focus on accurately classifying pixels within the interior of objects, while the boundary pixels are often treated as a derivative of the interior pixels, resulting in suboptimal performance around object boundaries.
In this paper, we argue that the boundary regions carry significant information that can be exploited to improve the segmentation performance.
To this end, we propose a novel approach called Boundary-informed Classification (Boa), which explicitly models the boundary regions to capture the additional information.
Boa first detects boundary pixels using a simple yet effective boundary detector, and then utilizes a boundary-informed loss function to enhance the classification of boundary pixels during training.
In the inference stage, we develop an adaptive inference mechanism that can effectively utilize the boundary information for accurate segmentation.
When extensively evaluated on four semantic image segmentation benchmarks, Boa achieves promising results, outperforming the state-of-the-art approaches, especially in terms of boundary accuracy.

In this work, we aim to segment splenomegaly in ultrasound images, a segmentation task that has not been explored in the literature.
We propose to use global convolutional kernels, which we name splenomegaly kernels (SMKs), that are designed to capture global appearance patterns of splenomegaly in ultrasound images.

We also propose to use conditional generative adversarial networks (cGANS) to generate synthetic ultrasound images from which we can extract additional SMKs that capture a wider variety of appearance patterns.
We show that our approach achieves a high segmentation performance, even when the number of training examples is relatively low.
Color image segmentation has always been an active research topic due to its wide applications in image processing area.
In this paper, we present a color image segmentation method based on seeded region growing and merging technique.
Specifically, we propose to use square elemental regions as the basic unit to extract the region information.
In the proposed method, the color image first undergoes the Gaussian smoothing operation, and the smoothing result is followed by the binary thresholding process to produce the initial segmentation.
Then, the seeded region growing and merging technique is applied to the binary image sequentially to produce the final segmentation result.
In the proposed method, the region growing process is performed within each square elemental region, and the region merging process is performed among the adjacent square elemental regions.
Therefore, the proposed method is named as square elemental region-based seeded region growing and merging method.
Compared with the other seeded region growing and merging methods that use the pixel as the basic unit, the proposed method can achieve more satisfactory segmentation results.
Experiments on a number of color images, including the Berkeley segmentation dataset, show the promising performance of the proposed method.
We present a novel eye-based interaction technique for image editing.
Given a rough sketch as input, our system uses gaze-tracking to collect a user's eye movements.
These eye movements are then used to iteratively refine a generated image using a conditional generative adversarial network (CGAN).
We demonstrate that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance in terms of image quality, and provides a fun and intuitive interaction for image creation.
In a user study, we show that our approach is preferred by users compared to alternative methods.
Medical image segmentation plays a crucial role in medical image analysis.
In this study, we focus on the segmentation of brain MRI (Magnetic Resonance Imaging) images and propose a method based on multi-modal convolutional neural network (MCNN).

The proposed method combines T1-weighted, T2-weighted and fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) images for segmentation, using three different image fusion schemes: early fusion, late fusion and multi-scale late fusion.
The objective is to investigate the effect of image fusion scheme on the performance of MCNN.
Our results show that the multi-scale late fusion scheme provides the best segmentation performance in terms of dice similarity coefficient and intersection over union.
Recent progress in historical document image segmentation is reviewed.
Then, a new approach is proposed which combines hierarchical segmentation with unsupervised learning.
A deep neural network is initialized with a linear discriminant analysis classifier trained on manually labeled pixels that are easily separable.
An image is segmented by iteratively labeling the most confident regions in a bottom-up fashion, starting from the end of the hierarchy, where the regions are smallest.
The proposed method is evaluated on the Public Domain Data Set (PDDS) and the authors' dataset of historical Chinese documents, and compared with four recent state-of-the-art methods on the PDDS.
Results show that the proposed method performs favorably against the other methods in terms of segmentation quality and speed.
In this paper, we propose a novel FPGA based parallelized architecture of an efficient graph based image segmentation algorithm.

The proposed algorithm is based on a hierarchical graph representation of the image, where the nodes of the graph represent the pixels of the image and the edges of the graph represent the similarities between the pixels.
The algorithm consists of two main steps: a node classification step and an edge weighting step.
The node classification step is used to classify the pixels of the image into different classes, based on the similarities between the pixels.
The edge weighting step is used to assign weights to the edges of the graph, based on the similarities between the pixels and the class of the pixels.
The proposed algorithm is implemented on an FPGA platform, which provides a high-performance and low-power implementation.
The algorithm is parallelized to take advantage of the parallel processing capabilities of the FPGA.
The experimental results show that the proposed algorithm achieves a high segmentation quality and a fast processing speed.

Due to the ever increasing size of digital images, there is a need for efficient and fast image segmentation algorithms.
In this paper we present a novel parallelized architecture for segmentation of large grayscale images using graph based segmentation techniques.

The proposed architecture is based on a hierarchical graph representation of the image, where the nodes of the graph represent the pixels of the image and the edges of the graph represent the similarities between the pixels.
The algorithm consists of two main steps: a node classification step and an edge weighting step.
The node classification step is used to classify the pixels of the image into different segments, based on the similarities between the pixels.
The edge weighting step is used to assign weights to the edges of the graph, based on the similarities between the pixels and the segment that the pixels belong to.
The proposed architecture is designed to be implemented on a field programmable gate array (FPGA) platform, which can provide a high performance and low power implementation.
The architecture is parallelized to take advantage of the parallel processing capabilities of the FPGA.
