DeepIGeoS is a deep learning framework for medical image segmentation, which introduces an interactive geodesic method based on the geodesic active contour without edges (GAC-WE) model.
Unlike the original GAC-WE model, which optimizes the contour directly, our method optimizes the geodesic distance map instead, allowing for more intuitive user interactions.
We employ a deep neural network to learn the geodesic distance map from the image, which can be trained in an unsupervised manner.
During the segmentation process, the user can freely adjust the contour by editing the geodesic distance map, and the network will update the map according to the user's input.
Our method has been evaluated on the MIT-BIH Arterial Tree andLiver CT images.
Compared to the original GAC-WE model, our method achieved a similar performance with significantly fewer parameters and without any edge detection modules.

Recent studies in the analysis of neonatal brain MRI datasets have demonstrated the potential of using 4D atlases for labeling cerebrovasculature, however, label fusion across time-points in longitudinal MR studies has not been addressed so far.
In this work, we present a label fusion approach to combine the label information from a 4D atlas across multiple time-points based on a previously proposed 4D atlas construction pipeline.

In the context of a neonatal cerebrovascular study, we demonstrate the efficacy of our approach on a real-world dataset, showing that our method can yield more accurate labeling results compared to state-of-the-art approaches.
Recent progress in conditional score estimation (CSE) has enabled state-of-the-art performance on a variety of computer vision tasks.

However, existing CSE methods are mainly designed for segmenting objects in images with simple shapes or with well-defined boundaries, and they often struggle to accurately segment objects with complex shapes or object instances with poor boundary contrast.
In this paper, we propose a new approach to image segmentation based on iterative inference from CSE.
Our approach iteratively refines the segmentation results by simultaneously estimating object boundaries and the conditional scores.

Specifically, given initial guesses for object boundaries and conditional scores, we iteratively update them by minimizing a joint energy function that measures the dissimilarity between the predicted and ground truth segmentations.
We also introduce an effective boundary refinement module that selectively refines object boundaries based on the confidence of the predicted boundaries.
Our approach can handle instances with complex shapes and/or poor boundary contrast, and is efficient and easy to optimize.

We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on the PASCAL VOC 2012 segmentation benchmark, where our method achieves competitive performance to the state-of-the-art methods while being much faster to optimize.
Recent progress in artificial intelligence has enabled the automation of various agriculture-related tasks, such as crop and weed detection.
However, creating a large and diverse dataset for training deep learning models can be a time-consuming and laborious process, which can hinder the development of accurate and robust models.
In this paper, we present a data generation framework that automatically creates a large and diverse dataset for training deep learning models to detect crops and weeds.
Our framework utilizes a combination of image segmentation, edge detection, and geometric projection algorithms to generate synthetic training data that closely resembles real-world images.
Furthermore, our framework can rapidly create datasets of various sizes and crop types, making it suitable for a wide range of applications.

We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through extensive experiments, showing that our framework can significantly improve the accuracy and robustness of deep learning models for crop and weed detection.
In this paper, a new boundary detection technique is proposed which adapts locally to the image noise and the object boundary regions in the image.
It is based on an iterative algorithm the convergence of which is guaranteed.
In each iteration, the algorithm updates the estimate of the boundary by pooling the information from the gradient magnitude and the gradient direction obtained from the image segmentation mask.

Since the proposed technique is capable of local adaptation, the performance of the algorithm degrades slowly in the presence of noise compared to other existing techniques and the performance is significantly better than those techniques in low-contrast images.
The proposed technique does not require any parameters to be tuned and therefore makes it easy to use in any type of application.
Finally, the performance of the proposed technique is compared to other existing techniques using various evaluation metrics.
The experimental results demonstrate the superiority of the proposed technique.
Deep learning has achieved great success in image segmentation, however, most existing works focus on the indoor scene which usually has a large number of training images.
For the aerial image segmentation, the collection of a large amount of training data is costly and time-consuming, and the diversity of scenes is another challenge.
Online maps provide a new perspective to acquire training data.
In this paper, we propose a learning approach for aerial image segmentation from online maps, which has the advantages of low cost and fast training speed.
We first extract the building footprint and road vector information from online maps, and then generate labeled images for training.
Finally, we design a deep neural network to learn the segmentation model from the generated images.
The experimental results on two public-available datasets show the effectiveness of our approach.
We introduce a new architecture for 3D convolutional neural networks (CNNs) that aims to improve the representation power of 3D CNNs while maintaining a compact structure and efficient training.

Our key idea is to factorize the 3D convolutional layer into a stack of 2D convolutional layers, allowing the network to utilize the powerful 2D CNN representations while retaining the 3D structure for handling longitudinal information.
We show that this factorization leads to a compact and efficient network that achieves better performance on a variety of 3D CNN benchmarks.
In addition, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our architecture on the challenging task of brain parcellation, where we achieve state-of-the-art performance.
Our 3D CNN architecture consists of a stack of 2D CNNs, where each 2D CNN processes a slice of the input volume.
This enables the network to utilize the powerful 2D CNN representations while retaining the 3D structure for handling longitudinal information.
The 2D CNNs are connected via a 3D pooling layer that aggregates the representations from the 2D CNNs.
We introduce a new 3D pooling layer that performs max-pooling along the third dimension, reducing the spatial dimensions of the representations while retaining the important information.
We evaluate our architecture on the challenging task of brain parcellation, where the goal is to segment the brain into different regions.
We achieve state-of-the-art performance on the public Brain Parcellation challenge 2017 dataset, outperforming the previous state-of-the-art by a large margin.
Our network is able to learn robust representations that capture the structural and anatomical properties of the brain, despite the limited amount of training data.
Our work demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed architecture in improving the representation power of 3D CNNs while maintaining a compact structure and efficient training.
We believe that our architecture will pave the way for more powerful and efficient 3D CNNs that can tackle a wide range of 3D data processing tasks.
We propose a new loss function for image segmentation using 3D fully convolutional deep networks.
Our loss function is based on the Tversky index, which is a measure of perceptual similarity between two images.
We show that our loss function is able to improve the performance of state-of-the-art 3D fully convolutional deep networks for image segmentation.
We evaluate our method on the Cityscapes and KITTI datasets, and show that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on both datasets.
Our code and models are available at https://github.com/junqiu/TverskyLossFunction.
We present an efficient graph cuts based technique for segmenting kidneys in ultrasound (US) images.
Graph cuts methods have been widely used in image processing and computer vision for image segmentation.
However, most existing methods rely on the initial segmentation results to obtain the final segmentation.
In this work, we develop an adaptive graph cuts technique that can simultaneously consider the global and local features of the kidneys in US images.
It can be used for the initial segmentation or as a stand-alone technique.
Furthermore, we integrate multiple feature maps, including edge, regional, and texture information, into the graph cuts framework to achieve more accurate segmentation results.
The experimental results on US images obtained from patients with kidney stones indicate that the proposed method is effective in segmenting kidneys and yields promising results.
DeepLab is a novel deep convolutional neural network architecture designed for semantic image segmentation.
The key component of DeepLab is a densely connected conditional random field (CRF) module that is connected to a deep convolutional neural network (DCNN) in a end-to-end training manner.
This CRF module leverages the spatial coherence prior in image segmentation and makes the network focus on hard examples for training.
We show that the CRF module can be integrated with the DCNN in an efficient way without deteriorating the convergence property.
Our network is trained by minimizing the conditional logistic likelihood of the CRF, which is an alternating optimization process.

We further propose an atrous convolution technique to effectively increase the field of view of the convolutional layers and an adaptive convolution kernel size technique to improve the performance in the image boundary.
Our network is applied to the PASCAL VOC 2012 segmentation challenge.
Without any further tuning, our network outperforms the current state-of-the-art methods for this benchmark by a large margin of +5.7% in terms of pixel accuracy and +4.0% in terms of mean accuracy.
Recent works have shown that deep neural networks (DNNs) can learn meaningful shape representations.
However, existing methods require extensive training and suffer from the dataset imbalance problem, i.e., the scarcity of labeled objects with respect to the background.
In this paper, we present a simple yet effective approach for object discovery via cohesion measurement.
Given a group of points in the 3D space, our method can automatically discover the objects with coherent structures.
We propose a novel cohesion measurement by exploring the intrinsic relationship between points, which captures the object boundaries in a learnable manner.
We further develop an efficient algorithm to optimize the cohesion measurement with guaranteed convergence.
The experimental results on both synthetic and real datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach for object discovery, outperforming the state-of-the-art methods.
Recent advances in deep learning have achieved remarkable performance in medical image segmentation in a single modality.
However, in real clinical settings, medical images are often acquired in multiple modalities, each providing different information.
In this paper, we present a multi-task learning framework for joint segmentation of anatomical structures in CT and MRI.

Our framework learns a shared representation across different modalities from their corresponding annotated image pairs, and is based on a deep architecture that explicitly models anatomical correspondences between the modalities.

We evaluate our method on multi-modal segmentation of the prostate, and show that it performs competitively to state-of-the-art single-modality segmentation methods while learning anatomical correspondences across modalities, thus demonstrating the promise of multi-task learning for medical image segmentation in multiple modalities.
We present a novel approach for learning tree potentials in conditional random fields (CRFs) for image segmentation.
Our method is based on structured output learning (SOL), which allows us to train the CRF using a linear split solver, such as L-BFGS.
Our approach utilizes a tree-structured output representation, where each node represents an intermediate segmentation result and only the leaf nodes correspond to the final segmentation.
We introduce an objective function that optimizes the tree potentials to enforce spatial coherence and a smooth transition from the intermediate to the final segmentation.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on two public image segmentation benchmarks, and show that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance.
We present a method for skin lesion segmentation in dermoscopic images, tailored for the ISIC 2017 Skin Lesion Segmentation Challenge.
The method is based on a convolutional neural network, trained on ISIC 2016 training and validation datasets.
We use k-means clustering to select the most relevant features and ensemble of regressions to improve the segmentation map.
We ranked 8th in ISIC 2017 Skin Lesion Segmentation Challenge.

Medical image segmentation is typically formulated as an iterative estimation problem, with each iteration updating an initial guess for the segmentation through comparison with a reference (often a labeled image).
In this paper we propose a simple method for learning the input to such an iterative process, by comparing the current segmentation with the reference using a normalized input representation.
This learned input can then be used in place of the original image input in subsequent iterations, resulting in a significant improvement in segmentation accuracy.

We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on three different segmentation problems: myocardial segmentation in cardiac MR images, tumor segmentation in MR breast images, and hippocampus segmentation in T1-weighted MR brain images.
In all cases, we achieve substantial improvements over the baseline methods.
We present a new algorithm for image segmentation based on grouping pixels together that belong to the same object.
Our method incorporates a priori knowledge of object geometry in the form of an overlapping group sparsity model.
This model is a generalization of the traditional group sparsity model, where groups of pixels can overlap, enabling better segmentation of objects that overlap in the image.

The algorithm is based on minimizing an objective function that encourages sparsity in the group labels, as well as a fidelity term that compares the predicted pixel labels to the ground truth labels.
We demonstrate the performance of our method on the public available Cityscapes dataset, where we achieve state-of-the-art segmentation results.
We present a novel framework for automatic prostate segmentation in ultrasound (US) images.
Our method is based on fine-grained recurrent neural networks (RNNs), which are designed to capture the complex anatomical structures and patterns in US images.
The proposed method consists of two main components: a coarse segmentation network and a fine-grained segmentation network.
The coarse segmentation network is based on a conventional RNN, while the fine-grained segmentation network is based on a long-short term memory (LSTM) RNN.
We evaluate our method on a large dataset of US images and compare it to other state-of-the-art methods.
Our results show that our method achieves competitive performance and is able to handle large variations in the appearance and shape of the prostate.
We present a shape-sampler for image segmentation based on a nonparametric shape prior, built upon the monte carlo belief propagation framework.
Our approach addresses the issue of combinatorial explosion by parameterizing a shape prior as a probabilistic distribution, and efficiently sampling from this distribution using MCMC methods.

We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on a benchmark dataset, showing that our method compares favorably with state-of-the-art segmentation methods while providing a structured shape prior.
We present a theoretical analysis of active contours on graphs.
We show that the energy of an active contour on a graph is minimized when the contour is a geodesic, and we characterize the first and second variations of the energy.
We show that the eigenvectors of the laplacian of the graph are parallel transported along geodesics, and we use this result to demonstrate the convergence of active contours to geodesics.
Finally, we present a new algorithm for implementing active contours on graphs.
Our results establish the mathematical foundation for active contours on graphs and provide a basis for their application to a variety of problems in image processing and computer vision.
Recent works on semantic segmentation largely focus on designing models with better expressive power to leverage abundant annotated image data for training.
However, these models are known to be susceptible to the inherent ambiguity of pixel-level annotations, and their complexity can make them difficult to optimize.

In this paper, we take a different approach and treat energy learning as a combinatorial problem, where the goal is to design an energy function that can effectively encode segmentations for a specific task.

Our key observation is that when the energy function is a composition of simple parts, the search for a good segmentation can be formulated as a combinatorial optimization problem, for which efficient algorithms exist.
To learn a good composition of parts, we propose a novel framework called Combinatorial Energy Learning (CEL).

Given a database of image segmentations, CEL learns a segmentation energy function as a weighted composition of a set of predefined atomic energies, where the weights are optimized via combinatorial optimization.
We show that this approach can produce segmentation energies that are as effective as state-of-the-art models while being an order of magnitude faster to evaluate.
In addition, by formulating the learning problem as a combinatorial optimization problem, CEL is able to bypass the need for annotated images during the learning process.

We demonstrate the effectiveness of CEL on both indoor and outdoor segmentation benchmarks, where CEL achieves competitive performance to state-of-the-art models while being an order of magnitude faster to evaluate.
We present a large-scale dataset for material recognition named MatNet, which contains over five thousand labeled samples of forty-eight common materials.

To acquire this dataset, we built a multi-camera light-field capture system, and developed an effective pipeline to synthesize 4D light-field images from stereo pairs of images, given the depth information.
To the best of our knowledge, MatNet is the first 4D light-field dataset for material recognition.
We further contribute two CNN architectures designed for material recognition: a simple but effective CNN called MatNet-Conv, and a more complex CNN called MatNet-ResNet.
Our extensive experiments show that our methods achieve top-tier performance on two public material recognition benchmarks, namely CAMEO and MatNet.
Recent advances in electron microscopy (EM) have made it possible to automate the process of imaging large cells and tissues with nanoscale resolution.
However, manual analysis of EM images remains a bottleneck in understanding cell structure and organization.
In this paper, we present a semi-supervised learning framework for segmentation of EM images by seeking a hierarchical merge tree of labeled pixels.
Given an image with only a few user-provided labels, our approach seeks an accurate segmentation through a sparse merge tree of labels that respects a hierarchical organization of labels.
We introduce a new graph neural network architecture tailored to our semi-supervised segmentation framework.
We show that the proposed method performs favorably compared with state-of-the-art segmentation methods on both simulated and real EM images.
We present a new architecture for effective superpixel extraction, based on a shallow convolutional network, trained with a large collection of image segments.
Our architecture is based on a series of bicubic-sampling operations, which we term bilateral inceptions, that explicitly model the pixel-edge correspondence.
During training, we enforce a global consistency on the pixels and edges, while permitting local variations in the responses.
This is achieved by a new loss function that is inspired by theedge-aware energy of the bilateral filter.
Our approach is fast, and extracts superpixels on the CPU in linear time with respect to the number of pixels.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on the 2015 Berkeley Segmentation Dataset, obtaining state-of-the-art results.
We present a method for segmenting images based on the content of screens present in the image.
Our method comprises two stages: in the first stage we identify regions in the image that contain screens, and in the second stage we segment the content displayed on those screens.
Our proposed method is fully automatic, and is able to handle a variety of screen content, including text, images, and videos.
We evaluate our method on a new dataset we created, as well as on publicly available datasets, and show that it performs better than state-of-the-art methods.
Our screen content segmentation algorithm proceeds by modeling the image as a sparse combination of dictionary elements, where each dictionary element corresponds to a candidate screen content patch.
We simultaneously identify regions containing screens, and segment the content on the screens by selecting the appropriate dictionary elements.
Within a screen region, we further refine the segmentation by minimizing a total variation energy, which allows us to handle screens that are distorted, occluded, or viewed from a perspective.

In order to effectively handle textual content, we introduce a text-specific dictionary learned from a set of handwritten digits, and show that it effectively improves performance on images with text.
Our algorithm performs well on a variety of screen content, including natural images, textual content, and videos.
We evaluate our method on a new dataset we created, which contains a variety of screen content, including natural images, text, and web-browsers.
We also evaluate our method on two publicly available datasets.
In all cases, we show that our method performs better than state-of-the-art screen content segmentation methods.

diagnosis extraction.

Efficient piecewise training of deep structured models for semantic segmentation

Semantic segmentation is the task of assigning semantic labels to each pixel in an input image.

While deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have achieved remarkable performance in this task, training such models is still a computationally expensive task, especially for large datasets and models.
In this paper, we present a method for training deep structured models for semantic segmentation that is more efficient than existing methods.

Our method is based on the idea of training the model in a piecewise fashion, where the model is trained on a subset of the data and then the trained model is used to predict the labels for the remaining data.
This allows us to train the model on a much smaller subset of the data, which reduces the computational cost of training.
Our experiments show that our method is able to achieve comparable performance to existing methods while reducing the computational cost of training by up to 50%.
Recent progresses in deep learning have advanced semantic image segmentation towards accuracy in categorizing individual pixels in an image and recognizing objects in the real world.
However, most existing semantic segmentation algorithms treat categorization and recognition as two separate tasks, regardless of their tight relationship in semantics.
In this paper, we bridge the gap between category-level and instance-level semantic segmentation with a unified framework, called simultaneous category-instance segmentation (SCIS).

Specifically, we formulate category-level and instance-level segmentation as a multi-task learning problem, such that the mutual interactions between category-level and instance-level segmentation can be effectively exploited for performance improvement.
A novel architecture, named Feature Pyramid Network with Grouping (FPN-G), is developed to effectively fuse multi-scale contextual information and decode the segmentation results.
Extensive experiments on the PASCAL VOC 2012 and Cityscapes datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in bridging the gap between category-level and instance-level segmentation.

Without using any instance-level annotated data, our approach achieves 83.1% in terms of F-measure on the PASCAL VOC 2012 dataset, outperforming the state-of-the-art fully-supervised instance-level segmentation methods.
Moreover, the category-level performance of our approach is only a 1.6% drop compared with DenseCap, which benefits from instance-level annotations.
Code is available at: https://github.com/YxyangTao/SCIS.

Semantic image segmentation has achieved remarkable performance on various benchmarks,
driven by deep learning with ever-growing model complexity.

However,

We introduce a context module that captures high-order

We then

Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on the Cityscapes

Recent results on salient object detection take a top-down approach, in which the model first detects the foreground and then refines it to obtain the final salient regions.
Most existing works focus on designing effective refinement modules to improve the quality of the predicted saliency maps.
In this work, we argue that a key problem of current top-down methods is the quality of the initial foreground map, which is usually obtained by thresholding or clamping the output of an encoder.
To address this problem, we propose a classifier-guided approach that refines the initial foreground map with a classifier.
Specifically, we train a support vector machine (SVM) classifier with image-level labels to predict whether a pixel is in the foreground or not.
Since the classifier is trained with image-level labels, it is able to exploit global information and capture the underlying object-like structures.
Extensive experiments on the salient object detection benchmark datasets validate the effectiveness of our approach compared to the state-of-the-art methods.
We present a new large dataset of electron microscopy images of synapses, along with a novel method for automatically identifying synapses in these images.
We trained a deep learning model on a large dataset of images manually annotated by human experts, and used it to predict the presence of synapses in a new dataset of images.
The model achieved a high accuracy, with an F1 score of 0.9369 on the test set.
We also present a new method for validating the accuracy of our model, which we used to evaluate the performance of our model on a separate validation set.
Finally, we present a quantitative analysis of the characteristics of the synapses in our dataset, and compare them to previous studies.
Traditional fuzzy C-means (FCM) clustering algorithms suffer from the occurrence of local minima in iterative optimization of the objective function during the clustering process.
We propose a kernelized weighted SUSAN based FCM clustering algorithm to segment images affected by Gaussian noise.
Noisy images degrade the quality of feature vectors for traditional FCM algorithms that are extracted from the original images.
In the proposed algorithm, a kernelization technique is employed during the feature extraction to mitigate the effects of noise.
Then, to further improve the quality of feature vectors, a weighted strategy is introduced where the weights are determined by using the SUSAN (symmetric unambiguous structures and anomalies) test.
The SUSAN based weights can effectively reduce the influence of outliers in the feature vectors.
In addition, the proposed algorithm utilizes the watershed algorithm to overcome the difficulty of determining the number of clusters for traditional FCM algorithms.
The proposed algorithm is evaluated using two benchmark noisy image datasets.
The experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm compared to four state-of-the-art FCM algorithms.

Integrated Inference and Learning of Neural Factors in Structural Support Vector Machines

While neural factorization models can express complex distributed computations,
most inference algorithms for structural SVM relax the modular structure
imposed by these models, resulting in a factor graph that is not
necessarily sparse or tree-like.

In this paper, we propose a new
algorithm for exact inference that respects the given factorization
structure, and show that the resulting graph has a tree-like structure;
i.e., can be written as an oriented tree.

We then use this inference
algorithm as the basis for a new algorithm for learning the weights of
the factors in a neural factorization machine.

The experimental results
show that our method compares favorably with state-of-the-art
algorithms for learning neural factorization machines.

Keywords: Neural Factorization Machines, Structural SVM, Graphical Models,
Tree-based Learning.
Graph entropies: recent progress in estimating graph entropies from data and applications in image processing is surveyed.
Graph entropy is a measure of randomness in graph structures.
Various entropy estimates are reviewed, including the spectral entropy, the distance-based entropy (also known as cut-entropy), and the recently developed interference-based entropy.
Applications of graph entropies in image processing, such as image segmentation and edge-preserving image filtering, are discussed.
In particular, a new edge-preserving smoothing filter based on the estimated cut-entropy is presented.
The new filter is shown to be effective in reducing the noise in the image while preserving the edges.
The relationship between the graph entropy and the graph Laplacian is also discussed.
Image segmentation remains a challenging problem in image processing, despite the considerable progress made in the last few decades
No single segmentation algorithm works well for all types of images.

Most segmentation algorithms assume that the image pixels are related to each other in a smooth and gradual way, and that the boundaries of the objects in the image can be described by a set of smooth curves.
However, this assumption is not always valid, and there are many images where the boundaries of the objects are abrupt and noisy, and the pixels are not related to each other in a smooth way.
For such images, traditional segmentation algorithms often fail to produce satisfactory results.
In recent years, there has been considerable interest in the use of entropy measures in image processing [3-5].
Entropy measures can be used to quantify the randomness or uncertainty in an image, and this information can be used to improve the performance of image segmentation algorithms.
In [6], it is shown that the entropy of an image can be estimated directly from the image data, without any prior knowledge of the image or the objects in it.
This estimate of the entropy is based on the observation that the entropy of an image is equal to the average entropy of the pixels in the image.
The entropy of a pixel is defined as the average entropy of the pixels in its neighborhood.
This neighborhood entropy can be estimated from the image data, using a distance-based approach.
The distance-based approach is based on the observation that the entropy of a pixel is proportional to the average distance between the pixel and its neighbors.
A fast algorithm for estimating the neighborhood entropy is presented, based on the use of a binary tree.
This algorithm is shown to be effective in reducing the computation time required for estimating the entropy of an image.
In this paper, we present a new image segmentation method based on active contours without edges.
Unlike the original active contour without edges model, we propose to use a regional active contour model, which can handle the ambiguity of the initial contour placement in the image without edges.
Our method is based on the variational level set framework, in which we introduce a new energy functional combining both the regional and the traditional smoothness terms.
The regional term encourages the contour to partition the image into spatially coherent regions, while the smoothness term enforces the contour to be smooth and compact.
To optimize the energy functional, we propose to use a new gradient descent algorithm which is specifically designed to handle the regional term.
In order to improve the efficiency of our method, we introduce a machine learning component to approximate the regional term in the energy functional.
In particular, we train a fully connected neural network to predict the regional term from the gradient of the smoothed image.
We show that our method is able to handle various types of images, and can produce spatially coherent segmentations.
Our method is evaluated on the public available Cityscapes dataset, and compared with four state-of-the-art image segmentation methods.
The experimental results show the advantages of our method over the competitors in terms of segmentation quality.
The "message passing" paradigm is widely used for inference in graphical models, but the messages themselves have usually been treated as auxiliary variables rather than first-class citizens.
In this paper, we show that the messages carry predictive information that can be leveraged by a neural network to improve inference.
In particular, we propose a "message passing neural network" (MPNN) that combines the strengths of graphical models and deep learning.
Our MPNN uses the messages from a graphical model as input to a neural network that performs inference in a different, potentially larger, graphical model.
Since the MPNN can be trained end-to-end, it is able to "learn" good messages that improve performance.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on two canonical inference problems: graphical model inference and natural language inference.
Our results show that the MPNN achieves state-of-the-art performance on a variety of datasets.
Clustering based image segmentation is an important problem in digital image processing.
In this paper, we propose a novel approach towards clustering based image segmentation.
Our approach is based on a new clustering algorithm that we call the Generalized Median Clustering (GMC).
The GMC is a variation of the K-Means clustering algorithm.
It is designed to work well with high-dimensional data such as images.
We evaluate the performance of our approach using a variety of images.
The results show that our approach is effective in segmenting images.
We also present a variation of our approach that is based on a new clustering algorithm called the Median-Ball Clustering (MBC).
The MBC is a variation of the GMC.
It is designed to work well with sparse data such as medical images.
We evaluate the performance of our sparse data variation using a variety of medical images.
The results show that our sparse data variation is effective in segmenting medical images.
Deep learning has shown promising results for medical image segmentation, but adopting deep learning models in clinical practice remains challenging.
In this paper, we survey the state-of-the-art deep learning techniques specific to medical image segmentation and discuss the challenges and opportunities for clinical adoption.
We first provide an overview of the most commonly used deep learning architectures, including fully convolutional networks (FCNs), U-Net, and Mask R-CNN.
We then survey the most commonly used loss functions, including pixel-wise loss, contour loss, and shape prior loss.
We then discuss the challenges of deep learning for medical image segmentation, including data scarcity, annotation difficulty, model size, and computational requirements.
We conclude by discussing the opportunities for future research, including multi-modal segmentation, semi-supervised learning, and domain generalization.

Abstract
Traditional image segmentation methods produce binary images, which
may not reflect the fuzzy regions in the original image.

Fuzzy segmentation methods can produce more accurate
segmentation results, but are often computationally expensive
and difficult to use.

In this paper, we present a new method
for fuzzy image segmentation that is both efficient and easy
to use.

Our method is based on a self-configuring fuzzy
segmentation algorithm that can evolve to produce a good
segmentation of the image.

The efficiency of the algorithm
comes from the fact that it only produces the necessary number
of segments, rather than segmenting the entire image.

The
ease of use of our method comes from the fact that it is a
fully automatic algorithm that does not require any user
interaction.

We present results showing that our method
can produce good segmentations of a variety of images, and
that it is faster than other fuzzy segmentation methods.

We consider the problem of learning conditional random fields (CRFs) via the Bethe approximation.
Previous work has shown that the Bethe free energy has a simple expression in terms of marginals of the CRF, and that these marginals can be efficiently computed via the forward-backward algorithm.
However, computing the free energy still requires performing summations over the entire CRF, which can be computationally expensive.
In this paper, we propose an alternative expression for the Bethe free energy based on the concept of message passing, and show that it can be efficiently computed via the map decoding algorithm.

Our approach is based on the observation that the Bethe free energy can be viewed as the difference between the marginal likelihoods of two CRFs, one in which all variables are conditioned on, and one in which a subset of variables is conditioned on.
We show that the map decoding algorithm can be used to efficiently compute these marginal likelihoods, and that the difference between them corresponds to the Bethe free energy.
Our experiments show that on a standard CRF benchmark, our approach is faster and more accurate than the previously proposed method based on the forward-backward algorithm.
We present a fast constraint propagation algorithm for image segmentation based on label fusion of watershed segments.
The approach is motivated by the shape prior of watershed segments, which reflects the local connectivity of the image pixels.

The proposed algorithm efficiently computes a score for each pixel based on the constraints from the watershed segmentation and fuses the scores of neighboring segments to obtain the final segmentation.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach on a variety of images, and show that it produces a segmentation that is more accurate and coherent compared to existing algorithms.
The proposed algorithm is fast enough to be used in real-time applications.

This paper proposes an unsupervised image segmentation method based on global and local criteria optimization.
It consists in minimizing an energy function which takes into account both gradient and similarity terms through a Bayesian network.
This network models the spatial dependence between pixels, and allows the use of various criteria at different scales.
We perform an iterative optimization of the energy function, which alternately minimizes a gradient descent and a similarity term.
The optimization of the latter is performed by propagating evidence through the Bayesian network.

This method does not require any initialization or parameter tuning, and allows to obtain competitive results compared to state-of-the-art unsupervised segmentation methods, while being simpler and faster.
We present a technique for the forward and backward propagation of convolutional neural networks that is optimized for pixelwise classification tasks.
Our method achieves a significant speedup compared to standard techniques, with a negligible reduction in accuracy.
We present results showing that our method can speed up the training process by as much as a factor of two, with no loss in accuracy.

We also show that our method can be used to improve the performance of existing convolutional neural networks, resulting in a significant increase in accuracy with only a small increase in training time.
Our method is based on a simple yet effective technique for optimizing the forward and backward propagation of convolutional neural networks.
We believe that our method will be useful for many applications, including the training of large-scale convolutional neural networks.

Fast Edge Detection Using Structured Forests

Edge detection is a fundamental step in many computer vision applications, but it is also a challenging task.
In this paper, we present a new edge detection method based on structured forests.
Our approach is fast, accurate, and easy to use.
We achieve this by combining the advantages of both the structured and the random forests.
The structured forest is used to extract the edges from the image, while the random forest is used to remove the noise and to improve the accuracy of the edge detection.
Our method is fast because it uses a parallel implementation of the structured forest, which allows us to process multiple images at once.
We demonstrate the performance of our method on a variety of images, and show that it is competitive with state-of-the-art edge detection methods.
Person re-identification (ReID) has achieved remarkable progress in recent years with the advancement of deep learning.

However, the existing ReID methods are typically trained and tested under a closed-set scenario, where all the persons in the training set also appear in the test set, which restricts their applicability in real-world scenarios.
In this paper, we tackle the open-set person ReID problem, where the test set may contain persons never seen during training.
Specifically, we propose a novel open-set aware feature embedding module (OFEM) to augment existing ReID models for open-set ReID.
In OFEM, we adopt an effective dropout technique to enhance the generalization ability of ReID models.
In addition, we propose a novel open-set ranking loss to explicitly enforce the model to learn the open-set information.
Furthermore, a simple yet effective ensemble method is proposed to boost the performance of open-set ReID.
We evaluate OFEM on three open-set person ReID benchmarks, and achieve superior performance over the state-of-the-art.
We present a method for fast pathological lung segmentation directly in thoracic CT scans, based on optimal sampling of keypoints.
Our method is tailored to the typically large amount of noise and artefacts in pathological scans.
At its core is a new algorithm for near-optimal keypoint sampling, i.e., approximately minimizing an upper bound on the expected segmentation error.
This is achieved by a greedy algorithm that iteratively selects the most informative keypoint to sample, i.e., the one that guarantees the largest decrease in the upper bound.
We show that our approach is fast, typically requiring under 5 minutes of computation time on a single core, thereby allowing for interactivity.

We demonstrate through extensive experiments on real patient data that our method is accurate, successfully segmenting 95% of lung voxels on average at an under 5% false positive rate, and outperforming state-of-the-art segmentation methods.
Semantic image segmentation is the process of classifying each pixel in an image into one of a pre-defined set of classes, such as sky, road, car, pedestrian.
We introduce a novel approach for semantic image segmentation that incorporates near-infrared (NIR) information into the process.
Our approach uses a deep learning architecture called a U-Net, which is designed to take advantage of the multi-scale contextual information in the image.
We train our U-Net on a large dataset of images that includes both visible wavelength and NIR images, and we evaluate its performance on the Cityscapes dataset.

Our results show that incorporating NIR information into the segmentation process can improve the accuracy of the segmentation, especially in cases where the visible wavelength images are unclear or ambiguous.
We also find that our approach is able to generalize well to images that were not in our training dataset, demonstrating the effectiveness of our approach in real-world applications.
In this paper, we propose a variational image segmentation model coupled with image restoration achievements.
Firstly, we adopt a variational model to achieve image segmentation, and the model is based on the Mumford-Shah functional.
Secondly, we couple the proposed model with image restoration achievements for improving the segmentation performance.
Thirdly, we propose a fast algorithm to solve the proposed model efficiently.
Finally, we perform comprehensive experiments on synthetic and real-world images to validate the effectiveness of the proposed model.
The results demonstrate that the proposed model is able to produce high-quality segmentation results.

We consider the problem of making a minimum number of moves to transform a given initial configuration of objects into a target configuration, where each move may involve flipping an edge between two objects (e.g., swapping the two objects).
This may model, for example, inserting a barrier between two objects in a network, or moving them closer together.
We seek a solution that minimizes an energy function that generalizes the submodular pairwise energies, and is defined using a symmetric and monotone set function that is not necessarily submodular.
This energy may model, for example, the total length of the edges involved in the moves.
We first present a polynomial-time algorithm that outputs an optimal solution when the energy function is submodular.
This algorithm extends a recent algorithm of Feige, Krause, Naor, and Ron for the special case in which the energy function is the sum of edge weights.

Our algorithm is based on a novel technique for handling the general submodular set function in an efficient way, by using a greedy tiered approach that iteratively adds subsets of nodes to the solution.
We then present an algorithm for the general case that has a approximation guarantee of $(1 - 1/e)$, by reducing the problem to a convex optimization problem.
This approximation guarantee is the best possible in the non-submodular case, and nearly matches the approximation guarantee of the known algorithm for the submodular case.
In this paper a new algorithm is presented for clustering categorical data.
This algorithm is an extension of the Fuzzy C-Means (FCM) algorithm for continuous vector data.

In contrast to the FCM algorithm, which requires the specification of a single parameter defining the granularity of clustering, the new algorithm incorporates a degree of uncertainty, or fuzziness, in the specification of the cluster membership, making it more flexible and able to capture the inherent uncertainty in clustering.
This algorithm has been developed to perform clustering on a new data type, referred to as vector membership (VM) data.
VM data combines categorical and vector data in a single data representation.
The proposed algorithm partitions VM data according to the belonging degrees of the constituent vectors to different clusters.
An application of this algorithm is demonstrated in the context of image segmentation.
The algorithm is applied to segment images based on the VM data obtained from the MPEG-7 descriptor, which represents shape and motion information in a local spatio-temporal neighbourhood.

Recent advances in machine learning have spurred great hopes for artificial intelligence to make a lasting impact on society, akin to other scientific advancements such as quantum mechanics or biotechnology.

However, machine learning systems that are trained to excel at natural language processing, for instance, require large amounts of data to be labeled, which is often collected in a non-transparent fashion without user consent.
This has led to an ongoing debate about the ethical implications of machine learning, and recent research has shown that the collection of data can be harmful to individuals and society.
In this paper, we propose a new method for enforcing statistical properties of data that mitigates the need to collect large amounts of data.
Our method is based on a convex optimization formulation that minimizes the difference between the empirical distribution of the data and a specified target distribution.
We show that our approach can be used to enforce statistical properties of data, such as the mean or the variance, and that it can be used to reduce the impact of outliers or noise in the data.
Our method is computationally efficient and can be applied to a wide range of problems in machine learning and statistics.
We demonstrate the performance of our method on a number of examples, including a simulation study and a real-world dataset, and compare it to existing methods for enforcing statistics.
Live-wire 3D medical images segmentation is a challenging problem in image processing.
In this paper, we propose a novel method for live-wire 3D medical images segmentation based on a combination of geometric and topological features.

Our method utilizes the geometric feature of the live-wire algorithm, which can effectively capture the local structure of the object, and the topological feature of the 3D medical images, which can describe the global structure of the object.
By combining these two features, our method can achieve accurate segmentation results.
We evaluate our method on a public 3D medical images segmentation dataset, and the results show that our method can achieve better performance compared to the state-of-the-art methods.
Recent works on image segmentation often assume that all pixels in an image are relatively evenly focused, and that blur is either constrained or appropriately modeled.
However, real-world images often include significant variations in focus, which can adversely impact the performance of segmentation algorithms.
In this paper, we seek to address this deficiency by developing a robust segmentation algorithm that operates under significant defocus.
Towards this goal, we first characterize the effects of defocus on pixel labels, and then propose a new energy function that mitigates the impact of defocus.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on a benchmark dataset, showing that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance even when operating in significantly defocused images.
Extraction of gray image from a color image is very important and it is the first step of extraction process in any image processing application.
A new approach is proposed to extract the gray image using fuzzy logic.
In this paper, RGB components of color image are considered as input for fuzzy system.
These inputs are fuzzified and processed by fuzzy logic to obtain a single output which is the gray value corresponding to that pixel.
The proposed method is tested on various images and results are also compared with existing methods.
The proposed method produced better results in terms of contrast and brightness.
Recent progress in image segmentation is significantly advanced by the 3D model assisted approach, which utilizes a 3D model to provide prior knowledge for the segmentation task.
Given a query image and a set of 3D models, the goal is to find the optimal 3D model which best explains the query image.

However, the existing 3D model assisted methods usually assume that the surface of the 3D model is composed of a finite number of segments, which is not suitable for scanning objects with complex surfaces, where significant texture variations and geometric structures usually exist in a single segment.
In this paper, we propose a new 3D model assisted image segmentation method to overcome the above limitations.
The key idea is to formulate the segmentation problem as a non-parametric binary labeling problem on the surface of the 3D model, and then solve it using a conditional random field (CRF) model.
To efficiently compute the CRF energy, we propose a new algorithm called the multi-scale graph cut algorithm, which approximates the CRF energy by a graph cut energy on a multi-scale graph structure.
The experimental results on both synthetic and real-world data sets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.
In this paper, we propose a linear framework for image segmentation and inpainting that involves a curvature penalty.
Our approach is based on the minimization of a functional that consists of an edge-stopping term, a region-size regularization term, and a curvature penalty term.

The edge-stopping term ensures that the solution remains close to the initial image, the region-size regularization term encourages the solution to have a prescribed number of regions, and the curvature penalty term helps to preserve the curvature of the initial image.
The resulting functional is minimized via a linear programming algorithm.

We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on a variety of image segmentation and inpainting problems, and show that our method produces results that are comparable to, or better than, state-of-the-art methods.
Our approach offers several advantages over existing methods for image segmentation and inpainting.
First, our method is simple and efficient, as it involves the minimization of a linear functional.
This makes it easier to implement and faster to compute than methods that involve the minimization of non-linear functionals.
Second, our method is able to produce results that are comparable to, or better than, state-of-the-art methods for image segmentation and inpainting.
This is because our method incorporates a curvature penalty, which helps to preserve the curvature of the initial image and produces more accurate results.
Third, our method is flexible and can be used to segment and inpaint images of different types, including medical images, satellite images, and images of objects in the real world.
This is because our method involves a region-size regularization term, which allows us to prescribe the number of regions that we want the solution to have.
A new multi-environment model (MEM) is presented for estimating the motility of individual Caenorhabditis elegans worms from images.
The approach estimates the worm's pose, size, and shape for each video frame, and additionally, estimates a set of parameters that characterize the worm's motility.
These motility parameters facilitate comparison across different worms, and moreover, they can be used to detect changes in a single worm's behavior over time.
The parameters include a crawling velocity, a muscle contraction velocity, and a set of parameters that characterize the worm's compliance to external forces.
This last set of parameters can be used to detect changes in the worm's elasticity and its tendency to buckle.
The approach is evaluated on a new dataset that contains images of C. elegans worms collected in a variety of environments (liquid, solid, and sand) and a variety of orientations.
In these new experiments, the worms are sometimes out of focus, and they sometimes crawl on the bottom of the dish, which can produce ambiguous appearances.
In addition, the evaluation compares the new motility parameters to other features that have been used for C. elegans motility analysis, namely joint angles and silhouette curvature.
In this paper, we propose a topological image segmentation technique based on the topological derivative for automatic recognition of sign language.

In order to segment the input hand gesture sequences from the video sequences, we adopt the watershed transformation to obtain the topological derivative of the gradient magnitude of the video frames.
Since the gradient magnitude does not satisfy the assumption of the topological derivative, we apply an isotropic filter to obtain a suitable input for the watershed transformation.
The use of isotropic filter prevents the gradient from being dominated by few directions and makes the watershed based segmentation technique more effective and robust.
The segmented regions are then subjected to a classification based on the statistical features extracted from the normalized RGB histogram of the regions.
In the next stage, a feature selection based on the Fisher score is applied to reduce the dimensionality and to obtain a set of features that are most relevant to the classification task.
Finally, the k-NN classifier is used as the classifier for the classification of the gesture sequences.
The proposed method has been tested on Texas Instrument DLP Sign Language Gesture Database and has achieved a recognition rate of 95.6%.

We show that the min-cut based clustering framework recently introduced by us, as well as a variety of other graph clustering algorithms, can be viewed in a new information- theoretic light, as special cases of a common algorithm for extracting independent signal from a noisy graph via spectral partitioning in the Stieltjes-Wasserstein (SW) space.

Our analysis provides new insights into the behavior of these algorithms on graphs with certain types of spectra, and suggests a direction for future research on graph clustering beyond the widely studied graph Laplacian setting.
In this paper, we study $L^2$ well-posedness of boundary value problems for parabolic systems with measurable coefficients.
We show that, for suitable function spaces, the existence and uniqueness of a solution can be obtained by using a fixed point theorem.
Furthermore, we establish a priori estimates for the solution in terms of the boundary data and the initial data.
Here we report on the design and construction of a variable-temperature environmental capsule for in situ scanning electron microscopy in gases and liquids at ambient conditions.
The device enables the investigation of materials as they react in varying environmental conditions.
We focused on minimizing the volume of the environmental capsule to achieve better resolution and to be able to perform experiments on a broad range of length scales, from nanoscale to macroscale.
We provide details of the design, fabrication and operation of the device and examples of how it can be used to obtain high-resolution images and spectra of materials in aqueous solutions and gases.
This environmental capsule provides the basis for a wide range of experiments aimed at understanding the behavior of materials in realistic environments.
We give an effective version of the Skolem-Mahler-Lech theorem for Diophantine equations satisfied by a finite generated algebra over a polynomial ring in infinitely many variables.
As an application, we give an effective version of the Lang-Weil estimate for the height of the solutions of a system of linear Diophantine equations with coefficients in a finitely generated domain.
We give a simple proof of recent results of Chen-Wang on the topology of blow-ups in generalized complex geometry.
Our approach is to use a technique due to Chen-Hörmander for simplifying the expression of the Chern-Simons function associated to a pseudo-Hermitian manifold.
This simplifies the topology of the blow-up in terms of the topology of the boundary of the domain in question.
We describe a new crystalline form whose unit cell is an icosahedron and whose lattice vector is the golden ratio.

We show that this quasicrystal is related to a particular packing of regular tetrahedra, and we present a geometric construction of this packing using a single tetrahedron and an icosahedral angle trisector.

We prove that the only convex polyhedra that pack into our quasicrystal are regular tetrahedra and irregular dodecahedra, and we present computer images of these packing figures which demonstrate their intricacy and beauty.
We introduce the basic notions of detection of hidden structures (detectability) in amorphous materials and complex physical systems, and develop their mathematical foundations.

In particular, we consider here finite systems and focus on the detection of hidden periodic structures; extensions to quasi-periodic and aperiodic structures, as well as to infinite systems, are also discussed.

Various applications of these notions are presented, ranging from ideal glasses to networks and from lattice systems to finite algebras, in order to illustrate the usefulness and power of the detectability approach.
Copula correlation is a novel dependence measure for continuous variables that overcomes the limitations of traditional measures such as Pearson's correlation.
