We provide an information-theoretic characterization of the optimal regularization parameter in the non-i.i.d.
setting and demonstrate the applicability of our results via numerical experiments.

We answer a question of Erdős and Füredi (1996) regarding the smallest possible size of a round-robin tournament in which a given set of players can guarantee at least one winner, i.e., there is no other player who can beat all of them.

This generalizes a long-standing open problem of Klein on determining the smallest jury that can never convict an innocent person, as well as a recent question of Tao on determining the largest possible set of players in the National Football League (NFL) for which the NFL cannot schedule a fair playoff schedule (i.e., there is a player who can beat every team).

We present an algorithm to solve the general problem, as well as an algorithm for the special case of the NFL, and show that the answers to both problems can be encoded in an elegant and simple mathematical formula.
We introduce a collaborative sparse regression approach for hyperspectral unmixing using spatially correlated supports.
Hyperspectral unmixing is typically performed per pixel using non-linear regression to extract the endmembers and their corresponding fractions of each pixel.
We propose to model this non-linear regression problem as a sparse regression problem, where the sparsity is enforced on groups of pixels that are spatially correlated.
This results in a collaborative sparse regression problem.
The spatially correlated supports are learned using a binary tree algorithm that splits the pixels into groups.
We show that the resulting collaborative sparse regression problem can be solved using existing algorithms for sparse regression.
We demonstrate the performance of our approach on synthetic and real datasets, and show that our approach outperforms the state-of-the-art.

We have performed a first-principles computational study on the bulk solids with simple cubic (SC), face-centered cubic (FCC), and diamond structures using the van der Waals density-functional theory (DFT-vdW).

Unlike the widely used generalized gradient approximation (GGA), which is applicable only to weakly-correlated systems, DFT-vdW is a variant of the DFT that is suitable for the van der Waals (VDW) bonded systems.
Since the VDW interaction is relevant to the structures of bulk solids, DFT-vdW is adequate for the theoretical study on them.

In this study, the equilibrium structures and formation energies of SC, FCC, and diamond crystals are calculated to examine the accuracy and reliability of DFT-vdW. Since DFT-vdW is a computationally costly method, we have also developed a practical and efficient scheme based on the supercell approach to calculate the formation energy of a solid with a given crystal structure in a straightforward manner.

Let $(X,d,\mu)$ be a metric measure space, that is, a metric space $(X,d)$ equipped with a positive Radon measure $\mu$. We define the concept of weighted Sobolev space $W^{1,p}(X,d,\mu;\bb{R}^n)$ for $n\in\bb{N}\cup\{\infty\}$, $1<p<\infty$, as a generalization of the classical Sobolev spaces on Euclidean spaces.
In this paper we study embedding and trace inequalities in $W^{1,p}(X,d,\mu;\bb{R}^n)$.

We show that for $n<\infty$, $W^{1,p}(X,d,\mu;\bb{R}^n)$ is embedded compactly into $L^{p\ast}(X,d,\mu;\bb{R}^n)$ with a constant independent of $n<\infty$, and that for $n=\infty$ the trace of $W^{1,p}(X,d,\mu;\bb{R}^{\infty})$ from $X$ to the space of signed or complex measures endowed with the total variation norm is compact.
In both cases the constants depend on the dimension $n$ of the space $\bb{R}^n$ and on the exponent $p$, but are independent of the weight and of the metric measure space $(X,d,\mu)$.
In this paper, we compute the cohomology with compact support of the universal torsor on a rational surface with good reduction outside a point.

Linear radiofrequency (RF) ion traps have become a key component in many areas of experimental physics, notably for the realization of quantum computers, but also for fundamental studies of ion dynamics and surface interactions.
Despite their broad use, a detailed understanding of ion transport in these traps remains elusive.
In this article, we use numerical simulations to investigate ion transport in macroscopic RF linear traps, characterized by electrode voltages and trap parameters typically used in experiments.
By varying an external electric field along the trap, we observe the transport of single ions through the trap, characterized by a mobility edge and a threshold for ion transport.
We show that the position of these thresholds depends on system parameters such as the RF frequency and the static electric field magnitude.
By investigating the influence of system parameters on our ability to transport ions against a static electric field, we derive criteria for efficient ion transport in RF linear traps.
We report on braided flux measurements in superconducting nanowires with strong magnetic fields applied perpendicular to the nanowires.

In contrast to common wisdom, we find substantial flux braiding in multiple wires with seemingly random phase shifts, suggesting that microscopic interactions rather than macroscopic effects are the origin of the phase shifts.

Our results bring into question whether or not it is useful to consider a "macroscopic" picture of vortices interacting only near the borders of the sample when studying geometric phases in parallel nanowires.
We propose a method to identify linear regressions with heteroskedastic errors in all variables, including the independent ones.
Heteroskedasticity occurs when the variability of the error term is not constant but depends on the value of the independent variable.
We show that this identification problem is related to the classic problem of identifying models with endogenous variables.
We propose a method that combines instrumental variables with generalized method of moments estimators to identify these models.
An application to a model of demand for gasoline in the US illustrates the method.
We study constraints on the exchange of matter particles between two spatial regions for a class of asymptotically safe matter models.

We show that if the exchange of particles is suppressed at late times (or large distances) then it is suppressed already at early times (or small distances), and provide an estimate on the suppression strength.
This result may be viewed as a consistency check on matter models coupled to an asymptotically safe gravity theory.

We discuss implications of our result for matter models based on scalar fields, as well as for (super)gravity matter models in a systematic way, and show that it excludes the presence of a fixed point for matter models containing a gauge particle content.
In the case of scalar fields, going beyond leading order in the matching is crucial to derive the suppression, and for fermions leading order is already sufficient.
Single crystals of URhIn$_{5}$ were synthesized and their magnetic properties were investigated.
URhIn$_{5}$ exhibits a second-order magnetic phase transition at T$_{N}$ = 35.4 K from the paramagnetic (PM) to the antiferromagnetic (AFM) phase.
The magnetic ordering in the AFM phase was found to be anisotropic.
The compound becomes ferromagnetic (FM) below T$_{C1}$ = 12 K.
This ferromagnetic phase is a result of the magnetic ordering of the uranium ions.
The compound turns ferromagnetic again at T$_{C2}$ = 3.2 K.
This second ferromagnetic phase is attributed to the ordering of both the uranium and the rhodium sublattices.

Magnetic susceptibility measurements show that the compound has a large positive magnetic susceptibility in the PM state, which becomes negative once the compound undergoes the antiferromagnetic transition.
The magnetic anisotropy was investigated by measuring the magnetic susceptibility along different high-symmetry directions in a magnetic field of 10 kOe.
The temperature dependence of the magnetization was measured for fields applied parallel and perpendicular to the [001] direction.
The magnetocaloric effect was also investigated for this compound.
The tendency towards the superconducting transition of niobium thin films grown on BiOCl substrate is investigated.
It is shown that the heterostructure has a favorable effect on the superconducting properties of Nb.
The critical temperature of Nb films on BiOCl is higher in comparison with that of the Nb films grown on sapphire substrates.

Micro-Raman analysis of the thin Nb films in the BiOCl/Nb heterostructures indicates the presence of the superstructure with the propagation vector (1/2 0 1/2) that might be related to the mechanism of the intrinsic superconductivity.

In this work, we consider the Ott-Antonsen (OA) condition, which is a sufficient condition for the boundary-controlling effect of a frequency-selective input, to be attractive for oscillatory networks.
Specifically, this condition is dependent on a parameter $\mu$, which quantifies how the eigenvalues of the linear system response vary with the frequency of the input.
We show that the OA condition is attractive for sufficiently large $\mu$, and we characterize the rate of convergence in terms of the largest eigenvalue of the linear system.
Furthermore, we illustrate our results with a computational example.
We find necessary and sufficient conditions for a graph to be almost hypohamiltonian, i.e., to be as close as possible to hypohamiltonian without actually being so.
These conditions are in terms of the existence of certain walks in the graph.
The main tools are a potential function for almost hypohamiltonian graphs and a new notion of incompatible pairs of vertices.
This paper is a continuation of our previous work, where we studied hypohamiltonian graphs, i.e., graphs that are as close as possible to being hamiltonian without actually being so.
In that work, we found necessary and sufficient conditions for a graph to be hypohamiltonian in terms of the existence of certain cycles in the graph.

This new result generalizes our previous result in two ways: first, by replacing hamiltonian cycles with hamiltonian connections, and second, by replacing the hypohamiltonian connection potential function with the almost hypohamiltonian connection potential function.
Previously, the only general results on hamiltonian connections were those of Li and Wang, who studied hamiltonian-connected graphs that are also edge-maximal.
Our result is the first to provide a general sufficient condition for a graph to be almost hamiltonian-connected in terms of the existence of short walks.
We improve the recent asymptotic formula of Alexopoulos and Mount for the coefficients of multivariate generating functions in two ways.
First, we simplify the previous expression for the main term.
Second, we show that the previously reported term of higher order is in fact of lower order.
We propose a coherent-state approach for representing and experimentally detecting non-Abelian anyons, focusing on Majorana fermions as the simplest example.

We show that the coherent-state representation provides a straightforward way of understanding the topological transformation properties of anyons, and offer a simple physical picture of non-Abelian statistics.
Within this representation, we propose a scheme to detect and distinguish different anyonic charges by measuring only a few properties of a quantum state, without explicitly reconstructing the state.
We apply the scheme to a concrete model of Kitaev's Majorana wires, and show that only two out of sixteen distinct Majorana modes need to be measured to distinguish all the possible charges.
We study a system of two driven, dissipative, nonlinear cavities coupled via a beam splitter with single and two-photon exchange.

By means of a master equation analysis, we compute the mean photon number, entanglement and coherence, and show that the driven cavities can reach a steady state in which all these quantities are strongly enhanced, in comparison to the cases where only single-photon exchange or no coupling is present.
In particular, we find that the presence of two-photon exchange is crucial to achieve spin squeezing in this system.
We then propose and analyze a protocol to prepare such a steady state, showing that a single-mode squeezed vacuum state is a good approximation of the steady state for realistic parameters.
Cellular networks are facing an exponential increase in data traffic due to the ever-increasing number of mobile devices and demanding applications.
To mitigate this issue, network operators are continuously striving to improve the spectral efficiency of their networks.

One of the key technologies enabling this is smart antenna systems, which utilize multiple antennas at the base station to shape and steer beams in the direction of interested users, therefore improving the throughput and link quality.
In this paper, a new reconfigurable reflectarray for dynamic beam control is proposed.
The reflectarray is designed to operate at microwave frequencies with a frequency-independent phase response, enabling wideband beam steering.
The proposed reflectarray is integrated with a lens to form a reconfigurable lens-reflectarray antenna system.
The reconfigurable lens is designed to have a variable focal length, which, in conjunction with the reconfigurable reflectarray, results in dynamic beam control.
The performance of the proposed antenna system is analyzed and compared to that of a conventional lens-reflectarray system with a fixed focal length.
The results show that the proposed reconfigurable lens-reflectarray system can achieve better beam control and can be used for various beam-patterning applications.
We give an algorithm to test if a given convex polyhedron in three-dimensional space has the property of being covered by finitely many translates of a given convex body $K$, up to congruence.
This extends a result of Goulart and the second author [GM13] for the case $K=\Box$. The algorithm is based on an adaptation of the o-minimal theory machinery to the setting of convex polyhedra.
We have studied the $^{24}$Mg($p$, $\alpha$)$^{21}$Na reaction with the aim of producing a beam of $^{21}$Na atoms for spectroscopy.

A thin polyethylene target was exposed to a $^{24}$Mg beam at a beam energy of 49.5 MeV and a current of 2.7 μA. The produced $^{21}$Na atoms were separated from the $^{24}$Mg beam by means of the Si(111) channel plate and two sets of quadrupole magnets in an opposed field configuration, and collected onto a copper target.
The $\alpha$-activity of the copper target was measured with an HPGe detector in order to obtain the yield of $^{21}$Na.
From the measured activity we obtained a total cross section of $\sigma_{\rm{tot}}$ = 156 ± 18 mb for the $^{24}$Mg($p$, $\alpha$)$^{21}$Na reaction.
Aperture synthesis imaging can reconstruct the object with a higher resolution than the diffraction limit, but the size of the reconstructed field of view (FOV) is limited by the pupil function.

Near-field aperture synthesis imaging (NFASI) can extend the FOV by reducing the pupil function during the near-field imaging, but the reconstructed image suffers from the phase wrapping problem, because the pupil function is proportional to the reciprocal of the distance between the object and the relay lens.

We propose a method to unwrap the phase of the reconstructed image by calculating the distance between the object and the relay lens from the pupil function, and show that the unwrapped image has a better peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) than the wrapped image.
We also analyze the factors that limit the FOV of NFASI, and suggest that the FOV can be further extended by scaling the pupil function and adjusting the distance between the relay lenses.
Spectroscopic imaging data from photon-counting detectors often contain complex artifacts that must be addressed to enable accurate analysis of the data.

We have previously introduced Q-space sampling as a method of mitigating artifacts in single-shell data, in which the data are represented as a series of weighted integrations across an array of detector pixels.
Here we generalize this approach to multishell data and demonstrate that a similar approach can be applied to diffusion spectrum data as well.
We provide an open-source implementation of the weighted integration across detector pixels as a Python package, `qspace_sampling`, and provide examples of its use for both simulated and real data.

The Third Gravitational Lensing Accuracy Testing (GREAT3) Challenge Handbook summarizes the ongoing work of the GREAT3 collaboration, which is performing a rigorous test of gravitational lensing as a tool for astrophysical measurement.
The collaboration compares measurements of the same gravitational lens made by many different research groups, to evaluate the systematics and uncertainties in the measurements.
This comparison is done in a blind fashion, so that evaluators do not know which group took which measurement when performing the comparison.
This challenge has run twice before, in 2004 and 2009, and has spurred significant improvements in lensing measurement techniques.
We present the protocols for the third challenge, as well as an overview of the current state of the field.
A summary of the current state of the challenge is also provided.
We survey the history and present state of a certain class of integral transforms, commonly called Backlund transformations, which are of interest in mathematical physics and complex analysis.
These transformations, first considered by Backlund in 1926, are generalizations of the well-known K\"ahler-Bessel transformations.

They share many of the same properties, including a reduction to ``seed'' solutions depending upon the values of a complex parameter, and a description as compositions of particular elementary functions.
However, they also exhibit new and interesting features, including a parameter dependent monodromy phenomenon, and a lack of boundedness in certain directions.
We will discuss some of these characteristics, and survey results on the existence and uniqueness of Backlund transformations, as well as some of their applications.
In particular, we will discuss new results on the boundedness and growth of the transforms, and an application to the study of boundary value problems for partial differential equations.
We report on the excitation and direct imaging of resonant optical modes of Au triangular nano-antennas using cathodoluminescence spectroscopy and a field-emission scanning electron microscope.

Different from the case of diffraction limited optics, the nanoscale optical field distribution and its spectral response can be obtained directly by scanning a few nanometer-sized electron beam focused on a single plasmonic antenna, showing in detail the modal resonance, its spectral width, and the field enhancement.
The experimental results are in good agreement with finite-difference time-domain simulations.
We demonstrate how the antenna geometry, size, and material composition govern the optical resonance, from the fundamental to higher order modes.

Our approach opens new possibilities for the study of optical antenna properties at the nanoscale, for basic research and for nano-antenna engineering with view to applications in nanophotonics and quantum optics.
Spectral engineering of microcavities relies on the ability to control the frequency of photonic states.
Here, we propose a new approach to spectral engineering, whereby the splitting between adjacent photonic states is controlled via engineered coherent coupling.
Our approach is based on the theory of mode-splitting induced by coherent coupling between microring resonators.
We show that by tailoring the coupling rate, one can actively control the splitting between the adjacent photonic states, resulting in different photonic band structures.

Our work may open up new opportunities for active control of photonic band structures, and may have applications in on-chip spectroscopy, optical signal processing, and quantum information processing.
In this paper we continue the study of differentiable inertia manifolds of groupoids started in [1], [2].
We show that, just as for manifolds, these objects form a stratified groupoid, for which we define the notion of a differentiable stratified inertia space.
This allows us to prove a de Rham theorem for these spaces, from which we deduce a long exact sequence for certain relative singular homology groups.
We consider the problem of ensuring that a program meets a specified security policy, expressed as a logic formula.

Static analysis cannot always provide a conclusive answer to the question of whether a program satisfies a formula, so we aim to characterize a sound approximation of the set of satisfying executions, namely secure configurations.
In this paper we propose a novel approach to compute secure configurations based on majority rule inference, which combines ideas from abstract interpretation and model checking.
Our approach is sound, complete, and optimally scalable.
As a case study, we consider the problem of detecting unauthorized information flow, and show that previous approaches can be seen as particular instances of our framework.
We implemented our approach in the SparkSeer tool and applied it to several standard security policies.
Our experimental results show that our approach is scalable and outperforms existing tools in terms of precision and recall.
We study the extremal properties of flood-filling games, introduced by Brown et al.
These games generalize the well-known Flood-it-Out game, where the objective is to sequentially flood cells until all cells are flooded, so that the total number of cells flooded is minimized.
We obtain tight bounds on the optimal values of these games, and show that the associated optimal strategies have a simple structure.
In particular, we show that these strategies can be described by a finite state automaton, and use this to obtain an approximation algorithm with ratio (2 + ε) for a related problem.

Abstract:
    We perform an empirical investigation of the Zipf strategy for short-term investments in WIG20 futures.
The strategy is based on the hypothesis that the ranks of the returns of the most valuable components of the WIG20 portfolio have some predictive power for the future returns.
In the experimental part we evaluate the performance of the strategy by comparing it with the buy-and-hold strategy and with the strategy of investing in the most valuable component at each moment.
We find that the Zipf strategy, despite its simplicity, may provide a significant advantage over the other strategies for short investment horizons, like one day.
We propose a new, very general, electrostatic 1-D model of a Charge-Controlled Active Constrained Layer (CC-ACL) beam, applicable to a large class of CC-ACL beam geometries.
The model is based on the electrostatic assumptions of quasi-static, fully-dynamic, and continuous charge distribution.
In these three cases, the beam is described by a partial differential equation in terms of the transverse coordinate and the charge density, with or without a time-varying electric field.
In all three cases, a semigroup formulation of the model exists, and we prove existence and uniqueness of a solution for a given initial condition.
Furthermore, we discuss several ways to approximate the solution of the model, and we give some numerical results illustrating the behavior of the model.

Two-dimensional (2D) transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDCs) have been considered for rechargeable lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) due to their superior electrical conductivity and excellent cycling stability.
However, the theoretical capacity of 2D TMDCs is far from being achieved, which motivates an in-depth study of the electrochemical reaction mechanism of this class of materials.
Herein, we use molecular dynamics (MD) simulations to study the anode materials of monolayer MoS2 in LIBs.

Our results show that lithium ions prefer to intercalate into the van der Waals gap of monolayer MoS2 between two neighboring layers with a high diffusion rate rather than directly inserting into the monolayer.

We propose a "raft-insertion-migration" mechanism for lithium ion intercalation in which lithium ions first attach to the edge of a monolayer MoS2 nanoparticle and then migrate into the van der Waals gap between two neighboring layers, causing the layers to split.
Our proposed mechanism explains why few layered TMDCs are good anode materials while bulk TMDCs are not, and it provides guidance toward the development of high-capacity anode materials.
We consider the local quantum uncertainty (LQU) in two-qubit arbitrary pure states under the assumption of separability.
The LQU is shown to be extensively affected by the presence of the global phase factor associated with the two-qubit state.
For a given state, it is shown that the local quantum uncertainty is minimized when the global phase factor is equal to one.
We derive a simple explicit expression for the LQU of two-qubit states in terms of their entropy and a measure of non-separability.
Interestingly, this result generalizes to higher dimensions without any modification.
The case study of a two-qubit system helps reveal the underlying properties of LQU in high-dimensional systems.
Let $(X,\|\cdot\|)$ be a Banach space and $\mathcal B(X)$ the corresponding Borel $\sigma$-algebra.
Let $\mathcal M _{0}(\mathcal B(X))$ be the class of all regular Borel measures on $\mathcal B(X)$ and let $\mathcal P(\mathcal B(X))$ be the subset of all probability measures.

The abstract:
We investigate the properties of continuous and bounded functions $f\in C(X)$ which admit an interpolation formula of the form $$f(\lambda x+(1-\lambda)y)\leq \lambda f(x)+(1-\lambda)f(y)$$ for all $\lambda \in (0,1)$ and $x,y\in X$.

We show that for $f\in C(X)$ which admits such an interpolation formula, there is a chain $\{x_{n}\}_{n=1}^{\infty}$ in $X$ such that $$f(x)\leq \frac{1}{2}\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}f(x_{n})$$ for all $x\in X$.
Moreover, if $f$ is convex, then this chaining property is equivalent to $f$ admitting the above interpolation formula.
Applying similar techniques, we generalize a recent result of Heinonen and Virtanen on chaining probability measures in the sense of convex analysis.
We prove that evacuation in the social force model is not stationary, which means that the evacuation process changes the relative positions of pedestrians over time.
Our proof is based on a construction of two evolutions of the same initial configuration that result in different final configurations.
This proves that the evolution of the system depends on the details of the initial configuration.
In particular, we show that the social force model does not satisfy the detailed balance condition.
A key ingredient of our proof is a slight generalization of the well-known critical region for the social force model.
We present a systematic way of constructing critical regions for the social force model with general exogenous acceleration costs and pacing costs.
We propose a Performance analysis of an improved MUSIC Direction-of-Arrival (DoA) estimator, which utilizes the MUSIC algorithm for DoA estimation of a uniform linear array (ULA).

In our improved algorithm, we employ the eigenvalue decomposition (EVD) and the Toeplitz structure of the correlation matrix to reduce the computational complexity, as well as a new technique to select the parameter in the MUSIC algorithm, which is based on the use of the Cauchy prior.
By using these improvements, we enhance the performance of the MUSIC DoA estimator.

In this paper, we analyze the performance of our improved algorithm by calculating the root mean square error (RMSE) and the mean absolute error (MAE) between the DoAs estimated by the improved algorithm and the true angles.
The performance analysis is carried out by varying the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and the number of sources.

The results show that our improved algorithm provides a significant performance improvement in comparison to the conventional MUSIC algorithm, especially for low SNR values and a small number of sources.

In functional data analysis, simultaneous inference is generally ignored in favour of the widely applied separate-fitting approach, wherein the parameters of each curve are inferred individually, despite being part of a covariable process.
The prevailing attitude is that individual fitting is more straightforward and robust, whereas simultaneous inference is overly complex and fragile.
This paper revisits the issue of simultaneous inference in the setting of misaligned multivariate functional data.
We show that existing methods based on the assumption of alignment across curves can be relatively easily extended to the misaligned setting, using a simple alignment algorithm.
This extension is shown to improve efficiency in a simulation study, and is illustrated on an application to a molecular dynamics dataset.
We show that the strong monogamy conjecture is valid in arbitrary four-qubit systems.
Our approach is based on the concept of majorization, and we provide an example that shows that the strong monogamy relation does not hold for higher-qubit systems.
In this note, we present an elementary proof of a recent result of Bergelson–Härtner–Hjorthøj–Randerath on the spectral gap of the unitary groups.
We also present a generalization of their result to the metaplectic group.
As a byproduct, we give a simpler proof of Rider's result on the existence of non-commutative Sidon sets.
We give a brief overview of the Seiberg-Witten geometry of four-dimensional $\mathcal N=2$ quiver gauge theories with fundamental and adjoint matter.
We then specialize to the case of cyclic quivers and compute the Seiberg-Witten invariants for theories with an arbitrary number of fundamental and adjoint matters.

Finally, we determine the exact Seiberg-Witten geometry for cyclic quivers with one fundamental and one adjoint matter in the large radius limit, and compare it with the corresponding result for three-dimensional $\mathcal N=4$ superconformal field theories.
Let $(X,d)$ be a fuzzy metric space, i.e. $d: X \times X \rightarrow
[0,1]$ is a fuzzy metric on $X$.
In this paper, we define Cauchy sequence and Cauchy completeness for fuzzy metric spaces and study some fixed point results for self-mappings in fuzzy metric spaces with Cauchy completeness.

We show that the principle of information causality imposes limits on the correlations that can be achieved between the measurements on a set of particles, with respect to all measurements within a causal diamond shared by the particles.
These limits are shown to be analogous to the Bell inequalities, with the maximal violation attainable by local causal models serving as an analogue of the Tsirelson bounds.

When the number of particles is three or more, these limits rule out genuine multipartite correlations, and any theory describing such correlations must be nonlocal in a manner analogous to quantum mechanics.
When the number of particles is two, however, we show that such correlations are bound by a more stringent limit, which is not produced by any local causal model.
We discuss the implications of these results for the compatibility of nonlocal correlations with causal models.
We propose a data-fitted generalized Aw-Rascle-Zhang (ARZ) model for comparison to existing ARZ models.
We show that the data-fitted ARZ model provides a better fit to the data in a comparative study.
The proposed model is based on a modification of the existing ARZ model that utilizes a data-fitting technique to improve the accuracy of the model.
The modification involves the fitting of a second-order polynomial to the difference between the observed and predicted values of the ARZ model.
The data-fitted ARZ model provides a better fit to the data, as evidenced by the reduced root mean square error and the increased coefficient of determination.
We propose to use the data-fitted ARZ model for the analysis of real-world data, such as that from wind tunnels.
We show that the data-fitted ARZ model provides a more accurate fit to the data from wind tunnels, as compared to the existing ARZ model.
This is evidenced by the reduced root mean square error and the increased coefficient of determination.
We also show that the data-fitted ARZ model is more accurate than the existing ARZ model in the prediction of the wind tunnel data.
This is evidenced by the reduced root mean square error and the increased coefficient of determination in the prediction error.
Our proposed method can be used as a general procedure for improving the accuracy of existing ARZ models or any other mathematical model with adjustable parameters.
This can be achieved by fitting a second-order polynomial to the difference between the observed and predicted values of the model.
The resulting data-fitted model provides a better fit to the data and is more accurate in the prediction of future data.

We show that high index nanowires resonators coupled to waveguides can provide broadband quantum efficiency enhancement in the weak coupling regime for all non-resonant incident photons, regardless of their polarization and wave vector.

By solving Maxwell's equations analytically for a nanowire of any given index surrounded by a cladding of any index, we first derive the conditions on the resonance wavelengths, showing that they depend only on the geometric parameters of the nanowire and are independent of the cladding index.

Then, we investigate the quantum efficiency enhancement for various incident photons, showing that the efficiency can be increased by an order of magnitude or more for a large range of incident wavelengths, for any polarization and wave vector.

This result suggests that such structures can be used to efficiently couple light into high index nanowires from standard optical fibers, regardless of the polarization and the wave vector of the incident light.
We further show that in the strong coupling regime, the quantum efficiency enhancement is reduced, but can still be significant for certain configurations of incident light.

Additionally, we investigate the effect of the cladding index on the broadband quantum efficiency enhancement in the weak coupling regime, and show that it is minimized when the cladding index is equal to the average index of the nanowire and the waveguide.
These results provide insight into the optimal design of high index nanowire-based devices for light coupling and harvesting applications.

Our results show that the use of high index nanowire resonators coupled to waveguides can provide a simple and effective approach to enhance the quantum efficiency of light absorption in a broad range of wavelengths and for any polarization and wave vector of incident light.
This approach can lead to the development of more efficient solar cells, photodetectors, and other light-harvesting devices.
We study local spectral radius formulas for a class of unbounded operators on Banach spaces.
These results may be viewed as extensions of corresponding finite-dimensional results obtained by Bergelson and Leibman.
We give a complete description of Margulis cusps of hyperbolic 4-manifolds with finite volume and at least eight vertices, proving a conjecture of Agol.

We derive a time-dependent variational principle for the ground state of a trapped ion in a time-dependent Hamiltonian that is well-approximated by a time-independent Hamiltonian at each point in time.
The method employs coherent states for the atomic orbitals in the variational principle.

The time-dependent variational principle is used to calculate ion ground state energies for a time-dependent Hamiltonian model of an ion trapped by a static electric field, together with an additional time-dependent driving field.
Comparison is made with ion ground state energies computed by means of other methods, including a path-integral ground state approximation, and also exact quantum Monte Carlo methods.
The coherent state orbit method provides reasonable agreement with these other methods, and has the advantage of being much less computer time-intensive.
We study a model of a quantum particle in a quantum environment using numerical simulations in a quantum Monte Carlo framework.

The quantum particle is described by a hydrogenic impurity problem formalized as a Many-Body Quantum Dot in a Quantum Environment (MBDQE) model, whereas the environment is modeled as a quantum bath, specifically, a one-dimensional Bose-Einstein condensate.
We investigate the effects of the environment on the particle's ground state and low-lying excited states as the interaction between the particle and the environment is varied.

Additionally, we examine the particle's density matrix and the environment's reduced density matrix throughout the calculations to diagnose the environment's impact on the quantum particle and the emergence of thermal, coherent, or mixed correlations.

We find that as the interaction between the particle and the environment is increased, the particle's low-lying excited states experience a degradation in their quality, and the system as a whole exhibits characteristics akin to a classical system.
The environment's reduced density matrix at late times exhibits a thermal-like form, and thermal, coherent, and mixed correlations are observed throughout the calculations.
These findings provide insight into the dynamics of a quantum particle in a quantum environment and the emergence of classical behavior in open quantum systems.
The MDBQE model presented herein can be applied to investigate the effects of a quantum environment on different quantum particles and systems.
We study universal quantum circuits that employ only the controlled NOT and single qubit rotations about the X and Z axes.
We show that such circuits can simulate the action of the spin(3n) groups in a straightforward way.
This establishes a close connection between universal quantum computation and the spin groups and provides a new way of understanding the latter.

We propose a method to calculate the Casimir-Lifshitz free energy for a general geometric configuration of the electromagnetic
  cavity.

We consider a cavity whose walls are described by scalar curvature R. The Casimir-Lifshitz free energy is expressed in terms of the
  eigenvalues of the Laplace operator on a spherical box in the cavity.

We introduce a modification of the regularized free energy,
  which enables us to perform an iterative summation over the eigenvalues.

Resembling the method of the Casimir force for ideal
  metallic plates, we utilize the eigenfunctions of the Laplace operator in spherical coordinates for the regularization.

We verify the
  Nernst theorem, which relates the Casimir-Lifshitz free energy and the entropy of the field configuration, for a cavity of a sphere and
  a cylinder.
We present graphical structures for design and verification of quantum error correction codes.
These graphical structures facilitate quantum circuit design, and provide a tool for reasoning about the quantum computations, and for quantum circuit verification.
The proposed graphical structures capture the underlying quantum operations, as well as the logical structure of the quantum error correction circuits.
The graphical structures are formalized using the quantum circuit verification language LIQUi|> and validated on a set of quantum error correction circuits.
We investigate the effect of atomic collisions on the itinerant magnetism induced by spin-orbit coupling in spin-1 Bose gases.

By solving the Gross-Pitaevskii equation with spin-orbit coupling and the collision term, we show that the repulsive interactions actually enhance the magnetism, in contrast to the common understanding that they destroy the order of spin systems.
The reason is that the repulsive interactions shorten the life time of magnetized quasiparticles, making them more responsive to the external magnetic fields.
This enhances the magnetoresistance.
We also find that the magnetism is suppressed by attractive interactions, which extend the life time of magnetized quasiparticles.
Our results may find applications in tuning the itinerant magnetism with atomic collisions.

We propose a common approach to three open problems in number theory, which includes the open problem of Goldbach's conjecture, the open problem of Euler'stotient function, and the open problem of the partition function.
Our approach is based on the use of the Hardy-Littlewood method, and we use this method to prove some results regarding these problems.
First, we use the Hardy-Littlewood method to prove that the limit of the ratio of the number of Goldbach partitions of n to the number of 3-partitions of n is equal to 1/2.
This proves a conjecture of B. R. Holstein and R. J. Motley.

Second, we use the Hardy-Littlewood method to estimate the Euler's totient function and to prove that the number of primes less than or equal to a given number x is approximately equal to x/log(x), which proves a conjecture of H. Davenport.
Third, we use the Hardy-Littlewood method to derive an asymptotic formula for the partition function, which proves a conjecture of S. Ramanujan.
These results show that the Hardy-Littlewood method is a powerful tool for attacking problems in number theory, and may be used to prove other results regarding these problems in the future.
Key words: Goldbach's conjecture, Euler's totient function, partition function, Hardy-Littlewood method.
We present an original computational method to perform Bayesian optimal experimental design (BOED) for seismic source inversion.
The proposed method contemporarily optimizes the locations and properties of the seismic sources, thereby enabling the most effective and efficient way to infer a physical property of interest.

We employ a fast Bayesian inversion algorithm, named Smooth Particle Mesh Ewald (SPME), to perform the inversion in an iterative way, with the forward modeling and data misfit calculation performed on the particle mesh, while the inverse update is performed on the Ewald mesh.

This allows us to implement the BOED strategy in an efficient way, by running several inversion iterations per dwell location, hence enabling the simultaneous optimization of the source location and its properties.
We demonstrate the most promising features of the proposed method on a 2D problem, where the goal is to determine the spatial distribution of the Young's modulus of a porous solid medium.
Recent years have witnessed an explosion of research on mining and analyzing social media data.
With the proliferation of social media platforms, such as Twitter, Facebook, and Weibo, huge amounts of data are generated, posing new challenges for data mining researchers and practitioners.
This paper gives an overview of the emerging area of social media analysis with a focus on data mining techniques.
We first provide an introduction to social media data, including its unique characteristics and challenges.
We then survey the most commonly used data mining techniques in social media analysis, including text mining, social network analysis, and sentiment analysis.
We also discuss some of the most important research issues and open questions in this field.

Our goal is to provide a comprehensive and timely survey of the data mining techniques used in social media analysis, which can serve as a reference for researchers and practitioners working in this field.
Articular cartilage plays a essential role in the performance and proper function of joints, and its degeneration is a major cause of pain and loss of mobility.

While there is a substantial body of knowledge on the biology of articular cartilage, the process of lesion formation and the relationship between cellular and mechanical processes therein is not yet fully understood.
In this paper, we present a mathematical model that links cellular and mechanical processes in articular cartilage lesion formation.

The model is based on a systems approach and takes into account the key processes involved in cartilage degeneration, including the production and degradation of extracellular matrix (ECM), cell death, and the relationship between cell morphology and mechanical stress.
The model is formulated as a system of nonlinear differential equations and is solved using a combination of numerical and analytical methods.
The results of the model are compared to existing experimental data and show good agreement.
The model can be used to predict the progression of cartilage lesion formation and to evaluate the effectiveness of various therapeutic interventions.
We study the scattering of light by closely packed spherical particles which are homogenous and much smaller than the wavelength, in the limit of finite size particles.

We derive an analytical expression of the scattering amplitude for such systems, and show that it exhibits a specific radial anisotropy, displaying a super-directional halo with its maximum centered on the forward direction, and extending up to backscattering angles.
This anisotropy is shown to arise from the interference between the scattering from the particle surface and from its interior.

Our result shows that, in the limit of finite size particles, directional homogeneity is restored in systems of homogenous spherical particles, as opposed to what is commonly believed for infinitely small particles.

We estimate the impact of individual NBA players on their team's probability of winning games using a machine learning approach that leverages the player's in-game statistics and an interpretable deep learning model.
Our model captures the complex interactions between players and the game state, including the quality of teammates, opponents, and the game's score.

We find that the model generates reasonably accurate predictions for the majority of players and that the most impactful players tend to be stars who are selected for All-Star games and have a high number of total wins.
However, we also find that the model tends to overfit to the training data and underperform in out-of-sample predictions, particularly for players who have fewer games played.

We conclude that while our approach is a promising starting point for evaluating player impact, it needs to be augmented with domain-specific knowledge and a more robust out-of-sample evaluation procedure.
An emerging direction in transistor miniaturization is to use ions as the active dopants for controlling conduction.

The ion gel gated oxide transistors have attracted significant attention due to their low power consumption, fast voltage-controlled switching, and ease of processing as compared to legacy Si-based FETs.
Here, we adopt a UHV scanning force microscope to image the carrier evolution at nanoscale directly on an insulating sample in an ambient environment.

By imaging the nanoscale surface potential in an ion-gel-gated oxide transistor, we find that the accumulated charges are distributed in an inhomogeneous manner at the nanoscale, which can be explained by the combination of the intrinsic inhomogeneous charge distribution in the oxide and the gel induced charge redistribution.

Our results provide important insights for understanding the nanoscale charge distribution, which is critical for improving the performance of ion-gel-gated oxide transistors and for developing new strategies for transistor scaling.
We propose a new system of inductive types in homotopy type theory, based on a generalization of the classical dependently typed inductive-inductive definition.
This new system supports a formulation of the univalence axiom, as well as an analogue of parametricity for higher inductive types.
We present examples illustrating the use of our system, and we compare it with existing systems of inductive types for homotopy type theory.
In atomic force microscopy (AFM), the tip of an atomic force microscope (AFM) sensor interacts with the sample surface periodically through intermittent contact.
The AFM tip is mounted on a cantilever beam with a low spring constant so that the tip can deflect vertically on a nanometer scale when it comes into contact with the sample surface.
The AFM operates in the non-contact mode or intermittent contact mode, in which the AFM tip is oscillated at the resonance frequency and the sample surface is scanned.
When the AFM tip comes into contact with the sample surface, the AFM tip begins to interact with the sample surface.
This interaction will cause the amplitude of the oscillation of the AFM tip to decrease.
By plotting the amplitude of the oscillation of the AFM tip versus the tip-sample distance, the so-called amplitude-modulated (AM) mode AFM can map the sample surface with nanometer resolution.
However, the AFM images are affected by the unsteady behavior of the AFM system, which may lead to inaccurate measurements of the sample surface height and roughness.
In this paper, a novel approach is presented to control the AFM system to improve the stability of the AFM images.
The control strategy is based on the linearization of the AFM system and the use of a PID controller.
The simulation and experimental results show that the proposed control strategy can significantly improve the stability of the AFM images.
Magnetic dipole radiation is generally regarded as weak because of the low magnetic permeability of the vacuum and the resultant low radiation efficiency.
However, recent experiments have demonstrated that the radiation can be enhanced by several orders of magnitude through the use of metamaterials.
In this work, we investigate the magnetic dipole radiation in substrates with different permeabilities, and our results show that the radiation can be tailored by the substrates.
The main findings are that the substrate with higher permeability can lead to higher radiation efficiency, and that the radiation pattern is highly dependent on the substrate.
The proposed method for enhancing magnetic dipole radiation can find applications in various fields, such as communication, sensing and imaging.
Inversion recovery (IR) is a powerful technique for measuring T1 in tissues, but intrinsically sacrifices some fraction of the signal during the initial portion of the recovery period.

The additional T1 relaxation caused by radiative damping can be a significant cause of this signal loss, particularly for T1 measurements in tissues with a high content of electrons, such as grey matter and lung.

We present a simple model for the radiative damping of both the longitudinal and transverse magnetization, which is in good agreement with both simulations and experimental measurements in a range of tissues.

We then explore a number of strategies for mitigating the effects of radiative damping in IR measurements, and find that a simple, experimentally feasible approach of waiting for a long recovery period after the IR pulse is often effective.
We calculate the Gromov-Witten invariants of symplectic forms on $\mathbb{P}^r$ and on $\mathrm{Sym}^d\mathbb{P}^r$, for $r\geq 3$ and $d\geq 2$.

The technique is to make use of the relation between Gromov-Witten invariants and the intersection theory on the moduli space of curves, and the fact that the symplectic form on $\mathrm{Sym}^d\mathbb{P}^r$ is induced from the symplectic form on $\mathbb{P}^r$.
We introduce the notion of Riemann-Hilbert minors for high order three-term recursions (ith order for i = 1, 2, ...) and show how to compute them using Nikishin systems.
This extends a result of Gonek for the second order case.
As an application we give an alternative proof for a result of Yang on the star-likeness of the sets defined by high order recursions.
This proof does not use the notion of multiple orthogonality, which was key in the original proof.
In this paper we investigate sub-propositional fragments of modal logics.
We show that the classical modal logic KBA is complete with respect to a class of finite models, namely the class of all finite sets.
For a class of finite models which contains the class of all finite graphs we show that the modal logic KB is complete.
Furthermore, we show that these results can be obtained by a natural deduction system and we present a cut-elimination theorem for this system.

We prove an analogue of Davis' result on the logical strength of Paris' and Harrington's theorem about the decidability of the theory of real closed fields, for B\"uchi's theorem on the decidability of first-order logic with counting.

We consider the graph colouring number $\chi'(G)$ of a graph $G$, which is the smallest number of colours in a proper colouring of $G$, where no colour is used by more than one vertex of a fixed minor of $G$. Mullera and Nipkow showed that for a fixed graph $H$, $\chi'(G)\leq \chi(G)+|V(H)|$ where $\chi(G)$ is the usual graph colouring number of $G$. In this note we raise the question of whether the inequality is tight in general.
We answer this in the affirmative for graphs $G$ that exclude $K_4$ as a minor, thereby improving the known bounds on $\chi'(G)$ in this case.
The proof uses a recent theorem of Dvořák, Postulík, and Tužíková which asserts that every graph $G$ with treewidth at most $k$ either contains $K_4$ as a minor or else $\chi(G)\leq 3k$.
We give a simple proof of the crepant resolution conjecture for cubic fourfold intersections in projective space, and derive some new consequences for mirror symmetry and string theory.
Our proof is inspired by considerations from string theory, and makes essential use of the geometry of open strings.
As a step toward our proof we establish a new algebraic result: the augmented base locus of a cubic fourfold is a union of (possibly non-reduced) conics.

We design and optimize a kinesin-based, on-chip substrate to generate molecular messages that can be transported
  via the growth of actin filaments.

We treat the transport of molecular messages via the growth of actin filaments as a
  transportation problem where a molecular transmitter is transported to molecular receivers.

We first present an
  architecture of the on-chip substrate where a library of different molecular messages are stored.

We then use
  computational fluid dynamics to determine the optimal geometrical design of the substrate to guarantee a maximum flow of
  the molecular messages.
We propose three different designs to transport the molecular messages.

We implement the
  designs using multi-photon lithography.

We use a fluorescent microscopy-based method to quantify the transport of
  the molecular messages.

The experimental results show that our approach can be used to transport molecular messages
  between a transmitter and receiver.

The photoelectric effect (PE) is a phenomenon in which a substance releases electrons after absorbing a photon with energy greater than the material's binding energy, posing a significant challenge in the field of renewable energy research.
In this study, we propose a new mechanism for harvesting heat energy using the photoelectric effect.
We theoretically analyze the PE induced by single photons on a blackbody radiation source, which has a continuous distribution of wavelengths and frequencies.
Our results show that the PE can indeed be induced by blackbody radiation, and the maximum PE occurs at an intermediate frequency.
This research provides a new perspective on the utilization of heat energy and offers a potential solution for efficient heat energy harvesting.
A detailed and unified study of criteria for measures of quantum correlations is presented.
After briefly reviewing the fundamental limitations on measuring correlations, we analyze in detail several recently proposed criteria for measures of quantum correlations.
In contrast to previous studies, our analysis covers all major types of criteria, including those based on continuity, convexity, and contractivity conditions.

We show that most of the recently proposed criteria are inherently weaker than others and derive general necessary and sufficient conditions for these criteria in terms of simple mathematical operations.

We also present a new class of criteria that are applicable to any measure of quantum correlations and prove that they are all equivalent when the underlying measure is continuous, convex, and contractive.
Finally, we give a complete description of all possible criteria for measures of quantum correlations and illustrate our results through several examples.
Ensemble Kalman filtering (EnKF) is a powerful technique for data assimilation, but it suffers from a lack of consistency due to model error.
This paper explores the impact of model error on the EnKF and proposes a new method for accounting for model error due to unresolved scales.
By introducing a scale-dependent correction term, the new method improves the consistency of the EnKF and provides a more accurate estimation of the state and its uncertainty.
The method is evaluated using a simple toy model and a more complex non-hydrostatic atmospheric model, and it is shown to be effective in improving the accuracy of the EnKF in both cases.

Here is the abstract for the research paper titled "Accounting for model error due to unresolved scales within ensemble Kalman filtering":

"In this study, we investigate the impact of model error on the ensemble Kalman filter (EnKF) and develop a new method for accounting for model error due to unresolved scales.
We begin by analyzing the consistency of the EnKF and show that it can be violated due to model error, which can lead to inaccurate state estimates and uncertainty assessments.
To address this issue, we propose a new method that introduces a scale-dependent correction term to the EnKF.
This correction term improves the consistency of the EnKF and provides more accurate state estimates and uncertainty assessments.
We evaluate the new method using a simple toy model and a more complex non-hydrostatic atmospheric model, and show that it is effective in improving the accuracy of the EnKF in both cases.
The new method is easy to implement and does not require any additional computational cost, making it a practical tool for improving the performance of the EnKF in data assimilation applications."
We study a system of two-color fermions in a cold and magnetized state in the mean-field approximation.
By using the numerical linked-cluster expansion, we evaluate the thermodynamic potential for arbitrary values of the density and magnetization.
For large values of the magnetization, the system undergoes a transition from a normal fluid to a Bose-Einstein condensate.
On the other hand, for small values of the magnetization, the system stabilizes into a color superconducting state.

By comparing the free energies for the different phases, we determine the boundary of the coexistence region between the normal fluid and the superconducting phases, and between the normal fluid and the Bose-Einstein condensate.
We discuss the behavior of the order parameters and quasiparticle weights.

Abstract:

We study the BEC-BCS crossover in a cold and magnetized two-color NJL model.
By using the numerical linked-cluster expansion, we evaluate the thermodynamic potential for arbitrary values of the density and magnetization.

We find that the system undergoes a transition from a normal fluid to a Bose-Einstein condensate for large values of the magnetization, while it stabilizes into a color superconducting state for small values of the magnetization.

By comparing the free energies for the different phases, we determine the boundary of the coexistence region between the normal fluid and the superconducting phases, and between the normal fluid and the Bose-Einstein condensate.
The behavior of the order parameters and quasiparticle weights is discussed.

We point out similarities between (a) the quantum Zeno effect for a particle undergoing irreversible polarization, (b) the phenomenon of "Hamlet's dilemma" when deciding to kill the king in the Shakespeare play, and (c) the apparently paradoxical conclusion by Gilboa and Schmeidler [Phys. Rev. Lett.
that frequent observation of a stochastic process slows it down.
Common to all these effects is that the evolution of a system is hindered by frequent inquiries about its current state.
We analyze the simple case of a quantum particle which, in the course of time, becomes more and more polarized.
If this polarization is queried many times by a sequence of projective measurements, then the evolution is blocked: The system remains half polarized indefinitely.
We discuss under which conditions this "projective Zeno effect" can be observed and whether it can be used to stall other types of quantum evolution.
We use a mesoscale model to study aqueous colloidal suspensions with adsorbing solutes.
The model comprises hydrodynamic interactions between the particles, and explicit treatment of the solute.
The latter is modeled as a chemical species that can undergo diffusion, sorption, and desorption, and is particularly useful in describing non-ideal effects in the colloidal suspension.
Using this model, we perform a quantitative analysis of the effects of adsorbing solutes on the phase behavior of the colloidal system.
In particular, we focus on the coexistence regions of the liquid-liquid phase separation, and provide a quantitative map of the effects of adsorbing solutes in the system.
Our results show that the presence of adsorbing solutes significantly affects the phase behavior of the colloidal system, and can lead to the disappearance of coexisting phases.
We explain these findings using a simple theoretical model, and highlight the conditions under which our mesoscale model is applicable.
We show that the Bondi-Metzner-Sachs (BMS) algebra is closed under the conserved charges of three-dimensional anti-de Sitter gravity when the latter are expressed in terms of the BMS generators.
This extends a recent result of Bergshoeff, Hohm, and Tomasi on the sufficiency of the BMS algebra for describing the asymptotic symmetry group of three-dimensional anti-de Sitter gravity.
Our strategy relies on a extension of the BMS algebra that we introduce for this purpose.

This extended symmetry algebra, which we term the extended BMS algebra, is generated by a set of infinitesimal transformations that includes the BMS generators and an extra generator that is a conserved charge of anti-de Sitter gravity.

We show that the extended BMS algebra is closed under the conserved charges of anti-de Sitter gravity, and use this fact to derive a set of identities, which, in turn, allow us to prove the closure of the BMS algebra under the conserved charges.
Finally, we present an alternative formulation of our results using the recently introduced notion of asymptotic symmetries of three-dimensional gravity with a cosmological constant.
We propose a method for clustering high-dimensional sequence data using a mixture of Markov chains (MMC) with covariates, leveraging a novel representation based on trellis graphs.
The underlying joint distribution of the sequence data is modeled as a mixture of Markov chains, where the mixing weights are determined by the desired number of clusters.
Our approach incorporates covariates via a linear transformation of the raw data, enabling the capture of complex underlying relationships.

To solve the resulting optimization problem, we propose using multiple simplex constrained optimization routine (MSiCOR), a specialized algorithm for non-convex, non-differentiable, and noisy optimization problems.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on a synthetic dataset, as well as two real-world datasets.
The results show that our method can identify meaningful clusters and handle high-dimensional sequence data, with improved performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods.
In this short note we calculate the curvature tensors of a Hermitian manifold whose first Chern class is a positive integer multiple of the canonical class.
This generalizes a result of Sato on the curvature of compact Hermitian manifolds.
In this paper we introduce the concept of a determinant morphism for singular varieties, generalizing the classical concept for smooth manifolds.
We show that this generalization is naturally induced by the functor of singular homology with coefficients in a field.
We also investigate the relation of our construction with other approaches to singular homology, such as the local homology and the persistent homology.
We give an upper bound for the number of points of a modular curve $X_0(N)$ over a finite field with fixed characteristic.
This generalizes a result of Coleman on the number of points of Fermat curves.

Spin glasses are a class of nonequilibrium statistical mechanics models with strong randomness and non-linear interactions that have been studied for more than thirty years but remain very controversial.
A new approach to study the glass transition and the properties of the glassy state in such models, using domain dynamics (DD), has recently been proposed.

This approach is based on the existence of a finite-temperature phase transition, the so-called critical dynamic transition (CDT), which is associated with the proliferation of dynamically generated domains.
Here, we extend this approach to random-field Ising models (RFIMs), which are known to be simpler than spin glasses, and present numerical evidence that RFIMs undergo a CDT.
At this transition, we observe the growth of finite-size domains, which are characterized by an exponential decay of their magnetization with respect to their size.
This magnetization decay is influenced by the thermal noise and clashes with the naive picture of a frozen-in magnetization in the domains.
Finally, we discuss the implications of our results for the understanding of the spin-glass problem.
We explore the acousto-mechanical response of a microbubble in an acoustic field.
We show that the bubble's response can be described by a simple mechanical model consisting of a mass attached to a spring.
The mass represents the gas in the bubble, and the spring represents the shell.
We find that the bubble's resonance frequency is proportional to the square root of the acoustic driving frequency.
We also show that the bubble's response can be described by a simple electrical circuit model consisting of a resistor and a capacitor.
The resistor represents the drag force on the bubble, and the capacitor represents the spring force.
We hope that our results will help designers of sonographic imaging systems and therapeutic ultrasound devices to improve the resolution and sensitivity of their instruments.
We study collective spontaneous emission from a system of quantum dots which are electrically controlled in a one-dimensional array.
The quantum dots are described by the multi-mode Hartree-Fock theory, including the quantum defect, and the array is embedded in a photonic crystal.

By calculating the emission spectrum and the electric field distribution, we show the existence of the hybrid light-matter states, which are formed by the strong coupling between the quantum dots and the photonic crystal cavity.
The hybrid states show anti-crossing behavior with the uncoupled states of the quantum dots and the photonic crystal cavity.

By means of the renormalization group technique, we investigate the quantum phase transition between the normal and the superradiant phases, and determine the critical number of quantum dots for the transition.
The critical parameters are sensitive to both the quantum defects and the coupling between the dots and the photonic crystal.
Recent developments in nanoscale electronics have enabled a new paradigm in computing, referred to as "neuromorphic computing".

In this paradigm, artificial systems are designed to process information in a way that is analogous to the way the brain processes information, using asynchronous, event-driven, and adaptive algorithms.
One of the key components of such systems is a new type of memory device, referred to as an "event-driven synaptic device".

Event-driven synaptic devices are designed to emulate the behavior of synapses in the brain, which are fundamentally analog devices, but can also be used as digital memory devices in neuromorphic computing systems.
In this paper, we explore the use of a new type of event-driven synaptic device, based on the concept of "signal focusing through active transport".

This device is designed to improve the signal-to-noise ratio of the synaptic connection, by actively transporting the synaptic signal from the pre-synaptic to the post-synaptic electrode via a molecular motor.
The molecular motor is driven by a current flowing through the device, and transports the signal in a direction that is perpendicular to the current flow.
The signal is then focused through a narrow channel, which is gated by a memristor.
The memristor is used to control the flow of the signal through the channel, and can be used to modulate the strength of the synaptic connection.
We analyze the behavior of this device using a combination of numerical simulations and analytical calculations.
We find that the device has a number of attractive properties, including a high signal-to-noise ratio, a low power consumption, and a high efficiency.
We also find that the device is robust to variations in the parameters of the device, such as the size of the channel and the strength of the memristor.
We believe that this device has the potential to be a useful component in future neuromorphic computing systems.
We propose a methodology for estimating high-dimensional models using higher-order estimating equations.
By incorporating higher-order relationships between the variables in the model, our approach allows for improved precision in the estimates and increased statistical efficiency.

Our methodology is particularly useful for high-dimensional models where the number of observations is limited and the classical least squares estimation may result in biased and inefficient estimates.
We demonstrate the performance of our approach through a simulation study and an application to a real data set.
The software implementing our methodology is available at https://github.com/lmesterton/higher-order-estimating-equations.
We present an extension of the LTLvis motion planning interface, designed to express and solve motion planning problems using an expressive temporal logic, Linear Temporal Logic (LTL).
In contrast to existing work, our approach allows users to easily specify a wide range of motion planning problems, while still enjoying the benefits of automated planning algorithms.

In particular, we contribute the following: (1) we extend the LTLvis interface to handle non-safety properties, (2) we propose an algorithm for planning in the resulting formalism that is sound, complete, and runs in polynomial time, and (3) we provide a proof of soundness and completeness of our approach.
We demonstrate the applicability of our approach on several examples, including a physical robot and a virtual robot in a simulated environment.
We introduce the edge clique cover of a graph, which generalizes the well-known vertex clique cover.
Given a claw-free graph, we propose an efficient algorithm to find an edge clique cover of a claw-free graph.
Furthermore, we derive a tight upper bound on the size of an edge clique cover of a claw-free graph.
Operating a large-volume time projection chamber (TPC) nuclear detector in a high background environment close to a major nuclear power station necessitates careful study of the backgrounds.
The main contributors to the background in the EXO-200 TPC are naturally occurring radioisotopes in the surrounding rock and soil as well as cosmic rays and radon gas.
Radon-222 decays into a series of alpha particles, which produce many low-energy electrons, positrons, and photons that are difficult to distinguish from real events.
We present here models of the expected background rates in EXO-200 due to these sources as well as measurements of the background rates in a water-filled TPC.
We consider thin games with symmetry in the sense of Bergelson and Sinkey (2008).
A concurrent variant of Hyland and Ong's game is introduced and shown to have the same distribution as the symmetric thin doubling game.
This answers positively a question of Bergelson and Sinkey (2008).
We study interference between two single photons and two-photon spontaneous superposition using a polarization-based quantum eraser setup.

The two-photon state is produced by an spontaneous parametric down-conversion photon pair source, and the photons are sent through a polarization beam splitter, with one arm containing a quantum eraser and the other a half-wave plate, which can be used to change the polarization of a photon.
The two photons are then measured using two polarization-sensitive detectors.

We find that when the half-wave plate is not set to a special angle, the two-photon coincidence rate shows an interference pattern, with maxima and minima corresponding to the two different polarization settings of the quantum eraser.
However, when the half-wave plate is set to a special angle, we observe that the two-photon coincidence rate is always at its maximum, independent of the polarization setting of the quantum eraser.
This demonstrates a breakdown of the spontaneous superposition of the two-photon state, and is explained by a simple classical model.
We prove a dimensional decrease of the average singular value for complex random matrices, both planar and upper triangular.
This extends an earlier result of Bai for real random matrices.
In fact, our techniques yield the same result for real planar matrices as well.
Our approach is to treat the complex and real cases on the same footing using tools from complex analysis, in particular the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality and Paley–Wiener theorems.
We consider secure communication from a transmitter to multiple receivers in the presence of an eavesdropper.

We propose a new scheme for selecting a jammer (a legitimate receiver acting as a jammer) to degrade the eavesdropper's signal-to-noise ratio, and show that the scheme achieves the single-user degrees-of-freedom (DoF) for secure communication, i.e., the total DoF of the jammer selection scheme and the secure communication scheme are equal.
Furthermore, we derive a jammer scaling law, which states that the total DoF of our scheme grows linearly with the number of legitimate receivers.
Finally, we propose a simple power allocation strategy to achieve the proposed jammer selection scheme.
We use a Monte Carlo code to study surface sputtering due to dual and rotated ion beams.

This code, which explicitly takes into account binary collisions between ions and surface atoms, as well as multiple collisions, shadowing in dual ion beams, and angular distribution of sputtered particles, yields a sputtering yield as a function of the incidence angle of the ion beam(s).
The sputtering yield has a maximum at an angle which depends on the parameters of the collision.
The effect of rotated ion beams is to increase this maximum angle.
Our results are in a good agreement with previously available experimental data.
We present algorithms for scheduling moldable tasks on homogeneous multiprocessors.
In many practical cases, the tasks arriving at a scheduler can be modified to increase their feasibility for the available resources.
We refer to such tasks as moldable.
We first present a polynomial-time algorithm that computes an online optimal schedule for moldable tasks under sum-completion-time (SCH) scheduling, which minimizes the makespan.
This algorithm is based on an optimal offline-algorithm that computes a schedule in which tasks are released at their release times.
We then consider the more practical scenario where the arrival times of tasks are given and the tasks may be modified only within a given preprocessing time.

We present an algorithm that is parameterized by two numbers, namely, a tuning parameter that controls the tradeoff between the makespan and the preprocessing time, and another parameter that specifies an upper bound on the makespan.
Our algorithm runs in time linear in the size of the input and the preprocessing time, and it always computes a schedule whose makespan is within an additive factor of the upper bound.
This factor can be arbitrarily close to 1 if the tuning parameter is chosen carefully.
We implement our algorithm and conduct an experimental evaluation to assess its performance in terms of the makespan and the preprocessing time.
We study the topology of surfaces for molecular Stark energy, alignment, and orientation generated by combined permanent and induced electric dipole interactions.
The topology of surfaces provides a geometric framework to understand the behavior of these interactions.
We find that the Stark energy surface is always homeomorphic to a sphere, but the alignment and orientation surfaces can have much more complex topologies.
In particular, we identify a class of molecules for which the orientation surface has the topology of a torus.
We also find that the alignment surface can have the topology of a sphere, a torus, or a Klein bottle, depending on the relative strengths of the permanent and induced dipole interactions.
Our results provide a new way to understand the behavior of molecular Stark energy, alignment, and orientation based on the topology of the corresponding surfaces.
We believe that this approach will be useful for predicting and understanding the behavior of molecules in electric fields and for designing new materials with desired properties.

We demonstrate a terahertz coherent perfect absorber with broadband and energy-concentrating properties based on a self-complementary metasurface.
The absorber consists of a periodic array of subwavelength metallic split-ring resonators on a thin dielectric substrate.

By tuning the geometrical parameters of the split-ring resonators, we achieve near-perfect absorption across a wide spectral range from 600 GHz to 930 GHz, with an absorption bandwidth of >430 GHz, which is ~25% of the free-space wavelength at 930 GHz.
Most notably, the calculated absorption depth is >99.999% across the entire operating band.

We also investigate the effects of fabrication tolerances and find that the designed perfect absorber is quite robust against variations in both the split-ring resonator dimensions and the thickness of the dielectric substrate.

Our results show that terahertz coherent perfect absorbers based on self-complementary metasurfaces provide a promising approach for efficient radiation absorption in the terahertz frequency range with potential applications in secure communication, sensing, and imaging.
We give a construction of A-infinity algebras for nonorientable Lagrangians with vanishing odd Chern-Simons function, and show that they have a structure of equivariant A-infinity algebra.
This extends the result of Liu-Tong for orientable case, and partially answers to a question raised by Liu-Tong.
