Sunflower-free sets are closely related to the notorious vector covering problem: Given a set $S$ of vectors, find the smallest subset of vectors that covers S.
This problem is known to be NP-hard, and it is believed that it is unlikely to have a polynomial-time solution.
In this paper, we present an upper bound on the size of a smallest sunflower-free set in terms of the size of the universe and the size of the ground set.
This bound shows that the size of a smallest sunflower-free set is essentially the same as the size of a smallest vector cover.
We also present a nearly matching lower bound.
We give a brief overview of the eigensurface topology of the spherical quantum pendulum and its relation to supersymmetry.
In particular we discuss how the supersymmetry of the model is reflected in the eigensurface topology and how this can be used to understand the properties of the model.
We also discuss some recent results on the supersymmetry and eigensurface topology of the spherical quantum pendulum.
We perform the first systematic study of the oscillations in solar jets observed with the Solar Optical Telescope (SOT) of the Hinode mission.
We have identified oscillating structures in 26 jets during 2007-2009, mainly in the chromosphere, but also in the transition region and in the corona.
These oscillations are likely to be driven by the reconnection process in coronal loops.
We have characterized the oscillations using time-distance diagrams, and measured the proper motions of several hundreds of oscillating points.
These measurements allow us to investigate, for the first time, the spatial dependence of the oscillation period in a jet, with the period increasing with height.

We have also found that the oscillations are likely to be radially propagating away from the jet axis with a propagation speed of about 20 km/s in the chromosphere, and 40 km/s in the transition region.
Our observations suggest that the oscillations are driven by a viscosity in the plasma, which is in agreement with the theoretical prediction of Maruyama et al.

We discuss the nature of this viscosity and show that the observed proper motions are consistent with the oscillations being driven by either the viscous reconnection itself or the global oscillations of the reconnected flux tubes.
The latter would require, however, that the oscillations be radially propagating, which has not been observed in any other oscillating structures in the solar atmosphere.

We study the limit distribution of the maximum likelihood estimator of the shape parameter of a log-concave density in finite samples, and develop a confidence region based on the asymptotic distribution.
The limit distribution is found to be Gaussian under minimal conditions on the log-concave density.
An intuitive explanation of the limit distribution is also provided.
We introduce the notion of type one generalized Calabi-Yaus, which include the well-known notion of almost Hermitian structure.
This class of almost complex structures appears in the study of the geometric structures of pseudosymmetric spaces and nearly Kähler manifolds.
We prepare the groundwork for a local study of these structures, and illustrate some of the differences between the type one generalized Calabi-Yaus and the almost Hermitian structures.

"Coherent averaging" is a technique used in quantum mechanics and other fields to calculate the expected value of a variable over a set of possible outcomes, given some probability distribution.
The expected value is a measure of the average value of a variable over a set of outcomes, and it can be used to predict the behavior of a system.
The coherent averaging method can be used to calculate the expected value of a variable in a system that is described by a set of linear equations.
The method can be used to find the solution to a set of linear equations, given some initial conditions and a set of probabilities for the outcomes of the variables in the system.

We present a new method for coherent averaging, inspired by the classical Monte Carlo method.
Our method is based on the idea of constructing a sequence of trial states, and updating the trial states using the Born rule and the linearity of the evolution.
We demonstrate that the coherent average of an observable A is given by the average of the observable over the sequence of trial states.
We apply our method to calculate the coherent average of the energy for a harmonic oscillator, and show that our method agrees with the classical Monte Carlo method.
We perform the first systematic investigation of the universality of the luminosity-metallicity (L-Z) and mass-metallicity (M-Z) relations for compact galaxies at 0 < z < 3.

We compile a sample of ~104 galaxies with stellar mass < 10^9 M⊙ and circumgalactic medium metallicity measurements from 11 studies of local and high-redshift galaxies, spanning four orders of magnitude in luminosity and eight orders of magnitude in mass.

In agreement with previous studies, we find that the L-Z relation for compact galaxies is not universal, but instead depends on luminosity, with the faintest galaxies exhibiting the highest metallicities.

However, we find that the M-Z relation is universal, independent of mass, and that this relation holds over an order of magnitude longer than previously reported, from the Milky Way to dwarf galaxies a factor of ~100 times less massive.

We show that this lack of evolution in the M-Z relation implies that the star-formation histories and chemical enrichment histories of these galaxies must be closely coupled over nearly all of their lifetimes.

Using stellar population models, we demonstrate that this coupling can be achieved if the duration of star formation is proportional to the gas mass of the galaxy and if the gas is mixed well with the stars at all times.
Finally, we combine our results on the M-Z relation with results from the literature on the relation between stellar mass and halo mass to conclude that ~2
× 10^5 M⊙ worth of metals must be produced within galaxies in order for them to reach the observed metallicity of the Universe today.
We show how to use lexicographic approximations to obtain existence results for FPTAS of integer programs.
We illustrate our approach by designing such an FPTAS for the median optimization problem.
We calculate the particle creation rates of scalar and fermionic fields in an inflationary universe described by the excited-de Sitter (eds) vacuum state.
The eds vacuum is a nontrivial state with a global U(1) symmetry, which remains invariant under the evolution of the inflating background.
We find that the creation rates can be suppressed compared to the standard result, depending on the details of the model.
We identify a physical mechanism responsible for the suppression, and show that it is related to the presence of hybrid eds-curvaton excitations in the universe.

Finally, we calculate the creation rates of particles produced during the evolution of the eds vacuum around a local minimum of the potential, and discuss the implications of our results for the production of primordial black holes.
We report on the dielectric properties of single crystal MoS2.
The dielectric constant and dielectric loss in the THz region (0.5-6.0 THz) and visible region (400-1100 nm) have been measured.
The single crystal MoS2 was synthesized by chemical vapor transport method using iodine as transport agent.
The dielectric constant of the synthesized MoS2 crystal increases with increase in frequency in the THz region and it shows opposite trend in the visible region.
The real part of the dielectric constant, ε′, in the THz region is about 8.4+1.8i, and 4.4 +0.25i in the visible region at 10 GHz and 5800 nm respectively.
The dielectric loss, ε″, is about 10-3 in the THz region and 10-4 in the visible region at the same frequency.
The trends in the dielectric property of MoS2 are explained on the basis of the existing models.

We introduce spatially adaptive stochastic multigrid methods for efficiently solving the fluid-structure systems with thermal fluctuations modeled by the Navier-Stokes equations coupled with the equations for thermal conduction and structural deformation.
We consider a simplified problem in which the structural deformation is linear, and the fluid flow is governed by the three-dimensional Navier-Stokes equations with random thermal forcing.
The resulting system for the velocity field is shown to be implicitly defined on the random thermal field, which represents the effect of thermal fluctuations.
We propose a spatially adaptive stochastic multigrid method to approximate this system.
The spatial adaptation is implemented by refining the grid in regions with fast spatial variations and coarsening the grid in regions with slow spatial variations in the random thermal field.
This adaptation strategy is shown to reduce the computational cost by up to a factor of 8, while maintaining the same accuracy as a uniform grid.
In this paper we introduce some new solutions for the T-system with principal coefficients.
By using these solutions, we construct an new infinite class of combinatorial proofs for some special cases of Rogers-Ramanujan type identities.
Finally, we obtain an new interpretation of these solutions in terms of q-hypergeometric functions.
We introduce and study a new family of inequalities motivated by the second law of thermodynamics, whereby entropy is maximized, subject to a constraint.
The new inequalities involve the quantum relative entropy, and are applicable to arbitrary states living on an arbitrary finite-dimensional quantum system.
We present some properties of these new inequalities, and discuss their use in the context of quantum information theory.
We present a novel saturable absorber based on a multiple-quantum-well structure with a wetting layer 2 (WS2) surface.
The sample was grown by molecular beam epitaxy.
The WS2 absorber exhibits a clear saturation behavior at a pump power of 75 μJ/cm2, which is promising for the passive Q-switching operation of diode-pumped solid-state lasers.
In particular, the WS2-based saturable absorber can be effectively used for the mode-locked laser operation.

The measured laser parameters are in good agreement with the results obtained from numerical solutions of the rate equations for a laser model including the saturable absorber and the dispersive mirror.

Let $(V_n)$ be the sequence of vertex transitive graphs which tile the plane, namely $V_1=K_2$, and $V_{n+1}$ is the graph which has $n$-fold rotational symmetry, and which is obtained from $V_n$ by adding a new vertex connected to every vertex of $V_n$. It is known that $V_n$ is always vertex transitive for $n\ge 3$.
We investigate the distribution of spacing between the projections of the vertices when they are projected along a fixed direction.
In particular, we prove that, regardless of the direction, almost all vertex pairs project within a constant distance, and that every direction yields the same result.
This settles a conjecture of Behzad, Lin, and Yeo.
We report on the fabrication of a new type of neutron detector that utilizes the reaction 10B(n, α) 7Li to detect neutrons.
The device consists of micron-size boron powder contained within the core of a cylindrical detector.
Upon capture of a neutron, the boron-10 powder emits alpha particles and lithium-7 ions.
An ionization chamber surrounds the boron core and detects the resultant charged particles to provide detection capability.
We report here on the fabrication techniques, radiation hardness, and initial response characteristics of the detector.
We find that the detector response is proportional to the number of atoms contained within the detector, providing a high intrinsic efficiency for neutron detection.
A high-resolution, time-to-digital-converter-based (TDC-based) data acquisition board has been designed and built for the NA62 experiment at CERN.
It is equipped with three TDCs able to measure with picosecond resolution the arrival time of signals coming from the experimental apparatus.
The TDCs have been produced adopting a dedicated ASIC, featuring a 6 b resolution and a dead time of 3.3 ns.
The board is capable of acquiring eight analog signals with 12-bit resolution, digitizing them with a sampling frequency of either 40 or 80 MHz.
The board transmits the data through the PCI express bus to a commercial processor card where the data are stored and processed.
A software framework, based on the Linux OS and on the EPICS distributed control system, has been developed to control and read out the data from the TDC-based board.
Quantum physics is inherently causal, but standard quantum mechanics is acausal, that is, it allows causal order to be violated.
Retrocausal models restore causal order at the cost of abandoning the linearity of standard quantum mechanics and are motivated by a desire to under-stand the quantum measurement process.
For such models to be well defined, one must require that they are faithful to the linear quantum theory, that is, that they reproduce the predictions of linear quantum theory.

We study this faithfulness condition for a simple retrocausal model and show that it implies a severe restriction on the class of allowable retrocausal models—one that may be impossible to satisfy in practice.
Thus, we raise an interesting question about the viability of retrocausal models.
At the same time, we show that our simple model captures non-trivial features of quantum theory, suggesting that it may be a useful conceptual tool for understanding the quantum measurement process.
We study two ways of enumerating ordered trees, using generating functions.
Both are based on the concept of triangulation, i.e. embedding the tree in a convex way in the plane, so that each internal vertex has exactly three incident edges.

Given such a triangulation, we can either consider the order on the vertices induced by considering the bottom-up order on the edges (keeping edges oriented), or we can order the vertices bottom-up by considering the vertices in the order they are removed from the convex closure (unoriented).
We show that these two orderings give rise to different generating functions, and we study some of their properties.
in particular we relate the generating functions to those of planar maps, and we determine the generating function for ordered trees with a fixed number of vertices and edges.
Tobacco use is increasingly recognized as having originated and become entrenched in certain civilizations as a result of complex interactions between society and tobacco.
These interactions were deeply influenced by the cultural, economic, and demographic features of these civilizations.
In this study, we build a mathematical model to study the effect of societal individualism on the prevalence of smoking.
We find that the transition from collectivism to individualism resulted in an initial increase in smoking prevalence, followed by a decline.
The initial increase was driven by the switching of women from non-smoking to smoking, while the subsequent decline was driven by the switching of men from smoking to non-smoking.
Our study provides a quantitative framework to understand the influence of societal individualism on the prevalence of smoking.
We consider the notion of equivalence for multi-letter quantum finite automata (QLFA), which was recently defined by Hindia.

We show that the proposed definition of equivalence is not compatible with the intuitive expectation that testing equivalence of QLFA should be easier than testing acceptance, and we propose a new definition that does satisfy this expectation.
We also show that our new definition enjoys a number of desirable properties, and we develop techniques for testing equivalence that are based on these properties.
In particular, we show that the problem of testing equivalence of QLFA is in RE, and we develop an algorithm that is asymptotically optimal (in terms of the sizes of the QLFA involved).
We present day-to-day group numbers for sunspot groups and pores in Edition-2 of the UWGS, extending from January 1849 to June 2018.
A new method for "grouping" images automatically is outlined that is relatively unaffected by group proximity, and is free from the human bias involved in visual grouping.
This new dataset can be used as is, or as a starting point for future analyses, as it includes all UWGS features through 2018, including merged groups, and groups that were previously missed.
Implementing this grouping algorithm, we find the median sunspot group lifetime is 18.1 ± 2.1 days, though this varies significantly with group size.
We also use this dataset to calculate new values for the sunspot number, including a new "daily" sunspot number extending from 1849-2018, and a new "Group Sunspot Number" extending from 1976-2018.
These new numbers are useful for, among other things, establishing the solar cycle variation in activity despite the changing number of observed sunspots over time.
We propose and analyze a new scheme for photonic quantum information processing with multiphoton maximally entangled states, based on weak nonlinearities.
It relies on a specific nonlinear interaction between photons in a coherent state, induced by a weakly driven nonlinear crystal, for which four-photon events are resonant.

This enables the possibility of generating multiphoton entanglement and of performing gate operations by means of linear optics, without needing strong nonlinear interactions in small quantum optical systems.
The scheme is suitable for integrated photonic technologies and for scalable quantum information processing with multiphoton entangled states.
A challenging problem in probabilistic modeling is to capture complex, heterogeneous structures in the data, while maintaining the ability to adapt to new, unseen data.

While numerous prior distributions exist to model different kinds of heterogeneity, they typically assume a fixed set of parameters or a fixed underlying structure, which may not always be appropriate for the data at hand.
In this paper, we propose a new class of dynamic adaptive mixture models that capture complex, changing relationships in the data, and adapt to new, unseen data in an online fashion.
These models combine the benefits of non-stationary probabilistic models, which can capture changing relationships, with the flexibility and interpretability of mixture models.

In particular, we build on the idea of probabilistic programming, and develop a new class of dynamic adaptive mixture models that leverage probabilistic programs to dynamically evolve the underlying mixture model structure based on new, unseen data.
This allows the model to adapt to changing relationships in the data while maintaining the ability to interpret the resulting model in terms of a traditional mixture model.

We demonstrate the performance of our new class of models on a number of synthetic and real-world datasets, and show that they can capture complex, changing relationships in the data while adapting to new, unseen data in an online fashion.
Let $(X_t)_{t\ge 0}$ be a homogeneous Markov chain with values in a countable probability group $G$.
We give a necessary and sufficient condition for mixing and double recurrence in $G$ in terms of the convergence of the associated coset averages.
This extends earlier results for mixing and double recurrence for countable Markov groups.
We consider a renewal process in which the interarrival times themselves form a renewal process with generally dependent intervals.
We derive two renewal theorems for this class of processes.
As an application, we show that the renewal process of the intervals supports a constant speed geodesic flow on the unit interval which preserves the renewal structure.
This solution concept generalizes the Brownian motion on the unit interval in a natural way, but its infinitesimal generator is not conservative, in contrast to the Brownian case.
We prove a version of Jorgensen's inequality for purely loxodromic surface groups with at most one end, and give an application to 2-generator free Kleinian groups.
In this paper, we present a classification of almost Abelian Lie algebras, a class of non-Abelian Lie algebras with a commutative derived subalgebra.
First, we establish a one-to-one correspondence between almost Abelian Lie algebras and pairs of abelian Lie algebras and automorphisms of abelian Lie algebras.
Then, we show that the structure of almost Abelian Lie algebras is determined by the corresponding pair, and we use this structure to define a grading on almost Abelian Lie algebras.
Finally, we use the grading to define a partial order on the set of almost Abelian Lie algebras, and we use this partial order to obtain a classification of almost Abelian Lie algebras.
We present hydrogen index (HI) measurements for a sample of blue compact dwarf (BCD) galaxies observed with the Green Bank Telescope (GBT).
These galaxies are among the most metal-deficient systems known and span a wide range in metallicity (-5.3 <
The BCDs, on average, follow the well-known correlation between HI content and metallicity observed in larger galaxies, despite their low masses and modified star formation histories.
This result demonstrates that the HI content-metallicity relationship is a fundamental one for galaxies independently of their mass and star formation history.
We also find that the scatter around the HI content-metallicity relationship is much larger among BCDs than in larger galaxies, increasing from 0.19 dex in galaxies >10^10^M_☉ to 0.3 dex in BCDs.
This result suggests that the HI content-metallicity relationship breaks down in low-mass galaxies with modified star formation histories.
In order to explore the origin of this scatter, we compare our HI data with stellar population models.
The models predict higher HI contents than are observed for the BCDs, suggesting that additional, unknown physics is required to produce the observed HI content-metallicity relationship in BCDs.
This physics could include non-canonical initial mass function, enhanced stellar death rates from massive stars, or scouring of gas from the galaxies by supermassive black holes.

Alternatively, many of our BCDs may be transitioning to becoming dwarf galaxies with passive stellar populations, which are not well-represented in the simple star formation histories used to model them.
We show that quantum spin Hall insulators can be obtained in geometrically frustrated square lattices at zero temperature, without any magnetic field nor spin-orbit coupling.

The necessary and sufficient condition for the quantum spin Hall phase is that the nearest-neighbor interaction is stronger (weaker) than the next-nearest-neighbor interaction on one direction of the lattice, and vice-versa on the perpendicular direction.
The protection of the quantum spin Hall phase is based on a topological property of the many-body spectrum, the presence of a protected point node at the corners of the Brillouin zone.
We discuss the robustness of our prediction in the presence of disorders and strains.
This paper proposes a new method for controlling and analyzing self-organizing systems, based on the principles of thermodynamics and fractal-cluster theory.
The method is applied to various examples, including the growth of plants, the spread of diseases, and the evolution of species.
The results show that the proposed method is effective in controlling and analyzing self-organizing systems, and that it can be used to understand and predict their behavior.

The research was conducted as part of a larger project on the development of new methods for controlling and analyzing complex systems, and the results are expected to have significant implications for the field.

We give an elementary proof of the recent result of Matveev and Finkelnstein who described diophantine approximations for translation surfaces in $\mathbb{C}^*$. In particular we show that a translation surface is approximated by translates of a plane convex body in $\mathbb{C}^*$ if and only if it is semi-convex at infinity.
We apply this result to prove new geometric descriptions of planar resonant sets.

"We introduce a new framework for distributed optimization based on information diffusion over random networks.
Our framework is inspired by the "diffusion adaptation" technique introduced by Allen et al.
[2018] to scale gradient descent, where the computation of each gradient step is distributed across a network of machines.

In this work, we consider the more general problem of distributed optimization of a convex objective function, where we have multiple loss functions, each with its own parameter vector, and the goal is to find a common set of parameters that optimizes all loss functions.

We study a new family of tail risk constraints using the concept of maximum entropy as developed by Shannon, which we refer to as Shannon Entropy (ShEn) constraints.

We show that maximization of Shannon entropy subject to a given probability constraint is equivalent to minimizing the relative entropy, also known as Kullback-Leiber divergence, between the probability distribution and its tail probability constraint.
As a result, ShEn constraints provide a natural geometric interpretation of tail risk constraints.

Furthermore, we show that ShEn constraints are closely related to the maximum entropy approach in statistical physics, as well as to the concept of minimizing relative entropy in the field of information theory.
Finally, we demonstrate how ShEn constraints can be used to construct new tail risk measures for use in quantitative finance and beyond.

We consider a simplified Ericksen--Leslie system that describes the motion of a nematic liquid crystal layer, which is subjected to uniform magnetic field and time-dependent boundary driving forces, in two dimensions.
Various external fields, such as the magnetic field and the boundary driving forces, play the role of external factors that affect the flow of the nematic liquid crystal.
We establish the well-posedness of the system and study the optimal boundary control of the system.

More precisely, we characterize the optimal control strategy by using the optimal control theory for elliptic systems, and we prove that our control strategy is optimal in a strong sense by using the energy method.
In this paper we provide a purely algebraic approach to a generalized version of the Jacobian conjecture proved by P. Callahan and J. Smillie
[The Jacobian conjecture for algebraic varieties, J. Amer.
Math.
As an application of our methods, we obtain a new algebraic proof of a result of G. Kempf on the Jacobian conjecture for elliptic curves.
We introduce a new invariant of closed 7-manifolds which generalizes the well-known analytic invariant for closed 8-manifolds defined by Donaldson.

This new invariant involves counts of special holomorphic disks and sextics on manifolds with cone angle less than \pi/7, and hence can be viewed as providing evidence that such manifolds are ``close'' to S^7.
Along the way, we establish a result about the symmetry of the Gromov-Witten invariants of 7-manifolds which is best possible in a certain sense.
We study the Schwinger effect in AdS$_5$ with a probe D3-brane at rest.

By calculating the correlation function of the stress-energy tensor, we find that the D3-brane accelerates in the presence of a background electric field, and shocks as a result of the Cerenkov radiation it emits.
We then place the D3-brane in a rotating frame, calculating the correlation functions in the presence of both an electric and a magnetic field.
We observe that the D3-brane continues to accelerate in the electric field, but is slowed down by the magnetic field, and find the drag force acting on the D3-brane.
We introduce a path integral representation of the Lorentzian spinfoam model, and study its asymptotics for large data.

In the large data limit, the path integral boils down to a classical geometric object, characterized by a Riemannian metric and a symplectic form, living on the space of spin networks encoded in the graph.
This result provides a rigorous foundation for the hope that the Lorentzian spinfoam model may be used to define a quantum theory of gravity with a classical limit.

The symplectic form is shown to be related to the spin foam continuum limit of the classical Euclidean theory, and the metric is shown to be related to a discrete version of the Poincar\'e-Hopf theorem, formulated on a spectral triple.
The construction of the spin foam geometry is independent of the graph topology, and thus provides a new, topology-free definition of simplicial geometry.
We introduce the notion of height for piecewise-testable (PT) languages, generalizing the concept of width for regular languages.
Given an alphabet of size n, a PT language L has height at most h if each characteristic word of L has length at most h, and L is infinite otherwise.

We show that for every infinite PT language L over an alphabet of size n, there is an equivalent PT language of height at most n. This result implies that the height of PT languages is unbounded when the alphabet size is unbounded.
We also show that the height of PT languages is strictly smaller than the width of regular languages, thus providing another perspective on the difference between the two classes.
Furthermore, we prove that the height of a PT language is equal to the maximum height of its syntactic congruence classes, generalizing a result about the width of regular languages.
We investigate the complexity of the logic of subword concatenations, which is a fragment of first-order logic capturing PT languages.
We show that the satisfiability problem for this logic is NP-complete, even when the languages involved are regular.
On the positive side, we show that the height of a PT language can be decided in polynomial time.
An original technique named tunable coupled-mode dispersion compensation is proposed and demonstrated in this work.

Unlike the conventional dispersion compensation techniques, this new method can intrinsically and simultaneously compensate the material and waveguide dispersion, which arises from the intrinsic nature of the proposed dispersion compensator.
The device is composed of a pair of essentially linear waveguides that are coupled by an adjustable air-gap.
By adjusting the air-gap, the coupled-mode dispersion of the proposed device can be tuned in a wide range.
The device is designed by using a dispersion-relation approach, and the basic operating principle is verified by employing a finite-difference time-domain simulation.
Furthermore, the proposed device is applied to on-chip resonant four-wave mixing, and an ultra-flat dispersion profile is obtained over a wide band.
An optimal design is proposed for the resonant four-wave mixing application, and the conversion efficiency is significantly improved compared to the case without the proposed dispersion compensation.

We propose a general construction of "foliated" backgrounds for M-theory compactifications, building on the recently proposed geometric construction of M-theory compactifications on twisted compactifications of CY 3-folds.
These backgrounds generalize the warped product construction, and provide a new class of examples for M-theory compactifications, with nontrivial topology and dynamics.
The dynamics includes both higher-dimensional gravity and a U(1) gauge field, arising as the m=0 reducing gauge field of M-theory.
We analyze the low energy effective actions for these theories, and show that they can be described by a single, nontrivial function of the radial variable only, for a large class of examples.
We propose a generalization of the warped AdS_3 solution, where the warping function and the 3-form flux are functions of the U(1) gauge field.

We show that this generalization is motivated by a desire to have a well-defined bulk stress tensor, and that for a large class of examples, the low energy effective action is independent of the 3-form flux.
We present a systematic and exact procedure for two-dimensionalizing three-dimensional, inviscid, turbulent flows using a mapping onto a curved background.
This method can be viewed as a generalization of previous procedures for simplifying turbulent flows.
The governing flow equations are solved in a curvilinear coordinate system, with the curvature imposed to guarantee that the streamlines on the two-dimensional surface are geodesics.
For flows with large Reynolds numbers, this procedure reduces the flow to a two-dimensional, time-dependent flow with a curvilinear velocity profile.
The flow possesses a modulated equilibrium state that undergoes periodic oscillations around this equilibrium.
This two-dimensionalization procedure leads to a drastic reduction in the computational cost of simulating the flow, thereby allowing for much longer integration times and finer spatial resolutions.

The dynamics of the most unstable modes in the two-dimensional flow are investigated, and the primary oscillation frequency is compared to that obtained in three-dimensional direct numerical simulations.
Let $D$ be a non-zero commutative Noetherian ring with unity, generated by $n$ elements as a ring.
Denoting by $\mathcal{I}\subseteq \mathrm{Discr}(D)$ the full invariant subring of $D$, it is known that $\mathcal{I}$ is a finitely generated $D$-algebra, and, in particular, Noetherian as well.
We prove that $\mathrm{Discr}(D)$ has effective results for the invariant theory of $\mathcal{I}$, and obtain some new results in this direction.
An ordered exchange graph is an exchange graph in which the edges appear in a specified order.

We study ordered exchange graphs for the case in which the underlying graph is a tree, and show that they can be used to recursively define systems of linear equations, in a way that is analogous to the definition of ordered tuples of integers.

We define a notion of solvability for such systems, and show that a necessary and sufficient condition for a system to be solvable is for a certain tree-width measure of the exchange graph to be bounded.

We show an upper bound on the quantifier depth of graph differentiation, proving that quantifier depth is bounded by O(n + m), where n is the number of nodes in the graph and m is the number of edges.
This answers a question posed by Makowsky, Slutzki and Urquhart in [MSU09].
We present a logical characterization of the bound in the form of a logical formula expressing that a graph is diffable.
This characterization makes the proof rigorous and clarifies the relationship between graph differentiation and quantifier depth.

The all-switches strategy, which recently has been shown to achieve approximation ratios close to the information-theoretic optimum for the Boolean satisfiability problem (SAT), hinges on the idea of synthesizing a satisfiable assignment by iteratively flipping subsets of variables.
This strategy and its variations have been shown to perform well on a variety of combinatorial problems, including the graph coloring problem.
In this paper, we investigate the complexity of improving the solution produced by the all-switches strategy in the graph coloring problem.
We show that this problem is NP-hard to solve, even when the underlying graph is a tree, and propose a polynomial-time heuristic algorithm to find an improved coloring.
We also show that the all-switches strategy can be used to solve other problems such as the maximum independent set problem and the minimum dominating set problem.
We introduce the concept of higher Auslander-Reiten sequences and give a reconstruction theorem in this setting.
This concept contains as special cases the classical Auslander-Reiten theory of modules over a ring and the theory of $t$-structures on a triangulated category.
We also give a characterization of when the sequence is a higher Auslander-Reiten sequence in terms of refinement of $t$-structures.
Finally, we apply these results to give a new proof of a recent result of Bondal and Zhang on constructing projective generators.
We introduce some new notions of equivalence for the Riemann Hypothesis that extend the usual equivalence with other well-known problems in number theory.
We show that the Riemann Hypothesis is equivalent to the truth of the Robin Inequality, and to the convergence of the generalized Lagarias criterion.
We study electron reflection from a potential barrier in a heterostructure, where the electron spin can flip during the reflection.

We find that the spin-flip probability obtained by solving the Schrödinger–Poisson system for a rigid impurity atom is significantly increased by the interface electronic states, which are taken into account by the interface-transparent boundary conditions.
This increase is more pronounced for a barrier with a tail (a graded interface).

We also find that the results obtained within the framework of standard boundary conditions, which account for the interface electronic states via the matching of the wave functions and the continuation of the eigenstates, are in a very good agreement with those obtained by solving the Schrödinger–Poisson system with interface-transparent boundary conditions.
We discuss an approach to Earth of asteroid (99942)
Apophis forecasted by NASA on 19 of December 2023.
Apophis impact probabilities for the years 2029, 2036, and 2053 are based on NASA JPL solution 27.
We recalculate these probabilities using two other solutions 20 and 25 according to which Apophis should miss the Earth on 2029 and 2053, but might impact on 2036.
There are two scenarios for 2029.
The first scenario, based on solution 27, is that Apophis might impact Earth on 2029.
The second scenario, based on solutions 20 and 25, is that Apophis will almost ricochet from the Earth on 2029.

This second scenario is confirmed by independent calculations of three groups from Russia, Italy, and the U.S.A. 

We discuss probabilities for these scenarios.
We also quantify how much the gravitational action of the Moon on Apophis is capable to deflect its trajectory.
We conclude that the scenario of an almost ricochet of Apophis on 13 of April 2029, supported by solutions 20 and 25, is much more likely than the impact scenario supported by solution 27.
This conclusion is also supported by a publication of NASA JPL published after solution 27.
In this note, we present a simple proof of the quantitative subspace theorem of Gurvits and Barnum
[IEEE Trans. Inf.
The proof relies on only the basic properties of random matrices and the tail bounds for the eigenvalues of random matrices.
Compared to the original proof, the new proof is more self-contained and does not rely on the probabilistic method.
The quantitative subspace theorem of Gurvits and Barnum is a key tool in the study of the capacity of random networks.
It provides an upper bound on the capacity of a random network in terms of the rank of a random matrix.
The bound is tight and matches the lower bound up to a constant factor.
The theorem has found many applications in the theory of random networks, including the proof of the cut-set bound and the proof of the broadcast bound.
The new proof of the quantitative subspace theorem is simple and straightforward.
It only relies on the basic properties of random matrices and the tail bounds for the eigenvalues of random matrices.
The proof is more self-contained and does not rely on the probabilistic method.
This makes it easier to read and understand, and it is hoped that it will encourage more researchers to use the quantitative subspace theorem in their work.
In this paper, a serious game system utilizing the game AI engine is proposed for human environmental consciousness education in residents' daily life.
In recent years, the environmental consciousness of residents has been decreasing in Japan, although it is necessary to enhance it for the sustainable development of the nation.

To increase the environmental consciousness of residents, this research develops a serious game system that provides an environmental consciousness education in residents' daily life through the game.
We focused on the fact that the residents' awareness of environmental problems is generally low, and it is necessary to provide information on environmental problems in a timely manner.

The purpose of this research is to propose a method of providing information on environmental problems in a timely manner and to develop a serious game system for human environmental consciousness education that utilizes the game AI engine.
The proposed method utilizes the game AI engine to automatically generate a scenario for a serious game that suits the user's environment.

In addition, this method utilizes the characteristics of the game AI engine, which can generate a scenario that suits the user's environment, to provide information on environmental problems in a timely manner.
The results of a survey conducted to evaluate the proposed method indicate that the users were able to understand the environmental problems more easily than before.

We give a simple proof of a recent result of H. Chen and C. Wuthrich according to which, given a sequence of natural numbers $(a_n)$ such that $\sum_{n \geq 1} \frac{a_n}{n} \lt \infty$, we have $\limsup_{x \to \infty} x^{-1+\frac{2}{3}} \sum_{n \leq x} a_n \lt 1$.
We analyze the computational performance of several existing algorithms for solving linear equality- constrained least squares problems (LECLS).

These algorithms include the classical Gauss-elimination with equality constraints (GE), the augmented Gauss-elimination (AG), the Jacobi-conjugate-gradient (JCG), and a variant of JCG with a closed-form solution to the linear system at each iteration.

We also propose a new algorithm, which is a variant of JCG, to solve LECLS by using a recently developed preconditioner for solving linear systems involving the sum of a diagonal matrix and a sparse matrix.
This new algorithm is termed Diagonal-plus-sparse Jacobi-conjugate-gradient (DPSJCG).
We implement these algorithms in MATLAB and compare their performance on a set of test problems.
Our experimental results show that, on our test problems, the DPSJCG algorithm outperforms the other algorithms in terms of the number of iterations required to reach a given accuracy.

The abstract for this paper is as follows:

This paper looks at a game-theoretic solution concept for a wireless power control game, where the players correspond to the base stations of a multi-cell wireless communication system and the utility of each base station is a function of the transmitted power of all base stations.
We study how the game-theoretic solution concept can be used to understand the behaviour of the game and design corresponding algorithms to implement a game-theoretic solution.
This paper focuses on the following three observations: (1) A game-theoretic solution concept can provide a framework for understanding the behaviour of the wireless power control game.
(2) The proposed solution concept is robust to the noise and interference in the system.
(3) The proposed game-theoretic solution concept can be used to design a distributed algorithm that implements the solution concept in a distributed way.

This paper concludes by discussing how the game-theoretic solution concept can be used to understand the behaviour of the wireless power control game and design algorithms that implement the solution concept.

We prove that the sets of provend and provable numbers are analytic, and describe the complexity of the associated analytic sets.

In particular, we show that the set of provable numbers is a $G_\delta$, and show how to effectively describe a dense subset of this $G_\delta$. We also show that the set of provend numbers is co-analytic, and that it has a natural description as a union of $G_\delta$ sets.
These results can be viewed as a generalization of a result of Stevo Todorčević on the analytic co-density of the set of recursive numbers.

We prove a Hirzebruch-type inequality for the L^2-norm of certain harmonic maps from a Riemann surface to projective space, and use it to show that a configuration of cuspidal curves of fixed degree in P^2 is bounded in L^2-norm by a linear function of the degree.
This gives a positive answer to a question of Yau.
Let π be a permutation expressing a number as a sum of parts.
We give a complete characterization of the possibility of expressing π as a concatenation of two (or more) core partitions, i.e., partitions avoiding the patterns 1324 and 4321.
This characterizes those permutations expressible as a sum of two (or more) "almost symmetric" parts.
We derive several results of interest regarding the parameterizations of such permutations, and of related families of permutations.

We demonstrate a measurement-device-independent quantum key distribution protocol using modified coherent states with a continuous-wave laser, in order to distribute a cryptographic key with a provable security, though without post-processing.
The modified coherent states are produced by inserting a phase plate in the optical path of the laser, in order to obtain two different states in terms of the phase and the transverse profile.
We first show that these two states are distinguishable with a high fidelity by using a homodyne detection, and then discuss the possibility to apply the MDI-QKD protocol based on them.

From the experimental data, we calculate the secure key rate and evaluate the realistic secure key rates by taking into account the detection efficiency and the dark count rate of the actual homodyne detector.
The results demonstrate that our scheme can achieve secure key rates of order of 1 Mb/s for realistic parameters, which is promising for practical applications.
We introduce the notion of common knowledge systems for explicit evidence.

In these systems, each piece of information is labeled as either common knowledge or not, and the system operates correctly as long as the set of common knowledge atoms is consistent with a specified theory.
This framework gives a clear and intuitive way to formalize various intuitive properties, and seems to capture the way human beings actually reason about information.
We explore this framework, proving several results about common knowledge systems, including the completeness and soundness of a specific proof system for these properties.

We show that the Hamiltonian formalism for the generalized Einstein-Scalar-Maxwell (ESM) theories in dimensions is uniquely defined by a set of first-class constraints in arbitrary dimension $D$, without any need of gauge fixing conditions.
This extends the previous results in dimensions, where the same approach was applied.

The approach used here relies on the study of the symmetries of the theory, and, in particular, on the analysis of the residual symmetry group, which is shown to be non-Abelian and to depend on the dimension.
This group is shown to be always of type ISO(D,1), with a distinguished generator that corresponds to the Hamiltonian constraint.
This generator generates a non-compact subgroup of ISO(D,1), which is the residual symmetry group of the theory.
This group depends on the particular choice of the scalar field and its coupling to the Maxwell field.
It turns out that, in spite of the non-Abelian character of ISO(D,1), the first-class constraints algebra is always Abelian for all choices of the theory.
We show that the Hamiltonian constraint is generated by an intrinsic scalar field potential, which is always attractive, and does not depend on the electromagnetic field.
We derive the conditions that the scalar field must satisfy in order to be a valid quantum field, and show that they are always satisfied provided that the scalar field potential is not too flat.

We consider solitons in a globally coupled hard-core bosonic system, which is described by the Gross-Pitaevskii type equations with the repulsive delta interaction and a two-body attractive/repulsive potential.
There exist two different types of solitons in the system, the bright and dark solitons.
By using the variational method, some new results on these solitons are obtained.
It is shown that the attractive interaction always stabilizes the bright solitons, while the repulsive interaction always destabilizes the bright solitons.
The effect of the two-body potential on the solitons is discussed.
The dark solitons always exist in the system if the two-body potential is attractive enough, while they may disappear if the two-body potential is repulsive.
The effect of the hard-core constraint on the solitons is also discussed.
Let $\mathcal S$ be either the space $C^m(\mathbb R^n)$ or the space $C^{\infty}(\mathbb R^n)$ of all real-valued $m$-times or infinitely differentiable functions on $\mathbb R^n$, respectively.

For a subset $\mathcal T \subset \mathcal S$ we define the Whitney distortion functional as $\mathcal W(\mathcal T) = \inf_{\pi \in \Pi(\mathcal T)} \sum_{T \in \mathcal T} \sum_{\pi(T) = T'} \|T - T'\|^2$, where $\Pi(\mathcal T)$ is the set of all bijections $\pi:\mathcal T \to
\mathcal T$ and the infimum is taken over all such permutations.
We say that a subset $\mathcal T \subset \mathcal S$ is an $\varepsilon$-extension of a subset $\mathcal S' \subset \mathcal S$ if $\mathcal W(\mathcal T) \leq

\varepsilon$. In this note we prove a structural result for $\varepsilon$-extensions of $C^m(\mathbb R^n)$ and $C^{\infty}(\mathbb R^n)$ and use it to obtain new results on interpolation and alignment of data.
We consider the drop policy of shared-memory switches, where multiple queues are stored in a single shared memory.
Each queue can be implemented as a linked list or as a skip list.
When a packet arrives, it can be added at the end of a linked list.
If the linked list becomes saturated, the drop decision can be made based on the packet's priority and the packet's head-of-line (HOL) blocking cost.
The HOL blocking cost can be the packet's finishing time, or it can be the packet's finishing time plus a fixed cost.
We analyze the competitive ratio of these drop policies.
When the HOL blocking cost is the finishing time, the competitive ratio is 1.5.
When the HOL blocking cost is the finishing time plus a fixed cost, the competitive ratio is 2.
When implementing queues as skip lists, the competitive ratio improves to 1.25 and 1.5, respectively.
These results generalize the previously known competitive ratio of 1.25 for the pure-priority drop algorithm for shared-memory switches with linked-list queues.

Let $\mu$ be a finite positive measure on the complex plane $\C$. The famous Fejér kernel $K_\mu(z,w)=\frac{1}{z\bar{w}}\frac{1-\bar{w}\mu(dz)}{1-\bar{z}\mu(dz)}$ is linked to the spectral theory of $\mu$-symmetric Dirac operators via the Fejér-type inequalities for arbitrary Dirac masses $\{m_j\}$. We generalize a recent result of Volkovsky and Wang, relating the flatness of the Fejér kernel $K_\mu$ to the existence of certain kind of eigenvectors of $\mu$-symmetric Dirac operators.
In particular, we show that if $\mu$ is an arbitrary finite measure then $K_\mu$ is flat if and only if certain eigenvectors of $\mu$-symmetric Dirac operators exist.
Also, if $\mu$ is a pure point measure then $K_\mu$ is flat if and only if all Dirac masses $m_j$ are equal.
Let $(X,d)$ be a complete proper geodesic metric space.
We give an overview of the theory of Morse boundaries of metric spaces, with a focus on geodesic spaces.
In particular, we describe the minimal and maximal Morse boundaries, and we characterize when the Morse boundary is discrete.
We give a complete description of the conormal map for the adjoint representation of a finite reductive group G in characteristic p>0.
This provides a solution to a question of Grobner and an extension of a result of Duchene for special linear groups in characteristic 0.
Also, we derive some consequences on the structure of G and describe the image of the conormal map when G is a classical group (including the unitary groups).

The ion implantation of As, P, and B was performed in a commercial a-SiO2 single crystal, using pulsed ion beams of various wide-range energies with plasma flood before and after the implantation, as well as after a thermal annealing of the implants.

The activation of implanted ions, observed only after annealing, reaches a maximum at a substrate temperature of 950 °C and depends on ion energy, on the type of plasma used for the flood, and on the position of the sample during ion implantation.
The paper also reports the observation of octahedral crystallization of a-SiO2, which is explained by the formation of an amorphous phase by the implantation of the ions used in this work.
A multilayer neural oscillator consisting of excitatory and inhibitory neurons is considered.
The system is subjected to periodic unidirectional modulation of the inhibitory potency, mimicking changes in the neuromodulatory tone.
Depending on the frequency of this modulation, two types of behavior emerge: phase resetting or mode switching.
In the former case, the system responds to the modulation with a periodic waveform, while in the latter, the system exhibits an aperiodic waveform.
The boundary between these two regimes is characterized by a canard explosion, where several coexisting periodic and aperiodic solutions appear.
For each type of solution, the conditions for emergence are determined.
The impact of noise and parameter uncertainty on the system's response is then investigated.
The induced uncertainty in the system's behavior is measured by the divergence of the eigenvalues of the transfer operator.

It is shown that the deterministic canard explosion bifurcation implies a divergence of the eigenvalues of the transfer operator with a specific signature, which is robust to parameter uncertainty and noise.
We present a double auction pricing mechanism for off-grid prosumers to buy and sell electricity in a regional network.
The mechanism is designed to operate in real-time, based on local measurements of generation and consumption, and allows prosumers to automatically submit their bids as linear functions of time.
The auction algorithm is designed to ensure that the resulting prices are efficient and equitable, and to handle scenarios where the demand for electricity exceeds the available supply.
The mechanism is implemented in a prototype system and evaluated using simulation experiments.
The results show that the mechanism can effectively balance the supply and demand of electricity in the network and provide fair prices to prosumers.

Introduction:
The increasing penetration of renewable energy sources in the electricity grid has led to the emergence of prosumers, who are both consumers and producers of electricity
In regional areas where the grid is not well-established, prosumers may rely on local renewable energy sources such as solar or wind power to meet their electricity needs.
In these situations, there is a need for a mechanism to enable prosumers to buy and sell electricity in a fair and efficient manner.
Our proposed solution is a double auction pricing mechanism that enables prosumers to automatically submit their bids as linear functions of time.
This allows prosumers to express their preferences for when they want to buy or sell electricity, and to update their bids in real-time based on local measurements of generation and consumption.
The auction algorithm is designed to ensure that the resulting prices are efficient and equitable, and to handle scenarios where the demand for electricity exceeds the available supply.
The mechanism is implemented in a prototype system and evaluated using simulation experiments.
The results show that the mechanism can effectively balance the supply and demand of electricity in the network and provide fair prices to prosumers.

Conclusion:
We have presented a novel double auction pricing mechanism for off-grid prosumers to buy and sell electricity in a regional network.
The mechanism is designed to operate in real-time, based on local measurements of generation and consumption, and allows prosumers to automatically submit their bids as linear functions of time.
The auction algorithm is designed to ensure that the resulting prices are efficient and equitable, and to handle scenarios where the demand for electricity exceeds the available supply.
The mechanism is evaluated using simulation experiments and the results show that it can effectively balance the supply and demand of electricity in the network and provide fair prices to prosumers.
We develop a model theory for M[G], the core model of a compact cardinal, as introduced by Jensen in his groundbreaking essay.

Our development is considerably different from Jensen's own development in the original essay; however, our main result, a reflection principle for M[G], is essentially the same as Jensen's main result.
We also present some new model-theoretic and diagrammatic methods for dealing with M[G]-definable relations, and we prove a generalization of a result of Shelah on quantifier elimination in M[G].
We consider the problem of refining a trace that represents a solution to a labelled Markov decision process (LMDP).

We propose an algorithm that takes as input an LMDP together with a trace that satisfies the specification of the LMDP, and outputs a refined trace, which still satisfies the specification, and yet exhibits a desired behavioural property expressed as an LTL formula.
The input trace is assumed to be provided by an oracle, which can be any source of information, but is typically a model checker.
We formalise the refinement problem within the framework of LMDPs and present an algorithm that iteratively queries the oracle to obtain a refined trace.
The algorithm is proven correct, in the sense that it always outputs a refined trace, and we present experimental results that demonstrate the effectiveness of the approach.
We introduce and study the notion of descent c-Wilf equivalence, a generalization of descent Wilf equivalence from the ring to the c-ring setting.
We show that descent c-Wilf equivalence is a congruence and characterize the c-rings which are descent c-Wilf equivalent to the trivial c-ring.
We also present an example of a c-ring which is not descent c-Wilf equivalent to any finite c-ring.
Hyperspectral and multispectral images, taken at a same scene, carry complementary information.
However, the lack of spectral overlap between the two types of data constitutes a fundamental obstacle to fusing them appropriately.
In this paper, we propose to overcome this limitation by exploring the sparse representation of color images, which have a sparse representation in the hyperspectral domain.
We build a dictionary adapted to hyperspectral images, using the K-means algorithm, and show that the sparse representation of color images can be accurately approximated using this dictionary.

Furthermore, we demonstrate that the concatenation of the sparse approximation with the original hyperspectral image produces a rich representation of the scene that can be effectively used for image fusion.

The proposed method is evaluated on two datasets, and the results show that it produces enhanced fused images, preserving the color appearance of the multispectral data and the spectral information of the hyperspectral data.
Coalgebras are algebraic structures that capture state and transition functions of reactive systems.
In this paper, we propose a novel approach for fair simulation of nondeterministic and probabilistic Büchi automata based on a coalgebraic construction.

Our approach is motivated by the desire to obtain a fair simulation result that is sound with respect to the initial state and any reachable state, and complete in the sense that any fair simulation relation computed is a bisimulation.
We present our results in the setting of traced coalgebras due to their suitability for systems with infinite behavior.
We show that our proposed construction is sound and complete, and we present a complexity analysis of our algorithms.
We study the tails of the sum of digits distributions for prime numbers.
This study is motivated by recent developments in the analysis of the prime number algorithm SAW for integer factoring.
We prove new bounds for the tail distribution of the sum of digits of prime numbers, and we show that the tails of this distribution achieve the predicted bounds.

These results show that the distribution of the sum of the digits of prime numbers has interesting properties, which could possibly be useful in number theory and in the analysis of algorithms that use prime numbers.
We consider the problem of finding the longest palindromic and symmetric repeats in a sequence under gap conditions.
That is, we seek repeats that are allowed to have gaps and we aim to find the longest such repeats.
We show that this problem is fixed-parameter tractable, and present an algorithm that runs in time 2O(n^3 + n^2 k^2), where n is the length of the input sequence and k is the maximum gap size.
This result is based on a novel technique for counting overlaps, which may be of independent interest.
We implement our algorithm and show that it is efficient on real-world data.
We use the behavior of gravitational clustering in an arbitrary cosmological background to isolate the relativistic effects due to the expansion of space.

We consider a toy model where matter is described by a Gaussian random field, and show that the evolution of the matter perturbations can be described by a simple, universal function of redshift, independent of the details of the model.
This result allows us to define a "relativistic contribution" to the growth of structure, which we show can be separated from the "classical" contribution.

Our formalism is consistent with the observational predictions for the growth of structure in a flat LCDM model, but it is invariant under cosmological rescalings, and therefore allows us to make predictions in an arbitrary cosmological background.
We show that the relativistic contribution to the growth of structure is negative at all scales, and that it becomes dominant at sufficiently large scales.

The classical contribution, on the other hand, exhibits a transition from positive to negative growth at small scales, which we show is a general feature of any gravity theory that descends from Newtonian gravity in the appropriate limit.
We introduce the concept of hybrid hypercomputing as a potential paradigm for future advancement of computational ability.
It unifies classical and quantum computation within a single formal framework, based on the notion of hypercomputation.
We discuss how hybrid hypercomputing may be achieved, and present a classification of computational processes.
This formalism may be useful for guiding future research in this direction.
We present a new algorithm for Boolean operations on triangulated surfaces, namely, union, intersection, and difference.
Our algorithm is based on a new approach to handle overlapping triangles.
It simplifies the surface, and then applies the standard Boolean operations for non-overlapping triangles.
As a result, it obtains a simpler surface with possibly overlapping triangles, which can be handled by our new approach.
Our algorithm is simple, efficient, and easy to implement.
Moreover, it is robust, even when the input surfaces have many overlapping triangles, and when the input surfaces have large void (i.e., empty) components.

We calculate the higher-order QCD corrections to the fragmentation of a gluon into an S-wave quarkonium state (such as the J/ψ) in next-to-leading logarithmic (NLL) accuracy, and show that they do not vanish in the collinear limit.
The inclusion of these corrections affects the fragmentation function at small x, and thereby the rapidity distribution of the quarkonium in hadron collisions.
We present the all-order factorization theorem for the gluon-fragmentation function in the color-singlet channel, and derive the NLL soft and collinear contributions.

The collinear contribution receives significant corrections from the gluon distribution function and the quarkonium wave function, which amount to non-vanishing contributions to the S-wave scattering amplitude in the collinear limit.
We evaluate these corrections for the J/ψ and ψ(2S) in a simplified model, and find that they can reach ~5% of the leading order prediction, depending on the rapidity distribution.
We propose a simple quantitative method to analyze point sets.
Our method uses the circle defined by the vertices of a triangle with the query point as its center, termed the quarter circle.
For each point of the quarter circle, we count the number of points of the set lying inside the circle defined by this point, termed the local point density.
We then study the distribution of these local densities for the whole point set and compare it to the distribution of local densities for random points.

We show that our method provides a graphical tool for the analysis of point datasets, and can be used as a first step toward identifying whether a given point set has the properties of a uniform distribution, a clustered distribution, or a mixture of both.
We implement our method on several point sets occurring in practical applications, and demonstrate its efficiency by comparing its results with those obtained by other methods.
We present a high-order adaptive Spectral Element (SE) method for solving optimal control problems governed by partial differential equations (PDEs).

The method is based on the Gegenbauer polynomial approximation and it is applied to solve numerically a class of nonlinear optimal control problems, namely, the infinite-time optimal control problems for PDEs.
The optimal control problems are discretized by the SE method, which is shown to achieve a higher accuracy compared to the standard Galerkin method.
The convergence analysis of the discretization is presented, and the optimal control problems are solved iteratively by using a Newton method.
The proposed method is applied to solve several test examples, including a two-dimensional Burger's equation and a three-dimensional semilinear heat equation.
The results show that the method is effective and efficient for solving optimal control problems.
Let Σ be the skew-product of the polynomial skew curve C^2 and itself defined by (x,y)∈C^2×C^2: (x,y)→(x+y,xy).

We give a complete description of the postcritical set of Σ, that is, the set of all points that are mapped to by some iterate of Σ. In particular, we prove that its complement has a natural structure of algebraic variety, and we describe how this variety is related to the polynomial Σ defines on it.

We propose and analyze a new Stein character for scaled sums of squared independent Gaussian variables, and use it to prove the almost sure convergence of some sample quantiles based on scaled sums of squared independent Gaussian variables, namely the scaled sample median and the scaled sample squared median, to their respective theoretical distributions.

An application of our result shows that the quantiles of some asymptotically chi-square distributed statistics, like the sample median and the sample variance, converge to their theoretical distributions at an optimal rate.
We propose and analyze a teleportation protocol utilizing nonlocality of individual Majorana bound states in a semiconductor nanowire.
The protocol makes use of a joint measurement on two out of three particles, which are each in one of the two Bell states.
After the measurement, the state of the unmeasured particle is nonlocally determined.
We analyze the feasibility of our protocol by considering concrete realizations, both theoretical and experimental, for the necessary components.
The utilization of Majorana fermions in a topological quantum computer is thus extended to communication applications.
We explore the feasibility of using social media data from Twitter to predict intraday changes in exchange rates.
Our hypothesis is that Twitter sentiment can predict the direction of exchange rate movements.

We find that sentiment is a leading indicator of exchange rate changes and that positive sentiment has a greater forecasting power for appreciating exchange rates compared to negative sentiment for depreciating rates.
We also explore the theory that the tone of tweets may be related to the level of uncertainty in the market and find some support for this theory.

Additionally, we find that the predictive power of sentiment varies across different currencies, and that the level of impact of Twitter sentiment is highest for the Canadian dollar, followed by the British pound, and then the euro.
Our results suggest that social media data can be a valuable tool for predicting intraday exchange rate movements.

We perform an in-depth analysis of the evolution of the Twitter social network, the massive online social network servicing 330 million users, by analyzing the graph properties of its social graph from 2007 to 2014.
In particular, we study the evolution of six graph properties: size, average degree, clustering, modularity, path length, and triangle abundance.

These properties capture important aspects of the network’s structure such as the number of nodes and edges, the density and connectedness of the graph, and the community structure present in the network.
By studying the time dependence of these properties, we aim to gain insights into the evolution of the Twitter social network and how it changes over time.
Our analysis shows that the Twitter social network has grown significantly since it was launched in 2006, with a steady increase in the number of users and tweets over time.
The average degree has also increased steadily, indicating that users are increasingly connecting with each other on the network.
The clustering and modularity measures show that the network has a high degree of community structure, with users clustering into groups based on their interests and affiliations.
The path length has decreased over time, indicating that it is becoming easier for users to connect with each other on the network.
The triangle abundance has increased, indicating that there are more closed loops of friendship in the network.
Our analysis provides valuable insights into the evolution of the Twitter social network and how it changes over time, and can be used to inform the development of future social networking platforms.

Recent works on anomaly detection in time series of relational data represented as graphs either
directly compute statistics on the graph or transform the problem into a time series one and
apply existing techniques.

In both cases, these approaches do not exploit the redundancy of
repeatedly monitoring a set of relations.

In this paper, we propose a framework for
anomaly detection in time series of graphs that first computes local statistics for each
relation and then aggregates them.

We show that our framework can naturally handle
different types of anomalies, has good statistical efficiency, and is able to detect
anomalies even when the anomalies do not present in the training data.

Finally, we
validate the effectiveness of our approach against state-of-the-art techniques on two
real-world datasets.

Let $\mathcal{A}$ be a unital complex algebra and let $\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{A})$ be the set of all commuting elements of $\mathcal{A}.$ Let $\mathfrak{A}$ and $\mathfrak{B}$ be two unital subalgebras of $\mathcal{A}$ with $\mathfrak{A}\subseteq\mathfrak{B}.$ It is shown that the restriction homomorphism from $\mathcal{A}$-module algebra $_{\mathfrak{B}}\mathfrak{A}$ to the $\mathcal{A}$-module algebra $_{\mathfrak{A}}\mathfrak{A}$ induces an isomorphism between the quotient modules $_{\mathfrak{B}}\mathfrak{A}/\mathfrak{B}_{\mathfrak{A}}$ and $_{\mathfrak{A}}\mathfrak{A}/\mathfrak{A}_{\mathfrak{A}}$ and consequently an isomorphism between the $\mathcal{A}$-algebras $\mathfrak{A}/\mathfrak{B}_{\mathfrak{A}}$ and $\mathfrak{A}/\mathfrak{A}_{\mathfrak{A}}.$ Furthermore, if $\mathfrak{B}\supseteq \mathfrak{A}^2,\; \mathfrak{B}\neq \mathfrak{A}^2$ and $\mathfrak{A}\neq 0,$ then the above isomorphism identifies the $\mathcal{A}$-ideal $\mathfrak{A}\mathfrak{B}^{-1}\mathfrak{A}$ with the radical of the algebra $\mathfrak{A}/\mathfrak{A}_{\mathfrak{A}}.$

This paper studies fair division and redistricting problems, which include optimally dividing a heterogeneous resource among individuals (with different preferences over the items) and fairly drawing borders of districts to accommodate a given population in a way that everyone has nearly equal political power.
Both problems are fundamental in many real-world applications, yet they pose significant challenges to each other in terms of the solutions.
We first show that the classic optimization approach, which optimally solves the fair division problem, can lead to extremely unfair district borders in the redistricting problem.
For instance, it may produce districts in which most voters are minorities in their own districts.
Then we propose a new paradigm to study these problems, by viewing them as a heterogeneous matching problem, and design efficient algorithms that optimize fairness in both problems simultaneously.
In particular, our algorithms ensure that after division, each district is composed of individuals who have nearly equal preference for the items (or political power).
We implement our algorithms in a software package called FERENDA (Fair Division and Redistricting Endpoint), which is the first comprehensive system for joint fair division and redistricting.
We evaluate the performance of our algorithms on real-world data, and demonstrate that they can produce equitable outcomes in terms of both division and redistricting.

Let $\mathbf{p}$ be a prime, and let $\mathcal{T}(\mathbf{p})$ be the category of torsion-free $\mathbf{p}$-modules of rank 1 over algebraically closed fields of characteristic $\mathbf{p}$. The Auslander-Reiten triangle theory gives a decomposition into simple modules of the canonical module of any algebra in $\mathcal{T}(\mathbf{p})$. We give a formula for the decomposition numbers in this case, and we use this to compute the perfection complex of any self-injective algebra in $\mathcal{T}(\mathbf{p})$.
In this paper, we introduce the concept of an additive deformation of a Hopf algebra.

We show that the tensor algebra T(G) of a group G equipped with the unique Hopf algebra structure such that T(G) ≃ ℝ₂[G] as a vector space, where ℝ₂[G] is the group ring of G, is an additive deformation of ℝ₂[G].
We also show that any additive deformation of ℝ₂[G] is isomorphic to a deformation of T(G).
The British university sector has been at the forefront of web development and delivery of online information and services from the early days of the World Wide Web.

The aim of the project described in this paper is to map the UK webspace by automatically analysing the contents of the websites of UK universities, in order to identify trends over time, and to provide a definitive record of the development of web provision and online services within UK Higher Education.
In this paper we describe the initial findings from an analysis of the web spaces of UK universities over a period of three years, from 2004 to 2006.
The analysis reveals a rapid growth in the size of web spaces, increasing from around 520 million pages in 2004 to over 1.1 billion pages in 2006.
Over the same period the level of accessible content increased significantly, from around 820 million pages in 2004 to over 970 million pages in 2006.
The number of websites hosted also increased substantially, from around 26,000 in 2004 to over 41,000 in 2006.
We perform the first self-consistent numerical study of coulomb screening in linear coasting nuclear burning.

We consider a wide range of nuclear fuels, including those relevant to the early universe as well as those relevant to hypernovae and neutron star mergers, and use screening to calculate the binding energy per baryon of the resulting nuclei during the coasting phase.
We show that screening significantly softens the binding energy, resulting in a substantial increase in the baryon number of the burned nuclei.
This has important implications for nucleosynthesis in these systems, as the increased baryon number leads to a higher mass for the resulting nuclei and a lower neutron-to-proton ratio.
Our results demonstrate the importance of including coulomb screening in numerical simulations of these phenomena.

We perform the first large-scale analysis of petition growth and success rates on the UK No. 10 Downing Street website, spanning over 13 years (from February 2006 to June 2019) and including 415,348 petitions.
We find that the number of signatures received increases with petition age, and this relationship is steeper for more recent years.

We also find a significant linear relationship between the mean signature rate per day and the median number of signatures received, which implies that getting signatures quickly is important for petition success.
Next, we show that a small number of petitions receive a large fraction of the signatures, and that this is more pronounced in recent years.
Finally, we show that success rates have decreased over time and that a "threshold model" where a fixed number of signatures leads to an outcome is not supported by the data.
However, a logistic regression model with petition signature velocity as a significant predictor of success is supported by the data.

This model implies that the probability of success is related to how quickly a petition receives signatures in the first few days of its life, and can be used to predict the outcome of a petition with a given signature velocity.
We introduce a new algorithm for estimating the inverse covariance matrix of a multivariate Gaussian distribution with a given covariance matrix, based on the L0 norm.
The algorithm is applicable to both dense and sparse covariance matrices, and is shown to produce accurate estimates in a variety of scenarios, compared to existing methods.
The proposed algorithm is motivated by the observation that the inverse covariance matrix satisfies a system of linear equations, which can be formulated as a sparse recovery problem.
The algorithm is evaluated on both synthetic and real-world datasets, and is shown to be competitive with existing methods in terms of accuracy and speed.
The L0 norm sparse inverse covariance estimation algorithm has potential applications in many fields, including finance, genetics, and image processing.

Cooperative communications, where multiple base stations collaborate to transmit to a user, has been proposed as a solution to this problem.
In this paper, we investigate the potential of uplink-downlink rate balancing, where the data is transmitted in a cooperative manner in the uplink and the downlink.
We propose a method for allocating resources between the uplink and downlink based on the user's channel conditions and the network's traffic load.

Our results show that significant performance improvements can be achieved through the use of uplink-downlink rate balancing, particularly in scenarios with high traffic loads or users with poor channel conditions.
