Abstract:
Inverse covariance matrix estimation is a fundamental problem in statistics, but it becomes challenging when the dimensionality of the dataset is very high.

The L0 sparse inverse covariance (LSIC) estimation algorithm provides a solution to this problem by estimating the inverse covariance matrix with a small number of nonzero elements, making it suitable for high-dimensional data.
In this paper, we provide a comprehensive review of the LSIC estimation algorithm, including its theoretical background, algorithmic steps, and applications.
We also discuss the challenges and limitations of the algorithm, and explore potential extensions and improvements.
The LSIC estimation algorithm has a wide range of applications in various fields such as finance, genetics, and machine learning.
We believe that this work will provide a valuable resource for researchers and practitioners interested in inverse covariance matrix estimation and high-dimensional data analysis.
The paper examines the challenges of uplink-downlink rate balancing in cooperating cellular networks, where a base station's capacity is shared among multiple users.
It explores the factors that contribute to the imbalance, including the asymmetry in user distribution and the varying signal-to-noise ratios in the uplink and downlink.
The paper then proposes a solution that utilizes traffic adaptive modulation and coding to dynamically adjust the modulation and coding schemes based on the changing traffic conditions.
This approach provides a more balanced distribution of resources and improves the overall performance of the network.
The simulation results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed scheme in mitigating the uplink-downlink rate imbalance and enhancing the network's throughput and coverage.

We investigate the separation of the intensity and warping effects in image registration, namely, the registration of images taken under similar viewpoints of the same scene but with different intensities.
We show that the logarithm of the intensity image can be viewed as the image of a scalar field, the logarithmic intensity, that carries the “geometric” (or warping) information of the image.
The intensity information is then recovered by exponentiating the logarithmic intensity image, a simple and effective procedure.

We propose an algorithm that uses this decomposition for registering intensity images, and show that, in the absence of intensity variations, it reduces to the well-known Lucas-Kanade algorithm for registering images that have undergone translation, scale change, and rotation.
We explore the theoretical properties of the proposed algorithm, and discuss procedures for estimating the parameter of the intensity function that is to be recovered.

We implement the proposed algorithm and compare its performance with that of several other state-of-the-art image registration methods, both in terms of accuracy and speed, on a standard image dataset.
Enforcing Mutual Consistency of Hard Regions for Semi-supervised Medical Image Segmentation.
Many state-of-the-art semantic segmentation methods utilize a pre-defined dataset, such as the Labeled Similarity Learning (LSL) dataset, which consists of accurately annotated images.
However, in reality, the availability of such datasets is usually very limited, and annotating a large number of images is costly and time-consuming.
This paper explores a semi-supervised approach for medical image segmentation that utilizes a small set of labeled images and a large set of unlabeled images from the same domain.
We propose a new method to enforce the mutual consistency of hard regions (MCHR) in the feature space for semi-supervised medical image segmentation.
Given a small set of labeled images, our method can effectively utilize a large set of unlabeled images to improve the segmentation performance.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on three different public datasets: the LSL, the ISBI challenge, and the IVC dataset.
The experimental results show that our approach can achieve significant improvements over the state-of-the-art semi-supervised segmentation methods.
Urban sense segmentation, which aims to assign semantic labels to pixels in urban scenes, is a fundamental task for many applications such as autonomous driving and robotic perception.
Recent advances in this field have achieved remarkable performance mainly based on two-stream architectures that separately learn global and local features.
However, these methods usually rely on heuristic designs to fuse global and local features, which limits their performance.
In this paper, we propose a hybrid transformer to learn adaptive global-local representations for urban sense segmentation.

Specifically, we design a global-local attention module to model the interactions between global and local features, allowing the model to focus on different aspects of the input in a self-adaptive manner.
Furthermore, a hierarchical transformer structure is introduced to capture the contextual information at multiple levels of granularity.
We evaluate our method on the Cityscapes and CamVid datasets, and the results show that our approach outperforms the state-of-the-art methods by a large margin under different settings.
Recent advances in supervised learning have propelled the state-of-the-art in medical image segmentation.
However, the lack of labeled training data in medical imaging hinders the model performance.
In this work, we tackle this problem by introducing a new training strategy named MISSFormer, which utilizes both labeled and unlabeled data for training effective segmentation models.
We propose to use a transformer encoder as the backbone for the segmentation model, as it is capable of capturing long-range dependencies in medical images.
In order to cope with the scarcity of labeled data, we introduce a new loss function that utilizes unlabeled data to provide additional information for training.
We evaluate our method on three public medical image segmentation benchmarks, and our model achieves state-of-the-art performance.
Our code and models are available at https://github.com/AI4MedicineLab/MISSFormer.
Medical image segmentation benefits from increased availability of annotated images across various domains, which enables domain generalization.

However, directly applying existing domain generalization (DG) approaches to medical image segmentation is challenging, as the desired output is a segment map instead of a classifier, and the segments are highly overlapping, creating numerous label relations that should be preserved across domains.
In this paper, we present a hierarchical consistency framework for domain generalization on medical image segmentation (HCDG).
Given a set of image domains, our approach learns a hierarchy of segmentations, each acting as an intermediate representation to capture progressively finer details in the image domains.

These segmentations are paired with a consistency term that enforces consistency among the segment maps within each level of the hierarchy and across levels, while still allowing differences in the finer details.
We show that our approach is able to effectively capture the underlying structure of segment maps across domains while maintaining the desired segmentations.
Our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on four publicly available medical image segmentation datasets.
Recent advances in multimedia technologies have made it possible to collect large volumes of video, audio, and text data.
This has led to a need for effective methods of automatic labeling, or auto labeling, of this data.
Auto labeling refers to the process of using machine learning techniques to assign labels to multimedia data without human intervention.
In this paper, we provide a survey of the most common machine learning techniques used for auto labeling of video, audio, and text data.
We focus on techniques that are most commonly used for a particular type of data, and we provide a brief overview of the strengths and weaknesses of each technique.
This paper aims to provide a comprehensive and informative guide for researchers and practitioners who are interested in using machine learning techniques for auto labeling of multimedia data.
Recent works have shown that bounding box annotations in object detection can be utilized to supervise instance-level segmentation, bypassing the need for expensive pixel-level annotations.
However, these works rely on heavily-annotated datasets, where instances are annotated both with bounding boxes and masks, which are scarce in medical imaging.

In this paper, we exploit domain adaptation to learn from abundantly available bounding box annotations in natural images and transfer the knowledge to medical images without requiring any mask annotations on the target domain.
Specifically, we propose a Box-Adapt framework that consists of a bounding box detector adapted from natural images and a segmentation model with a box-aware encoder.
We condition the encoder on the detection results, enforcing it to learn instance-level representations that reason about the presence and location of instances given the bounding boxes.

Experiments on the abdominal CT and lung CT segments of the MedSeg dataset show that our approach outperforms previous state-of-the-art methods that use only bounding box annotations by a large margin.
Current state-of-the-art semantic image segmentation methods mostly rely on convolutional neural networks (CNNs) with various architectural designs.
Despite the successful performance of CNNs, it still poses some challenges for achieving precise predictions in segmented images.
Recently, Transformer networks have become the go-to option for various computer vision tasks, especially in image classification and object detection.
In this paper, we explore the potential of Transformer networks, namely the Fully Transformer Network (FTN), for semantic image segmentation.
Specifically, we design a simple yet effective FTN architecture to demonstrate the advantages of using Transformers for image segmentation.
The proposed FTN applies a series of Transformer encoders to extract features from input images and obtains segmentation results via a segmentation decoder.
To handle the segmentation with variable numbers of objects, we propose a novel object-wise training strategy for the segmentation decoder.

The experimental results on the Cityscapes and Mapillary Vistas datasets show the effectiveness of the proposed method, achieving competitive performance compared to state-of-the-art segmentation models.
We present a self-paced contrastive learning (SPCL) framework for semi-supervised medical image segmentation with meta-labels.
Meta-labels, derived from the anatomical label of the image, are used to augment the data and improve the generalization performance.

Our approach is to learn a discriminative embedding space for meta-label-conditioned segmentation, where the similarity between the embeddings of the same meta-label is maximized, and the similarity between different meta-label embeddings is minimized.
This is achieved by formulating the learning problem as a maximization-minimization problem on a meta-label-aware loss function, which is solved by the SPCL algorithm.

Our experimental results on three public available abdominal CT image segmentation benchmarks, including the abdominal CT image segmentation challenge (ACTC) 2020 dataset, show that our method outperforms the state-of-the-art semi-supervised learning methods in terms of segmentation performance.
We present a new framework for fully-automatic segmentation of anatomical structures in 3D medical images, where the shape of the structure is modeled as a 3D bounding box.
Unlike previous works on 3D bounding box segmentation, our method does not require any user-provided 3D initialization, making it fully automatic.

Our framework is built upon a novel joint segmentation and 3D bounding box estimation pipeline, where an initial guess of the bounding box is automatically estimated in 2D space and then refined in 3D space with a learned prior.

We show that our method is able to accurately segment 3D volumes of various anatomical structures, and that the use of a 3D bounding box prior leads to more accurate and robust segmentation results compared to state-of-the-art fully-automatic segmentation methods.
Our code and trained models will be publicly available.
We present a maximum likelihood method for reconstructing the parameters of overlapping Gaussian noise models on binary data.
The method is applied to the problem of neuron reconstruction from randomly sampled binary images of cortical activity.
We show that the usual hidden Markov modeling techniques for fitting these models are biased when the data is sparse, and that the bias can be eliminated by expectation-maximization reweighting.

In a simulation study and an application to real cortical data, we show that the method yields accurate estimates of the modeled neurons' firing rates and spatial fields, despite the typically very limited amounts of data available in practical applications.
Recent progresses in few-shot learning have achieved remarkable performance in image segmentation, but most of them still rely on a sufficiently large dataset for training.
In this work, we tackle the few-shot medical image segmentation task under the scenario of limited training data.
Specifically, we collected 112 lesion-specific datasets with only a few images of lesions for training and a large number of images of normal tissues.
To overcome the challenge of limited training data, we propose a Recurrent Mask Refinement (RMR) framework that iteratively refines the segmentation mask in a label propagation manner.

The proposed RMR framework is built upon a basic segmentation framework, and the key difference is that it effectively integrates the prior knowledge of the lesion with only a few labeled images and further refines the segmentation results in a recursive manner.
We evaluate our method on two public breast cancer segmentation benchmarks and a cervical cell detection benchmark, and experimental results show the effectiveness of the proposed method.
Recent works in visual object recognition typically operate on fixed sets of predefined objects or entities of interest.
In this work, we introduce a new task of open-world entity segmentation, where the set of entities is not predefined but is rather determined by the data itself.
We present an approach for open-world entity segmentation that discovers entities in an unsupervised manner, followed by an iterative refinement process that learns to localize and segment them.
The unsupervised entity discovery is based on a variation of the non-parametric Dirichlet process, while the iterative refinement process is solved as a constrained optimization problem.

We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach on the task of instance-level segmentation of 40 different entity classes in the OpenWorld dataset, which contains over 100,000 images and requires zero-shot instance segmentation.
Our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on this benchmark.

Crosslink-Net introduces a simple yet effective encoder segmentation network via fusing vertical and horizontal convolutions, which can be built in a flexible way for various applications with promising results.
The core idea is to adopt a double-branch encoder network that integrates both horizontal and vertical convolutions to capture different kinds of structures in the input images.
Then, a fusion module is designed to effectively combine the features from the two branches.

The horizontal branch focuses on the correlation among pixels in the same row while the vertical one considers the correlation among pixels in the same column, which can capture both texture and shape information in the image.

In the fusion module, the horizontal and vertical features are independently processed via several convolutional layers with different kernel sizes and then concatenated to produce the final feature representation.
We evaluate our approach on the Cityscapes and COCO-stuff segmentation benchmarks and achieve state-of-the-art results.
We present a method for creating predictive models of the housing market using image features.
We show that our model performs better than a baseline prediction model that does not use image features.
In particular, we find that nighttime images improve the performance of our model.
Our best model uses a sparse-coding vectorization of image features from a collection of houses, and spatial and temporal information about the houses.
We show that predictions made using image features are improving over time and that the improvements are consistent with a model that learns from the data.

Our results demonstrate that image features can be useful for predicting the housing market, and that more complex models that utilize additional data sources and features can perform better than simpler models.
However, our results also suggest that the choice of image features and the way in which they are used in the model can have a significant impact on performance.
Therefore, it is important to carefully consider the choice and application of image features when developing predictive models for the housing market or other complex systems.
Domain shift, caused by variations in acquisition protocols, affects the performance of medical image segmentation.
In this work, we aim to segment magnetic resonance images (MRI) of the prostate, which exhibit significant domain shift due to variations in resolution, field of view, and contrast enhancement.
We propose to leverage a pre-trained U-Net with a modified cost function that includes a domain adaptation (DA) term.
On a dataset of 320 MR images, our method achieves a 6.7 percentage point higher segmentation F1-score compared to U-Net without domain adaptation.
Through qualitative and quantitative analysis, we demonstrate that our method is especially effective in difficult cases that exhibit large domain shift.
Our analysis also shows that including the DA term in the cost function improves performance for U-Net layers at multiple levels of the network.
Medical segmentation is a fundamental task in medical imaging.
It refers to the process of partitioning an image into multiple segments, each corresponding to a different anatomical structure.
This paper presents a new perspective on medical segmentation by introducing a novel approach based on matting.

Matting is a technique commonly used in image processing to extract transparent objects from an image, and has been widely used in computer vision applications such as image editing and photo manipulation.
In this work, we propose to use a matting-based approach for medical segmentation, which we refer to as medical matting.
Our method leverages the inherent uncertainty of matting algorithms to handle the challenges associated with medical images, such as noise, artifacts, and partial occlusions.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on a variety of medical image datasets, and show that it can achieve state-of-the-art performance in terms of segmentation accuracy and efficiency.
Recent advances in MRI acquisition enable scanning of the entire heart at once, making it possible to reconstruct a volumetric model of patient-specific cardiac chambers.
This model can be used for help in surgical planning; however, it is challenging to manually segment the boundary of the cardiac chambers in the volume.
We present a method for automatic segmentation of the left ventricle (LV) and right ventricle (RV) in cardiac MRI volumes using a transformer-based model.
Our method reaches a F1 score of 0.91 on in-distribution testing data, and 0.80 on out-of-distribution data.
In addition, our model generalizes to segment the RV in datasets where the RV was not present in the training data.
We show that our model generalizes well to unseen datasets and out-of-distribution data in an open-world setting, despite only being trained on a fixed set of segments.
Recent progress in segmentation algorithms driven by large-scale annotated image datasets has advanced the state-of-the-art in medical image analysis.

However, manual annotation work is costly and time-consuming, which hinders the generalization performance of deep learning models in medical image analysis tasks, especially when only a small amount of annotated data is available.
In this paper, we present a cooperative training strategy with latent space data augmentation (COLA) to enhance the generalization performance of deep learning models for medical image segmentation.

Compared with conventional data augmentation methods, COLA introduces few-shot segmentation labels into the latent space of a pre-trained segmentation model to generate more diverse augmented samples for training.
We implement COLA on three public breast histopathology image datasets with different annotation sizes.

Results show that our method significantly improves the performance of state-of-the-art segmentation models in terms of segmentation accuracy and robustness, especially when only a small amount of annotated data is available.
Strided tensor networks (STNs) offer an efficient representation for atomic and molecular structures, and can be used to accelerate machine learning predictions.

In this work, we extend supervised learning with STNs to the segmentation of two-dimensional (2D) structures, such as the partitioning of molecular graphs into functional groups, or segmentation of 2D images.
We introduce a new architecture, the strided fully connected network, and demonstrate its efficacy on molecular segmentation tasks.

This new architecture improves upon the prior state-of-the-art method on the CASA benchmark, a commonly used dataset for molecular segmentation comprised of annotated structures, with a correctly classified instance of the development dataset.
We introduce a simple and effective method for poisoning the search space in neural architecture search (NAS).
Our method introduces hundreds of thousands of noisy architectures into the search space that mimic the architectures being searched but have slightly modified operations.

During search, these noisy architectures are favored by the NAS algorithm due to their initial good performance, thereby counteracting the evaluation bias and improving the generalization performance of the final architecture.

We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on both image classification and natural language processing tasks, improving the final architectures' top-1 accuracy on CIFAR-10 and EM/F1 score on the Penn Treebank (PTB) dataset compared to baseline methods.
Recent progress in deep learning allows training models to translate between different domains, such as image style transfer and point cloud-to-image translation.
However, most existing works focus on preserving the object structure or the geometry of the objects without considering the semantic meanings of the objects.

In this paper, we tackle the problem of multi-modal domain translation from LiDAR point clouds to panoramic color images, which enables us to preserve both the geometry and the semantics of the objects in the translated images.
Specifically, we propose a novel framework that consists of two components: a geometry-aware translator and a semantics-aware translator.

The geometry-aware translator aims to capture the geometric structure of the objects and the spatial layout of the scene, while the semantics-aware translator aims to capture the object categories and their part relationships.
To train the two components, we propose a new loss function that combines the geometry-aware loss and the semantics-aware loss into a unified framework.
We validate our approach on the challenging KITTI dataset, and the results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach.
Head overcoat (HOC) thickness is an important diagnostic indicator for multiple sclerosis (MS), which can be automatically measured using magnetic resonance (MR) images.
However, existing methods usually require additional manual corrections or optimizations, which is inconvenient for clinical use.
In this paper, we propose a novel automatic HOC thickness measurement method based on deep learning.
Our method is based on a NASNet-Large-Decoder net pre-trained on a large dataset of abdominal MR images.
We fine-tune the pre-trained model on a small dataset of MS patients including T1-weighted (T1W), T2-weighted (T2W), and fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) images.

The proposed method was validated on MS patients and healthy controls, and compared with two commonly used methods: manual drawing of regions of interest (ROIs) and an automatic method based on random forests (RFs).
The results show that the proposed method outperforms RF-based and manual methods in terms of agreement with the gold standard, which is the manual measurement by radiologists.
The proposed method could potentially serve as a useful tool for automatic HOC thickness measurement.
Recent works have shown that training vision transformers (ViTs) with millions of parameters can outperform their convolutional neural network (CNN) counterparts on image classification tasks.
However, training ViTs still poses several challenges: models are sensitive to (1) the quality and amount of data, (2) the augmentation strategies, and (3) the regularization techniques.
In this work, we investigate how these components impact the performance and generalization of ViTs.
We find that training ViTs with higher quality data improves performance significantly, and larger models require more data to maintain performance.
We show that the right augmentation strategy can boost the performance of a ViT, particularly when the amount of data is not sufficient.
We further explore several regularization techniques and demonstrate their effectiveness in improving generalization.
Finally, we propose a set of best practices for training ViTs, validated by a curated collection of benchmark experiments.
When applying these best practices, we achieve state-of-the-art performance on ImageNet-1K, a popular image classification benchmark.

Recent progress in referring expression comprehension has enabled referring queries on images (e.g., which girl is swimming?).

However, most of the prior work focused on answering referring queries with a single object instance, while it is often the case that there can be multiple instances in an image corresponding to a referring expression.

It is challenging to identify all the instances for a given referring expression since the instances could be of different object categories specified in the referring expression, have different scales, and/or occlude each other.

In this paper, we present a cascaded multi-model fusion (CMF) approach for referring image segmentation, which takes a referring expression as input and outputs a segmented image with all the instances labeled.
Our approach effectively combines both appearance and geometry information for instance segmentation.
Specifically, we first generate initial segmentations using appearance models (e.g., CNN features), and then refine them based on geometric constraints in a cascaded fashion.
We perform exhaustive experiments on three benchmark referring expression segmentation datasets, and the results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach against the state-of-the-art methods.

Recent progress in sketch colorization is primarily focused on convolutional neural networks (CNNs), where the input is usually represented by images.
However, sketches are generally more challenging for CNNs to process because of their abstract and often incomplete nature.
In this paper, we propose a new approach to sketch colorization that leverages the power of segmentation models.
Our method trains a segmentation model to classify pixels in colored images into foreground and background, and then uses the predicted mask to color the corresponding regions in a sketch.
To train our segmentation model, we introduce an adversarial loss that encourages the model to produce masks that are perceptually similar to those produced by humans.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on the public SketchColorization dataset, and show that our method outperforms the current state-of-the-art in sketch colorization.
Medical image segmentation serves as a fundamental step for various cardiac image analysis tasks.
In this paper, we focus on left ventricle contouring in cardiac images and present a novel framework based on deep reinforcement learning.
Our framework consists of a pre-trained convolutional neural network (CNN) for initial region proposal generation and a reinforcement learning (RL) agent that learns to generate the final contour.
We employ a deep Q-network (DQN) architecture as our RL agent, which is trained using a loss function that combines both the accuracy and the smoothness terms of the contour.

To handle the significant variation in the shape and size of the left ventricle across different patients, we propose an adaptive bounding box mechanism that provides the RL agent with a fixed-size input while accommodating varying ventricle sizes.
We evaluate our method on the publicly available MICCAI 2012 cardiac segmentation challenge dataset and achieve competitive results compared to state-of-the-art methods.
Recent works usually utilize contrastive learning to improve the representation power of deep models under the supervised setting.

However, most of them follow a deterministic sampling method, i.e., the positive and negative samples are sampled from the easy and hard examples respectively in the same way for all the training examples.
In this paper, we argue that this deterministic sampling may limit the performance of contrastive learning since the hard examples for different training examples could be different.
Thus, we propose a novel attention-guided contrastive learning framework to improve the model performance.

We randomly sample hard examples for each training example according to the attention map, and our experiments show that this random but attention-guided sampling can improve the performance of contrastive learning for semantic segmentation.
Specifically, our model achieves 79.7% mIOU on the Cityscapes dataset, which is 80% of the Waymo dataset.
The accurate classification of abnormal red blood cells (RBCs) using automated hematology analyzers is critical for the diagnosis of various blood disorders.
However, current methods based on single-channel analysis and traditional machine learning algorithms have limited performance, particularly for complex abnormalities.
In this study, we propose a novel approach for vision-based abnormal RBC classification using a multi-channel deep learning architecture.
Our method utilizes the spatial and spectral information of RBCs in multiple color channels to capture the morphological and color features of abnormalities.
We extract multi-channel features from the blood cell images and feed them into a deep neural network for classification.

We evaluated our method on a large dataset of peripheral blood smear images, and the results show that our approach significantly improves the accuracy of abnormal RBC classification compared to state-of-the-art methods.
Our method achieves an overall accuracy of 97.3% and an F1-score of 96.8% on the test set, outperforming traditional machine learning algorithms by a large margin.
The proposed method is also robust to variations in image quality and sample preparation, which is crucial for practical applications in low-resource settings.
Deep learning methods have been applied to medical image segmentation, such as for SPECT/CT images.
However, most existing works focus on binary or discrete segmentation, which limits their clinical usability.
In this work, we aim to learn fuzzy clustering for continuous SPECT/CT segmentation.

We construct a fuzzy clustering framework based on convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and utilize intermediate activations for segmentation instead of the final softmax layer, which enables the model to produce continuous segmentation outputs.

We train the CNN using a novel learning algorithm that minimizes the global mis-classification error of the intermediate activations via stochastic gradient descent (SGD), which is challenging due to the non-differentiabilities of the activations.
We evaluate our method on the MIT-BIH dataset and compare it with state-of-the-art binary and discrete segmentation methods.
Our results show that our method achieves the best segmentation performance in terms of Dice similarity coefficient and average surface distance while producing continuous segmentation outputs.

Abstract:
We introduce SemSegLoss, a Python package providing a collection of state-of-the-art loss functions for training semantic segmentation models.
It facilitates transfer learning and model evaluation by implementing popular loss functions associated with published semantic segmentation models.
We include a carefully curated collection of readable and reproducible source code examples that span a wide range of publication settings and network architectures.

This package simplifies the implementation life-cycle of semantic segmentation models, increases reproducibility in computer vision, and will continue to grow as a collaborative resource for the community.
In this work, we conduct a thorough analysis of the package and examples, provide technical guidance on their usage, and outline future improvements.
Example applications using SemSegLoss are available at <https://github.com/SemSegLoss/SemSegLoss>.
