Recent progress in contrastive representation learning shows that it is essential to learn a good discriminative embedding for semi-supervised learning.

In this paper, we extend the recently proposed momentum contrastive learning (MoCL) to 3D voxel-wise representation learning for semi-supervised volumetric medical image segmentation, which is a typical 3D instance-level segmentation problem.
In our method, we exploit the intrinsic correlation among voxels within the same instance and employ a voxel-wise classifier to enhance the discrimination of embeddings for different segments.
Furthermore, we introduce a momentum contrastive learning (MoCL) framework to aggregate the intrinsic correlations and update the embeddings.
Specifically, we first compute the correlation among voxels within each class and then adaptively adjust the learning rate for different voxels according to the correlation confidence.

The experimental results on three public datasets, i.e., MRI Knee, MRI Abdominal, and MRI Brain, demonstrate the superiority of the proposed method compared to the state-of-the-art semi-supervised learning methods.
We introduce a general framework for joint boundary-aware segmentation and cutout, which can be applied to both indoor and outdoor scenes, for mobile and web applications.
It is the first approach to simultaneously estimate objects and their boundaries in a feed-forward manner.
A boundary-aware segmentation network (BoaNet) is developed to predict object boundaries and segment objects in an end-to-end trainable fashion.

In the BoaNet, a novel boundary-aware skip connection is proposed to couple the feature representations of fine and coarse scales, forcing the network to focus on both the object regions and their boundaries in an explicit manner.
Furthermore, we propose a cutout augmentation method to train the BoaNet, which can not only improve the generalization performance but also enhance the diversity of the training data.
When tested on four benchmark datasets, the BoaNet yields state-of-the-art results.
In addition, the BoaNet has been successfully deployed on mobile and web applications for real-time object segmentation tasks.
Encoder Fusion Network with Co-Attention Embedding (EFN-CAE) is a new deep learning architecture designed for the task of referring image segmentation.
EFN-CAE leverages a fusion of high-level and low-level features learned by two encoders to highlight the referred objects in the image.
Furthermore, a co-attention mechanism is introduced to model the relationship between the referring expression and the image, generating spatial attention weights to focus on the relevant areas.
The referred regions are obtained by fusing global and local features of the image using the attention weights.
In addition, we introduce a novel referredness measure to weigh the importance of each referred region.
This measure is learned jointly with the segmentation network.
We evaluate EFN-CAE on the ReferItSeg dataset, and our model achieves state-of-the-art performance.
Recent progress in pixel-level image segmentation has largely been driven by large convolutional neural networks trained on fully-labeled images with pixel-wise annotations.
However, annotating images pixel-wise is expensive, and for objects that occupy a small proportion of the image (e.g. a few pixels), the annotation cost can be disproportionately large.
This is a particular problem for in-the-wild object segmentation, where even a small number of object instances can require a large amount of effort.
In this paper we explore the problem of training segmentation models using only a small amount of global shape information for training, without any pixel-wise annotations.
We show that even when only trained with a few simple shape descriptors (e.g. bounding box, and segmentation mask), a segmentation model can accurately localize objects in the test image.

We present an approach for learning to segment new objects, given a small number of training examples, each only containing a bounding box and a segmentation mask, and show that our approach is effective in segmenting a wide variety of objects.
Our model performs competitively with state-of-the-art baselines for in-the-wild object segmentation while being significantly more efficient to train.

Recent works on semantic image segmentation often leverage large amounts of annotational data, which are obtained by labeling the pixels in images to distinguish the objects in the images from the background.
However, the quality of the labels varies significantly since the labels are usually generated by different people or different AI/machine learning models.
In this paper, we exploit a simple yet effective technique to improve the discriminative power of pixel-level annotations for image segmentation, by conditioning on metadata of images.

We show that the proposed approach, which we refer to as Linear Conditioning, can effectively boost the performance of semantic image segmentation models without requiring additional training data or modification to the existing segmentation models.

In particular, our experimental results on the Cityscapes dataset show that the proposed approach can improve the F1-score of well-established segmentation models such as PSPNet and DeepLabv3 by 5.7% and 3.0% respectively, and obtain gains of up to 10.7% over the baseline method when compared to the state-of-the-art methods in terms of the F1-score.
Recent advances in deep learning have achieved remarkable performance in semantic image segmentation.
However, training deep segmentation models requires a large amount of labeled images, which are difficult to obtain.
Data augmentation is a useful technique to generate more training samples by applying different transformations to the original images.
Most data augmentation methods focus on image-level augmentation, which applies the same transformation to all objects in an image.
This is a limitation for semantic image segmentation, as it cannot increase the diversity of objects in an image.
In this paper, we introduce a new data augmentation method called ObjectAug, which performs object-level data augmentation for semantic image segmentation.
ObjectAug can generate images with more diverse objects by adapting instance-level labeling and instance-level transformations.
We implement ObjectAug in two ways: (1) adapting instance-level labeling to object-level labeling, and (2) adapting instance-level transformations to object-level transformations.
We conduct extensive experiments on two popular semantic image segmentation datasets, namely Cityscapes and COCO-Seg.
The results show that ObjectAug significantly improves the performance of semantic image segmentation models, especially when the model is trained with a limited number of labeled images.

Recent works in semantic segmentation have demonstrated the potential of learning from weakly-annotated data when a limited number of training images are annotated by a small number of unreliable and inconsistent labels.

However, existing methods usually assume that the uncertainty is induced only by the limited training data and fail to model the uncertainty coming from the variability of the annotator, which is particularly significant in the case of few/no-training-data settings.
In this paper, we argue that the spatial smoothness prior learned from the reliable regions should not be too strong when the reliability of the annotations starts to degrade.
We introduce a spatially varying label smoothing (SVLS) approach to capture the uncertainty from annotator variability in semantic segmentation.
Specifically, given the initial annotations, we estimate the reliability map that indicates the level of confidence in the annotations.
Then, we spatially adjust the label smoothing strength according to the reliability map.
In this way, our method robustly captures the uncertainty from both data and annotator variability when only a few training images are annotated.
We validate our method on both the Cityscapes and Mapillary Vistas datasets with and without training data.
Without any training data, our method outperforms the state-of-the-art methods that assume only data uncertainty, achieving 68.3% mIOU on Cityscapes and 79.4% mIOU on Mapillary Vistas.
Deep learning models have shown promising results for medical image segmentation tasks.
However, training deep learning models for medical image segmentation is a challenging task due to the limitations of labeled training data and the variability of imaging protocols and scanner types.
In this paper, we present a two-layer ensemble of deep learning models for medical image segmentation.
The first layer is a collection of shallow models trained on a small amount of labeled data.
The second layer is a collection of deep models trained on a larger amount of labeled data.
The shallow models are used to initialize the deep models and the deep models are used to refine the predictions of the shallow models.
We evaluate our approach on the ISBI 2017 cardiac segmentation challenge and show that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance.
We present a new framework for scale-space filtering of images, termed Hierarchical Image Peeling (HIP).

HIP is motivated by the observation that digital images can be interpreted as composed of a collection of hierarchical layers, and that many image processing operations may be interpreted as converting an initial configuration of layers into a final configuration.

HIP formalizes this intuition using a hierarchical representation of images, and develops a general scheme for performing local filtering operations that propagate through the hierarchy, updating the layers as they go.
HIP is particularly well-suited to scaling operations, which progressively convolve an image by a scaling kernel.
We show how a wide variety of existing scaling methods, including Gaussian blur, bilateral filtering, and Guided Image Filtering, can be expressed concisely as instances of the HIP framework.

We further demonstrate that the framework is rich enough to accommodate a variety of additional operations, such as reshaping and reparameterization, that are difficult to perform efficiently within the standard image filtering paradigm.
Our implementation of HIP is efficient, and able to accelerate existing image filtering methods by a factor of 100, while providing increased flexibility and expressiveness.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of HIP on a variety of image processing tasks, and show results that are either not possible, or computationally infeasible, with standard image filtering methods.
We address the problem of out-of-distribution (OOD) detection for neural networks, which lacks a clean solution due to the absence of ground truth in the real world.
Unlike existing OOD detection methods that require some form of ground truth for calibration, we propose a simple and general method that detects OOD data without any ground truth.
We observe that neural networks have different responses to in-distribution and OOD data arising from their ability to model the data generating process.

In particular, the distributions of the neural network's intermediate activations are modeled via kernel density estimation (KDE), and the detection is based on a simple statistical test for the intermediate activations.
Our method is completely self-supervised, and does not require any ground truth, anomaly detection, or access to the true data distribution.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet.
Our code is available at this https URL.

Recent works have shown that the use of differentiable topology optimization
can be effective for unsupervised learning of meaningful representations of
data.

We propose DiNTS (Differentiable Neural Network Topology Search), a
method that combines the benefits of differentiable programming with
topological search, for unsupervised 3D medical image segmentation.

In
DiNTS, a differentiable evolution model is learned from a database of
medical images, which can then be used to segment new medical images by
topologically searching for a valid segmentation in a huge search
space.

We show that this approach is able to learn a valid segmentation
in a fraction of a second, and that it generalizes across patients and
modalities.
Learning deformable image registration from optimization: perspective, modules, bilevel training and beyond.
Deformable image registration is a classic problem in medical imaging with wide range of applications, such as surgical planning, target localization, and image fusion.
Recent advances in deep learning have sparked interest in learning-based approaches to deformable image registration.

However, training deep neural networks for this task is challenging, because the network is required to learn a nonlinear registration mapping under a non-differentiable similarity measure, which hinders the use of gradient-based optimization algorithms.
In this paper, we provide a perspective on learning deformable image registration, with a focus on optimization-based approaches.
We discuss the challenges and opportunities in training deep neural networks for this task, and review recent advances in the field.
We also discuss the potential of bilevel optimization, a promising direction for learning-based deformable image registration.
Our goal is to provide a comprehensive overview of the field and identify future research directions.
Recent progress in image co-segmentation has primarily focused on developing effective models for pairwise similarity learning.
However, most existing works assume that the similarity between image regions is independent of the image's context, which is not necessarily true in real applications.
In this paper, we propose a novel approach to image co-segmentation via deep metric learning, which takes into account the contextual information of images.
Specifically, we propose to use a convolutional neural network (CNN) to learn a context-dependent distance metric between image regions.
The proposed metric takes pairs of regions and their corresponding images as input and learns to measure the similarity between the regions while considering the contextual information of the images.
To optimize the proposed metric, we develop a new co-segmentation loss function that encourages consistent and coherent segmentations across images.
The proposed approach has been evaluated on five standard co-segmentation benchmarks, and the results show that our method outperforms the state-of-the-art approaches.
We present a semi-supervised learning method for the segmentation of eye images.
We utilize a convolutional neural network (CNN) architecture, referred to as the Augmented CNN (ACNN), which leverages the power of supervised learning and the robustness of unsupervised learning.

Our approach is based on the assumption that eye images can be represented in a low-dimensional feature space where data points of the same class are closer to each other than data points of different classes.
The ACNN utilizes a low-dimensional embedding function to map input eye images into a low-dimensional feature space, where a linear classifier is then applied for segmentation.
To train our embedding function, we utilize a small set of labeled eye images and a large set of unlabeled eye images.
Our experimental results show that the proposed method achieves state-of-the-art performance on the ISBI eye segmentation benchmark.

Recent works have demonstrated the ability to train MLPs on aggregated graphs, where nodes represent entire graphs and the edges represent similarities between these graphs, with performance that scales with the amount of graph data.
However, in order to do so they rely on having access to large amounts of fully labeled data, which is often difficult and expensive to obtain, especially for medical image analysis.
In this work, we propose a semi-supervised approach to train MLPs on aggregated graphs, by leveraging unlabeled data and a few fully labeled examples.
Since the aggregation of graphs introduces non-transitive relationships between the nodes, we cannot directly apply standard semi-supervised learning approaches based on graph cuts.
To overcome this, we propose a novel approach based on the Diffuse Interface Method, a general framework for optimal transport of probability distributions.

We derive a sufficient condition for identifying well-founded nodes, i.e., nodes for which the semi-supervised training is able to identify the correct class, and show that our approach is able to identify well-founded nodes for a wide range of semi-supervised learning problems on aggregated graphs.
Finally, we propose a fast matrix-vector product for aggregated graphs that is key for the scalability of our method.

We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on two challenging medical image analysis problems: cell classification and lesion segmentation in digital pathology, where the availability of fully labeled data is limited.
A new approach to image segmentation based on the principal component analysis is presented.
This approach is applied to the segmentation of in vitro cell colonies in bright field images.
The individual cells are the basic elements for the segmentation, and therefore an appropriate estimation of cell regions is essential.
In order to achieve this goal, a new filtering technique that utilizes the spatial dependence of the pixel intensity in the image is proposed.
This technique, named as the self-guided filter, is used to preprocess the image, and the resulting image is then provided as the input to the proposed segmentation method.

In this method, the image is decomposed into its principal components, and the segmentation is performed on the dominant principal component, which carries most of the useful information for segmentation.
The proposed method is evaluated using four different benchmark segmentation algorithms.
The results show that the proposed method is comparable to the gold standard watershed algorithm in terms of segmentation quality, and it has the advantage of computational efficiency.
We present a novel approach for enhancing 3D morphological feature representation in convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for semantic segmentation of medical images.
Our method involves extracting 3D morphological features from medical images using morphological operations, which are then used as input to a CNN.
We propose a new block design, called the residual block, which enhances the representation of the extracted features by learning residual mappings.
The proposed residual block is designed to mitigate the information loss caused by linear transformations in traditional convolutional layers, such as downsampling and normalization.
We evaluate our method on the task of semantic segmentation of abdominal computed tomography (CT) scans, and show that it achieves state-of-the-art performance.
Our code and dataset are publicly available.
We present a semi-supervised segmentation approach to localize retinal layers in optical coherence tomography (OCT) images based on a learned prior of layer geometry.
We model the uncertainty arising from the limited training data to constrain the segmentation.
Given a small set of ground truth segmentations, our approach learns a convolutional neural network that predicts layer segmentations and uncertainties.
We introduce a novel boundary-driven loss function that mimics the gold standard of an expert annotator, who typically iterates over layer boundaries until a satisfactory result is reached.
We show that this loss function leads to a learned prior that is able to generalize to unseen data, as indicated by estimated uncertainties.
We evaluate our approach on two public OCT image datasets, and show that it compares favorably to existing state-of-the-art methods while being much faster in practice.
Face mask has become an essential accessory since the COVID-19 pandemic began.
This research aims to address the problem of mask detection and extraction from video sequences.
We present a simple, fast, and effective approach that utilizes a coupled appearance and motion model.
It is trained in a weakly-supervised manner on video clips with ground truth mask bounding boxes.
We introduce a novel Mask Flow Network (MFN) that estimates the flow of masked faces in video frames.
Our approach operates on a single frame in the video and does not rely on face tracking, making it efficient and applicable to videos with challenging poses and facial occlusions.
We evaluate our approach on the 300-hour YouTube Faces dataset, achieving state-of-the-art performance with fast runtime.
Code is available at https://github.com/AI4Finance-Foundation/Mask- Extraction-in-Video-Sequence.

Recent progress in convolutional neural network (CNN) architecture design, such as designing more complex architectures or the use of pre-trained models, has led to significant improvements in image segmentation accuracy.
However, these sophisticated architectures often suffer from overfitting when applied to real-world datasets.
While regularization methods can be applied to mitigate overfitting, they may not be sufficient when the dataset is imbalanced.
In this work, we investigate the impact of class imbalance on overfitting in CNNs for image segmentation.
We find that when the dataset is imbalanced, the CNN tends to overfit more severely, especially when the imbalance ratio is high.
Furthermore, we observe that the overfitting is more pronounced in the early stages of training.
To address this issue, we propose a new regularization method that uses class imbalance as a regularization term.
We evaluate our method on two public datasets, and show that it significantly reduces overfitting, improving segmentation accuracy compared to other regularization methods.
The results suggest that careful data balancing is important to achieve high accuracy in image segmentation with deep CNNs.
We present a simple and efficient self-paced co-training framework for semi-supervised image segmentation.
Our approach leverages the power of consistency, a principle inspired by self-supervised learning, to enforce mutual consistency between label and pixel predictions.
This enables the model to make use of all available labels, even those only available as weakly-supervised pseudo-labels.

We introduce a new consistency loss that enforces agreement at the pixel level between high-level features for both labeled and unlabeled images, and show that it is able to improve performance on semi-supervised segmentation benchmarks.
Our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on the MIT-Adobe FiveK dataset with a single model, in both labeled and semi-supervised settings.
Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) has achieved promising results in image synthesis.
In this paper, we propose a GAN based approach for enhancing the resolution of underdrawings, which are often found in sketches and preliminary drawings in the shading stage.

We train a GAN to generate realistic underdrawings that resemble the given underdrawing, and then use a style transfer technique to combine the generated underdrawing with the given image, producing a high resolution result.
To train the GAN, we use a dataset of underdrawings extracted from images of faces, and we evaluate our approach on a dataset of faces with underdrawings.
Our results show that the proposed method can effectively recover the details in underdrawings while preserving the style of the given image.
Recent results in semantic segmentation, especially in biomedical imaging, have been driven by large-scale annotated datasets.
However, annotating dense pixel-level labels is expensive, and for some applications, the availability of trained experts to perform the annotation is limited.

We introduce a new paradigm called DSAL: Deeply Supervised Active Learning from Strong and Weak Labelers, that aims to minimize the amount of annotation required for training, while learning a model that performs no worse than the baseline that uses all the labels.
In DSAL, a weak annotator performs initial annotation, and a strong annotator cleans up the errors of the weak annotator.
This cleaning process generates strongly supervised training examples in a semi-supervised active learning setting.

We show that this training paradigm is effective for training deep learning models for biomedical image segmentation, and that the resulting models perform competitively with respect to models trained with all the labels.
Recent progress in segmentation of medical images has been driven by large datasets and powerful convolutional neural networks.
However, expert-labeled datasets remain a costly and laborious method of ground truth generation.
We present a new active learning strategy that reduces the amount of labeled data required for network training while maintaining segmentation accuracy.
Our method works in two stages.
First, a convolutional neural network is trained using an initial small set of labeled images.
These are used to learn a probabilistic model of the segmentation performance, specifically a confusion matrix that relates true and predicted segment labels.
Second, active learning is used to select future images for labeling.
This is guided by the predicted confusion matrix, which identifies the most informative images for labeling based on the current state of the model.

We apply our method to simulate the active learning of a prostate MRI segmentation model, and show that the method requires only ~25% of the images in the dataset to achieve >90% of the segmentation performance of the fully-trained network.
Recent works have shown that the use of probabilistic segmentation models provides a number of advantages compared to classical deterministic models.

However, most probabilistic segmentation models assume that the uncertainty is independent across locations, an assumption that is not valid when the spatial coherence of the uncertainty is notable, as is the case in most real world scenarios.
In this work, we address this limitation by proposing Stochastic Segmentation Networks (SSN), a new class of models for producing spatially coherent segmentation maps with associated uncertainty.

SSN combine a spatial aggregation of uncertainty maps, produced by multiple instances of a segmentation model, with an additional spatial transformation step that allows the resulting uncertainty to be spatially correlated.
We show that this model is able to capture meaningful structures in the uncertainty, and provide improved performance compared to state of the art methods on ACDC and VOC2012 segmentation benchmarks.

Recent progress in domain adaptation (DA) has advanced the state-of-the-art in many applications, but most of these methods assume that the source and target domains are fully paired, which restricts their applicability in many real-world scenarios.
In this paper, we tackle the more challenging setting of multi-source domain adaptation (MSDA), where only a subset of domains are paired, and the target domain has no labeled data.

To overcome this limitation, we propose a new framework, which we call mDALU (multi-source Domain Adaptation and Label Unification), to adapt to the target domain with no labeled data using information from the source domains.
Our key insight is that, even in the case of only partial pairings, there still exists useful information in the distributions of the domain-specific features, which can be utilized for MSDA.
We cast the MSDA problem to a novel meta-learning framework, which enables the model to learn from the source domains and unify their knowledge to adapt to the target domain.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on several benchmark datasets for image classification.
We introduce morphological networks (MOR), a novel neural architecture that combines the strengths of morphological neurons (MORs) with the design principles of neural networks.

MORs are similar to cellular neurons in that they are composed of multiple operationally-connected morphological subunits, and compute a real-valued activation based on the inputs and the geometry of the subunits.
However, unlike cellular neurons, the subunits of MORs are not pre-wired but are instead wired via connections to other neurons, either within a layer or across layers.

We show that MORs inherit several key advantages of cellular neurons: they can implement recurrent and attentional dynamics on top of feed-forward computation; they are robust to additive noise due to their divisive normalization property; and they are well-suited for performing complex-valued computations.
Furthermore, we show that, despite their greater complexity, MORs can be trained efficiently using standard gradient-based optimization.

We evaluate MORs on an image classification task, and show that a network of MORs can match the performance of a fully-connected network with a fraction of the number of parameters, and improves upon a network of cellular neurons.
Medical image segmentation is an active research field, producing a large variety of methods and a vast amount of published works.

Compared to other medical image processing tasks, the field of segmentation is particularly challenging since it requires methods to correctly classify voxels or pixels in a large variety of shapes present in different medical images.
Among the different approaches to address this problem, a particular class of methods relies on using loss functions that are able to leverage available information in the form of a prior.
In these methods, the network is trained to classify pixels or voxels together with a confidence value measuring the reliability of the predicted class.

This confidence value is then used to compute the final segmentation mask, where pixels or voxels with a confidence value above a certain threshold are considered part of the foreground, while the others are assigned to the background.
In this paper, we provide an extensive survey on this class of prior-based loss functions for medical image segmentation.
We focus on highlighting the specific design choices done in the different published works, together with a comprehensive evaluation of their performance.
We finally point out open questions and possible research directions.
Semantic image segmentation remains an open problem in computer vision with notable challenges in discriminating fine-grained visual context and accurately localizing objects of interest.
In this paper, we propose to leverage the power of lateral inhibition to address these challenges.
Specifically, we propose a novel module, referred to as gated dilated convolution (GDC), that adaptively computes contextual responses in a self-supervised manner.

GDC introduces a gate that mitigates the lack of locality in conventional dilated convolutions, enabling the network to focus on relevant contextual information and inhibit the responses to irrelevant areas.
We implement GDC in a U-Net like architecture, referred to as GDC-Net, and demonstrate its effectiveness on semantic image segmentation.

In particular, GDC-Net achieves state-of-the-art performance on the PASCAL VOC 2012 semantic image segmentation benchmark, significantly improving the F-measure from 87.4 to 89.5 on the challenging `segmentation-uncertainty` test set, and reducing the gap to the fully supervised baseline from 11.2 to 4.7.
Recent advances in deep learning have achieved remarkable performance in image segmentation tasks.
This survey provides a comprehensive overview of the state-of-the-art deep learning techniques for image segmentation.
We first give an introduction to the image segmentation problem and discuss the importance of this problem in computer vision.
We then survey the recently proposed deep learning based approaches for image segmentation, including fully convolutional networks, U-Net, and Mask R-CNN.
We also discuss the limitations of these approaches and explore the potential for future research.
Finally, we conclude by highlighting the most important contributions of this survey.
Recent progress in contrastive learning shows promising performance in image segmentation with insufficient annotations.
However, most existing methods focus on learning either global or local features, but not both.
In this work, we present a simple yet effective approach to learn global and local features for medical image segmentation with limited annotations.
We first use a convolutional neural network to extract a global feature vector for each image.
Then, we use a simple yet effective approach to extract local features around the predicted boundary.
Finally, we minimize the divergence between the global and local features for training.
Specifically, we minimize the squared Euclidean distance for global features and the cosine distance for local features.
We perform comprehensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets, and the results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach compared to the state-of-the-art methods.
Medical image analysis benefits from automated segmentation to assist pathologists in diagnosing cancer.
In this work, we develop an adaptive segmentation framework for gastric histopathology images based on a hierarchical conditional random field (CRF).
We use a multi-scale segmentation strategy to capture the different sizes of nuclei, which are the most important foreground components.
The nuclei are first detected using a Gaussian mixture model (GMM) and then segmented using the CRF.
The CRF is defined on a hierarchical set of images, obtained by applying Gaussian filters at different scales to the original image.
This allows the CRF to capture both small and large nuclei.
The adaptation is implemented by learning a separate weight for each Gaussian filter scale, which are then combined to produce the final segmentation.
We compare our method to existing works using the challenging dataset from the 2016 MICCAI Gastric Histopathology Image Segmentation (GHIS) challenge.
Our method achieves a Dice similarity coefficient of 0.5391 and a Hausdorff distance of 29.4 pixels on the challenge dataset.
Semantic segmentation of high-resolution satellite imagery is a fundamental task for extracting useful information.
However, the severe variation of scales in the same scene poses a great challenge for pixel-level labeling.
In this paper, we propose a new approach for semantic segmentation of high-resolution satellite imagery, named PP-LinkNet.
It leverages a multi-stage training strategy to learn the hierarchical representations of pixels, which can effectively capture both local and global characteristics of the data.
Specifically, a pyramid pooling module is proposed to encode multi-scale contextual information, and a link-net module is designed to capture the global relationships between pixels.
The whole network is trained in an end-to-end manner, allowing effective gradient flow through the pyramid and link structures.
We evaluate our approach on the challenging semantic segmentation benchmark, and demonstrate that it achieves state-of-the-art performance.

Many state-of-the-art segmentation models exploit domain-specific information for better performance but rely on either 1) assuming the availability of domain-specific segmentation models or 2) using heuristic normalization schemes that do not perform well when the distribution of the data is complex.
In this paper, we aim to address both of these issues.
We propose a realistic image normalization (RIN) approach towards learning a single segmentation model that is able to adapt to multiple domains while maintaining performance.
Our approach first estimates the domain-specificity in the image and then compensates for it by adjusting the image pixel-wise so that the distribution becomes more uniform.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on three publicly available datasets, and show the advantages against prior art on both segmented and unsegmented images.
Semantic image segmentation is a fundamental task in computer vision with a wide range of applications.
Deep learning methods have shown promising results in this area, but real-time performance is still a challenge.
This survey provides a comprehensive overview of recent advances in deep learning methods for semantic image segmentation in real-time.
We focus on two main aspects: accuracy and efficiency.
We review state-of-the-art algorithms and evaluate their performance on standard benchmarks.
We also discuss the trade-offs between accuracy and efficiency and explore potential solutions to improve both.
Our goal is to provide a comprehensive reference for researchers and developers working on semantic image segmentation in real-time.
Recent progress in 3D medical image segmentation has benefited from effective architectures designed for image-based tasks, especially those with encoder-decoder structures.
However, in medical imaging, images are not simply arranged pixels, but structured data, where each pixel is associated with a discrete label that forms a hierarchical graph structure.
This graph structure, referred to as the segment hierarchy, represents the spatial and semantic relationships between different anatomical structures in medical images.
In this paper, we argue that effectively utilizing the segment hierarchy during inference is crucial for capturing the underlying structures of medical images.
To this end, we propose UXNet, a novel encoder-decoder architecture that explicitly models the segment hierarchy in 3D medical image segmentation.
UXNet searches for multi-level feature aggregation strategies to effectively integrate information from different levels of the hierarchy during inference.
We evaluate UXNet on the task of abdominal organ segmentation in abdominal CTs and compare it with state-of-the-art methods on the public dataset abdominal_segmentation.org.
Our results show that UXNet improves over the baseline by a large margin and compares favorably with the state-of-the-art on the public leaderboard.
We present a random style transfer approach to domain generalization based on a unified representation learning framework.
In this approach, we use a pre-trained convolutional neural network (CNN) as the prior knowledge to extract features for domain generalization.
To achieve this, we propose a random style transfer mechanism that can flexibly integrate both shape and spatial information for domain generalization.
We show that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods on two benchmarks, specifically for the dataset of SUN and SCUT-CT.

Arrival of patients at the emergency department (ED) with unclear diagnosis and referral patterns pose a great challenge to healthcare systems in deciding on the optimal treatment or referral strategy.

In this paper, we aim to introduce a novel framework for the utilization of electronic health records (EHRs) for referring patients to the right department in the hospital at the point of arrival to the ED, to facilitate quick and efficient patient routing.
The proposed approach is based on a deep learning architecture that utilizes the EHRs effectively for accurate decision-making in patient referral at the ED.
We propose a framework that is based on a variational approach to encode the inherent uncertainty within the deep learning architecture.

The framework is evaluated on a real-world dataset from a major hospital, and the results show that the proposed approach is able to outperform the state-of-the-art approaches for patient referral at EDs.
Towards semantic video segmentation, the state-of-the-art primarily relies on dense optical flow for effective motion compensation.
However, computing optical flow is memory-intensive and computationally costly, especially for video frames of high resolution.

In this paper, we tackle the challenge of developing an effective and efficient framework for semantic video segmentation, which can readily take advantage of compressed-domain motion knowledge without requiring optical flow.

To this end, we propose TapLab, a semantic video segmentation framework that taps into compressed-domain motion knowledge by extensively exploiting motion compensation mechanisms available in modern video coding standards (e.g., MPEG).

Specifically, we reformulate the traditional semantic video segmentation pipeline by integrating compressed-domain motion compensation at each step, ranging from feature extraction to spatial propagation and temporal aggregation.
Furthermore, we introduce a novel sparse-grid optical flow field, which is efficiently computed from the compressed video stream and aids in refining the motion compensation.
On the popular Cityscapes and KITTI datasets, experimental results show that our TapLab framework is on par with or even outperforms the state-of-the-art methods while being several times faster.
Recent progress in segmentation of medical images typically relies on large amounts of annotated training data.
However, different diseases might require different segmentation strategies due to distinct anatomical changes, and it can be difficult to obtain large-scale annotated data for all domains.
We propose a framework to learn a disease-specific segmentation model for MRI brain images using only a small labeled sample of healthy and diseased images.

Our framework is based on the observation that anatomical structures of the brain, as well as most diseases, manifest themselves in spatially coherent patterns, which can be captured by learned spatial filters.
We propose to learn a shared low-dimensional embedding of brain images, where the embedding is optimized to (1) capture disease-specific spatial patterns and (2) be useful for segmentation.
The embedding is learned via a conditional cycle consistency loss, which ensures that the embedding encodes spatial relationships both within and between images.
We then use the embedding to adapt a segmentation model trained on a different dataset, without needing to annotate the images in the new domain.
Our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on multiple datasets for multiple diseases, while using only a small fraction of the labeled data required by other methods.
Medical image segmentation is a fundamental task in clinical workflows, enabling various downstream analyses.
Despite the success of deep learning methods, most state-of-the-art approaches struggle with segmenting rare anatomical structures due to the lack of training data.
We propose an uncertainty-aware loss function to train normalizing flows for segmentation of rare structures.
We model uncertainty via a Bayesian approach, where the latent space is modeled as a Gaussian distribution conditioned on the image data.
We propose a novel uncertainty-aware loss function that utilizes the uncertainty predictions to emphasize the misclassified pixels.

We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach on three different rare anatomy segmentation datasets, where our model outperforms the state-of-the-art in terms of segmentation accuracy and uncertainty estimation.
We present a fully automated active contour model that is trained from end to end to segment images of buildings in aerial imagery.

The network is composed of a convolutional backbone network, followed by an attention module that performs the active contour energy computation, and followed finally by a segmentation head that outputs a segmentation mask.

Since there are no predefined contour models that can handle this problem, we propose an attention module that takes in the features from the backbone network and computes an attention map where regions of importance for the contour are highlighted.
We train the entire network end-to-end to optimize over the active contour energy and the segmentation mask.
We validate our approach on a new dataset we created where ground truth segmentation masks were manually created by leveraging the Google Building Maker tool.
We show that our fully automated model is on par with the manually created building contours, thus demonstrating the potential for automated image segmentation in this problem domain.
Fast panoptic segmentation is a fundamental task for many computer vision applications.
Existing methods usually concatenate prediction branches for different categories, yielding a huge increase in model size and computation.
In this work, we propose a lightweight and efficient approach for fast panoptic segmentation, termed AinnoSeg.
Specifically, we introduce a weight-shared U-Net whose output channels are dynamically determined by the intermediate features.

A key insight is that the hierarchical features in the U-Net can be naturally aligned with the panoptic segmentation hierarchy (i.e., instance-level, stuff-level, and thing-level), and therefore the U-Net can be adapted to different parts of the hierarchy with different output channels.
This adaptability allows us to selectively enlarge the capacity for hard instances (e.g., small stuff) while keeping a small model size for easy instances (e.g., large things).
We show that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on the camvid and cityscapes datasets with a model size 14\times and 4\times smaller than the previous best method, respectively.

Recent works on semantic image segmentation often
use encoder-decoder networks as the main architecture.

Encoder-decoder networks inherently assume a
single-stage inference, where the predicted
segmentation output is refined by transposing
features from the encoder via skip connections.

In
this paper, we argue that this single-stage
inference is sub-optimal for segmentation as it
ignores the spatial coherence in the output
space.

Consequently, we propose Deep
Decoders, a simple and effective approach that
incorporates spatial coherence into encoder-
decoder networks for semantic image
segmentation.

Deep Decoders utilize multiple
stages of decoding in an end-to-end trainable
fashion, where each stage upsamples the
coarse output to yield a more detailed
segmentation.

Our experiments on the VOC 2012
segmentation benchmark show that our approach
yields a significant improvement in segmentation
quality while being efficient enough to be
practically applicable.
Semantic segmentation is a fundamental task in computer vision with a wide range of applications.
However, training such models requires large amounts of accurately annotated data, which is difficult and expensive to obtain.
In this paper, we tackle the problem of limited data and annotations in semantic segmentation by proposing a new approach that combines the use of image-based and instance-based training data.
We show that by using a multi-task learning framework, we can effectively leverage both types of data to improve the performance of semantic segmentation models.
Furthermore, we present a new instance-based loss function that utilizes an ensemble of instance-based models to improve the robustness of our approach.

We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on the Cityscapes and CamVid datasets, achieving state-of-the-art performance on both datasets with a significant reduction in the amount of training data required.

Towards Unsupervised Learning for Instrument Segmentation in Robotic Surgery with Cycle-Consistent Adversarial Networks

Preoperative imaging is instrumental for surgical planning however, current planning methods do not sufficiently depict instrument location or configuration, information that is useful for determining surgical strategy.
We propose an unsupervised learning framework for the segmentation of surgical instruments in fluoroscopic images.
Our method consists of a cycle-consistent adversarial network (CycleGAN) with additional clinical prior knowledge incorporated into the loss function.
We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach on a novel dataset of 30 robotic surgery fluoroscopic sequences, achieving a dice coefficient of 0.8021.

Recent advances in medical imaging, such as magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and computed tomography (CT), have led to a vast amount of data that must be processed, with the aim of extracting relevant information for radiologists.
This has created a great demand for efficient and effective image processing techniques.
We present a novel approach for the mining of corrupted pixels in medical images, which has the potential to significantly improve the efficiency of image processing.
Our approach utilizes the concept of meta-learning, where a machine learning model is trained on a large dataset of images and their corresponding corrupted pixels.
The model is then used to extract the corrupted pixels from new images, with the aim of utilizing the extracted information for subsequent image processing tasks.

We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on a variety of medical image datasets, including MRI and CT images, and show that it can significantly improve the efficiency of image processing tasks.
K-means is simple and efficient, but it suffers from two well-known problems: it converges to local minima and sensitivity to the initial cluster centers.
In this paper, we follow a fuzzy approach for the $C$-means algorithm, which has been shown to be more robust and is more likely to converge to the global solution.
Following this, we employ the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence as a measure of similarity between two probability distributions to define the fuzzy $C$-means (FCM) algorithm.

Additionally, we propose a morphological reconstruction approach to improve the final cluster shape, and we utilize wavelet frames to handle multi-scale information and to improve the efficiency of the algorithm.
The proposed method is evaluated on several benchmark segmentation datasets, and the results show the efficacy of the proposed approach compared to state-of-the-art algorithms.

Learning-based anatomical segmentation is often performed in an unsupervised manner, relying on strong assumptions about the data distribution, and yielding implausible segmentations that require tedious post-processing.
In this paper, we explore the use of denoising autoencoders (DAEs) for learning-based segmentation post-processing.
We introduce a new framework, which we call Post-DAE, that improves the accuracy of segmentation by refining the predictions of any learning-based method.
In particular, we show that DAEs, originally proposed as an unsupervised method for image denoising, can be used to enhance segmentation by encouraging consistency between neighboring segments.

We demonstrate the effectiveness of the method on synthetic and real images, and show that our approach improves upon state-of-the-art unsupervised segmentation methods for the task of abdominal organ segmentation.

We present a new method for cardiac segmentation that provides strong anatomical guarantees, i.e., it computes a segmentation where each voxel is labeled according to the tissue type that dominates anatomically.
This is made possible by a new explicit anatomical prior based on a distance transform of the left ventricle surface, which is used to regularize the segmentation.
We show that the proposed method is competitive with state-of-the-art cardiac segmentation methods, while providing better anatomical accuracy, as verified against manual annotations.
We present a Bayesian optimization (BO) framework for optimizing complex systems that can be decomposed into subsystems, where the collaboration between subsystems follows a specific model.

These systems often arise in applications where a user can choose among a collection of tools or algorithms to solve a problem, and the performance of the overall system depends on the choice and collaboration of these subsystems.
We introduce a "modular" black-box model that captures the collaboration between subsystems, along with switching costs that arise when changing the composition of the system.
We propose a novel BO algorithm that optimizes the system's structure (i.e., the choice and configuration of subsystems) and its parameters via a probabilistic representation of the search space.
We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach on simulated problems and a real-world scenario of optimizing the hyperparameters of a machine learning pipeline composed of modular components.
Recent advances in deep learning have propelled the fields of image processing and computer vision to a level never seen before.
One of the most successful applications of deep learning is in image segmentation, which is the process of partitioning an image into multiple segments.
This paper provides a survey of the current state of research in image segmentation using deep convolutional neural networks.
We begin by providing a brief overview of the most commonly used image segmentation techniques.
We then review the recent advances in image segmentation using deep learning, including the use of fully convolutional networks, atrous convolution, and recursive partitioning.
We then discuss the advantages and limitations of each approach.
Finally, we provide a summary of the current state of the art in image segmentation using deep learning and identify potential future research directions.
Recent works have shown that training segmentation models with noisy labels can improve performance on real-world datasets.
However, these methods assume that the annotation layers present in the training data perfectly align with the ground truth segments, an assumption that does not hold in practice.

In this paper, we show that the commonly used annotation refinement techniques, which are applied to align the annotations, introduce significant errors that negatively impact the performance of the model.
We propose a simple yet effective framework to learn a segmentation model from misaligned and noisy labels.
We introduce a new architecture, called Shift, that leverages the inherent geometric structure of segmentation models to explicitly model the label shift as a learnable layer.

We show that our method consistently improves upon the state of the art on the Cityscapes and Mapillary Vistas datasets without any annotation refinement step and even when only trained on synthetic data.
Electrocardiograms (ECGs) are indispensable for the diagnosis of cardiac abnormalities, but the process of manually annotating ECG waveforms is labor-intensive and time-consuming.
Recently, deep learning models have been proposed for ECG delineation, but these models require a large amount of manually annotated data for training.
In this work, we present ECG-DelNet, a deep learning model for ECG delineation that can be trained using a mixed quality dataset, containing both manually annotated and automatically annotated data.
We show that our model can learn to delineate ECG waveforms with high accuracy, even when trained on a mixed quality dataset.
Our model is composed of a convolutional neural network (CNN) followed by a region-based fully connected neural network (FNN).
We evaluate our model on a large dataset of ambulatory ECGs and show that it outperforms the state-of-the-art in ECG delineation.
Code is available at https://github.com/AI4ECG/ECG-DelNet.
We introduce a new framework for multitask learning (MTL) to improve natural language understanding (NLU).
Our method performs MTL with an ensemble of task-specific models, all of which are trained with supervised learning (SL) and are initially identical.
We then jointly train the ensemble on a mixture of tasks, using a small amount of labeled data for each task.
This enables the models to specialize on their respective tasks, yet they can still borrow information from each other to improve on all tasks.
We evaluate our method on a state-of-the-art NLU system, where we achieve a relative improvement of 1.7% in task-agnostic F1 score.
We present a novel architecture for cell image segmentation called Feedback U-net (F-U-net).
F-U-net combines the strengths of the U-net and CycleGAN architectures to create a robust and accurate cell image segmentation model.

The U-net architecture allows for the use of an encoder-decoder structure with skip connections, which helps to improve the model's performance by providing high-level features to the decoder network.

The CycleGAN architecture enables the model to learn a mapping between the source and target domains, which is useful for segmenting cells in images from different modalities or with different characteristics.
We evaluate F-U-net on two cell image segmentation datasets, and results show that it significantly improves over the U-net architecture in terms of accuracy and efficiency.
F-U-net has several notable features.
Firstly, a feedback connection is added on the decoder side of U-net to refine the output of the last layer.

Secondly, a CycleGAN-like architecture is used to learn the underlying transformation between the source and target domains, which helps to improve the segmentation performance for images in different modalities/backgrounds.
Thirdly, we design an adaptive loss function to effectively train the model on both labeled and unlabeled data.

Experiment results on two public cell image segmentation benchmarks, namely the Cell Segmentation Challenge 2017 (CSC2017) and PubMed Central (PMC), show that the proposed method achieves the state-of-the-art performance.
Code is available at https://github.com/AI4Finance-Foundation/Feedback-Unet.
A deep learning based convolutional neural network (CNN) has been shown to achieve great performance for medical image segmentation.
However, it remains a challenge to train such networks with limited training data.
In this paper, we present a novel ensemble based deep CNN framework for semi-supervised medical image segmentation, which is trained on both labeled and unlabeled data.
Our framework utilizes an ensemble of CNNs to boost the segmentation performance.
We adopt a weighted majority voting scheme to combine the outputs from individual CNNs, where the weights are learned from the labeled data.
Furthermore, we introduce a novel data augmentation technique to generate more training samples from the unlabeled data.
The proposed method is evaluated on the abdominal CT image dataset from the CAMELYON16 challenge.
Quantitative and qualitative results show that our method can achieve competitive performance compared to the state-of-the-art semi-supervised learning methods.
Recent progress in real-time video segmentation is evaluated mostly based on latency, regardless of the stability of the output and the complexity of the scene.

In this work, we first argue that the current evaluation metric is unfair, since the performance of the model depends on the input video, and then propose a fair metric by considering the segmentation quality and the complexity of the scene.
We build an end-to-end real-time video segmentation framework that can predict the trade-off between the segmentation quality and the latency with a single forward pass.
The framework consists of a backbone network and a quality-latency predictor network.
Given the predicted quality-latency scores, we develop an adaptive aggregation strategy to output the final segmentation results.
Since the proposed framework is end-to-end trainable, we alleviate the lack of training data and alleviate the discontinuity of the learned latencies by using data augmentation and a continuity loss.
We optimize the predictor network with a novel fairness objective to measure the unfairness of the current metric.
Our method achieves real-time performance with high efficiency and fairness.
Deep learning has resulted in great advances in biomedical image segmentation, especially in recent years.
However, designing an effective deep learning architecture still requires extensive experimentation, making it a tedious and time-consuming task.
In this paper, we present an automated design pipeline for deep learning that is tailored to biomedical image segmentation.
Our pipeline is based on a meta-learning approach, where a set of candidate architectures are pre-defined and a neural network is used to select the best architecture from the candidate set.

We evaluate our approach on three publicly available biomedical image segmentation datasets, and show that our automated design pipeline can produce models that are either comparable or significantly better than the state-of-the-art.
We will make our source code and trained models publicly available.
Recent progresses in few-shot segmentation mainly focus on designing metric learning objectives or embedding structures to improve the adaptability of the networks for few-shot scenarios.
These methods usually require a significant number of reference samples for each class to build the adaptability.
However, in real-world applications, it is expensive or even impossible to collect a large number of references for all classes, which hinders the promotion of few-shot segmentation models.
In this paper, we tackle this problem from a network design perspective.
We propose a Cross-Reference Network (CRNet) that can utilize the reference samples of other classes to improve the representation of the current class.

Specifically, we design a cross-reference module that leverages the reference samples of different classes to refine the feature representations of the current instance through a consensus learning process.
We conduct extensive experiments on three public datasets, and the results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach against other few-shot segmentation methods.
We propose a neural network approach for optimizing stochastic processes that can be expressed as constrained optimization problems with a large number of dimensions.
The proposed method is motivated by optimal stopping problems, where the goal is to choose a stopping time for a given stochastic process that maximizes the expected cumulative rewards.
We introduce a deep neural network that learns a ranking of the response surfaces over the decision space, without relying on the explicit form of the reward function.
We show that the proposed approach can effectively optimize a wide class of reward functions, including possibly non-differentiable and non-convex functions.

We demonstrate the performance of our method on a synthetic problem and two optimal stopping problems: maximizing the expected lifetime of a stochastic process and maximizing the expected cumulative rewards in a sequential classification problem.
Our results show that the proposed method can effectively optimize these problems and improve the state-of-the-art.
Object detection and classification are important tasks in computer vision, with many applications in various fields.
However, these tasks become challenging in cluttered backgrounds, where multiple objects are present in a single image, leading to decreased performance in both accuracy and efficiency.
In this paper, we explore methods to improve the learning effectiveness for object detection and classification in cluttered backgrounds.

We propose a new approach that utilizes a multi-scale convolutional neural network (CNN) to extract features from images, and a hierarchical classification framework to improve the accuracy of object detection and classification.

The proposed method is evaluated on two standard datasets, and the results show that it significantly improves the performance of object detection and classification in cluttered backgrounds compared to the state-of-the-art approaches.
We present a novel approach to 3D object detection that utilizes semi-supervised learning and multi-view training.
Our method leverages uncertainty awareness during training to improve the performance of 3D object detection.
We introduce a new co-training scheme that uses a single-view detector as a strong prior to guide the training of a multi-view detector.
Furthermore, we propose an uncertainty-aware loss function that encourages the model to produce confident and accurate predictions.
Our method significantly improves over previous state-of-the-art approaches on the KITTI dataset, achieving a mean average precision of 82.4% on the test set.
Code is available at: https://github.com/NVlabs/
Uncertainty-Aware-Multi-View-Co-Training.
We consider the problem of optimizing a surrogate function that mimics a linear-fractional utility function in a binary classification problem.
The surrogate is defined as a linear combination of the true utility function and a set of convex, differentiable functions.
The optimization problem is posed as a constrained maximization problem, with the surrogate function as the objective function and the true utility function as a constraint.

We propose a method for calibrating the weights of the surrogate function to maximize the difference between the surrogate function and the true utility function, while maintaining a positive semidefinite covariance matrix of the surrogate function.
The proposed method is evaluated on a set of simulated data and compared to existing methods for maximizing the true utility function.
The results show that the proposed method can perform well in a variety of scenarios and can provide an effective surrogate for the true utility function.
We propose a residual-sparse fuzzy $C$-means clustering method for image segmentation.
It benefits from the prior knowledge that the objects in the image to be segmented are composed of a finite number of pixels, i.e., the object size is bounded by a small value.
It incorporates two techniques: morphological reconstruction and wavelet frames.
In the morphological reconstruction, the initial fuzzy $C$-means result is refined by iteratively adding pixels, which can improve the accuracy of the result.
Wavelet frames are used to extract the multiscale information of the image, and they can provide the prior knowledge of the object size.
The proposed method is evaluated on several images, and the experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.
We present a one-pass attention network for brain tumor segmentation, which is trained end-to-end.

Unlike most existing methods that learn to attend to the most relevant features independently for each task (i.e., tumor versus non-tumor), our approach learns a common attention module for all tasks.
This module attends to the most relevant features while suppressing the irrelevant ones in a task-independent fashion.
We show that this cross-task guided attention mechanism improves performance on all tasks and results in better generalization.
We evaluate our method on the BraTS 2018 dataset and achieve promising results, outperforming the state-of-the-art methods for most of the metrics.
We present an approach for training Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) when some (or all) of the true data is missing or incomplete.

Our method extends recent work on factorised discriminators, which decomposes the discriminator network into a parallel stack of components, each of which focuses on a different aspect of the input data.

By training the discriminator to learn a generic factor whilst maintaining a component specifically for the incomplete data, our approach treats the incomplete data as an auxiliary task, encouraging the generator to learn a robust representation that captures the shared information between the incomplete and complete data.
We demonstrate our approach on several datasets, showing that it is competitive with, or improves upon, state-of-the-art GAN methods for handling incomplete data.
In this paper, we present a hierarchical modeling approach for multidimensional data, which advantageously allows for regular decomposition of the solution space.

In contrast with standard nonlinear modeling, wherein the solution space is implicitly defined by the nonlinear equation system, here we rely on algebraic tensor decompositions, specifically, on the hierarchical tensor representation of multivariate functions.

We show that, under very general assumptions, the solution of the hierarchical modeling problem can be sought in the regular tensor manifold, as opposed to the high-dimensional space of the full tensor rank.

We discuss the connections between the hierarchical approach and other topics from the recent literature on low-rank tensor approximation, and present a systematic way for modeling data with complex structures in a hierarchical setting.
In particular, when the data are generated by a stationary process, we provide a natural generalization of the classical multivariate spectral decomposition.
We also introduce a new technique for estimating the parameters of the hierarchical model, which exploits the low-rank structure of the solution space and is shown to be numerically efficient.
The methodology is illustrated through several applications to simulated and real data.
Deep learning segmentation networks for rectal cancer microscopy images often show strong model variance, which hampers generalization performance.
We attribute this to the limited amount of training data available, which leads to overfitting.
To mitigate this problem, we propose a simple yet effective approach to reduce the model variance of a segmentation network.
Our approach consists of training the network with data augmentation on a larger dataset, and then fine-tuning the network on the target dataset with a lower amount of labeled data.
We compare our method to other approaches for model variance reduction, such as training on a larger dataset without data augmentation, and model selection using validation performance.

Our results show that our method improves the mean Dice similarity coefficient by 5.2% compared to training on the full dataset without data augmentation, and by 3.2% compared to model selection using validation performance.
Furthermore, it reduces the maximum Dice coefficient variation among five different runs by 40.7%.
An active contour model is proposed for image segmentation based on the eikonal region growing technique.
Unlike existing methods, our model is driven by a priori knowledge that can be easily specified by the user.
The key component of our model is a region growing technique that can quickly and automatically produce a good initial contour as well as a collection of accurate seed points for region growing.
An efficient implementation of the proposed method is realized using the recently developed dynamic programming framework for 1-fold and 2-fold image segmentation.
The performance of the proposed method is compared with three state-of-the-art active contour models, and the results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.
We present a novel end-to-end differentiable decomposition framework for training convolutional neural network (CNN) based conditional random fields (CRFs).
Under this framework, the CNN-CRF is decomposed into a convolutional layer and a CRF layer, with the convolutional layer outputting particle filters for the CRF layer.
The particle filters are obtained by solving a convolutional-deconvolutional (c-d) network via a differentiable approximation.
During training, the gradients of the CNN-CRF with respect to the CRF layer and the convolutional layer are calculated via the chain rule and the backpropagation algorithm.
Our framework is capable of effectively training deep CNN-CRFs with multiple layers.
We validate our framework on a number of benchmark datasets, and demonstrate its effectiveness and efficiency.
Recent advances in medical imaging technology have led to a vast amount of data available for training deep learning models for image segmentation.
However, manual segmentation remains a time-consuming and tedious task, despite recent developments in the field of medical image segmentation.
In this work, we present a novel approach for medical image segmentation based on hierarchical attention networks.
Our method employs a multi-scale hierarchical attention module that utilizes attention weights to focus on relevant features at multiple scales.
Furthermore, we introduce a novel boundary refinement module that utilizes morphological operations to improve the accuracy of the segmentation output.
We evaluate our method on the ISBI 2017 Challenge dataset and achieve competitive results compared to other state-of-the-art methods.
Our code and trained models are available at https://github.com/zhang-zhy/hani.
Abstract— We present a framework for training a deep neural network for automated weed detection in aerial imagery with context.
Our approach combines a convolutional neural network (CNN) for feature extraction with a support vector machine (SVM) for classification.
The CNN is trained on a dataset of aerial images containing a variety of weeds and background contexts.
The SVM is trained on the features extracted by the CNN from a separate dataset of images containing only weeds and background.
Our approach achieves a high accuracy rate of 92.7% for weed detection in aerial imagery.
Furthermore, our approach is able to detect weeds in imagery containing a variety of background contexts, such as fields, roads, and water bodies.
Our work is a novel application of deep learning for weed detection in aerial imagery.
To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work that combines a CNN with an SVM for this purpose.
We believe that our approach can be applied to other object detection tasks in aerial imagery, and potentially in other domains as well.
Medical image segmentation is a fundamental but challenging task in medical imaging.
In this paper, we present a novel semi-supervised segmentation framework to effectively utilize the abundant unlabeled images for training.

Specifically, we impose a consistency constraint on the segmentations of the unlabeled images under a variety of transformations, where the transformations include rigid transformations (rotation, translation, and scaling), elastic transformations (rigid and non-rigid deformations), and intensity transformations (contrast and brightness adjustments).

We learn a segmentation network under the consistency constraint via a maximum a posteriori (MAP) framework, where the posterior is defined by a probabilistic model that characterizes the consistency relation.
We optimize the segmentation network and the probabilistic model alternately.
We evaluate our method on the MIT-BIH and INRIA-MedSeg segmentation benchmarks, and experimental results show that our method outperforms the state-of-the-art semi-supervised segmentation methods.

Current unsupervised video object segmentation (VOS) methods mostly utilize either optical flow or temporal convolutions to model the temporal coherence, which may not model the objectness properly, leading to degraded performance.
In this paper, we propose a simple but effective anchor diffusion module to improve the performance.
It refines the segmentation results at both frame level and pixel level by modeling the temporal coherence properly.

Specifically, given the initial segmentation results, we propagate the segmentation confidence from the confident pixels to their adjacent pixels in the same object via anchor points, which can keep the spatial information and guide the diffusion effectively.
Furthermore, a threshold-free method is proposed to refine the segmentation results at the pixel level, which can effectively capture the object boundaries.
The proposed method is simple to implement and can be easily integrated into any existing frameworks.
We validate the effectiveness of our approach on VOC2012, where our method achieves a F-measure of 81.1% on the test set, outperforming all existing unsupervised methods.
We present a novel framework for few-shot segmentation of volumetric images, such as those acquired by MRI, CT, or ultrasound.
Our method leverages the prior knowledge provided by a pre-trained convolutional neural network (CNN) and a set of few labeled example volumes to learn a new CNN for segmenting novel input volumes.

We introduce a novel module, termed Squeeze & Excite, that regularly samples and fuses features across layers, enabling the model to leverage informative features from the prior and learn new features from few labeled examples.
Our method performs competitively with state-of-the-art approaches on multiple volumetric image segmentation benchmarks while requiring only a fraction of the labeled training data.
In a quantitative evaluation, we show that our approach excels in few-shot segmentation tasks where the support set size is small, exhibiting strong generalization performance.
We present a simple and efficient approach for semantic segmentation based on convolutional neural networks (CNNs).
Our method combines a CNN architecture with a level set loss function to learn pixel-level class labels.
The network takes an input image and produces a binary segmentation mask for each class.
We train the network using a set of labeled images and show that the proposed method can achieve accurate segmentation results.
The trained network can be used for semantic segmentation of novel images.
We compare our method to other state-of-the-art approaches on two standard benchmark datasets, and show that it achieves competitive performance.
The network architecture and implementation details are made available to facilitate further research.

In this paper, we propose a novel approach to 
cross-stain histopathology image segmentation based on a dual adaptive pyramid network (DAPNet).
The DAPNet is composed of two adaptive pyramid networks (APNs), each designed to segment a specific stain in the histopathology image.

The proposed method was tested on a dataset of 
histopathology images from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) project.
The experimental results show that the proposed method achieves state-of-the-art performance in terms of segmentation accuracy and runtime.

Introduction: 
Histopathology image segmentation refers to the process of identifying and classifying pixel regions in histopathology images based on the presence of specific stains.
This process is crucial for accurate analysis and interpretation of histopathology images, which are widely used in medical diagnosis and research.
However, segmentation of histopathology images is a challenging task due to the presence of complex structures, noise, and staining variations.
Numerous approaches have been proposed for histopathology image segmentation.
These approaches can be broadly classified into two categories: stain-specific segmentation and cross-stain segmentation.
Stain-specific segmentation methods operate on a single stain and segment pixels based on the presence of that stain.
In contrast, cross-stain segmentation methods operate on multiple stains and segment pixels based on the presence of multiple stains.
Cross-stain segmentation is more challenging than stain-specific segmentation due to the additional complexity of dealing with multiple stains.
However, it is also more versatile and can be used to segment pixels that are stained with any of the input stains.
Therefore, cross-stain segmentation has received considerable attention in recent years.

Our proposed method: 
We propose a novel approach to cross-stain histopathology image segmentation based on a dual adaptive pyramid network (DAPNet).
The DAPNet is composed of two adaptive pyramid networks (APNs), each designed to segment a specific stain in the histopathology image.
The APNs are trained on a large dataset of histopathology images and learn to adapt to different input stains and tissue types.

Recent progress in deep learning has advanced the field of perception, enabling us to extract high-level information from raw sensory data.
