In this paper, we propose a novel approach to incorporate confidence estimation from deep learning into risk-aware planning.

Our approach utilizes confidence estimation from deep learning to quantify this uncertainty, and incorporates it into the planning process.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in a simulated urban driving scenario, where the planner must decide between multiple actions, each with its associated risk and uncertainty.

Recent works have shown that network compression can effectively reduce the resource footprint of deep learning models without sacrificing performance on inference.

In this paper, we propose a novel approach, called CC-Net, to perform network compression guided by image complexity.
Our key insight is that simpler images contain less information and therefore require fewer parameters to achieve a given performance.
We leverage this observation and design an effective framework that automatically generates simplified biomedical images to guide network compression.
Specifically, we first utilize an autoencoder to learn a low-dimensional encoded representation for input images.
Then, we propose a complexity measurement to estimate the complexity of the encoded images, which is used to guide compression.

Our approach can handle both object instances and object classes, and is able to deal with large deformations of the input image due to perspective, occlusions, and background.

Toward panoptic segmentation, which directly predicts instance-level segmentation masks and instance labels for each pixel, we find that existing methods suffer from two limitations: (1) Most existing methods rely on post-processing steps that are expensive in terms of computational cost, and (2) Existing panoptic segmentation benchmarks include only coarse pixel-level ground truth, which hampers the training of dense prediction models.

By adapting the mask-scoring module in the detection framework, our method achieves comparable performance to the state-of-the-art methods while being much faster.
In addition, to tackle the lack of dense ground truth, we present a new dataset, called , which has instance-level segmentation masks as ground truth.
The proposed method achieves top performance on the and benchmarks, while being more than 2x faster than the next best method.

Arterial spin labeling (ASL) allows for non-invasive estimation of arterial blood flow without the need for contrast agents.

However, at lower arterial input pressures, the flow in the arteries is characterized by a transition from steady flow to unsteady flow, which manifests as a decorrelation of the ASL signal in space and/or time.
In this work, we derive a new generalized model for the flow-independent ASL signal, which we show captures the decorrelation due to unsteady flow.
The proposed model can be fit to ASL data in a least-squares sense, resulting in a spatial map of the effective input arterial blood flow, which we term the arterial input function (AIF).
We show via simulation that the AIF is capable of recovering the ground truth input flow in the presence of both spatially-varying and time-varying decorrelation.
We further validate our method on both simulated and in vivo ASL data.
We present a skin lesion segmentation model based on deep convolutional encoder-decoder architecture with aggregated multi-resolution skip connections.
The proposed model takes advantage of both encoder and decoder pathways to capture multi-scale contextual information for accurate segmentation.

In order to effectively exploit the rich spatial information of medical images, we introduce a novel aggregated skip connection module that computes attention weights for each pixel and aggregates multi-scale features by assigning different weights to the input features of different resolutions.
The proposed model was evaluated on the ISBI 2019 Skin Lesion Segmentation Challenge dataset and achieved promising results compared to the state-of-the-art methods.
Our method achieved 0.901 mean accuracy on the validation dataset, which is 2.7% higher than the second best method.
We show how to solve the graph cut segmentation problem using a quantum algorithm.
In particular, we use the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) to find the maximum weighted clique in a weighted undirected graph, which is in general an NP-hard problem.

This algorithm relies on a particular instance of the graph, due to Kargar and Montavon, that transforms the maximization of the weighted clique problem into a quadratic unconstrained binary optimization problem (QUBO).

We implement a quantum processor based on the D-Wave 2000Q machine to solve this QUBO problem and show that, for a wide range of parameters, the obtained segmentation is in agreement with the ground truth segmentations.
To the best of our knowledge, this is the first application of quantum computing to the graph cut problem.
We present a systematic approach to scene understanding for autonomous manipulation, leveraging recent advances in deep learning.
In this work, we consider the task of picking objects from cluttered scenes, a key capability for autonomous robots.
We introduce a novel deep architecture, termed Object-Context Embedding (OCE), that fuses object detection and semantic scene understanding.
Our approach jointly reasons about the presence of objects, their contexts, and their interactions, enabling the robot to adapt its decisions to the scene at test-time.

In particular, we achieve 79% pick success on the challenging Object Discovery and Learning (ODL) dataset, significantly improving upon the prior state of the art.
Efficient Smoothing of Dilated Convolutions for Image Segmentation.
In this paper, we improve the efficiency of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for image segmentation tasks.

We observe that existing works either suffer from decreased performance due to the downsampling of multi-scale inputs or the increased computational cost for processing these inputs entirely, resulting in slow inference especially on architectures with many dilated convolutional layers.

To address these issues, we propose an efficient smoothing method for dilated convolutions, which is designed to reduce the computational cost of processing inputs with many dilation layers while maintaining the performance.

Our method works by adaptively adjusting the dilation rate of each layer based on the local structure of the input, allowing the network to concentrate on the most informative regions while suppressing the computational cost on less important areas.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on two public segmentation benchmarks, Cityscapes and CamVid, with state-of-the-art performance and improved efficiency.
Our source code is available at https://github.com/NVlabs/efficient-smoothing-of-dilated-convolutions.

We consider the estimation of nonlinear Markov random fields (MRFs) when the available data consists of independent copies of the MRF, and the goal is to reproduce the underlying conditional distributions.
We focus on feedforward neural networks as approximators, and develop an algorithm for learning the network parameters via backpropagation.
The method is derived by extending a connection formula for Bayesian neural networks to the MRF setting.
The main challenge is to devise an appropriate approximation to the intractable ensemble of conditional distributions.
This is overcome by utilizing the chain rule of probability, and expressing the network as a composition of conditional distributions.
We illustrate the method through numerical experiments, comparing the proposed approach to alternative methods for learning MRFs.
In this paper, we present an automatic brain image segmentation method based on differential geometric features of multimodal MRI.
The proposed method incorporates a new type of feature, namely the differential geometric feature, which has not been used in brain image segmentation before.
This feature captures the local geometric structure of images, and it is robust against noise, artifacts, and variations in appearance.
To extract the differential geometric features of multimodal MRI brain images, we propose a new algorithm called the differential geometric feature extraction algorithm.
The proposed algorithm is simple, efficient, and easy to implement.
We also propose a new segmentation algorithm called the differential geometric feature segmentation algorithm, which is based on the extracted differential geometric features.
The proposed segmentation algorithm is fully automatic, and it is capable of segmenting brain images accurately and reliably.
We evaluated the proposed method on a public dataset, and the results show that the proposed method is effective in brain image segmentation.

We introduce Superpixel-based Data Augmentation (SPDA), a simple and effective data augmentation technique for biomedical image segmentation.
SPDA creates augmented training sets by preserving geometric consistency and anatomical correspondence between the original and augmented images.

SPDA improves upon existing data augmentation techniques by introducing a superpixel-based segmentation that simplifies the augmentation process and allows for more precise anatomical correspondence between original and augmented images.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of SPDA on three publicly available segmentation benchmarks for neurological MRI, cardiac MRI, and histopathology images.
For the Brain Tumor Segmentation Challenge, SPDA achieves a Dice score of 95.3% on the validation dataset, outperforming the current state-of-the-art by 1.2%.
For the Cardiac Image Segmentation Benchmark, SPDA achieves a Dice score of 96.2% on the validation dataset, outperforming the current state-of-the-art by 5.7%.

We present an efficient and accurate approach for colorectal tumor segmentation based on 3D U-Net.

Our method extends the 2D U-Net architecture to include 3D pooling and striding operations, enabling the network to effectively capture spatial dependencies and contextual information in volumetric data.
To enhance performance, we introduce a region-of-interest (RoI) pooling layer that allows the network to focus on the most relevant tumor regions.

Arterial spin labeling (ASL) is a non-invasive approach to imaging the cerebral vascular anatomy and physiology without the need for contrast agents.

However, the process of segmenting the ASL images into various tissue types such as gray matter (GM), white matter (WM), and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) is a challenging task, mainly due to the complex anatomy and the low SNR.
In this work, we propose an architecture consisting of a series of residual units, referred to as MultiResUNet, for the purpose of segmenting ASL images.
In this new architecture, we eliminate the contraction path in the U-Net to reduce the number of parameters without losing the representation power of the network.

We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on a publicly available dataset, and show that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance in terms of Dice similarity coefficient and Hausdorff distance on both the T1- and T2-weighted ASL images.
Recent progress in convolutional neural networks (CNNs) has propelled medical image segmentation performance closer to human-level accuracy.
However, the creation of robust segmentation models capable of explaining their decisions in clinical practice remains a challenge.

We present a novel approach towards explaining segmentation models by estimating the aleatoric uncertainty, defined as the uncertainty due to variability in the data, with a test-time augmentation (TA) strategy.
Our approach consists of training a segmentation model on a sparse subset of the labeled data and subsequently estimating aleatoric uncertainty for the entire dataset during test-time.
We demonstrate that our proposed approach achieves higher prediction accuracy and better uncertainty estimation compared to baseline methods.

In particular, our proposed method improves average precision at the voxel level by up to 4.24% and reduces the Mean Absolute Error of the uncertainty estimation by up to 30.87% compared to the state-of-the-art.
We further show the effectiveness of our method in segmenting medical images and illustrate its utility in providing trustworthy explanations for segmentation models.

We tackle the problem of semi-supervised image-to-image translation, where the training process is performed using a small amount of labeled source and target images and a large number of unlabeled images.
We propose a novel framework that utilizes a conditional adversarial network (CAN) to learn a joint distribution of images from the source and target domains.
Our approach is based on the intuition that the unlabeled images in both domains contain valuable information that can be used to learn a robust translation model.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on two benchmark datasets, and show that our approach outperforms the state-of-the-art in semi-supervised image translation.
Recent advancements in Machine Learning have enabled the creation of powerful malware detection models.
Deep learning in particular has drawn considerable attention, as it demonstrates strong performance in numerous domains.
Despite these advances, there exists a concern that deep learning models could be fooled by carefully crafted adversarial examples.
In this work, we aim to investigate this concern by evaluating the vulnerability of an end-to-end deep learning malware detection system to adversarial examples.
We successfully generate adversarial examples that deceive the detector at a significant rate.
We further explore the transferability of these examples across different datasets, models, and attack types.
The results confirm the transferability of our crafted examples, demonstrating their broad applicability.
We perform a detailed analysis to understand the reasons behind the detector's vulnerability.
We find that the detector's performance can be explained by its over-reliance on a small set of features.
We also explore potential defenses against adversarial attacks, and demonstrate the limitations of existing techniques in the context of malware detection.
Semantic segmentation of traffic participant objects is a fundamental task for analyzing multi-modal transportation systems.
We propose an approach to improving the quality of ground truth (GT) annotation for training deep learning models that segment images of traffic participant objects.
Our approach uses a two-stage process.
In the first stage, we use an initial set of GT segments labeled by an expert to learn a deep learning-based segmentation model.
In the second stage, we use the trained model to segment the input images, and we use the segmented images to aid the annotation process of the GT used to train the model.
We iteratively improve the GT annotation by manually correcting the errors in the segmented images.
Our approach can be applied to any semantic segmentation problem, especially when there is a lack of sufficiently labeled training data.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on a new dataset we created for segmenting traffic participant objects in street images.
Our approach improves the F1-score of the baseline model by 7.7 points on average.
Deep learning provides a powerful set of techniques for medical image processing tasks, enabling accurate and precise measurements and classifications.
This paper provides a gentle introduction to the field, including a review of the most commonly used deep learning architectures and algorithms.
The paper also discusses the challenges and opportunities of deep learning in medical image processing, and provides a set of guidelines for successful application of these techniques.
Finally, the paper includes a number of case studies to illustrate the use of deep learning in medical image processing.
We introduce a new fully-automatic segmentation algorithm that we call Pixel Objectness (Po).

Po operates directly on the pixel level, and can therefore be applied to any image without any a-priori knowledge about the objects present - Po learns everything it needs to know from a single image in a fully unsupervised manner.
Furthermore, Po can be made very fast (around 1 Hz on a CPU), so that it can be applied to each frame of a video in real-time.
We demonstrate very promising results for Po on a wide variety of images and video sequences, and introduce a new YouTube dataset of 30 everyday objects in the context of a typical home environment.
We present a weakly supervised instance segmentation method, which utilizes a hybrid network with a multi-scale aggregation (MSA) module and a feature pyramid network (FPN) module.
The proposed method weakly supervises instance segmentation by classifying each pixel as an object or a background, and then segments the objects by exploiting the spatial dependencies among pixels.
The MSA module effectively utilizes the multi-scale features for accurate classification, while the FPN module refines the features at each level of the feature pyramid.
Our method achieves the state-of-the-art performance on the VOC2012 and VOC2017 datasets with a single model, and the best performance on the VOC2012 dataset compared to prior art.
Our source code and models are available at https://github.com/Dai-Jun-Wang/Weakly-Supervised-Instance-Segmentation-using-Hybrid-Network.
Successive 3D U-Net architectures combined with a contour loss are used to automatically segment the left atrium (LA) from short-axis cardiac images.
In comparison to other chambers, the LA is often more challenging to segment due to its anisotropic shape and location adjacent to the pulmonary veins, which have similar intensities.
In this work, a novel contour loss is proposed to enforce the network to predict object contours as well as pixel-wise labels.
The contour loss is combined with a 3D U-Nets architecture, which is trained using a successive approach, where an initial segmentation is used to constrain the segmentation of the LA.
The network is evaluated on 50 short-axis cardiac images and compared to an experienced clinician's manual segmentation and a state-of-the-art deep learning model.
The proposed method achieves a 4.35% mean absolute error, which is a 22.7% relative improvement compared to the baseline model.
Recent advances in deep learning have achieved significant performance improvements in various computer vision tasks.
However, the lack of training data remains a challenging problem, especially for small datasets or new classes.
In this paper, we present a new approach to segmenting images without any training data.
Our method, called SUSAN (Segment Unannotated image Structure using Adversarial Network), learns to segment images using only the image itself as input.
We employ an adversarial network to transform the input image into a structured representation, which is then used to segment the image.
Our experiments show that SUSAN can achieve competitive performance compared to state-of-the-art methods on the MIT-CBCL and PASCAL-Context datasets.
We present a novel approach for multi-organ segmentation based on deep learning and multi-planar reconstruction.
Our method, termed deep multi-planar co-training, leverages the coherence among anatomically adjacent organs in the same patient to improve performance.

It consists of two main components: (i) a fully-automatic multi-planar reconstruction algorithm that reconstructs multiple orthogonal planes from a single axial CT scan, and (ii) a deep learning framework for joint organ segmentation on the reconstructed planes.
Multi-planar reconstruction enables the training of much larger datasets, significantly improving the performance of the segmentation network.

We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach on the task of multi-organ segmentation in the abdominal region, achieving state-of-the-art performance on the publicly available abdominal CT segmentation challenge.
Recent advances in medical imaging, such as MRI and CT, have led to a treasure trove of 3D data, which is laborious to label due to its multi-modal and volumetric nature.
We tackle the few-shot 3D multi-modal medical image segmentation problem, where a small number of labeled examples are available for each class.
We propose a novel few-shot learning framework that leverages a generative adversarial network (GAN) to synthesize additional labeled examples for training.
Our framework consists of a segmentation network trained using few-shot learning with a GAN, and a discriminator network that distinguishes between real and synthesized examples.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on 3D brain tumor and abdominal organ segmentation tasks, where we achieve state-of-the-art performance compared to other few-shot learning methods.

We address the problem of weakly-supervised learning for image segmentation, which requires the learner to refine initial segmentations that are produced by a segmentation algorithm that does not take into account object class labels.

We propose a method that combines three components: a deep neural network that outputs segmentation masks, a procedure for learning the deep network from a small number of user-provided bounding boxes, and a saliency map that is used to weigh the contribution of different pixels to the learning process.

We show that our method competes favorably with state-of-the-art image segmentation algorithms, both in terms of precision and recall, while requiring no more than a few bounding boxes for each class, and we explore a variety of strategies for improving performance.
We present a light-weight RefineNet for fast semantic segmentation, aiming to achieve both accuracy and efficiency.

To achieve fast inference, we introduce a new network architecture called Light-Weight RefineNet, which removes the redundant skip connections in the original RefineNet and replaces all pooling operations with strided convolutions.
To improve the accuracy, we propose to use Atrous Convolution to capture more context in the original image.

Our experiments on the Cityscapes dataset show that our method can achieve a speedup of about 4x with only a small drop in accuracy (from 82.2% to 80.7%) compared to the original RefineNet, and a speedup of about 10x with an acceptable accuracy (78.5%) compared to the Fully-Connected CRFs baseline.
In addition, our model is about 40% faster than the state-of-the-art MobileNet-based methods while achieving similar accuracy.
The source code and models are available at: this https URL.
We introduce a new class of energy networks (EnNs) for adversarial learning.
These networks extend the standard discriminator by learning a low-dimensional energy representation of the input data, which facilitates more robust and generalizable predictions.
We show that EnNs can be trained in a discriminative fashion, without requiring any modifications to the standard GAN objective.
Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of EnNs on image classification and few-shot learning tasks, where they achieve state-of-the-art performance.
Notably, EnNs exhibit strong generalization performance on novel adversarial attacks, even when trained on attacks they have never seen before.
Recent progress in clinical imaging devices has led to a significant increase in the size of medical images, posing a challenge for most existing segmentation models.
Although deep learning models for image segmentation have shown promising results, their applicability is limited due to the computational resources and expertise required for training.
In this paper, we present nnU-Net, a lightweight and flexible framework for U-Net-based medical image segmentation.
nnU-Net addresses the limitations of current models in resource-constrained environments by adapting the architecture based on available resources, resulting in improved performance and efficiency.
Our approach automatically adjusts the number of layers and parameters of the U-Net model using a learned scaling factor, enabling efficient segmentation on large images without sacrificing accuracy.
We evaluate our method on three public datasets: ISBI 2017 Cardiac MRI Segmentation Challenge, abdominal CT, and pulmonary CT.
Our results show that nnU-Net provides a reliable and efficient solution for U-Net-based medical image segmentation, improving performance and reducing memory requirements.

Abstract:
We overview some modern convex optimization tools that have been recently used in medical image analysis.
We focus on statistical parametric mapping (SPM) and the famous X-Engine, and demonstrate their relationship through convex optimization.
New developments on SPM, such as the use of wavelet frames and Gaussian mixtures, are introduced.
We also discuss recent advances on X-Engine, including a generalization of the level-crossing method, a joint MAP-EM algorithm, and a new initialization method.
Finally, we demonstrate the use of these methods in the analysis of Alzheimer's disease, where both SPM and X-Engine have been employed for the first time.
Recent works in dense image prediction typically exploit architectural arrangements at multiple scales to leverage multi-scale information and achieve better performance.
In this work, we perform an in-depth study and discover that the efficiency of multi-scale architectures varies significantly with different dense prediction tasks.
In particular, efficient architectures for natural image super-resolution (NI_SR) are not necessarily efficient for other tasks, and vice versa.
This inspires us to search for efficient multi-scale architectures for different dense prediction tasks.
We discover a few effective strategies for each specific task, including global information modulation, feature fusion, and spatial transformer networks.

Furthermore, we find that efficient architectures for dense prediction are typically composed of a small number of repeated modules with specific structures, which is different from the architectures designed for image classification.

Finally, we propose a set of efficient multi-scale architectures for four dense prediction tasks, including NI_SR, semantic segmentation, portrait segmentation, and object detection, and demonstrate their superior performance compared to the state-of-the-art.
We present a novel approach for retinal vessel segmentation based on generative adversarial networks (GANs).
Our method requires only a few annotated vessel samples, yet it can synthesize a large amount of training samples with an arbitrary level of granularity.
The synthesis is performed by a conditional GAN, where the vessel structures are conditioned on the retinal images.
We introduce an attention module to improve the conditioning capability of the GAN.
We optimize the GAN based on a novel loss function that enforces the segmentation performance with a given level of granularity.
We evaluate our method on two public retinal image datasets, and experimental results show the efficacy of our approach.
Iris recognition is widely used in automated human identification systems.
Several studies have demonstrated that the iris is a robust biometric trait for identity matching, even for subjects with refractive errors.
However, it is not clear if cataract, a significant cause of refractive error, influences iris recognition performance.
In this study, we investigated the impact of cataract on iris recognition performance.
We collected iris images of subjects with and without cataract from two different iris recognition systems, and used these images to test their performance.
Our results show that cataract significantly influences iris recognition performance.
Systems using images from subjects with cataract achieved significantly lower matching accuracy and much higher false acceptance rates.
When comparing the performance of the two systems, the one including subjects with cataract achieved a lower accuracy of approximately 50% of the other system.

Our results suggest that iris recognition systems need to be adapted to cope with cataract, for example by using spectral information rather than just intensity information, or by including additional preprocessing steps such as segmentation and registration.
We present a semantic image segmentation model based on an encoder-decoder architecture that utilizes atrous separable convolution.
Our model achieves state-of-the-art performance on the Cityscapes dataset, despite using a significantly smaller number of parameters and training images than previous approaches.
We introduce a new module, the atrous separable convolution module, which performs well on semantic image segmentation tasks and is also suitable for deployment on resource-constrained devices.
Our model is trained using a multi-scale training strategy and supervised pixel-level semantic image segmentation datasets.
In addition, we introduce a new metric for evaluating semantic image segmentation models, which we call the inter-pixel variance.
Our model achieves a high score on this metric, indicating that it is able to produce spatially coherent predictions.
Automated machine learning-based medical image segmentation is crucial for radiological diagnosis, however, it faces the challenge of requiring extensive training data to achieve high performance.
We present a method for generating synthetic medical image data with HoloLens and Unity in order to mitigate the need for large labelled datasets.
In order to learn a segmentation model using only a small labelled dataset, we employ few-shot learning with a semantic segmentation model.
We show that our approach achieves similar performance to training on a larger dataset, and that the use of synthetically generated data improves generalisation performance.
Current techniques for automated labeling of cardiac MR images are often not accurate enough for clinical use.
In this paper, we propose a method for improving the accuracy of automated labeling.
Our method is based on the fusion of labels from multiple atlases, using a neural network to combine the labels.
We show that our method is effective in improving the accuracy of automated labeling, and that it is able to generalize to images that are not included in the training set.
Our method, which we call Neural Multi-Atlas Label Fusion, combines labels from multiple atlases, with a neural network that is trained on a set of training images.
The neural network learns to combine the labels from the atlases in a way that is optimal for the training images.
We then test the neural network on a set of test images, and evaluate the performance using a metric such as the F1-score.
Our results show that our method is able to improve the accuracy of automated labeling, and that it is able to generalize to images that are not included in the training set.
We also show that our method is able to improve the accuracy of the labels for images that are difficult to label, such as those with low contrast or noise.
Our method is suitable for clinical use, as it is able to produce accurate labels for a wide range of images, and can be used to automate the labeling process.
It can also be used to improve the accuracy of other imaging techniques, such as CT imaging.
We present an approach for clearing noisy annotations in computed tomography (CT) imaging.
Our method comprises two steps.
First, we use a convolutional neural network (CNN) to produce segmentations of the CT images.

Our CNN takes as input both the CT images and the noisy annotations, and outputs a segmentation that emphasizes the regions that the noisy annotations have labeled correctly, and de-emphasizes incorrectly-labeled regions.
Second, we introduce a post-processing step in which we run a thresholding algorithm to clean up the segmentation produced by the CNN.
In the thresholding step, we assume that a small neighborhood of voxels in the segmentation should be labeled correctly so long as most of the voxels in that neighborhood are labeled correctly.
We assess our method on a public CT image dataset, and demonstrate significant improvements over the state of the art.
Self-supervised learning has become a powerful tool for many vision tasks, but training robust optical flow models is still challenging.
In this paper, we propose a simple and effective approach for optical flow prediction, by framing the problem as a similarity learning task.
Our approach is based on cross-pixel similarity, which we show can be learned efficiently by a simple network architecture.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on the recent NYUv2 dataset, achieving better performance than other self-supervised methods.
We also show that our model is able to learn flow similarities that are robust to large displacements as well as local intensity and texture variations.
In this paper, we propose a novel approach for semantic segmentation of pelvic magnetic resonance (MR) images.
Our method combines pyramid pooling and attention mechanism to capture both global and local information.
We first apply pyramid pooling to extract multi-scale features from the input images.
Then, we employ an attention mechanism to weigh the importance of different features for accurate segmentation.
The proposed method was evaluated on a public dataset consisting of pelvic MR images.
The experimental results show that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance in terms of both accuracy and speed.
Furthermore, our approach is able to segment images that are difficult to classify using traditional methods.
The code and dataset used in this work are available at https://github.com/AI4Finance-Foundation/Pyramid-Pooling-and-Attention-Mechanism-for-Pelvic-MR-Image-Semantic-Segmentation.
Recent advances in convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have achieved remarkable performance in image-related tasks.
However, the trained models are often obtained from a source domain where the images are usually different from the test images in the target domain.
Domain adaptation aims to reduce the distribution gap between the source and target domains for better generalization performance.

In this paper, we focus on unsupervised cross-modality domain adaptation of CNNs for biomedical image segmentation, where ample labeled source data in one modality (e.g., computed tomography (CT)) are available, but only limited labeled data in another modality (e.g., magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)) for the target domain.
To overcome the domain shift, we propose a novel unsupervised cross-modality domain adaptation framework based on the cycle-consistent adversarial loss.
We train the network with a cycle-consistent adversarial loss, which enforces the consistency between the source and target domains by using only unpaired data.
Our experimental results on four public datasets for biomedical image segmentation show the effectiveness of our approach compared to other state-of-the-art domain adaptation methods.

Recent progress in deep learning has propelled the performance of medical image segmentation models, yet these are trained and tested on the same dataset, limiting their generalizability to new domains, such as acquisitions of different vendors, or from different hospitals.
In this work, we aim to learn a segmentation model that is capable of adapting to new domains without any labeled examples from the target domain.
Specifically, we generate synthetic medical images from a generative model, and use these synthetics to train a segmentation model capable of operating on real medical images from a new domain.
We introduce a task driven loss for the generative model that encourages the generation of images with segmentation labels similar to the training data.
We show improved performance over baseline methods for chest X-ray image segmentation, as well as anecdotal improvements on MRI brain image segmentation.
We present a new neural network architecture for the dense estimation of labeled datasets and for labeling points in a feature space.
The key idea in our approach is to explicitly model the uncertainty in both the density estimation and labeling tasks, which prior work has generally ignored.

This is beneficial in two ways: (1) it allows us to capture the characteristics of the uncertainty in both tasks, and (2) it simplifies the architecture by avoiding the need for a multi-layer perception (MLP) module, which is commonly used in prior work.
In addition, we propose a new "hourglass" architecture that models the uncertainty in a feed-forward manner, and show that it performs on par with state-of-the-art methods on both tasks.
Recent progresses in deep learning greatly boosted the research on accurate and efficient biomedical image segmentation.
However, the lack of large amount of manually annotated images, especially for clinical images, restricts its wide application.
In this paper, we present a novel approach called BoxNet for biomedical image segmentation using boxes only annotation, which is simple, fast and easy to be applied.
Given very few box annotations, BoxNet could automatically recover the precise boundaries of the objects, as well as the full pixel-level segmentation masks.

Furthermore, to the best of our knowledge, we establish the first box only annotation dataset with ground truth segmentation masks for pancreatic cancer computed tomography (CT) images, which is named as BoxCT.
BoxCT dataset is publicly available and can be used for training and evaluating segmentation models.
We evaluate BoxNet on four public abdominal CT image datasets.
The experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of BoxNet, and its superiority over the state-of-the-art approaches.
Deep learning has recently achieved great performance in image segmentation, but the mechanisms that lead to these results are not well understood.
In this paper, we investigate the utilization of a deep structured prediction model for fine image segmentation that inherently promotes complex relationships between labeled pixels.
We introduce a novel architecture that combines ideas from set propagation - allowing the model to reason about relationships between pixels - with an attention mechanism over object instances.
We show that our model discovers an interpretable hierarchy of object instances and pixel relationships, while achieving state-of-the-art performance on the Cityscapes segmentation benchmark.

In a thorough empirical analysis, we uncover that (1) set relationships derived by the model correspond to meaningful object structures, (2) these relationships are crucial for segmentation performance, and (3) our model's attention over object instances is able to learn contextual object interactions.
Finally, we present an analysis of what limits the performance of our model on the Cityscapes dataset and discuss potential ways to overcome these limitations.
We present a method for segmenting images into piecewise flat regions, which explicitly models the spatial layout of the regions as a small number of flat sheets.
This model is an instance of a manifold in a high-dimensional space, where the intrinsic dimension of the manifold corresponds to the number of sheets.
We propose a variation of the classic spectral clustering algorithm that efficiently computes an embedding of a given dataset in the space of flat sheets, defined by a set of sample vectors.
The embedding is computed by minimizing the variance of data points in the embedded space under a nonconvex constraint that enforces flatness, as measured by the sample vectors.

We apply the algorithm to synthetic and real images, and show that the piecewise flat segmentation provides a good fit to ground truth segmentations, while being more efficient than competing methods in terms of runtime and the amount of labeled training data required.
Dense connections between representation levels have proven crucial for learning strong semantic representations.
Recent works have introduced architectures that iteratively refine a densely connected representation hierarchy using an encoder-decoder structure.

However, these methods do not explicitly enforce connections between intermediate representations, resulting in them being unable to effectively rely on information from higher-level features during the refinement process.
To address this, we propose a simple yet effective method that explicitly encourages the reuse of high-level features during refinement.
We show that our approach, which we call Reuse Refinement, allows for better utilization of the representation hierarchy and improves performance across various dense connection models.

We conduct extensive experiments on ACDC and Cityscapes datasets, and demonstrate the superiority of our approach compared to related methods, especially when trained on datasets with limited training data.
Multi-channel image segmentation is a classical problem in image processing, with many applications in areas such as medical imaging, remote sensing, and video processing.
In this paper, we propose a new approach to multi-channel image segmentation based on component trees.
Our method utilizes the derivative information of the image channels to build a hierarchy of segments, which can be recursively split into smaller segments.
The proposed method is simple to implement and efficient to compute, and it can handle images with different numbers of channels.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on a number of challenging segmentation problems, including a remotely sensed image dataset and a multi-channel medical imaging dataset.
Our results show that the proposed method can achieve accurate segmentation results and is competitive with state-of-the-art methods.
Recent works on portrait segmentation usually emphasize the accuracy of the segmentation results, while ignoring the boundary sensitivity of the predicted masks.
In this paper, we present a boundary-sensitive network (BSNet) for portrait segmentation, which effectively improves the boundary accuracy of the predicted masks.
Specifically, we propose to use a boundary-sensitive loss (BSLoss) to optimize the network.
In addition, we introduce a boundary-sensitive module (BSM) into the network architecture, which is designed to refine the boundaries of the predicted masks.
By combining the BSLoss and the BSM, our BSNet can produce much more accurate boundaries without sacrificing the overall segmentation performance.
In the experimental part, we conduct comprehensive experiments on the publicly available Portrait Segmentation Benchmark.
The results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach compared to the state-of-the-art methods.
Superpixels are image segments formed by grouping neighboring pixels that have similar intensities.
In this paper, we apply superpixels to segment several landmarks in running rodents.
We acquired videos of running mice and rats, and detected and segmented the thorax, abdomen, and tail of the rodents without any prior knowledge about the shape or size of the rodents.
The proposed method can be used for tracking landmarks of running rodents in typical laboratory cages as well as in variously shaped running environments.
Deep learning has emerged as a powerful tool for medical image segmentation, enabling the development of accurate and automated methods for extracting meaningful information from medical images.
This paper provides an overview of the current state of deep learning for medical image segmentation and discusses the challenges and opportunities in this field.
We first introduce the concept of deep learning and its application to medical image segmentation.
We then review the most commonly used deep learning architectures for medical image segmentation, including fully connected networks, convolutional neural networks, and recurrent neural networks.
We then discuss the challenges of training deep learning models on medical image data, including the lack of large, labeled datasets and the need for domain-specific knowledge.

We finally discuss the opportunities for future research in this field, including the potential for transfer learning and multi-task learning to improve the performance of deep learning models for medical image segmentation.

Recent works on universal adversarial perturbations (UAP) have shown that it is possible to find adversarial examples that are able to misclassify any given neural network model across a wide range of architectures and hyperparameters.

The existing attacks that are capable of finding such examples typically require an increasing amount of computational resources as the number of model parameters increases, and a fixed computational budget can afford only a small perturbation that is often not successful at misclassifying the most vulnerable models.
In this work, we propose Recurrent Segmentation, a method that, given a fixed computational budget, is capable of finding successful adversarial examples for a wide variety of models.

Our approach iteratively applies a standard perturbation to a small subset of the input pixels (a pixel subset) and uses the model's uncertainty over the class prediction as a measure of the success of the perturbation.
We then repeat the process on a new pixel subset and aggregate the perturbations to build a successful perturbation for the whole image.

We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on CIFAR-10 with a fixed budget of 256 computational steps, finding successful perturbations for a wide variety of models, including ResNet-20, ResNet-32, ResNet-50, ResNet-110, and ResNet-152.
Our approach also substantially improves upon the state-of-the-art UAP found by Chen et al.
We present a long-term visual localization system that utilizes semantic segmentations of the training images to improve performance.
We pretrain a convolutional neural network (CNN) on the ImageNet dataset, and use the CNN to extract features from both the training and test images.
We then use a support vector machine (SVM) to classify the images into 1000 fine-grained object classes.
To segment the images, we propagate the activations of the last layer of the CNN through an iterative graph cuts algorithm.

To localize a query image, we first classify the query image using the SVM, then we segment the query image using the trained segmentations from the training images, and finally we localize the query image by matching the segmented query image with the segmented training images.

In addition, we implement several strategies to improve localization performance, including a prior based on the training images' geographic location information, and “in-session localization,” which utilizes object classes that are unique to the session to improve localization.
We evaluate our method on the previously unseen Rocky Mountains dataset, which contains 765 query images and 3418 training images.
Without any geographic prior, our method achieves a mean localization error of 122.7 meters.
With geographic prior and in-session localization, our method achieves a mean localization error of 85.0 meters.
We present a deep learning based approach for inpainting high-resolution textures.
We train a convolutional neural network (CNN) to synthesize texture samples based on an input image of clean regions and their corresponding dirty regions that contain textures to be inpainted.
To enable learning at multiple scales, we employ an adaptive atrous convolutional layer that can adaptively adjust the output resolution.
During training, we adopt the recently proposed focal loss to address the class imbalance issue between the clean and dirty regions.
We also propose a novel geometry-aware loss that can preserve the geometric details during texture synthesis.

We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through a wide range of quantitative and qualitative results, showing that our network can effectively restore high-resolution textures while maintaining the fine details of the input image.

Current state-of-the-art self-supervised semantic segmentation methods achieve impressive performance, but they rely on large amounts of manually designed architectural components and their hyperparameters.
In this paper, we approach the problem of self-supervised semantic segmentation from a different angle.

We propose a mix-and-match approach where we assemble a semantic segmentation network by combining off-the-shelf components from a large repository of pre-trained models, specifically tailoring our approach to the self-supervised setting.
To this end, we introduce a new training regime for self-supervised segmentation, where we replace the normalisation layers of the segmentation network with random normalisation layers.
This removes the need for manual tuning of many components, as well as allowing us to use segmentation networks as a black-box that is trained without accessing the internal representations.
We evaluate our approach on ACDC and Cityscapes and show that our approach is able to achieve results that are competitive with the state-of-the-art, while requiring less manual design effort.
We present an automated framework for cardiac diagnosis based on segmentation of the left ventricle (LV) in cardiac magnetic resonance images (CMRIs).
In this framework, we employ a fully convolutional multi-scale residual densenet (MS-RD-DenseNet) for LV segmentation and an ensemble of classifiers for automated cardiac diagnosis.
To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work that uses a fully convolutional MS-RD-DenseNet for cardiac MRI segmentation and ensembled classifiers for cardiac diagnosis.
We evaluated our method on 320 CMRI slices from 50 patients and obtained a Dice similarity coefficient (DSC) of 95.88% for LV segmentation.
Furthermore, the ensemble classifier achieved an accuracy of 84.25% for cardiac diagnosis.
Our method provides a powerful and effective approach for cardiac diagnosis based on CMRI.
Recent progress in video object segmentation has mainly focused on standardized datasets and rigid settings.
However, in many real-world applications, object appearances vary greatly across different cameras, viewpoints, and environments (in the wild).
To tackle this challenge, we propose a new framework that actively learns a structured model for video object segmentation from interacting with users.

Specifically, given a video and an initial bounding box from a user, our framework outputs a refined bounding box by automatically exploring various object appearances in the video via an interactive process.
We formulate the interactive video object segmentation as a structured output prediction problem with a novel spatiotemporal graph structure, where the graph topology is learned from data.

To effectively exploit the graph structure for accurate segmentation, we propose an attention-guided graph neural network that selectively focuses on relevant regions and updates the segmentation result.
Our method can be easily deployed on various platforms, including but not limited to desktops, laptops, tablets, and smartphones to enable efficient and effective interactive segmentation.
We evaluate our method on VOC2012, where our framework outperforms the state-of-the-art approach.
Our code and models are available at https://github.com/AI4Finance-Foundation/Interactive-Video-Object-Segmentation.
We present a real-time multi-object tracking (MOT) system that is trained entirely in a category-agnostic manner, i.e., without any category-specific bounding box labels whatsoever.
Despite this, our system performs comparably with state-of-the-art MOT methods on the MOT17 benchmark, while being significantly more general and flexible.
In particular, our method achieves ~80% MOT accuracy (mAP) on MOT17, compared to ~64% achieved by the current literature.
Furthermore, we achieve this without any use of ground truth bounding boxes during training, or any other kind of strong supervision.
To achieve these results, we leverage a recently proposed object tracker called Generalized Association (GA) that is trained using only image-level labels.
We then show that GA is actually equivalent to a network that combines a Siamese Network with a one-shot detector (SSD), and use this observation to improve GA's tracking performance.
Finally, we implement a simple tracking refinement model that uses Kalman filtering to refine the object trajectories output by GA.
This improves the mAP of our overall system to 80%.
We reexamine the recently proposed Atrous Convolution (AC) for semantic image segmentation.

Despite its popularity, we show that the performance of AC deteriorates as the average stride length in the encoder increases, which is crucial for preserving spatial information and resisting overfitting.

Through analysis and experiments, we find that this limitation arises from the sharing of the atrous rate among different convolutional layers, which restricts the adaptability of the atrous rate to feature hierarchies.
To address this problem, we propose a simple yet effective method called Adaptive Atrous Rate (AAR), which adaptively estimates the atrous rate for each layer.
AAR not only improves the segmentation performance but also significantly reduces the memory usage and accelerates the training process.
We implement the state-of-the-art segmentation models with AAR and demonstrate its advantage over the models with the original AC on multiple datasets, including Cityscapes and ACDC.
Our code and models are available at https://github.com/cszn/AAR.
Recent advances in convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have promoted the development of various automatic organ segmentation methods.
However, the spine, as an important organ, has not attracted enough attention owing to its complex shape and sparse annotation.
In this paper, we present a deep learning framework for automatic spine segmentation, which benefits from redundant generation of class labels.
Specifically, given the annotation of a single slice, our method can generate artificially labeled slices from both above and below the annotated slice.
Then, a 3D CNN is trained in an end-to-end manner to learn the mapping from the input MR volumes to the segmentation masks of the spine.
The network is composed of a contracting path and an expanding path, which can effectively capture the spatial and channel information, respectively.
To handle the variability of spine size across different patients, we introduce a simple yet effective scale normalization technique to the contracting path.
On the other hand, to effectively utilize the redundant information, we propose a stacked hourglass network to model the long-range dependencies and capture the global context in the expanding path.
The extensive experiments on the public spinal cord segmentation challenge 2017 dataset validate the effectiveness of our method, especially when trained with limited annotations.

We present a new class of efficient and invariant convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for dense prediction tasks, where the input is an image and the output is a vector of intensities corresponding to each pixel.

Our CNNs are based on a new building block called the “pixel-level convolutional layer”, which operates directly on the pixel values of the input image, and implements a form of spatial pooling via a learnt unary activation function.

We show that this layer implements a form of non-linear scale-invariant filtering, and can be used to construct a dense prediction network that achieves state-of-the-art performance on the NYC-Depth v2 dataset, while having relatively low computational complexity relative to other methods.
We present an analysis of the architectural properties of our network and discuss how it relates to other work on CNNs for dense prediction.
Fast Recurrent Fully Convolutional Networks for Direct Perception in Autonomous Driving
In this paper, we introduce a new class of models for direct perception in autonomous driving, which we refer to as Fast Recurrent Fully Convolutional Networks (FR-FCNs).

Our approach leverages recent advances in fully convolutional neural networks and recurrent neural networks to learn hierarchical representations of the input sensory data, in a manner that is both efficient and effective.

We show that FR-FCNs can be trained end-to-end to directly predict semantic road layouts from input sensory data, without the need for post-processing steps such as graph optimization or iterative refinement.

We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on the task of autonomous driving in simulated environments, and show that our models can predict semantic road layouts with high accuracy and efficiency.
Keywords: autonomous driving, direct perception, sensory data, semantic road layout, recurrent neural networks, fully convolutional networks.

Abstract:

We introduce a new class of models for direct perception in autonomous driving, based on recent advances in fully convolutional neural networks and recurrent neural networks.
Our approach learns hierarchical representations of input sensory data in a single forward pass, without the need for post-processing steps such as graph optimization or iterative refinement.

We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on the task of autonomous driving in simulated environments, and show that it outperforms existing state-of-the-art models in terms of accuracy and efficiency.
The proposed method can directly predict semantic road layouts from input sensory data, providing a powerful tool for autonomous driving systems.
Our approach is fast, efficient, and general, and can be applied to a wide range of autonomous driving scenarios.
We believe that it will make a significant contribution to the field of autonomous driving, and will help to advance the state-of-the-art in direct perception for autonomous vehicles.
We introduce a new class of models for semantic segmentation, termed dense-forecasts, trained by means of a novel consistency criterion that we refer to as dense-forecast consistency.

Specifically, we argue that, in contrast to existing segmentation models, it is necessary to produce detailed and precise forecasts, i.e. predictions for every pixel in an input image, for each class, in order to successfully learn a per-class segmentation.

To this end, we propose a fully convolutional architecture, termed denseNet, based on depth-wise separable convolutions, that is easy to train and yields state-of-the-art performance on the Cityscapes dataset.

To solve the aforementioned dense-forecast consistency, we further introduce a new training objective, termed pixel-wise smoothness, which ensures, at training time, that the forecasts produced by each layer are consistent with the forecasts produced by the preceding layer.
This criterion allows the network to successfully learn to produce consistent, high quality forecasts, and hence, per-class segmentations.
We evaluate our proposed approach on the Cityscapes dataset and achieve a mean Intersection over Union of 0.839, which is a new state-of-the-art on this dataset.
Recent advances in deep learning have achieved significant performance improvements in medical image segmentation.
However, training these models usually requires large amounts of manually annotated medical images, which are difficult to obtain.
In this paper, we present an approach for interactive medical image segmentation using deep learning with image-specific fine-tuning.
We start by training a deep learning model on a large dataset of synthetic images to obtain a good initial estimate of the segmentation.
We then fine-tune the model using a small number of manually annotated medical images specific to the patient and clinical site.
The fine-tuning process is performed using a small number of interactions with the user, who provides feedback on the initial estimate.
Our approach has been evaluated on a dataset of abdominal CT scans and compared to a fully-supervised approach.
The results show that our approach can achieve similar performance with significantly less manual annotation.

Recent works have shown that geometric and topological patterns of neural activity contain valuable information for downstream tasks, such as object recognition.
In this paper, we study the problem of learning spatial propagation networks (SPNs) for recognizing objects using cortical microcircuit geometry.
We propose a novel SPN architecture that is trained using a novel learning algorithm.
The SPN is designed to capture geometric and topological features of input activity patterns in a way that is suitable for recognition tasks.
The learning algorithm is based on a novel distance metric that measures the dissimilarity between the geometric and topological features of input and output activity patterns.

We present a scalable variational inference algorithm for estimating the posterior of Bayesian log-supermodular models.

We exploit the structure of the posterior to propose an original algorithm, called Scalable Variational Inference for Log-supermodular Models (SVIL), that combines the benefits of both coordinate and reweighting variational inference.

We show that SVIL possesses several desirable properties: (i) it is coordinate-ascent, allowing for a fast convergence; (ii) it is reweighting-like, reducing the variance of the estimates; (iii) it is scalable, as it only requires evaluating a surrogate of the log-supermodular model; and (iv) it is easy to implement, as it relies on a single parameter.
We assess the performance of SVIL on a synthetic dataset, and compare it to other state-of-the-art variational inference algorithms.
The results show that our algorithm is very effective in terms of sample efficiency and quality of the estimates.
Recent works in clothing parsing often rely on large amounts of labeled image data for training.
However, collecting pixel-level annotated images of clothes is tedious and expensive.
To mitigate this, we propose a self-supervised approach for learning joint image segmentation and labeling models for clothing.
Our approach leverages the abundant unlabeled images available on the web alongside a small set of labeled images.
We introduce a new parsing module that up-samples coarse segmentation maps to dense pixel labels.
This module is trained by self-supervised objectives that encourage the model to reconstruct the image texture and to produce coherent segmentations.
We show that our approach compares favorably to previous work on the Pascal VOC 2012 clothing parsing dataset, and that our model generalizes to images not seen during training.
In this paper, we propose a new method for segmenting meaningful objects in SAR images.
The proposed method is based on a multi-scale non-local active contour model.
The non-local operation is implemented by a Gaussian weighted distance map, which can describe the long-range spatial dependence with a single parameter.
In the multi-scale framework, a series of Gaussian weighted distance maps are employed as the internal energy and the external energy of the active contour model, respectively.
By minimizing the energy function, a series of active contours are generated in different scales.
Finally, the segmentation result is obtained by combining the information from the multi-scale active contours.
The proposed method is evaluated on the Sentinel-1 dataset.
The experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.
We consider the setting where a pre-defined set of candidates is available for all positions in a structured prediction task.
This is common in many applications, such as parsing a sentence where the set of possible syntactic parses is finite and known in advance.
A candidate constrained conditional random field (CCRF) models the likelihood of the gold parse given the input, while enforcing that the predicted parse is among the candidates.

We provide a generalization of the candidate constrained approach that enables an arbitrary marginal distribution on the candidates, and introduces a loss awareness mechanism that biases the model towards parses that have not been previously seen during training.
We show that this is a strict generalization of the original CCRF model, and provide a learning algorithm that is applicable to both models.

Our experimental evaluation on a biological event extraction task shows that our model improves F1 score by 2.9 points compared to the original CCRF model, and by 1.2 points compared to the strongest baseline.
We present a new optimization algorithm for training structural support vector machines (SVM) on arbitrary metric spaces.
Training structural SVMs with a costly max-oracle using smoothing techniques is known to be a challenging non-smooth, non-convex optimization problem.
In this paper we propose a block-coordinate Frank-Wolfe algorithm that uses a multi-plane method to select the next variable to orthogonalize.
We show that the algorithm is able to exploit the structure of the optimization problem through the use of a particular class of concave functions as well as a novel lazy selection strategy.
We implement the algorithm in the context of SVM regression for graphs and images and demonstrate improvements in optimization speed over state-of-the-art techniques.
Deep face identification models have shown promising results but mainly rely on face images of extreme resolutions, e.g., <1024x1024.
In this work, we aim to learn a face representation that can identify faces from low-resolution images, which is more practical in real-world applications.
We propose to use second-order pooling for face representation learning.

Given a face image, it first applies a convolutional layer to output channel features, then applies another convolutional layer to the channel features, and finally applies max pooling to the second-order responses.
We show that the proposed method, compared with state-of-the-art methods based on first-order pooling, is more robust to low resolutions and is more transferable to unseen datasets.
Moreover, it achieves better performance in face identification.

Abstract: CIDI-Lung-Seg: A Single-Click Annotation Tool for Automatic Delineation of Lungs from CT Scans

Automatic segmentation of lungs in CT scans is a fundamental step towards computer-aided detection, diagnosis, and treatment of pulmonary diseases.
However, it remains a challenging task, mainly due to the lungs' intricate structures and their proximity to the heart and other organs.
In this paper, we present a single-click annotation tool, called CIDI-Lung-Seg, for efficient and effective delineation of lungs in CT scans.
Our approach is based on a deep learning model that utilizes a conditional instance-discrimination inference (CIDI) framework to improve the segmentation performance.

We evaluated our method on 320 CT scans from the public LUNA16 dataset, and the results showed that CIDI-Lung-Seg achieved a mean dice similarity coefficient of 0.9378, outperforming the state-of-the-art.
Our tool is designed to be user-friendly and can be easily operated by radiologists and clinicians without extensive knowledge of computer vision or deep learning.
It enables users to quickly and accurately delineate the lungs in CT scans, saving time and effort in the diagnosis and treatment of pulmonary diseases.
We believe that CIDI-Lung-Seg has the potential to significantly aid in the analysis of CT scans and improve the efficiency of clinical workflows.
Recent works have shown that the choice of loss function can significantly impact the quality of learned representations in NLP models.
Unfortunately, a single annotation-specific loss function is unable to capture the multiple utility aspects of a given task.

To address this issue, we propose a novel approach called Multi-utility Learning (MU-Learning) that is capable of leveraging multiple annotation-specific loss functions during training to improve performance on a given task.
We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach on the task of multi-hop question-answering, where we show that our model achieves state-of-the-art performance on a benchmark dataset.
We perform a comprehensive analysis to demonstrate that our model learns task-agnostic and task-specific representations that are capable of capturing the multiple utility aspects of the given task.
Chilies are one of the most important cash crops in Mexico and it is the second most important vegetable after the tomato.
Time consuming and tedious manual inspection is currently done in agriculture to estimate the percentage of defects in the harvested produce.
Defect inspection is needed for proper grading and to determine if the produce meets the stringent quality requirements of the exporter.
This work focuses on defect segmentation of chili pepper X-ray images.
Successful segmentation was achieved using a texture based approach.
A Gabor filter is used as a texture descriptor.
The descriptors are then used to classify the defect regions via a support vector machine.
The method was tested on a database of 117 images and achieved a 97.64% accuracy rate with a 0.96 F-measure.
Detection of symmetric abnormalities in MRI brain images is an important step in the screening of brain tumors.
In this paper, we present a method to detect brain tumors by analyzing the mathematical symmetry of the MRI images and their spatial derivatives.
We find that the abnormal regions produced by brain tumors have different levels of symmetry than normal brain tissues.
In our method, the MRI images are smoothed to reduce the effect of noise and improve the symmetry of the images.
The mathematical symmetry of the images is then analyzed by calculating the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix of the image pixels.
The eigenvalues represent the variance and correlation between the pixels in the image.
The spatial derivatives of the image are calculated to improve the contrast between the abnormal and normal regions.
The eigenvalues of the covariance matrix of the spatial derivatives are then used to detect the abnormal regions in the image.
The method has been tested on a database of MRI brain images and has been shown to be effective in detecting brain tumors.
The method has a sensitivity of 97.5% and a specificity of 96.2%.
We present a new approach for the interactive segmentation of objects in binary images based on active contours.
Our method aims at achieving two objectives: accuracy in shape and speed of evolution.

We combine edge-based active contours with a contour template approach: we evolve the contour towards the object boundary by minimizing an energy that includes an edge term and a template matching term.
The template is a statistical model of the object boundary that is constructed from a set of training examples.
It can be seen as an accurate prior within the active contour framework.
We perform experiments on a variety of images and show that our method is competitive with state-of-the-art interactive segmentation methods, while being much faster.
In addition, we show that our approach is able to produce accurate segmentations for objects that are difficult to segment using existing methods.

We present an algorithm for constrained MAP inference in hidden Markov models that iteratively constructs a multi-dimensional parametric mincut graph, whose edges carry a weight that corresponds to the posterior probability of the corresponding state assignment.
The mincut graph is constructed incrementally, maintaining a collection of candidate state assignments that progressively win support in the data.
We provide an intuitive explanation for the algorithm's behavior in terms of a dynamic programming formulation, and show that the algorithm runs in linear time, achieving computational scalability.
In an application to segmenting short DNA sequences, the algorithm is shown to yield significant improvements in running time over the greedy algorithm commonly used in practice.
An image segmentation method based on a contrario selection of optimal partitions is presented.
The method aims to find a good compromise between the segmentation accuracy and the number of segments generated.
It is based on a genetic algorithm that selects pixels to optimize an energy function.
In contrast to most previous work on genetic image segmentation, the algorithm searches for a good segmentation without any a priori constraint on the number of segments.
Instead, it searches for the optimal segmentation in an unbounded solution space.
An evaluation of the method on several images shows that it is very efficient in finding a good segmentation that closely approximates the optimal segmentation.
Image segmentation is the process of partitioning an image into multiple segments, thereby simplifying the representation of image data.
The segmentation of video sequences is an extension of this technique, where each video frame is segmented individually.
We present a novel approach to image segmentation in video sequences, based on a probabilistic model.
Our method utilizes the temporal coherence of video frames, where we estimate the probability of each pixel belonging to a particular segment using a Bayesian framework.
We incorporate a prior probability distribution defined by a Gaussian mixture model and a likelihood function defined by the pixel intensity.
By maximizing the joint probability of the segments across the video frames, we achieve accurate segmentation results while maintaining temporal coherence.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on benchmark datasets, showing improved performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods.
Abstract— Image extraction is important in many applications, such as in the medical field, in order to diagnose patients.
In these applications the boundaries of regions in images have important information.
In this paper we propose a novel method to extract images based on feature based fuzzy rule base.
The proposed method extracts the important information in a region in an image in a efficient and effective way.
The proposed method is evaluated on the synthetic dataset.
The experimental results show the effectiveness of the proposed method.

A maximal flow $f$ in a graph $G$ is called combinatorial if for every directed edge $e$ in the support of $f$, the capacity of $e$ is equal to $1$, and $f$ is continuous if it is the limit of a sequence of combinatorial flows.
It is well known that every maximal flow in a graph is the limit of continuous maximal flows.
In this paper, we investigate the combinatorial structure of continuous maximal flows.

We show that a necessary condition for a system of homogeneous equations in the edges and vertices of $G$ to have a continuous maximal flow solution is that the equations should be consistent, and we present an algorithm to check consistency.
We apply these results to solve the longstanding open problem of finding an interpretation of continuous maximal flows in terms of graph theory and linear programming.
Along the way, we develop several new theoretical and computational tools, including a new algorithm for solving systems of linear inequalities.
Automatic image segmentation is a classic problem in image processing, with many applications in areas such as medical imaging, remote sensing, and biological imaging.
In this paper, we present an automatic image segmentation method based on dynamic region merging.
Our method combines the advantages of both region-based and edge-based segmentation methods, while avoiding the drawbacks of each.
The proposed method is efficient, automatic, and does not require any user interaction.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on a variety of images, including those with complex shapes and textures.
We also compare our method to other state-of-the-art segmentation methods, and show that it performs favorably in terms of segmentation quality and efficiency.
We present a new image segmentation algorithm that utilizes weak shape prior to achieve state-of-the-art performance.
Our approach combines the strengths of both the watershed transform and the level set method while avoiding their drawbacks.
Like the watershed transform, our algorithm segments images based on the locations of local maxima in the gradient magnitude of a smoothed image.
However, instead of using the gradient magnitude directly, we estimate it using a convolutional neural network (CNN).
By learning a mapping from the input image to a Gaussian scale space, the CNN is able to discover local maxima in an adaptive manner, without any parameter tuning.

Furthermore, we introduce a novel weak shape prior term into the energy functional of the level set method, which regularizes the segmentation boundaries to be smooth and coherent with the image structures.
Our experimental results on the Berkeley Segmentation Dataset show that our approach outperforms the watershed transform and the level set method in terms of segmentation quality.

Introduction
Image segmentation is a fundamental problem in image processing and computer vision, with many applications in various fields.
The level set method \citeben2000level and the watershed transform \citeferreira1997watershed are two popular segmentation algorithms that have been widely used in practice.

The level set method is a powerful technique for evolving fronts in an image based on an energy functional, but it can be difficult to tune the parameters of the method to achieve good segmentation results.

The watershed transform is a popular alternative that is simple to use and does not require any parameter tuning, but it can produce oversegmented or inaccurate results on images with complex structures.
In this paper, we present a new image segmentation algorithm that combines the strengths of both the watershed transform and the level set method while avoiding their drawbacks.
Our approach utilizes a weak shape prior to achieve state-of-the-art performance.
We estimate the gradient magnitude of a smoothed image using a convolutional neural network (CNN), which discovers local maxima in an adaptive manner without any parameter tuning.

Furthermore, we introduce a novel weak shape prior term into the energy functional of the level set method, which regularizes the segmentation boundaries to be smooth and coherent with the image structures.

Our experimental results on the Berkeley Segmentation Dataset \citemartin2001database show that our approach outperforms the watershed transform and the level set method in terms of segmentation quality.
Our approach is simple to use and does not require any parameter tuning, making it suitable for various applications in image processing and computer vision.
