In this study, we propose a method for fish recognition based on a combination of robust feature selection, image segmentation, and geometrical parameter techniques using artificial neural network and decision tree classifiers.
The proposed method was tested on a database of fish images and compared with other state-of-the-art fish recognition methods.
The results show that the proposed method achieves a higher accuracy than the other methods in recognizing fish.
The proposed method combines robust feature selection, image segmentation, and geometrical parameter techniques to extract the most relevant features from fish images.
The use of artificial neural network and decision tree classifiers allows the proposed method to capture the complex relationships between the features and the classes.

The proposed method achieved an accuracy of 98.25% on the database of fish images, compared to 94.48% for support vector machine (SVM) and 95.45% for principal component analysis (PCA), two other state-of-the-art fish recognition methods.
The proposed method has several advantages over other fish recognition methods.
First, it uses a combination of robust feature selection, image segmentation, and geometrical parameter techniques to extract the most relevant features from fish images.
This ensures that the extracted features are the most representative of the fish images.
Second, the use of artificial neural network and decision tree classifiers allows the proposed method to capture the complex relationships between the features and the classes.
This enables the proposed method to recognize fish more accurately than other methods.
Third, the proposed method is able to handle high-dimensional feature spaces and large datasets, which are common in fish recognition problems.
Finally, the proposed method is simple, fast, and easy to implement, which makes it suitable for real-time applications.
Recognizing fish is an important task in many applications such as fish population monitoring, fish habitat mapping, and fish behavior analysis.
There are many approaches to recognizing fish, but they have some limitations.

This study proposes a new method for recognizing fish based on a combination of robust feature selection, image segmentation, and geometrical parameter techniques using artificial neural network and decision tree classifiers.
The proposed method is evaluated on a database of fish images and compared with other state-of-the-art fish recognition methods.
The results show that the proposed method is more accurate than other methods in recognizing fish.
We present a new algorithm for interactive structural image segmentation based on a sparse deformation field.
The algorithm is fast and produces smooth, seamless segment boundaries.
The method iteratively improves a preliminary segmentation by interacting with the user to modify boundaries, and propagating these changes through the image using a sparse deformation field.
We introduce a new feature for evaluating the interaction and a new stopping criterion based on it.
We implement the algorithm in a new interactive segmentation software tool, SparseWatershed, which is available as open-source software.
On a public dataset, we show that our algorithm is significantly faster than state-of-the-art methods while producing segmentations of comparable quality.
Diluted magnetic Sb/GdTe and Sn/CrTe quantum wells were grown by molecular beam epitaxy.
Magnetic properties of these systems are strongly dependent on the content of the nonmagnetic atoms Sb or Sn.
Increasing the Sb or Sn content leads to a decrease of the Curie temperature and an increase of the paramagnetic effect.
The de Haas-van Alpen effect was observed in all the samples and revealed an electron paramagnetic behavior with a g factor close to 2.57.
The g factor in all the samples was found to be independent of the nonmagnetic atom content and the magnetic field applied along the growth direction.

Comparison of the magnetic properties for the two different types of nonmagnetic atoms indicates that the behavior can be explained by an isotropic Heisenberg model with an exchange constant J = 0.037 meV. 

Possible origins of the diluted magnetic behavior and the exchange interaction in these systems are discussed.
We perform 3D general relativistic hydrodynamical simulations of self-gravitating boson stars in the presence of various feedback mechanisms arising from particle interactions.
These feedback mechanisms are modeled through different equations of state, which describe the pressure as a function of density for a given particle interaction model.

We consider three types of particle interactions - repulsive delta-function interactions, attractive delta-function interactions, and hard sphere interactions - and we examine corresponding equations of state that are derived using effective potential theory.
In each case, we examine the stability of the resulting equilibrium configurations.
For the attractive interaction case, we find that the configurations are stable against radial perturbations, while for the repulsive case, the configurations are unstable.
The hard sphere interactions lead to mildly bound, unstable objects.
We examine the density profiles and gravitational properties of the resulting equilibrium configurations in detail.
Our simulations show that the self-gravity of the boson stars is very mild.
The gravitational redshift $z$ is typically around $10^{-3}$, which is almost completely due to the self-gravity of the object.
The gravitational mass of the objects is many times their baryonic mass.
We also find that the radius of the equilibrium configurations is proportional to the inverse square root of the mass, which suggests that the objects are (very mildly) bound.
The velocity field is predominantly tangential, with a small radial component that is proportional to the density gradient.
This indicates that the objects are supported by rotation rather than pressure.
The specific angular momentum is proportional to the mass, which suggests that the objects are not rotating rigidly.
We also examine the stability of the equilibrium configurations to various types of perturbations.
We find that the objects are most stable to axisymmetric perturbations, followed by non-axisymmetric perturbations of degree 2, and are least stable to non-axisymmetric perturbations of degree 4.
The stability of the objects to non-axisymmetric perturbations of degree 3 is unclear.
We also find that the objects are more stable to perturbations that are orthogonal to the velocity field than to perturbations that are parallel to the velocity field.
This suggests that the objects are most likely to undergo axisymmetric or triaxial collapse, rather than becoming oblate or prolate spheroids.

We prove that the classical Navier slip model of the moving contact line problem, when applied to a Newtonian fluid of zero viscosity, is in fact equivalent to the no-slip boundary condition, thus providing a theoretical justification for a frequent and long-standing empirical assumption.
Furthermore, we obtain similar results for a class of related boundary conditions that includes the Navier condition as a limiting case.
Finally, we present numerical evidence indicating that, when the slip length is very small, the fluid flow may be well-described by the no-slip condition.
Recent studies have started to examine Twitter activity during political protests.
This paper reviews studies of Twitter activity during Occupy Wall Street, the Arab Spring, and the Russian elections.
All of the studies examined were quantitative, analyzing tweets about these events.

This paper identifies four biases in the studies: a geographic bias that excludes analysis of Twitter activity in non-English languages; an temporal bias that examines the events only during the time they are 'newsworthy'; a bias that examines only negative events; and a bias that examines only large events.
It suggests that future studies examine a longer time period, a broader set of events, and a more diverse set of outcomes.
Let $\{p_k\}$ be the increasing listing of primes.
Kempner and Irwin computed that the sum of the reciprocals of the squared prime gaps converges to $\frac{7}{16}$. In this note we improve upon this result by obtaining the limit as $\frac{35}{72}$.
We address the problem of multi-target tracking of asynchronous objects, as encountered in asynchronous video sequences analysis or multi-sensor surveillance.
We propose to handle the corresponding measurement models as superpositional; i.e., we allow for multiple objects to be present in any given measurement.
This modeling leads to a tractable, yet general, representation of measurements in terms of labeled random finite sets (RFS).
We propose a particle filter that maintains an RFS representation of the state, and propose an efficient algorithm for predicting the evolution of the state RFS.
The algorithm operates on the principle of forward filtering backward sampling, and is significantly faster than existing methods that operate on the principle of backward sampling forward filtering.
Finally, we demonstrate the efficacy of our approach on a real-world problem of airplane tracking in asynchronous radar sequences.
We introduce the notion of datatype-defining rewrite systems.
These are rewrite systems in which each rule is defined by a functional datatype.
This framework is sufficiently expressive to define the rewrite relations for natural numbers and integers.
The framework is formalized in the setting of denotational semantics with explicit substitution, and a sound and complete proof principle is provided.
Abstract: Special relativity emerged from the general relativity context where the equivalence principle plays a key role.

In this paper, we revisit the relativity theory without assuming the equivalence principle, and show that it can be refounded on the light postulate alone, where the light postulate is in fact a direct consequence of the relativity principle.
The relativity principle is shown to be the only option for a consistent theory, and we derive the Lorentz transformation and the energy-momentum relation of particles from it.
Some of implications of the relativity principle are then explored.
We introduce European and Asian Greeks for exponential Levy processes using the probabilistic representation of the exponential Levy processes in terms of a pure jump process.
Asian Greeks are sensitivities of the asset price to the changes in the underlying model parameters, which are the jump intensity and the jump size distribution.
European Greeks are sensitivities of the asset price to the changes in the underlying model parameters, which are the drift and the volatility.
This approach paves the way for developing a jump diffusion framework for exponential Levy processes.
Reproducibility in data analysis is a growing concern in introductory statistics, as students are increasingly working with large datasets and complex models.
R Markdown is a powerful tool for creating reproducible data analyses, but it is underutilized in introductory statistics.
This paper describes a project that introduces R Markdown to undergraduate students in a statistical inquiry course.
In groups, the students replicated a data analysis of a case study, first using only Excel and Word, then using R Markdown.
The project was evaluated through interviews, surveys, and observations.
The results suggest that R Markdown helped the students to be more precise in their reporting, use correct statistical methods, and work collaboratively.
Moreover, the students appreciated the opportunity to use a tool that is widely used in the statistical community.
Keywords: reproducibility; data analysis; R Markdown; case study; introductory statistics; statistical inquiry

We introduce a new asymmetric three person hat game, played according to the rules of the well-known "six hat" game, with the following modification: each player, prior to the game starting, must declare a positive integer m to the other players, being rigidly committed to this value for the rest of the game.

The players then proceed playing the game, following the normal rules of the "six hat" game, namely they take turns, each player placing one of their hats on their head, with the constraint that there cannot be more than one hat of the same color on the table at any given time.

We examine the game in the presence of various different rationality assumptions about the players, and relate the resulting game to the classical "six hat" game, as well as to a game introduced by Ebert in 2008, where players are similarly restricted in the number of items of a certain type they are allowed to have at a given time.
We present a simple parallel algorithm for computing Voronoi diagrams and Delaunay graphs.
It is based on a subdivision algorithm that recursively divides the plane into a bounded number of cells.
This subdivision is done by performing a sequence of projections onto the sites defining the Voronoi diagram.
These projections clip the cells of the subdivision, creating new cells and partially defining the desired diagram.
We give an $O(n\log n)$ time complexity bound for the algorithm, where $n$ is the number of sites in the diagram.
This bound is asymptotically better than the $O(n^2)$ bound given for the serial algorithm.
Furthermore, we present a simple technique for distributing the cells of the subdivision over a parallel computer.
This technique gives a cell traversal algorithm with $O(\log n)$ overhead, and allows the algorithm to be implemented on any parallel computer.
Abstract—Service composition enables the creation of complex applications from building blocks that are simple and already available.
These building blocks are services that are described abstractly by contracts, and executed dynamically at runtime.

We aim to specify service contracts using automata, which are a formal method for describing the behavior of services, and to orchestrate a collection of such services using recursive automata composition.
In this paper we contribute three main results.
First, we formally define an SML-based domain specific language, called Recursive Service Contracts (RSC), for specifying service contracts.
Second, we show that RSC can be executed recursively, yielding an execution of the composed services.
Third, we implement a runtime system that executes compositions of RSC specifications, and we evaluate its performance and scalability.

We prove a recent conjecture of Berndt, which states that the Charlier polynomials of non-negative integer index k transition to the Hermite function H_k under the inverse square root transformation ξ → i√ξ.
This answers in the affirmative a question posed by Ng in the case k is not an odd integer.
We address the problem of constructing a smooth receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve estimator based on a finite set of ordered hypotheses.

Existing smoothing techniques for ROC curves require the estimator of the positive predictive value (PPV) to be strictly increasing in order to guarantee the convergence of the smoothed ROC curve to the true ROC curve.
In this paper, we show that this requirement can be relaxed by using a log-concave density estimate of the PPV instead of a strictly increasing estimate.
We derive the conditions under which the proposed estimator is consistent and discuss the advantages of using a log-concave density estimate.
Furthermore, we introduce a new smoothing technique that utilizes a weighted average of the ordered hypotheses to improve the smoothness of the estimator.
The experimental results indicate that the proposed approach performs better in terms of mean squared error and produces a more symmetric ROC curve compared to the existing methods.
We consider the confinement phase of massive Schwinger model and carbon-nanotubes of different diameters.
We calculate the mass and the charge of the composite fermions and compare the results with the experimental data available for different-sized carbon-nanotubes.
The results can be explained on the basis of the scaling property of the massive Schwinger model with the help of an appropriate transformation of variables.
We show that the experimental data for different-sized carbon-nanotubes can be explained by a massive Schwinger model with an effective confinement/
Higgs parameter ρ ∼ D − 1.
We then discuss the extended massive Schwinger model.
The effective Lagrangian of the model has an additional interaction term ∝ Tr(F2) in addition to the standard confinement interaction ∝ Tr(F2)

We show that this term is irrelevant for the critical phenomena of the model but affects the value of the composite fermion mass and the scaling of the correlation length with the mass and the charge.
Finally we argue that this term can play an important role in arresting the delocalization of electrons when the nanotube diameter is small.
We propose a new quasi-likelihood method for estimating the parameters of a spatial point process, assuming that the locations of the points are known.
The method is based on the idea of matching the observed data with a set of candidate spatial point processes, with each process specified by a set of parameters.
The likelihood function is then approximated by a quasi-likelihood function, which allows for a more efficient estimation algorithm.
We apply the method to a set of simulated data and show that it performs well in terms of accuracy and efficiency.
We also apply the method to a real data set and demonstrate that it can be used to estimate the parameters of a spatial point process with high precision.
The paper proposes a novel method for estimating the parameters of a spatial point process.
The method is based on the idea of quasi-likelihood, which allows for a more efficient estimation algorithm.
The paper applies the method to simulated and real data and shows that it performs well in terms of accuracy and efficiency.
The paper is important because it introduces a new method for estimating the parameters of a spatial point process.
This method can be used to improve the accuracy and efficiency of estimation, which can be beneficial for various applications such as spatial statistics and geographic information systems.
We propose a new test statistic for a specified smooth function of the parameters under the alternative based on smoothing the profile likelihood ratio (PLR) function using B-splines.
The new test is shown to be asymptotically normal under the null and equivalent to the PLR test when the nuisance parameter is absent.
We illustrate the test via a numerical example.
We show that a simple assumption on the quantum effective action, namely that it is bounded below, is a strong indication for the avoidance of singularities in Quantum Einstein Gravity.
This is in sharp contrast to classical general relativity, where non-trivial bounds on the effective action are not known to exist.

We discuss under which assumptions on the UV-completion of quantum gravity one may prove the avoidance of singularities and provide an example where the assumption of a lower bound on the effective action is not satisfied.
We also give a heuristic argument, based on the existence of a UV-completion containing only marginal operators, for the avoidance of singularities in Quantum Einstein Gravity.

We consider the problem of distributing a given square matrix, whose entries are drawn from a probability distribution, across a graph, in a way that preserves as much as possible the spectral properties of the original matrix.

We propose a method that is inspired by the idea of minimizing the Kullback-Leiber divergence between row and column margins of the distributed matrix, and has a form similar to the well-known graph Laplacian.
In particular, our method optimizes for the weights of a graph, given the entries of this matrix.

We show that our method recovers the original matrix satisfactorily, in the sense that the spectral properties of the original matrix are well-preserved by the graph, and the difference between the original matrix and its reconstruction has small spectral norm.
Finally we propose a simple variant that is suited for matrices with zero-mean entries.

Let $G=(V,E)$ be a simple graph, and $\mathcal{C}$ a family of circuits in $G$. Let $\mathcal{A}(G,\mathcal{C})$ be the associated ambigraph, and $\mathcal{M}(G,\mathcal{C})$ the corresponding matroid.
We give a necessary and sufficient condition for $\mathcal{M}(G,\mathcal{C})$ to be representable over the field ${\mathbb{Q}}(t)$, based on generalized Whitney formulas.
This generalizes a recent result of C. Rautenbach and A. Van Tuyl.
We are constructing a large area multilayer supermirrored detector for ultracold neutrons.
This project aims to provide a tool to study the fundamental properties of the neutron, in particular its quantum states, as well as for precision measurements and fundamental physics experiments.
The detector consists of a series of thin supermirrored copper and nickel layers alternated with a layer of emulsion.
We describe here the design of the detector and its assembly, as well as some of the challenges we have encountered along the way.
Rigid foam films are commonly used in the food industry as a packaging material due to their ability to provide insulation and reduce food waste.
However, these films are known to have holes and cracks that can reduce their effectiveness.
In this research, we use a combination of experimental and numerical methods to investigate the effect of holes and cracks on the thermal conductivity of rigid foam films.

We find that the presence of holes and cracks can significantly reduce the thermal conductivity of the film, and that the reduction in thermal conductivity is dependent on the size and shape of the holes and cracks.
We also find that the thermal conductivity of the film is inversely proportional to the thickness of the film.
Understanding the impact of holes and cracks on the thermal conductivity of rigid foam films is important for improving the performance of these materials as food packaging.

By optimizing the size and shape of the holes and cracks, as well as the thickness of the film, the thermal conductivity of the film can be reduced, leading to improved insulation and reduced food waste.
The findings of this research can also be applied to other applications where rigid foam films are used as insulation, such as in building and construction materials.

Complex arithmetic random waves are widely used in scientific research and have a variety of applications in physics, mathematics, and other fields.
In this paper, we explore the phenomenon of phase singularities in complex arithmetic random waves.
We define a new concept called "phase singularity strength" and analyze its properties.
We find that the phase singularity strength is related to the variance of the complex amplitude of the wave.
We also explore the relationship between the phase singularity strength and the wave's frequency and show that it is a decreasing function of the frequency.
These findings could have implications for understanding wave propagation and complex arithmetic random waves.

We demonstrate the existence of strongly confined planar mesoscopic photonic crystal cavities supported by the lattice periodicity alone, without the assistance of sharp Bragg mirrors or waveguide coupling.
Planar cavities are appealing due to their ease of fabrication and compatibility with existing planar photonics circuits.
We show that such cavities can have very high quality factors and small mode volumes, comparable to those of three-dimensional photonic crystal cavities.
We identify a broad parameter range in which these cavities possess a dark-mode spectrum, in which only a single unattenuated mode exists within a spectral range of interest.
This parameter range is particularly useful for applications in cavity quantum electrodynamics and optical filtering.
We present a design strategy for such mesoscopic cavities and provide examples of their applicability.
We propose accelerated stochastic variants of the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM) for convex optimization problems with noisy gradients.
Our methods are inspired by the accelerated stochastic gradient (ASG) methods for online convex optimization, where proximal mappings are replaced with stochastic approximations.

We show that the resulting accelerated stochastic ADMM (AS-ADMM) methods achieve linear convergence of order O(1/t) for smooth problems, and O(1/t^2) for non-smooth problems, under suitable assumptions.
We introduce a variance reduction technique that enhances the convergence of AS-ADMM, and show that the method can achieve linear convergence of order O(1/t) for non-smooth problems as well.

The proposed methods are evaluated on a set of benchmark problems, and the results show that our methods compare favorably with other stochastic ADMM methods in terms of the number of iterations and the variance of the estimates.
Quantum cryptography, in its original form of quantum key distribution (QKD), can provide two remote parties with a common secret key known only to them.
This key is then used as a one-time pad for encrypting messages.
QKD is information-theoretically secure against any attack, including those with quantum computers.
Unfortunately, it requires the establishment of a quantum channel between the two parties, which is not under active development for long-distance communication.
It has therefore been generally assumed that quantum cryptography is useful only for short-distance applications.
In this survey, we show that this assumption is incorrect.
We present several quantum cryptography protocols that do not rely on the existence of a quantum channel.
Most of these protocols are not information-theoretically secure, but they provide security against a quantum computer.
We also discuss the so-called post-quantum cryptography, in which classical algorithms are used to provide security against quantum computers.
We explain why many post-quantum cryptography schemes are susceptible to attacks by a quantum computer and present a few schemes that are secure against it.
We show that b-coloring a graph is NP-hard on co-bipartite graphs, thus answering positively a question posed by Feizi and Akbari.
Furthermore, we show that b-coloring is polynomially solvable on tree-cographs, i.e., cographs with a tree as their condensation.

We present the results of deep X-ray observations of two cometary blue compact dwarf (BCD) galaxies, Mrk 59 and Mrk 71, aimed at studying the nature of the excess soft X-ray emission recently discovered in these objects.
The observations were performed with Chandra ACIS-S on 2005 November 22 (Mrk 59) and 2005 December 2 (Mrk 71) for a total exposure of ~70 ks and ~140 ks, respectively.

The X-ray images of both galaxies are well fitted by a model in which the emission is dominated by a point source, most likely the active nucleus, at the galaxy's center, and a diffuse, unresolved component.
The latter is spatially coincident with the optical emission and accounts for ~70% of the total X-ray flux in both galaxies.
The spectrum of this diffuse component is well fitted by an absorbed power law with a photon index of ~1 and a cutoff at ~1 keV.
The absorbed fluxes of the nuclei are ~2.5
and ~1.2 × 10^−13 erg s^−1, respectively, consistent with being dominated by LLAGN activity.
The nuclear hardness ratios are also consistent with this interpretation.
The luminosities and absorption-corrected sizes of the diffuse components are consistent with being due to the superposition of many X-ray point sources, i.e., star formation activity.
We compare the observed X-ray properties of Mrk 59 and Mrk 71 with those of other BCD galaxies with and without nuclear activity, and with the X-ray properties of the Small Magellanic Cloud.

These comparisons show that the nuclear activity in Mrk 59 and Mrk 71 does not contribute significantly to their soft X-ray emission and that these two galaxies are good candidates for having a superposition of many X-ray point sources as their dominant emission mechanism.

We also find that the X-ray properties of BCD galaxies are generally consistent with those of normal star-forming galaxies, supporting the hypothesis that the nature of the dominant emission mechanism is similar in both populations.
Information theoretic privacy defines the amount of residual information that an attacker can infer about an input given access to the output of a deterministic, memoryless, and unbiased algorithm.
When the input is chosen from a known distribution, this quantity can be characterized by the Kullback-Leiber divergence.

We consider algorithms that are allowed to emit independent side information at a cost in entropy, and give tight characterizations of the price of privacy in terms of divergence from the input distribution in several settings.
In particular, we show that any such algorithm that amplifies privacy at all must leak at least as much information as a noisy channel with a uniform output distribution, up to a logarithmic factor.
We also show that if the output is constrained to be independent of the side information, then such an algorithm must have zero privacy.
Finally, we consider a model where the attacker can perform quantum queries and show that quantum side information does not improve the situation significantly.
In this paper, we propose a novel compressive beamforming (CBF) approach for multiple-snapshot beamforming.

Unlike the conventional CBF approach which requires a long training sequence to obtain a high-quality beam pattern, our proposed approach can obtain a high-quality beam pattern from only a short training sequence, while maintaining the same beam pattern quality as that of the conventional CBF approach.
Furthermore, the proposed approach can simultaneously obtain multiple beam patterns, each of which has a high quality.

The proposed approach is based on the conventional CBF approach, which consists of two steps: (1) the determination of the beam pattern which maximizes the variance of the information vector obtained by performing beamforming on the measured data vector, and (2) the utilization of the determined beam pattern to compress the measured data vector.
In the proposed approach, we modify the first step of the conventional CBF approach.
In particular, we use the concept of the majorization-minimization (MM) algorithm to obtain a high-quality beam pattern from only a short training sequence.
Furthermore, we modify the second step of the conventional CBF approach to simultaneously obtain multiple beam patterns, each of which has a high quality.
The proposed approach is validated through numerical experiments.
A reduct of a unary structure is a first-order structure with at most one element in each extension of a given first-order language.

A dichotomy theorem says that a property of reducts of unary structures holds, if and only if it holds for all reducts of unary structures and there is an infinite family of unary structures for which the property is satisfied, and there is an infinite family of unary structures for which the property is not satisfied.
We prove a dichotomy theorem for first-order reducts of unary structures, which answers a question of Bergelson and Sinakis.
To prove this result, we introduce a new technique that we call the density argument, which may be of independent interest.

We consider the problem of PCA-based dimension reduction where the data matrix has a known low-rank plus additive error structure, arising in various applications including incompletely supervised learning, and spectral graph clustering.
A main challenge in this problem is the inability to directly apply the eigenvalue decomposition (EVD) of the data matrix, as the EVD of a matrix with such structure is not guaranteed to exist.

We overcome this challenge by developing a new approach that robustly estimates a low-rank matrix from a small number of its entries, and leverages the estimated low-rank matrix for subsequent dimension reduction via PCA.
We prove that our approach enjoys a convergence rate of O(√n) for correctly recovering the low-rank matrix, and O(1/n) for subsequent dimension reduction via PCA, where n is the size of the data.
We further develop an efficient algorithm to compute the proposed approach.
We apply our proposed approach to incompletely supervised learning, and spectral graph clustering, and demonstrate its effectiveness via comprehensive experiments.

We consider the graph labeling problem in which each vertex of a graph is assigned a unique label in such a way that no label appears in the label of a properly colored vertex in any proper coloring of the graph.
In this paper, we present an approach that extends the list-antimagic labeling algorithm for edge-weighted graphs to vertex-weighted graphs.
The algorithm utilizes an optimal merging approach to obtain a list-antimagic labeling of the vertices, with the objective of minimizing the sum of the labels.
We present an implementation of this approach and include a computational study of several vertex-weighted graphs.

The results demonstrate that our approach can produce list-antimagic labelings with a small number of labels, and that the running time is reasonable for graphs with a large number of vertices and edges.
Black phosphorus field effect transistors (BP-FETs) have attracted considerable attention as an alternative to graphene due to their promising electrical properties and ease of fabrication.
In this work, we investigate the environmental, thermal, and electrical susceptibility of BP-FETs.
By testing the devices in controlled environments, we find that the environmental conditions, such as oxygen and moisture, have a significant impact on the device performance.
We also study the thermal properties of BP-FETs and find that they exhibit a positive thermal coefficient of resistance, which indicates that the devices are sensitive to temperature changes.

Finally, we investigate the electrical properties of BP-FETs and find that they exhibit a nonlinear current-voltage relationship and a high on/off ratio, which makes them suitable for digital applications.
Our results provide valuable insights into the performance of BP-FETs under different environmental, thermal, and electrical conditions.
We study gravitational waves in a compact extra dimension model where the bulk scalar field has a linear equation of state.
This model was shown to be an idealized scenario for the aether paradigm, where the aether is the scalar field in the bulk.
We calculate the dispersion relations for gravitational waves both in the bulk and on the boundary, and show that only on the boundary do gravitational waves propagate at the speed of light.
In the bulk, gravitational waves propagate at a different speed, which may be identified as the aether wind.

We analyze the constraint on the parameter space given by the recent LIGO detection of gravitational waves, and find that it is consistent with the aether model for sufficiently small extra dimensions, but disfavors large extra dimensions regardless of the choice of linear equation of state.
Action or state based formalisms are usually employed in different domains of computer science to specify and reason about systems.
In this paper we show that state/event based formalisms can be viewed as a particular and popular case of action or state based formalisms.

On the one hand, this helps to understand and characterize the expressive power of state/event based formalisms, and on the other hand, it highlights new possibilities for the refinement and/or extension of state/event based formalisms.
An important practical aspect in the application of nanophotonics is the efficient transmission of electromagnetic waves through sub-wavelength apertures.
In this paper, we investigate the transmission of electromagnetic waves through a sub-wavelength nano-hole in a two-dimensional plasmonic layer.
We show that the transmission coefficient is closely related to the shape of the hole.
In particular, we find excellent transmission coefficients when the hole is a circular dot or a square.
We also find that the transmission coefficient can be greatly enhanced by a factor of up to 4 when the incident angle is around 18 degrees.
Our results may offer designing guidelines for efficient sub-wavelength filters and antennas in nanophotonics.
We introduce the Hanf number of a graph, which is the least positive integer that cannot be formed by the graph's adjacency list.
We present an algorithm to compute the Hanf number of a graph, given an adjacency image of the graph.

The algorithm is based on the observation that the Hanf number of a graph can be calculated by dividing the graph into layers using breadth-first search and calculating the maximum depth of each layer.
We implement this algorithm and show that it is very fast, resulting in a new graph parameter which is efficient to compute.
A witness structure is a particular kind of combinatorial structure associated to a polynomial map, which encodes interesting information about the roots of the polynomial in question.
In this paper, we use witness structures to construct a new family of topologically meaningful complexes associated to systems of polynomial equations, called immediate snapshot complexes.
These complexes encode the topological information of systems of equations in a way that is analogous to how witness structures encode algebraic information.

We show that these complexes are always homotopy equivalent to a particular kind of complex involvingWITner spectra, and we use this fact to compute the homotopy type of the complex associated to a system of equations in terms of the roots of the polynomials in question.
We propose an alternative equation of motion approach to the single-impurity Anderson model based on a functional renormalization group scheme.
By working directly with the correlation function, our approach provides a systematic and parameter-free way to take into account the frequency dependence of the self-energy.
This allows us to investigate the spectral properties of the model at finite frequencies beyond the commonly used approximation of the frequency-independent self-energy.
Within our approach, we derive an effective low-energy theory that captures the universal features of the model.
We show that the self-energy obtained within our approach is consistent with the frequency-dependent self-energy obtained from the linearized Boltzmann equation of motion approach.
Our approach provides a way to investigate the effects of the frequency-dependent self-energy on the spectral properties of the model.
We find that the frequency-dependent self-energy has a significant effect on the spectral function even at low frequencies.
In particular, we show that the self-energy renormalizes the quasiparticle weight and modifies the low-energy features of the spectral function.
We also show that the self-energy has a negligible effect on the spectral function at high frequencies.
Our work provides a new approach to study the frequency-dependent self-energy of the single-impurity Anderson model.
Our approach can be applied to other many-body systems with frequency-dependent self-energy.
We present an algorithm for the vertex cover $P_3$ problem on graphs of bounded treewidth.
This algorithm is an improvement over the existing algorithm of Chan et al.
[23], which was designed to solve the more general vertex cover problem.
Our algorithm utilizes a novel approach based on dynamic programming, and allows us to solve the $P_3$ problem in polynomial time for graphs of bounded treewidth.
We also include a complexity analysis of our algorithm, and discuss its performance in comparison to existing algorithms for the vertex cover problem.
We show that a ring cavity can be used to synchronize Bloch oscillations in an atomic Bose-Einstein condensate.
By sending a laser pulse into the cavity when the atomic spin is oriented perpendicular to the cavity field, the atomic spin is driven coherently.

When the driving frequency matches the frequency of the Bloch oscillations, an effective negative atom-field coupling occurs, which leads to synchronization of the atomic precession and of the light field inside the cavity.
We determine the conditions for the synchronization to occur, and we show that it is possible to induce synchronization for any initial condition of the atomic spin.
The proposed setup can be used to produce a well-defined common atomic state, which is promising for applications in quantum information processing.
We introduce the notion of a locally standard torus action on a simplicial poset.
This is analogous to the well-known notion for groups, but with a topology induced by the order filtration on the simplicial poset.
We show that the h'-vector of a simplicial poset with a locally standard torus action satisfies an analog of the Garsia-Haiman formula.
This generalizes a result of McCutcheon and Miller for standard torus actions on groups.
We introduce a new probabilistic model for hierarchical structures in documents based on the Cont-Bouchaud model for polymers in disordered media.
The model is induced by a nested partition process where each node of the hierarchy is associated with a partition of the underlying set.
We derive an expression for the average similarity between the cont-bouchaud fingerprints of two documents.
This expression involves an overlap probability between the two partitions associated with the documents.
We show that the average similarity is able to capture the similarities between the documents in terms of their hierarchical structure.
We continue our study of the global Fukaya category begun in our previous paper
After briefly recalling the definition of the global Fukaya category, we discuss various examples, including singular connections and vanishing cycles, and explain how they relate to our definition.

We then prove a technical result on functoriality of the global Fukaya category with respect to a bijection on the set of exact Lagrangian submanifolds, which generalizes a result of Abouzaid and Smith

Finally, we give several examples of computations of the global Fukaya category in the case of affine manifolds, and explain how to use our functoriality result to establish an isomorphism in the case of affine bundles.

We report the results of 134.2 live-days of solar neutrino measurements by the Super-Kamiokande-IV experiment, which has adopted an analytic method based on the world's most precise neutrino energy calibration to search for pep-nova oscillations in the solar neutrino flux.
No significant deviation is found.

Combined with previous results, we obtain the 90% C.L. upper limit on the pep-nova mixing parameter, |U^2_{e1}|<0.071 at ν^{}_e<0.1 GeV and |U^2_{e1}|<0.095 at ν^{}_e<0.2 GeV, which correspond to <1.4% and <1.1% effects, respectively, at the 90% C.L..

We report on electrical transport measurements through few-layer graphene/boron-nitride/few-layer graphene structures with encapsulated boron-nitride (h-BN) layers, as a function of graphene layer number and gate voltage.
In contrast to most transport studies on few-layer graphene, we do not rely on the availability of sharp graphene contacts, nor on an interaction with the substrate.
This allows us to study few-layer graphene transport in a setup optimized for cleanliness and isolation from contaminants and the substrate, thus probing the intrinsic few-layer graphene properties.
By studying the evolution of the quantum Hall effect as a function of layer number, we determine the layer-dependent charge neutrality levels of few-layer graphene.
We observe a clear signature of the formation of a gate-tunable band gap in the monolayer and bilayer cases.
Our results provide insight into the layer-dependent physics of few-layer graphene, and evidence for a gate-tunable band gap in these systems.
We present a stable and efficient pseudospectral scheme for the approximation of partial differential equations (PDEs) using Barycentric Gegenbauer quadratures.
These are high-order accurate, total-variation-diminishing (TVD), and entropy-stable for a wide range of linear and nonlinear PDEs in convection dominated regimes.
We demonstrate that the Barycentric Gegenbauer quadratures achieve their optimal order of accuracy in the absence of dispersion effects, such as stiffness and nonlinearity.
We introduce suitable techniques to handle nonlinearity and dispersion in a stable manner.
Our approach is based on a modulation technique that introduces extra variables to decouple the nonlinear and dispersive effects from the TVD property.
We demonstrate the efficacy of the method through numerical examples.

We present a systematic construction of well-posed smoothed finite element discretizations for fluid-structure interaction (FSI) systems with quasi-steady inflow and/or outflow conditions, on arbitrary spatial domains.

The key ingredient that enables the construction of well-posed schemes is a stabilized space-time finite element pair that captures the dominant features of the convective terms in the FSI system; this pair is constructed via a transformation of Duhamel's principle.
The well-posedness of the discretizations is demonstrated via a discrete maximum principle for steady problems and via energy methods for unsteady problems.
To solve the resulting linear systems efficiently, we propose a class of robust diagonal preconditioners.
These preconditioners are suitable for problems with many rigid bodies and are easy to implement.

Furthermore, we show that each preconditioner is numerically robust, i.e., it is asymptotically efficient for all instances of a problem class, provided that a certain condition number bound is satisfied.
This preconditioning strategy has been implemented successfully in the finite element code FENICS.
The study of ideal theory in finite rings has many applications in computer science and mathematics.
It serves as a theoretical foundation for cryptography, and many of its problems are NP-hard.
In this paper, we present a quantum algorithm for solving the ideal membership problem, wherein given a finite ring and an ideal I, one wants to determine whether a given element
x is in I.
We improve the known quantum bounds and show that, for a fixed finite ring of size n, the ideal membership problem can be solved in time O(n^3 log(n)).
This is the first example of a problem in ideal theory that can be solved efficiently on a quantum computer.
We use high-speed imaging and numerical modelling to investigate water droplet penetration inside narrow, open-ended pores, characterised by a diameter of ∼1 mm.
In particular, we analyse the dependence of capillary influx and splashing on droplet size and on the initial contact angle.
We find that the closed pore generates a stronger capillary force, which results in a more effective attraction of the liquid.
Interestingly, we observe that, before completing the penetration, the liquid protrudes from the pore, wets the external surface, and finally detaches.
The total ingress time is significantly longer than the cavity emptying time, thus revealing that the liquid evacuation is controlled by capillary inertia.
We quantify the liquid protrusion length as a function of the contact angle and find that it corresponds to the meniscus pinning regime.

Our results show that the open-ended pore is a relevant scenario to improve the understanding of droplet impact and capillary influx, which are relevant in many applications involving porous media, including in biomedical devices and in oil production.

Let $\mathcal{A}$ be the set of all analytic convex domains in $\mathbb{C}^n$. Denoting by $\mathfrak{L}(\mathcal{A})$ the length spectrum and $\mathfrak{A}(\mathcal{A})$ the area spectrum of a domain $\Omega \in \mathcal{A}$, respectively, we prove that any sequence $\{\Omega_j\} \subset \mathcal{A}$ such that $\mathfrak{L}(\Omega_j) \to 0$ and $\mathfrak{A}(\Omega_j) \to 0$ as $j \to \infty$ admits a subsequence converging to a ball $B \subset \mathbb{C}^n$.
This solves a question suggested by Ahlfors and Bers.
We present a family of reduced modeling techniques for the a posteriori analysis of nonlinear multiphase problems in elastodynamics.

In contrast to standard reduced modeling techniques, which construct a single reduced-order model throughout the computation, the technique presented here constructs a sequence of reduced-order models, with each model in the sequence being tailored to the particular eigensolution of the full problem that is being computed.
This approach is inspired by recent work on reduced relative entropy fabrication, and adapts that methodology to the setting of nonlinear elastodynamics.
In order to demonstrate the efficacy of the approach, we consider a model problem involving a nonlinear damped wave equation with a modal perturbation in an interior region of the domain.

We demonstrate that the sequence of reduced-order models produced converges to the full solution of the problem as the mesh is refined, and that the error in the prediction of the full solution can be controlled via a posteriori error estimation techniques.
Model predictive control (MPC) is applied to a coupled tank liquid level system in this work.
In this system, the liquid levels in two tanks, which are connected by a pipe, are controlled.
The control objective is to transfer liquid from one tank to another while maintaining the liquid levels in both tanks at desired levels.
The model of the system is derived using a mass balance approach on the liquid levels in the tanks.
The controller is designed using a linear quadratic regulator (LQR) approach.
The controller is tested on a set of realistic scenarios, and the results are compared with those obtained using a PID controller.
The results show that the MPC controller can effectively control the liquid levels in the coupled tank system, and it can handle large and fast changes in the system inputs and disturbances.
In this paper, a model predictive control (MPC) scheme is presented for controlling the liquid level in a coupled tank system.
The system comprises two tanks connected by a pipe.
The objective is to transfer liquid from one tank to another while maintaining the liquid levels in both tanks at desired levels.
A mass balance model of the system is derived, and the controller is designed using linear quadratic regulator (LQR) methodology.
The controller is evaluated using a set of realistic scenarios, and its performance is compared with that of a PID controller.
Results show that the MPC controller is able to effectively control the liquid levels in the coupled tank system, even in the presence of large and fast changes in the system inputs and disturbances.
We consider arrangements of n objects in a line that avoid a crossing.
We investigate the minimal number of crossings for a generalized Euler permutation, a standard tableau of rectangular shape, and a column strict array.
In the case of the generalized Euler permutation, we give an exact formula for this number and we provide an asymptotic formula in the other two cases.

Recent progress in the controlled generation of individual x-ray photons for imaging at a free-electron laser (XFEL) facility lays the foundation for a new regime of imaging – single-photon counting (SPC) imaging.
In SPC imaging, the detected intensity at each image pixel is determined by counting the number of detected photons arriving within a fixed-length shutter time.
In this paper, we investigate the benefits as well as the associated challenges of SPC imaging, as compared to conventional (i.e. integrating) imaging, in a variety of scientific applications.

To this end, we have developed a simulation framework, which models the entire photon generation, propagation, and detection process at an XFEL facility, and which is suitable for performing fully-sequential simulations, wherein each detected photon's arrival time and pixel position is determined stochastically.
In this paper we present the formalism and the numerical methods employed in this simulation framework.

We then explore, through a series of numerical simulations, the relative benefits of SPC imaging as compared to conventional imaging in the context of three scientific applications: (a) phase imaging to recover a weak object transmission function; (b) diffraction imaging to determine an object's lattice; (c) imaging through strongly scattering media.
We provide a brief survey of sequential decision problems, where the available options or their outcomes depend on some hidden type.
We then introduce a new formalism, called generic solutions, for their solution.
This formalism generalizes both previous work on decision problems with types and work on point-based decision procedures.

We show that generic solutions enjoy nice computational properties: the resulting decision problem is still decidable, and can be solved by a linear number of calls to a standard decision procedure for a single-agent problem.
We present a historical survey of the proofs of Euclid's theorem on the infinitude of primes, ranging from 300 BC to the present, focusing on the modern approaches.
In addition, we introduce a new proof based on the idea of the difference between two consecutive numbers being divisible by all integers less than or equal to the larger of the two.
This proof is particularly elegant because it relies only on the concept of divisibility, making it accessible to mathematicians at all levels.
We study the topology of the eigensurfaces of the planar quantum pendulum using supersymmetry.
By constructing an infinite-dimensional supersymmetric algebra, we relate the eigensurfaces of the quantum pendulum to those of a supersymmetric partner Hamiltonian.
The latter is shown to have a bulk-edge correspondence, with edge modes residing on the boundary of the Brillouin zone.

The eigensurface topology is then determined by calculating the Jones polynomial of the unknotting tunnels of the original pendulum, and relating it to the Jones polynomial of the unknotting tunnels of the supersymmetric partner.
This provides a topological explanation for the bulk-edge correspondence in the quantum pendulum.
We propose a class of dynamic spatial autoregressive (DSAR) models with autoregressive (AR) and heteroskedastic disturbances, which are modeled as a first-order autoregressive process.

The proposed model allows for different weights for the spatial and temporal autocorrelations and captures the dynamic dependence among the spatial units, both in the mean and in the volatility, while remaining applicable in high-dimensional settings.
We propose a penalized maximum likelihood estimation procedure that allows for efficient estimation of the model parameters in large panels.
We study the theoretical properties of the estimator and derive the large sample normality of the estimator in a semi-parametric bootstrap procedure.
Finally, we illustrate the application of the proposed method using a real data example.
We report on a coherent photodetector based on self-assembled quantum wells (QWs) in a single AlGaAs/GaAs nanowire (NW).

The 3D quantum well structures are formed by phase-breaking dislocations introduced by a quantum corral technique, in which a quantum well template is fabricated beneath the nanowire, utilizing the substrate as an aperture.
The photodetector shows response times as short as 11 ps with a responsivity of 18 mA/W at a wavelength of 976 nm.
The fast response is attributed to the suppression of Auger recombination in the QWs.
Our results demonstrate the potential of using coherent photodetectors based on quantum wells in single nanowires for fast optical communication.
Keywords: Nanowire, quantum well, dislocation, photodetector, quantum corral, ultrafast photoresponse
We determine the fractal dimension of SAT formulas, showing that it is strictly greater than 1, namely 2.025.

Since the unique graph with fractal dimension 2 is the complete graph, every SAT formula with n variables and m clauses contains a subformula that is isomorphic to a subformula of K_n, the complete graph on n vertices.
We also show that the fractal dimension of SAT formulas is not affected by the specific instance of variables.
Password cracking is the art of recovering passwords from data that has been stored in or transmitted by a computer system.
Computer security is essential everywhere, especially in organizations that handle confidential data, to protect the interest of the users, organizations, and nations.
Due to this importance, the area of computer security, especially the authentication phase, has received a lot of attention recently.
Researchers have developed many solutions to various security problems, including the password cracking problem.

This paper surveys the state-of-the-art of password cracking, including password crackings statistical analysis and the most popular cracking techniques, such as Dictionary, Brute-Force, and Hybrid cracking techniques.
It also surveys the state-of-the-art of password countermeasures, including password policy and password storage.
We discuss the future direction of research on password cracking and countermeasures.
In this paper we present a systematic study of domination parameters based on the number of dominated neighbours.
We show that these parameters are capable of inferring several known parameters, and that they may become alternative tools in algorithmic ecology.

In particular, we show that each of three classical invariants of plant competition (the competitive ratio, the dominance ratio, and the participation ratio) can be inferred from the number of neighbours dominated with two sons, and we present a condition ensuring that these relations hold in a wide variety of situations.

We also show that the parameter first observed by Bascompte and Lloret can be used to infer the amount of variation in individual quality, and we introduce a new parameter, the dominance index, for quantifying the hierarchical structure of a population.
This parameter is based on the number of neighbours dominated with two sons, and on the number of neighbours dominating two sons.
We show that the dominance index is related to the variance of individual quality, and that it can be used to quantify the impact of abiotic factors on the hierarchical structure of populations.
Finally, we present a simple algorithm for computing the dominance index, and we show that it can be used to solve the all-pairs shortest paths problem on trees in polynomial time.

We show that the resonances of open quantum systems possessing discrete spectrum can overlap, forming complex patterns, even in the absence of decoherence or thermal activation, generalizing the phenomenon of avoided crossings.

The overlapping of resonances occurs when the eigenstates of the system couple to common (shared) environmental modes, resulting in eigenstates that are a priori distinct acquiring a non-zero overlap.
We provide a systematic method to identify overlapping resonances in multi-level systems, and apply this method to several examples, both artificial and real, drawn from the literature.
In all cases, we find that overlapping resonances are connected by complex eigenvectors, rendering the spectrum non-degenerate, and impacting the system's spectral function.

We discuss the physical implications of overlapping resonances, and show that they can give rise to level-crossing thermalization, where an initially pure state thermalizes by evolving through a sequence of overlapping resonances.
In this paper, we define a monoid of invertibility preserving maps on a set and study its properties.
We use this monoid to construct a group of invertibility preserving maps on a set.
We apply these results to construct a group of isometries on a vector space and use this group to study the structure of Clifford algebras.

Our algorithm is based on a new set of metrics for evaluating the performance of clustering and relational ambiguity resolution algorithms.
Our metrics are designed to be more sensitive to the underlying structure of the data and to the relationships between the data points.
We evaluate our algorithm on a variety of text data sets and show that it is more accurate and efficient than the existing algorithms in the literature.
We also show that our algorithm is able to handle relational ambiguity in text data, which is not handled by the existing algorithms in the literature.
Our algorithm is a promising step towards a more effective and efficient clustering and relational ambiguity resolution algorithm for text data."
We present a new numerical method for solving the spherical harmonics moment equations of radiative transfer in the Earth's atmosphere.
The new method, called StaRMAP (STAGgered Radiative Moments APproach), is a second-order accurate approximation of the exact radiative transfer equation.
It is based on a staggered grid arrangement of the spherical harmonics moments, which allows for an efficient and accurate solution of the radiative transfer equation.
We describe the basic idea of StaRMAP and present a set of test problems to evaluate the accuracy and performance of the new method.
The radiative transfer equation is a basic equation in atmospheric radiation, which describes how solar and terrestrial radiation is absorbed, scattered, and re-emitted in the Earth's atmosphere.
It is a complex nonlinear partial differential equation, which can be simplified by using the spherical harmonics moments.
These moments correspond to the coefficients of the spherical harmonics expansion of the radiation field, and they can be solved using a set of linear equations.
StaRMAP is a new method for solving the spherical harmonics moment equations of radiative transfer.
It is based on a staggered grid arrangement of the spherical harmonics moments, which allows for an efficient and accurate solution of the radiative transfer equation.
The method is second-order accurate, which means that it approximates the exact solution of the radiative transfer equation to second-order accuracy.
This makes it a very accurate method for solving the radiative transfer equation.
We present a set of test problems to evaluate the accuracy and performance of StaRMAP.
These test problems are designed to test the accuracy and performance of the new method in a variety of scenarios.
We find that StaRMAP is a very accurate and efficient method for solving the spherical harmonics moment equations of radiative transfer.
It is able to solve the test problems to second-order accuracy and is faster than other methods for solving the radiative transfer equation.
In this paper, we discuss the equations of the inverse kinematics problem, in which the end-effector of a robot is posed in terms of the joint variables.

We show that, depending on the underlying representation, the inverse kinematics problem can be formulated as a nonlinear system of up to six equations, and we discuss the conditions under which this is possible.
We also show that, in general, the inverse kinematics problem cannot be formulated as a linear system of four equations, and we discuss the reasons for this.
We study a planar four-Fermi model in a tilted magnetic field using the functional renormalization group (FRG).
We find a chiral phase transition line in the plane of the tilt angle and the coupling constant of the four-Fermi term.
The chiral phase transition is of second order along the entire line.
There is a critical point at a tilt angle of 45$^{\circ}$, where the correlation length exponent $\nu$ changes its value from 1 to 2.
Along the line, the universality class is identical to that of the three-dimensional Ising model.
We also analyze the FRG equations for the tilted axial next-nearest-neighbor Ising model in order to understand the appearance of the Ising universality class in the four-Fermi model.
We give a necessary and sufficient condition for a real analytic family of complex structures to be analytically conjugate to a family of complex structures with vanishing first derivative.

This condition is sufficient to ensure the integrability of the generalized complex structure, and implies the existence of a symplectic form and a almost-complex structure on the symplectic form, both invariant under the complex structure.

We apply our results to the setting of toric generalized complex structures, and give an example of a family of generalized complex structures which is not analytically conjugate to a family with vanishing first derivative.
WavePacket is a Matlab package devoted to the numerical solution of quantum dynamics in closed systems.
It can handle both finite-dimensional and infinite-dimensional systems, the latter being described by Gaussian wavefunctions.

The package implements a set of numerical techniques for the propagation of Gaussian wavepackets, both in the position space (numerical propagation in the configuration interaction picture) and in the momentum space (numerical propagation in the Heisenberg picture).
The propagation can be done in both the energy representation and in the representation of any other variable, like the angular momentum.
The package can also perform the exact diagonalization of the Hamiltonian of a many-body system described by means of a finite-dimensional Hilbert space.
WavePacket can be used as a simple and reliable tool for teaching and researching basic aspects of quantum mechanics.
The package, as well as tutorials on how to use it, can be downloaded from http://www.uca.es/ WavePacket.
We present an original approach to design ultra-compact supercontinuum sources based on two-soliton modulation instability in microstructured fibers.
Our design strategy combines experimental data with numerical simulations within a genetic algorithm optimization procedure.
The objective function to be minimized comprises two terms: a data fitting term to adjust the experimental data and a spectral distortion term to optimize the spectral flatness of the supercontinuum.
We present optimization results for a number of experimentally realizable fiber configurations.
The proposed optimization procedure leads to considerably narrower spectral envelopes and improved spectral flatness of the supercontinuum compared to previous results.
We discuss the applicability of this method for other microstructured fiber configurations.
In the paper, we show that every normed space X is angularly equivalent to a normed space of rational angles.
This answers a question posed by G. Schechtman.

We give a simple and conceptual proof of a theorem of Alexeev and Brion, which says that a rational surface singularity is simple if and only if it admits a weighted projective line structure of genus 0.
This theorem gives also a necessary and sufficient condition for a weighted projective line to be homogeneous, extending a result of Keel.
We give an upper bound for the negativity of arrangements of curves transversal to a line, in terms of the classical Harbourne constant of the arrangement.
This provides a new upper bound for the maximum negativity of all arrangements of $n$ curves in the projective plane, improving a recent result of Chan.

Multi-hop Diffusion LMS accurately estimates the parameters of a linear dynamic system with multiple sensors and a parameter-update controller placed on every link of a communication network, with a provable guarantee on estimation accuracy and a finite-time convergence result, under a communication energy constraint.

The algorithm combines the benefits of diffusion and cascade (or multi-hop) algorithms, i.e., it allows the sensors to exchange their estimates over a multi-hop communication network, and at the same time, it compensates for the distortion of the estimates due to the communication process.

The proposed algorithm is especially suitable for resource-constrained sensor networks, such as wireless sensor networks, where the energy consumption of the communication process should be minimized.
The theoretical findings are validated through simulation results.
We propose and analyze thin-disk laser pump schemes that allow for a large number of amplification passes while maintaining a relatively low pump absorption per pass.

The thin-disk lasers are configured to have a relatively low pump-light-to-laser-light efficiency, which allows them to have higher pump absorption per pass, and larger number of passes while maintaining moderate pump source quality.
This approach can extend the thickness limit of the laser crystal due to heat effects, and can also allow for a more efficient laser operation by operating the laser at higher output power.

The proposed pump schemes can be used for laser crystals that have high quantum defect, such as Nd:YAG, and Nd:YLF, and also for laser crystals that have relatively low quantum defect, such as Nd:Glass and Nd:YVO4.
The proposed pump schemes can also be used for other laser crystals such as Yb:YAG, and Yb:YLF.
We analyze the potential efficiency, and output power limitations of the proposed pump schemes, and discuss the trade-offs between the laser performance, and the pump configuration.
We give a new, combinatorial definition of the Theta-invariant, a classic homology invariant of oriented 3-manifolds.
Our definition uses Heegaard diagrams, a familiar way to describe 3-manifolds.
Up to homotopy, our definition is analogous to the way the Kauffman polynomial is defined using Kauffman diagrams.

As an application, we prove the Kauffman- Thistlethwaite conjecture that a bracket polynomial is homotopic to a Kauffman polynomial if and only if it is equal to its Taylor expansion plus higher-order corrections.
We present a new model reduction technique for efficient simulation of flow in heterogeneous porous media, which accounts for both the nonlinearity of the flow and the heterogeneity of the medium.

Our method combines a global nonlinear model reduction technique, which captures the overall behavior of the flow, with a local model reduction technique, which captures the fine-scale behavior of the flow in each individual cell of the porous medium.

The global model reduction is based on a nonlinear singular value decomposition (SVD) of the flow equation, which identifies the most important modes of the flow and allows for the reduction of the flow problem to a small number of dimensions.
The local model reduction is based on a cell-specific approximation of the flow equation, which captures the fine-scale behavior of the flow in each individual cell of the porous medium.
The cell-specific approximation is constructed using a local nonlinear SVD of the flow equation, which identifies the most important modes of the flow within each cell.

The global-local model reduction technique is demonstrated on a variety of example flows in heterogeneous porous media, and it is shown to provide significant improvements in computational efficiency compared to conventional full-scale simulations, while maintaining accurate predictions of the flow behavior.
We report on a time-resolved study of periodic surface structures formed in fused silica following illumination with a focused femtosecond laser pulse.
A single pulse was capable of producing a clearly visible periodic surface structure, the periodicity of which decreased with increasing fluence.
Experimental measurements revealed that the periodicity of the resulting surface grating decreased with increasing laser pulse intensity as a power law with an exponent of −0.20 �± 0.01.
Comparable measurements carried out on bulk silica exposed to the same laser field intensity indicate that the surface plays a crucial role in the development of periodic structures.
We consider Bayesian variable selection problems in high-dimensional settings, where both the number of covariates and the sample size are large.
We propose a new Bayesian variable selection method for grouped covariates that incorporates the group structure in a natural way.

We demonstrate that our method has attractive theoretical and practical properties, including improved frequentist coverage properties compared to existing Bayesian variable selection methods for high-dimensional data.
We illustrate our method through a simulation study and an application to a real data set.
We introduce a novel information geometric formalism for the spatially homogeneous Boltzmann equation, with emphasis on the Curty-Ford-Merritt (CFM) collision operator.
This formalism is motivated by the structure of the CFM operator, which preserves an invariant measure and a conserved quantity that plays the role of a Hamiltonian.

By suitably adapting the information geometric formalism developed for the Ising model, we show that the CFM Boltzmann equation corresponds to a Riemannian submersion, with the Hamiltonian playing the role of the submersion metric.
This allows one to employ the theory of Riemannian submersions to study the long-time behavior of solutions, as well as the local well-posedness of the CFM equation.

We investigate the possibility of using simple architectures to outperform deeper and more complex ones, investigating both potential advantages of using simple architectures and the possibility of finding more robust solutions.
Our investigations show that simple architectures can outperform deeper and more complex ones, and that a robust solution can be found by using a combination of both complex and simple architectures.
We present a simple architecture, a kind of Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) with a single convolutional layer, that achieves state-of-the-art performance on the CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 datasets.
We show that our simple architecture is able to achieve this performance by taking advantage of the structure of the input data and the specific problem definition.
We also show that our architecture is able to generalize well to different datasets and problem definitions.
We give an introduction to stochastic partial differential equations (SPDEs).
After recalling the definition and properties of classical Gaussian SPDEs, we discuss existence and uniqueness results for general nonlinear SPDEs in a Gaussian setting.

We then turn to a class of nonlinear SPDEs in the Gaussian setting which possess a unique solution and focus on the question of obtaining a probabilistic representation for the solution in terms of a stochastic flow of maps.
Here the underlying stochastic flow is solution to a stochastic differential equation with a countable number of Brownian drivers.
We present a general approach for obtaining such a representation under mild conditions on the coefficients of the SPDE.

As a concrete example, we consider a class of nonlinear SPDEs that are associated to a stochastic flow of maps that is generated by a stochastic differential equation with a countable number of Brownian drivers.
We discuss existence, uniqueness and probabilistic representation results for this class of SPDEs.
An application of our results to the study of a stochastic flow of maps arising in the study of stochastic resonance is given.
Throughout this paper, we assume that the reader is familiar with the basic theory of SPDEs, stochastic integration and the theory of stochastic flows of maps.

Introduction

Stochastic partial differential equations (SPDEs) are an important class of stochastic models that are used to describe the behavior of a wide range of physical, biological and financial systems.
These equations generalize classical partial differential equations (PDEs) by introducing a stochastic term into the equation.
This stochastic term can be used to model a variety of phenomena, such as noise, random fluctuations and uncertainty in the system.
SPDEs can be classified into two main categories: linear and nonlinear.
Linear SPDEs are those in which the nonlinearity in the equation is a linear function of the unknown function and its derivatives.
Nonlinear SPDEs are those in which the nonlinearity in the equation is a nonlinear function of the unknown function and its derivatives.
The study of SPDEs is a rapidly developing field, and many new results and techniques have been developed in the past few years.
One of the main challenges in the study of SPDEs is the lack of closed-form solutions.
This is due to the fact that the stochastic term introduces a high degree of randomness into the equation, making it difficult to find exact solutions.
However, there are many existence and uniqueness results for SPDEs, and these results can be used to obtain approximate solutions
We study the problem of covert communication over classical-quantum channels.
We show that quantum states, which are suitable for secure quantum communication, can be used for cheating in covert communication.
Thus, the capacity of the cheating strategy, called covert capacity, is shown to be zero, under certain assumptions, if the channel is memoryless and classical-quantum.

In this case, we provide a rigorous definition of covert capacity, which is consistent with the usual definition of classical covert capacity, and obtain an inner bound, which is tight up to a constant factor.
The result generalizes previous results on classical-quantum channels to the case of covert communication.
We present a new method for three-dimensional (3D) tracking of colloidal particles in a microfluidic environment using digital holographic microscopy (DHM) and joint reconstruction.
In DHM, a laser beam is split into a reference beam and an object beam, which is scattered by the sample.
The interference between the reference and object beams is recorded on a camera, producing a hologram containing phase information about the sample.
We then develop an algorithm for reconstructing the 3D trajectory of a colloidal particle from a sequence of such holograms.
The algorithm is based on joint reconstruction of the particle position in the hologram plane and its 3D position, using a Bayesian approach.
We show that our method is more accurate and robust than previous methods, and can track multiple particles simultaneously.
We demonstrate the performance of our method on simulated and real data, and show that it can be used to study the Brownian motion of colloidal particles in a microfluidic environment.

In DHM, a laser beam is split into a reference beam and an object beam, which is scattered by the sample.
The interference between the reference and object beams is recorded on a CCD camera, producing a hologram containing both amplitude and phase information about the sample.
We then develop a new algorithm for reconstructing the 3D trajectory of a colloidal particle from a sequence of such holograms.

We show that our method is more accurate and robust than previous methods, and can simultaneously track multiple particles.
Finally, we demonstrate the performance of our method on both simulated and real data.
