Charlier polynomials are a family of orthogonal polynomials that arise in the study of quantum mechanics and statistical mechanics.
The Hermite function, on the other hand, is a special function that is widely used in various areas of mathematics and physics.
The paper presents a detailed analysis of the relationship between Charlier polynomials and the Hermite function, including their respective properties and applications.
The results of this study provide valuable insights into the mathematical and physical connections between these two important mathematical objects.
Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves are widely used in various fields to evaluate the performance of binary classifiers.
However, estimating the ROC curve from data can be challenging, especially when the underlying density is unknown or difficult to estimate.
In this paper, we propose a new method for estimating smooth ROC curves based on log-concave density estimates.
We show that our estimator is consistent and achieves the optimal rate of convergence under mild assumptions.
We also provide a simulation study to demonstrate the performance of our method compared to existing approaches.
Our results suggest that the proposed estimator can accurately estimate smooth ROC curves even in the presence of complex underlying densities.
This has important implications for the evaluation and comparison of binary classifiers in practice.
In this paper, we investigate the confinement phase in carbon-nanotubes using the extended massive Schwinger model.
We analyze the behavior of the model in the presence of an external magnetic field and study the effects of different parameters on the confinement phase.
Our results show that the confinement phase is strongly influenced by the external magnetic field and the parameters of the model.
We also discuss the implications of our findings for the understanding of confinement in carbon-nanotubes and propose future directions for research in this area.
This paper introduces a new approach for modeling spatial point processes using quasi-likelihood methods.
Spatial point processes are commonly used to model the distribution of events or objects in space, such as the locations of trees in a forest or the occurrence of disease cases in a region.
Traditional methods for modeling spatial point processes often rely on assumptions about the underlying distribution, which may not always be appropriate or feasible.
The proposed quasi-likelihood approach offers a flexible and robust alternative by allowing for the estimation of the mean intensity function without making strong assumptions about the distribution.
The paper presents the theoretical framework for the quasi-likelihood method and demonstrates its application through simulation studies and real-world examples.
The results show that the quasi-likelihood approach can accurately estimate the mean intensity function and provide reliable inference for spatial point processes.
Overall, this paper provides a valuable contribution to the field of spatial statistics by offering a new and flexible method for modeling spatial point processes.
This paper proposes a smoothed p-value test for hypothesis testing when there is a nuisance parameter under the alternative hypothesis.
The proposed method involves smoothing the p-value function using a kernel density estimator.
The authors show that the smoothed p-value test has better power properties compared to existing methods, especially when the nuisance parameter is large.
The performance of the proposed method is evaluated through simulation studies and real data examples.
The results demonstrate the effectiveness of the smoothed p-value test in various scenarios, making it a valuable tool for hypothesis testing in the presence of a nuisance parameter.
In this paper, we investigate the avoidance of singularities in asymptotically safe Quantum Einstein Gravity.
We propose a modified version of the theory that incorporates a non-singular behavior at the Planck scale.
We analyze the renormalization group flow of the theory and show that it exhibits a fixed point at high energies, indicating the existence of a non-trivial ultraviolet fixed point.
We also study the behavior of the theory near the singularity and find that it is characterized by a bounce, where the curvature reaches a maximum and then decreases.
This bounce effectively avoids the singularity and leads to a non-singular evolution of the universe.
Our results provide a promising framework for addressing the singularity problem in quantum gravity and open up new avenues for further research in this field.
In this paper, we propose a novel method for constructing a non-negative low rank and sparse graph with data-adaptive features.
We first introduce a new framework that combines non-negative matrix factorization and sparse coding to learn a low rank and sparse representation of the data.
We then use this representation to construct a graph that captures the underlying structure of the data.
Our method is data-adaptive, meaning that it can adapt to different types of data and learn features that are specific to the given dataset.
We evaluate the performance of our method on several real-world datasets and compare it to existing methods.
The results show that our method outperforms existing methods in terms of both accuracy and efficiency.
Overall, our method provides a powerful tool for constructing graphs with data-adaptive features, which can be used in various applications such as clustering, classification, and anomaly detection.
This paper presents generalized Whitney formulas for broken circuits in ambigraphs and matroids.
The authors extend the classical Whitney formulas to include broken circuits, which are circuits that contain a pair of parallel edges.
The authors provide a combinatorial interpretation of these formulas and prove their correctness.
They also discuss the implications of these formulas for the study of ambigraphs and matroids.
Overall, this paper contributes to the understanding of broken circuits in these mathematical structures and provides a useful tool for further research in the field.
This paper presents the design and performance of a multilayer surface detector for ultracold neutrons (UCNs).
The detector consists of alternating layers of boron and lithium fluoride, which are optimized for high efficiency and low background noise.
The detector is capable of detecting UCNs with energies below 100 neV, making it suitable for a wide range of experiments in the field of ultracold neutron physics.
The performance of the detector is characterized in terms of its detection efficiency, background noise, and energy resolution.
The results show that the detector achieves a high detection efficiency of 95% for UCNs with energies below 10 neV, and a low background noise level of 0.1 counts per second.
The energy resolution of the detector is found to be 1 neV, which is sufficient for many UCN experiments.
Overall, the multilayer surface detector presented in this paper offers a promising solution for the detection of UCNs in a variety of experimental setups.
This paper investigates the formation and behavior of holes and cracks in rigid foam films.
The study focuses on the effects of various factors, such as film thickness, foam density, and environmental conditions, on the formation and growth of these defects.
Experimental and numerical methods are employed to analyze the mechanisms behind hole and crack formation, as well as their impact on the overall mechanical properties of the foam films.
The findings of this study provide valuable insights into the design and manufacturing of rigid foam films, with potential applications in packaging, insulation, and other industries.
This paper investigates the occurrence and properties of phase singularities in complex arithmetic random waves.
Phase singularities are points in a wave where the phase is undefined or discontinuous.
The authors use numerical simulations to study the distribution and behavior of phase singularities in complex arithmetic random waves.
They find that the number of phase singularities increases with the complexity of the wave and that their distribution follows a statistical pattern.
The authors also analyze the relationship between phase singularities and the amplitude of the wave, finding that the amplitude can affect the behavior of phase singularities.
Overall, this study provides insights into the behavior of phase singularities in complex arithmetic random waves and contributes to the understanding of wave phenomena.
This paper presents a study on stable planar mesoscopic photonic crystal cavities.
The authors investigate the design and fabrication of these cavities, focusing on their stability and performance.
The study includes simulations and experimental measurements to evaluate the cavity's quality factor, mode volume, and resonant wavelength.
The results show that the planar mesoscopic photonic crystal cavities exhibit high stability and performance, making them suitable for various applications in photonics and optoelectronics.
The findings of this study contribute to the development of efficient and reliable photonic devices.
This paper presents an accelerated stochastic alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) algorithm with variance reduction for solving large-scale optimization problems.
The proposed algorithm incorporates a variance reduction technique to reduce the computational cost of stochastic gradient estimation.
The algorithm is shown to converge to the optimal solution at a faster rate compared to existing stochastic ADMM algorithms.
Numerical experiments on various optimization problems demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of the proposed algorithm.
The results suggest that the accelerated stochastic ADMM with variance reduction is a promising approach for solving large-scale optimization problems.
Quantum cryptography has revolutionized the field of secure communication by leveraging the principles of quantum mechanics to provide unconditional security.
Quantum key distribution (QKD) is the most well-known application of quantum cryptography, which allows two parties to establish a secret key over an insecure channel.
However, QKD is limited in terms of its practicality and scalability.
This paper explores the concept of quantum cryptography beyond QKD, focusing on alternative approaches that can enhance the security and efficiency of cryptographic protocols.
We discuss various techniques such as quantum coin flipping, quantum secret sharing, and quantum oblivious transfer, which offer new possibilities for secure communication.
Additionally, we analyze the challenges and potential applications of these advanced quantum cryptographic protocols.
By going beyond QKD, we aim to contribute to the development of more robust and versatile quantum cryptographic systems that can meet the demands of future secure communication networks.
The paper investigates the complexity of the b-coloring problem on co-bipartite graphs and tree-cographs.
The b-coloring problem involves assigning colors to the vertices of a graph such that no two adjacent vertices have the same color, and the number of colors used is minimized.
The authors prove that the b-coloring problem is NP-hard on co-bipartite graphs, meaning that it is computationally difficult to find an optimal solution.
However, they also show that the problem can be solved in polynomial time on tree-cographs, which are a special class of graphs.
This result provides insight into the complexity of the b-coloring problem on different types of graphs and contributes to the understanding of graph coloring algorithms.
This paper presents a study of the X-ray properties of two cometary blue compact dwarf galaxies, Mrk 59 and Mrk 71.

X-ray observations were conducted using the Chandra X-ray Observatory, and the data was analyzed to determine the X-ray luminosity, spectral properties, and X-ray source populations in these galaxies.
The results show that both Mrk 59 and Mrk 71 exhibit X-ray emission, with Mrk 59 showing a higher X-ray luminosity.
The X-ray spectra of both galaxies indicate the presence of thermal emission, possibly from hot gas associated with star formation activity.
Additionally, a number of X-ray sources were detected in both galaxies, including potential X-ray binaries and supernova remnants.
These findings provide valuable insights into the X-ray properties of cometary blue compact dwarf galaxies and contribute to our understanding of the processes driving their evolution.
Privacy amplification is a crucial step in secure communication protocols, where two parties aim to establish a shared secret key over an insecure channel.
Non-signaling privacy amplification protocols are designed to ensure that an eavesdropper cannot gain any information about the shared key.
In this paper, we prove the impossibility of achieving non-signaling privacy amplification.

We demonstrate that any protocol that claims to achieve non-signaling privacy amplification must either leak information to the eavesdropper or result in a shared key that is not uniformly distributed.
Our proof is based on information-theoretic arguments and provides a fundamental limitation on the achievable level of privacy in secure communication protocols.
This result has implications for the design and analysis of privacy amplification protocols and highlights the need for alternative approaches to achieve secure communication.
This paper presents a novel approach to compressive beamforming, a technique used in ultrasound imaging to improve image quality and resolution.
The proposed method, called multiple and single snapshot compressive beamforming, combines multiple snapshots of the ultrasound data to enhance the reconstruction of the beamformed image.
The authors demonstrate the effectiveness of their approach through simulations and experiments, showing improved image quality compared to traditional compressive beamforming methods.
The proposed method has the potential to significantly improve the performance of ultrasound imaging systems, leading to better diagnosis and treatment of various medical conditions.
This paper presents a dichotomy theorem for first-order reducts of unary structures.
A unary structure is a structure with a single unary relation.
The dichotomy theorem states that every first-order reduct of a unary structure is either a disjoint union of cliques or a disjoint union of cliques and isolated vertices.
The proof of this theorem involves a reduction to a simpler problem and the use of a combinatorial argument.
This result has applications in various areas of mathematics and computer science, including model theory and complexity theory.
This paper presents a robust principal component analysis (PCA) algorithm that incorporates partial subspace knowledge.
Traditional PCA methods assume that the data lies entirely in a low-dimensional subspace, which may not be accurate in real-world scenarios.
The proposed algorithm leverages partial subspace knowledge to improve the accuracy of PCA.
The algorithm is based on a convex optimization framework and utilizes a nuclear norm penalty to encourage low-rank solutions.

Experimental results on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm in accurately recovering the underlying subspace structure even when only partial knowledge is available.
The algorithm also outperforms existing robust PCA methods in terms of robustness and computational efficiency.
Overall, this paper provides a valuable contribution to the field of robust PCA and offers a practical solution for scenarios where only partial subspace knowledge is available.
This paper introduces the concept of list-antimagic labeling for vertex-weighted graphs.

A list-antimagic labeling is a labeling of the vertices of a graph such that the sum of the labels of the vertices adjacent to any given vertex is different from the sum of the labels of the vertices adjacent to any other vertex.
The authors provide a characterization of graphs that admit list-antimagic labelings and present algorithms for constructing such labelings.
They also investigate the relationship between list-antimagic labelings and other types of labelings, such as antimagic and supermagic labelings.
The paper concludes with several open problems and directions for future research in this area.
Black phosphorus (BP) has emerged as a promising material for field effect transistors (FETs) due to its unique electronic properties.
However, the environmental, thermal, and electrical susceptibility of BP FETs remains poorly understood.
In this study, we investigate the effects of environmental factors such as humidity and oxygen exposure on the performance of BP FETs.
We also examine the thermal stability of BP FETs under different operating conditions.
Furthermore, we analyze the electrical susceptibility of BP FETs to external stimuli such as light and magnetic fields.
Our results provide valuable insights into the limitations and potential applications of BP FETs in various environmental and operational conditions.
This paper investigates the presence of aether terms in a space-time with a compact extra dimension.
The authors propose a modified theory of gravity that includes a compact extra dimension and a non-zero aether field.
They derive the equations of motion for the metric and the aether field, and study the behavior of the solutions.

The authors find that the aether terms can have significant effects on the dynamics of the space-time, leading to new phenomena such as the generation of gravitational waves and the modification of the gravitational force.
The results of this study provide insights into the possible existence and properties of aether in a space-time with a compact extra dimension.
This paper explores the differences between state/event based logics and purely action or state based logics.
It examines the advantages and disadvantages of each approach and discusses their applications in various domains such as artificial intelligence, robotics, and software engineering.
The paper also presents a comparative analysis of the two logics based on their expressiveness, computational complexity, and ease of implementation.

The findings suggest that state/event based logics are more suitable for modeling dynamic systems with complex behaviors, while purely action or state based logics are better suited for simpler systems with well-defined actions and states.
The paper concludes with recommendations for future research in this area.
This paper investigates the transmission of electromagnetic waves through a subwavelength nano-hole in a two-dimensional plasmonic layer.
The plasmonic layer consists of a periodic array of metallic nanostructures, which exhibit strong plasmonic resonances.
The authors use numerical simulations to study the transmission properties of the nano-hole, including the transmission efficiency and the transmission spectrum.
They find that the transmission efficiency is strongly dependent on the size and shape of the nano-hole, as well as the incident angle and polarization of the electromagnetic wave.
The transmission spectrum shows multiple resonances, which can be tuned by adjusting the parameters of the plasmonic layer.
The results of this study provide valuable insights into the design and optimization of plasmonic devices for applications such as sensing, imaging, and energy harvesting.
This paper introduces a novel method for generating Hanf numbers using accessible images.
Hanf numbers are a mathematical concept that represents the number of accessible points in a graph.
The proposed method utilizes image processing techniques to convert images into graphs, and then applies graph theory algorithms to calculate the corresponding Hanf numbers.
The results show that the proposed method is effective in generating Hanf numbers and can be applied to a wide range of images.
This research contributes to the field of graph theory and provides a new approach for calculating Hanf numbers.
This paper introduces the concept of witness structures and immediate snapshot complexes as a way to study the combinatorial structure of simplicial complexes.
Witness structures are a generalization of simplicial complexes that allow for the representation of higher-dimensional combinatorial structures.
Immediate snapshot complexes are a specific type of witness structure that capture the combinatorial structure of a system at a specific point in time.
The paper presents algorithms for constructing witness structures and immediate snapshot complexes, as well as techniques for analyzing their properties.
The authors demonstrate the utility of these concepts by applying them to various real-world examples, including social networks and biological systems.
Overall, this paper provides a novel framework for studying the combinatorial structure of complex systems and offers new insights into their behavior.
The single-impurity Anderson model is a widely studied model in condensed matter physics that describes the interaction between a localized impurity and a conduction electron bath.
In this paper, we propose an alternative equation of motion approach to study the dynamics of the single-impurity Anderson model.
Our approach is based on a generalized equation of motion for the impurity Green's function, which allows us to capture the non-equilibrium dynamics of the system.
We apply our approach to calculate the impurity spectral function and the impurity occupation number as a function of time.
Our results show good agreement with previous numerical and analytical studies, demonstrating the effectiveness of our alternative equation of motion approach.
This approach provides a valuable tool for studying the dynamics of the single-impurity Anderson model and can be extended to other impurity models in condensed matter physics.
The vertex cover $P_3$ problem is a well-known NP-hard problem in graph theory.
In this paper, we propose an improved algorithm for solving this problem on graphs of bounded treewidth.
Our algorithm utilizes a dynamic programming approach and takes advantage of the tree decomposition of the graph.
We show that our algorithm has a time complexity of O(n^3), where n is the number of vertices in the graph.
We also provide experimental results that demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of our algorithm compared to existing algorithms.
Overall, our algorithm offers a significant improvement in solving the vertex cover $P_3$ problem on graphs of bounded treewidth.
This paper investigates the synchronization of Bloch oscillations in a system consisting of a ring cavity and a semiconductor quantum well.
The authors demonstrate that by controlling the parameters of the ring cavity, it is possible to synchronize the Bloch oscillations of the quantum well with the cavity field.
This synchronization is achieved by adjusting the detuning between the cavity resonance and the energy of the quantum well exciton.
The authors provide experimental evidence of this synchronization and discuss its potential applications in the field of optoelectronics.
Overall, this study contributes to the understanding of the dynamics of Bloch oscillations and provides a new approach for controlling and manipulating these oscillations in semiconductor systems.
This paper investigates the relationship between locally standard torus actions and h'-vectors of simplicial posets.
The authors define locally standard torus actions and provide examples to illustrate their properties.
They then prove a theorem that relates the h'-vector of a simplicial poset to the number of fixed points of a locally standard torus action on its order complex.
The authors also discuss the implications of this theorem for the study of combinatorial commutative algebra and algebraic topology.
Overall, this paper contributes to our understanding of the connections between torus actions and the combinatorial structure of simplicial posets.
The Hierarchical Cont-Bouchaud model is a mathematical framework that aims to capture the hierarchical structure of financial markets.
This model builds upon the Cont-Bouchaud model, which is a widely used model for describing the dynamics of financial prices.
The Hierarchical Cont-Bouchaud model introduces a hierarchical structure to the Cont-Bouchaud model by considering multiple levels of agents with different time horizons.
Each level of agents is responsible for making decisions at different time scales, which allows for a more realistic representation of the dynamics of financial markets.
The model is able to reproduce several stylized facts of financial markets, such as fat-tailed price distributions and volatility clustering.
Furthermore, the Hierarchical Cont-Bouchaud model provides insights into the role of different levels of agents in the formation of market dynamics.
Overall, this paper presents a novel approach to modeling financial markets that takes into account the hierarchical structure of market participants.
This paper explores various applications of the Global Fukaya category II, including singular connections and quantum obstruction theory.
The Global Fukaya category II is a mathematical framework that allows for the study of symplectic geometry and mirror symmetry.
The paper discusses the construction of singular connections within this framework and their implications for quantum obstruction theory.
Additionally, the paper explores other potential applications of the Global Fukaya category II in the field of symplectic geometry.
Overall, this paper contributes to the understanding and development of the Global Fukaya category II and its applications in various areas of mathematics.
The Super-Kamiokande experiment is a large water Cherenkov detector located in Japan that has been used to study solar neutrinos for over two decades.
In this paper, we present the results from the fourth phase of the Super-Kamiokande experiment (Super-Kamiokande-IV), which ran from 2008 to 2014.
We discuss the improvements made to the detector during this phase, including the addition of new photomultiplier tubes and a water purification system.
We also describe the data analysis techniques used to measure the flux and energy spectrum of solar neutrinos.
Our results are consistent with previous measurements and provide further evidence for the existence of neutrino oscillations.
We also discuss the implications of our measurements for solar physics and neutrino physics.
Overall, the Super-Kamiokande-IV experiment has provided valuable insights into the properties of solar neutrinos and has contributed to our understanding of fundamental physics.
In this paper, we report on the direct observation of a gate tunable band-gap in electrical transport in ABC-trilayer graphene.
We demonstrate that by applying a gate voltage, the band-gap in the trilayer graphene can be tuned, leading to significant changes in the electrical transport properties.
We use a combination of scanning tunneling microscopy and spectroscopy to directly measure the band-gap and observe its tunability.
Our results provide important insights into the electronic properties of trilayer graphene and open up new possibilities for its use in electronic devices.
This paper presents a high-order, stable, and efficient pseudospectral method using barycentric Gegenbauer quadratures.
The method is based on the spectral collocation approach and utilizes the barycentric interpolation formula to compute the derivative matrix.
The stability and accuracy of the method are analyzed, and it is shown that the method achieves exponential convergence for smooth functions.
The efficiency of the method is demonstrated through numerical experiments, where it is compared to other pseudospectral methods.
The results show that the proposed method outperforms existing methods in terms of accuracy and computational efficiency.
Overall, this paper provides a novel and effective approach for solving differential equations using pseudospectral methods.
This paper investigates the well-posedness and robust preconditioners for the discretized fluid-structure interaction (FSI) systems.
The FSI systems are commonly used to model the interaction between fluid and solid structures in various engineering applications.
The authors propose a numerical discretization scheme for the FSI systems and analyze its well-posedness properties.
They also develop robust preconditioners to improve the efficiency and accuracy of the numerical solution.
The effectiveness of the proposed methods is demonstrated through numerical experiments.
The results show that the well-posedness and robust preconditioners significantly enhance the stability and convergence of the FSI simulations.
This research contributes to the understanding and improvement of numerical methods for FSI problems, which have important implications for engineering design and analysis.
This paper presents a novel approach for efficient quantum processing of ideals in finite rings.
We propose a quantum algorithm that leverages the properties of finite rings to perform operations on ideals with significantly reduced computational complexity compared to classical methods.
Our algorithm utilizes quantum Fourier transforms and modular exponentiation techniques to efficiently compute the generators and elements of ideals.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through extensive simulations on various finite rings, showing significant speedup compared to classical algorithms.
Our findings have implications for a wide range of applications in cryptography, coding theory, and number theory, where efficient processing of ideals is crucial.
This paper investigates the impact of droplets near a millimeter-sized hole, comparing the behavior of a closed pit with an open-ended pore.
The study utilizes high-speed imaging techniques to capture the droplet impact dynamics and analyzes the resulting splash and spreading behavior.
The results show that the presence of an open-ended pore significantly affects the droplet impact, leading to different splash and spreading characteristics compared to a closed pit.
The findings provide valuable insights into the understanding of droplet impact near small holes and have potential applications in various fields such as microfluidics and surface engineering.
This paper investigates the length and area spectrum of analytic convex domains.
The length spectrum refers to the set of lengths of closed geodesics on the boundary of a domain, while the area spectrum refers to the set of areas of all compact subsets of the domain.
The authors prove that for a large class of analytic convex domains, the length spectrum is discrete and has no accumulation points.
They also establish a relationship between the length and area spectrum, showing that the area spectrum is determined by the length spectrum.
These results have implications for the study of geometric properties of convex domains and provide a deeper understanding of the relationship between length and area in analytic convex domains.
This paper presents reduced relative entropy techniques for the a posteriori analysis of multiphase problems in elastodynamics.
The authors propose a method to compute the relative entropy between the true solution and an approximation, which allows for the quantification of the error in the approximation.
The method is applied to a multiphase problem in elastodynamics, and the results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed technique in accurately estimating the error.
The authors also discuss the computational aspects of the method and provide numerical examples to illustrate its performance.
Overall, the paper provides a valuable contribution to the field of elastodynamics and offers a new approach for a posteriori analysis of multiphase problems.
This paper presents the application of Model Predictive Control (MPC) to a coupled tank liquid level system.
The system consists of two tanks connected by a pipe, and the objective is to control the liquid levels in both tanks.
The MPC algorithm is used to predict the future behavior of the system and optimize the control inputs to achieve the desired setpoints.
The paper describes the mathematical model of the system, the formulation of the MPC problem, and the implementation of the controller.
Experimental results are presented to demonstrate the effectiveness of the MPC approach in controlling the liquid levels in the coupled tank system.
The results show that the MPC controller is able to track the setpoints accurately and maintain the desired liquid levels in both tanks, even in the presence of disturbances.
Overall, the paper highlights the potential of MPC for controlling complex and nonlinear systems like the coupled tank liquid level system.
This paper investigates the asymptotic behavior of minimal overlapping patterns for generalized Euler permutations, standard tableaux of rectangular shape, and column strict arrays.
The authors provide explicit formulas for the generating functions of these patterns and use them to derive the asymptotic behavior.
They also establish connections between these patterns and other combinatorial objects, such as Dyck paths and Motzkin paths.
The results obtained in this paper contribute to the understanding of the combinatorial properties of these objects and provide insights into their asymptotic behavior.
This paper investigates the single-photon-counting (SPC) modes of imaging using an X-ray free-electron laser (XFEL) source.
The XFEL source provides ultrafast and intense X-ray pulses, which enable the detection of individual photons.
The authors discuss the advantages and challenges of SPC imaging, including its potential for high-resolution imaging and its sensitivity to radiation damage.
They also present experimental results demonstrating the feasibility of SPC imaging using an XFEL source.

The findings of this study contribute to the understanding and development of SPC imaging techniques for XFEL sources, with potential applications in various fields such as biology, materials science, and chemistry.
This paper explores the use of dependent types in the context of sequential decision problems.
It presents a generic solution that leverages dependent types to model and solve a wide range of sequential decision problems.
The paper demonstrates the effectiveness of this approach through several case studies, showing how the generic solution can be applied to different problem domains.

The results indicate that dependent types offer a powerful tool for modeling and solving sequential decision problems, and that the generic solution presented in this paper is a promising approach for addressing such problems in a flexible and efficient manner.
Euclid's theorem on the infinitude of primes is a fundamental result in number theory that states there are infinitely many prime numbers.
This paper provides a comprehensive historical survey of the various proofs of this theorem from its original formulation by Euclid in 300 B.C. to the present day.
The survey covers both classical and modern approaches, highlighting the key ideas and techniques used in each proof.
Additionally, the paper presents a new proof of Euclid's theorem, offering a fresh perspective on this well-known result.
The new proof utilizes a novel approach that combines elements from different proof techniques, resulting in a concise and elegant argument.

Overall, this paper offers a comprehensive overview of the proofs of Euclid's theorem on the infinitude of primes, shedding light on the development of this important result throughout history and presenting a new proof that contributes to the ongoing exploration of prime numbers.
In this paper, we investigate the relationship between supersymmetry and the eigensurface topology of the planar quantum pendulum.
We first introduce the concept of supersymmetry and its application in quantum mechanics.
We then analyze the eigensurface topology of the planar quantum pendulum and show that it exhibits a rich structure with multiple connected components.
We further demonstrate that the eigensurface topology can be understood in terms of supersymmetry, where the different connected components correspond to different supermultiplets.
Finally, we discuss the implications of our findings and potential future directions for research in this area.
This paper introduces a new class of dynamic spatial autoregressive (SAR) models that incorporate both autoregressive and heteroskedastic disturbances.
The proposed models allow for the joint modeling of spatial dependence and heteroskedasticity, which are common features in many spatial datasets.
The paper presents the theoretical framework for these models and develops estimation and inference procedures.
The performance of the proposed models is evaluated through a simulation study and an empirical application to real-world data.
The results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed models in capturing both spatial dependence and heteroskedasticity, and highlight their potential for improving the analysis of spatial data.
This paper presents a study on ultrafast photodetection in the quantum wells of single AlGaAs/GaAs-based nanowires.

The authors investigate the optical properties of these nanowires using time-resolved photoluminescence spectroscopy and find that they exhibit ultrafast carrier dynamics with a response time of less than 1 picosecond.
They also demonstrate that the photodetection efficiency of these nanowires can be enhanced by engineering the quantum well structure.
The results of this study provide valuable insights into the potential applications of AlGaAs/GaAs-based nanowires in ultrafast photodetection devices.
This paper investigates the fractal dimension of SAT formulas, which are logical formulas used in the field of computer science to represent Boolean satisfiability problems.
The fractal dimension is a measure of the complexity or irregularity of a geometric object, and in this study, it is used to analyze the structure of SAT formulas.
The authors propose a method to calculate the fractal dimension of SAT formulas based on their graphical representation.
They apply this method to a large set of SAT formulas and analyze the relationship between the fractal dimension and other properties of the formulas, such as their size and satisfiability.

The results show that the fractal dimension can provide valuable insights into the structure and complexity of SAT formulas, and may have implications for the development of more efficient algorithms for solving Boolean satisfiability problems.
This paper presents a comprehensive survey of password cracking techniques and countermeasures in computer security.
Passwords are widely used as a means of authentication in various systems, making them a prime target for attackers.
The survey covers different types of password cracking attacks, including offline and online attacks, as well as the tools and methods used by attackers.
It also discusses various countermeasures that can be employed to enhance password security, such as password policies, two-factor authentication, and password hashing algorithms.
The paper concludes with a discussion on the limitations and future directions of password cracking and countermeasures.

This survey provides a valuable resource for researchers and practitioners in the field of computer security to understand the current state of password cracking techniques and the measures that can be taken to mitigate the risks associated with weak passwords.
This paper explores the interrelations and algorithmic consequences of domination parameters with the number 2.
Domination parameters are used to measure the extent to which a set of vertices in a graph dominates the remaining vertices.

The authors investigate the relationships between different domination parameters with the number 2, such as the total domination number, the paired domination number, and the double domination number.
They also discuss the algorithmic consequences of these interrelations, including the complexity of computing these parameters and the existence of efficient algorithms for finding optimal solutions.
The findings of this study provide insights into the theoretical foundations and practical applications of domination parameters with the number 2 in graph theory and algorithm design.
This paper investigates the phenomenon of overlapping resonances in open quantum systems.
Resonances occur when the energy of a system matches the energy of an external driving force, leading to enhanced response.
In open quantum systems, resonances can overlap due to the presence of multiple driving forces or the coupling of different modes.
The authors develop a theoretical framework to describe the dynamics of overlapping resonances and analyze their effects on the system's behavior.
They demonstrate that overlapping resonances can lead to complex and non-intuitive phenomena, such as the emergence of new resonant states and the modification of resonance widths.
The findings have implications for various fields, including quantum information processing and quantum sensing, where understanding and controlling resonances is crucial.
The paper concludes with suggestions for future research directions in this area.
This paper investigates the compositions of invertibility preserving maps for certain monoids and their application to Clifford algebras.
The authors explore the properties of these maps and provide examples of their application in the context of Clifford algebras.
The results of this study contribute to a deeper understanding of the structure and properties of these monoids and their relationship to Clifford algebras.
This paper explores the challenges and potential solutions in clustering natural data, specifically focusing on the issue of relational ambiguity.
The authors propose a novel approach that combines text data and natural data to improve clustering accuracy.
The study demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed method through experiments on various datasets.
The findings suggest that incorporating relational information can significantly enhance clustering performance, particularly in cases where the data contains ambiguous relationships.
The paper concludes by discussing the implications of these findings and suggesting future research directions in the field of clustering natural data.

This paper presents a new numerical method called StaRMAP (Second order staggered grid method for spherical harmonics moment equations of radiative transfer) for solving the radiative transfer equations in spherical geometry.
The method is based on a second order accurate staggered grid discretization of the equations, which allows for efficient and accurate computation of the radiative fluxes and source terms.
The method is validated against analytical solutions and compared to other existing methods, demonstrating its accuracy and efficiency.
The paper also discusses the implementation details and computational considerations of the method.
Overall, StaRMAP provides a robust and efficient numerical tool for solving radiative transfer problems in spherical geometry.

The inverse kinematics problem is a fundamental problem in robotics and computer graphics, which involves determining the joint angles of a robot or the pose of a virtual character given a desired end-effector position or pose.
In this paper, we present a comprehensive analysis of the equations of the inverse kinematics problem for various types of robots and characters.
We derive the general form of the equations and discuss their properties and solutions.
We also propose a novel approach for solving the inverse kinematics problem based on optimization techniques.
Our approach is able to handle complex kinematic chains and non-linear constraints, and it provides accurate and efficient solutions.
We validate our approach through extensive experiments on different robotic systems and virtual characters.
The results demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of our method in solving the inverse kinematics problem.

Overall, this paper contributes to the understanding and advancement of the inverse kinematics problem, and it provides a valuable resource for researchers and practitioners in the field of robotics and computer graphics.
In this paper, we investigate the chiral phase transition in a planar four-Fermi model in the presence of a tilted magnetic field.
We use a mean-field approximation to study the behavior of the chiral condensate and the quark number density as a function of temperature and magnetic field strength.

We find that the chiral phase transition is significantly affected by the presence of the tilted magnetic field, leading to a modification of the critical temperature and the order of the phase transition.
Our results provide insights into the role of magnetic fields in the chiral symmetry breaking and may have implications for the study of QCD phase diagram in the presence of strong magnetic fields.
This paper introduces the concept of stable generalized complex structures, which are a generalization of stable complex structures in the context of generalized complex geometry.
The authors define stable generalized complex structures and study their properties, including stability conditions and deformations.
They also provide examples of stable generalized complex structures and discuss their relationship with stable complex structures.
The paper concludes with some open questions and directions for future research in this area.
This paper presents WavePacket, a Matlab package designed for numerical quantum dynamics simulations.
The package is specifically tailored for closed quantum systems and discrete variable representations.

The paper provides an overview of the package's capabilities and features, including the ability to solve the time-dependent Schrödinger equation, simulate quantum dynamics in various potential energy surfaces, and analyze the results using a range of visualization tools.
The paper also discusses the underlying mathematical and computational techniques employed by WavePacket, such as the discrete variable representation method.
Overall, WavePacket offers a user-friendly and versatile platform for studying quantum dynamics in closed systems, making it a valuable tool for researchers in the field.
This paper presents a novel approach to optimizing supercontinuum generation in dual-soliton based light sources using genetic algorithms.
The authors propose a grid platform for parallel computing, which allows for efficient exploration of the parameter space.
The genetic algorithm is used to search for the optimal combination of input pulse parameters, such as pulse duration and peak power, to achieve the desired supercontinuum spectrum.
The results show that the proposed approach outperforms traditional optimization methods in terms of both speed and accuracy.
This research has important implications for the development of high-performance light sources for various applications in optics and photonics.
This paper investigates the concept of angular equivalence in normed spaces.
Angular equivalence is a relation between two normed spaces that captures the similarity of their unit spheres.
The authors provide a formal definition of angular equivalence and explore its properties.
They also study the relationship between angular equivalence and other notions of equivalence in normed spaces, such as isomorphism and isometric isomorphism.
The paper concludes with several examples and applications of angular equivalence in various areas of mathematics.
Overall, this work contributes to a deeper understanding of the structure and properties of normed spaces.
This paper explores the relationship between weighted projective lines and rational surface singularities.
Weighted projective lines are a generalization of projective lines, where the points are weighted by positive integers.
Rational surface singularities are singular points on a surface that can be resolved by a sequence of blow-ups.

The authors investigate the classification of weighted projective lines and rational surface singularities, and establish a correspondence between certain classes of weighted projective lines and rational surface singularities.
They also study the properties of these objects, such as their automorphism groups and their resolutions.
The results of this study provide a deeper understanding of the geometry and topology of weighted projective lines and rational surface singularities.
This paper explores the concept of bounded negativity in the context of transversal arrangements of curves.
The authors introduce the notion of Harbourne constants, which measure the maximum number of negative intersections between curves in an arrangement.
They provide a detailed analysis of the relationship between bounded negativity and Harbourne constants, and present several results and conjectures in this area.
The paper also includes computational experiments and examples to illustrate the concepts and findings.
Overall, this research contributes to a deeper understanding of the structure and properties of transversal arrangements of curves.
This paper proposes a multi-hop diffusion least mean squares (LMS) algorithm for energy-constrained distributed estimation in wireless sensor networks.
The algorithm aims to minimize the energy consumption while maintaining accurate estimation performance.
The proposed algorithm utilizes a multi-hop diffusion strategy to distribute the estimation task among the sensor nodes, reducing the energy consumption of each individual node.
The algorithm also incorporates an adaptive step-size mechanism to improve convergence speed and accuracy.
Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed algorithm achieves significant energy savings compared to existing algorithms, while maintaining comparable estimation performance.
The algorithm is particularly suitable for energy-constrained sensor networks where prolonging network lifetime is a critical requirement.
This paper presents a study on thin-disk laser pump schemes that can accommodate a large number of passes and moderate pump source quality.
The authors propose a novel pump scheme that utilizes a combination of multiple pump sources and a reflective pump cavity to achieve efficient pumping of the thin-disk laser.
The performance of the proposed pump scheme is evaluated through numerical simulations and compared with other existing pump schemes.

The results show that the proposed pump scheme can achieve higher pump efficiency and better beam quality, making it suitable for applications that require a large number of passes and moderate pump source quality.
The paper presents a combinatorial definition of the Theta-invariant, a topological invariant associated with Heegaard diagrams.
The authors introduce a new combinatorial model for Heegaard diagrams and use it to define the Theta-invariant in terms of certain combinatorial structures.
They prove that this definition is equivalent to the classical definition of the Theta-invariant and provide examples to illustrate its usefulness.
The paper concludes with a discussion of potential applications and future directions for research.
This paper presents a global-local nonlinear model reduction approach for simulating flows in heterogeneous porous media.
The proposed method combines global model reduction techniques with local nonlinear models to accurately capture the complex behavior of the flow.

The global model reduction is achieved through the use of proper orthogonal decomposition (POD) and reduced basis methods, while the local nonlinear models are constructed using a combination of local POD and radial basis function interpolation.
The effectiveness of the proposed approach is demonstrated through numerical experiments on a variety of heterogeneous porous media.

The results show that the global-local nonlinear model reduction approach is able to accurately capture the flow behavior while significantly reducing the computational cost compared to traditional full-order models.
This paper presents a time-resolved measurement technique for studying the formation of periodic surface structures induced by single pulse femtosecond laser irradiation.
The authors use a pump-probe setup to measure the temporal evolution of the surface structure formation process with sub-picosecond resolution.

The results show that the formation of periodic surface structures occurs within a few hundred femtoseconds after laser irradiation, and the formation process is highly dependent on the laser fluence.
The findings provide valuable insights into the dynamics of laser-induced surface structuring and can contribute to the development of advanced laser processing techniques.
This paper presents a Bayesian variable selection method for high-dimensional settings with grouped covariates.
The proposed method utilizes a hierarchical prior structure to model the grouping structure of the covariates and incorporates a spike-and-slab prior to perform variable selection.
The method is able to handle high-dimensional data and effectively select relevant variables while accounting for the correlation structure among the covariates.

The performance of the method is evaluated through simulation studies and real data analysis, demonstrating its superiority over existing methods in terms of variable selection accuracy and prediction performance.
Overall, the proposed method provides a flexible and efficient approach for variable selection in high-dimensional settings with grouped covariates.
This paper presents a formalism for the spatially homogeneous Boltzmann equation using information geometry.
The Boltzmann equation describes the evolution of a gas of particles and is commonly used in statistical mechanics and fluid dynamics.
The information geometry formalism provides a geometric framework for studying the properties of probability distributions.
The authors derive the information geometry of the Boltzmann equation and show how it can be used to analyze the dynamics of the system.
They also discuss the connection between the information geometry formalism and other approaches to studying the Boltzmann equation.
The results of this study provide new insights into the behavior of the spatially homogeneous Boltzmann equation and may have implications for understanding complex systems in physics and biology.
In recent years, there has been a growing trend in the field of deep learning to develop increasingly complex and deep neural network architectures.
However, this paper argues that simpler architectures can often outperform their deeper and more complex counterparts.
The authors present a series of experiments comparing the performance of simple and complex architectures on various tasks, including image classification and natural language processing.
The results consistently show that the simpler architectures achieve comparable or even better performance than the more complex ones.
The authors also discuss the potential reasons behind this phenomenon, such as the increased risk of overfitting in deeper architectures.

Overall, this paper highlights the importance of considering simplicity in neural network design and challenges the prevailing notion that deeper and more complex architectures always lead to better performance.
This paper provides an introduction to stochastic partial differential equations (SPDEs).
SPDEs are a class of equations that involve both random and deterministic components, making them a powerful tool for modeling complex systems with inherent uncertainty.
The paper begins by introducing the basic concepts of probability theory and stochastic processes, which form the foundation for understanding SPDEs.
It then discusses the different types of SPDEs, including linear and nonlinear equations, and provides examples of their applications in various fields such as finance, physics, and biology.
The paper also covers numerical methods for solving SPDEs, including finite difference and Monte Carlo methods.
Overall, this paper serves as a comprehensive introduction to the theory and applications of SPDEs, making it a valuable resource for researchers and practitioners in the field.
This paper investigates the possibility of covert communication over classical-quantum channels.
Covert communication refers to the transmission of information without being detected by an eavesdropper.
The authors propose a protocol that utilizes the principles of quantum mechanics to achieve covert communication.
They analyze the security of the protocol against various eavesdropping strategies and provide theoretical bounds on the achievable covert communication rates.
The results show that covert communication is indeed possible over classical-quantum channels, although the achievable rates are limited by the inherent noise and imperfections in the channel.
The findings of this study have implications for the design of secure communication systems and can contribute to the development of covert communication techniques in practical scenarios.
This paper presents a method for tracking the Brownian motion of colloidal particles in three dimensions using digital holographic microscopy and joint reconstruction.
The authors propose a joint reconstruction algorithm that combines multiple holograms of the same particle to improve the accuracy of the tracking.
The algorithm takes into account the diffraction effects and noise in the holograms to estimate the position and orientation of the particles.
The authors validate the method using both simulated and experimental data, and demonstrate its ability to accurately track the motion of colloidal particles in three dimensions.
The proposed method has potential applications in various fields, including biophysics and materials science.
In this paper, we investigate the relationship between compactness and sequential compactness in topological spaces.
We introduce the notion of compactness with respect to a set of filters and study its properties.
We then explore the relationship between compactness with respect to a set of filters and sequential compactness in products of topological spaces.

We provide several characterizations of compactness with respect to a set of filters and establish conditions under which products of sequentially compact spaces are compact with respect to a set of filters.
Our results contribute to the understanding of the interplay between compactness and sequential compactness in topological spaces.
This paper presents a comprehensive review of multi-fidelity models, which are mathematical models that combine data from multiple sources with varying levels of accuracy and cost.

The review covers various aspects of multi-fidelity modeling, including the different types of multi-fidelity models, their applications in different fields, and the challenges and limitations associated with their use.
The paper also discusses the advantages and disadvantages of multi-fidelity models compared to single-fidelity models, and provides recommendations for future research in this area.
Overall, this review aims to provide a comprehensive understanding of multi-fidelity models and their potential for improving the accuracy and efficiency of mathematical modeling in various domains.

In this paper, we investigate the length of an s-increasing sequence of r-tuples, where an s-increasing sequence is defined as a sequence in which each element is greater than or equal to the previous element, and an r-tuple is a sequence of r elements.
We provide a formula for calculating the length of such a sequence and prove its correctness.
Additionally, we explore the relationship between the length of an s-increasing sequence and the values of s and r.
Our findings have implications in various fields, including combinatorics and optimization.
This paper explores the complexity of dynamic mechanism design, which involves designing mechanisms that can adapt and update their rules over time.
The authors analyze the computational complexity of dynamic mechanism design problems and provide insights into the inherent challenges and limitations of designing such mechanisms.
They present a framework for characterizing the complexity of dynamic mechanism design problems and discuss various computational techniques that can be used to solve them.
The paper also highlights the importance of considering computational complexity in the design of dynamic mechanisms and suggests future research directions in this area.
This paper explores the regional development of digital humanities research in Taiwan through a case study.
The study examines the current state of digital humanities research in Taiwan, including the research topics, methodologies, and collaborations.

The paper also investigates the challenges and opportunities faced by digital humanities researchers in Taiwan, such as limited funding and resources, as well as the potential for international collaborations.
The findings of this study provide insights into the regional development of digital humanities research in Taiwan and offer recommendations for future research and collaboration in the field.
In this paper, we study the existence and properties of traveling wave solutions for a bistable equation with nonlocal diffusion.
The equation describes the spread of a population in a heterogeneous environment, where the diffusion is nonlocal and depends on the integral of the population density over a certain range.
We prove the existence of traveling wave solutions by constructing suitable sub and super solutions and using the theory of monotone semiflows.
We also investigate the properties of these traveling waves, such as their speed and shape, and show that they exhibit a transition from a slow to a fast wave as the diffusion range increases.
Our results provide insights into the dynamics of population spread in heterogeneous environments and have potential applications in various fields, such as ecology and epidemiology.
This paper explores the relationship between game characterizations and lower cones in the Weihrauch degrees.
The Weihrauch degrees are a hierarchy of complexity classes for computable analysis, and game characterizations are a way to describe these classes using games.
The authors provide a detailed analysis of the lower cones in the Weihrauch degrees and show how they can be characterized using certain types of games.
They also investigate the connections between different types of lower cones and provide examples to illustrate their findings.
Overall, this paper contributes to our understanding of the Weihrauch degrees and provides insights into the structure of lower cones in this hierarchy.
This paper presents a comprehensive review of the field of temporal condensed matter physics in gas-filled photonic crystal fibers.
The study focuses on the unique properties and applications of these fibers, which allow for the manipulation and control of light at the nanoscale.
The authors discuss the various techniques and experimental setups used to study the temporal dynamics of light in these fibers, including ultrafast spectroscopy and time-resolved imaging.
They also explore the potential applications of gas-filled photonic crystal fibers in areas such as telecommunications, sensing, and quantum information processing.
Overall, this paper provides a valuable resource for researchers interested in the emerging field of temporal condensed matter physics in gas-filled photonic crystal fibers.
The paper presents a generalization of the Salem-Zygmund inequality for locally sub-Gaussian random variables, random trigonometric polynomials, and random circulant matrices.
The Salem-Zygmund inequality is a well-known result in probability theory that provides bounds on the tails of random variables.
The authors extend this inequality to the aforementioned classes of random variables and matrices, and provide explicit bounds for their tails.
The results are derived using techniques from Fourier analysis and concentration inequalities.
The paper also includes numerical experiments to illustrate the applicability of the derived bounds.
Overall, the paper contributes to the understanding of the tail behavior of these classes of random variables and matrices, and provides useful tools for their analysis.
This paper presents a Kripke semantics for Martin-Löf's extensional type theory (ETT).
The semantics is based on a notion of possible worlds and a relation of truth between worlds and formulas.
The paper defines the syntax and semantics of ETT and shows how the Kripke semantics can be used to interpret the type theory.
The paper also discusses the relationship between the Kripke semantics and other semantic approaches to ETT, such as the intensional type theory and the categorical semantics.
The paper concludes with some remarks on the philosophical implications of the Kripke semantics for ETT.
This paper investigates the modal and excitation asymmetries in magneto-dielectric particle chains.
The authors analyze the behavior of these chains under different excitation conditions and study the effects of particle size and spacing on the modal properties.
The results show that the modal and excitation asymmetries are influenced by the magnetic and dielectric properties of the particles, as well as the chain configuration.
The findings of this study provide valuable insights into the design and optimization of magneto-dielectric particle chains for various applications in photonics and metamaterials.
In this paper, we present a Monte Carlo study of a spin-3/2 Blume-Emery-Griffiths (BEG) model on a honeycomb lattice.
The BEG model is a lattice spin model that incorporates both Ising and Potts-like interactions.
The honeycomb lattice is a two-dimensional lattice with a hexagonal structure.
We investigate the phase diagram and critical behavior of the spin-3/2 BEG model on the honeycomb lattice using Monte Carlo simulations.

Our results show the presence of a first-order phase transition between a paramagnetic phase and a ferromagnetic phase, as well as a continuous phase transition between the ferromagnetic phase and an antiferromagnetic phase.
We also analyze the critical exponents associated with the continuous phase transition and compare them with theoretical predictions.
Overall, our study provides insights into the behavior of the spin-3/2 BEG model on a honeycomb lattice and contributes to the understanding of complex spin systems on non-trivial lattice structures.
In this paper, we propose a new iterative protocol called $\mathcal {C}-$IBI for deriving coarse-grained models of complex fluids.
The protocol targets cumulative coordination, which is a measure of the local ordering of particles in the system.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of $\mathcal {C}-$IBI by applying it to multi-component complex fluids and comparing the results to existing methods.
Our findings show that $\mathcal {C}-$IBI is able to accurately capture the structural and thermodynamic properties of the system, making it a promising approach for coarse-graining complex fluids.
This paper investigates the control of light absorption and emission in quantum dots through the use of a surface-plasmon field.
The authors demonstrate that by manipulating the properties of the surface-plasmon field, they can modulate the absorption and emission spectra of the quantum dots.
This control over the quantum-dot light-matter interaction has potential applications in areas such as quantum information processing and optoelectronics.
The findings of this study contribute to the understanding of surface-plasmon interactions with quantum dots and provide a basis for further research in this field.
We investigate the formation and dynamics of self-maintaining defect/droplets in a system of two interacting Bose-Einstein condensates.
By numerically solving the Gross-Pitaevskii equation, we find that the interaction between the condensates leads to the formation of stable defect/droplets that persist over long timescales.
These defect/droplets are characterized by a localized density depletion surrounded by a ring of enhanced density.

We analyze the properties of these defect/droplets, including their size, shape, and stability, and discuss their potential applications in the field of quantum optics and quantum information processing.
Our results provide insights into the behavior of interacting Bose-Einstein condensates and contribute to the understanding of self-maintaining defect/droplets in quantum systems.
This paper investigates the deformations of symmetric simple modular Lie (super)algebras.
The authors provide a classification of these deformations and study their properties.
They also explore the relationship between these deformations and the cohomology of the underlying Lie (super)algebra.
The results of this study contribute to the understanding of the structure and deformations of symmetric simple modular Lie (super)algebras.
This paper presents a novel approach to energy harvesting using a geometric thermoelectric pump.
Traditional energy harvesting methods rely on the Seebeck and pyroelectric effects, which have limitations in terms of efficiency and power output.
The proposed geometric thermoelectric pump overcomes these limitations by utilizing the geometric properties of the material to generate a temperature gradient and induce an electric current.
The authors demonstrate the feasibility of this approach through theoretical analysis and experimental results.
The geometric thermoelectric pump offers a promising alternative for energy harvesting applications, with potential for higher efficiency and power output compared to traditional methods.
This paper presents a model for understanding social dynamics in a collaborative environment.
The model takes into account the opinions and conflicts among individuals and aims to identify consensus among them.
The authors propose a mathematical framework that incorporates various factors such as individual preferences, influence of others, and the evolution of opinions over time.
The model is validated through simulations and case studies, demonstrating its effectiveness in capturing the complex dynamics of social interactions.
The findings of this study contribute to the understanding of collaborative environments and can be applied to various domains such as online communities, team decision-making, and social networks.
This paper presents a note on $s_0$ nonmeasurable unions, which are a type of nonmeasurable set in measure theory.
The concept of $s_0$ nonmeasurable unions is introduced and their properties are explored.
It is shown that $s_0$ nonmeasurable unions have certain characteristics that distinguish them from other types of nonmeasurable sets.
The paper also discusses the implications of $s_0$ nonmeasurable unions in the context of measure theory and provides examples to illustrate their behavior.
Overall, this note contributes to the understanding of nonmeasurable sets and their properties in measure theory.
This paper investigates the sample complexity of auctions with side information.
The authors analyze the number of samples required to achieve a certain level of accuracy in estimating the optimal auction outcome.
They consider a setting where bidders have access to side information that can potentially improve their bidding strategies.
The authors provide theoretical bounds on the sample complexity for different types of side information, including private values and correlated values.
They also propose algorithms that exploit the side information to reduce the sample complexity.
The results of this study have implications for the design and implementation of auctions in various domains, such as online advertising and spectrum auctions.
This paper presents experimental constructions of binary matrices with good peak-sidelobe distances.
The peak-sidelobe distance is a measure of the quality of a binary matrix, with a larger distance indicating better performance.
The authors propose two different constructions based on different mathematical techniques.
The first construction is based on the theory of finite fields, while the second construction is based on the theory of combinatorial designs.
The experimental results show that both constructions yield binary matrices with significantly better peak-sidelobe distances compared to existing constructions.

These results have important implications for applications such as radar and sonar signal processing, where binary matrices with good peak-sidelobe distances are crucial for accurate detection and classification.
This paper investigates the use of inorganic high-k nanostructured materials to reduce the Coulomb interaction in organic solar cells.
The authors demonstrate that the introduction of these materials leads to a significant reduction in the Coulomb interaction, resulting in improved device performance.
The study provides a detailed analysis of the electronic properties of the nanostructured materials and their impact on the device performance.
The findings suggest that the use of inorganic high-k nanostructured materials can be a promising approach to enhance the efficiency of organic solar cells.

This paper investigates the stability and monotonicity properties of certain discretizations of the Biot's model, which is a mathematical model used to describe the behavior of fluid-saturated porous media.
The authors analyze two different discretization schemes and prove that they both exhibit stability and monotonicity under certain conditions.

The stability property ensures that the numerical solution of the discretized model remains bounded and does not blow up, while the monotonicity property guarantees that the solution preserves the ordering of the initial data.
These properties are important for the accuracy and reliability of numerical simulations of the Biot's model.
The authors provide numerical experiments to validate their theoretical results and demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed discretization schemes.

Overall, this paper contributes to the understanding and development of numerical methods for the Biot's model, which has applications in various fields such as geomechanics and petroleum engineering.
This paper investigates the heights of points with bounded ramification in algebraic number fields.
The authors establish a general framework for studying the heights of such points and provide explicit formulas for calculating their heights in certain cases.
They also prove several results regarding the behavior of these heights under various operations, such as multiplication and addition.
The paper concludes with some applications of these results to the study of elliptic curves and modular forms.
Overall, this work contributes to our understanding of the arithmetic properties of points with bounded ramification and provides useful tools for further research in this area.
In this paper, we present a linear kernel for the Planar Total Dominating Set problem.
The Planar Total Dominating Set problem is a well-known NP-hard problem in graph theory, where the goal is to find a minimum set of vertices that dominate all other vertices in a planar graph.
We propose a linear-time algorithm that constructs a kernel of size O(k), where k is the size of the optimal solution.
Our algorithm is based on a reduction technique that allows us to reduce the problem to a smaller instance while preserving the solution.
We provide a detailed analysis of the algorithm's time complexity and correctness, and present experimental results that demonstrate its efficiency and effectiveness.
Our linear kernel for the Planar Total Dominating Set problem contributes to the field of parameterized complexity by providing a more efficient algorithm for solving this problem in practice.
This paper presents a higher-order perspective on nominal unification, a fundamental operation in computational logic and programming languages.
Nominal unification is concerned with finding substitutions that make two given nominal terms equal.

The higher-order perspective allows us to reason about nominal unification in a more expressive and flexible way, by treating nominal terms as first-class objects and incorporating higher-order functions into the unification process.
We provide a formal framework for higher-order nominal unification and develop an algorithm that can efficiently solve nominal unification problems.
We also demonstrate the practical utility of our approach by applying it to various examples from the literature.

Our results show that the higher-order perspective on nominal unification offers new insights and techniques for solving nominal unification problems, and has the potential to advance the field of computational logic and programming languages.
This paper investigates the language equivalence problem for multi-measurement quantum finite automata (MM-QFAs) and proves its undecidability.
MM-QFAs are a model of computation that extends the capabilities of classical finite automata by incorporating quantum measurements.
The language equivalence problem for MM-QFAs asks whether two given MM-QFAs recognize the same language.
The paper presents a reduction from the halting problem of Turing machines to the language equivalence problem for MM-QFAs, demonstrating that the latter is undecidable.
This result has implications for the study of quantum computation and highlights the limitations of MM-QFAs as a computational model.
This paper introduces a new measure of non-linear large-scale structure in the form of three-point phase correlations.

The authors propose a method to calculate these correlations using Fourier transforms and demonstrate their usefulness in characterizing the non-linear clustering of galaxies in cosmological simulations.

The results show that three-point phase correlations capture information beyond traditional two-point statistics and can provide valuable insights into the formation and evolution of large-scale structures in the universe.
The authors suggest that this new measure can be a powerful tool for studying the non-linear dynamics of the cosmic web.

The abstract for the academic paper titled "Local energy balance, specific heats and the Oberbeck-Boussinesq approximation" discusses the relationship between the local energy balance and the specific heats in the context of the Oberbeck-Boussinesq approximation.
The Oberbeck-Boussinesq approximation is a commonly used simplification in fluid dynamics that assumes the density variations in a fluid are small compared to the mean density.
The paper presents a detailed analysis of the energy balance equation and the specific heats in the context of this approximation.

The authors derive expressions for the specific heats in terms of the temperature and density variations, and discuss the implications of these expressions for the accuracy of the Oberbeck-Boussinesq approximation.
The results of the analysis provide insights into the limitations and applicability of the Oberbeck-Boussinesq approximation in various fluid flow scenarios.

The findings of this study have implications for the understanding and modeling of fluid dynamics in a wide range of applications, including atmospheric and oceanic sciences, geophysics, and engineering.
