To tackle this issue, we propose a parameter decoupling strategy, in which we decouple the parameters into two parts: architecture parameters and appearance parameters.
We then fine-tune the network separately on both supervised and unsupervised datasets, with the architecture parameters kept fixed.

In this way, our method can effectively leverage the rich annotations from the supervised dataset and the abundant unlabeled samples from the unsupervised dataset, thereby achieving better performance in 3D left atrium segmentation.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on the publicly available MIT-BIH dataset.
Our method achieves an accuracy of 97.43% on the test set, outperforming the state-of-the-art fully supervised segmentation methods.

Towards Robust and Generalized Medical Image Segmentation Framework

Medical image segmentation is a fundamental step towards computerized
diagnosis and assists physicians in locating abnormalities to
provide anatomical context.

In this paper, we present a
segmentation framework that is built upon a fully connected
convolutional neural network (FC-CNN).

We use a multilayer
FC-CNN architecture because of its ability to handle
small sample sizes, as well as its capability to learn
complex and composite underlying structures.

Our network
has three convolutional layers and two fully connected
layers.

We introduce a new region-based loss function
that preserves both global and local structures, and only
requires a small number of training samples.

Finally, we
use an adaptive weighted sampling strategy to obtain a
better generalized segmentation framework.

In our experiment,
we applied our model to segment lumbar vertebrae structures
from MRI images.

Our method achieved a 93.9% segmentation
accuracy on the testing dataset.

We present a methodology to perform neural architecture search (NAS) in operational contexts, where the available computational resources are limited and the search for the optimal model should be performed in a short time frame.
Our case of study is remote sensing, where the available datasets are typically small and there is a need to deploy models quickly with limited computational resources.
We present a methodology to perform NAS using a single GPU, and show that our approach is able to find optimal models for the VIOLET dataset, a common benchmark in the remote sensing community.
Our approach is based on a genetic algorithm coupled with a simple search space defined by a set of architectural building blocks.

We show that our approach is able to find models that outperform the current state-of-the-art models for the VIOLET dataset in terms of prediction accuracy, while requiring fewer computational resources.
Our methodology is easily adaptable to other datasets and can be used to find optimal models for a wide range of remote sensing tasks.
Recent progress in deep learning has boosted the development of medical image segmentation models.
However, most existing works focus on 2D images or 3D volumes without considering the inherent hierarchical structure of medical images.
In this paper, we present a Pyramid Medical Transformer (PMT) to effectively exploit the pyramid structure of medical images for segmentation.
Specifically, we design a Light-weight Attention Module (LAM) to capture the global and local information at different levels of the image pyramid.
Moreover, to effectively integrate multi-scale information, we propose a Scale-aware Attention (SA) module that can focus on different scales of features adaptively.
Furthermore, a Pyramid-aware Tokenization (PAT) strategy is proposed to selectively preserve the useful information from the low-level features for each token.
Experiments on four public datasets, including MRI thigh bones, MRI cardiac, X-ray lungs, and X-ray kidneys, demonstrate the effectiveness of our PMT model compared to other state-of-the-art methods.
We present a novel approach for ultra-high resolution image segmentation based on a locality-aware contextual correlation (LACC) model.
Our approach exploits the contextual information of the image via a correlation prior, which captures the dependence between pixels belonging to the same object.
To efficiently compute the correlation prior, we introduce a locality constraint that encourages similarity between pixels within a localized region.
The LACC model is learned in a fully unsupervised manner via a variant of the expectation-maximization algorithm that optimizes the trade-off between the correlation prior and the locality prior.

We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on the semantic segmentation of very high resolution remote sensing images, where the fine spatial granularity of the objects poses a challenge for most existing techniques.
When compared to other state-of-the-art unsupervised segmentation methods, our approach achieves superior performance in terms of both accuracy and efficiency.
Recent progress in semantic segmentation is primarily driven by two types of contextual information: image-level and semantic-level.
However, existing methods usually integrate the two types of contextual information separately on either feature level or decision level.
In this paper, we argue that the complementary information between image-level and semantic-level contexts could be further exploited by jointly integrating them into a unified framework.

Specifically, we develop a novel Integration of Semantic-level and Image-level Networks (ISNet), which integrates image-level and semantic-level contexts in a symmetric and cooperative way for semantic segmentation.
It not only effectively combines the advantages of both contexts but also provides an explicit integration mechanism to balance their contributions.
The proposed ISNet is simple to implement and can be conveniently embedded into any existing segmentation frameworks.
We evaluate ISNet on four widely-used semantic segmentation benchmarks, where experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach.
Arxiv abstract:
We present a novel semi-supervised learning framework for few-shot medical image segmentation, which we refer to as PoissonSeg.
In medical image analysis, acquiring manually annotated images for training can be expensive, and transferring pre-trained models to new sites and modalities is challenging.

To tackle these problems, we exploit a recently proposed poisson learning framework, which enables us to leverage abundant unlabeled data and prior knowledge, and develop a new framework that is suitable for few-shot learning.

In our method, we minimize a poisson loss that enforces the agreement between segmentations and the prior knowledge, and a segmentation difference loss that encourages the agreement between predictions and a few labeled images.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on three different abdominal image segmentation benchmarks, and show that our method outperforms the state-of-the-art approaches for few-shot learning.

Recent advances in medical image segmentation have achieved remarkable performance using supervised learning, but training a model from scratch requires a large amount of labeled medical images, which are difficult to obtain.
In this work, we aim to reduce the gap between supervised and unsupervised learning for medical image segmentation.
In particular, we investigate contrastive learning as a simple and effective approach.

However, standard contrastive learning pipelines are not directly applicable due to the following challenges: 1) medical images are typically labeled at the voxel-level, rendering it difficult to directly compute pairwise similarity/difference; 2) there is a domain gap between synthetic augmentation and real clinical data; and 3) unlabeled data are imbalanced, as only a few pathologies are annotated.
To address these issues, we propose SimCVD, a simple yet effective approach to contrastive learning for medical image segmentation.
SimCVD distills a teacher model into a student model in a voxel-wise manner, leveraging abundant unlabeled data and only a small amount of labeled data.
Specifically, it generates pseudo-labels by pairing the teacher and student models, and then performs hard example mining to obtain a balanced training set for the student model.
We show that SimCVD significantly improves segmentation performance on multiple datasets for different pathologies, including liver and prostate cancer, with only 10% of labeled data.
We present a novel semi-supervised learning (SSL) approach to address the 2D medical image segmentation problem.

The proposed method utilizes a contrastive learning strategy, which maximizes the similarity between the labeled and unlabeled data, and minimizes the similarity between different unlabeled data samples.
To achieve this, we adopt a supervised clustering algorithm that utilizes a labeled data pool to generate pseudo-labels for unlabeled data.

We optimize the clustering algorithm parameters to minimize the contrastive loss, which measures the similarity between the labeled and unlabeled data, and the cross-entropy loss, which measures the similarity between different unlabeled data.
Furthermore, we introduce a data augmentation technique that generates additional training samples by applying geometric transformations to the original data.
The proposed method is evaluated on the 2D abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) segmentation benchmark from the 2018 Medical Image Computing and Computer Assisted Intervention (MICCAI) challenge.
The experimental results show that our method outperforms the state-of-the-art SSL approaches in terms of segmentation accuracy.
Recent progress in medical image segmentation has benefited from the release of large, manually annotated image datasets.
However, a significant portion of these datasets contain noisy, inconsistent, or missing labels, particularly in regions of interest for segmentation.

We present a simple yet effective approach to address these issues: we treat the segmentation annotations as a distribution and seek to find a mode of this distribution that agrees with the majority of the annotations while being smooth and coherent.

We employ a type of differentiable neural architecture known as a normalizing flow, which has recently shown success in density estimation, to learn a valid segmentation model in an unsupervised manner from these inconsistent annotations.

Since medical images often exhibit local structures with global smoothness, we propose a hierarchical flow architecture that is capable of capturing both local and global modes of the segmentation distribution in an unsupervised manner.
We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach on a public dataset with inconsistent annotations and achieve state-of-the-art performance in terms of both precision and F1 score.

Recent progress in transductive segmentation substantially improved performance on specific datasets, but these methods tend to forget previously learned knowledge when trained on a new dataset, indicating an inability to generalize between datasets.
In this work, we analyze transductive segmentation from a self-training perspective, and propose a self-training framework with uncertainty estimation for transductive image segmentation.
We find that existing state-of-the-art transductive models are poorly initialized and show that self-training can help.
We further explore the effect of uncertainty estimation in transductive segmentation, and find that it plays a crucial role in selecting supportive data for self-training.
Our method significantly improves segmentation performance on multiple datasets with different annotations, and achieves state-of-the-art performance on the challenging MIT-Adobe FiveK dataset.
Abstract: With the rapid development of artificial intelligence, it has become possible to use big data and machine learning to identify and map vulnerable populations.
This paper explores the use of AI to map vulnerable populations in Chicago, Illinois.
We use a combination of demographic data, social vulnerability data, and AI to create a map of vulnerable populations in the city.
The map is then used to identify areas of the city that are most vulnerable to environmental and social stressors.
Our results show that the most vulnerable areas of the city are those with a high concentration of low-income and minority residents.
These areas are also the most susceptible to environmental and social stressors, such as air pollution and crime.
We conclude that AI can be a powerful tool for identifying and mapping vulnerable populations, and that it can help policymakers and researchers to better understand the needs of these populations.
Vessel-CAPTCHA: An Efficient Learning Framework for Vessel Annotation and Segmentation.
In this paper, we present a learning framework, namely Vessel-CAPTCHA, for the fully automatic vessel annotation and segmentation in 3D rotational angiography (3DRA) sequences.
Unlike most existing methods which rely on handcrafted features, our approach learns a deep neural network to extract features directly from the raw input images.
The network is composed of several convolutional layers with pooling operations, followed by fully connected layers for classification.
To cope with the scarcity of annotated training samples, we adopt a bootstrapping strategy to train the network in an unsupervised manner, which is named as Vessel-CAPTCHA.

In this approach, a vesselness measure is learned to select the regions of interest (ROIs) that are likely to be vessels, and these ROIs are then used to train a second network for the final vessel segmentation.
The proposed method has been evaluated on a publicly available 3DRA dataset with manual annotations.
Our method achieves a mean accuracy of 94.3% on the vessel annotation and 92.5% on the vessel segmentation, outperforming the state-of-the-art approaches.
ArXiv abstract: TransClaw U-Net is an innovative variant of Claw U-Net, which explicitly leverages the power of Transformers.
It replaces the traditional convolutional layer in the contracting path of Claw U-Net with a Transformer encoder, and inserts a Transformer decoder into the expansive path.
Specifically, we utilize a pre-trained BERT model as the underlying Transformer architecture, which is optimized for contextual embeddings.
In the training process, we keep the encoder fixed and only update the decoder.
We evaluate our method on the ISBI challenge and the Cityscapes dataset, and show that it achieves competitive performance compared with other state-of-the-art methods.
Our code and model are available at: https://github.com/XiaohongWang001/TransClawUNet.
In this paper, we propose a hierarchical self-supervised learning (HSSL) approach for medical image segmentation.

The proposed method leverages the power of multi-domain data aggregation (MDDA) and uses a hierarchical learning framework to integrate information from different medical image domains, such as computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI).
The MDDA approach enables the training of a segmentation model that is robust to domain variations and able to generalize well to unseen data.
The HSSL framework learns a hierarchy of features from the aggregated data, with the lower levels capturing fine-grained details and the higher levels learning more abstract representations.

We evaluate the proposed method on the ISLES 2017 segmentation challenge dataset for liver and tumor segmentation in CT and MRI, and show that it significantly improves over the baseline method in terms of segmentation performance.
We consider the problem of modeling component partitions of a collection of objects, as encountered in image segmentation.
A partition can be described as a labeled graph, where the nodes correspond to objects and the edges correspond to spatial relationships.
We propose a framework for modeling a large collection of such graphs, under a sparse assumption that any two graphs in the collection are related by a small number of edge edits.
The edges can be added, deleted, or altered in the edit step; we allow each type of edit to have its own cost, which reflects the prior knowledge about the relationships between the objects.

We formulate the graph edit distance as a linear program and introduce a regularization term that encourages solutions to obey a natural graphical constraint: a solution should represent a partition of the objects into components that do not overlap.
This regularization term is allowed to be somewhat flexible, in that it is permitted to have gaps in its support, so that its zeros precisely encode the known component structure.
We derive a linear programming formulation for the flexible regularization term and show that the resulting optimization problem can be solved efficiently.
We apply the proposed method to the image segmentation problem, and demonstrate results on both synthetic and real image data.
We present a quality-aware memory network (QAMN) for interactive volumetric image segmentation.
Unlike most existing deep learning-based methods that output an entire 3D volume result, our approach interacts with a user by taking advantage of intermediate outputs from a memory network.
A novel quality-awareness module is introduced to maintain the quality of segmentation results by preserving prominent structures and preventing excessive blending of object boundaries.
We employ a multi-scale architecture to handle objects of various sizes within the volume.
Our method can output segmentation results at different levels of detail, enabling the user to interactively adjust the trade-off between accuracy and rendering speed.
In validation on interactive segmentation of isotropic and anisotropic volumetric images, we demonstrate the efficacy of our approach against state-of-the-art methods.
Code is available at https://github.com/VITA-Group/QAMN.
Recent advances in medical imaging technology have led to a vast amount of big volumetric data, which poses great challenges for accurate and efficient segmentation.

Although deep learning models have achieved remarkable performance in 2D image segmentation, directly applying these models to 3D medical image segmentation is hindered by the lack of large-scale annotated 3D datasets and the computational complexity of training 3D models.
In this paper, we present UTNet, a hybrid transformer architecture designed for medical image segmentation.

UTNet integrates a pyramid attention module (PAM) into the transformer encoder, which not only enables the model to effectively capture multi-scale contextual information but also reduces the computational complexity compared to pure 3D models.

Furthermore, a novel spatial-channel attention module (SCAM) is proposed to adaptively weigh the features from different encoder layers and channels, thereby improving the representation ability of the model.
Our extensive experiments on four public datasets, including MRI, CT, and ultrasound images, demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in segmenting different anatomical structures.
Compared to state-of-the-art methods, our model achieves improved performance in most cases and is more efficient in terms of computational speed.
The code and models have been made publicly available at https://github.com/AI4MedicineLab/UTNet.

We present a method for segmentation with multiple acceptable annotations, where the ground truth is specified as a set of examples, each of which is labeled with a different segmentation, yet each of which is considered correct.
A single segmentation is then predicted that is guaranteed to be an acceptable annotation.

We demonstrate the utility of this approach in the problem of myocardial segmentation in contrast echocardiography, where ground truth annotations are often difficult to agree upon, yet multiple experts may agree on the set of example segmentations.
We show that our approach can use as few as two example segmentations to learn a new segmentation and that using more example segmentations results in more accurate predictions.
Furthermore, our approach naturally handles missing or incorrect annotations, provided that there are enough correct examples in the training set.
Recent progress in deep learning has achieved great performance in biomedical image segmentation, especially with the popularization of U-Net and its variants.
However, these models usually rely on a large number of training samples and a large amount of computational resources, which are difficult to obtain in the field of biomedical imaging.

In this paper, we propose a multi-compound transformer for accurate biomedical image segmentation, which can effectively utilize both image-level and pixel-level information, and segment both small and large anatomical structures with fewer training samples.
The multi-compound transformer combines the advantages of encoders and decoders, and can effectively capture both local and global information.
We evaluate our method on four public datasets, and the results show that our method outperforms the state-of-the-art methods.
We present an approach for semi-supervised segmentation of images that combines global and local Mutual Information (MI) regularization.
Our method leverages a large amount of unlabeled data to boost the performance of supervised segmentation, while still retaining the ability to adapt to image specific properties.
We introduce a new MI regularization term that encourages labeled and unlabeled pixels to have similar segment assignments.

This regularization term is combined with a supervised term that enforces agreement between labeled pixels and a segmentation mask, and a global MI regularization term that encourages all pixels of a given segment to be assigned the same label.
The resulting energy function is optimized using a graph cuts algorithm that efficiently handles the irregular pixel adjacency present in images.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on semantic segmentation of indoor and outdoor scenes.
Recent progress in medical image segmentation has benefited from large labeled datasets and powerful convolutional neural networks (CNNs), but manual labeling is expensive and error-prone.
We propose a simple yet effective semi-supervised learning method for medical image segmentation that leverages a small labeled fraction of data and a large fraction of weakly-supervised data.
Specifically, we propagate label uncertainty from the labeled to the weakly-supervised examples via an adversarial process.
This enables the model to learn from all data while selectively trusting the labeled data when it agrees with the weakly-supervised data and the latter is more certain.
We apply our method to multiple medical image segmentation tasks, and show that our method consistently improves over the state-of-the-art across a variety of metrics.

In particular, on the MRI knee dataset, our method achieves a DSC of 0.88, outperforming all other methods; and on the abdominal CT dataset, our method achieves a DSC of 0.82, outperforming all but two methods.
We present a simple, yet effective approach to learn a positional contrastive loss suitable for volumetric medical image segmentation.
Our loss combines a standard contrastive loss with a positional loss, which models the spatial consistency of the predicted segmentation within a support volume.
This allows us to use the popular dilated convolutional neural network architecture for segmentation, while retaining 3D spatial information in the output.
We evaluate our method on the ISLES 2020 segmentation challenge and achieve the best performance among all submissions for the lung and kidney segmentation tasks.
Code is available at https://github.com/AUTOMATIC1111/Positional-Contrastive-Learning.
Optimal latent vector alignment for unsupervised domain adaptation in medical image segmentation

Abstract In this paper, we address the problem of unsupervised domain adaptation in medical image segmentation, where the goal is to learn a segmentation model from a source domain that is capable of generalizing to a target domain without the need for labeled examples in the target domain.

We propose a new algorithm for optimal latent vector alignment, which aligns the latent vector representations of images in the source and target domains in a way that minimizes the difference in distribution between the two domains.

This alignment is achieved by optimizing a cost function that measures the similarity between the latent vector representations of images in the two domains, while simultaneously minimizing the difference in distribution between the two domains.

We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on a challenging dataset of abdominal CT scans, and show that our algorithm is able to improve the performance of a state-of-the-art unsupervised domain adaptation algorithm by a significant margin.
Deep learning models have achieved great success in medical image segmentation, however, training such models usually requires a large amount of labeled data.
In this work, we present a novel approach for medical image segmentation that combines the strengths of the U-Net and Swin Transformer architectures while only requiring unlabeled data for training.
We name our new model DS-TransUNet, which is composed of a Swin Transformer encoder and a U-Net decoder.
The Swin Transformer encoder utilizes self-supervised learning to extract image features without the need for labeled data, while the U-Net decoder uses these features for segmentation.

We evaluate DS-TransUNet on three different medical image segmentation datasets (Parkinsons, ALS, and Knee Osteoarthritis) and show that it achieves state-of-the-art performance while being trained using only unlabeled data.
Our code and models are available at https://github.com/VITA-Group/DS-TransUNet.
Recent works have shown that few-shot learning, the ability to use few labeled examples to build accurate models for new classes, can be successfully applied to image segmentation tasks.
In this paper, we extend this idea to the domain of medical image segmentation, where the availability of labeled images is even more limited.
We introduce a new meta-learning framework that uses implicit gradients to learn a universal segmentation model from a small number of labeled images.

Our key insight is that medical images can be characterized by a small number of dominant features, and we use a meta-learning approach to identify and weigh these features in a way that is consistent with the limited labeled data.
This allows us to build a robust and generalizable segmentation model that is able to handle new classes with only a few labeled examples.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on a challenging dataset of abdominal CT scans, where we achieve state-of-the-art performance in few-shot segmentation.
Recent works have shown that deep neural networks are vulnerable to adversarial attacks, where carefully crafted input perturbations can cause the network to misclassify with high confidence.
Such attacks can be particularly damaging in the real-world, where adversaries have access to the output of a classifier and can craft patches to degrade its performance.

We present a method for attacking vision systems using patches of arbitrary size and shape, which can be applied remotely without access to the original training images or any information about the training process.
When the patches are constrained to be imperceptible, we achieve success rates of up to 100% on convolutional neural networks for image classification.
To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work on remote patch attacks, which expand the scope of adversarial attacks and highlight a new vulnerability of deep learning systems.
Detection of Adversarial and Anomalous Inputs using Normalizing Flows.
William Falcon, Zhijing Guo, Pengbo Li, Yuantao Gu, Yuanzhong Xu, and Beihang Wang.
In AAAI'22.
Abstract.
Large-scale recognition systems are increasingly susceptible to input deformations resulting from both unintentional noise and malicious attacks.
In this paper, we present a simple yet effective method for detecting anomalous and adversarial inputs.
We model the distribution of normal inputs via a bijective neural network, which we refer to as a normalizing flow.
Since the normalizing flow is onto, any input can be transformed to a normal input via the inverse of the flow.
We then define a detector via a binary classifier that discriminates between samples from the true distribution versus samples from the transformed distribution.
This framework is applicable to any recognition model and performs favorably compared to prior art on a wide range of benchmarks, including CIFAR-10, ImageNet, and PyTorch's Detectron2.
We show that our method is robust against attacks in white-box and black-box settings, and also effective at detecting inputs with unintentional noise.
We introduce a new image segmentation algorithm called BoundarySqueeze that incorporates intuitive notions of object boundaries into a variational framework.
Our approach combines a non-local boundary energy with a local TV regularization, formulated as a continuous non-smooth optimization problem.

This non-smooth energy is realized by a novel boundary-penalized TV (BP-TV) model that we introduce in this paper, and is inspired by the observation that object boundaries are typically characterized by rapid changes in image intensity.
We show that the BP-TV energy is a natural generalization of the TV energy that is capable of better handling image regions with complex, irregular object boundaries.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on a benchmark dataset, as well as several challenging real-world image segmentation applications.
We present a novel approach towards effective voxel-level abdominal multi-organ segmentation using siamese representation learning.

In this work, we design a 3D voxel-level siamese network, namely Voxel-wise Siamese Network (VSN), which encodes the similarities and differences between the two input organs within each voxel, and leverages the global organ-level information for accurate segmentation.
Specifically, we propose a novel voxel-wise fusion module to effectively aggregate the voxel-level and organ-level information for multi-organ segmentation.
The proposed method was evaluated on the abdominal organ segmentation dataset from the 2018 MedIAI Segmentation Challenge.
Our method achieved a high segmentation accuracy with an average Dice similarity coefficient of 95.72% for liver, 92.10% for stomach, and 90.37% for kidneys across eight subjects.
Recent advances in neuro-modification have enabled direct interface with large-scale neural circuits.
However, such interfaces often suffer from noise or artifacts that can lead to erroneous reads/writes.
We introduce a method for identifying and correcting such errors, leveraging the natural image prior and a trained image classifier.
We apply our approach to a spatial-probing, optogenetics-based neural recording paradigm and a deep learning framework for semantic image segmentation.
Our method correctly identifies and repairs 75% of the circuit errors in our dataset, improving performance to that of the correct circuit reads without any overhead in runtime.
We present an algorithm for geodesic active contours based on characteristic functions.

The evolution of the contour is governed by an energy functional that comprises an external energy term defined by the characteristic function and an internal energy term proportional to the geodesic distance between the initial contour and the current contour.
The characteristic function is defined by a series of indicator functions that are designed to capture specific features in the image.
The algorithm is efficient and allows for the use of a large number of indicators.
We demonstrate the performance of our algorithm on several 2D and 3D segmentation examples.
In this paper, we present a method for the automatic segmentation of citrus, which is a basic but challenging step toward a fully automated citrus inspection system.
We propose a method that combines supervised and un-supervised learning.
Supervised learning is used to learn the mapping from input images to a segmentation mask (binary image) using a convolutional neural network (CNN).
Un-supervised learning is used to improve the segmentation results from the CNN by incorporating prior knowledge about the objects to be segmented.
We demonstrate the performance of our method on a dataset of over 4000 images.
In particular, we show that our method is able to achieve a F1-score of 0.83, which is a significant improvement over the state-of-the-art.
Our approach can be divided into three steps: (1) pre-processing, (2) supervised learning, and (3) un-supervised learning.
The pre-processing step involves converting the input image to a format suitable for the CNN.
This includes scaling the image to a fixed size and converting it to a grayscale image.
The supervised learning step involves training a CNN to learn the mapping from the pre-processed image to a segmentation mask.
The un-supervised learning step involves improving the segmentation results from the CNN by incorporating prior knowledge about the objects to be segmented.
This includes applying a morphological operation to the segmentation mask to remove small regions and to close gaps between regions.
It also includes a graph cut step to improve the accuracy of the segmentation.
The graph cut step uses a cost function that takes into account the prior knowledge about the objects to be segmented.
Deep learning algorithms have been demonstrated to achieve excellent performance on image classification, object detection, and segmentation tasks.
However, these algorithms require a vast amount of memory and computational resources to operate effectively.

In this paper, we propose a new algorithm, termed Cascaded and Separable Structures of Dilated Convolution (CASSOD-Net), which is designed to reduce the memory and computational requirements of deep learning algorithms.
CASSOD-Net is composed of multiple cascaded and separable structures of dilated convolution, which are designed to reduce the number of parameters and computations required by the network.

The proposed algorithm has been demonstrated to achieve excellent performance on a variety of image classification and object detection tasks, while requiring fewer parameters and computations than traditional deep learning algorithms.
Recent advances in deep learning have achieved significant performance improvements for medical image segmentation.
However, most of these approaches require large amounts of interactive labeling effort, which is expensive and time-consuming, and often impractical in clinical environments.
In this paper, we present MIDeepSeg, a semi-supervised segmentation approach that minimizes the amount of interactive labeling effort required for training.
Instead of using a fixed amount of labeled and unlabeled data, we iteratively add labeled data to the training set during training, which we call “minimally interactive” labeling.
Our approach uses a simple yet effective deep learning architecture, and can be used to segment unseen objects from medical images.

We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on the task of brain tumor segmentation from T1-weighted MRI, and show that our approach achieves comparable performance to state-of-the-art fully-supervised methods, while requiring significantly less labeling effort.
Recent results on supervised learning with large datasets require an infeasible amount of human-labeled data.
To alleviate the labeling bottleneck, we propose DatasetGAN, a novel framework that leverages generative adversarial networks (GANs) to create labeled data efficiently.
It automatically identifies the underlying data distribution of the unlabeled data and synthesizes labeled data based on it, thereby converting unlabeled data into labeled data.
Compared to the conventional data co-training approach that uses GANs, DatasetGAN directly generates labeled data instead of unlabeled data, which is more efficient in terms of the data utilization.
We demonstrate the efficacy of DatasetGAN on four real-world datasets, in which it achieves up to 90% reduction in the labeled data requirement while maintaining the same accuracy.
Abstract: Labeled data are essential for training deep neural networks.
However, labeling data can be expensive and time-consuming, especially for large datasets.
This work proposes DatasetGAN, a novel framework that leverages generative adversarial networks to create labeled data efficiently.
It automatically identifies the underlying data distribution of unlabeled data and synthesizes labeled data based on it, converting unlabeled data into labeled data.
Compared to co-training with GANs, DatasetGAN directly generates labeled data, which is more efficient in terms of data utilization.
We demonstrate the efficacy of DatasetGAN on several real-world datasets, achieving up to 90% reduction in labeled data requirements while maintaining the same accuracy.
We present an image segmentation model based on the Product of Experts architecture, where the experts are defined by a MRF-UNet.

The MRF-UNet combines the strengths of the U-Net and the MRF models: the former's ability to encode multi-scale contextual information, and the latter's ability to express rich, hierarchical relationships between pixels.
In the proposed model, the MRF-UNet is trained end-to-end, allowing for efficient segmentation of medical and natural images.
We validate the model on the MIT-CBCL and the ISBI 2017 cardiac segmentation benchmark.
Our model achieves competitive results to state-of-the-art methods on both datasets, while being more efficient in terms of runtime.
Deep learning ensembles have shown promising results for medical image segmentation.
However, they require large amounts of data and training time when training on small datasets.

We propose a deep learning ensemble method, called deep ensembles based on Stochastic Activation Selection (S2EN), which trains ensemble networks with shared weights, each consisting of randomly selected activation functions from a pre-defined activation pool.

Since the ensemble networks share weights and the selected activation functions act as regularization, the proposed method reduces the amount of training data and time needed to achieve high performance, making it suitable for training with small datasets.

We applied the proposed method to polyp segmentation in colorectal endoscopic videos, and compared it with a recently proposed deep learning ensemble method as well as a state-of-the-art deep learning method based on a two-stream network.
The proposed method achieved a 3.6% and 2.8% improvement in F1-score on the validation and test datasets, respectively, compared to the next best method.
Code is available at https://github.com/naverlab/S2EN.
We present a method for decomposing a 3D scene into objects via unsupervised volume segmentation.
Our method is based on the observation that object surfaces exhibit a higher curvature than the background.
We leverage this property to develop a curvature-based volume segmentation method.
We compute a curvature potential directly in the voxel space using a Gauss-Newton technique for efficient non-differentiable structure and motion estimation.
Furthermore, we propose an iterative refinement framework to optimize the segmentation.
We evaluate our method on the ShapeNet part segmentation benchmark and show that our method outperforms the state-of-the-art on both the car and airplane categories.

Our method achieves a mean accuracy of 84.4% and 89.4% on the car and airplane categories, respectively, compared to the second best method, which achieves a mean accuracy of 79.4% and 86.2%, respectively.
Object-centric image segmentation evaluation is typically performed by measuring the Intersection over Union (IoU) between the ground truth (GT) and predicted segmentations.

However, in scenarios where the GT is provided as a set of bounding boxes (BBs), the commonly used Average IoU (AvgIoU) metric treats each bounding box as a separate segment, ignoring the objects they bound.
In this work, we propose a novel Boundary IoU (BgIoU) metric that utilizes the boundaries of objects in GT BBs for evaluation.
We show that BgIoU better aligns with the intrinsic goal of segmentation, providing a tighter upper bound on the IoU between the true object boundaries and the predicted boundaries.

Furthermore, we present an efficient implementation of BgIoU based on a bounding box distance transform, which allows us to compute BgIoU with a computational complexity of ~3*N*M, similar to the conventional IoU. We perform a comprehensive evaluation of BgIoU on two public datasets, demonstrating its superiority over state-of-the-art metrics for object-centric evaluation.
Recent works have demonstrated the power of Transformer architectures in tasks like machine translation, text summarization, and question answering.
However, one drawback of these models is their lack of interpretability, making it difficult to understand why they make certain predictions.
We present a generic attention-model-based method for interpreting Transformer predictions in a way that highlights the most important parts of the input that influenced the model's decision.

We demonstrate our method on bi-modal and encoder-decoder Transformers in three tasks (machine translation, text summarization, and question answering), and show that our method is able to explain the model's predictions, giving users and developers insight into how the model makes its decisions.
We present a simple, fast, and effective training strategy for learning deformable image registration models, which we call Test-Time Training (TT).
In TT, the model is trained only on a random subsample of the training data, and tested directly on the withheld majority of the data.
We show that registration performance of the model on the test set improves as the model is trained, and that the improvement persists over a wide range of training subsample sizes.
We perform detailed analysis to understand the cause of this phenomenon, and show that it is due to the model learning to imitate the transformation behavior of the withheld data.
We perform experiments on two benchmark deformable image registration datasets, and show that TT results in improved performance compared to training on the full dataset.
The TT strategy enables training large registration models on data with stringent privacy requirements, and could be useful in a variety of other registration scenarios.
Recent works on color transfer for images often ignore the regions of the image that lie behind objects, and consequently, the colors of these background regions are not harmonized.
We introduce a method for detecting objects in an image, and use the resulting segmentation as an input to a color transfer algorithm.
We propose a novel weighted-color-distance function that emphasizes the contributions of the dominant colors in each segment, and incorporates an image-dependent weight-assignment heuristic.
The proposed method enables the colors of the background regions to be harmonized, even when they are partially obscured by objects.
We evaluate our approach using the CLEAR 2008 and 2010 benchmark datasets, and compare the results to state-of-the-art color transfer methods.
Recent progress in medical image segmentation has largely been achieved by pre-training large models on large-scale, open-domain datasets, and then fine-tuning on in-domain data.
However, fine-tuning tends to cause model capacity reduction and suffers from the lack of available in-domain training data.
In this paper, we attempt to address both issues.
We propose a Margin Preserving Self-paced Contrastive Learning (MPSCL) framework for unsupervised domain adaptation of medical image segmentation.

Specifically, we use a margin-preserving learning scheme to alleviate the capacity reduction of the fine-tuning process, and a self-paced learning strategy, which allows the model to select the most informative data samples for adaptation, to address the data scarcity problem.
We apply the proposed method to adapt a pre-trained model from abdominal CT to abdominal MRI segmentation with promising results.
Recent progress in semantic segmentation largely concentrates on image-based approaches.

However, for cities with tall buildings and dense streets, the perspective of aerial images shows a significant deviation from the ground images, making it challenging to directly apply the image-based methods.
To this end, we propose a novel framework, named PointFlow, for aerial image segmentation.
It models the semantics propagation in a point-based manner, allowing us to handle the large-scale perspective variation and thus ease the segmentations on aerial images.
In particular, given a sparse set of points, our framework flows the semantics from source points to target points in an iterative manner.
At each iteration, we estimate a sparse semantic label field from the current point predictions, and then update the point predictions by propagating the estimated label field.
In this way, our framework effectively integrates the global context information in a bottom-up fashion.
We evaluate our method on three public datasets for aerial image segmentation, and experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach against other state-of-the-art methods.
Recent works on omnidirectional image segmentation have shown the efficacy of incorporating contextual information across different ranges for accurate pixel-level labeling.
However, existing methods mainly rely on either a limited number of fixed ranges or a single modulated range, which may not adequately capture the rich variations in the omni-range context.
In this paper, we present an Omni-Range Context module that can flexibly capture the omni-range context from a set of input features.

Specifically, given a set of input features, our module can be flexibly configured to use a sub-set of features with specific ranges of interest, enabling the model to focus on the most relevant context.
We show that the proposed module can be easily integrated into existing segmentation frameworks to enhance their performance.
When evaluated on four standard benchmarks for omnidirectional segmentation, our method achieves state-of-the-art performance.
Code is available at https://github.com/AI4Finance-Foundation/Omnidirectional-Segmentation.

Recent progress in 3D medical image segmentation has benefited from both convolutional neural network (CNN) and transformer-based architectures, but their individual limitations hinder performance and efficiency.
To address these limitations, we present CoTr, a simple and efficient hybrid architecture that combines the strengths of CNN and transformer-based models.
Our approach dynamically allocates the tasks of feature extraction and segmentation across the two architectures based on the image size, enabling efficient training and inference on large images.

We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on three challenging 3D medical image segmentation tasks: abdominal organ segmentation from CT, pulmonary nodule segmentation from CT, and hippocampus segmentation from T1-weighted MRI.
Our model achieves state-of-the-art performance on all three datasets, significantly improving over previous methods, while being more efficient for segmentation on large images.
Code is available at https://github.com/ interpreteur/CoTr.

Recent progress in image segmentation, especially for nuclei images, has
been driven by large-scale annotated datasets.

However, manual
annotation is costly, and the resulting datasets are subject to
annotation errors and bias.

We present a data augmentation
approach to address these issues: given a nuclei image and its
ground truth segmentation, our algorithm generates new nuclei images
with the same segmentation.

Our method is based on a
generative neural network that learns to convert label maps to
images.

Because our network is trained to preserve the segmentation
rather than the appearance of individual nuclei, it can also
correct segmentation errors in the input image, and it is
capable of generating images with nuclei of different sizes and
shapes.

We show that our method, when used for data augmentation
during training, improves the performance of a U-Net
segmentation model for in vitro and in vivo nuclei images,
leading to significant improvements in segmentation accuracy
and speed.

Furthermore, because our method also provides a probabilistic
image synthesis, it can be used to quantify the uncertainty in
the generated images, which we demonstrate can be used for
estimating segmentation uncertainty.

Recent progresses in deep learning have achieved remarkable performance in specialized image segmentation tasks, yet their usage remains limited to the domain they are trained on, lacking the ability to generalize to unseen domains.

In this paper, we tackle the problem of segmenting medical images acquired from different domains (e.g., different institutions or different modalities) by designing a MixSearch framework that learns a universal segmentation architecture applicable to all domains.

Given a set of domains with limited labeled samples each, our approach first utilizes domain-specific pre-trained models as fixed initialized prior models to build domain-adaptive segmentation architectures, and then a meta-learning based approach is introduced to refine these prior models into domain-generalized segmentation architectures.
Specifically, we propose a novel progressive meta-learning framework, where a sequence of few-shot learners with increasing complexity are learned in an iterative manner.
Each few-shot learner is first fine-tuned with domain-specific data to adapt to individual domains and then further trained on the mixed dataset to learn domain-generalization.

We evaluate our method on segmenting lymph nodes from different institutions in the CAMELYON-train and -test datasets, as well as segmenting pulmonary nodules in CT images from two different institutions, and achieve state-of-the-art performance.
We show how to use the split Bregman algorithm to find the global minimum of the self-repelling snake model on a compact set.
In particular, we consider the model where the potential is the sum of a Gaussian and a barrier, with the latter having a global minimum.
We show that the split Bregman algorithm is able to find a minimizer of this model, and we present a scheme to make the algorithm more efficient in terms of computational complexity.
Additionally, we show that our algorithm is able to find the global minimum of the model in a reasonable amount of time, and we present some preliminary computational results.

Recent works have shown that encoders based on pre-trained Transformers, particularly ViTs, set new standards for the quality of the learned representations for natural images, outperforming traditional convolutional neural networks.
In this work, we adapt Transformers for medical image segmentation.
In particular, we propose to use Transformers as encoders, predicting segmentations as a whole image classification.
To adapt the Transformers to this task, we modify the classification layer to take into account the label hierarchy and handle overlapping segments.
We present a new Transformer encoder based on ViT, called TransUNet, that outperforms the current state-of-the-art methods for segmentation on multiple benchmarks for both 2D and 3D medical images.
Our code is available at https://github.com/DPichenaux/TransUNet.
Deep learning segmentation of fluorescence microscopy images with missing markers can be greatly improved by utilizing uncertainty estimation.
This paper proposes a novel method to estimate the uncertainty of the deep learning model, which considers the missing markers and spatial correlation of the image.
The proposed method is based on a fully convolutional network with a residual connection and a side output for uncertainty estimation.
The uncertainty estimation is achieved by introducing a temperature parameter to the side output, which is optimized along with the main output during the training process.
The proposed method has been evaluated on a public dataset and compared with other state-of-the-art methods in terms of segmentation performance and uncertainty estimation.

The experimental results show that the proposed method can effectively estimate the uncertainty of the segmentation output and improve the segmentation performance, especially when the input images contain missing markers.
The code and additional results are available at: https://github.com/CVMI-Lab/Uncertainty-Deep-Learning-Segmentation.
Personal fixation-based object segmentation with object localization and boundary preservation.
Object segmentation significantly benefits various computer vision applications.
Most existing methods rely on a fully supervised training process, requiring a large number of labeled images for each class.
However, collecting a large number of images with ground truth for every application is expensive and time-consuming.
In this paper, we exploit the idea of utilizing personal fixations from a small number of users to train an object segmentation model.
We propose a new framework that can localize objects and preserve boundaries via a learned attention mechanism.
The proposed method utilizes a sparse-coded fixation dataset, which is naturally personal, to learn a generic object segmentation model.
We show that our method can achieve promising results on both personal and public datasets, outperforming existing state-of-the-art methods in terms of both accuracy and efficiency.
We present a graph-based framework for natural image segmentation based on affinity fusion.
Our approach leverages the multi-scale graph structure to capture the image context and fuse the multi-scale segmentation results.
By iteratively refining the graph representation and updating the segmentation, our algorithm effectively combines both global and local information for accurate segmentation.
We introduce a novel affinity learning scheme to adaptively estimate the affinity matrix, which measures the similarity between pixels.
The proposed method is fully automatic, parameter-free, and is able to handle any image size.
We evaluate our approach on the VOC 2012 segmentation benchmark and achieve competitive results compared to the state-of-the-art methods.
We present an approach for unpaired image segmentation that learns a deep neural network with class-specific affinities for multiple modalities.
Our network leverages domain-specific knowledge by learning to reason about the relationships between individual pixels and image classes of different modalities.
We formulate the image segmentation problem as a maximum a posteriori inference in a Bayesian framework, where the posterior is defined by a deep convolutional network.
Our approach is trained end-to-end in a semi-supervised manner, given only a small number of paired training examples.

We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on three real-world multimodal segmentation datasets, achieving state-of-the-art performance on the largest dataset, which contains complex information in both image and semantic domains.
Arrival of autonomous driving has been underway for several years and continues to be an area of active research.
The state-of-the-art autonomous vehicles have features including environmental perception, localization, and planning.
All these functionalities heavily rely on the perception capability of the vehicle.
In this paper, we describe our approach for stereo computer vision to capture the vehicle surroundings in 3D, which serves as the main sensing modality for static and dynamic objects in the scene.
We highlight the challenges we faced in practical autonomous driving scenarios and the approaches we took to address them.
Our solution comprises various components including efficient stereo estimation, dense 3D point cloud segmentation, and object detection and tracking in 3D.
We explain the choices of the individual components and how they fit together to deliver a capable stereo computer vision system.
We evaluate our system on the KITTI dataset and discuss how it generalizes to new domains.
Learning robust object representations is a core challenge in computer vision.
Most existing works rely on a large amount of labeled images to learn these object representations.
In this paper, we present an approach to object segmentation that is trained using only image-level labels.
Our approach is based on a careful analysis of the image-level label and a novel message passing architecture that leverages the inherent multi-scale nature of the labeling process.

We show that our approach is able to learn robust object representations and produce state-of-the-art results on the PASCAL VOC segmentation challenge with minimal training data, and is able to outperform other state-of-the-art approaches that use orders of magnitude more labeled data.
Recent progress in deep learning has achieved remarkable performance in medical image segmentation.
However, these methods often require large amounts of manually annotated training data, which is difficult to obtain for medical image segmentation.
We present a new framework for medical image segmentation that addresses the problem of limited training data.
Our approach combines a U-Net architecture with a reinforcement learning agent that learns to segment new images by playing a segmentation game.
The agent uses anatomical knowledge to form a short-term reward and a long-term reward that is optimized to minimize segmenter bias.
We demonstrate the efficacy of our method on three different medical image segmentation tasks: abdominal CT, cardiac MRI, and brain tumor segmentation from MRI.

Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on the abdominal CT and cardiac MRI segmentation tasks, and improves upon the prior state-of-the-art method on the brain tumor segmentation task despite using less than half of the training data.
In this paper, we address the problem of segmenting overlapping wear particles in 3D point clouds collected from used metal parts.
We propose a novel deep learning approach that utilizes a few labeled data and addresses the imbalance in the sample.
We first generate a large number of synthetic point clouds containing randomly placed and oriented wear particles.
We then train a deep neural network using the generated data and a small set of labeled point clouds.
The trained network is used to segment the wear particles in new point clouds.
The proposed approach is evaluated on a large dataset of real-world point clouds.
Compared to the state-of-the-art, the proposed approach achieves a significant improvement in segmentation accuracy.
Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have become a popular framework for unsupervised learning of image compression.
While these methods can generate visually appealing images, they generally lack the ability to faithfully reproduce the input noise distribution in the generated images.
To address this, we propose a novel distance measure for GANs based on the Normalised Laplacian Pyramid (NLP).
The proposed distance measure provides a mechanism to enforce perceptual consistency on the generated images, allowing the GAN to reproduce the input noise distribution in a more effective way.

We show that the proposed distance measure outperforms the state-of-the-art methods in terms of the quality of the generated images, as measured by the Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) and the Inception Score (IS).

Introduction: 
Recent advances in deep learning have enabled the development of powerful generative models for image compression.
One of the most successful frameworks is the Generative Adversarial Network (GAN), which consists of a generator and a discriminator network.
The generator network learns to transform random noise into realistic images, while the discriminator network tries to distinguish the generated images from real images.
The training process of GANs is based on an adversarial game, in which the generator and discriminator are trained simultaneously to improve the quality of the generated images.
While GANs have shown promising results in generating visually appealing images, they generally lack the ability to faithfully reproduce the input noise distribution in the generated images.

This limitation can be attributed to the fact that the existing distance measures, such as the popular Fréchet Inception Distance (FID), do not provide an effective mechanism for enforcing perceptual consistency on the generated images.

To address this limitation, we propose a novel distance measure for GANs based on the Normalised Laplacian Pyramid (NLP).
The NLP is a multi-scale image representation that captures local and global image characteristics.
It has been successfully used for image denoising, compression and other image processing tasks.
The proposed distance measure uses the NLP to compare the generated image with the input noise distribution.

By evaluating the similarity between the NLP representations of the generated image and the input noise, we can enforce perceptual consistency on the generated images, allowing the GAN to reproduce the input noise distribution in a more effective way.

Recent progress in video semantic segmentation has primarily relied on effective use of temporal information, which is challenging to obtain due to the inherent distortion in optical flow estimation.
To mitigate this issue, we propose a distortion-aware feature correction module that explicitly estimates and removes the distortion introduced by flow estimation.
Our correction module consists of two components: a distortion estimator and a correction layer.
The distortion estimator accurately estimates the distortion in the flow field via a convolutional layer that compares features from the current and next frames.
The correction layer then leverages the estimated distortion to correct the feature representation for better alignment.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on the Cityscapes and Mapillary Vistas datasets, where our method achieves significant performance gains over the state of the art.
Further analysis shows the advantage of our approach in capturing temporal dependencies and the robustness of our method to different levels of flow quality.
Recent progress in deep learning enables numerous applications of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) in medical image analysis, especially in image segmentation.

However, most of the existing methods treat image segmentation as a binary-wise or pixel-wise classification problem and thus segment the objects in a constant scale, which may cause the loss of object boundary information or lead to uneven segmentation results for objects with different sizes.
In this paper, we propose a 3D deep coarse-to-fine framework to achieve volumetric medical image segmentation, which can preserve the boundary information and handle objects with different sizes.
Within our framework, we first utilize a 3D CNN to extract multi-scale features and then adopt a conditional random field (CRF) to refine the segmentation results on each scale.
To effectively train the 3D CNN, we further propose a novel 3D adversarial example generation method, which can add diversity to the training samples and thus accelerate the training process.
The proposed method has been evaluated on the ISBI challenge 2016 and 2017 segmentation datasets and compared with other state-of-the-art methods.
The experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.
We present a novel approach towards training a segmentation model for catheter filaments in 3D frustum ultrasound (US) using only sparsely-labeled training data.
Towards this end, we propose an innovative weakly-supervised loss that utilizes both the readily available 2D US images and the 3D US volume, which is reconstructed from the 2D slices.
We show that our approach effectively leverages the rich 3D information for training robust 2D detectors for catheter segmentation, while only requiring a small amount of 3D annotation.
In particular, given a single 3D slice labeled with tube contours, our method can learn to segment catheters in all 2D slices of the frustum.
We evaluate our approach on 40 clinical cases, and demonstrate that our method yields accurate catheter segmentations in 2D slices.

Our pipeline, illustrated in Figure 1, consists of (1) 2D detection in individual US slices, (2) 3D tube contour prediction in reconstructed volumes, and (3) weakly-supervised loss for training 2D detectors.
2D detection is performed by a 2D convolutional neural network (CNN) based on the popular Mask R-CNN framework.
To enable 3D tube contour prediction, we first reconstruct the 3D volume of the ultrasound from the individual 2D slices, and then run 2D detectors in the 3D volume for tube contour prediction.
Specifically, for each slice, we apply the 2D detector to the reconstructed volume, and produce tube contours in the 3D space.

However, since the 3D volume is reconstructed from slices, the resulting tube contours are not directly usable for training 2D detectors due to the following challenges: (1) the contours are not aligned with the 2D slices, and (2) the contours are not quantized to the same resolution as the 2D US slices.
To address these issues, we propose a weakly-supervised loss that aligns and resamples the 3D contours to the 2D slices.
Given a sparse set of 3D labeled slices, our approach enables the 2D detectors to learn from the 3D annotations without requiring additional 2D annotations.
Deep learning models have achieved great performance in semantic segmentation of fundus images.
However, these models are heavily dependent on large amounts of manually labeled training data, which are difficult to obtain for specialty domains like ophthalmology.
In this paper, we present a domain-oriented feature embedding (DoFE) approach to enhance the generalizability of deep learning models for fundus image segmentation.
DoFE learns a low-dimensional feature representation that captures domain-specific information from unlabeled specialty datasets.
We then employ these domain-specific features as additional input to a deep learning model trained on a large dataset of natural images.
This enables the model to leverage the domain-specific information and achieve better generalization performance on unseen datasets.
We evaluate our approach on the MIT-BIH and DRIVE datasets for segmentation of retinal fundus images.
Our results show that DoFE improves the performance of deep learning models on both datasets, even when trained on natural image datasets only.
We present a method for training a deep neural network for pixel-level image segmentation of aerial images using imperfect polyline labels.
We tackle the problem of annotation errors in the provided polyline labels, which are often present in crowdsourced datasets.
Our key insight is to leverage the structural information of polyline labels to propagate labels across the entire image.
We formulate the image segmentation as a conditional random field (CRF) and propose a deep CRF architecture that incorporates a convolutional neural network (CNN) as its feature extractor.
We train the network end-to-end from image to segmentation, enabling the network to learn to refine incorrect or incomplete labels.

We evaluate our method on a public dataset with pixel-level and polyline-level annotations, and show that our method can effectively correct annotation errors in polyline labels and produce pixel-level segmentation results of high quality.
We introduce a new benchmark for weakly supervised medical image segmentation, which we call Segmentation of Synonyms (Segsyn).
Given a list of synonyms representing the labels for a given image, the goal is to produce a segmentation mask where each label is assigned to the regions containing the structure it denotes.
We show that while state-of-the-art medical image segmentation methods perform poorly on this benchmark, models pre-trained for natural image segmentation perform remarkably well.
We conduct an extensive study to identify and analyze the reasons behind these performance differences.
Finally, we propose a simple method to improve the performance of medical image segmentation models on Segsyn without access to any labeled medical data.
Our code and dataset are available at https://github.com/BBillot/SegSyn.
Abstract: We present LAMP, a method for training Large Deep Nets with Automated Model Parallelism for Image Segmentation.

LAMP dynamically partitions a deep neural network into compute units that can be distributed across multiple GPUs, allowing for efficient training of very large models that would be infeasible on a single GPU.
Our method is based on a novel architecture that automatically partitions a deep neural network into parallel beams, each of which can be computed in parallel on a separate GPU.
This enables training of models with hundreds of layers and millions of parameters at scales well beyond what is currently possible on a single GPU.

We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on the challenging task of semantic image segmentation, where we achieve state-of-the-art performance on the Cityscapes dataset, outperforming prior methods by a large margin.
Our method is highly general and can be applied to a wide range of deep learning tasks.
We address the problem of recognizing objects in images using sparse representation.

In contrast to recent works on sparse representation that rely on the computation of local features (e.g., edges, gradients, etc.), we propose to use contour information as a priori knowledge to improve the performance of object recognition.
We define a novel dissimilarity between contours, based on the concept of stickiness, that measures the extent to which contours stick together in the image.
This dissimilarity is used within a sparse representation framework to recognize objects in images.
We evaluate the performance of our method on two standard benchmarks, showing that our method outperforms the state-of-the-art in object recognition.
This paper proposes a method for the segmentation of land use and land cover (LULC) in RGB satellite images using an Fully Convolutional Network (FCN-8).
The FCN-8 is a convolutional neural network (CNN) model designed for image segmentation tasks.
The model is composed of eight convolutional layers, followed by a max pooling layer and a fully connected layer.
The FCN-8 model was trained on a dataset of RGB satellite images and their corresponding LULC labels.
The training process involved the use of a cross-entropy loss function and an optimizer algorithm to minimize the difference between the predicted LULC labels and the ground truth labels.
The trained model was then evaluated on a separate test dataset, and the results were compared to those obtained using a conventional watershed-based approach.
The FCN-8 model achieved a higher accuracy and recall compared to the watershed-based approach, while also reducing the overall processing time.
The proposed method demonstrates the potential of using deep learning techniques for LULC segmentation in RGB satellite images.
We present a new image labeling algorithm that combines Markov random fields (MRFs) with neural networks in a multiresolution framework.
Our approach uses a MRF optimized via the belief propagation algorithm to label pixels in an image, with the MRF's parameters learned via a neural network.
We introduce a novel upsampling/fusion strategy that combines high-resolution and low-resolution labeled images to obtain precise and reliable object boundaries.
This multiresolution strategy is particularly important in the context of MRFs, where labeled object boundaries are typically difficult to estimate due to the inherent smoothing of the MRF.
Our algorithm is fully automatic, and is able to handle images of varying resolution and size without any modification.
We present quantitative and qualitative results on both synthetic and real world image datasets.
We address the problem of training an agent to learn from its mistakes in the context of a reinforcement learning (RL) task.
We propose a method that combines reinforcement learning with attention mechanism and error-driven learning.
The attention mechanism is used to focus on the errors made by the agent, while the error-driven learning component utilizes the attention information to update the policy of the agent.
Using the Euclidean distance as a measure of error, we show that the proposed method can be used to find the optimal policy that minimizes the error.
We perform extensive experiments on the Atari 2600 game Breakout using two different error definitions.
The results show that the proposed method can improve the score of the agent significantly over the baseline methods.

Introduction

Reinforcement learning (RL) is a type of machine learning (ML) where an agent learns to make decisions by interacting with its environment.
The agent receives rewards for performing actions that lead to desired outcomes, and learns to make better decisions over time by optimizing its policy.
A key challenge in RL is dealing with the credit assignment problem, which occurs when the agent's policy is suboptimal and leads to errors.
The agent needs to identify the errors and update its policy accordingly in order to improve its performance.
Our method is inspired by the phenomenon of error-driven learning, which is observed in humans and animals.
When a person or animal makes an error, they tend to pay attention to the error and adjust their behavior to avoid making the same error in the future.
In this paper, we propose a method that combines RL with attention mechanism and error-driven learning.
The attention mechanism is used to focus on the errors made by the agent, while the error-driven learning component utilizes the attention information to update the policy of the agent.
We show that the proposed method can be used to find the optimal policy that minimizes the error.
We perform extensive experiments on the Atari 2600 game Breakout using two different error definitions.
The results show that the proposed method can improve the score of the agent significantly over the baseline methods.

Related Work

There is a growing body of research that combines RL with attention mechanism.
These methods often use attention to focus on relevant information in the environment, or to learn a policy that is robust to changes in the environment.
There is also research that combines RL with error-driven learning.
These methods often use errors to update the policy of the agent, but they do not use attention to focus on the errors.
