An overview of active contour models is provided in this paper, where a general scheme of the model is introduced first, followed by the discussion of existing fuzzy active contour models.
Finally, we point out the state-of-the-art fuzzy active contour models in image segmentation with a discussion.
Optical satellite imagery is a valuable source of information for greenhouse detection.
However, manually drawing bounding boxes around greenhouses is a tedious and time-consuming task.
In this paper, we present a deep learning-based approach to automatically segment greenhouses from high-resolution optical satellite imagery.
Our approach employs a U-Net architecture, trained on a large dataset of manually annotated images.
We evaluate our method on a separate test dataset, and compare it to a traditional machine learning approach, as well as to manual segmentation.

Our results show that our deep learning-based approach achieves a high accuracy and significantly reduces the time required for segmentation, making it a powerful tool for greenhouse detection on optical satellite imagery.
Recent progress in deep learning allows training models to learn image segmentation from labeled images, but training data with ground truth is often not available in practice.
Unsupervised learning offers a appealing alternative but learning meaningful representations of images without guidance remains challenging.
In this paper, we exploit differentiable kernel clustering as a building block for learning an effective image representation without any labels.
Our method clusters image patches in a way that captures local structures and, at the same time, is differentiable with respect to the inputs.
This property enables training by minimizing an appropriate energy function on a graph, which is defined by the image gradients.
We show that the resulting algorithm is capable of simultaneously clustering image patches and segmenting the image in a supervised manner, given only the image itself as input.
We evaluate our approach on the semantic segmentation of natural images and show that it achieves state-of-the-art performance in terms of segmentation quality.

Recent advances in superpixel-based segmentation have relied on a fully-supervised setting, where both the segmentations and the soft labels (i.e., the probability images) are available during training.
In many real-world applications, including medical imaging, fully-supervised training data are difficult to obtain, and manual labeling is expensive and time-consuming.
We overcome this limitation by introducing a new training scheme for superpixel-based segmentation, which only requires hard segmentations as training labels.
Our method is based on a softening of the hard labels via a supervised contrastive loss, which is learned by leveraging image pairs.

We show that our approach, named superpixel-guided label softening (SGLS), compares favorably to the state-of-the-art on three public benchmarks for cardiac and abdominal imaging, where only hard segmentations are available.
Code is available at https://github.com/CVMI-Lab/SGLS.
Recent advances in medical imaging, such as MRI, have been instrumental in the diagnosis and treatment of various medical conditions.
However, the sensitive nature of medical data has prompted the need for secure and effective image segmentation techniques.
In this paper, we propose BUNET, a blind medical image segmentation framework based on the Secure UNet architecture.
BUNET combines the security and privacy of blind segmentation with the effectiveness of deep learning to provide a robust and efficient solution to medical image segmentation.
In our approach, we utilize a secure artificial intelligence (AI) module that performs blind segmentation on encrypted image data.
The module is trained using unlabeled, encrypted image data and a small amount of labeled, encrypted image data.

During training, the encrypted image data is processed within the secure AI module, which prevents the exposure of the raw image data to the outside world, including the trainer and other participants in the training process.
Our proposed method is evaluated on a public dataset, and we compare its performance with that of a conventional UNet.
The results show that BUNET achieves a similar performance to the UNet while providing the additional security and privacy benefits of blind segmentation.
We believe that our proposed method can be widely used in various medical image segmentation tasks, particularly in situations where data privacy and security are crucial.
By combining the strengths of deep learning and blind segmentation, BUNET presents a practical and effective solution towards secure and private medical image segmentation.
Superpixel segmentation is a fundamental step for many computer vision applications.
In this paper, we present an efficient superpixel segmentation approach based on dynamic and iterative spanning forests.
Our method leverages the benefits of both pixel-level and region-level information, combining the advantages of traditional pixel-based segmentation techniques and recent region-based methods.

Specifically, we iteratively construct a spanning forest over an evolving graph, where each node represents a pixel and each edge encodes appearance and spatial similarities between neighboring pixels.
By dynamically updating the spanning forest at each iteration, our method is able to capture the gradual convergence of the segmentation process.
We evaluate our approach on several benchmark datasets, and the results demonstrate its effectiveness and efficiency compared to state-of-the-art superpixel segmentation methods.
We present a new approach to image segmentation based on recent advances in interactive segmentation using particles.
The scheme utilizes the intuitive concept of region competition and cooperation, formed by the spatial distribution of particles.
We construct a complex network from the particle system, and the segmentation is achieved by partitioning the network into independent components.
Specifically, the nodes of the network are the particles, and the edges are determined by the relative spatial distributions of the particles.
Particles that are close to each other are connected with high affinity, while those that are further apart are connected with less affinity.
The partitioning of the network is achieved by assigning a label to each node based on the affinity of its neighboring nodes.
The labeling is performed using a modified version of the Fortune algorithm, which takes into account the affinity between nodes.
The segmentation is refined by allowing particles to move and change their affinity with their neighbors in response to user input.
The scheme is fully automatic, and the only user input required is to draw a few lines to define the regions of interest.
The approach is shown to be effective and efficient on a variety of images, including those with complex shapes and textures.

Abstract
This paper presents an automated pavement crack segmentation approach using a U-Net-based convolutional neural network (CNN).
The U-Net architecture, developed for biomedical image processing, is adapted to pavement crack image segmentation.
The proposed method consists of three steps: image acquisition, preprocessing, and crack segmentation using a U-Net-based CNN.
In the image acquisition step, pavement images are collected using a vehicle-mounted mobile device.
In the preprocessing step, the images are preprocessed to enhance the contrast and reduce noise.
In the segmentation step, the U-Net-based CNN is utilized to automatically segment the pavement cracks.
The proposed method was evaluated using a large dataset of pavement images collected from different roads.
The results show that the proposed method can effectively segment pavement cracks with high accuracy.
The proposed method reduces the workload and improves the efficiency of pavement crack segmentation.
We present a fully automated segmentation algorithm that simultaneously detects regions, edges, and contours within image structures.
The proposed method is based on a deep neural network that learns to predict pixel-level labels for different segmentation tasks from image structures.
The network is composed of multiple modules, including a region module for region segmentation, an edge module for edge detection, and a contour module for contour detection.

The modules are designed to work jointly and to produce compatible predictions, enabling the network to reason about the relationships between different segmentation tasks and to leverage the strengths of different tasks for improved performance.
We train the network using a novel loss function that combines region, edge, and contour segmentation losses, as well as a regularization loss based on image smoothness.

The proposed method is evaluated on a public dataset, and results show that the joint learning of region, edge, and contour information leads to improved segmentation performance compared to single-task approaches.

Deep learning has enabled rapid advances in facial analysis, but most studies focus on learning a single deformable shape model across a variety of poses, while the variation of shapes across pose is often ignored.

We argue that shape variations associated with pose are important, and learn a deformable shape model that discovers the underlying factor structure of shape variations within and across poses, while constraining the factor loading to be pose-invariant.

Our framework, which we term Constrained Mixtures of Factor Analyzers (CMFA), models intra-class shape variations as a mixture of factor analyzers, and inter-class differences via a logistic mixture model.
We learn the entire CMFA model end-to-end, with novel off-the-shelf loss functions for the various components.
In a series of experiments, we show our model outperforms strong baseline methods in terms of accuracy and shape diversity for recognition, and runs in reasonable time.
Abstract: We present a fully-convolutional neural network (FCNN) architecture for joint segmentation of medical images: ACNN.
Architectures are described for the two major medical image types: scalar images (e.g., MRI) and vectorized images (e.g., CT).
For scalar images, an adaptive pooling module enables the network to handle images of different resolutions, while a multichannel input enables effective utilization of multi-contrast MRI scans.
For vectorized images, a hybrid FCNN architecture is proposed to handle both axial and coronal slices.

We evaluate ACNN on four public medical image segmentation benchmarks, ISBI 2011 Liver Tumor Segmentation, ISBI 2013 Pancreas Segmentation, MIAS 2016 Liver and Lung Segmentation, and 2018 Cardiac Tissue Segmentation, and achieve top performance on all datasets, significantly improving over the state-of-the-art.
In particular, on the MIAS 2016 Liver and Lung Segmentation dataset, our method achieves a high segmentation F1-score of 92.43%, significantly outperforming the next best method by 5.7%.
Code is available at: https://github.com/DLTMI/ACNN.

Automated image segmentation is a crucial step in the analysis of concrete petrographic images, as it involves the identification and classification of different types of grains and voids in the images.
In this paper, we present a deep learning-based approach to automated image segmentation that uses a U-Net neural network architecture to achieve accurate and efficient segmentation.
The U-Net model is trained on a large dataset of concrete petrographic images and learns to segment the images based on the grain and void structures present in the images.
We evaluate the performance of the U-Net model on a separate test dataset and compare its performance to that of a traditional threshold-based segmentation approach.
The results show that the U-Net model is able to achieve significantly better segmentation accuracy and efficiency compared to the traditional approach.

The proposed method has the potential to significantly reduce the time and effort required for concrete petrographic analysis, and could be applied to a wide range of image analysis tasks in the field of materials science.
Recent works in image segmentation commonly utilize multi-task learning to improve the performance of pixel-level classification.
We propose a novel approach to multi-task learning for image segmentation, which we refer to as recursive approximation tasks.
Our method forms a chain of tasks, where each subsequent task approximates the output of the previous one.
At the first level of the chain, we have a coarse segmentation, and at the last level, we obtain the final segmentation.
We show that our approach allows us to learn a better segmentation in a shorter amount of training time compared to the state-of-the-art methods on the Cityscapes and Mapillary Vistas datasets.

We evaluate our method on four benchmark datasets (Cityscapes, Mapillary Vistas, CamVid, and Scannet) in terms of segmentation quality and training speed, and show its superiority via quantitative comparisons with other state-of-the-art methods.
Our code is available at https://github.com/autonomousvision/cat_plus_moc.
We present a novel semi-supervised segmentation model, which we refer to as TransCon, that is designed to address the issues of lacking training data for medical image segmentation.
TransCon learns a transformation consistent self-ensembling (TCSE) model that leverages abundant unlabeled data to enhance the segmentation performance of a given labeled data.

We employ a canonical correlation analysis (CCA) to find the maximal linear correlation between the labeled and unlabeled data, and then use the learned transformation to project the labeled images onto a new feature space where the distributions of the labeled and unlabeled data can be artificially made similar.
We then train a segmentation model on the augmented data in the new feature space.

Since the transformation is learned from the whole dataset, including the labeled and unlabeled data, the segmentation performance on the labeled data can be improved without losing its generalization capability to the unlabeled data.
We evaluate our method on the ISBI challenge 2016 semi-supervised segmentation benchmark.
In comparison to the current state-of-the-art methods, our method achieves a 12.2% relative improvement in dice coefficient on the test set of the abdominal dataset without any training data leakage.
Recent few-shot segmentation approaches leverage extensive image annotations to learn image-level embeddings and generate segmentations for new images.

These methods tend to fail when the intrinsic structure of objects in images differs from the annotated images, as is the case when objects are photographed from different viewpoints, occlusions, or backgrounds.
In this work, we propose SimPropNet, a viewpoint-invariant few-shot segmentation model.

It learns a similarity metric in a self-supervised manner from the image-level embeddings of the base classes and effectively leverages the available support images at test time to accurately localize objects in the query images.

We propagate the similarity from the support images to the query image via a novel attention mechanism that selectively focuses on the support regions that are most informative for few-shot segmentation.
This enables our method to effectively segment objects in query images that are viewed from different viewpoints than the support images.

We validate the effectiveness of our approach on both the PASCAL VOC 2012 and Cityscapes segmentation benchmarks with few-shot segmentation settings, where we outperform the state-of-the-art by a large margin.
We present a deep learning based approach to automatically segment nerve fibers in corneal confocal microscopic images using a spatially constrained U-Net.
Our approach achieves this while utilizing only inaccurate bounding box annotations for training.

We demonstrate that significant segmentation performance can be achieved with a relatively small number of training samples when the network is constrained to the spatial support of the ground truth bounding boxes while being invariant to their accurate placement.
We achieve a macro-averaged F1-score of 0.91, significantly outperforming previous state-of-the-art methods.
Code for our approach is available at https://github.com/Seyed-Mohsen/U-Net-for-Nerve-Fiber-Segmentation.

Towards panoptic segmentation, which simultaneously segmenting objects and assigning them instance IDs, a recent trend is toward encoding semantic attributes, such as objectness and borderness, to improve performance.

We find that existing works either omit or only partially encode important but secondary attributes, such as similarity to background and similarity to other objects, which could provide additional useful information.
In this work, we propose a simple, effective, and modular network, called the generator evaluator-selector (GES) net, to jointly encode nine semantic attributes for improved panoptic segmentation.

We show that the GES net improves performance of state-of-the-art methods on the cityscapes dataset, and can be integrated with existing works to improve performance with only negligible increase in computational cost.
Semantic image segmentation of urban street scenes is a fundamental step towards intelligent transportation systems.
In this paper, we present a real-time high-performance method for semantic image segmentation of urban street scenes.
Our method is based on a deep learning architecture called Convolutional Neural Network (CNN).
We use a pre-trained CNN model trained on the ImageNet dataset to extract features from the input images.
We then fine-tune the CNN model on a new dataset specifically designed for semantic image segmentation of urban street scenes.
Our method achieves accurate segmentation results and runs in real-time, making it suitable for applications such as autonomous driving and traffic monitoring.
We present a novel framework for multi-class semantic segmentation, named RSS-Net, which is trained with a weakly-supervised learning strategy that utilizes an FMCW radar.

To overcome the lack of sufficiently annotated images, we exploit the complementary information from radar, which acquires implicit semantic segmentation information in the form of range and Doppler measurements.
These measurements are then converted into image-like representations as regional features and fed into a convolutional neural network (CNN) for training.
We evaluate our method on the Cityscapes dataset and demonstrate that the proposed method achieves promising results compared to the state-of-the-art semi-weakly-supervised methods.

Gen-LaneNet: A Generalized and Scalable Approach for 3D Lane Detection

We propose a general and scalable approach for 3D lane detection, called Gen-LaneNet, which is able to detect lanes from a variety of 3D point cloud datasets, without any prior knowledge of the specific dataset.
Our approach is based on a deep neural network that takes a 3D point cloud as input and outputs a set of lane boundaries.
The network is composed of a encoder and a decoder, which are based on the PointNet and DecagonNet architectures, respectively.
The encoder extracts a set of features from the input point cloud, while the decoder uses these features to output the final lane boundaries.
Our approach is designed to be general and scalable, so that it can be easily extended to detect lanes in new datasets.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on two public datasets, and show that it outperforms the state-of-the-art in 3D lane detection.

Recent works have shown that the latent space of variational autoencoders (VAEs) can be used for out-of-distribution (OOD) detection, by monitoring the distance between the encoded vectors in the validation set and the data distribution in the latent space.
In this work, we argue that such techniques cannot be directly applied to multi-label datasets, as the latent space of standard VAEs is not guaranteed to be well-conditioned w.r.t.
the label information.
To overcome this limitation, we propose to use the latent space of $β$-VAEs, for which we prove that the label information is indeed well-conditioned.
We conduct a comprehensive evaluation of our method in the context of image classification, leveraging three different datasets, and a realistic simulation of OOD data.
Our experimental results show the effectiveness of the proposed approach compared to the state-of-the-art.
Recent results on image segmentation could be improved both in accuracy and efficiency, especially when only a small amount of labeled data is available.
In this paper, we exploit self-correcting networks (SCN) to boost the performance of semantic image segmentation.

We train SCNs in an semi-supervised learning setting, where a small amount of labeled data is available for training, and exploit a large amount of unlabeled data to implicitly learn to correct the segmentation errors.
Specifically, we train two SCNs, one produces segmentation maps with only pixel-level supervision, and the other produces segmentation maps by refining the former with image-level supervision.
We show that the latter can be effectively trained with only unlabeled data.
In the experimental part, we demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method on the PASCAL VOC 2012 segmentation benchmark.
Without using any extra training data, our method achieves 78.3% mean accuracy on the VOC 2012 test set, which is a relative improvement of 2.7% over the state-of-the-art.
Brain tumor segmentation refers to the process of identifying and distinguishing tumor regions from healthy ones in MRI scans, which is of primary importance in clinical oncology practice.
Recently, deep learning models have been successfully applied to this task.
However, existing methods usually concentrate on either appearance or texture information, and only a few of them consider both modalities, which limits their performance in challenging cases.
In this paper, we present a novel approach to robust brain tumor segmentation via feature disentanglement and gated fusion.

Our solution can not only effectively leverage both appearance and texture information from multimodal images but also disentangle the trustworthy features from the unreliable ones, which is achieved by a gate module.

Specifically, we design a sparse-matching based gate module to assess the reliability of the features from each modality, and the features passing the gate can be fused together for final segmentation.
Experimental results on a public dataset validate the effectiveness of our approach compared to the state-of-the-art methods.

We introduce a new image segmentation framework called PointRend, which models image segmentation as a rendering problem, where the goal is to assign appropriate colors to the pixels of an input image based on the image's structure and existing object boundaries.
PointRend extends an existing approach called Semantic Softpooling, which uses a deep neural network to produce a soft segmentation label image that emphasizes regions with object boundaries.
These regions are then refined using a novel post-processing procedure involving a rendering step that assigns colors to pixels based on their proximity to object boundaries.
We show that the rendering step can be optimized end-to-end using a gradient descent algorithm that minimizes rendering energy.

This optimization procedure produces a segmentation that improves upon the input to the network and approaches the performance of a fully supervised energy-based method without requiring any ground truth segmentations at training time.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on the Cityscapes and CamVid datasets, obtaining state-of-the-art results.
Abdominal CT images provide fine-grained details of the liver anatomy, which is widely used for clinical diagnosis and intervention.
However, the complex anatomical structures in CT images make liver segmentation a challenging task, even for expert radiologists.
In this paper, we present an auto-context neural network together with a self-supervised contour attention module to address the segmentation challenge.

The auto-context module captures the global context by aggregating all positions and channels of the input features, while the self-supervised contour attention module is designed to capture the contour information of the objects, without any additional contour information in the training phase.
We evaluate our method on the 2018 ISBI Liver Segmentation Challenge.

Compared to the state-of-the-art methods, our approach produces segmentation results with better accuracy and spatial coherence, ultimately improving the F1-score from 87.1% to 89.4% on the challenge dataset.
Unsupervised learning allows computational finding of intrinsic patterns in data without explicit alignment to known structures.

We present an unsupervised learning framework for the discovery of communities in transactional data, such as found in electronic medical records, collaborative filtering systems, and social networks.

Our framework addresses the problem of detecting communities in a sparse transactional data matrix where each row and column corresponds to an entity (e.g., a patient, user, or peer) and each sparse element indicates a transaction (e.g., a diagnosis, a movie rating, or a communication).
The problem is inherently unsupervised because there is no known ground truth for communities; computational approaches must mine for communities without any alignment to known structures.
Compared to previous work, we propose a new precise definition for the quality of a community detection mapping in terms of popular visualization techniques.
This allows a direct evaluation of the quality of a detected mapping without relying on external ground truth.
We then present a novel algorithm for community detection that is shown via theoretic analysis and experiments to precisely optimize this quality function.

Finally, we demonstrate the utility of our approach on a real-world, large-scale transactional dataset from digital pathology, where we discover previously unknown structures in tissue whole-slide images.
We consider the problem of minimizing a submodular function plus a convex penalty term, subject to a cardinality constraint on a subset of the variables.
This problem generalizes many classic problems in combinatorial optimization, including the famous vertex cover problem.
We give a simple and intuitive linear programming (LP) based algorithm for this problem, which translates the non-convex submodular objective into a convex one.
This allows us to apply standard LP solvers, such as the simplex method or interior point methods.
We show that our algorithm is robust, i.e., it continues to produce an optimal solution even if the submodular function is modified by a small additive error.
We perform a thorough experimental evaluation of our algorithm on a wide variety of instances drawn from the vertex cover problem, set cover problem, and a cooperative modeling application.
This evaluation demonstrates the effectiveness and robustness of our approach.

We show that deep-learning-based segmentation methods based on convolutional neural networks (CNN) with access to a large, labeled image atlas can achieve nearly perfect generalization performance when trained with only a few labeled examples.

Our main result is that CNNs for segmentation can be trained with a number of labeled examples that is several orders of magnitude smaller than what would be needed using other approaches, such as superpixels or textures.
We show that this advantage arises because the CNN learns to exploit global, anatomical structures present in the images, which provides substantial regularization.

This is a radical departure from the standard deep-learning approach of training on very large datasets, and it opens up new possibilities for training deep-learning systems on resource-limited platforms, such as smartphones, laptops, or small servers.

Our experiments show that the error of our optimized, sparse-training CNN is only 5.7% relative to that of a fully-trained CNN that uses all available training data, despite having only 1/500 as many labeled pixels.
Recent works on video semantic segmentation usually treat each frame in a video as independent, which ignores the temporal redundancy among the frames.
In this paper, we propose a novel framework to exploit the temporal redundancy for accurate video segmentation.
Given a video of arbitrary length, our framework first propagate the labels from the reference frame to other frames through a learned propagation network.
Then, we refine the predicted results of each frame through a refinement network to obtain the segmentation results of the frame.
We optimize the objective functions of the propagation and refinement networks respectively during training.
Experimental results on the Vimeo90K dataset show that our method outperforms the state-of-the-art approaches.
Code is available at: this https URL.
In this paper, we present a multi-focus image fusion method based on the similarity characteristics of images.

In order to measure the similarity between the reference image and the target image, the traditional image fusion algorithm converts the RGB image into the YCbCr color space, and the luminance channel is extracted for processing.
Due to the ambiguity of the YCbCr color space, the similarity measurement between the reference image and the target image has some errors.

In order to solve this problem, we propose a method for similarity measurement between images based on the deep learning framework, which can extract more image details and obtain more accurate measurement results.
Then, we construct a multi-focus image fusion model based on the similarity characteristics of images, which can better preserve the details of the image and improve the quality of the fused image.
Finally, we conduct comprehensive experiments on the UC-Merced dataset to validate the effectiveness of the proposed method.
The results show that the proposed method can achieve better performance in terms of peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR), structural similarity (SSIM), and visual effect.

Recent progress in representation learning has achieved remarkable results in many computer vision tasks, but the obtained models are usually trained on large-scale datasets and require a large amount of memory to store the intermediate results.
In this paper, we present OASIS, a new approach for efficient memory-saving representation learning for image segmentation.

Given a set of images, OASIS trains a shared atlas representation in a one-pass manner, simultaneously learning segmentations for all images, and producing an aligned atlas set that significantly reduces the memory cost while retaining the accuracy.

OASIS is built upon a simple yet effective idea: producing an aligned set of atlases such that each atlas provides dense correspondences to all images in the dataset, and then learning a shared representation across these atlases.
We provide a theoretical analysis to guide the design of our algorithm, and prove that OASIS converges to the optimal solution given sufficient iterations.

We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on three public segmentation benchmarks, where OASIS achieves comparable or even better performance compared with the state-of-the-art, while using less memory and being more efficient.
Recent progress in 3D medical image segmentation has primarily relied on supervised learning approaches, in which a large amount of labeled expert-drawn contours are used to train a model.
This process can be time-consuming and expensive, which motivates the investigation of assisted segmentation frameworks where the expert's time is used efficiently.
In this paper, we present an assisted segmentation framework where a multi-agent reinforcement learning system iteratively refines a preliminary segmentation in an interactive manner with a user.
In each iteration, the user provides sparse label updates through a GUI by pointing at voxels and pushing a button to indicate if the voxel should be added or removed from the segmentation.

Our multi-agent system consists of a primary agent that predicts expected label updates based on the user's input, and multiple secondary agents that attempt to predict the user's input given the current context.
Secondary agents are explicitly trained to mimic the user's behavior in that they incentivize the same action as the user on the same voxels given the current context.

The rewards are tuned such that the primary agent is incentivized to produce label predictions that match the user's input, and secondary agents are incentivized to produce inputs that match the user's actual input.
Consequently, the primary agent improves over time, as do the secondary agents.

Because the secondary agents are trained using only the user's input, they can be successfully used to initialize the primary agent on a new dataset, thus enabling the model to quickly adapt to new cases.
We present experiments on both synthetic and real MRI brain images that demonstrate the efficacy of our approach compared to single-agent models.
We present a computerized method for threat recognition within 3D CT images for baggage security screening.
An adaptive algorithm is presented that analyzes 3D CT slices, applies a series of feature extraction filters, and automatically recognizes threat items.
The system is designed to be an auxiliary tool for mitigating the workload of a human operator who ultimately makes the final decision.
In order to train the system, a database of 3D CT slices is created containing a broad range of potential threat and non-threat items.
Each slice is labeled by an expert operator and serves as the training data set.
A variety of features are extracted from each slice of the training data, and a threat recognition algorithm is developed using a probabilistic approach.

In order to mitigate the effect of highly variable positioning of bags within the CT scanner, an adaptive algorithm is developed that accurately registers the 3D CT slices to a reference coordinate system.
Registration is important because the features used for threat recognition are position dependent.
The adaptive registration algorithm utilizes a prior threat map to reduce the search space and increase accuracy.
Thus, the system is able to adapt to variations in bag positioning while retaining a high degree of accuracy.
Image segmentation is the process of partitioning an image into multiple segments.
It has various applications in many fields, ranging from object extraction in images to medical image analysis.
While there exist many segmentation algorithms, most of them do not provide a measure of quality for the produced segmentation.

In this paper, we introduce the Quality Assurance Network (QANet), a deep learning architecture to predict the quality of segmentation output, given the input image and the corresponding ground truth.
We propose to use a pair of segmentation models with symmetric architectures and an additional symmetric quality prediction model.
Our quality prediction model is trained to predict whether the segmentation result is correct and the ground truth is incorrect or vice versa.
We train all models using a multi-task learning approach to ensure that the predicted quality scores are closely aligned with human perception.
We evaluate our approach on the Cityscapes dataset and achieve significant improvements over the state-of-the-art.
Further, we provide an extensive analysis on how our method deals with difficult segments and the relations between the quality predictions and the human-annotated quality scores.

We present a novel gated conditional random field (CRF) loss for weakly supervised semantic image segmentation, which combines the benefits of supervised and unsupervised training while mitigating their respective shortcomings.
Whereas supervised segmentation typically provides precise but sparse training labels, unsupervised methods exhibit smooth but inconsistent predictions.

By conditioning the CRF on a mask obtained from a segmentation confidence map, we provide stronger guidance to the model where it is more uncertain, producing more consistent and accurate segmentations.
Furthermore, our method is able to explicitly leverage additional supervision, despite its noise, to further improve performance.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on the PASCAL VOC 2012 semantic image segmentation benchmark, obtaining state-of-the-art performance.
Code is available at https://github.com/NVlabs/paced-crf.
We propose a novel framework for the segmentation of liver tissues in 3D ultrasound images based on a deeply self-supervised contour embedded neural network (CDC-ENet).
The proposed method utilizes a contour embedding technique to effectively capture the contextual information of the input images, which is further enriched by a multi-scale aggregation module.

Within the proposed framework, the self-supervised learning mechanism enables the network to learn robust features from the raw image data without the need for manual annotation, which is particularly beneficial for the scarce medical image datasets.

The performance of the proposed method was evaluated on a public dataset, where it achieved a mean Dice similarity coefficient of 95.1% on the segmentations of the liver tissues, outperforming the state-of-the-art methods.
Post-mortem identification is an important task of forensic science, and the iris is a biologically unique region for human identification.
However, the process of post-mortem iris image segmentation is extremely challenging due to the absence of ocular illumination and specularity.
In this paper, we propose a deep learning based approach for post-mortem iris image segmentation, which is lightweight and efficient.
Our approach is composed of a coarse segmentation network, which is a lightweight ResNet18 with an attention module, and a refined segmentation network, which is a U-Net with an attention module.
We train our networks using a hybrid loss function, which combines dice loss and mse loss.
Our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on a public post-mortem iris image segmentation benchmark while being much faster than other approaches.
In addition, we have collected the first post-mortem iris image dataset, which contains 5,552 images from 154 donors with different post-mortem times.
Large model support is critical for TensorFlow to manage ever-growing machine learning models.
We present a systematic approach to building large models in TensorFlow by graph rewriting.
This approach is designed to work with existing TensorFlow code and APIs, and it does not require changes to the TensorFlow source code.
We introduce a new API that allows users to specify rewrite rules for TensorFlow graphs.
We then present a series of rewrite rules that can be used to efficiently execute large models on hardware accelerators.
The rewrite rules can be combined in different ways to support a variety of model sizes and hardware configurations.
We present an evaluation of our approach on a large-scale image recognition model and show that it can achieve significant speedups over the original model.
Recent advances in 4D MRI imaging have made it possible to longitudinally acquire whole-tumor MRI volumes as a 4D dataset, with each 4D-volume acquired over several minutes, for a given patient.

However, due to the limitation of computational resources, it is challenging to utilize the 4D dataset for tumor growth prediction, which requires modeling the complex spatio-temporal correlations and the varying growth rates across different patients.

In this paper, we propose a novel Spatio-Temporal Convolutional LSTM (STCL) model, which learns to predict tumor growth rates by utilizing both spatial and temporal information from the 4D longitudinal patient data.

We introduce a spatio-temporal convolutional layer, which performs 3D convolution on each slice of the 4D volume, and a stack of LSTM layers that model the temporal dependencies at each spatial location.

We optimize the entire STCL model using a stacked sparse-reward learning framework, which incorporates a sparse-reward structure to push the model towards learning the sparse representations of the highly varying growth rates.

Finally, we evaluate our method on a large dataset of 4D MRI longitudinal volumes from glioblastoma patients, and show that our method achieves significant performance improvement over the state-of-the-art.
We present a framework for phase-aware collaborative segmentation of images, with application to hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) stained histopathology images.

In the absence of ground truth for the challenging task of pixel-level segmentation of histopathology images, we leverage collaborations among multiple annotators, where each annotator benefits from the annotations of other annotators.
In order to encourage collaboration, we design a loss function that enforces agreement among collaborating annotators.

To handle the variability in annotations among different annotators, we propose a phase-aware collaborative network that encourages agreement in the early phases of annotation, but allows for more diversity in later phases.
Our phase-aware collaborative network is trained in a distributed fashion, where each annotator only communicates with a small subset of other annotators.
We demonstrate the efficacy of our method on a public H&E stained histopathology image dataset, where we achieve a significant improvement in segmentation quality compared to baseline methods.
In this paper, we propose a novel automatic image pixel clustering based on mussels wandering optimization (MWO).
Compared with the traditional K-means clustering algorithm, the proposed method can produce more accurate clustering results.
In the proposed method, we represent the pixel values of an image by a set of random features, and then MWO is used to optimize the clustering results according to the random features.
By adjusting the random features, the proposed method can produce more accurate clustering results.
Moreover, a series of experimental results show that the proposed method can produce more accurate clustering results than the K-means algorithm.
Introduction: In this paper, a novel image pixel clustering algorithm based on mussels wandering optimization (MWO) is proposed.
Compared to traditional K-means clustering algorithms, the proposed method can produce more accurate results.
It represents pixel values as random features in an image, and then MWO optimizes the clustering results based on these random features.
The proposed method can produce more accurate clustering results by adjusting these random features.
In addition, we present a series of experimental results to show the superiority of the proposed method over the traditional K-means algorithm.

We present a customizable architecture search method for semantic segmentation.

Unlike existing works which adopt an architecture search strategy specific to the design space, our approach allows the user to customize the search process with different strategies, including evolutionary algorithms (EAs) and reinforcement learning (RL).
To achieve this, we first formulate the architecture search as a meta learning problem, such that different search strategies can be used to optimize the same objective.
We then develop a meta trainer that learns a good policy network from a user specified search strategy in a few iterations.
With the policy network, the search strategy is then fine-tuned within a few more iterations to find the optimal architecture.

We show that our approach allows the user to not only customize the search process, but also achieve better performance compared to the state of the art methods on the Cityscapes dataset with MobileNetV2 as the backbone.
Code is available at https://github.com/microsoft/arch_search_semseg.
We present a novel approach to weakly supervised image segmentation based on a deep geodesic prior learned from a sparse set of annotated images.
Our approach leverages the geometric structure of the scene as captured by the deep prior to propagate labels across images in a self-supervised manner.
We introduce a new loss function that optimizes the predicted labels by enforcing agreement with the geodesic distances predicted by the deep prior.
We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach on the challenging task of segmenting pixels in 20 classes from a weak supervisory signal in the form of image-level labels.
Our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on the PASCAL VOC 2012 segmentation benchmark.
We introduce a novel framework for parsing freehand sketches composed of line drawings and composed shapes.
We tackle the parsing problem in the wild, where the shapes and their compositions in the sketch are not predefined and can take any form.
To this end, we design a deep fully convolutional neural network that directly predicts a pixel-wise labeling of the sketch, treating the parsing problem as a pixel-level classification task.
This approach allows our network to be parse-free, in that it does not require training examples of specific parsings of the sketch.

In order to handle the variability and ambiguity of sketches in the wild, we propose a new architecture, SFSegNet, which is based on dilated fully convolutional networks and incorporates both shape and composition cues within a single architecture.

We present a deep learning based approach for the segmentation of nuclei in immunofluorescence images.
We address the lack of large-scale annotated training data by employing a data generation strategy that utilizes a database of segmented cells.
We first train a deep learning based edge detector to locally refine the segmentation of cells.
In a second step, the detected edges are used as strong image features for a pixel-based segmentation.
We present a comparison of different deep learning architectures with respect to their performance and computational requirements.
We show that the proposed approach allows for segmenting images of high-throughput screens with varying fluorescence intensities, noise, and staining qualities.
Finally, we present a performance analysis of the proposed approach in terms of its generalization performance.

Recent progress in both the diagnostic efficacy of OCT and the advent of deep learning for OCT image analysis has paved the way for a more systematic and widespread use of OCT within the practice of ophthalmology.
In this work, we present a novel framework for OCT segmentation of retinal layers, which we call Adaptive CONtour-based Deep Architecture (ACONDA).

ACONDA leverages recent advances in both adaptive boundary prediction and entropy-driven adversarial learning to achieve state-of-the-art performance on the large-scale public dataset 1003G. In particular, through extensive experiments, we show that ACONDA achieves superior performance to the current state-of-the-art methods on four commonly used evaluation metrics.
Recent works on semantic segmentation with RGB-D sensors take a class-agnostic approach and segment objects in a per-pixel manner without explicit recognition of object classes.

In this paper, we argue that recognizing object classes could provide valuable prior knowledge for pixel-level segmentation, and designing a unified framework for both class discovery and segmentation could make the process more efficient and effective.
To this end, we propose a novel Incremental Class Discovery (ICD) framework for semantic segmentation with RGB-D sensing.
It incrementally discovers object classes while simultaneously refining pixel-level predictions.
Specifically, we formulate class discovery as a binary classification problem, where each class candidate is scored based on features computed from both the RGB and depth channels.
During training, our framework alternates between refining class predictions and updating pixel-level predictions.
We show that the proposed ICD framework is able to discover object classes and yield state-of-the-art segmentation performance on the NYU Depth V2 dataset.
We present a new model for video segmentation that adapts convolutional LSTM architectures for efficient inference.
Our model uses a separable convolutional architecture that reduces the computational requirements by factor of four without a noticeable drop in performance.

This is in contrast to state-of-the-art video segmentation models that use standard convolutional LSTM architectures and have a time complexity of O(N^2) in inference, where N is the number of pixels in the frame.

To achieve this, we use a simple yet effective strategy of breaking the convolutional LSTM layers into separable convolutions that approximately halve the computational complexity of the layer, whilst only losing a small amount of performance.
In addition, we propose a "Channel-Wise ConvLSTM" layer to reduce the number of parameters and computations.

We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on the Cityscapes and CamVid datasets, where we achieve a 77.3% FPS gain with a 2.7% drop in mIOU over the state-of-the-art CULane model with a similar architecture.

Understanding deep networks via interpretable models has attracted growing attention, but existing methods either result in high computational complexity or output interpretations that are not faithful enough to the original network.

In this paper, we propose a novel Divide-and-Conquer strategy that aims to interpret deep networks by dividing the interpretation task into smaller sub-problems, which can be solved efficiently and effectively.
Our key insight is that the interpretations of individual layers in a deep network contain certain structural information that can be utilized to infer the interpretations of the entire network.
We formalize this idea as a specific Divide-and-Conquer problem, for which we propose an efficient algorithm to solve it.
Finally, we conduct experiments on a number of benchmark datasets, and the results demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed approach.
We present a novel approach to axon-myelin segmentation on histology images based on deep active learning.

Our method leverages the power of deep learning algorithms to learn a robust feature representation from a sparse set of training examples, and an active learning strategy to query the most informative training examples to improve the segmentation performance.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on a large dataset of histology images, and show that our method outperforms the state-of-the-art in axon-myelin segmentation.
Our approach can be applied to other image segmentation tasks, and has the potential to significantly reduce the amount of manual labeling required for training deep learning models.
We introduce a novel external memory algorithm for computing maximum flow in dense graph, which arises in image segmentation.
Our algorithm is based on the push-relabel algorithm but incorporates several new ideas.
We use an innovative data structure, called dual-directed binary heap, for efficient vertex relabeling.
This allows us to limit the frequency of expensive vertex relabeling operations, and leads to significant performance improvement.
Our algorithm also includes a new compact representation for the adjacency matrix, as well as a simple and efficient mechanism for maintaining and updating the adjacency matrix.
In particular, our algorithm does not need to construct the adjacency matrix explicitly, and has near-linear time complexity in the number of vertices for the underlying sparse graph.

We show that the max-flow algorithm attains a linear convergence rate, and the overall segmentation algorithm has a linear convergence rate in the number of pixels when the image is segmented using the max-flow algorithm.
We present a partially reversible U-Net for memory-efficient volumetric image segmentation that reduces the memory footprint compared to the original U-Net architecture while maintaining performance.
The proposed network incorporates reversible layers, enabling the computation of intermediate features on-the-fly without storing them entirely in memory.

We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach on the challenging task of volumetric image segmentation, achieving favorable results compared to the original U-Net architecture while reducing the memory usage by up to 50%.
The proposed network is especially advantageous for memory-constrained environments, enabling the segmentation of large volumetric images that were previously inaccessible.
Many works in computer vision have applied data augmentation for training models that generalize to unseen domains.
In this paper, we question whether data augmentation is always needed for good generalization.
surpris-ingly, we find that for some datasets with synthetic data, data augmentation can even hurt model generalization.
We show that this is because the augmentation is already implicitly inside the data generation process, rendering the standard data augmentation procedure unnecessary and even detrimental.

Based on this insight, we propose a simple data preprocessing method that removes the augmentation from the training data, and demonstrates improved generalization performance on both synthetic and real-world data.
Our code and dataset are available at https://github.com/AI4Finance-Foundation/FinSAIGeneration.
Deep learning-based label fusion methods have become a vital component for effective and robust multi-atlas segmentation.
However, most existing methods rely on hand-crafted features, which limits their performance.
In this paper, we present VoteNet, a deep learning-based label fusion method for multi-atlas segmentation.
Instead of hand-crafted features, VoteNet utilizes a deep learning architecture to learn effective features directly from the data.
Our method is based on a simple yet effective idea: we train a deep neural network to learn a fusion function that takes as input the label maps from multiple atlases, and outputs a fused label map.
We train our network using a novel loss function that combines both the Dice coefficient and the Hausdorff distance, which allows us to optimize for both accuracy and spatial consistency.
Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on the challenging multi-atlas segmentation benchmark ISBI 2017.
Code is available at: https://github.com/ interpreteur/votenet.
We present a fast neural architecture search (NAS) algorithm for semantic segmentation.
In contrast to most prior work on NAS for image classification, we do not search for the final model architecture, but rather for a sub-network that is subsequently trained as an auxiliary cell.
This formulation allows us to apply many of the existing NAS algorithms designed for classification tasks with minimal changes.

We modify the categorical cross-entropy loss for segmentation by adding a consistency term that enforces similarity between the outputs of the auxiliary cell and the ground truth map, while keeping the classification loss unchanged.
This consistency regularization significantly improves the quality of the searched architectures without increasing the computational cost of search.
We perform an exhaustive search on CIFAR-FS and Cityscapes and show that our method finds architectures that are more accurate and significantly more compact than the prior art.
Code is available at https://github.com/tensorflow/tpu/tree/master/models/official/efficientnet.
We explore the problem of presentation attacks (PAs) on iris recognition systems.
PAs are typically made by modifying a live sample with a synthetic eye image, obtained from a database, that fools the recognition system into accepting an impostor as a legitimate user.
We propose a baseline approach to detect presentation attacks against iris recognition that is tailored to open source iris recognition software.
Our approach relies on testing a subject's iris against a database of enrolled irises without the subject's image ever being enrolled in the database.
Our baseline uses three heuristics based on the geometry of iris recognition and can detect some presentation attacks with as few as 50 enrolled irises.
We evaluate our approach on the OpenIRIS database.
Small target detection (SDT) plays a vital role in search and rescue (SAR) operations, especially in complex terrain.
However, the existing SDT algorithms face challenges in effectively detecting targets in cluttered and noisy environments.
In this paper, we propose a novel approach to SDT using distributed deep learning (DL) and synthetic data generation (SDG).
Our method utilizes a distributed DL framework to train a deep neural network (DNN) on a large dataset of synthetic images generated using SDG.
The synthetic data is generated by a computer-vision based simulation, which mimics the characteristics of real-world SAR images.

The proposed method is evaluated on a challenging dataset of real-world SAR images, and the results show that our approach significantly outperforms the state-of-the-art SDT algorithms in terms of both accuracy and speed.
Our method achieves an F1-score of 0.83, outperforming the previous state-of-the-art by 11.3%
In this paper, we study the problem of region homogeneity from a mathematical perspective.
We propose a new definition of region homogeneity based on the concept of logarithmic image processing.
Our definition is motivated by the observation that the logarithm of a pixel intensity value is a more robust representation of the pixel value in the presence of noise and interference.
This leads to a new framework for image processing based on logarithmic image spaces.
We show that the problem of region homogeneity can be formulated as a optimization problem in this new framework.
We propose an algorithm to solve the optimization problem and show that the solution is a continuous function of the input image.
We also show that the algorithm is applicable to region growing algorithms, which are commonly used in image processing and analysis.
Finally, we demonstrate the performance of our algorithm on a set of images and compare it with existing algorithms.
The results show that our algorithm is more robust to noise and interference and produces more accurate results.
We present a new approach for segmenting 3D tomography images of porous media, based on 3D quantum cuts.

This approach combines the 3D cut forest algorithm with recent advances in tomography image reconstruction, namely, the continuous positional and orientational ambiguity resolution via quantum transport.
We show that the 3D quantum cuts, via a simple data-driven cutoff, can provide a prior map for segmentation of the pore space.
In particular, we show that, given an appropriate threshold, the prior map is guaranteed to be non-empty, open, and connected.
Furthermore, the map can be evaluated rapidly, making it suitable for 3D segmentation of tomography images.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on synthetic and real tomography images.
Recent advances in medical imaging technology have led to large amounts of labeled image data for segmentation of anatomical structures.
However, annotating large-scale datasets is expensive, and this cost increases with the complexity of the images.
In this work, we focus on one-shot segmentation, where only a small labeled dataset of a specific modality and contrast is available.
We propose a data augmentation method that uses a generative adversarial network (GAN) to transform images from a given dataset to synthetic images from other modalities or contrasts.
We train a segmentation network with the augmented data and show that it generalizes better to unseen data than a network trained with the original data alone.
Our method is particularly useful for one-shot segmentation problems, where there is no opportunity for fine-tuning.
Recent progresses in MRI acquisition techniques have led to an explosion of big imaging data, posing a tremendous challenge for expert manual segmentation.

Meanwhile, compared with the abundant labeled images from different domains, the few-shot segmentation setting, where only a few images of specific domains are available for training, is more practical in real-world applications.
In this work, we exploit the intrinsic hierarchical structure of segmenting brain MR images from different domains with a deep heteroscedastic multi-task learning (HMT) framework.
Specifically, we design a weighted cross-entropy loss to incorporate the heteroscedastic noise of unlabeled data from different domains in an automatic manner.

Furthermore, to effectively utilize the limited labeled data, we propose a knowledge distillation strategy that explicitly trains a thinner student network with the learned knowledge from a thicker teacher network pre-trained on abundant data.
When trained on a few-shot setting, our method outperforms the state-of-the-art methods for brain MRI segmentation on multiple public datasets, including ISLES, LLC and ADNI.
The code is available at https://github.com/VITA-Group/Few-shot-brain-segmentation.
In this work, we propose a feature fusion encoder-decoder network (FE-Net) for automatic liver lesion segmentation.

The proposed method combines multi-scale features from multiple modalities, including computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), using a feature fusion encoder-decoder architecture.
The encoder utilizes shared learning across all modalities, while the decoder performs modality-specific segmentation.

We evaluate our method on the public available LLIA dataset, which contains 256 CT and 256 MRI slices of livers with and without lesions, and achieve a mean Dice similarity coefficient of 95.4% on the CT slices and 94.2% on the MRI slices.
MobileNetV2 is a family of image classification models of varying complexity, designed to improve the performance and efficiency of mobile vision applications.
It achieves this by improving the depth-wise convolutional layer of MobileNet to incorporate point-wise convolutional layers.
Additionally, it introduces a new layer called the linear bottleneck, which is a point-wise layer with a reduced number of output channels.
This allows the model to have a shallower network depth, reducing the number of parameters and computations, while still achieving a high level of performance.
The paper demonstrates the effectiveness of MobileNetV2 on multiple image classification benchmarks.
On the ImageNet dataset, the model achieves a top-1 accuracy of 86.6%, which is a 2.1% improvement over the original MobileNet.
Additionally, the model achieves a top-5 accuracy of 96.6%, outperforming the original MobileNet by 3.1%.
The paper also explores the use of the MobileNetV2 architecture in a variety of applications, including object detection, semantic segmentation, and image captioning.
In these tasks, the model demonstrates competitive performance, despite its reduced complexity.
The authors also conducted extensive experiments to evaluate the performance and efficiency of the model on various hardware platforms, including CPU, GPU, and mobile devices.
The paper concludes by discussing the potential for further research on the MobileNetV2 architecture.

The authors suggest that future work could focus on improving the model's performance in more complex and diverse datasets, as well as exploring the use of the model in other applications such as video classification and natural language processing.
We present an approach for the segmentation of roots in soil images using a U-Net architecture.
We use a supervised learning approach, in which a training set of soil images with manually segmented root regions is used to learn the optimal values of the weights and biases in the U-Net model.

During training, we utilize a root-specific loss function that encourages the network to learn features correlated with root regions while ignoring other objects typically found in soil images, such as stones and knots in the wood.
We evaluate the performance of our model on a separate test set of images and compare it to other state-of-the-art segmentation methods.
Our model achieves a high accuracy on the test set and is able to segment roots in a wide variety of images with varying soil conditions and root orientations.

Automatic segmentation of PET data into physiological regions and compartments, followed by use of these data for training, has the potential to overcome the lack of available CT-PET aligned datasets, and make it possible to train models that can exploit the additional information available in PET data.

In this work, we present a fully automatic method for segmenting 18F-FDG PET images into various physiological regions (blood, grey matter, white matter, and cerebrospinal fluid) and compartments (bound and free).
The segmentation is based on a convolutional neural network, trained using a small number of manually annotated images.

We show that the method is able to generalize well to unseen data, and that the automatically segmented images can be used to train a model for predicting corresponding CT values, while outperforming a model trained using only manually segmented images.
We present an approach for fine-grained semantic segmentation of motion capture (MOCAP) data.
Our method leverages the temporal coherence in MOCAP sequences to achieve improved segmentation performance.
We propose the use of dilated temporal fully-convolutional networks (DTFCN) to capture the long-range dependencies in the input sequences.
Our DTFCN is composed of a spatial stream, which performs segmentation of individual frames, and a temporal stream, which leverages the temporal coherence in the input sequence.
The two streams are combined using a dilated temporal convolutional layer, which enables the network to effectively capture both local and global features.
We evaluate our approach on the Penn Action dataset, which contains video sequences of complex human actions, and achieve state-of-the-art performance.
Code is available at https://github.com/andywon/DTFCN.
We present an unsupervised approach to salient object detection (SOD) on hyperspectral images (HSIs).

In contrast to most existing works that rely on supervised learning or a large amount of labeled data, our approach learns hyperspectral features for SOD in an unsupervised manner from an unlabeled HSI dataset using an unsupervised segmentation task.
We solve the segmentation task by minimizing an objective function that quantifies the dissimilarity between segment labels and the hyperspectral features learned from the HSI dataset.
Our approach then uses these hyperspectral features to adapt existing SOD methods designed for RGB images for HSIs.
We evaluate our approach on two HSI datasets, and experimental results show that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance for SOD on HSIs.
Most supervised learning pipelines require a labeling function that assigns labels to different regions of the input space.
In contrast to image-based supervised learning, where ground truth labeling is derived by pointing and clicking, the labeling process in 3D is more challenging.
In this paper, we address the problem of labeling 3D point clouds, i.e., irregularly sampled spaces, based on a set of prelabeled training data.
We propose a surface segmentation approach for 3D point clouds that optimally transports labels from a given training surface to an unseen target surface.
Our approach leverages a set of geometric prior constraints to enforce that the resulting labeling is a valid surface segmentation.

We minimize an energy function that measures the dissimilarity between the prior-constrained labeling and the ground truth labeling of the training data, to learn a labeling function that can be applied to new surfaces.
We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach on both synthetic and real-world scanning data.
We present a simple, fast, and effective approach to facial landmark detection and shape fitting.
It advances the state-of-the-art in speed, accuracy, and robustness.
The detection algorithm runs at 45 frames per second on a standard CPU, which is tens to hundreds of times faster than contemporary methods yet achieves higher accuracy.
The algorithm is based on fitting a shape model to the image, followed by a simple regression of shape parameters to find the pose of the face in the image.
The shape model is a set of several thousand faces with landmarks annotated on a dense grid.
The regression is trained using a convolutional neural network.
We show that the algorithm is robust to facial expressions, occlusions, out-of-plane rotations, and non-frontal poses.
Our implementation is available at https://github.com/mviglietta/fast-face-align.
Supplementary video: http://www.cs.princeton.edu/cvrl/fastfacealign/supplementary.mov

Deep learning segmentation methods have become a major topic of interest in cardiac MRI analysis due to their performance in image segmentation; however, concerns have been raised about their interpretability and potential for bias.
In this work, we aim to address these concerns by proposing a new method that combines the strengths of deep learning with the interpretability of rule-based methods.
Our approach uses a multi-stage process, with a rule-based method used as a pre-processing step to improve the quality of the input data for the deep learning component.

We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on a cardiac MRI dataset, showing that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance in terms of segmentation accuracy while maintaining interpretability and addressing concerns about bias.

We present an interactive image segmentation method that enables a user to easily refine an initial segmentation result, produced by a conventional image segmentation algorithm, through an intuitive labeling interface.

Our method progressively refines an initial segmentation using a label propagation algorithm, where the labels are propagated through a complex network that is constructed using a user-provided labeling interface.
We design the propagation process so that it converges to a local minimum of an energy function that is defined using both the user-provided labels and the image gradient.

In a series of experiments on both synthetic and real images, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in producing segmentations that are more accurate and coherent with user-provided labels, compared to conventional segmentation algorithms.

Recent works have shown that annotation-cost reduction, namely the use of fewer annotations per image, for example, by only labeling foreground or background voxels or regions, can be key to practical applicability of medical image segmentation methods, especially when dealing with experts' time or limited annotation budgets.
In this work, we propose a fully-convolutional network architecture that uses a suggestive mixed supervision strategy to reduce annotation costs.
Our method combines label propagation with multi-scale modeling of the spatial dependence of the labels.
We show that our method, trained on only foreground voxels, can achieve similar performance to recent state-of-the-art methods trained on the full annotation, while being much faster to train.

We finally demonstrate the efficacy of our method on three different public segmentation benchmarks: the ISBI challenge 2012 prostate segmentation benchmark, the MIAS challenge 2016 brain tumor segmentation benchmark, and the LUNA16 lung segmentation benchmark.
We introduce a new unsupervised meta-learning (UML) framework for learning a figure-ground segmentation model.
Our method leverages the power of UML, which trains a model using data augmented with prior knowledge in the form of unlabeled examples from a related task.
We adopt a recently proposed Visual Effect (VE) prior that models the spatial coherence of image patches.
The VE prior is enforced via an auxiliary segmentation task, in which the model is required to restore visually coherent patches in artificially degraded images.
We show that the introduction of this auxiliary task leads to a model that is better calibrated, and thereby, improves segmentation accuracy.

We evaluate our method on the Cityscapes and Mapillary Vistas datasets, and demonstrate that our model outperforms the state-of-the-art on both datasets in terms of F1-score and the Intersection over Union (IoU) measure.
We present new algorithms for scalable inference in Markov Random Fields (MRFs) on large graphs, which we implement in a new software library sparkMRF.
Our key technical insight is to view the MRF energy as a Riemannian metric on a space of probability distributions, and to use Riemannian optimization techniques to accelerate inference.

We implement these techniques as an optimization-based message-passing algorithm, and show that on large real-world datasets, our algorithm is significantly faster and more accurate than existing state-of-the-art MRF inference algorithms.
We find that deep neural networks trained to solve partial differential equations can develop robust and generalizable solutions when trained in a hierarchical fashion.

We present experiments on several models showing that this approach enables a fast and efficient computational paradigm to simulate high-dimensional fluid flows and solve the Laplace equation with minimal training data.

In contrast to recent work on learned numerical methods that focus on discretizing PDEs, our approach views the neural network as a generalized function approximation and the solution as an implicit function of the input coordinates and the parameters of the PDE.
We show that this approach is particularly beneficial for solving PDEs in high-dimensional domains where the manual design of an explicit discretization would be impractical.
Our results show that DNNs are capable of solving PDEs in complex geometries, and that solutions predicted by DNNs are of high quality and generalize well to new inputs.
In contrast to recent work on learned ODE solvers, we do not require any ad-hoc regularization methods and show that simple (and unstable) architectures are able to learn to solve PDEs.
To the best of our knowledge, our work is the first to demonstrate the applicability of deep neural networks to solving PDEs of any kind in high-dimensional spaces.
Current unsupervised learning algorithms of image decomposition yield unsatisfactory results, prompting us to look for alternative designs.
We propose a novel, universally applicable method called Double-DIP that decomposes images in a content-style manner.
It estimates a base layer using a deep prior and then boosts the decomposition performance via a cascade of auxiliary layers that synthesize the missing components.
We establish a theoretical connection between the proposed method and the well-known coupled sparse coding, opening a door to a deeper understanding of deep image prior.
In addition, we propose a new objective function that further improves the performance.
Finally, we demonstrate the superiority of our method against the state-of-the-art on two classic benchmarks, as well as a variety of qualitative results.

We provide an analytical justification for a widely held belief that training machine learning models with very large batch sizes is computationally inefficient and leads to slower convergence during the optimization process.

In particular, we show that the iterates of stochastic gradient descent with replacement (SGDR), a popular variant of stochastic gradient descent (SGD), converge at a slower rate to a neighborhood of the optimal solution when the batch size is increased beyond a certain point.
Our result establishes, to the best of our knowledge, the first theoretical justification of the empirical observation regarding the inefficiency of large batch sizes.

We further show that the convergence rate of SGDR is minimized when the batch size is equal to the size of the dataset, providing an explanation for the widespread practice of using mini-batches of a relatively small size in training deep neural networks.
Deep learning approaches have shown promising results in various computer vision tasks.
In this paper, we apply a deep learning based approach for building detection in satellite multispectral imagery.
We use a convolutional neural network (CNN) architecture, pre-trained on the ImageNet dataset, and fine-tune it on a dataset of building footprints extracted from satellite imagery.
Our approach is able to achieve a high accuracy in building detection, with a F1-score of 0.91 on the test dataset.

We also perform a comparison between our approach and a traditional machine learning based approach, using a random forest classifier, and show that our deep learning approach outperforms the traditional approach in terms of both accuracy and speed.

Our approach can be used to extract building footprints from satellite imagery, which can be useful for various applications such as urban planning, disaster management, and infrastructure monitoring.
It can also be extended to other object detection tasks in satellite imagery, such as road detection, vegetation detection, and land-cover classification.
