Recent works in visual semantic segmentation have shown that the use of semantic segmentation as a teacher model helps virtual pilots learn to control in the real world.

In this paper, we argue that the use of virtual pilots i) limits the scalability of data collection, ii) limits the types of environments in which data can be collected, and iii) the policy learned with this approach is sub-optimal.
In contrast, we propose a framework where the teacher is trained directly in the real world.
Our framework performs convolutional neural network filtering of raw camera images and uses the output to train a policy in the real world.
We show that our method is able to learn a more robust policy end-to-end with only raw camera data and rudimentary sensing for state estimation.
We show that our method generalizes to unseen environments, and compare against state-of-the-art virtual-to-real methods on the semantic segmentation front.
Prostate segmentation in transrectal ultrasound (TRUS) images is a fundamental step towards automated prostate cancer detection.
In this paper, we present a 2D U-net variant for prostate segmentation in TRUS images.
In our method, we incorporate a bridged pathway to refine the features learned by the encoder.
Specifically, we concatenate the low-level features from the encoder with the corresponding features from the decoder, and feed them into a bridge pathway to enhance the quality of features.
We evaluate our method on a public dataset and achieve a dice similarity coefficient of 95.5%, which is 2.7% higher than the previous state-of-the-art.

Deep learning has become a popular tool for image-based medical applications, however, most works limit their focus to segmentation, ignoring the rich anatomical information available in medical images.
In this work, we present a novel framework for deep learning of anatomical structures called Deep Geodesic Learning (DGL).
DGL leverages geodesic distance and heat kernel signatures to model the symmetric positive-definite similarity between anatomical structures in a learned manner.

We show that geodesic distance, computed on a manifold learned by a deep network, can be used in a loss function to optimize the network towards accurate segmentation as well as accurate anatomical landmark localization.

We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach on challenging 3D medical image datasets, showing that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art deep learning works for segmentation, and that our framework can learn to accurately localize anatomical landmarks.
Automated cell count is an important problem in digital pathology.
In this paper, we propose a Field Of Interest (FOI) proposal generator network to assist in mitotic cell count (MC), a sub-problem of cell count.
Our network takes RGB patches corresponding to cell images as input and outputs an FOI proposal map, which can be used to generate rectangular FOI regions to assist the mitotic cell count.
We train our network using a weakly-supervised learning strategy, where only the image-level ground truth is needed.
Our network is able to exploit the prior knowledge of cell image distribution and the FOI proposal generation is formulated as a bounding box regression problem.
We implement our network using a lightweight CNN architecture to achieve real-time performance.
In addition, we introduce a novel adaptive training scheme to improve the generalization ability of the network.
Our method achieves a mean Absolute Measuring Error (AME) of 0.83 and a relative Measuring Error (ME) of 21.7% on the Digital Slide Archive (DSA) of the Mitotic Cell Count (MC) challenge.
We present a method for reconstructing images from their Fourier measurements based on a deep neural network.
Given a set of Fourier measurements y_k = |H_k *
x|^2, our goal is to reconstruct the image x that was convolved with the known kernel H_k.

Our approach relies on a deep neural network that operates on the Fourier domain, which we train using a novel loss function that encourages the network to reconstruct images that yield the measured Fourier coefficients.

We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on image reconstruction tasks with known and unknown blur kernels, and show that our method can reconstruct images more accurately and rapidly than state-of-the-art reconstruction algorithms while requiring less training data.
Semantic image segmentation has achieved remarkable progress in recent years.
With the rapid development of deep learning and the availability of large-scale datasets, many state-of-the-art models have been proposed to tackle this task.
In this paper, we provide a comprehensive review of recent progress in semantic image segmentation, focusing on deep learning based approaches.
We first give an overview of the history and basic concepts of semantic image segmentation.
Then, we discuss the challenges and limitations of traditional methods.

Next, we survey recent advances in deep learning based approaches, including fully convolutional networks (FCNs), atrous convolutional networks (ACNs), and densely connected fully convolutional networks (DCNs).
We also discuss the impact of different design choices, such as the use of skip connections, dilated convolutions, and cost volume optimization.
Furthermore, we review the recent progress in semantic image segmentation for specific applications, such as medical imaging and scene understanding.
We conclude the paper with a discussion on the current state-of-the-art models and the potential directions for future research.

We address the problem of semantic segmentation for robot perception, which is challenged by the bias introduced by the domain gap between the training data (typically images from a static camera) and the onboard sensor (a robot-moving camera).
Previous works tend to rely on large amounts of robot-moving data for training, which is difficult to obtain.
Instead, we investigate pre-training on synthetic data generated by a variety of virtual cameras, and then fine-tuning with limited real robot data.

Given that the synthetic data are generated using a different rendering engine than what the real robot sensors provide, a straightforward fine-tuning tends to result in a domain gap that reduces performance.

To overcome this, we propose a feature transfer method that can align the features learned from synthetic data with the real robot data, so that the fine-tuning can be performed in a largely domain-agnostic manner.
We show that our approach can significantly improve performance on real robot data, and moreover, our method is flexible and can be used with any state-of-the-art segmentation model.
Iris recognition is widely used in automated biometric identification systems.
In a perfect world, when capturing iris images, it would be done under tightly controlled conditions, and images would only be captured of healthy eyes.

However, in the real world, capturing iris images may be done under varying illumination conditions, and images may be captured of subjects with eye pathology (such as cataracts, corneal opacities, or hemorrhages).
When these conditions are combined, it makes the task of iris recognition more challenging, because the captured iris images may contain occlusions, or the iris texture may be degraded.
In this paper, we propose a method of iris recognition that is robust to such degradations.
Our method first locates the iris using a simple circularity test, and then performs texture-based matching in the region determined by the circularity test.

We determine the best matching methods to use on the iris texture by first creating a database of degraded iris images, and then testing four different matching methods (correlation, phase only correlation, local gradient correlation, and local phase gradient correlation) on this database.
Our results show that the local gradient correlation gives better results than the other three methods in all cases.
Then, given a query image, our system finds the closest match in the database, and retrieves the identity of the subject.

From our experiments using a realistic database with a wide range of degradation types, we show that our method is able to successfully recognize iris images that contain up to 30% occlusion from cataracts, with a false rejection rate of less than 1%.
Understanding how the brain connects its cells (neurons) to enable sophisticated behaviors involves tracing millions of neurons through complex networks.
We present a novel deep learning approach to understand the neural pathways in the zebrafish, a model organism for neurobiology.

We annotated tens of thousands of neurons and millions of synapses in electron microscope images, and then computed neural pathways that were trained to recognize synaptic connections in an automated fashion.
This approach allowed us to uncover synaptic connections in areas of the zebrafish brain that were not studied before.
Our results show that the deep learning approach can successfully reconstruct known neural pathways in the zebrafish and can discover new pathways that were not studied before.
This work brings the study of neural circuitry within reach of deep learning and offers a powerful new way of understanding the brain.
The task of segmenting objects in images is generally considered an inherently difficult problem, due to the immense variability in shapes, textures, and backgrounds in real-world images.

However, this variability is usually reduced in many real-world applications, such as medical imaging, satellite imaging, and manufacturing, where the classes of objects are hierarchical and nested, and the background shares a common texture or pattern.
In this paper, we exploit this additional knowledge of hierarchical nested classes in order to make the segmentation task easier.
In particular, we propose a multi-level activation strategy that combines the benefits of convolutional and recurrent neural networks while mitigating their respective drawbacks.
We show that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on two publicly available datasets, and is able to run in real-time.
We present a method for unsupervised learning of foreground object detection, based on clustering and density estimation.

It consists in the training of two components: a classifier that assigns to each pixel a label corresponding to the cluster to which the foreground object belongs, and a density estimator that models the background.
The labels are determined during training by a clustering procedure that identifies the regions of the image dominated by the foreground objects.
The resulting method is effective in detecting the foreground objects in a fully unsupervised manner.
We demonstrate the performance of the method on a synthetic dataset and on a difficult real-world dataset of people in crowded scenes.
Our method is related to the popular density-based clustering methods
[4, 5], however, it differs from them significantly in the way the foreground objects are modeled.
In particular, we rely on a careful treatment of the background to construct a method that is able to successfully detect the foreground objects.
Recent works on semantic segmentation could benefit from a larger amount of labeled training data, but annotating a lot of images is expensive and time-consuming.
To remedy this, a simple yet effective solution is to synthesize data via data augmentation.
In this work, we propose to use labeled images to synthesize confusing examples to train a confusion-aware network that reduces confusion errors in semantic segmentation.
We propose a network structure that uses a confusion loss to explicitly reduce confusion errors in semantic segmentation.
This structure is compatible with any network that uses a per-pixel loss, such as fully convolutional networks.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on the Cityscapes dataset, where our approach achieves 92.5% mean accuracy on the test set, compared to 88.4% achieved by a baseline network.
Our approach also improves performance on the confusing classes, such as road and sidewalk.
Deep learning networks have shown promising results in hyperintensity segmentation.
However, these methods require a large number of manually-labeled training samples, which are scarce in practice.
To overcome this limitation, we propose a data augmentation method using U-net with random initialization.
Since U-net is prone to overfit the training data, we use random initialization to prevent overfitting.
To improve the segmentation accuracy, we propose a post-processing method that refines the output of U-net.
We evaluate our method on the White Matter Hyperintensity Segmentation Challenge 2015 (WMHISC2015) dataset.
Our method achieves a mean accuracy of 94.43% on the test set, which exceeds the previous state-of-the-art method.
Deep learning approaches have demonstrated promising results for medical image segmentation tasks.
However, training such models usually requires a large amount of manually annotated images and can take days to weeks.
In this work, we present a method for fast training of deep neural networks for hippocampus segmentation using a patch-based canonical neural network architecture.

Our method utilizes a self-supervised pre-training approach to initialize the network weights using a small number of images and then fine-tunes the network using a limited number of manually annotated images.

We evaluate our method on the challenging task of hippocampus segmentation in near real-time MRI scans and demonstrate that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance while being orders of magnitude faster to train.
Liver and tumor segmentation from CT volumes is a fundamental task in clinical practice, which is also a challenging topic in medical image analysis.
In this paper, we propose a new hybrid densely connected UNet (H-DenseUNet) for efficient liver and tumor segmentation.
It integrates advantages of both fully convolutional and densely connected architectures, namely, an efficient encoder-decoder framework and a powerful multi-scale aggregation capability.

In H-DenseUNet, besides the common contracting and expanding paths in UNet, we add dense connections on the contracting path to enrich the information propagated from the high-level to the low-level features, which enables our network to effectively capture multi-scale information and handle large anatomical variations.

Furthermore, a hybrid attention mechanism is proposed to weigh the features before they are aggregated at each resolution level, which allows the network to focus on the interested regions and suppress the background interference.
In the experimental part, the efficiency and effectiveness of our method are validated on the public LiTS dataset.
Compared with the state-of-the-art methods, our approach achieves a higher segmentation accuracy under the same settings.
We present a simple yet effective approach for whole-body segmentation of human poses in images.
Our method is based on a keypoint representation of the human body using the publicly available COCO keypoint detection dataset.
We show that by suitably grouping the detected keypoints, it is possible to obtain a sparse representation of the human body that can be effectively used for whole-body segmentation.
Our approach is fast, and it can be used for real-time segmentation of human poses in images.
Furthermore, we present a method for transferring the segmentation mask from one image to another, which can further speed up the segmentation process.
Our method does not require any training data, and it can be used out of the box for whole-body segmentation of human poses in images.
Experiments on the COCO 2017 keypoint detection and segmentation challenges show that our approach is effective and efficient for whole-body segmentation of human poses in images.
Our project page is available at https://www.vision.caltech.edu/visipedia/KeypointTransfer.
Appendix: Additional results on the COCO test set are available in the full version of this paper.
Recent progress in deep learning enabled significant performance gains in medical image analysis.
In this work, we aim to segment renal vessels in contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) volumes.
We introduce a novel fully convolutional network architecture, called Kid-Net, specifically designed for this task.
The network is composed of a stem followed by two stages of residual blocks.

To effectively utilize the limited amount of labeled training data, we introduce a new residual block variant that employs a weighted sum of the input feature map and the output feature map of the previous layer, thereby reducing the necessary amount of labeled data.
We employ a pyramid pooling module that computes a multi-scale context map for each layer, providing the network with a robust representation to handle structures at various scales.
Furthermore, we introduce a new atrous convolution variant, which enables the use of a larger filter size and thus enhances the performance in terms of segmentation accuracy.
We evaluated our method on 100 CT volumes, where two experienced physicians manually annotated the renal vessels.
The proposed network achieved a mean Dice similarity coefficient of 0.88±0.02 on the test set.
We present NeuroNet: a novel approach for the fully automated reproduction of human brain image segmentation pipelines.
In contrast to most previous methods, which aim at reproducing a specific segmentation pipeline, here we aim to reproduce any given pipeline operated by a human expert.
A pipeline is described by the sequence of applications of a set of tools on the input image.
Tools are characterized by their parameter settings.
The goal is to find the best parameter settings to obtain a segmentation similar to the one obtained by the human expert.

This is solved as a meta-learning problem, in which the main learning objective is to reproduce accurately the segmentation of a large number of training examples, each corresponding to a different input image and pipeline.
NeuroNet is trained once and can then be used to segment new images, whose pipelines were not used during training.
In our evaluation, NeuroNet outperformed state-of-the-art methods for pipeline reproduction on multiple brain image segmentation benchmarks while being much faster.
Medical image segmentation is typically assessed by the variation of segmentations obtained from multiple experts.
A common assumption in this assessment is that all experts provide their own segmentation without any communication or coordination.
In reality, however, experts often discuss their segmentations, and they may even adjust their segmentations based on their peers' segmentations.
In this paper, we investigate the effect of such communication on the uncertainty of medical image segmentation.
We consider two types of communication: absolute agreement and relative agreement.

Absolute agreement refers to the case where all experts agree on a single segmentation, while relative agreement refers to the case where the experts adjust their segmentations so that they are consistent with an average segmentation.
We find that both types of communication can significantly reduce the uncertainty of the segmentation, but that relative agreement is more effective in doing so.

We also find that the uncertainty of the segmentation can be effectively estimated using only a small number of experts, but that the choice of which experts to use can have a significant effect on the estimated uncertainty.
We present a simple method to augment pretrained models with new anatomy and images, based on an in-depth analysis of the representations learned by the pretrained models.

Our method is motivated by the observation that while pretrained models are trained on a diverse set of images, they learn highly specific representations, making them ineffective when used out of distribution.

We find that this is because the representations learned are highly dependent on the presence of certain anatomy and that the absence of this anatomy often leads to the representations not being able to generalize well.
Our method addresses this limitation by learning a new representation that can exploit both the information in the pretrained model as well as the new anatomy and images.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on three different datasets: cardiac MRI, abdominal CT, and knee MRI.
For all three datasets, we show that our method improves performance compared to the state-of-the-art methods, while requiring less labeled data.
In this paper, we present a knowledge-based fully convolutional network (KFCN) that is designed for the segmentation of lung CT images.
The KFCN is based on a fully convolutional network (FCN) architecture, which has been successfully used for image segmentation tasks.
The KFCN incorporates anatomical knowledge in the form of prior knowledge and a prior-based loss function to improve the performance of the FCN.
The prior knowledge is in the form of a set of labeled example images, which are used to train the KFCN.
The prior-based loss function is designed to minimize the difference between the output of the KFCN and the prior knowledge.
We evaluated the performance of the KFCN on the public LUNA16 dataset and compared it to the performance of a fully-connected CRF as well as a number of state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods.
Our results show that the KFCN is comparable to the SOTA methods in terms of segmentation performance measured by the DSC and JD, and significantly better than the fully-connected CRF.
We present a convolutional implementation of conditional random fields (CRFs) for semantic image segmentation.
Our architecture retains the computational efficiency of pixel-based approaches while leveraging the label consistency enforced by CRFs.
We introduce a novel convolutional layer that computes the unnormalized log-likelihoods of the CRF.
This layer is differentiable, allowing for end-to-end training.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on the public NYU Depth V2 and PASCAL VOC 2012 semantic segmentation datasets.
Our network outperforms the state-of-the-art in both datasets in terms of segmentation accuracy measured by Intersection over Union, while maintaining real-time inference speed.
Code and models are available at http://www.cs.princeton.edu/~yang900/crf/.
In this paper, we present a new approach for left ventricle segmentation of cardiac MR images.
Our method is based on a hybrid forest that uses both decision trees and random forests.
We show that our method is able to achieve state-of-the-art performance on the MICCAI 2012 cardiac segmentation challenge dataset, while being much faster than other approaches.

We also demonstrate that our method is able to segment the left ventricle in a single slice of the dataset, which can be useful in clinical settings where the patient is unable to hold their breath for the entire scan.
Semantic image segmentation is crucial for understanding the content of an image, and it remains a challenging task.
One reason is the diversity of visual instances in the real world.
For example, accurately segmenting objects with complex shapes or textures can be difficult.
We present a novel locally adaptive learning loss (LALL) for semantic image segmentation, which adaptively reweights the learning process according to the local characteristics of each pixel.
The proposed method captures the underlying structure of the data by modeling the spatial dependence of pixel labels, and it can be integrated into any deep learning framework.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of LALL on semantic image segmentation, where it achieves state-of-the-art performance on the Cityscapes dataset with only a small number of training samples.
The code is made publicly available at https://github.com/Dai-JunWu/LALL.
We introduce the Lovász-softmax loss, a differentiable surrogate for the optimization of the intersection-over-union (IoU) measure commonly used for training detection models.

In this surrogate, the IoU is replaced with a differentiable upper bound, for which we provide a tight analysis that establishes a link between the Lovász-softmax loss and the optimization of the IoU. This result shows that, when optimizing the Lovász-softmax loss, the detection model converges to a locally optimal solution for the IoU measure, providing an explanation for the superior performance of models trained with this loss.

Furthermore, we show that the Lovász-softmax loss possesses the useful property of only depending on a model's predicted labels, and not the confidence scores, making it compatible with a variety of training procedures and architectures.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on the COCO dataset, obtaining state-of-the-art results with a ResNet50-based single-shot detector.
Code is available at https://github.com/IDSIA/ LovaszSoftmaxLoss.
In this paper, we address the problem of image segmentation.
In contrast to most existing works that use a vectorial representation, we propose to represent the image data in a lower-dimensional subspace.
In this subspace, a segmentation algorithm can be interpreted as a clustering algorithm on a graph.
The nodes of the graph are the subspace vectors, and an edge connects two nodes if their distance is smaller than a threshold.
The segmentation is achieved by partitioning the graph into several segments in such a way that the nodes within each segment are densely connected while the nodes from different segments are sparse.
To obtain a sparse decomposition, we apply a sparse decomposition algorithm on the graph.
The proposed method has been tested on synthetic and real images, and the experimental results show that it produces favorable results even with a small number of segments.
We present Ω-Net (Omega-Net), a fully automatic deep neural network (DNN) solution to cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) image analysis.
Ω-Net simultaneously detects cardiac views, segments out the myocardium, and identifies the orientation of the myocardium in a single network architecture.

This network is trained end-to-end in a multi-task learning framework, enabling the network to selectively reuse information and features from the previous tasks to enhance performance in the current task.

We evaluate Ω-Net on 400 cardiac MR cases, and achieve an average precision of 95.4%, recall of 92.0%, and F1-score of 94.2% for cardiac view detection; and 97.2% for myocardium segmentation with orientation identification.
In addition, we present a novel atrial segmentation technique, which achieves an F1-score of 97.6%.

The techniques described in this paper were used to generate the segmentation and orientation maps for the CMR images used in the recent CAMERA (Characterizing Atherosclerosis using Multiparametric Cardiac MR Imaging with Deep Learning and Radiomics) challenge.
This challenge was aimed at advancing the field of cardiac radiomics and computer-aided diagnosis.

Arxiv abstract:
Quantization of Fully Convolutional Networks for Accurate Biomedical Image Segmentation

We present an approach for the quantization of fully convolutional networks for accurate biomedical image segmentation.
We demonstrate that quantization, coupled with appropriate network design and training techniques, can produce segmentation models that are both accurate and efficient.
Our approach utilizes a combination of network architecture design, weight initialization, and training techniques to produce a model that is suitable for quantization.
The resulting model is then quantized by applying a linear quantization scheme to the weights and activation functions of the network.
We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach on the task of brain tumor segmentation from multimodal MRI images.
Our results show that our approach can produce a model that is both accurate and efficient, and that is suitable for use in a clinical setting.
Keywords: biomedical image segmentation, fully convolutional networks, quantization, brain tumor segmentation, MRI images.
Deep learning methods have achieved remarkable results in traffic sign detection.

Most of the existing methods separate the detection and boundary estimation stages, which incur errors propagating from the detection to the estimation and lead to performance degradation especially when the detection result is not accurate.
In this paper, we propose a novel framework to simultaneously detect traffic signs and estimate their boundaries in an end-to-end trainable manner.
We employ a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) architecture, named as Joint Object Detection and Boundary Estimation Network (JODaBEN), to perform the simultaneous detection and estimation tasks.

Specifically, we design a shared-weight feature pyramid network to extract multi-scale features for both detection and estimation, and a boundary-estimation-aware loss function to optimize the whole network.

Moreover, a series of experiments based on the German Traffic Sign Detection Benchmark (GTSDB) are conducted to evaluate the performance of the proposed method, and the results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach.
Automatic tooth segmentation in X-ray images is a classic problem in image processing.
Most of the work focuses on analyzing dental images, which are taken regularly by dentists for diagnosis and treatment planning.
In this paper, we perform a thorough survey of the most prominent methods and evaluate them on a newly introduced dataset.
We follow the trends in deep learning for dental image analysis.

In particular, we investigate the performance of well-known architectures such as VGG, ResNet, Inception, and EfficientNet in conjunction with both binary and categorical cross-entropy loss functions.
Our experimental results show that the categorical cross-entropy loss with ResNet50 architecture achieves the best performance in tooth segmentation on our dataset.
We also analyze the impact of different preprocessing techniques and evaluate the effectiveness of data augmentation.
Finally, we provide our perspectives on the future of dental image analysis towards the automatic detection of caries.
Deep learning has shown promising results for medical image analysis, particularly in image classification and segmentation tasks.
In this paper, we present a novel deep learning framework for the segmentation of pancreatic tumors on CT scans.
Our approach leverages graph-based representations and 3D convolutions to capture the complex structures and textures present in medical images.
We introduce a graph-based layer, called Logismos, that computes graph-based features within a deep learning architecture.
This enables the network to reason about the spatial relationships between pixels, facilitating the segmentation of tumors.
We evaluate our method on a public dataset of pancreatic CT scans and show that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance in terms of both accuracy and speed.
Our framework has the potential to improve the diagnosis and treatment of pancreatic cancer, which is one of the most deadly forms of cancer.
In this work, we present a computer vision pipeline for the automated determination of cardiac structure and function from two-dimensional echocardiography (2DE).

This pipeline begins with the detection of the heart in the image series, and then identifies the cardiac cycle, and subsequently tracks the cardiac wall motion and thickening throughout the cardiac cycle.
The output is a series of displacement maps representing the wall motion and thickening at each time point throughout the cardiac cycle.
We evaluate our method on a dataset of 2DE images and compare our results to ground truth displacement maps created by an expert sonographer.
Our method shows good agreement with the ground truth, with an average error of 0.16 mm for wall motion and 0.41 mm for thickening.
We then apply our method to the detection of cardiac disease by tracking the cardiac wall motion and thickening in a series of 2DE images from a patient with known cardiac disease.
Our method is able to detect the disease state by identifying a decrease in the wall motion and thickening in the affected region.
We show that our method is able to detect the disease state with a high degree of accuracy, and can be used to automatically identify cardiac disease in 2DE images.
This work presents a computer vision pipeline for the automated determination of cardiac structure and function from 2DE images.
Our method is able to detect the heart in the image series, identify the cardiac cycle, and track the cardiac wall motion and thickening throughout the cardiac cycle.
We evaluate our method on a dataset of 2DE images and compare our results to ground truth displacement maps created by an expert sonographer, and demonstrate its ability to detect cardiac disease.
The output of our pipeline can be used to assess cardiac function and detect cardiac disease with a high degree of accuracy.

Camera-trap images segmentation using multi-layer robust principal component analysis

Camera-trap photography is a powerful tool for studying wildlife populations.
However, the segmentation of animal regions in images is challenging due to variations in size, shape, and texture.
We present a novel algorithm for the segmentation of animal regions in camera-trap images based on robust principal component analysis (RPCA).
Our algorithm comprises an initial segmentation of the image using a Gaussian mixture model (GMM) followed by a series of RPCA-based refinements to improve the accuracy of the segmentation.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on a dataset of camera-trap images containing a variety of animals and backgrounds.
Our results show that the proposed method achieves a high degree of accuracy in segmenting animal regions, outperforming existing state-of-the-art methods in terms of both precision and recall.
The proposed method is able to handle images with complex backgrounds and overlapping animals, making it suitable for use in a wide range of wildlife photography applications.
We present a learning framework that utilizes abundant unlabeled data and limited labeled data for training robust CNN models in medical image analysis.

We particularly consider the problem of gastric tumor segmentation, in which the labeled data are often expensive to obtain since the expertise of experienced radiologists are required to manually annotate the regions of interest.
In this work, we establish a patch-based iterative learning framework, in which a patch-based CNN model is first trained to obtain initial predictions.
Then, a small number of patches with the most uncertain predictions are selected and labeled.
These labeled patches are then used to iteratively fine-tune the model.
Specifically, we implement a patch-based U-Net model for the gastric tumor segmentation.
In the experimental part, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed approach on a real-world dataset, in which only a small fraction of the whole dataset is labeled.
The experimental results show that our method can achieve comparable performance to fully-supervised learning when only 20% of the data is labeled.
In this work, we present a semi-supervised GrowCut algorithm to segment and classify regions of interest of mammographic images.
The algorithm is based on a fuzzy clustering technique that allows us to obtain probabilistic segmentation and classification results.
The proposed method is evaluated on a public mammographic database, where the ground truth was obtained through manual labeling by radiologists.
In order to assess the performance of the algorithm, we use several evaluation metrics, including accuracy, precision, recall and F1-score.
Furthermore, we present an experimental comparison with other state-of-the-art segmentation algorithms.
The obtained results show the effectiveness of the proposed method in both segmentation and classification tasks.

Recent works in crowd-based object segmentation have mostly relied on either a) labeling a new training dataset, b) using pre-trained models without adapting to the new dataset, or c) using complex models tuned on different datasets.
In this work, we tackle the problem of training a crowd-based object segmentation model from scratch, i.e., without any available pre-trained models or labeled training data.
To this end, we follow a data-centric approach leveraging click-stream data collected via an online annotation tool.
We propose a clickstream analysis framework that compensates for the limitations of the crowd by dynamically adapting the amount of labeling effort spent on each pixel.
This is done in a data-driven fashion using a deep neural network that predicts the quality of the crowd's annotations without ground truth.
We show that our approach, which is trained entirely on click-stream data, is able to achieve better performance than models trained on ground truth data alone.
Furthermore, we show that the clickstream analysis framework is able to nearly double the efficiency of the crowd, thereby reducing the time and cost of the labeling process.
W-Net is a deep learning model for fully unsupervised image segmentation.
It captures image structure by estimating locality-sensitive binary codes from deep features.
The model is built upon a multi-scale architecture, where the image is first processed by a series of convolutional layers followed by non-local operations.
By training the model without any labels, we are able to learn a robust segmentation model that is able to segment images in a variety of scenarios.
We demonstrate the performance of our model on the Cityscapes and KITTI datasets, and show that it achieves state-of-the-art performance on both datasets.

W-Net provides a powerful foundation for fully unsupervised image segmentation, and can be used to segment images in a variety of applications including autonomous driving, medical imaging, and remote sensing.
Brain tumor segmentation is a fundamental step in clinical MRI analysis, and an accurate and automatic segmentation method is demanded.
In this paper, we propose a deep learning model integrating fully convolutional neural networks (FCNNs) and conditional random fields (CRFs) for brain tumor segmentation.
Our model is based on the U-Net architecture, which is a FCNN that uses skip connections to capture multi-scale contextual information.
We modify the U-Net architecture to incorporate CRFs, which model the spatial dependencies between pixels and provide global constraints on the segmentation.
The proposed model is trained on a large dataset of MRI scans and evaluated on the BraTS 2018 validation dataset, which contains a wide variety of tumor types and clinical modalities.
Our model achieves state-of-the-art performance on the BraTS 2018 validation dataset, with an F1-score of 0.9143 and an area under the ROC curve (AUC-ROC) of 0.9149.
The proposed model is also evaluated on the BraTS 2020 validation dataset, and achieves an F1-score of 0.9132 and an AUC-ROC of 0.9145.
The model is made publicly available to facilitate further research and development.
Segment3D is a web-based application for collaborative segmentation of 3D images.
It is designed to enhance the accuracy and efficiency of segmenting images of shoot apical meristems (SAMs), the continuously growing tips of plant stems that regenerate the plant's aerial portions.
Segment3D helps users to interactively segment SAMs in 3D, while simultaneously viewing the annotations of other users.
In addition, it provides a text chat box to facilitate discussion between users, and displays a time stamped record of all user activities.
This collaborative approach can help to overcome the subjectivity and ambiguity in segmenting SAMs, and reduces the time per segment that a user requires to complete a segmentation.
Segment3D is implemented using HTML5, allowing it to be used in most modern browsers without the need for plugins.

Segment3D also employs several techniques to improve the performance of the application, including: (1) a novel method to render 3D images without relying on hardware acceleration; (2) a spatial indexing mechanism to efficiently load and display the 3D image; and (3) a compact representation of the 3D image using octree compression.
We present a comprehensive study on deep learning based cardiac MR image segmentation.

Compared to state-of-the-art 2D approaches, 3D segmentation networks have shown promising results but at a significant increase in computational cost and without a noticeable improvement in performance.
Our exploration of current 2D and 3D techniques reveals that 2D models perform poorly on long-axis slices, which contain valuable information for segmentation.
We resolve this issue by proposing a simple yet effective approach that enforces 2D models to output 3D segmentation results.
With this approach, we achieve better performance than 2D-only and 3D-only models on long-axis slices while keeping the computational requirements of 2D models.
Furthermore, we investigate the impact of popular data augmentation techniques on model performance.
Our results suggest that data augmentation greatly improves generalization performance and its effectiveness is data-dependent.
Code is available at https://github.com/AI4Cardio/CardioSegment.
We address the problem of automatic lung tumor contour annotation from 4D computed tomography (CT) scans, i.e., stacks of 3D CT volumes acquired over the treatment period.
Previously, we had developed a fully-automated algorithm based on a deformable model to track the tumor between volumes; however, it required 4 to 6 hours to run on a single patient.
In this paper, we revisit this problem with the goal to achieve real-time performance, i.e., under 30 minutes per patient.
Towards that end, we first identify the parts of the previous algorithm that accounted for the large run time.
We then develop strategies to speed up those parts.

In particular, we speed up the initialization of the deformable model by using an annotated reference scan; we speed up the deformation step by using a coarse-to-fine strategy that iteratively refines the contour; and we speed up the runtime by using all available volumes for the contour propagation, rather than just the two adjacent volumes.
We implement these ideas in a new algorithm, called Fast Barcode Retrieval for Consensus Contouring (FBRC).
FBRC runs on a single desktop computer in 17 minutes, which is an order of magnitude faster than our previous method.

In spite of the speed-up, the performance of FBRC is comparable to that of our previous algorithm, as measured by Dice score and Hausdorff distance between the automatically segmented tumor and the ground truth.
Recent progress in image segmentation is significantly driven by the advancement of deep learning.
However, most existing methods rely on a single neural network architecture, which may not be sufficient to capture the diversity and complexity of the natural world.
In this paper, we explore and exploit diversity for image segmentation.
We propose a modular neural network system, called DivNet, which consists of a collection of specialized neural networks.
Each network in DivNet is designed to focus on specific characteristics or variations in the images, and can be trained independently to improve the performance.
To efficiently explore the potential of the system, we develop a search strategy that automatically finds the best configuration of DivNet for a given image segmentation task.
We evaluate DivNet on four public benchmarks, and show that our method outperforms the state-of-the-art approaches.
Our code and models are available at https://github.com/AI4Finance-Foundation/DivNet.

We introduce rotation equivariant vector field networks (REFN), a new architecture for representation learning of 3D objects by learning a mapping from 3D meshes to a lower dimensional space while capturing both geometry and symmetry.

In contrast to recent works on learning symmetric representations, the proposed method is able to handle general input meshes with arbitrary topologies, and does not require any parameterization of the input, such as spherical harmonics.
The key idea is to construct a vector field on a space of input meshes, with the property that the rotation of the input object corresponds to a linear transformation of the vector field.
We show that this vector field can be modeled as a network, and introduce a specific architecture based on a U-Net like architecture with symmetric skip connections.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on the tasks of object classification and part segmentation on the ShapeNet dataset, showing improvements over state of the art methods.
Slack and margin rescaling are two recent extensions of the convex supermodular function class that have proven useful in multi-agent optimization.
We prove that both rescaling functions are continuous, increasing, and convex, thereby justifying their use as objective functions and learning constraints.
Furthermore, we show that both objective functions are closed under composition with linear functions, providing a new characterization of supermodularity.
Finally, we present a learning algorithm for margin-rescaled liner functions and use it to derive a new, tighter, convex relaxation of the non-convex multi-agent linear aggregation problem.

We present a novel approach for the automatic segmentation of cardiac substructures from magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and computed tomography (CT) using multi-planar deep segmentation networks (MP-DSNs).

Our method employs a combination of supervised and semi-supervised learning to overcome the limitations of existing approaches in handling large-scale data and the variability in the appearance of cardiac structures across patients.

We train our MP-DSNs using a combination of supervised and semi-supervised learning, where a small set of manually annotated images is used to learn a spatial-varying appearance model, and a large set of unlabeled images is used to learn a spatial-invariant segmentation model.
The proposed method was evaluated on 320 MRI and 256 CT slices from 32 patients, and achieved an average accuracy of 94.5% and 91.4% on the MRI and CT data, respectively.
The proposed method has the potential to improve the efficiency and accuracy of cardiac structure segmentation from MRI and CT, which may aid in the diagnosis and treatment of cardiac diseases.
Line patterns are very common in images.
They appear, for example, in aerial and satellite images, temperature maps, brightness temperature maps, and many other types of images.
The problem of line pattern delineation, i.e., segmenting a line pattern into individual lines, is therefore of practical importance.
In this paper we propose a new approach to line pattern delineation based on the use of B-COSFIRE filters.
These filters have good frequency response characteristics and are straightforward to implement.
In addition, a new gradient-based line selector is proposed.
The selector uses the gradient magnitude and direction at each pixel to determine whether the pixel belongs to a line.
The proposed approach was tested on several benchmark images and the results compared with those obtained using existing techniques.
The results show that the proposed approach is competitive with, and in some cases better than, those of the other techniques.

We introduce the notion of a dominant set for a binary image, which encapsulates, for a given pixel, the information of which class (black or white) dominates the local region of the image around this pixel.

We show that the problem of finding the dominant set has a natural correspondence with the well-known constrained segmentation problem in image processing, for which we present an efficient algorithm with a time complexity of O(n \log n), where n is the number of pixels.
Finally, we demonstrate the usefulness of dominant sets for the task of image segmentation, by means of experimental results on synthetic and real-world images.
Recent works have shown that training Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) on a large and diverse dataset usually leads to better generalization performance on the target domain.
However, for many real-world applications, the available dataset is limited in size and fails to provide sufficient diversity.
In this paper, we investigate the impact of dataset size and diversity on the generalization performance of CNNs.
We find that limited dataset not only leads to worse performance, but also makes the generalization more sensitive to the choice of architecture and hyperparameters.
We show that the error correcting process plays an important role in the generalization performance of CNNs.
In light of this finding, we propose a simple yet effective method, named Error Corrective Boosting (ECB), to improve the generalization performance of CNNs trained on a limited dataset.
Our method focuses on correcting the errors made by the model, and leverages the diversity of the limited dataset to boost the error correcting capability of the model.

We conduct extensive experiments on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 datasets, as well as the popular transfer learning benchmarks, and show that our method significantly improves the generalization performance of CNNs trained on a limited dataset.
Deep learning has recently become an important tool for the diagnosis and prognosis of various diseases.
We present a novel deep learning framework for the automated segmentation and function prediction of biventricular cardiac masses.
These masses result from either tumor growth or benign structural abnormalities and can be found in patients with primary cardiac tumors, metastases, or cardiomyopathies.
Our framework utilizes a fully convolutional neural network architecture combined with a 3D attention module to segment the masses from magnetic resonance (MR) images.
We then use the segmented masses to calculate a series of function metrics that have been shown to be predictive of adverse cardiac events.
We evaluated our method on 100 MR images and compared the results to those obtained with a support vector machine (SVM) and a fully automated mass segmentation (AMS) method.
Our method achieved an accuracy of 92% for the segmentation of cardiac masses, which was significantly higher than the SVM (p < 0.001) and AMS (p = 0.002) methods.
Furthermore, the framework was able to predict a series of function metrics with high accuracy.

The deep learning framework presented in this study can be used to automate the segmentation and function analysis of biventricular cardiac masses and could potentially improve the diagnosis and prognosis of patients with cardiac diseases.
We present a novel shape prior for multi-object segmentation based on gradient vector flow (GVF).
Our method optimally segments objects by minimizing an energy function that comprises a data term and a shape prior term.
The data term is based on a fully-convolutional network (FCN) that computes pixel-wise objectness and boundary maps.
The shape prior term is based on a novel GVF formulation that encourages coherent and accurate object boundaries.
We optimize the energy function via an iterative graph-based approach.
We evaluate our method on the 2016 Cityscapes and 2017 CamVid datasets, and show that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance.
Our code and model weights are available at: this https URL.
Semantic segmentation is a fundamental computer vision task with a wide array of applications.
In this paper, we explore the use of deep structured models for semantic segmentation.
These models are based on the idea of learning a hierarchical representation of the input data, with each level of the hierarchy capturing a different level of detail.
This allows the model to reason about the context of the input data, which is crucial for accurate semantic segmentation.
We evaluate our models on the Cityscapes and CamVid datasets, and show that they achieve state-of-the-art performance on both datasets.
We also show that our models are able to generalize well to unseen data, which is an important characteristic for semantic segmentation models.
Deep learning has recently demonstrated its potential in medical image processing, with achievements in various tasks such as image segmentation, classification, and registration.
However, there are still several challenges to be addressed in order to achieve robust and accurate results.
In this paper, we provide an overview of the current state of deep learning for medical image processing, and discuss some of the key challenges and future directions.
We highlight the need for large and diverse datasets, as well as the importance of domain expertise and clinical interpretation in the development of deep learning models for medical images.
We also discuss the potential of transfer learning and multi-task learning in improving the performance of deep learning models for medical image processing.
Finally, we outline several future research directions, including the use of more complex architectures, the integration of domain knowledge, and the development of robust and interpretable models.

Recent advances in tissue-clearing techniques have made it possible to image whole nervous systems with nanometer-scale resolution, enabling new possibilities for studying the structural connectivity of the brain, spinal cord, and peripheral nervous system.

The resulting data are of such size that automatic segmentation is the only currently feasible method for identifying individual neurons, but these segmentations are not yet accurate enough for quantitative analysis.

In this paper, we investigate several strategies for proofreading automatic segmentations of neurons in 3D, with an emphasis on the emerging technique of connectomics, which aims to map the connections between all neurons in a nervous system.

We find that proofreading strategies that are guided by an anatomical understanding of the tissue can achieve tens of percent improvements in segmentation accuracy, but require significant amounts of expert curation.
In contrast, strategies that are guided by simple heuristics can provide one-click corrections, but only achieve modest improvements in segmentation accuracy.

We introduce a user interface that combines both types of guidance, and demonstrates the potential for expert curation to produce substantial improvements in segmentation accuracy while still keeping the effort required of experts reasonable.
We present a fully automated method for white matter bundle segmentation that does not require any manual initialization or seed point selection.

Our approach utilizes a U-Net architecture with an iterative refinement strategy to directly segment white matter bundles in MR volume images without needing additional registrations or preprocessing steps.
We demonstrate that our method is both fast and accurate, and can handle a wide variety of white matter bundle shapes and sizes.
We evaluate our method on a large dataset of 25 subjects and show that it achieves state-of-the-art performance on white matter bundle segmentation.
Our code and dataset are publicly available at https://github.com/SrinathRR/WhiteMatterBundleSegmentation.
We present an approach for crowd-sourcing image segmentation, where the goal is to obtain pixel-level labels for all pixels in an input image.

Our method, which we call iaSTAPLE (interactive active learning for segmentation via online proximal learning and explicit annotation), leverages the recently proposed online proximal algorithm for adaptive sampling of hard examples, and integrates it with an interactive process where a user provides labels for a small number of pixels per iteration.

We perform an error analysis to understand the impact of the number of annotations required by the proximal learning algorithm, and conduct experiments on a public dataset to evaluate the performance of our method compared to state-of-the-art interactive segmentation methods.
We present a novel approach for training deep learning models for histopathology image segmentation that operates under weak supervision.
We constrain the model's attention to image regions that contain annotated cells, which we refer to as strong regions.
During training, the model learns to classify pixels in the strong regions while minimizing an attention loss that encourages it to attend to regions with cells and avoid those that do not.
We introduce a novel attention loss that rewards the model for attending to the strongest regions and penalizes it for attending to weak regions.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on three public histopathology image segmentation datasets, where we achieve state-of-the-art performance.

Abstract:

Deep learning (DL) has recently emerged as a powerful tool for machine health monitoring (MHM).
In this survey, we provide an overview of the current state of the art in DL for MHM, including key research challenges, opportunities, and limitations.
We begin by introducing the basic concepts of DL and MHM, and then review the different ways in which DL has been applied to MHM, including fault detection, diagnosis, and prognosis.
We then discuss the advantages and limitations of DL for MHM, and highlight key research challenges such as data acquisition, model selection, and deployment.
Finally, we provide a brief overview of the current state of the art in DL for MHM, and highlight potential research directions.
We hope that this survey will provide a comprehensive and informative overview of the current state of the art in DL for MHM, and inspire further research and development in this exciting field.
We study the problem of uniform information segmentation, i.e., dividing a given sequence of data into segments such that each segment receives an equal amount of information.

We consider a setting where a transmitter sends independent codewords over a binary erasure channel (BEC) to a receiver, and the goal is to design these codewords so that the receiver's uncertainty about the transmitted information is evenly distributed among the received segments.

We show that when the number of segments is a function of the blocklength, this problem is equivalent to the well-known uniform edge coverage problem from coding theory, and design an algorithm to find the maximum a-posteriori (MAP) assignment of each segment, given the received word.

We then consider the case where the number of segments is predetermined, and show that if the uncertainty in each segment is not evenly distributed, then there exists an alternative MAP assignment where the disparity in uncertainty between the segments is minimized.

We implement these algorithms to uniformly segment twenty artificial and real-world sequences, and compare the performance of our designs with uniform segment length and uniform entropy partitioning, both in terms of the disparity in uncertainty and the average segment length.
We present a fully-convolutional network for video segmentation which is able to produce pixel-wise segmentation masks for every frame in a video given a sufficiently long clip of consecutive frames.
Our network is built using a recurrent neural network architecture inside which we implement 3D convolutions to exploit the spatial-temporal volume of the input data.
We employ an attention mechanism which operates at the frame level to focus the network on the most relevant regions of the video clip.
Our network is trained end-to-end from pixel-level ground truth via a multi-scale segmentation loss.
We evaluate our method on the Cityscapes and CamVid datasets and achieve state-of-the-art results.
Active mean fields (AMFs) model image intensity as a dynamic fluid flowing under the influence of forces.

Here we study the equilibrium states of the discrete AMF model, and show that in closed form they provide a probabilistic interpretation of the Chan-Vese active contour model, as well as a discrete version of the Rudin-Osher-Fatemi (ROF) model with a pure jump process prior.
We characterize the continuum limits of our discrete model, and show that for appropriately chosen energies they coincide with the ROF model and a variant of the Chan-Vese model, respectively.

We demonstrate the utility of our approach on a series of images, where we compare our method to classical probabilistic segmentation methods, as well as to recent graph cuts and geodesic flows methods that are known to be closely related to the continuum AMF model.
Our approach is able to correctly segment difficult regions, including large smooth areas and areas with object boundaries.
Recent works have shown that Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) benefit 3D biomedical image segmentation, alleviating the shortcomings of conventional fully convolutional networks (FCNs).
Nonetheless, training end-to-end architectures that combine FCNs and RNNs is challenging due to the non-differentiability of slice-wise max pooling.
In this work, we propose a novel architecture that combines FCNs and RNNs, termed Recurrent Fully Convolutional Network (RFCN), which is trained end-to-end.
We overcome the non-differentiability issue by using a differentiable pooling technique.
We assess the proposed architecture on the challenging task of myocardial segmentation in cardiac MR images.
Our method achieves a competitive performance in comparison to state-of-the-art methods, without any pre-processing steps such as initializing the network with a pre-trained FCN.
Code is available at: https://github.com/yzsl/R-FCN.
We consider the problem of learning the parameters of log-supermodular distributions, which includes distributive lattice models as a special case.
We introduce a novel algorithm called Learning Optimal Hierarchical Abstract models (LOHA), which form a partition of the sample space given the parameters of the distribution.

We show that LOHA induces a greedy search over the space of hierarchical abstract models (HAM), and that the resulting parameter learning algorithm is asymptotically optimal in terms of expected Kullback-Leiber divergence, matching the lower bound up to a constant factor, improving upon the previous state of the art.

We further show that this greedy algorithm can be executed in distributed fashion, each processor holding a subset of the samples and communicating with others holding corresponding subsets, which induces a natural parallel version of LOHA.
We illustrate the use of our method on a real world dataset.

The abstract is as follows:

We present a simple and effective approach for video semantic segmentation, built upon the state-of-the-art Mask R-CNN architecture.

By adapting the architecture to process video streams efficiently, without performing expensive per-frame computations, our Clockwork Convnets achieve real-time performance at a fraction of the computational cost.
We introduce a temporal module that efficiently aggregates information across frames, driven by a clock mechanism that regulates the flow of information.
Our solution is trained in a single stage, without the need for any post-processing steps.
We validate our approach on the Cityscapes and CamVid datasets, and provide qualitative and quantitative analysis of the proposed technique.

We find that, despite having a very simple computational interface, the Neutro-Connectedness Cut (NCC) converges significantly faster than the Sinkhorn algorithm on a difficult benchmark of large-scale semi-supervised node classification.
In contrast to most graph-based semi-supervised learning algorithms, NCC is not based on kerneling, and interconnects nodes in a graph in a way that is analogue to classical linear algebra.
We introduce a new variant of NCC, which we term weighted NCC, that enables us to incorporate additional information in the form of node features.

We implement both NCC and weighted NCC in Apache Spark, and show that they can achieve convergence several orders of magnitude faster than the Sinkhorn algorithm on a real-world network with ground truth labels.
We present a technique for improving the performance of random walker image segmentation and registration algorithms.
Our method involves precomputing and storing intermediate results for a fixed set of input parameters.
By storing these precomputed results, we are able to significantly reduce the time required to compute the final result for any given input image.
We find that our method is particularly useful for segmentation and registration problems that involve large images or a large number of images.
Our method is adaptable in the sense that it can be used with any random walker algorithm that utilizes a graphical model representation.
We present experimental results demonstrating the effectiveness of our method on a number of different images.

We present a multi-task learning framework, DeepSaliency, for joint training of a deep neural network (DNN) for image saliency detection and for learning the underlying salient object characteristics.
Our method learns a shared deep representation between the two tasks: predicting saliency maps and predicting object masks in salient regions.
We introduce a novel salient object characteristic mining loss that enforces the DNN to learn a deep representation that can be used to selectively mine salient object characteristics.
Our method also naturally leverages an ensemble of predicted object masks for robustly segmenting salient objects.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on four publicly available datasets, comparing to the state-of-the-art methods on both saliency detection and salient object segmentation.
In particular, our model achieves the state-of-the-art performance on the MIT-CBCL and UCFSports datasets with a significant margin.
Code is available at: https://github.com/michuanhd/DeepSaliency.
We show how to use a model of social dynamics, specifically the Deffuant-Weisbuch model, for unsupervised image segmentation.
In this model, pixels or regions compete for labels in an iterative process of local refinement and global competition.

We introduce a novel multi-scale implementation that allows the model to simultaneously identify objects at multiple scales, and show improvements in segmentation quality as compared to previous approaches.

We demonstrate the performance of our algorithm on the Berkeley Segmentation Dataset and show that it computes reasonable segmentations without any parameter tuning or training, and provides a viable alternative to existing approaches in terms of both running time and memory usage.
Arxiv is a powerful new tool for computer vision.
We present a technique for the automatic formation of a hierarchy of superpixels from a single image, where the hierarchy is induced by pixel similarity.
This unsupervised approach produces a tree of nested superpixels, each of which is a dense region of pixels that is itself a segmentation of the image.
We demonstrate that the fine-grain segmentation produced by our approach, without any parameter tuning, closely rivals state-of-the-art superpixel methods in both run-time and quality.
We further present a novel extension of our technique to video data, where our method automatically detects and tracks objects in motion.

Previous approaches to superpixel segmentation have relied on a priori knowledge of the underlying image structure, by either modeling the spatial relationship between pixels or by adapting techniques from vector quantization.
In contrast, our approach is entirely unsupervised and does not make any assumptions about the image other than it can be decomposed into a hierarchical arrangement of groups of similar pixels.
To achieve this, we adopt a spectral technique whereby pixels are clustered according to similarity in the eigenspace of a large collection of pixel descriptors.
This enables our approach to discover structures in the image that are both global and local in nature.
Our technique can be viewed as a multiresolution segmentation method, but one that is entirely automatic and parameter-free.
We evaluate our approach on the seminal Berkeley Segmentation Dataset

[2], and show that our method, without any parameter tuning, compares favorably with the current state-of-the-art superpixel methods in terms of both run-time and segmentation quality as measured by the F-measure.
We further demonstrate that our technique is able to discover a hierarchical arrangement of superpixels, with finer-grain segments being formed from the merger of larger ones.
We further demonstrate an application of our segmentation technique to the problem of object detection and tracking in video.
We show that our approach is able to detect and track objects in motion, without any a priori knowledge of object location or appearance, or any parameter tuning.
This opens the door to a new class of completely unsupervised video analysis methods that are able to discover object structure from raw video data.
We present a novel approach for joint image segmentation and deconvolution of ultrasound (US) images using a hierarchical Bayesian model based on generalized Gaussian priors.
The model is designed to handle the challenges of US image reconstruction, such as the presence of noise, speckle, and complex tissue structures.

By incorporating a prior distribution that captures the statistical properties of real US images, the model is able to effectively regularize the reconstruction process and improve the quality of the estimated image.
The proposed method is evaluated on a clinical dataset consisting of US images of the liver and compared to state-of-the-art algorithms.
The results show that the proposed method achieves improved segmentation and deconvolution performance compared to the baseline algorithm.
Furthermore, the proposed method is able to recover finer details in the estimated image, resulting in improved visualization of anatomical structures.
The proposed method has the potential to improve the diagnostic accuracy of US imaging and assist in the detection and characterization of lesions and other abnormalities.
We present an approach to semantic segmentation based on a very deep fully convolutional network.

This architecture, which consists of 8 convolutional layers followed by a context prediction layer, is trained directly on the pixels of the images and their corresponding semantic labels in the dataset.
Without any parameter tuning or network architecture modifications, our method achieves a mean accuracy of 86.8% on the NYUv2 dataset, a 1.2% increase over the previous state-of-the-art.
We further improve the performance to 89.2% by adding skip connections, a technique recently proposed for training very deep networks.
On the challenging PASCAL VOC 2012 dataset with its complex object contexts, our model achieves a mean accuracy of 79.8%, which is a 1.6% improvement over the previous best result.
Adaptive segmentation is crucial in image processing and computer vision.
In this paper, we propose a novel unsupervised color image segmentation method based on the Voronoi region (VR), which is derived from the Voronoi diagram (VD).
Specifically, we first construct a VD of the image based on the ISO data, and then compute the VR of each pixel.
By analyzing the relationship between the colors of the pixels in each VR, a novel unsupervised segmentation method is then proposed to segment the image.
The proposed method has been tested on a variety of images, and the experimental results demonstrate its effectiveness and superiority compared to some state-of-the-art algorithms.
Recent progress in semantic segmentation largely benefited from the advances of deep learning.
However, directly applying deep learning to instance-based video description is difficult due to the uncertainty and the diversity of the instance-level semantics.

In this paper, we argue that the instance-level semantics should be described in a coarse-to-fine manner and propose a multi-scale multiple instance video description network (MMVDN) to tackle the video description problem.
Specifically, we decompose the video description process into three scales: low, middle, and high, each of which takes a coarse-to-fine approach.
We design a Pyramid Pooling Module (PPM) to capture the global and local instance-level semantics at each scale.
Moreover, we propose a Recurrent Pyramid Pooling Module (RPPM) to capture the temporal consistency of the instance-level semantics across frames.
The proposed MMVDN effectively utilizes the structural information of the instances, which tends to be helpful for describing the instance-level semantics.
We evaluate our method on the VOC2012 and the Cityscapes datasets for instance-based video description and achieve competitive results when compared with the state-of-the-art methods.
We have developed a method to increase the spatial resolution of SMAP soil moisture data from the native L3 resolution of 1km to 9km.
This method uses a kernel machine approach to combine the original SMAP L3 soil moisture data with meteorological data as well as a moisture calibration.

In an effort to make the dataset generated reproducible, all code and required data inputs have been made public and the dataset generated by the code provided has been uploaded to the SMAP science team's data archive.
In this paper, we describe the methodology and evaluate the performance of the resulting high resolution soil moisture dataset against various in situ benchmarks.
We conclude that at 9km resolution our methodology provides a robust increase in resolution over the 1km product without a significant loss in information.
We present a simple and efficient approach for learning a high-level prior for semantic segmentation, which is a strong predictor of ground-truth segment maps.

By training a convolutional neural network (CNN) to predict segment maps as directly as possible given the input image, we learn a prior over segment labels that has high-level knowledge of the scene.
This prior enables a new semi-supervised learning framework that is applicable to most state-of-the-art segmentation methods, and shows promising results on the PASCAL VOC 2012 dataset.
We also present an efficient variant that reduces the memory footprint of the CNN by factor of 64 at test time, while only suffering a small drop in accuracy.
We introduce a formalism of a segment-phrase table (SPT) for semantic segmentation, visual entailment and paraphrasing tasks.
It captures the universal hierarchy of semantic propositions of entities, their attributes and relationships in a fine-grained and compositional manner.

A neural network is trained to induce an SPT from unsupervised video and image captions, where each row corresponds to a phrase in a caption and each column corresponds to a segment in a video or image.
The cell entries capture the likelihood of the phrase explaining the segment based on a similarity metric.
An SPT factorizes the likelihood as a product of the individual phrase and segment probabilities, which enables the evaluation of paraphrases by simply summing their respective entries.
We show that an SPT can be used for visual entailment, where an SPT entry supports or refutes the presence of a phrase in a given segment.
We further show how an SPT can be used for semantic segmentation as an energy function that optimizes the segmentation by maximizing the likelihood of a caption.

Our experimental results on the VisualGenome dataset and YouTubeCooking dataset demonstrate that an SPT can be effectively learned from videos and image captions, outperforming previous work on semantic segmentation, visual entailment and paraphrasing.
Recent advances in imaging acquisition technology have resulted in a deluge of big data in the form of extremely large images.
Segmentation of organs and structures of interest in such images is a tedious, tedious and laborious task, the solution of which automatically segments images and accelerates the workflow.
In this paper, we present a systematic survey of recent methods of multi-atlas segmentation of biomedical images.
We compare the methods based on the type of atlas used, the segmentation algorithm, the similarity measure used and the evaluation metrics.
We also discuss the current challenges and future directions.
Our survey can serve as a useful reference for researchers interested in multi-atlas segmentation of biomedical images.

Abstract:
We present an architecture for biomedical image segmentation based on deep convolutional neural networks.
The network is designed to leverage the advantages of both encoder-decoder architecture and U-shaped architecture, whilst mitigating their drawbacks.

A key property of the proposed architecture is its ability to exploit the long range dependencies in the image, whilst maintaining the ability to effectively capture context information at various levels of granularity.
We refer to the proposed architecture as the U-Net.
We demonstrate the performance of our method on a challenging dataset of 20 manually annotated images from the ISBI challenge 2016.
Our method achieves a dice coefficient of 0.854, surpassing the dice coefficient of all other submissions to the challenge.
Code is available at: https://github.com/uo-bi/UNet.
Kernel spectral clustering (KSC) is a nonlinear dimension reduction technique and a general framework for clustering, pioneered by Davis et al. (2004).
It encompasses several other kernel-based methods, such as kernel PCA and kernel Fisher discriminant analysis (Kernel-FDD), as special cases.
This article provides a comprehensive introduction to KSC, covering the basic algorithm, theoretical properties, and practical tips for implementation.
We also discuss extensions of KSC, including kernel CCA and kernel MDS, and applications in text mining, image analysis, and bioinformatics.

Introduction

Spectral clustering is a popular technique for clustering and dimension reduction, originating from the spectral decomposition of symmetric positive semidefinite matrices.
It has been shown to be effective in a variety of applications, including image analysis, text mining, and bioinformatics.
The original spectral clustering algorithm, also known as spectral embedding, is a linear method, which works well when the data is linearly separable.
However, in many applications, the data are not linearly separable, and linear methods may not perform well.
This is where kernel spectral clustering (KSC) comes in.
KSC is a nonlinear dimension reduction technique that combines the power of kernel methods with the efficiency of spectral clustering.
It has been shown to be effective in a variety of applications, including image analysis, text mining, and bioinformatics.
The basic idea behind KSC is to project the data into a higher-dimensional space, where it can be linearly separated, and then apply a spectral clustering algorithm to the projected data.
In this article, we will introduce the basic concepts of KSC, including the algorithm itself, theoretical properties, and practical tips for implementation.

We will also discuss extensions of KSC, including kernel canonical correlation analysis (KCCA) and kernel multivariate statistical analysis (KMSA), and applications in text mining, image analysis, and bioinformatics.
