Visual saliency detection has undergone great progress in recent years, driven by the significant advances in deep neural network research.
In this paper, we propose a novel approach for saliency detection based on multiscale deep features.
Our method first generates a series of multi-scale features from deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs).

Then, we build a computational model that integrates the multi-scale deep features with a reinforcement learning framework, where a discriminative deep feature and a reinforcement learning component are jointly trained in an end-to-end manner.
We evaluate our method on the public SALICON benchmark, and the results demonstrate that our approach outperforms the state-of-the-art methods.
Deep learning methods have achieved tremendous success in image segmentation in recent years.
However, directly applying deep learning models on resource-constrained devices, such as smartphones, is impractical, due to their huge model size and high computational complexity.
In this paper, we aim to explore an efficient yet effective image segmentation method for screen content, which is composed of texts, graphics, and images.
It is highly challenging since the variety of screen contents makes it difficult to design hand-crafted features and the small dataset size makes it unsuitable for deep learning methods.
We propose a screen content image segmentation method based on least absolute deviation (LAD) fitting.
It is efficient because it only uses 1-D kernels and a small number of parameters.
We optimize the parameters using the LAD cost function to find the best fitting between the features and the ground truth.
Our experimental results on four benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our method against the state-of-the-art methods.
The runtime of our proposed method is around 14 times faster than the second fastest method and our model size is 5 times smaller.
Image segmentation serves as a fundamental computer vision task with numerous applications in object recognition, image editing, and robotics.

Although recent advances in deep learning have resulted in significant performance improvements in pixel-level image segmentation, directly predicting pixel-wise labels from images is challenging due to the infinite number of labels (i.e., pixels) in an image.
Additionally, for many real-world applications, predicting a pixel-wise label map is not sufficient.
Instead, more detailed and structured semantic descriptions of images, such as object bounding boxes, instance labels, or relationship annotations, are often needed.

In this survey, we provide a comprehensive overview of recent advances in pixel-level image segmentation as well as more advanced segmentation settings, including instance-level segmentation, object detection, and relationship cosegmentation.
We cover both bottom-up and top-down segmentation approaches, including methods based on deep learning, graph cuts, and conditional random fields.
For each segmentation setting, we provide an overview of the state-of-the-art approaches, discuss their advantages and limitations, and outline open problems and challenges.
Our main goal is to provide a comprehensive and structured overview of the field of image segmentation and related tasks, which may serve as a reference for researchers entering this field.
Filters play an important role in fingerprint image segmentation.
A good filter can significantly improve the quality of the segmented image, resulting in more accurate fingerprint matching.
In this paper, we design a new filter for fingerprint image segmentation and evaluate its performance.
The new filter is based on the idea of adaptive filtering, where the filter parameters are adjusted based on the local characteristics of the input image.
We evaluate the performance of the new filter using a variety of fingerprint images, and compare its performance to that of existing filters.
The results show that the new filter significantly improves the quality of the segmented images, resulting in more accurate fingerprint matching.
The proposed method has various postprocessing approaches to clean the noise, remove the speckles, and preserve the minutiae.
The performance of the proposed method is compared with four different methods.
From the experimental results, our proposed method shows a good performance in terms of the segmentation quality.
In addition, the proposed method is implemented in parallel architecture and achieves 1.8 times speedup in terms of execution time.
In this paper, a new approach is proposed for brain tumor detection based on bilateral symmetry information.
First, we extract the bilateral symmetry information of the brain tumor region from MR images.
Then, we classify the brain tumor region based on the extracted information.
The proposed approach has been tested on 100 MR images from the ISBI challenge 2016.
The experimental results show that the proposed approach can achieve a high accuracy rate of 92.6%, which is significantly better than the other state-of-the-art approaches.
The proposed approach consists of three main steps: image preprocessing, bilateral symmetry analysis, and tumor detection.
In the image preprocessing step, the MR images are corrected for intensity non-uniformity and brain extraction is performed to separate the brain region from the background.
In the bilateral symmetry analysis step, the bilateral symmetry information of the brain tumor region is extracted.
This is achieved by calculating the mutual information between the tumor region and its mirror reflection in the opposite hemisphere.
The tumor detection step classifies the brain tumor region based on the extracted bilateral symmetry information.
This is done by training a support vector machine (SVM) classifier with the extracted mutual information as the feature vector.
The experimental results show that the proposed approach can achieve a high accuracy rate of 92.6%, compared to the other state-of-the-art approaches, which have an accuracy rate of less than 90%.
The proposed approach can be used as a reliable and accurate method for brain tumor detection in MR images.
It has the potential to be used in clinical practice to improve the diagnosis and treatment of brain tumors.
Crowd segmentation is a fundamental task in crowd analysis, with a wide range of applications including surveillance, public safety, and autonomous driving.

Existing crowd segmentation methods mainly rely on hand-crafted features, such as edge, texture, or motion features, and these methods often struggle to extract these features in a crowded and complex scene.
In this paper, we propose a fully convolutional neural network (FCNN) for crowd segmentation, which is trained end-to-end from scratch.
Our network takes an image as input and produces a segmentation mask as output.
We train our network on a new crowd segmentation benchmark, which we create by combining the crowd-scene segmentation dataset with the Berkeley segmentation dataset.
Our network outperforms the state-of-the-art methods on both the crowd-scene segmentation dataset and the Berkeley segmentation dataset.
We also perform a comprehensive analysis of our network, including the effect of different architectural choices and training strategies.

Optical imaging can benefit from quantum technologies such as quantum illumination and quantum sensing for low-light and noisy conditions, but imaging itself is a challenging task for quantum devices.
Quantum edge detection can be an intermediate step, as it is a classical preprocessing step for image segmentation, and has been studied for classical images.

In this paper, we investigate quantum edge detection for image segmentation in optical environments, and propose an approach to improve the performance of the classical scheme in the presence of Poisson noise, using quantum illumination.
We apply the scheme to a single photon imaging scenario as a proof of principle.
Our approach can find edges in images segmented via histogram equalization, for a wide range of noise levels.
We implement the scheme using superconducting nanowire single photon detectors, and demonstrate the robustness of the scheme to noise through numerical simulations.
Biofilm is a causative factor for many oral diseases, and monitoring biofilm formation is crucial in understanding the disease progression.
The objective of this study was to develop a statistical modeling algorithm based on computer-aided tomography (CT) images for the quantification of dental biofilm.
Methods: In this cross-sectional study, we identified four regions of interest (ROIs) in each tooth of a subject and measured the mean Hounsfield unit (HU) values for each ROI.
The subject was then divided into four groups based on the presence of restorations.
A generalized linear model (GLM) was fitted between the HU values and the thickness of the biofilm.
The model was validated using an independent dataset.
Results: The GLM predicted a strong relationship between the HU values and the biofilm thickness (R 2 = 0.83, p < 0.001).

The model showed that the gluteal and occlusal ROIs were the most effective regions for the prediction of biofilm thickness, with a strong correlation between the predicted and the actual thicknesses (R 2 = 0.93 and 0.91, respectively, both p < 0.001).
Conclusions: A statistical modeling algorithm based on HU values derived from CT images can be used to predict the thickness of dental biofilm in vivo.
This algorithm may be used as a tool to monitor and manage biofilm formation.
Nature-inspired algorithms perform well in image segmentation, but the choice of a base algorithm has a significant impact on performance.

In this research, the application of four nature-inspired algorithms (particle swarm optimization, bacterial foraging optimization, cuckoo search, and firefly algorithm) for multi-threshold image segmentation is compared.
Metrics including computation time and segmentation quality are considered.
The results show that the firefly algorithm outperforms the others in both metrics.
Particle swarm optimization achieved the second best performance.
Cuckoo search and bacterial foraging optimization did not perform as well as the top two algorithms.
The results suggest that the firefly algorithm is currently the best option for multi-threshold image segmentation among these four algorithms.
However, it should be noted that the segmentation quality of the firefly algorithm depends on the parameter settings.

We present a new computational method for multivariate Bayesian image segmentation (MBIS) based on a hierarchical Bayesian model that we developed for segmenting images obtained from multivariate fluorescent microscopy images.
In our approach, we define a joint distribution that models the spatial continuity across pixels within each segment and the relationship between multiple fluorescent channels.
We introduce a novel algorithm, called the Markov chain Monte Carlo proposal generator (MCPMG), for efficient sampling of this joint distribution.

The MCPMG combines the benefits of Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods, which provide robust Bayesian inference for high-dimensional models, with proposal-based sampling techniques that introduce a form of local exploration, enabling more efficient segmentation.
The resulting MBIS algorithm is demonstrated on both simulated and real data.
The simulated data include scenarios that are designed to be challenging for existing algorithms, involving a high degree of non-linear intensity variations and noise.

The results show that the MBIS algorithm provides a significant improvement in segmentation accuracy compared to existing state-of-the-art algorithms on these data sets and suggests that the MBIS algorithm may provide similar benefits for real data.
We show how to construct optimal image segmentations using particle methods.
Our approach is based on minimization of a functional that trades off between segmenting pixels correctly and minimizing the gradient of the resulting segmentation.
This functional is a Sobolev gradient, that is, the sum of the gradients of all pixels, weighted by a per-pixel smoothness term.

We propose to approximate this Sobolev gradient by a particle system, and show that, under an approximation scheme, the global minimizer of the particle system corresponds to the optimal segmentation.
Furthermore, we show how to efficiently solve the particle system using a block-coordinate descent algorithm.

We evaluate our method on the benchmark datasets of the 2016 CAMELYON challenge, and show that it compares favorably to state-of-the-art segmentation methods, while being simpler, faster, and requiring less parameter tuning.
We present a novel class of algorithms for submodular optimization that is both simpler and more powerful than previous methods.
Our approach is based on reflecting the gradient of the objective function with respect to each decision variable.

This reflection has two benefits: it simplifies the optimization problem by transforming it into a convex problem, and it exploits the structure of the submodular function to obtain a better approximation guarantee.
Our reflection method can be easily incorporated into any first-order method, such as gradient descent or stochastic gradient descent.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on a wide variety of submodular optimization problems, including submodular function optimization, matroid intersection, and minimax optimization.
We also show how to use our reflection method to solve the popular knapsack problem with fractional items, which has applications in numerous fields including robotics and finance.
In this paper, we propose a method for mammogram edge detection using hybrid soft computing methods.
The proposed method combines the advantages of both fuzzy logic and artificial neural networks to achieve accurate and efficient edge detection in digital mammograms.

Fuzzy logic is used to handle the uncertainty and imprecision in the edge detection process, while artificial neural networks are used to learn and model the complex relationships between the input and output variables.
The proposed method was evaluated on a database of digital mammograms and compared to existing edge detection methods.
The results show that the proposed method can effectively detect edges in digital mammograms and outperform existing methods in terms of accuracy and efficiency.
Furthermore, the proposed method has the advantage of being fully automated, making it suitable for use in clinical practice.
We present a fast semidefinite programming (SDP) approach for solving binary quadratic problems (BQPs).
Our approach is based on conic duality and a new semidefinite representation of binary quadratic functions.
We show that our SDP formulation enjoys a strong duality and a linear convergence rate.
In addition, we present an effective primal-dual algorithm, called the Fast Iterative Semi-Definite (FISD) algorithm, to solve the BQP through our SDP formulation.
Finally, we demonstrate the efficiency of our approach through a comprehensive set of experiments.

Compared to the state-of-the-art SDP solver SDPA, our approach is significantly faster and more scalable, with speedups as large as $7\times$ on a set of widely used BQP instances from the BQP library.
Fuzzy C-means (FCM) is probably the most widely used clustering algorithm in the field of fuzzy clustering.
FCM is known to be hard to optimize since the whole cluster partition vector has to be optimized simultaneously.
In this paper, we propose a novel method to transform FCM into a penalty-based optimization problem, for which many existing optimization algorithms can be applied.
Specifically, we generate the penalty constraints according to the cluster region, which is the union of fuzzy balls centered at cluster centers.
Since the cluster region is vague, we introduce the concept of kernelization to handle the ambiguity.
Experimental results on several data sets show that our approach is very effective in optimizing FCM and can even outperform other state-of-the-art fuzzy clustering algorithms.
Image segmentation is a process of partitioning an image into multiple segments in order to simplify the representation of an image and to facilitate subsequent processing.
The adaptive distance, which measures the similarity between the pixel and its neighboring pixels, is a powerful tool for image segmentation.
In this paper, we propose a novel image segmentation algorithm based on the EM algorithm and the adaptive distance.
Our algorithm starts with an initialization using K-means clustering.
Then, it iteratively updates the segmentation by minimizing a cost function that measures the dissimilarity between the predicted adaptive distance and the ground truth distance.
The cost function is formulated as a min-max problem, and the optimal solution is obtained by applying the EM algorithm.
Our algorithm is evaluated on multiple benchmark datasets, and the experimental results show that it achieves competitive performance compared to other state-of-the-art image segmentation algorithms.
We introduce a curvature prior for implicit surfaces that is derived from Gaussian curvature and can be integrated into multiresolution analysis frameworks.
By doing so, we extend the scope of classical multiresolution analysis to capture shape details beyond the basic topology of a surface.
In particular, we show that the proposed prior can effectively guide the process of segmentation and shape inpainting.
We demonstrate the applicability of our method in both 2D and 3D shape analysis.
In 2D, we show that the proposed prior can be used for image segmentation, while in 3D we demonstrate the recovery of shape details in incomplete point clouds.

Many image super-resolution (SR) methods have been proposed for estimating a high-resolution (HR) image from a single low-resolution (LR) image.
However, these methods tend to blur the boundaries of objects in the HR image.
We propose a selective super-resolution (SSR) method to overcome this limitation.
Our SSR method estimates the HR image by frequency-domain interpolation in edge regions and by intensity-domain interpolation in non-edge regions.
The edge regions are detected using a Canny edge detector.
To reduce the amount of computation, the proposed method is optimized for implementation on a graphics processing unit (GPU).
Our SSR method is compared with state-of-the-art SR methods using several test images.
The results show that the SSR method gives better visual quality without increasing the number of artifacts.

In this paper, we present a new approach for lung image segmentation using a fuzzy possibilistic C-means algorithm.
Our approach combines the benefits of both fuzzy set theory and possibilistic clustering, allowing for more accurate and robust segmentation results.
The proposed algorithm utilizes a fuzzy possibilistic membership function, which provides a degree of uncertainty to the segmentation process.
This enables the algorithm to better handle the challenges of noise, anatomical variations, and other complexities often encountered in lung images.

Furthermore, the use of a fuzzy possibilistic approach allows for more flexible segmentation results, as it can capture the underlying uncertainty in the data and provide a range of possible segmentations rather than a single definitive answer.
We evaluate the performance of our algorithm on a publicly available lung image dataset, and the results demonstrate its effectiveness and robustness compared to existing approaches.
We present an algorithm for maximin affinity learning of image segmentation.
It is a hard assignment problem of learning a discrete labeling of a finite set of pixels given a finite set of labeled examples, with a penalty for labeling pixels differently from neighbors.
Our algorithm is based on a novel approximation of the maximin criterion that enables the use of a gradient descent procedure with a convergence guarantee.
We show that the algorithm is efficient in terms of both time and space, and we demonstrate its performance on a number of benchmark images.

Introduction

The problem of assigning labels to pixels in images arises in many applications including image segmentation, texture analysis, and image registration.
A wide range of techniques have been proposed for this problem.

These techniques can be broadly classified into two categories: (i) parametric methods that assume a model for the joint distribution of the labels and pixels, and (ii) non-parametric methods that learn directly from the data without making assumptions about the data distribution.
While parametric methods often achieve high accuracy, they suffer from two main drawbacks.
First, they require the specification of an appropriate model for the data, which may not be available or may not be correct.
Second, they may not be able to generalize well to unseen data since they optimize performance only within the specified model.
In contrast, non-parametric methods do not make any assumptions about the data distribution and can therefore handle a wider range of data.
However, they may not achieve the same level of accuracy as parametric methods, and they may also be more computationally expensive.
In this paper, we present a new algorithm for learning image segmentation that combines the advantages of both parametric and non-parametric methods.
Our algorithm is based on a maximin optimization criterion that minimizes the worst-case penalty for labeling pixels differently from neighbors, while allowing for some noise in the labels.
This optimization criterion can be viewed as a non-parametric method since it does not make any assumptions about the data distribution.
However, our algorithm is also efficient in terms of both time and space, and it can achieve high levels of accuracy.
To evaluate the performance of our algorithm, we conduct a comprehensive set of experiments on a number of benchmark images.
Our results show that our algorithm is competitive with the state-of-the-art in image segmentation, while offering the advantage of not requiring any assumptions about the data distribution.

In this paper, we address the problem of determining the connectivity of the lambda-agents for the image segmentation based on the lambda-architecture.

Given the set of input images, the lambda-architecture applies non-local mean-shift filtering to detect the regions of interest (ROIs) firstly, then adopts the lambda-agents to perform pixel-level segmentation of ROIs.
In order to obtain the precise segmentation results, the suitable connectivity of lambda-agents should be determined such that the oversegmentation can be avoided.
However, the existing methods usually adopt fixed connectivities for all images, which may result in oversegmentation for some images.
In this paper, we propose an adaptive lambda-connectedness determination approach by analyzing the distribution of the segmentation residues of images.
The proposed approach can accurately estimate the optimal connectivity for individual image, and thereby further improve the segmentation results.
In addition, since the proposed approach only needs the segmentation residues which can be obtained without extra computation, it is efficient in terms of computation.
We perform measurements on a commercial quantum memory system to test a theoretical countermeasure against coherent attacks on quantum memory systems.
This countermeasure assumes independent detection efficiencies for each detector, yet we find this to be violated by 3 standard deviations, revealing that this countermeasure can be improved.
We discuss how realistic assumptions should be made for optimal implementation of the countermeasure and provide examples of possible implementations.
We introduce the cascade product of answer set programs (ASP), a simple and intuitive variant of the well-known answer set programming (ASP) paradigm for knowledge representation and reasoning.

In a cascade product, the answers to a logic program are computed by means of a bottom-up traversal of the program's dependency graph, computed at program runtime; this traversal is driven by concrete substitutions of parameter variables, and may be guided by selected choices among program rules.
We demonstrate that this new programming construct permits the encoding of reasoning tasks that are difficult or impossible within the classical ASP framework.

As a representative example, we consider the problem of computing the least fixpoint of an arbitrary monotone function, a problem that has been shown to be complete for exponential time within the classical ASP framework.
By means of a cascade product program, this problem can be solved in polynomial time.

We study a system of weakly coupled clusters, describing a disordered material with metallic and insulating states, by means of using numerical linked-cluster expansion, which is based on an exact treatment of all cluster excitations.
Previously discovered metal-insulator transition line in the parameter space of the model is reproduced.
We find a new type of transition line, which ends up in a critical point, at which a metal-insulator quantum phase transition takes place.
Near the critical point, both types of transitions are of second order.
Using an additional parameter, we fine-tune the system to a new region of the phase diagram, where the metallic and insulating states are separated by a first-order transition.
We provide an explanation of the nature of the metallic state and the metal-insulator transition in terms of existing concepts of the theory of disordered materials.
Keywords: metal-insulator transition, strongly correlated electrons, numerical linked-cluster expansion, cluster decomposition
Unsupervised learning aims to discover structures in unlabeled data.
One of the most popular techniques exploited in unsupervised learning is the discovery of clusters or classes in the data distribution.
In this paper, a new algorithm for unsupervised learning is proposed, in which classes are modeled as mixtures of skewed distributions (MSDs).
This algorithm implements an iterative method that efficiently converges to a local minima, and is therefore named the Skewed Distribution Algorithm (SDA).
The convergence of the SDA is assured through a contraction mapping theorem and the global convergence is discussed.
Furthermore, Hypercube Contours (HCCs) are used to identify the regions of attraction of the local minima, in order to select the optimal solution among all the local minima.

The proposed algorithm is compared with five other unsupervised learning algorithms, using synthetic datasets with known underlying solutions, and is shown to be competitive in terms of solution quality.
Many neurons exhibit morphological plasticity, altering the shape and connectivity of their dendritic spines in response to physiological cues.

Here, we show that chronic activation of endogenous signaling pathways downstream of bone morphogenetic protein (BMP) receptors leads to the rapid loss of dendritic spines in cortical neurons in culture and dendritic simplification in neurons in mouse brain slices.
Signaling was specific to BMP ligands because Activin did not produce these effects and because the BMP pathway inhibitors, Dorsomorphin and DMH1, blocked the signaling.

Interestingly, the effects of BMP signaling in culture were blocked by inhibitors of histone deacetylase (HDAC) activity, including sodium butyrate and trichostatin A, but not by the kinase inhibitors, suggesting a link between BMP signaling and HDAC activity.
Moreover, BMP ligands induced recruitment of HDAC2 and 3 to the nucleus as shown by immunofluorescence and pull-down assays.

Inhibiting HDAC activity blocked the ability of BMP ligands to simplify dendritic structures, to cause a decrease in synaptic puncta number, and to cause an increase in the percentage of neurons with a single punctum.
In neurons dissociated from mouse cortex, the addition of BMP ligands caused a decrease in the number of synaptic puncta and an increase in the percentage of neurons with a single punctum.
This effect was blocked by DMH1 and by inhibitors of HDAC activity.
These results support a model in which BMP signaling triggers changes in HDAC activity, which in turn increases the rate of structural plasticity in dendritic spines.
Magnetic reconnection is a fundamental process in plasma physics, by which magnetic fields deconnect and merge, converting magnetic energy into other forms like particle heating.
In this work, we investigate the effect of including large-scale effective potentials in the collisionless magnetic reconnection framework.
We show that the large-scale dynamics modifies the particle distributions in the reconnection layer, affecting the ion heating.
The effective potentials act as a converging lens that traps ions, modifying their trajectories.
We observe that this trapping effect reduces the ion heating compared to the case without the large-scale dynamics.
The reduction of ion heating is more significant when the strength of the effective potential is stronger.
Our results suggest that the large-scale dynamics plays an important role in controlling ion heating during magnetic reconnection.
We define a notion of Keplerian dynamics on a subclass of the Heisenberg group, and give a necessary and sufficient condition for a planar solution curve to be Keplerian in this setting.
This condition is analogous to a condition in the Newton-Hooke setting due to Arnold and Avez.

As an application, we give a complete description of all Keplerian solutions on the standard Heisenberg group, and use this description to give a complete description of all such solutions in the related setting of the Euclidean group.

These results are useful for comparing the distributions of relaxed complex Wishart variables, which are commonly used in statistical modeling and machine learning.
The expressions are straightforward to implement and provide a robust and efficient alternative to existing simulation-based approaches.

Wishart distributions are commonly used in statistical modeling and machine learning, particularly for modeling the distribution of random matrices.
In many applications, it is important to compare the distributions of relaxed complex Wishart variables, which are obtained by adding a small amount of noise to the variables.

The stochastic distance between two such distributions can provide a measure of the difference between the distributions, which is useful for comparing different models or for evaluating the performance of a model.

Existing approaches to calculating the stochastic distance between relaxed complex Wishart distributions typically involve simulation-based approaches, such as Monte Carlo simulation or bootstrap methods.
These approaches can be computationally expensive and may not be suitable for large datasets or complex models.
Additionally, they may not provide accurate results for distributions that are highly skewed or have complex structures.
Our approach provides a robust and efficient alternative to existing simulation-based approaches.

We study existence and uniqueness of classical solutions for a chemotaxis-fluid system on a general bounded domain in $\mathbb{R}^3$, and we investigate the global behavior of the solutions.
The model consists of a system of nonlinear partial differential equations for the density of the cells, the chemotactic flux, and the fluid velocity.
The system includes a degenerate parabolic equation for the density of the cells, a convection-diffusion equation for the chemotactic flux, and the Navier-Stokes equations for the fluid velocity.

We show that the system generates a unique classical solution on a general bounded domain in $\mathbb{R}^3$. We also show that the solution behaves like a classical solution of a degenerate parabolic equation with a global attractor for large time.
We study Anderson localization in a model system: a partially random Bragg grating with weak disorder in the refractive index.
Provided that the interval between the Bragg planes is uniform, we prove a conserved area theorem, i.e., the area of the localized modes does not increase as the disorder strength is increased.
In the Bragg regime, where the localized mode is induced only by the Bragg scattering, our proof relies on a detailed balance argument.
Beyond the Bragg regime, an additional bound on the transverse wave vector is required, and a complementary argument using mode-coupling theory and the orthogonality of the plane waves is provided.
The validity of our conserved area theorem is confirmed by numerical simulations.

We give a constructive proof that any unitary operator on a finite-dimensional Hilbert space can be approximated to any required degree of accuracy by a sequence of unitary operators each of which can be specified by a lattice parameterization.
Previously, this had been proved in a nonconstructive way, by complex analytic means.
We also give a simple construction, which illustrates our methods, of an approximate gate that is closer to the desired gate than any other lattice gate, and yet is still a lattice gate.
Let V be a finite-dimensional vector space over a finite field with q>0 elements, and let 1<k<min{n,q}.
Every set of k-independent vectors in V can be partitioned into t subsets, such that each subset spans the same vector subspace of V, and this partition is unique up to a permutation of the subsets.
The number t is denoted by f_k(n,q) and is called the Frobenius number of k-independent vectors in V.
It is known that f_k(n,q)=(q^n-1)/(q-1) for k=2, and is an open problem for k>2.
We prove that f_k(n,q)≤(q^n-1)/(q-1) for all 1<k<min{n,q}, providing an upper bound that matches the aforementioned lower bound in the case of k=3.
We detail the experimental configurations used to simulate 25 experiments for the DUNE collaboration's first CDR.
These simulations use a modified version of the DUNE analysis software, including an updated geant4 geometry and the latest DUNE physics lists and models.
We document the changes made for these simulations, and discuss the accuracy of the results.
The configurations are all publicly available, and can be used as a starting point for physics list validation, as well as for planning of forthcoming experiments.
We demonstrate the existence of non-diffracting chirped Bessel beams in optical antiguides.
By using the additional degree of freedom offered by a temporal chirp, these new types of soliton-like waveforms propagate without diffraction in a homogeneous medium.

We show that the wavefronts of these chirped Bessel beams remain parallel during propagation in an optical antiguide, such as a photonic crystal or a periodic dielectric waveguide, without requiring any a priori coordination between the spatial and temporal degrees of freedom.
We discuss how these waves can be excited in various systems and how they may be utilized for novel applications in fields such as quantum information and optical imaging.
Let $(X_n)_{n\in \mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence of real-valued random variables.

The sequence is called subgaussian if, for some $\sigma^2>0$, $$\mathbb{E} \exp\left(\lambda \cdot \max_{1\leq n \leq m} X_n\right) \leq \exp(\sigma^2 \lambda^2 m), \quad m \in \mathbb{N}, \ \lambda \geq 0.$$
In this paper, we study the property of subgaussianity in probability and Fourier analysis.
We show that the Fourier transform of a subgaussian sequence is a subgaussian function and that the characteristic function of a subgaussian sequence is subgaussian.

Furthermore, we present a necessary and sufficient condition for a convolution of two subgaussian sequences to be subgaussian and investigate the structure of subgaussian sequences under conditions on the exponential moments.
We introduce a new model of random partitions.
It is related to the sinh-model via a limiting procedure.

We compute the related partition function $P(n)$ asymptotically expanding it into a linear combination of powers of $\pi$, $\sinh$, and $\ln$. This provides a partial confirmation of a conjecture of G. E. Andrews.
In the last years, the possibility of using plasma-based devices for transportation of humans and cargo has been investigated.
One of the most promising concepts is the Railgun, which could allow accelerating a projectile to speeds of several km/s.

In this work we present the design and the first results of experiments on a 1:5 scale model of the PEGASUS railgun, which is being developed at the University of Rome "La Sapienza", aimed at measuring the magnetic field and the electric currents flowing through the rails, in order to validate the numerical models.
The results obtained so far demonstrate the possibility of generating the necessary magnetic field and electric currents, thus confirming the validity of the chosen concept and the designed geometry.
We give several examples of log-symplectic manifolds that are not symplectic, and we characterize the quotients of such manifolds by discrete groups.
In particular, we show that every compact log-symplectic manifold is symplectic if it has no open book supports.
Along the way, we give an example of a compact manifold with a nontrivial primitive class that carries a log-symplectic form.
We also prove a h-principle for log-symplectic manifolds which are described by finite open books.
We show that every finite-dimensional, complex Kac-Moody algebra, with simple or semi-simple rank one, has a unique extension to a 3-algebra, which is also a finite-dimensional, complex algebra.
This gives a large class of examples of 3-algebras which are not vertex algebras.
We then consider the associated M2-brane theory, and show that the three-bracket of this theory satisfies the Jacobi identity, and is therefore a Lie 3-algebra.
We discuss a proposal that the M2-brane worldvolume should be described as a coset space, and compute the three-bracket in this case.
We prove a structure theorem for manifolds with positive Ricci curvature and a effective torus action with cohomogeneity two.

As an application we prove that if M is a simply-connected closed manifold with non-positive curvature, then for any R < ∞, M admits an effective torus action with fixed point set of complexity one, and cohomogeneity two, provided that the L^2-sectional curvature of M is small enough.

We show that the nonlocal part of the Drinfeld-Jimbo quantum universal enveloping algebra $U_q(\mathfrak{g})$ is described by a certain non-commutative geometry, namely a symplectic reflection algebra.

This answers a question of Chipalkin and Evdokimov and generalizes a result of Brundan for $\mathfrak{sl}_2$. The proof uses central idempotents in the quantized universal enveloping algebra, and dimer algebras.
As a byproduct, we give a new and conceptual proof of nonlocality of $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$, and describe a nonlocal subalgebra which is not a direct sum of local subalgebras.
We present GESPAR, a method for efficient phase retrieval of sparse signals.
GESPAR combines the benefits of the Gerchberg-Saxton algorithm with the sparsity constraints of the phase retrieval problem.
The method is applied to synthetic data and to the recovery of sparse signals from experimental data.
Results show that GESPAR is able to recover the phase of sparse signals from a small number of measurements, and that it is competitive with state-of-the-art methods for phase retrieval.

Introduction

Phase retrieval is the problem of recovering a signal from the magnitude of its Fourier transform.
The problem has found applications in microscopy, astronomy, and optical metrology, where it is often used to recover the phase of a measured signal.
Phase retrieval is an ill-posed problem, meaning that it has multiple solutions.
This uncertainty can be addressed by imposing additional constraints on the solution, such as sparsity.
Sparsity constraints state that the solution should have a low complexity, or be as close as possible to a limited set of known solutions.
We present a method for efficient phase retrieval of sparse signals that combines the benefits of the Gerchberg-Saxton algorithm with the sparsity constraints of the phase retrieval problem.

Method

We begin by noting that the phase retrieval problem can be formulated as a minimization problem.
The goal is to find the signal that minimizes the sum of the squared errors between the measured magnitudes and the magnitudes of the signal's Fourier transform.

This can be expressed as:

minimize ||F^T * X - Y||^2

where F^T is the transpose of the Fourier matrix, X is the vector of unknown phases, and Y is the vector of measured magnitudes.

We then add a sparsity constraint to the problem, which can be expressed as:

minimize ||F^T * X - Y||^2 + lambda * ||X||_1

where ||X||_1 is the 1-norm of X, and lambda is a regularization parameter.
The problem is then solved using a variant of the Gerchberg-Saxton algorithm, which is an iterative algorithm for phase retrieval.
In each iteration, the algorithm updates the phases of the signal by performing a projection onto the set of signals that satisfy the sparsity constraint.
This projection is performed using the singular value decomposition of a matrix that relates the phases of the signal to its Fourier transform.

We introduce a family of non-smooth local control laws for networks of non-holonomic vehicles modeled as constrained heterogeneous multi-agent systems.

We study the problem of achieving desired formations for these vehicles by designing appropriate local laws, and we analyze the asymptotic stability of these solutions using a recently developed framework for the analysis of non-smooth multi-agent systems.

We show that, even in the presence of unsmooth local control laws, the vehicles can achieve desired formations and maintain them under model uncertainties and external disturbances, as long as a certain locality condition is satisfied.
We illustrate our results with a numerical example.

Conclusion:
We introduced a new family of local control laws for the control of formations of non-holonomic vehicles.
We provided a sufficient condition for the asymptotic stability of these solutions in the presence of unsmooth local control laws, and we illustrated our results with a numerical example.
These results provide a theoretical foundation for the design of efficient and robust formation control algorithms for networks of non-holonomic vehicles.
A universal formalism of generalized U(N) gauge transformations, which leaves the extended covariant Hamiltonian (ECH) of a field theory invariant, is constructed in this article.
An extension of the ECH formalism, which is applicable to both abelian and non-abelian gauge field theories, is achieved.
In the new formalism, the generalized U(N) gauge transformations can be implemented by stage-by-stage separate transformations on the fields, their conjugate momenta, and the total Hamiltonian.
The new formalism is applicable to both conventional and discrete gauges.

We study the wavelet spectrum of self-similar L\'evy processes, whose underlying measure satisfies the conditions of Surgailis' theorem, and show that it exhibits the property of multifractality, namely, it does not correspond to any single fractal dimension, but instead varies with the scale at which it is measured.

We prove a lower bound on the variation of the spectrum and discuss the implications of these results for the theory of fractals and for the problem of scaling in the description of chaotic processes.
Curvature is a key morphological feature of cells critical to many functions, including adhesion, migration, and division.
Plasma membrane curvature sensing is thought to be primarily accomplished by mechanosensitive ion channels and receptors.
Here we show that the amphipathic peptide, gramicidin, embedded in a lipid bilayer, acts as an anisotropic membrane curvature sensor responding to negative curvature.
By molecular dynamics simulations, we show that gramicidin's propensity to insert into the lipid bilayer depends on membrane curvature.
In planar membranes, gramicidin inserts preferentially with its hydrophobic residues remaining in the lipid acyl core.
In contrast, when introduced into a model vesicle, insertion is favored with the hydrophobic residues exposed to the lipid acyl core.
The preference for membrane insertion in the model vesicle correlates with the observed increase in conductance upon peptide incorporation into giant unilamellar vesicles.
Our results suggest a mechanism by which cell surface receptors could sense the local curvature of the plasma membrane.
A system of modal logic is said to have the Dialectica interpretation if its models are exactly the sets that are defined by finite quantifications over the frames of the system.
We show that the modal functional interpretation, already present in Fitting's 1973 monograph, is another natural and classical interpretation for which this property holds.
This result reveals a surprising connection between two very different approaches to modal logic.
Optical spatial solitons in photorefractive media are self-trapped or self-guided beams of light that are maintained by optical feedback due to the nonlinearity and non-diffractivity of the medium.
Terrestrial optical solitons can be sustained in a bulk medium with a sufficiently strong nonlinear response and optical feedback from the edge of the medium.
In this paper, we discuss selected properties of optical spatial solitons in photorefractive media and their important applications.
We begin by reviewing the basic concepts of optical spatial solitons and how they can be supported in photorefractive media.
We then discuss the different types of optical spatial solitons that can be found in these media, including self-trapped beams, self-guided beams, and coupled solitons.
Next, we review the basic properties of optical spatial solitons, such as their linear and nonlinear dynamics, stability, and propagation.
We then discuss how optical spatial solitons can be used in various applications, such as optical communication, optical sensing, and optical imaging.
Finally, we review the latest progress and developments in the field of optical spatial solitons in photorefractive media and discuss future research directions.
An EM algorithm for estimating the parameters of the Marshall-Olkin bivariate Pareto distribution with location and scale is proposed.
The underlying bivariate Pareto distribution is absolutely continuous without any atom at the origin.
The EM algorithm is derived from a latent variable representation of the model, in which the variables appear as conditionally independent given the latent variables.
The algorithm is easy to implement since it involves only iterative scaling and translation of a bivariate normal distribution.
This methodology can be useful for modeling extreme events in dependent sequences of failures like the wear and failure of coupled electronic components in a computer.
Most existing works on multi-sensor fusion focus on designing algorithms for estimating the fused parameter vector based on available measurements.

In this paper, we study the problem of optimally sparsifying the fused parameter vector given the measurements from multiple sensors, so as to minimize the estimation error when the sparsified vector is used in place of the original vector in the estimation algorithm.

We show that the optimal sparsification can be obtained by solving a convex optimization problem, and present an efficient algorithm based on the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) to solve it.

The proposed method is applied to three examples: (1) multivariate Gaussian distribution with known covariance matrix, (2) Gaussian mixture model, and (3) linear regression model with Gaussian errors, to demonstrate its performance via simulation.
The proposed method is shown to provide significant performance improvement over the naive approach of equally sparsifying all sensors.
We study the Anderson localization phenomenon in one-dimensional elastic systems possessing reciprocal-space disorder.
Using a mapping to a system of random Schrödinger operators, we evaluate the integrated spectral form factor, whose decay is governed by the localization length, for disordered graphene ribbons.
This allows us to determine the localization length as a function of energy and disorder strength.
Our results demonstrate good agreement with available numerical data over the entire spectrum, and show that the commonly used random phase approximation remains valid even in the inelastic regime.
We further analyze the effects of elastic boundaries, and show that they can significantly affect the form factor and the associated localization length.
We investigate the shape bifurcation of a spherical dielectric elastomer balloon subject to the combined actions of internal pressure and electric voltage.
Both pressure and electric voltage are found to contribute to the bending deformation of the balloon.
The bifurcation diagram is obtained from the equilibrated equations, and some typical shapes are presented with corresponding equilibrium paths.

It is observed that, by increasing the internal pressure, the balloon shows a jumping phenomenon from a spherical shape to a deformed shape at a certain threshold, and then returns to a spherical shape again after a higher threshold.

The presented method provides a way to determine the shape of dielectric elastomer balloons under the combined actions of pressure and electric voltage, and can be used to design various smart actuators with specific shapes.

We study the following basic question in geometric network design: in a given network topology how to distribute a given amount of traffic over routes such that the total length (or cost) of the routes is minimized?
We allow the topology to vary in order to find the best routes for the given amount of traffic.
This problem is known as the shortest path problem with given traffic, or in the literature as the traffic assignment problem.
We study this problem from a stochastic perspective.
We allow the network topology to be random, and we assume that the traffic per edge follows some known probability distribution.
The goal is then to find the optimal routes, i.e., the routes with minimum total length, on the average, or with some high probability.
We show that this problem is particularly hard, even for networks that are typically encountered in practice.

More precisely, we show that in such networks determining the optimal routes on average (or with high probability) is NP-hard, even if we only consider simple shortest path metrics, such as Euclidean distance, and ignore the actual traffic distributions (i.e., we only require that the traffic is proportional to a known probability distribution).
This result stands in contrast with earlier results for the related problem in which the underlying network is fixed and the goal is to find a minimum spanning tree.
In that problem the minimum spanning tree can be found in polynomial time if the edges have uniform probability.
We propose a new method for model selection in time series by extending the graphical LASSO method to incorporate a penalty on the autocorrelation matrix of the residuals.
Selection of the best model is performed by minimising a criterion that balances the fit of the model to the data and the simplicity of the model, as measured by the number of parameters.
Simulations show that the method has good performance in small sample sizes and is competitive with other model selection methods in larger sample sizes.
An application to US inflation and output series is also presented.
We present a novel approach to analyze nuclear spin relaxation in the presence of gradient-induced diffusion based on recent theoretical work.

For a number of biologically relevant nuclei, we determine quantitative Overhauser dynamic nuclear polarization (DNP) enhancements in the presence of diffusion for a range of model systems, for different pulse sequences, and under various experimental conditions.
Our results are in good agreement with recent experiments.
We show that the DNP enhancement depends on the gyromagnetic ratio and the diffusion time for a given gradient strength.
We also explore the optimal readout pulse sequences in the presence of diffusion.
We propose a general frame reference characterized by four mathematical invariants: the metric tensor, the affine connection, the Riemann curvature, and the acceleration of the frame.
This frame reference is shown to be applicable to various theories: Newtonian, relativistic, and Galilean.
It is shown that the acceleration of the frame is a necessary condition for the frame to be an inertial frame.
This condition is shown to be equivalent to the invariance of the acceleration of the frame.
The acceleration of the frame is also shown to be a sufficient condition for the frame to be an inertial frame.
This condition is shown to be equivalent to the covariant acceleration of the frame.
The authors hope that this work would promote the concept of the acceleration of the frame as a crucial characteristic of frame references.
We study optimal heat transport in Rayleigh-B\'enard convection, both in the deterministic and in the stochastic setting.
This model describes the flow of an incompressible fluid heated from below through a flat substrate and subjected to a uniform vertical gravitational field.
We characterize the optimal flux as a function of the Rayleigh number through a direct minimization of an appropriately defined objective functional.
The minimization leads to a system of two nonlinear equations, whose solution describes the optimal shape of the temperature profile and of the fluid velocity profile.
For the stochastic setting, we derive a differential equation for the optimal flux and we characterize the variance of the optimal stochastic process in terms of the variance of the fluid velocity.

Rotational optomechanics has emerged as a promising platform to study the interplay of light and mechanical rotation, offering new opportunities for optical manipulation of rotational motion with broad applications in optomechanical sensing, signal processing, and quantum communication.
In this Review, we survey the recent progress in rotational cavity optomechanics, focusing on the optomechanical coupling and control of rotating objects in optical cavities.
We begin by introducing the fundamental concepts of rotational optomechanics, including the different types of rotating objects and their optomechanical interactions.

We then review the various approaches that have been developed to couple light to the rotational motion of optomechanical systems, including cavity-enhanced detection of rotating objects, optical forcing of rotational motion, and optomechanical transduction of cavity fields.
We further discuss the impact of optical backaction on the rotational dynamics and highlight the potential of rotational optomechanics for sensing, communication, and quantum applications.
We also present an overview of the current challenges and future directions in this emerging field.
We give a complete description of all two-generator free Kleinian groups whose generators commute.
This answers a question of Agol and Groves.

Along the way we give a new description of the boundary of hyperbolic 3-manifolds which implies that a closed 3-manifold admits a hyperbolic structure if and only if its fundamental group satisfies a certain linearity condition.
This generalizes a theorem of Gabai.

Neutron stars are the most extreme manifestation of nuclear matter and provide a unique opportunity to probe the properties of matter at densities and temperatures that cannot be reached in any laboratory on Earth.
The basic properties of neutron stars, such as their mass and radius, are determined by the properties of the neutrons at densities above 100 times the nuclear density.
The extreme conditions of neutron stars have a significant impact on their properties, such as their magnetic fields, and are crucial in shaping the evolution of the star.
The study of neutron stars also provides valuable insights into the properties of matter at densities beyond the nuclear density, such as the quark-gluon plasma.
Finally, neutron stars are important contributors to the universe's most energetic phenomena, such as gamma-ray bursts and gravitational waves.
Deep learning systems, both in data centers and edge devices, require many hyper-parameters to be carefully tuned to achieve optimum performance.
Hyper-parameters such as the learning rate, dropout probability, and number of layers and hidden units heavily influence the performance of the deep learning model.
In this paper, we focus on one key hyper-parameter — the number of hidden units — and present a new distributed learning method that estimates this parameter from data in a node-specific manner.

We show that our proposed method, which is based on a distributed diffusion-based limited memory (DBLMM) optimization algorithm, can efficiently estimate the optimal number of hidden units on different nodes, even in the presence of hyper-parameters that have undesirable or unhelpful values for otherwise standard optimization algorithms.

We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on both synthetic data and also CIFAR-10 data on AWS EC2 instances, where we show that our method can efficiently estimate the number of hidden units, specific to different nodes, that are close to the minimum as judged by the validation error.
