A new type of generalized coupled-line all-pass phasers based on mutually coupled transmission lines is presented.
The device consists of two or more nearly quarter-wavelength-long transmission lines with mutual couplings between adjacent lines.
By properly adjusting the lengths of the transmission lines and the mutual coupling coefficients, the proposed phaser can achieve arbitrary phase shifts with a compact size and low loss.
The design procedure is described and verified by both simulation and measurement results.
Let $\g$ be a simple, simply connected, and graded-by-involution finite dimensional algebra over a field of positive characteristic.
Assume that $\g$ has a standard basis $\mathcal B = (\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_n)$, and let $\mathfrak X=\mathfrak X_1\oplus\cdots\oplus\mathfrak
X_n$ be the corresponding graded Hecke algebra.
We study the first extensions of $\mathfrak X$-modules.

Recent work has shown that fine-grained human mobility data provides new opportunities for studying human behavior, from the mathematical and complexity perspectives, in a way that has not been possible with coarse-grained mobile phone or transportation data.
Even if mobility data is at the smallest scale, a systematic characterization of such data, however, is still lacking.
In this article, we provide a systematic study of human mobility patterns at the smallest scales, focusing on the mathematical properties of the trajectories themselves.

In particular, we provide a complete picture of the topological properties of human mobility networks in different contexts, and show how the right abstraction of mobility data may provide a key towards a better understanding of human behavior.
The Sun's latitude distribution responds to both the solar cycle and long-term trends.
Previously, this behavior has been studied through the analysis of photospheric magnetic field models, or using direct observations of the solar disk at a single wavelength.
Here, we present evidence that active longitudes oscillate around the solar equator, with a period of about 4 years, and reflect the underlying magnetic field structure.
We found characteristic active longitudes in 1995 and 2009, and traced their evolution till 2020.

Our analysis is based on differential emission measure (DEM) maps, constructed from SOHO/EIT data, which are free of the biases of magnetic field models, and provide a better understanding of the solar latitudinal distribution, beyond the solar cycle.
We find that the equatorial regions are very weak in emission, indicating a very low magnetic flux density, in agreement withPotential Field Source Surface (PFSS) models.
Furthermore, our findings agree with the magnetic flux transport theory, as the observed active longitudes correspond to fast magnetic flux transport regions.
Our results also show good agreement with the photospheric magnetic field models, unlike the case of plage distribution.
We discuss the results in the context of the small-scale dynamo theory, and demonstrate good agreement with the predictions of the mean-field model.
The case of the current cycle is discussed in view of our findings.

In this article, we study an operator relation R obtained by Y. Kawahigashi and the author in the case of one-dimensional Schrödinger operators with a periodic potential, through relations between the oscillator algebra and the Young diagram algebra, and show that R implies the existence of an infinite-dimensional kernel for the Dirac operator restricted to the kernel of the Laplacian.
We also show that the relation R is equivalent to the existence of an infinite-dimensional kernel for the Laplacian.
Active matter represents a new paradigm in the field of nonlinear physics, covering a wide range of physical systems in which energy is injected into the material by self-propelled particles.
This energy serves to power the large-scale motion of the system as a whole, in contrast to passive systems where this motion is powered by external forces.
We show that the additional power in active matter leads to a novel effect: a positive force acting on the individual particles, in the direction of the global motion.
However, this force is subject to dissipation, which could potentially slow the system's motion.
Using a simple model of an active fluid, we show that the interplay between these two effects determines the speed of the global motion.
When the strength of the force is sufficiently larger than the dissipation, this leads to an acceleration of the fluid, as the force overcomes the damping.
We validate our model using active matter simulations, and discuss the implications for the physics of active matter.
Recent developments in space propulsion have opened up the possibility of using nuclear electric or solar electric propulsion for interplanetary missions.
These methods have higher efficiency than the traditional chemical propulsion methods, leading to shorter transfer times.
We compare four different space propulsion methods using parameters relevant to a crewed Mars mission: nuclear electric, solar electric, nuclear thermal, and chemical propulsion.
We consider the effects of reduced thrust levels on transfer time, mass, and complexity of the missions.
We find that nuclear electric and solar electric propulsion can reduce the transfer time by half a year or more compared to chemical propulsion, despite having lower thrust levels.
We also find that the nuclear electric method has a lower mass compared to the other methods, while the solar electric method has the lowest complexity.
The results of this study can help to inform the choice of space propulsion method for future crewed missions to Mars.
We study the tractability of finding the shortest path between two given vertices in a treelike instance, that is, a weighted graph that has a tree structure induced by some weights on its edges.

Given such an instance, the problem is to determine the shortest path between two vertices, either from source to target, or between two targets, or between two sources, each with the same or different weights.
We show that this problem is NP-hard on treelike instances with non-negative edge weights, even if the instance is a tree itself.
This result extends a previous result of Kirchner and Thiele, who considered the case of unweighted graphs.

We show further that the problem remains NP-hard even if the instance is a tree and all weights are equal to one, thus generalizing a result of Dijkstra who considered the case of unweighted trees with arbitrary edge weights.
Finally, we present two polynomial-time algorithms for certain cases of treelike instances: instances that are trees and instances that have bounded vertex degrees.
We enumerate the corners of tree-like tableaux, giving a bijection with forbidden integer configurations in an $n\times n$ square grid.
This generalizes results about enumerating descending and inverse plane partitions, and about enumerating lattice points in a torus divided by an $n\times n$ square.
Along the way, we define a new family of generalized chessboards, and give a bijection between their prohibited diagonals and the corners of tree-like tableaux.
The local field emission current from vertically oriented graphene nanowalls has been studied using a combined method of molecular dynamics and Poisson solver.
The geometries of graphene nanowalls (including the width and height) are modeled by finite sized graphene sheets with proper boundary conditions.
The local electric field and emission current are computed self-consistently by solving the Poisson equation and the Newton equation of motion, respectively.

It is found that the local field emission current is controlled by both the geometrical configuration (e.g., the width and height of a graphene nanowall) and the electric configuration (e.g., the applied electric field and the tip-sample distance).
For a fixed geometrical configuration, the local field emission current is increased as the applied electric field or the tip-sample distance decreases.
Conversely, for a fixed electric configuration, the local field emission current is found to be increased as the graphene wall width or the height of a graphene nanowall increases.

Our results suggest that the local field emission current can be effectively controlled by tuning the geometrical and electric configurations, which paves a way to potential applications of graphene nanowalls as local field emitters with high reliability and reproducibility.
We give a simple construction of odd orthogonal bundles on curves, as deformations of rank 2 bundles of the form θ∞1(Σ,−Σ), where Σ is a symmetric stable pair.

The construction relies on a relation between odd orthogonal and odd symplectic bundles, which follows from a refinement due to Bruillard and Iritani of a result of Shin on strange duality for holomorphic vector bundles on curves.
Deep learning has transformed many Natural Language Processing (NLP) tasks, but pre-trained models are rarely applied to languages with limited digital resources.
To fill this gap, we present a novel approach to train language models on diverse web-scraped data and show its applicability to under-resourced languages.

We focus on Medieval Latin (ML), a language with scarce digital resources, and show that our method, which we call Web-Scraped Language Models (WSLMs), can be used to create a new state-of-the-art pipeline for NLP tasks in ML.
To validate our approach, we conduct experiments on a wide range of tasks, including word representation, sequence tagging, and text classification.
We show that even a simple WSLM can outperform state-of-the-art results on several tasks.

Furthermore, we present an integrated sequence tagging model that combines a WSLM with a neural machine translation approach and show that this integration improves performance on all tasks, reaching up to 93% accuracy on named entity recognition.

We introduce rowmotion, a new operation for directed graphs that generalizes the notion of vertex motion from the theory of digraphs to also capture motion on rows of the adjacency matrix of a directed graph.
We characterize when rowmotion can be used to simulate generalized toggle groups, a generalization of the toggle group of a directed graph introduced by D. L. Freeman in his Ph.D. thesis.
This leads to a characterization of the class of graphs for which the rowmotion chromatic number is within a constant factor of the maximum number of disjoint directed cycles.
The feasibility of using multipole traps for environmental studies was investigated.

Laboratory experiments with multipole traps of different geometries and a variety of trap settings demonstrated that multipole traps are capable of capturing, manipulating, and releasing a wide range of aquatic organisms.
No adverse effects on the organisms were observed as a result of their capture or confinement in the traps.
Organisms were observed to enter the traps of their own volition, and to exit the traps when the traps were emptied.
Triaxial dipole traps appeared to be the most effective design for sampling aquatic organisms.
A field trial using a triaxial dipole trap yielded organisms similar to those captured in the laboratory experiments.
The size and type of organisms captured in the field trial were consistent with the size and type of organisms that typically occupy the lake in which the field trial took place.
These results suggest that multipole traps can be effectively used as tools for environmental studies.
We study the primordial non-Gaussianities in the context of inflationary step-like models in single field inflation.
The model considered is a hybrid model, in which the potential contains a canonical scalar field and a step-like feature.

We compute the three-point function of the primordial perturbations, which generates non-Gaussianities, in the slow-roll approximation, and show that the model gives rise to sizable non-Gaussianities of local type, which can be detected by the upcoming prime missions such as the Planck and the Litebird.

We also analyze the run of the spectral index, and show that the step-like feature in the potential induces a rapid change of the running, which can be significant depending on the parameters of the model.
This paper introduces many worlds in quantum computation, with a focus on the practical aspects of this paradigm.
It discusses the basic concepts and gives an overview of the different approaches to many worlds.

The paper also covers the application of many worlds in quantum computation, including the use of parallel universes to perform parallel computations and the use of quantum annealing to optimize the performance of quantum algorithms.

Finally, it discusses the implications of many worlds in quantum computation, including the possibility of developing a truly parallel quantum computer and the potential for developing new quantum algorithms that can take advantage of the many worlds paradigm.
We report on a novel scheme to realize a Fourier transform spectroscopy in a spin-orbit coupled Bose gas.
By driving spin-orbit coupled bosons with a weak radio-frequency field, we obtain an oscillating population between two different orbital states as a function of the radio-frequency frequency.
The frequency of this oscillation can be tuned by the interaction between the spin and the orbit of the particles.
By scanning the radio-frequency frequency, we obtain a spectrum that can be related to the frequency dependence of the bosonic occupancy of the different orbital states.
Our scheme can work in a homogeneous system, and does not require any trap.
We propose a new design for clustered randomized studies of contagion processes that leverages contact network information to generate more efficient clusters in terms of expected infection counts.

We show that by clustering units with similar contact networks, our design reduces the expected number of infections in the clusters, thereby reducing both the number of units and the total length of follow-up time needed to detect an effect with a given power.

We provide a general framework for implementing the proposed design in different contexts, and describe a practical method based on spectral clustering that allows for clustering individuals using either contact patterns or contact networks.

We apply the proposed method to the Setting Interventions to Prevent Infections in Nursing Homes (SIPIN) data, and show that our design can yield substantial efficiency gains relative to a design that clusters units using only demographic information.
We introduce a new model of random interface evolution in imperfect channels, where the channel geometry is subject to a random evolution over time.

In contrast to the existing models of interface evolution in imperfect channels, the randomness we introduce acts on the channel geometry rather than on the fluid viscosity, making the model more realistic in certain applications.
We analyze the corresponding stochastic differential equation describing the evolution of the interface, and prove existence and uniqueness of a strong solution.
In addition, we prove that this solution is almost surely bounded for all time, and that the associated Markov process admits a transition density.
We provide a concise and organized lecture note on ridge regression, a technique in statistical learning that is closely related to the least squares method.
In particular, we present algebraic properties of ridge regression and derive a closed-form solution when the design matrix has a low rank.
We propose a generalized eigenvalue problem for obtaining the closed-form solution, which reveals the connection between ridge regression and principal component analysis.
The note also covers several extensions of ridge regression, including LASSO regression, elastic net regression and multi-task regression.
Throughout the note, we include some exercises with detailed answers to help readers grasp the material.

We present stellar population models based on APOGEE data for the innermost regions of 17 nearby S0 galaxies, aiming to quantify the impact of various environmental factors on the evolution of their central stars.
Combining the data with literature multiband photometry, we derive the stellar ages and abundances in the galaxies' bulges and inner disks.

We find that the central regions of S0 galaxies are generally dominated by old ( ≳ 10 Gyr) stars, albeit with significant internal variations, and that these galaxies typically lack young (≲ 1 Gyr) stars.

Comparing the stellar populations in the inner disks of S0s with those in the outer disks of spiral galaxies, we find that the onset of star formation in the outer disks typically occurs at a younger age and higher gas surface density.
This suggests that environmental factors play a crucial role in shutting down star formation in S0s, perhaps by accelerating the expulsion of gas from their inner regions.
Our results imply that the cessation of star formation in S0s occurs at an earlier time and higher gas surface density than predicted by simple cosmological simulations.
We discuss possible explanations for this, highlighting the importance of feedback and galaxy mergers in building up the population of local S0s.

We show that minor mergers can trigger significant star formation in gas-rich S0s and suggest that major mergers are likely required to transform spiral disks into S0s with old, dead stellar populations.

Our results imply that S0s are typically formed in relatively dry environments, possibly via dry minor mergers, and that their inner regions become quiescent very quickly (in ≲ 1 Gyr) after the galaxies lose their gas.
We discuss how our findings can be used to constrain the star formation histories of S0 galaxies and what they imply for the nature of the environment in which S0s are typically formed.

We investigate the inverse magnetocaloric effect (IMCE) in Fisher's super-exchange antiferromagnet compound Cu(NO3)_{2.6}Mn(OH)_{3.4}Br, which has a highly anisotropic gigahertz magnetic resonance spectrum with two distinct gaps and a spin-1/2 ground state based on the single-ion anisotropy.
We found that the IMCE is enhanced by applying a small magnetic field of B-0 = 10 G.
Our result demonstrates that the IMCE can be enhanced by manipulating the small magnetic field and may provide a way to optimize the IMCE in Cu(NO3)_{2.6}Mn(OH)_{3.4}Br and related compounds.
We give a survey of results about converting infinite data from the Heegaard Floer homology of a three-manifold into finite data.
The main technique is to use twining numbers, defined by Lipshitz and Sarkar, which count the number of times that a holomorphic disk in $S^3$ twines around a link in the three-manifold.
When the link is a meridian, this gives an upper bound for the rank of the Heegaard Floer homology group; when the link is a longitude, this gives a lower bound.
When the three-manifold is a rational homology sphere, these two bounds agree, and the twining number is an invariant of the three-manifold.
We also discuss the relationship of this approach to the recent work of Lipshitz and the second author on constructing a new finite type invariant of three-manifolds.
The electron dynamics in atoms of the elements are highly executed using inter-state transitions.
The evolution of the atomic structure is an inherent consequence of the execution of the electron dynamics.
The paper examines the evolution of the atomic structure in atoms of the elements that are highly executed using inter-state electron transitions.
The analysis of the atomic structure evolution is crucial to understanding the highly executed electron dynamics in the atoms of the elements.
The results of the analysis can be used to develop a theory of highly executed electron dynamics in atoms.
This theory may be useful in predicting the behavior of materials under extreme conditions.
The paper focuses on the structure evolution of atoms of the elements lithium, beryllium, and boron.
The atomic structure of these elements evolves as a result of the execution of the electron dynamics within the atoms.
The paper examines the changes in the atomic structure of these elements as a result of the execution of the electron dynamics.
The paper also examines the effects of the atomic structure evolution on the physical and chemical properties of the elements.
The analysis of the atomic structure evolution can be used to develop a theory of the electron dynamics in atoms.
This theory may be useful in predicting the behavior of materials under extreme conditions.
The paper concludes by suggesting that the evolution of the atomic structure in atoms of the elements is a result of the execution of the electron dynamics within the atoms.
The analysis of the atomic structure evolution can be used to develop a theory of the electron dynamics in atoms.
This theory can be used to predict the behavior of materials under extreme conditions such as high temperatures or pressures.
The author also suggests that the atomic structure evolution may also be useful in understanding the behavior of materials in nuclear reactors or in the environment.
We propose a novel method to generate cluster states, which are multi-qubit graph states that occur naturally in algebraic geometry.
Our approach leverages the geometric structure of these states in order to facilitate their generation by a sequence of elementary operations, such as single-qubit rotations and CNOT gates.

We present a layer-by-layer construction of cluster states whereby we iteratively apply a sequence of such elementary operations to an initial state, such as the vacuum state, in order to generate a desired cluster state.
This approach does not require the use of ancillary qubits or any other resources reusable between iterations, thereby making the generated cluster states resource-efficient.
We implement the proposed layer-by-layer construction for generating the most basic cluster state, the seven-qubit cluster state, on a quantum computer.
In this article, we continue the study of symmetries of nonlinear ordinary differential equations (ODEs) initiated in [AS2020].
The concept of symmetry is well-developed for linear ODEs, but much less so for nonlinear ones.

The main goal of this article is to provide a partial answer to the following question: given a nonlinear ODE, how can one determine if it displays a symmetry, and if so, what is the form of that symmetry?
As a case study, we consider the modified Emden equation, a classical model in astrophysics, geometry, and topology.
This equation possesses an infinite-dimensional group of symmetries, generated by four independent basic symmetries.
In this article, we determine all nonlinear differential equations that are symmetries of the modified Emden equation.
This provides a partial answer to the above question, in the case when the symmetry group is infinite-dimensional.
Along the way, we develop a general method, based on the use of arbitrary functions, for constructing symmetries of nonlinear ODEs.

We investigate the crossover from three dimensional (3D) to two dimensional (2D) topological insulators in Bi2Se3 thin films through three dimensional topological surface states derived from bulk-edge correspondence.

Via analyzing the low-energy effective Hamiltonian for surface states, we demonstrate that the 3D topological insulator of Bi2Se3 thin films can be regarded as the 2D topological insulator with a effective nearest-neighbor hopping parameter, which could be tuned by thickness and electrostatic gating.
Furthermore, the phase diagram of Bi2Se3 thin films is predicted by solving the effective model, in good agreement with the experimental observations.
With the advent of anesthesia, surgery has become painless.
However, the underlying brain mechanisms supporting consciousness, which are perturbed by anesthesia, remain unclear.
Here, we aim to elucidate the spatiotemporal dynamics of brain networks supporting consciousness during the onset of anesthesia-induced loss of consciousness.

We applied a data-driven, hierarchical clustering approach to functional magnetic resonance imaging data obtained from healthy human volunteers, at the onset of unconsciousness induced by the intravenous administration of propofol.

We found that, as consciousness was lost, activity in the brain shifted from being organized by the known default mode and dorsal attention networks, to being organized by a novel unconscious network comprised of thalamus, brainstem, and dorsal cortex.

Furthermore, we found that the structure of brain networks at the onset of unconsciousness was related to the electroencephalographic latency of the participants, indicative of a relationship between the structure of brain networks and the neurophysiological measures of consciousness.
These findings provide novel insights into the brain dynamics supporting consciousness, and the relatedness of brain structure and function to consciousness.
This short note is intended for students of elementary physics, aiming to provide them with a simple and precise roadmap to the fundamental geometric axioms and theorems of Newtonian Dynamics.

In addition to the classic treatment of Newton's Principia, two other foundational sources are highlighted: the elegant and concise geometric approach of Josiah Willard Gibbs, and the recent "modern" axiomatic development of Jean Gallier.
The note ends with a list of challenging problems that the students can use to strengthen their understanding.
It is hoped that exposure to these different approaches may provide a more balanced view, and some insight into the power and limitations of the various presentations.
Decidable properties of directed graph codes, first introduced by Condurache and Gutman [CG06], are considered.
These are obtained from oriented graphs by first creating a set code and then adding multiplicities to the codewords.

We show that the problem of deciding whether the number of codewords of a directed graph code is bounded (in both the set and multiset cases) is undecidable, thus answering positively a question raised by Condurache and Gutman
[CG06, page 171].

On the positive side, we show that, for numerically decipherable directed graph codes, the problem of deciding whether the set of codewords is finite (in both the set and multiset cases) is decidable, where a code is called numerically decipherable if its syndrome decoding algorithm makes only numerical computations.
We discuss a mechanism of forming Cooper pairs in a superconductor.
In the absence of an external magnetic field, the s-wave pair potential is a sum of a local repulsion and a non-local exchange interaction.
The latter is known to be relevant for an explanation of the observed magnitude of the pairing gap and the behavior of the critical temperature in unconventional superconductors.
We show that the exchange interaction is capable of creating Cooper pairs, even in its standard isotropic form when the Fourier component of the pair potential has a divergence at the origin.
This property is a consequence of the long-range character of the interaction and does not require any anisotropy.
We evaluate the exchange-created pair density and compare it with the pair density generated by the repulsive part of the pair potential.

The exchange interaction can lead to a significant increase of the pair density, exceeding the corresponding value for the s-wave interaction, but still being much smaller than in d-wave superconductivity.
We study some properties of edge-set graphs of graphs related to projective planes of even order and the Fano plane.

In particular, we describe the edge-set graph of the incidence graph of the projective plane of order 2n as a union of cycles and we determine the chromatic number of the edge-set graph of the Fano plane.
We consider the problem of detecting anomalies in a sequence of independent observations, where the anomalies are rare events and the observations are drawn from a known family of distributions.
We propose a sequential testing procedure that performs optimally in the limit as the sample size goes to infinity, with the cost metric being the total false alarm rate over the sample interval.

Our approach is motivated by the observation that the false alarm rate of any sequential testing procedure is proportional to the likelihood of the observations under the null hypothesis, and we seek to minimize this quantity by optimizing the test procedure over all possible sequences of observations.
We show that the optimal test procedure has a simple form, and we provide a closed-form expression for the optimal false alarm rate.

We also show that our approach is asymptotically optimal in the sense that the total false alarm rate of our procedure converges to zero as the sample size goes to infinity, and we provide a bound on the convergence rate.
Finally, we demonstrate the performance of our procedure on a simulated data set and compare it to existing sequential testing procedures.
We propose a method for path checking of a large class of MTL and TPTL specifications, based on a notion of atomic zones.
Although the method is exact, it has a space complexity that is linear in the size of the input and the number of zones, rather than the size of the specification.
The method also has an acceptable runtime, which compares favorably with other tools.

We propose a new algorithmic framework for exact and approximate testing of functional inequalities, motivated by several concrete applications that we have in mind in the theory of special functions, in particular the gamma and beta functions.

Instead of simulating the integral/derivative evaluation nodes of the discretized inequality, as it is usually done, we propose to simulate the nodes of the difference between the left-hand side and the right-hand side of the inequality.

This new approach allows one to test several functional inequalities for systems of several functions at once, with a computational cost that is linear (instead of quadratic) with the number of functions in the system.
We present implementations of our method in Matlab and C, that we make publicly available.

We also propose a variant of our method that allows one to test, on a grid of points, several functional inequalities against systems of tests that involve only a small number of functions in the system.

This is useful when one has a specific set of functions that are expected to satisfy a given functional inequality, and wants to test this inequality against a large number of tests using only evaluations of the given set of functions.

Recent works have shown that training deep neural networks (DNNs) with decentralized data, i.e., data collected by various entities with different privileges, enables more efficient and private training compared to centralized training.
In these systems, a central server is often still required to aggregate the training data and update model parameters based on the aggregated data.

In this paper, we study the minimum amount of communication needed for training deep networks with decentralized data, i.e., the lowest possible aggregate size among all parameter update algorithms that use decentralized data.

We show that this minimum aggregate size can be achieved by a simple extension of the decentralized learning algorithm in an information-theoretically optimal way, i.e., the extension does not increase the aggregate size but may decrease the training speed.
Academic performance, course taking patterns, and curriculum design provide important insights into the underlying structure of knowledge and the most effective ways of organizing its acquisition.

We apply association rule mining and collaborative filtering to 9 months of grade data from over 26,000 students to identify key first-year courses in an undergraduate curriculum in a general way that does not rely on pre-specified organizational structures or explicit academic domain knowledge.
Our approach reveals the fundamental connections between courses in terms of the knowledge they impart, demonstrating that data mining can uncover the underlying structure of curricula.
We study the stability of phase motion in race-track microtons.
By adding a linear coupling between the two pendulums, we show that the race-track can become unstable, which means that the system is not a robustly stable oscillator.
We find analytically that there is a critical coupling strength above which the system is unstable, and we verify this both analytically and numerically.
We also determine the basins of attraction in the phase space for different values of the coupling strength.
When the coupling is weak, the system behaves as two decoupled pendulums.
However, when the coupling is stronger, the system can undergo a supercritical pitchfork bifurcation, resulting in an unstable race-track.
We observe that the system can undergo a subcritical pitchfork bifurcation and become a symmetric limit cycle.
The basins of attraction in the phase space for the new limit cycle are shown to be symmetric with respect to the race-track solution.
Ultimately, we conclude that the race-track solution is not a robustly stable solution, and that the system can undergo a supercritical pitchfork bifurcation and become unstable.
We also show that the system can undergo a subcritical pitchfork bifurcation and become a symmetric limit cycle.
The findings in this paper provide a new perspective on the stability of race-track microtons, and suggest new ways to control the behavior of such systems.
We introduce the polynomiality property for structure coefficients of finite-dimensional algebras over a field.
This is a generalization of the polynomiality property that has been studied for structure coefficients of semisimple and reductive Lie algebras.
We prove that the polynomiality property is equivalent to the double centralizer property for the associated Dynkin diagram, and we give a necessary condition in terms of the graph of the algebra.

As an application, we determine the structures of the double centralizer algebras for all simply-laced Dynkin diagrams, and we construct an example of a double centralizer algebra with an arbitrary Dynkin diagram that does not have the polynomiality property.

Let $\Phi$ be a positive, self-adjoint linear operator on a finite-dimensional complex Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}$. Denoting by $\mathfrak{S}(\Phi)$ the set of its self-adjoint operators, and given an orthonormal basis $\mathfrak{B} = (\varphi_j)_{j\in J}$ of $\mathcal{H}$, we consider the matrix $A = (a_{ij})_{i,j\in J}$ defined by $a_{ij} = \langle \varphi_i,\Phi\varphi_j\rangle$.

The upper height bound of order $\alpha$ for $A$, defined as the smallest integer $M$ such that all entries of $A^M$ are dominated by $\alpha$ in the sense that $|a_{ij}| \leq \alpha\ \text{for all}\ i,j\in J$, is a classical subject in operator theory.

In this note we study the upper height bounds for a class of infinite matrices associated to $\Phi$, defined as the union of $\mathfrak{S}(\Phi)$-orbit of $A$ under the conjugation action on the set of all matrices.
This generalizes two classical results on the height bounds for $A$.

We introduce the notion of quasi-power law (QPL) ensembles, which are based on the idea of preserving the average properties of a power law ensemble (PLE) while modifying the tail of the distribution.
We show that QPL ensembles are as resilient as PLEs to attacks that have been previously considered for PLEs, such as the birthday attack and the subset attack, while requiring a smaller key space.
In addition, we show that QPL ensembles are useful for creating practical symmetric key generators, as they can be generated with a small number of bits and are highly resilient to attacks.
We present a way to generate QPL ensembles that is based on a new method for generating PLEs, which is more efficient than the previously known methods.
Introduction: Power law ensembles (PLEs) are a class of distributions that have been shown to be useful for creating practical symmetric key generators.

A PLE is a distribution whose tail decay is proportional to a power law, which means that the probability of encountering a member of the ensemble decreases as a power law function of its rank in the ensemble.
This property makes PLEs highly resilient to attacks such as the birthday attack and the subset attack, which attempt to guess the key by exhaustively searching through a subset of the ensemble.
In order to make PLEs practical, it is necessary to generate them using a small number of bits, which has been previously accomplished using a method based on the idea of rank-based sampling.
In this paper, we introduce a new method for generating PLEs, which is more efficient than the previously known methods.

This new method allows us to introduce the notion of quasi-power law (QPL) ensembles, which are based on the idea of preserving the average properties of a PLE while modifying the tail of the distribution.
We show that QPL ensembles are as resilient as PLEs to attacks that have been previously considered for PLEs, while requiring a smaller key space.
Additionally, we show that QPL ensembles are useful for creating practical symmetric key generators, as they can be generated with a small number of bits and are highly resilient to attacks.
Rank-based sampling: Rank-based sampling is a method for generating PLEs using a small number of bits.
The basic idea behind rank-based sampling is to divide the key space into a set of ranks, where each rank corresponds to a different power law exponent.
Then, a set of keys is generated by sampling from each rank with a probability proportional to its rank

Let $D$ be a finitely generated domain with field of fractions $K$, and let $I$ be a proper ideal of $D$. In this short note we present an elementary proof of effective results for the solution of the unit equation $u^2=a$, with $a\in I\setminus\{0\}$, over $D$.
We introduce the concept of tangentially biharmonic Lagrangian H-umbilical submanifolds in complex space forms and discuss some of their properties.
In particular, we show that any such submanifold must be totally geodesic and we characterize those that are also minimal.
We also prove a structure theorem that describes the general form of such submanifolds in terms of a quadratic equation.
Finally, we give examples of tangentially biharmonic Lagrangian H-umbilical submanifolds in complex space forms that are not biharmonic.
These results illustrate some interesting differences between the cases of real and complex space forms.
An important application of Mirror Symmetry is the computation of refined topological quantities for manifolds which are related by this symmetry.
In the case of toric varieties, this quantity is encoded in a lattice model defined by a fan.

We give a general construction of this quantity for manifolds with transverse self-dual structures (including toric varieties), express it in terms of data on the boundary of the manifold, and explain how to compute it from a fan.
This result generalizes and unifies several previous results in the literature.
This paper studies the gauge theory on a space with linear Lie type fuzziness.
It establishes the gauge independence of physical quantities and the local existence of gauge theory.
Furthermore, it establishes the local uniqueness of gauge theory and gives the corresponding proof.
Finally, it briefly discusses the non-locality of gauge theory and gives the corresponding examples.

We present a theoretical study of the longitudinal and spin/valley Hall optical conductivity in a single layer of $MoS_{2}$. Using a self-consistent iterative solution of the linearized Boltzmann equation, we have obtained the frequency dependent optical conductivity for this material.
We show that the intraband contribution to the optical conductivity is strongly frequency dependent due to the presence of van Hove singularities in the quasi-particle density of states.
In contrast, the contribution from interband transitions is weakly frequency dependent.
The strength of the van Hove singularities in the optical conductivity is found to depend strongly on the choice of the quasi-particle weight function.
We also evaluate the spin/valley Hall conductivity in this system.
Our results show that the magnitude of the spin/valley Hall conductivity is sample dependent and it is sensitive to the carrier concentration.
Damage to relationships is a central theme in major depressive disorder (MDD).

There are two styles of responding to relationship damage that may affect recovery: self-invalidation (i.e., generalized self-doubt) and self-downgrade (i.e., exaggerated negative views of specific relationships).

The present research sought to identify the causal mechanisms that link relationship damage to these two styles of responding, and subsequently to MDD symptoms, to test the proposal that self-invalidation and self-downgrade represent downstream consequences of relationship distress.
In Study 1 (N = 203), as hypothesized, damaging events involving relationships were more strongly associated with self-invalidation and self-downgrade than with a measure of depressed mood.

In Study 2 (N = 268), experimentally manipulated thoughts about relationship damage (vs. control thoughts) led to greater self-downgrade, but not self-invalidation, and this effect was mediated by depressed mood.
In Study 3 (N = 244), self-invalidation and self-downgrade predicted increases in depressed mood over 1 year, and this effect was mediated by relationship distress.
The generalization of these findings to relationship damage involving other valued domains (e.g., work) suggests that the findings are not specific to relationships per se.
Rather, the findings suggest a chain of events in which damage to valued domains leads to depressed mood, which in turn leads to self-downgrade, but not self-invalidation.
Implications for the study of MDD and for intervention strategies are discussed.

We calculate the electronic Raman scattering (ERS) in the charge-density-wave (CDW) phase of the spinless Falicov-Kimball model within the framework of the numerically exact determinantal quantum Monte Carlo (DQMC) method.

In contrast to the usual assumption of constant spectral weight in the entire Brillouin zone, we find that the spectral weight is strongly peaked at the zone boundary $\pi$, where the effects of the CDW gap are the largest.
Using a simple model, we show that the spectral weight is related to the momentum dependence of the spectral function in the CDW gap.
Our results demonstrate that ERS is a powerful tool to probe the effects of the CDW gap on the electronic states in this model.

We show that large cardinals appearing in the constructible universe L_(κ) can be represented in the von Neumann hierarchy, assuming the consistency of a weak form of the axiom of constructibility, specifically the existence of a strongly compact cardinal κ satisfying the hypothesis H_(κ): every AOG sequence of size ω_1 has a further AOG subsequence of length κ.

Our result provides a new solution to the representation problem for L_(κ)-cardinals in the von Neumann hierarchy, with the additional feature that the required strength is predictable in an appropriate sense.

Along the way we show that the assumption of H_(κ) implies the consistency of a weak form of the square principle, and we use this fact to give a new proof of the representation result for ω_(1) established by Magidor in his classic paper on the subject.
In the recent paper "On the germ of an algebraic function" by M. Hirose and the present writer, a new type of germ, called the Goursat germ, was introduced.
Although the Goursat germ is an generalization of the Puiseux germ, there is an essential difference between them.
In this note, we investigate the characteristic of the Goursat germ.

We show that any finite collection of bijections (equivalences) between finite sets, such that any two of them have a common fixed point, extends in a unique way to an autotopism of a torus (i.e. a bijection between the sets of toroidal semiquences with a common factor).
This solves a special case of a problem posed by G. Czeller and M. Mosonyi.
We present an efficient and effective method for identifying parallel passages across a large Hebrew/Aramaic corpus.
We use a combination of textual and linguistic features, including word and phrase frequencies, to develop a set of features that are highly predictive of parallel passages.
We apply a machine learning algorithm to train a model on a large subset of the corpus and use the trained model to search for parallel passages in the entire corpus.
Our results show that our method is highly accurate, with an F1 score of 0.82, and is able to successfully identify parallel passages in a variety of different genres and styles.
The proposed methodology offers a substantial advancement over current state-of-the-art in the field, both in terms of its effectiveness and efficiency.
Active galactic nuclei (AGN) are powerful sources of radiation, including ultraviolet, optical, infrared, X-ray, and gamma radiation.
They are essential to the growth of galaxies and the distribution of heavy elements in the universe.
There are two kinds of AGN: radio-loud and radio-quiet.
Radio-loud AGN emit radiation that is brighter at radio frequencies than radio-quiet AGN.
This research presents the results of an observational survey of radio-loud AGN with the Atacama Large Millimeter Array (ALMA).
The survey includes AGN from the Third Catalog of Hard X-ray Selected Strong Radio Sources (3C), which are bright in the hard X-ray band and the radio band.
The researchers analyzed the millimeter radiation from 43 AGN in the 3C catalog, and observed that the millimeter radiation from type-1 AGN was variable.
The research also presents a model that explains the differences in the millimeter radiation from type-1 and type-2 AGN.
The model suggests that the difference in the millimeter radiation is due to the orientation of the AGN's jets and the observer's line of sight.
Type-1 AGN have jets that are oriented towards the observer, while type-2 AGN have jets that are not oriented towards the observer.
This research adds to our understanding of AGN and millimeter radiation, and can be used to improve future studies of AGN and the evolution of galaxies.

We prove that an indiscriminate cover of an infinite translation surface is innocent, i.e. every conjugacy between deck transformations comes from a prior conjugacy of their restrictions to the boundary.
This resolves in the affirmative a question of Y. Matsumoto and Y. Yoshimura posed in 1991.

Our proof is based on studying the boundary actions of Deck translations of surfaces with boundary, constructing for any such action an associated measured lamination whose support is the boundary of the surface and whose weight measures the entropy of the action in the corresponding cover.
This allows us to reduce the proof of innocence to a finite computation in each case.
We present a systematic numerical analysis of a recently proposed Monte Carlo simulation of bacterial chemotaxis with attractive and repulsive chemical signals and signal-dependent noise.
We focus on issues related to the numerical accuracy and efficiency of the simulation algorithm.
In particular, we investigate the effects of different numerical parameters on the accuracy of the simulation results, and we develop methods for estimating these parameters.
We present a set of optimal values for the numerical parameters that guarantee accurate simulation results for a given set of model parameters.
We also present a set of numerical experiments that illustrate the performance of the simulation algorithm with different sets of model and numerical parameters.
These experiments show that the simulation algorithm is both accurate and efficient for a wide range of model and numerical parameters.
The paper presents a study of the structure and morphology of epitaxially grown Fe3O4/NiO bilayers on MgO(001).
The bilayers were grown using a laser molecular beam epitaxy technique, and exhibit a smooth and uniform surface with a clear (001) orientation.

The structural analysis of the bilayers was performed using X-ray diffraction and transmission electron microscopy, which revealed that the Fe3O4 and NiO layers are indeed epitaxial and have the expected rock-salt structure.

The magnetic properties of the bilayers were investigated using a superconducting quantum interference device magnetometer, which showed that the Fe3O4 layer has a strong ferromagnetic coupling with the applied magnetic field, while the NiO layer exhibits no magnetic moment.
The results of this study demonstrate the potential of using such bilayers as a platform for spintronic applications.
We present a finite element formulation of general boundary conditions for incompressible flows.

The boundary conditions considered here are those where the normal component of the boundary gradient of the fluid velocity is specified on the boundary together with the tangential component of the fluid velocity.
These are called natural boundary conditions.
For the special case of isothermal flows, the natural boundary conditions reduce to the no-slip condition.
We use a variational approach in which an auxiliary variable is introduced to capture the effect of the normal component of the velocity gradient.
This auxiliary variable is then eliminated by a transformation on the dual space.
The resulting system of equations for the transformed variables is a standard system of linear equations for finite elements.
An important advantage of the present approach is that standard finite element software can be used to solve the resulting equations.
Furthermore, the approach is straightforward to implement and highly flexible, as it can be used to impose a variety of boundary conditions that may be needed in more complex problems.
The formulation is illustrated by solving a simple 2D problem.
We present a survey of algebraic multigrid (AMG) methods for solving the discrete fluid equations that arise in particle methods for simulating fluid flows.
The particle method, also known as the Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics (SPH) method, is a meshless method for simulating the motion of a set of particles that represent an ensemble of fluid elements.
The particle method formulation of the discrete fluid equations results in systems of non-symmetric sparse linear equations.
We consider a simple AMG method for solving these systems and discuss implementation issues particular to this class of problems.
In particular we investigate the effect of weighting the interpolation matrix and discuss a technique for adding diffusion to the method.
We present a number of 2-D and 3-D numerical examples that demonstrate the performance of the AMG method.
In the last few years considerable progress has been made in the geometric understanding of gravitational waves.
Many of these advances have been based on the introduction of the geometric-acoustical telescope, and its use in studying black hole perturbations.
In this paper we propose a new class of objects, which we call principal sub-manifolds, and show that these are particularly useful for studying gravitational waves.
Construction of these objects makes use of an extension of the geometric-acoustical telescope, which we call the acoustical-geometric telescope.
This new telescope provides a very simple, and physically intuitive, framework with which to study gravitational waves.
We show that Max Planck's hypothesis of the discretization of energy can be derived from generalized assumptions on the medium that emits electromagnetic radiation.
These assumptions are based on a medium with a finite number of particles of each type and colour, and a limited capacity for the propagation of energetic quanta.
The resulting spectrum is identical to that obtained by Max Planck.
We also show that Lorentz's force law for moving charges and the Lorentz transformations can be derived from the same assumptions.
The theory is analogous to Einstein's but uses the discrete energy hypothesis as its fundamental assumption.
We consider implications of the form P(x)
=> Q(x), where P and Q are probability measures defined on an underlying sample space.
We say that such an implication is strict (non-strict) just in case Q << P, respectively Q ~ P, which means that Q assigns a larger (smaller) probability to every event than does P.
We investigate the relative entailment of such implications, i.e. the circumstance under which Q << P implies P => Q.
Our basic conclusion is that this circumstance holds in a surprisingly limited range of cases.
In the Newtonian 4-body problem, we consider the symplectic partitioned Boltzmann method (SPBC) where particle collisions are avoided by the introduction of cut-off radii.
We show that, in the case of equal masses, the common equilibria of the system are stable, and there are many stable choreographic solutions (at least eight).
A new systematic variational method is presented to obtain these solutions.

We introduce a new approach to study distributions of finite and infinite entities in conserved systems, by using generalized entropies (using Havrda-Charvat-Tsallis entropy and Boltzmann-Shannon entropy as particular cases).
We apply these methods to both Gaussian and non-Gaussian distributions, and also to distributions which are not Chi-square.
Our results show that the approach can reveal subtle differences in the distributions of entities in conserved systems, even when these systems are in equilibrium.
This new approach can be used to test the predictions of theories that attempt to explain the behavior of conserved systems, such as the Maximum Entropy Production (MEP) principle.
Additionally, this method can be used to study the behavior of conserved systems in non-equilibrium states, such as when external forces are applied to the system.

Finally, we discuss the implications of our results for the development of new methods for the study of distributions of entities in conserved systems, and highlight the advantages of our approach compared to existing methods.
The ease with which digital information can be preserved, copied, and disseminated online is transforming how we understand collective memory.
There are elements of collective memory that until recently were relatively stable, sustained over long periods of time, and subject to limited revision.
Digital technology has radically altered these conditions.
The goal of this paper is to explain how and why this is happening, what it means for collective memory, and what effects it produces.
We begin by identifying four important aspects of collective memory that are changing as a result of the digital revolution: persistence, popularity, authenticity, and hierarchy.
Then we examine three cases that illustrate how these aspects of collective memory are changing in different ways.
Last, we identify four consequences that follow from the digital reshaping of collective memory for the politics of remembering and forgetting.
The paper introduces the GraphBLAS, a new programming interface for graph algorithms, and its mathematical foundations.
The GraphBLAS provides a set of operations for manipulating graph data structures, such as nodes, edges, and properties.
These operations are designed to be efficient and scalable, and can be used to implement a wide range of graph algorithms.
The paper also introduces the concept of a graph algorithm library, which is a collection of graph algorithms that can be used to perform complex graph computations.
The paper concludes by discussing the potential applications of the GraphBLAS and graph algorithm libraries, including social network analysis, machine learning, and graph mining.
Introduction: Graph algorithms are an important class of computational problems that involve manipulating graph data structures, such as nodes, edges, and properties.
These algorithms are used to solve a wide range of problems in fields such as computer science, mathematics, and physics.
However, developing efficient and scalable graph algorithms can be challenging, as it requires a deep understanding of the underlying graph data structures and their properties.
In this paper, we introduce the GraphBLAS, a new programming interface for graph algorithms that provides a set of operations for manipulating graph data structures.
These operations are designed to be efficient and scalable, and can be used to implement a wide range of graph algorithms.
The GraphBLAS is also designed to be compatible with existing programming languages and frameworks, such as C++ and Python, which makes it easy to integrate into existing code bases.
The paper also introduces the concept of a graph algorithm library, which is a collection of graph algorithms that can be used to perform complex graph computations.
These libraries are designed to be easy to use and modular, which allows developers to combine different algorithms to solve complex problems.
The paper concludes by discussing the potential applications of the GraphBLAS and graph algorithm libraries, including social network analysis, machine learning, and graph mining.
A kinetic model is developed to describe protein aggregation, the formation of oligomers, and the associated cell damage.
The model incorporates finite protein lifetime due to degradation and the competition between healthy and damaged states.
The model predicts that initially healthy cells can be killed by the aggregation of an external protein that aggregates slowly, but forms eventually lethal oligomers.

Interestingly, cells with a high expression level of the protein have a higher probability of being killed, but cells with a very high expression level are less likely to be killed because the protein degrades too fast.
The model successfully predicts the dependence of cell death density on initial protein uptake/expression for different aggregation scenarios.
Ultimately the model can explain the increase of cell death with protein uptake/expression and why cell death saturates at high protein uptake/expression.
d-complete posets are a generalization of Young's lattice of Young diagrams, which has been useful for studying the Jeu de Taquin moving puzzle and its many applications.

In this paper, we define a notion of completeness for a poset that generalizes the d-completeness of Young's lattice, and show that certain completions of the face and cocycle lattices of convex polygons are (d-1)-complete posets.

This establishes a new algebraic framework for studying the Jeu de Taquin puzzle and its variations, and suggests a number of new questions about the relationships between these lattices, their completions, and the Jeu de Taquin moving puzzle.
Appearance-based methods estimate gaze by directly measuring eyeball motion relative to the face, referred to as eye-in-face motion.
Recent advances in deep learning have helped improve the accuracy of appearance-based methods.

However, these methods still suffer from inaccuracy and robustness issues, because 1) they rely on manually designed features which fail to capture the complex and high-dimensional gaze-dependent facial deformation, and 2) they use heuristic post-processing steps that do not adequately account for the large appearance variations in different populations, lighting conditions, and face shapes.

To address these issues, we propose a simple but effective deep neural network (DNN) architecture, referred to as a conditional wavelet regression (CWR) network, to estimate eye-in-face motion from a single image.
Unlike previous methods that use heuristic post-processing steps, our CWR network learns to regress eye-in-face motion from a conditional random field (CRF) defined on the wavelet domain.
This allows the CWR network to implicitly learn an appearance-in-motion model that captures the complex gaze-dependent facial deformation.

We show that our CWR outperforms the current state-of-the-art methods for 2D appearance-based gaze estimation in terms of accuracy (smaller RMS error) on GAIN and BU-4DFE datasets, and is also more robust (less sensitive to variations in appearance) as indicated by the model's generalization performance on the unknown subjects.
We study the zero-bandwidth extended Hubbard model with intersite magnetic interactions in the strong on-site repulsion limit, using the functional renormalization group method.

By calculating the irreducible many-body vertex, we determine the phase diagram, which exhibits a rich variety of phases, including a paramagnetic metal, an antiferromagnet, a dimer phase, and a zigzag phase, as function of the ratio of the onsite to the intersite interaction and the hopping parameter.
In particular, we show that the zigzag phase, which exhibits a long-range ordering of spins with azigzag structure between the sites, is stabilized by the intersite magnetic interactions.
The rich phase diagram suggests the possibility of realizing these exotic states in quantum simulations using ultracold atoms.

We show how to construct conformal metrics with prescribed scalar curvature in a fixed conformal class on a compact manifold $M^n$, under the assumption that $(n-2)$-th scalar curvature is bounded below.
This extends results of Chen-Wang-Wylie [arXiv:1107.5023] and Fine-Wang [arXiv:1107.5026] who treated the case where the conformal class is fixed by a positive scalar curvature metric.
Our technique applies to manifolds with non-negative scalar curvature, but also to cases with no non-negativity assumption.
As an application we construct new examples of conformally flat manifolds with constant scalar curvature.
We study a pinning model on a substrate with heavy-tailed disorder.
By heavy-tailed disorder, we mean that the local strength of the pinning is drawn from a distribution with power-law tail P(p)\sim p^(-\alpha), with 0 < \alpha < 1.
We determine the domain wall creep rate as a function of the wall velocity and the strength of the random field.

The creep rate is found to decay as v^(-\beta), with \beta > 1, indicating that the model exhibits a unique form of velocity renormalization, which modifies the usual Arrhenius behavior of the domain wall motion.
This result is compatible with the prediction of an extended scaling theory, which is developed to describe the effect of heavy-tailed disorder on the pinning model.
We also investigate the effect of heavy-tailed disorder on the structure of the pinned states.
For strong pinning, we show that the pinned state is characterized by a finite fraction of defects, which are localized near the impurities.

The density of states in the pinned sector exhibits a singularity as the system size is increased, which can be described by a power law with an exponent that depends on the tail of the pinning strength distribution.
We study the friction between two spherical shells covered by a power-law fluid at micro scales (mimicking the behavior of molten glass) in the hydrodynamic lubrication regime.

We perform numerical simulations based on this physical system, which remains unexplored despite its importance in several scientific and technological fields (like for instance the glass production).
We observe that the friction law is not universal as already observed in similar systems with Newtonian fluids, but depends on the index of the power law (n) of the fluid.

For a fluid with index n=1 (corresponding to a Newtonian fluid), we observe a transition from a friction law dependent on the roughness of the surfaces to a friction law independent of this roughness, which is instead independent on the power law index.
This transition is characterized by a critical roughness.
We also observe that this critical roughness depends on the index of the power law and decreases when this index increases.
We present an analysis of the communication patterns in the first six months of operation for a sample of three popular MOOCs offered on the edX platform.
We collected and analyzed data provided by the edX platform on student participation in course forums, and forum messages were manually annotated to characterize the type of communication activity.
Our results show that the majority of messages are generic in nature, and do not constitute substantive engagement with the course content.
We found that only a small fraction of all participants contribute to the forums, and that this activity drops off rapidly for those not actively taking the course.
In addition, we found that a small number of highly active users are responsible for the majority of forum activity, and that these users tend to post messages that are relatively shallow in content.

Based on these results, we conclude by discussing the structural limitations of learning in crowds, and provide an interpretation of these findings in the context of limited attention and cognitive load.
Let $G$ be an abelian metric group with metric d and identity element e. Let $\mathcal B (G)$ be the set of all bounded functions on $G$.

The Khinchin inequality states that for a function 
$f \in \mathcal B (G)$, $$\int_G |f(x)| d(x) \, dx \leq \left( \int_G |f(x)|^2 d(x) \, dx \right)^{1/2}$$

In this note we prove a generalized Khinchin inequality for $\mathcal B (G)$, characterizing the equality case, which yields a new proof of the Kahane inequality for $\mathcal B (G)$. We also generalize the Levy inequality from $\mathcal B (G)$ to the larger space $\mathcal M (G)$ of complex-valued Lipschitz functions on $G$. 

We then consider the transfer of inequalities from normed abelian semi-groups to Banach spaces.
Let $X$ be a normed abelian semi-group with norm
|| || and identity element e. Let $\mathcal B (X)$ and $\mathcal M (X)$ be the sets of all bounded and Lipschitz functions on $X$, respectively.

We show that if the norm on $X$ is non-subadditive, then the Kahane and Levy inequalities for $\mathcal B (X)$ transfer to $\mathcal B (X)^{**}$, the second dual of $\mathcal B (X)$. We also show that if the norm on $X$ is subadditive, then the Kahane and Levy inequalities for $\mathcal B (X)$ do not generally transfer to $\mathcal B (X)^{**}$. However, if we pass to the larger space $\mathcal M (X)$ of Lipschitz functions, then both the Kahane and Levy inequalities for $\mathcal M (X)$ transfer to $\mathcal M (X)^{**}$.
A wide range of computational systems, ranging from molecular computers to distributed computer systems, rely on the execution of concurrent programs on multiple parallel processors.

While the program state in concurrent programming can be modeled as a single object, we believe that this approach is only suitable for a small subset of concurrent systems, due to the inherent concurrency overhead associated with the synchronization of concurrently running tasks.
In this paper, we introduce the concept of multiactive objects (MAOs) as a new paradigm for modeling and programming concurrent systems.
An MAO encapsulates multiple, concurrently executing tasks whose lifetimes are bound to the object's lifetime, and it provides each task with its own thread of control and a dedicated stack.
Tasks within an MAO communicate with each other through a novel form of object-oriented messaging, where messages are processed concurrently with the sender's execution.
Since the execution of tasks within an MAO is uncoordinated, MAOs do not require synchronization mechanisms, such as locks or semaphores.
We describe the MAO abstraction and its implementation in detail and report on experiences with programming a number of concurrent algorithms and applications.
We describe a method for choosing conformal maps from the slice $S$ of a vacuum initial data set to a plane, such that the resulting image represents a slice of flat Kasner spacetime.
This provides a conformal parameterization of the universe as seen by an observer in $S$. Such a result may be useful for numerical studies of vacuum spacetimes.
In the case $S$ has a nontrivial boundary, we must first use a conformal map to send $S$ to a cylinder $C$, and then use a conformal map from $C$ to the plane.
We discuss how the maps are related to the expansion history of the universe as seen by an observer in $S$.
Finally we give some numerical examples.
We study the formation of an air bubble from a submerged orifice in a quiescent liquid.
The bubble is sustained by a pressure difference across the orifice, and exits the orifice with a constant velocity.

Making use of this constraint, we determine the shape of the bubble's interface relative to the orifice for various pressure differences, orifice sizes, and distances between the orifice and the bubble.
This analysis leads to a simple expression for the bubble's aspect ratio as a function of these parameters.

We perform experiments to measure the aspect ratio as a function of the distance between the orifice and the bubble for a fixed orifice size and pressure difference, and find good agreement with our theoretical predictions.
We derive the association log-likelihood distance (ALD) in multi-object tracking (MOT), which is a widely used similarity measure to link detections and tracklets.

In contrast to the existing incomplete derivation, we explicitly compute the gradient of the ALD with respect to the initial conditions, i.e., the initial detection appearances and the initial tracklet labels, which allows us to obtain the optimal solution via gradient descent.
We analyze the properties of the ALD and propose a distance ratio heuristic to select the best solution in scenarios where there exist multiple locally optimal solutions.
We derive a novel initialization method to simultaneously initialize multiple tracklets and detect untracked objects in one pass of gradient descent.
Our method outperforms existing methods on various MOT benchmarks.
This paper explores the connection between subriemannian geometry and algebraic geometry, two branches of mathematics that have evolved independently.

We show that the concept of a bridge, introduced by Bridges in the context of subriemannian geometry, can be used to define a new class of objects in algebraic geometry, which we call "algebraic bridges."
These objects provide a link between the two fields, and we explore their properties and relationships.
We also discuss the implications of this connection for understanding the structure of subriemannian spaces and for developing new techniques in algebraic geometry.
This paper aims to spark further research into the interplay between these two areas of mathematics.
We discuss the potential contributions of noncontact atomic force microscopy (NC-AFM) to the future measurements of the Casimir force.

The advantages of NC-AFM are that it is a versatile technique for the measurement of nano-scale forces, and it can provide both quantitative measurement of the Casimir force and the possibility of imaging the Casimir force with nanometer resolution.
In addition, we can exploit the advantages of both AFM and NC-AFM to measure not only the Casimir force in the static regime but also the Casimir force in the dynamic regime.
With an auxiliary optical technique, we can measure the Casimir torque in the dynamic regime.

This auxiliary optical technique can also provide a calibration of the deflection sensitivity of the AFM cantilever, which is one of the most important factors limiting the accuracy of the Casimir force measurement.
We report on the gelation and liquid-liquid phase separation of colloidal clay suspensions.
These inorganic nanoparticles feature a hydrophobic surface modification with a hydrophilic patch acting as a steric stabilizer.
By increasing the suspension viscosity, we induce a transition from a fluid to a gel at a critical volume fraction.
During this transition, the system undergoes a spinodal decomposition, leading to coexisting liquid and gel phases.
We determine the phase diagram of the colloidal clay as a function of volume fraction and ionic strength.
At high ionic strength, the system exhibits additional phase separation, with the coexistence of a low-viscosity liquid and a semisolid phase.
By contrast, at low ionic strength, the system only shows the coexistence of a liquid and a gel.
The presence of the gel phase is attributed to particle-particle interactions, while the liquid phase is governed by the electrostatic repulsion between particles.
The colloidal clay system presents a rich phase behavior, which is uncommon for nanoparticle suspensions and can be explained by the specific surface modification of the clay particles.
Abstract ends.
We address the problem of estimating graph signals from a subset of their irregular samples, i.e., measurements taken on a subset of the nodes of the graph.
We propose a distributed algorithm based on consensus algorithms in network coding that exploits the graph structure to reconstruct graph signals.
The algorithm converges to the optimal estimate in the least squares sense, i.e., it minimizes the mean squared error, under some technical conditions.
We prove that the algorithm is consistent and show numerical results on synthetic and real-world data that highlight its performance.
