The paper studies the role of natural convection in the dissolution of sessile droplets.
It presents a numerical study of the effect of natural convection on the dissolution rate of a sessile droplet resting on a solid surface.
The study focuses on the impact of key parameters such as the Bond number, the Weber number, and the Rayleigh number on the droplet dissolution rate.
The results show that natural convection has a significant impact on the dissolution rate, and that the Bond number is the most influential parameter.
The paper concludes by discussing the implications of these findings for droplet dissolution in various applications.

Abstract: We propose the construction of a three detector short-baseline neutrino oscillation experiment, to be called NuSkin, based on an exposure of several hundred million neutrinos to three near detectors in the Fermilab Booster Neutrino Beam.
The scientific goals of NuSkin include a precise measurement of the electron neutrino mixing angle \theta_e, sensitive searches for neutrino decay and the measurement of the neutrino charge radius.
The proposed experiment will also be able to perform sensitive searches for light dark matter and other rare forms of neutrino interaction.
Recent interest in the control of magnetization dynamics has led to the development of new techniques for manipulating the magnetic properties of materials.
In this study, we investigate the effect of interface anisotropy on the precession of magnetization initiated by laser heating.
We find that a $\pi$ phase shift occurs in the precession of magnetization when the material is heated by a laser.
This phase shift is a result of the interface anisotropy and the resulting change in the magnetic easy axis.
We also find that the direction of the phase shift depends on the direction of the applied magnetic field, and that the phase shift can be controlled by the direction of the magnetic field.
These findings could be useful for controlling the magnetic properties of materials and devices.
We provide new tight lower bounds on the oracle complexity of nonsmooth convex optimization, namely, of finding a zero of a nonsmooth convex function under affine equality and inequality constraints.
Our approach is via information theory.

We show that any measurement compression scheme based on a random Gaussian matrix generates a nonsmooth convex optimization problem that is as hard to solve as solving the corresponding linear programming problem optimally.
This result applies to a number of settings in which the objective is to measure some parameters that affect a latent variable, while minimizing the variance of the estimate.

We also provide a complementary result showing that when the measurements are not compressible, in the sense that they contain as much information as possible about the latent variable, then the corresponding nonsmooth convex optimization problem can be solved in polynomial time.
We extend the hypersequent calculus with a nested sequent notation, permitting conclusions to be displayed structurally, in an attempt to combine the advantages of both notations.
We propose a sound and complete proof system for this calculus, based on a systems-theoretic refinement of the original hypersequent calculus proof system.
We show that our proof system is sound and complete, and that cut-elimination is also obtained.
We investigate the interacting $F(R,T)$ gravity with modified Chaplygin gas in the Einstein frame for the flat FRW universe.

In particular, we explore the kinetic coupling and the potential coupling, and find that the system can undergo a cosmological phase transition from the decelerated expansion to the accelerated expansion induced by the potential coupling, while the kinetic coupling leads to the accelerated expansion without the phase transition.
We also examine the stability of the solution obtained by utilizing the shooting method.

However, the numerical solutions for the flat FRW universe with the kinetic coupling and the potential coupling cannot match the observational data well, which implies that the $F(R,T)$ gravity with the modified Chaplygin gas cannot adequately explain the evolution of our universe.
A fiber-coupled single-photon detector (APD) has been absolute calibrated using a comparison method.
The calibration dependence on detector parameters, such as temperature and biasing voltage, is analyzed.
It is shown that the detection efficiency of the APD obeys the Beer-Lambert law with the absorption of photons in the fiber of about 25% per meter.
The absolute efficiency of the detector is determined to be $(1.4 \pm 0.2) \times 10^{-9}$, which includes the reflection at the fiber connector of $(1.7 \pm 0.2)
The dark count rate is measured to be $900 \pm 200$ counts/s.
The detector resolution is estimated to be $3.5$ ns.
The purpose of this study is to develop and validate a mathematical model of kidney function which incorporates the effects of multiple myeloma (MM).
MM is a malignancy of plasma cells, which can result in elevated levels of serum albumin, and in the degradation of kidney function.
We develop a simple, mathematical model of the dynamics of kidney function (KF), and the interactions between MM and KF.
In particular, we allow for direct inhibition of renal filtration by soluble products of MM, as well as for the effect of decreased blood oxygen availability on KF.
We validate the model using data from three different studies of MM patients, and illustrate the use of the model by exploring the effects of MM on KF in a hypothetical patient.
We study the Random Online Dominance (ROD) algorithm for the Dominating Set problem, where the edges of the input graph are permuted randomly and independently with probability p.
This algorithm has an approximation ratio of 2+ep, hence it is 2-approximate for any e > 0.
We show that, surprisingly, the occurrence of certain permutations can make this approximation ratio as bad as 1+ep.
On the other hand, we show that other permutations guarantee an approximation ratio of at least 4/3.
We present a simple deterministic preprocessing step that uses only O(n) space and turns ROD into a 4/3-approximation algorithm on all input permutations.
Finally, we present experimental results that support our theoretical findings.

We propose and demonstrate an original concept of generation of few-cycle long-wavelength pulses in a dispersive medium with a carrier field shock formed from a femtosecond laser pulse with a spectral gate.
Modal expansion of a laser pulse in a microstructured fiber with a parabolic-index profile was observed both theoretically and experimentally.
A mechanism of the modal cleaning at the input face of the parabolic fiber due to the influence of the spectral gate is proposed.

Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a family of random variables defined on a probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal{F},P)$ and taking values in a measurable space $(\mathbb{R}^d,\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d))$. The family $\mathcal{F}$ is said to possess the noble means property if for every $B\in \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d)$, the tail probability $$\mathbb{P}\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \mathcal{F}(x_i) \in B\right) \to \mathbb{P}(X\in B)$$ as $n\to \infty$ for all sequences $x_1,x_2,\ldots$ independent of $\mathcal{F}$. In this note, we study a family of random variables which arises when considering a stationary sequence of random variables and its canonical process.
We show that this family possesses the noble means property.
We study quantization of conductivity decay in finite regular graphs in relation to the percolation threshold.
To this end we calculate the spectral form factor for a finite graph with periodic boundary conditions.
This allows us to determine the scaling of the conductivity with system size and to identify the critical point at which the conductivity becomes independent of system size.
In contrast to the case of the infinite plane graph, there is a sharp transition for any finite graph at a certain finite density.
However, we show that for graphs with a sufficiently high coordination number this sharp transition occurs at a density which is exponentially close to the critical density of the infinite plane.

Our results are consistent with the hypothesis that the conductivity of finite graph samples approaches the quantized values expected for the corresponding infinite graph as the sample size tends to infinity.

Abstract: 

We consider quantization of electrical conductivity in finite disordered graphs in relation to the metal-insulator transition.
In contrast to the case of the infinite plane, there is a sharp transition for any finite graph at a certain finite density.
We show, however, that for graphs with a sufficiently high coordination number, this sharp transition occurs at a density that is exponentially close to the critical density of the infinite plane.
Our results suggest that the conductivity of finite graph samples approaches the quantized values expected for the corresponding infinite graph as the sample size tends to infinity.
To study the metal-insulator transition in finite graphs, we calculate the spectral form factor, which describes the correlation between the eigenvalues of the Laplace operator.
For periodic graphs, this correlation function can be related to the conductivity via the spectral determinant.

Our calculation of the form factor allows us to determine the scaling of the conductivity with system size and to identify the critical point at which the conductivity becomes independent of system size.
This critical point occurs at a density that is sharply distinct from the critical density of the infinite plane.
For graphs with a high enough coordination number, we find that the two densities are exponentially close.

Our results suggest that the metal-insulator transition in finite graphs is governed by the same universal critical behavior as in the infinite plane, with only minor differences due to the finite size.

Two-dimensional (2D) materials offer a unique opportunity to combine different atoms in a single van der Waals heterostructure, with atomic precision, to create engineered meta-materials with unprecedented electrical, optical, and magnetic properties.

One of the current challenges is the lack of understanding of the fundamental dielectric properties of these meta-materials and how they originate from the properties of the constituting 2D materials.
Here, we present a first principles theory to calculate the dielectric function of a van der Waals heterostructure made up of two different 2D materials.
We show how the fundamental dielectric response is influenced by the properties of the individual layers, such as the atomic structure, the electronic states, and the optical transitions.

As an example, we calculate the dielectric functions of van der Waals heterostructures made up of h-BN and graphene, and we show that the fundamental dielectric response is influenced by both the intralayer and the interlayer physics, which include resonant states in both regions and a strong interlayer coupling.
The results agree well with recent measurements.
In this note, we present a multidimensional version of Szemerédi's theorem on arithmetic progressions for the set of primes.

Let $\mathcal{P}$ be the set of all primes and $\mathcal{P}^{(k)}$ the set of $k$-term arithmetic progressions of elements in $\mathcal{P}$. Let $\mathcal{D}$ be a multidimensional interval defined as $\mathcal{D}=\prod_{i=1}^{d} [a_i,b_i]$, where all the intervals $[a_i,b_i]$ are of the form $[x,x]$, $[x,y]$ or $[y,x]$.

Our result states that $$\liminf_{n\to \infty}\frac{\#\{A\in \mathcal{P}^{(k)}:\ A\subset \mathcal{D}\}}{\#\mathcal{P}^{(k)}\cdot \#\mathcal{D}}\ge 1-\frac{1}{(\log 2)^{d}}$$ which generalizes a recent result of Bergelson, Furstenberg and Tao.
Let $G$ be an algebraic group over a local field $K$. In this paper, we give a sufficient condition for $G(K)$ to have infinitely many points, and we give some examples.

A linear system response to a broadband random excitation can be quite different from the excitation when the excitation has certain spectral characteristics, in particular, when the excitation has line spectra or resonates with one of the system's modes.
In this paper, we provide a theoretical framework to analyze such phenomena in linear dynamics: mode expansion and shadowing.

We show that when a linear system is exposed to an excitation that has a line spectrum or resonance, the system can exhibit extraordinary responses, including slow decay and/or explosion of the response, due to the interaction between the modes and the nonlinearity of the system.
We derive general conditions for these phenomena to occur and demonstrate them with several examples, including a numerical example that exhibits extremely slow decay of the response.
Finally, we show that our theoretical framework can explain, interpret and extend a number of recent experiments and numerical simulations.

We present a simple, practical optimisation of the measurement of relativistic distortions in large-scale structure, focusing on the thermal and kinematic Sunyaev-Zel'dovich (tSZ and kSZ) effects as observable in galaxy surveys.

We optimise the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) for a given survey, finding that the SNR is optimised by splitting the survey area into many independent patches, and stacking the signal from patches that are seen at high angle to the line-of-sight to the cosmic microwave background (CMB).
This method - "stacking by angle" - reduces the noise from astrophysical contaminants and CMB anisotropies, while keeping the signal from the tSZ and kSZ effects coherent.
In narrow redshift bins, stacking by angle optimises the SNR even in patches as small as ∼5° (∼10⁶ galaxies).
However, in wide redshift bins where the survey is deeper, the SNR is optimised for patches with diameters of ∼30°-50° (∼10⁷-10⁸ galaxies).
We provide a simple form of the optimal survey mask for stacking by angle, and show that the optimal mask does not depend on the optional galaxy clustering measurement.

We provide a simple model for the signal and noise in the tSZ and kSZ effects, in order to translate our optimal survey strategy into a simple, practical optimisation that can be applied to any galaxy survey.
We study categorical-algebraic conditions that are related to the concept of protomodularity in abstract elementary toposes.

In particular, we show that a certain natural generalization of protomodularity, called strong protomodularity, is characterized by a universal property, and we introduce the concept of an S-protomodular category, which generalizes both protomodular and S-modular categories.

We show that S-protomodular categories satisfy a generalization of the Beck Condition BC^*, and we use this result to give a new proof of a result of Hofmann, Streicher, and the author on the existence of "relative" sums in any protomodular category.
We argue that gravity is an emergent phenomenon that arises from the geometrization of a classical scalar field, as suggested by the first few lines of Maxwell's equations.

This approach leads naturally to a classical field theory in a curved spacetime, and helps resolve several issues in the prevailing understanding of gravity, including the problems of boundary terms in a variational principle, the non-local nature of the Einstein-Hilbert action, and the deep connection between gravity and thermodynamics.
In this approach, the propagation of gravitational waves is a local phenomenon, and does not imply instantaneous action-at-a-distance, as commonly perceived.

We present a simple derivation of the stress-energy tensor for the gravitational field, and show that it satisfies the conservation of energy and momentum, and the local Lorentz invariance, without any need for a redefinition of the stress-energy tensor at the boundary as usually done in the stress-energy tensor for the Einstein-Hilbert action.

Specifically, we give an algorithm that runs in time $$2^{O(sd)}(sd + N)^{O(1)}$$ where $s$ is the number of monomials in , $d$ is the maximum degree of the input polynomials, and $N$ is the total number of coefficients.
This improves upon the best known runtime of $$2^{O(sd)}(sd + N)^{O(d)}$$ for polynomial matching, matching the best known runtime for factoring univariate polynomials of degree $d$.
We present a virtual microscope that enables the visualization and analysis of big data collections from various domains, with a particular emphasis on imaging and geometric data.

In many application domains, such as materials science, imaging, and remote sensing, the amounts of data collected from experiments can be so large that it becomes infeasible to study the data without extensive preprocessing.
We propose a framework for the visualization and analysis of big geometric data that is based on the concept of contextualization.

Our approach leverages the use of projections for the visualization of high-dimensional data and enables the user to interactively explore the data collections, with a particular emphasis on the identification of structures and patterns in the data.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through a series of examples from materials science and imaging.

We show the existence of interior bubbling solutions for the critical Lin-Ni-Takagi problem in dimension 3, i.e. minimal surfaces with topological genus zero and one boundary component, whose boundary curve is a criss-cross curve with four double points.
In this work, we develop a numerical method for radiative transfer in randomly textured slabs, which are uniformly coated with contaminant of known thickness and optical properties.
The method utilizes the scattered light technique, where the coated rough surface is replaced by an effective perfect diffuser.
This approach, when combined with the Monte Carlo method further enables us to model the radiative transfer in the contaminant layer and the substrate.
We present a numerical example to demonstrate the application of the method to calculate the reflectance of a rough silicon wafer coated with SiO2 of known thickness and refractive index.

We show that the coated rough surface exhibits higher reflectance than the bare substrate at near-normal incidence due to the multiple scattering in the rough surface and the additional reflections at the interface.
However, the reflectance decreases with increasing angle of incidence, and at some angle, the bare silicon becomes more reflective than the coated rough silicon.
The effects of the texture and coating parameters on the reflectance spectra are also investigated.

There has been a lot of interest in "differential privacy," a notion that captures resistance of a statistical database to adversarial inference about individuals contained in the database.
Recently, a Bayesian formalization of differential privacy has been put forth, linking the concept to expected loss in Bayesian inference.
In this note, we question the validity of this link in the general case.
More precisely, we show that expected loss does not satisfy a necessary condition for differential privacy when the adversary's prior distribution depends on the database.
We then suggest a modification of the Bayesian formulation to address this issue.
Appearance variations of facial images taken under different imaging conditions have become a major obstacle for facial recognition systems.
Image quality enhancement is a promising solution to this problem.
However, directly enhancing facial images is challenging due to the ambiguity of the facial structure and the large variety of possible appearances of the same identity.
In this paper, we aim to overcome these challenges by introducing a blind facial image quality enhancement approach that utilizes a patch-based optimization framework.
A patch refers to a subimage that is localized around a given pixel, and can be regarded as a semantic unit to capture the shared structure and appearance between facial images.
Specifically, we explore the non-rigid patches that enable adaptive refinement of the facial image in a content-aware manner.
The optimization of the non-rigid patches is formulated as a sparse representation based denoising approach, where the patch dictionary is learned from a set of training images.
We demonstrate through extensive experiments that the proposed approach outperforms the state-of-the-art methods in terms of both objective measurements and subjective visual evaluations.
This paper explores the application of information theoretic inequalities to superconformal field theory, with a focus on the bounds they provide for the scaling dimensions of composite operators.

The authors review several information theoretic inequalities, including the Shannon entropy power inequality, the Tsallis entropy power inequality, and the Bennett concentration inequality, and discuss their implications for superconformal field theory.
These inequalities provide bounds on the scaling dimensions of composite operators, which can be used to determine the admissibility of certain operators in the theory.
The authors also discuss the implications of these inequalities for the conformal bootstrap approach to superconformal field theory, and suggest future research directions in this area.
A novel chaotic image encryption scheme is proposed using generalized threshold function in this paper.
The generalized threshold function is constructed by concatenating a couple of standard threshold functions with some XOR operations.
The concatenated function makes the output histogram of the plain image unpredictable, which enhances the security of the proposed scheme.
In the proposed scheme, the plain image is encrypted via a couple of chaotic systems driven by two sets of control parameters.

In order to increase the entropy of the cipher image and make the histogram of the cipher image consistent with that of the original random noise, a random noise is added to the plain image before encryption.
Moreover, in order to resist the known-plaintext attack, the control parameters are generated from the key and the plain image.
A set of visual attacks resistant metrics is proposed to measure the resilience of the proposed scheme against various attacks.
The experimental results show that the proposed scheme is resistant to various attacks, and has a higher security compared to the existing schemes.

In the framework of classical electron beam physics, we derive a simple analytical expression for the linear polarization measurement (LPM) effect in sequential bremsstrahlung, in situations where the emission of a photon bremsstrahlung occurs in a medium of finite optical thickness.
Our formula is an extension of the well-known analytical expression for the LPM effect in linear bremsstrahlung.
It is derived by matching the solutions of the sequentially emitted photons' propagation in the external medium to the solutions of the homogeneous equation, with the help of the matching technique.
The resulting expression is simple, compact, and easy to implement in any Monte Carlo simulation that includes the radiative electron energy loss.
We report broadband ferromagnetic resonance (FMR) studies of epitaxial Co/Ti bilayer thin films.

It is found that the ferromagnetic resonance linewidths exhibit distinct frequency dependence, which cannot be described by the commonly used Kittel model that assumes uniform magnetization precession.

By taking into account the variation of the exchange field with resonance frequency, a modified Kittel model that includes the frequency dependence of the exchange field is able to describe our data, indicating that the simple Kittel model is insufficient to describe the FMR properties of these films.
The modified Kittel model provides a better understanding of the magnetization dynamics in ferromagnetic materials, and can be used to analyze and predict the FMR properties of similar systems.

These findings are important for developing a comprehensive understanding of the magnetization dynamics in ferromagnetic materials, and for advancing research on magnetic materials for applications in spintronics and magnetic recording.

The results presented in this paper provide new insights into the frequency dependence of the exchange field in Co/Ti bilayer thin films, and offer a practical guide for developing models that capture the complex behavior of ferromagnetic resonance in magnetic materials.
We study two-dimensional (2D) crystals of hard-core repulsive Yukawa particles with finite-range attraction, modeling e.g. charged colloidal particles in the presence of screening.
For the mono-disperse case we determine the phase diagram as a function of the coupling constants using numerical solutions of the corresponding Schrödinger equation.
Thereby, we focus on the particle density as the order parameter.
We find a rich phase diagram comprising a crystal phase, a fluid phase and a wet crystal phase.
In the wet crystal phase the particles are arranged in a crystal structure, however, the particle positions are shifted due to the long-range attractive interactions.
In addition, we determine the elastic moduli of these different phases, i.e., the Young's modulus and the shear modulus, as a function of the coupling constants.
For the polydisperse case we study the dependence of the elastic properties on the particle size distribution.

By comparing the elastic moduli of polydisperse crystals with the corresponding values for the mono-disperse case we determine the influence of polydispersity on the mechanical stability of the system.
Our results show that the Young's modulus of polydisperse crystals is always smaller than for the corresponding mono-disperse case.
This leads to an instability of the crystal phase already for small polydispersities.
The shear modulus depends in a more complicated way on the polydispersity.
We observe a maximum in the shear modulus as a function of the polydispersity for a certain range of coupling constants.
This maximum signals an optimized mechanical stability of the polydisperse crystal for this choice of parameters.
We introduce a quantum phase-space representation for systems whose configuration space is curved.
This representation is applicable to both constrained and unconstrained systems, and does not require a priori knowledge of either the coordinate system or the constraint structure of the system.

We show that the dynamics of the system is described by a symplectic master equation on the quantum phase space, and use this formalism to derive a conditional evolution for systems subject to non-conservative forces.
This approach provides a framework to study quantum phenomena in curved configuration spaces, such as the quantum mechanics in the presence of a cosmological constant.
This paper derives the time-variant optimum stepsize for normalized least mean square (NLMS) algorithms using Bayesian network (BN) perspectives.
The derivation is based on a linear noise model of the NLMS algorithm and utilizes the structure of a Bayesian network to capture the nonlinearities present in the algorithm.

Numerical results demonstrate the improved performance of the derived stepsize compared to a traditional fixed stepsize and show that the proposed method achieves faster convergence rates and improves the stability of the NLMS algorithm.
Quantum mechanics is founded on the notion of non-locality, making it radically different from classical mechanics that are locally deterministic.
By examining the double-slit experiment and Bell's theorem, we demonstrate that quantum mechanics is not only non-local, but it is also four-dimensional (4D).
This 4D view may provide a new understanding of quantum phenomena, such as entanglement and uncertainty, and a way to experimentally prove the 4D nature of quantum particles.
In this paper, we develop the 4D quantum theory and demonstrate that it is in perfect agreement with all the existing quantum predictions, with no need for the quantum state collapse.
Furthermore, we show that the 4D quantum theory can naturally explain the recent LHC entanglement experiment, in which quantum entanglement was shown to survive over distances of more than 15 km.
In addition, we propose a new Bell test experiment, using two entangled electrons instead of photons, which can definitively prove the 4D nature of quantum particles.
Recent progress in deep learning greatly boosted the performance of super-resolution (SR).
However, training an SR model with a large kernel size and sufficient multi-scale information still faces the challenge of requiring a large amount of data and computational resources.
Based on the observation that internal and external learnings have different requirements for data, we propose a low-rank decomposition (LRD) method for efficient SR model training.

The LRD decomposes the original convolution kernel into a low-rank and a sparse component, such that the internal and external learnings can be conducted on the low-rank and sparse components respectively.
Experiments on several benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach.

Our model with an internal learning-based kernel of size 11×11 achieves state-of-the-art performance on the NYU Depth-to-Surface and the Single-Image Super-Resolution benchmarks, while being more efficient in terms of computational resources and requiring less training data.

This answers positively an open question posed by G. E. Andrews.

Let V be a finite-dimensional vector space over a field of characteristic zero, furnished with a nondegenerate symmetric bilinear form ≤. Let SV be the symmetric algebra of V. Multi-fan algebras were defined by the authors as certain subalgebras of SYM(V), which include symmetric algebras of classical fans and of orthonormal multiplicities.
In this paper, we find necessary and sufficient conditions for a subalgebra of SYM(V) to be a multi-fan algebra, and completely describe all multi-fan algebras.
We study a non-autonomous Cahn-Hilliard-Darcy system with mass source modeling tumor growth in a bounded domain with no-flux boundary condition.
We show that the mass source term, which models the tumor growth, gives rise to a global attractor, provided that the cancer cells are dissipated to the extracellular fluid at a certain rate.
Otherwise, the system may not have a global attractor.
Moreover, the global attractor, if exists, is bounded in a certain function space.
In addition, we show that the system possesses a unique stationary solution.
We propose a general mechanism that relates fermionic T-duality and defects/solitons in field theories.

This mechanism is exemplified in a specific quantum field theory in two-dimensions, namely, a topological insulator described by a defects/solitons enriched Chern-Simons theory with fermionic flavors.

We show that if we turn on a certain space-time dependent background, the bulk theory possesses an emergent space-time supersymmetry, and the defects/solitons of the theory are described by super-Poincar\'{e} bundles.
Furthermore, the bulk theory is shown to be related to a stack of D-branes by the Fermionic T-duality, and the D-brane geometry is described by a super-Poincar\'{e} bundle as well.
Thus, we establish a connection between fermionic T-duality and defects/solitons in field theories, as well as a connection between defects/solitons and super-Poincar\'{e} bundles.
Many existing direction-of-arrival (DOA) estimation methods require a large number of snapshots and coherent paths to achieve acceptable performance.

In this paper, we analyze the subspace leakage phenomenon, which happens when the dimension of the signal subspace is smaller than that of the ambient noise subspace, and provides an interpretation of why fewer snapshots and coherent paths are needed for small-dimensional subspace.

We then propose a novel method to estimate the DOA based on the concept of subspace leakage, where the signal subspace is efficiently retrieved by projecting the data onto the noise subspace followed by whitening and truncation.
The proposed method further improves the DOA estimation performance by utilizing the second-order statistics of the received data.

Simulation results show that the proposed method can estimate the DOA with a small number of snapshots and coherent paths, and significantly outperforms the existing methods in terms of DOA estimation accuracy and robustness.

We present a new version of a code, previously developed by us, for the synthesis of galaxy spectra in the presence of dust, which includes a treatment of non-local thermodynamic equilibrium (NLTE) effects on the level of ionization equilibrium.

We then derive simple and practical recipes, based on the observed UV-to-IR spectral energy distributions (SEDs), for the estimation of the dust properties of galaxies (extinction coefficient and dust temperature), which can be useful for dust-obscuration corrected SED fitting, and for other applications.
The code and the recipes are applied to a sample of nearby galaxies, and the results are found to be consistent with the available observations.

Encouraged by these results, we then use the code to analyze the far-UV to near-IR rest-frame spectra of a dozen of galaxies at redshift larger than 2, for which the far-UV rest-frame spectra have been recently obtained with HST/COS, and for which the dust-attenuated SEDs are available in the literature.

The analysis reveals that a simple assumption of a single dust screen, located in the plane of the galaxy, can hardly explain the observed spectra, unless the optical depth of such a screen is very large (AV > 1).

This suggests that either the dust is not optimally mixed, or that an additional (optically thin) component of dust is present in the galaxy, or that the simple assumption of plane-parallel dust screen is not appropriate.
Alternatively, the observed spectra can be explained if the star-formation history of the galaxy is not well represented by a single burst at the galaxy's birth.
We also derive the attenuation curves of the galaxies, and find that they can be well represented by the Calzetti attenuation curve, with a slight difference in the shape of the far-UV rise.
This suggests that the assumption of a single attenuation curve, modified by a simple exponential cutoff, suitable for nearby galaxies, remains valid also at high redshift.
We show that a compact quantum group G takes the Baum-Connes property with respect to so(Y) G-crossed products if and only if G is a direct product of compact quantum groups.
This in particular applies to SU(n) and Spin(n) for n > 2, answering a question of Higson and Kasparov.

The approach relies on recent results of Crainic and Fernique on Kac envelopes for compact quantum groups, and on an idea of Brown and Guentner to use splitting maps for the construction of (pre-)crossed products.
We report experimental results of anomalous Hall effect (AHE) in Ge(1-x-y)Pb(x)Mn(y)Te composite systems with x=0.2 and 0.4, and y=0.025, 0.05, and 0.075.

The AHE shows a strong dependence on the ferromagnetic ordering in the MnTe sublattice, and an angular symmetry of the AHE oscillations, which is consistent with the theoretical prediction of an Ising-like anisotropy of the exchange interaction in MnTe.
Our results demonstrate the possibility of manipulating the AHE using magnetic field and temperature to reveal the symmetry of exchange interaction in ferromagnetic materials.
We present a methodology for estimating the semantic inflation rate of Wikipedia categories.
Given a category C, we identify a set of candidate categories based on the category's hypernymy/hyponymy links, and use distributional similarity to select the most likely expansions.
We propose several measures of category similarity and evaluate them on a manually annotated validation dataset.
Our results show that our approach achieves high accuracy and F1 score, and that the choice of similarity measure has a significant impact on performance.
We apply our method to a large collection of categories and use the resulting semantic inflation rates to gain insight into the nature of Wikipedia categories.

We show that the isospectral deformation of the free particle solution in one dimension generates infinitely many new integrable equations, namely, the complex KdV equations with various complex potentials.
This provides an example of new integrable equations obtained through the isospectral deformation of the soliton solution of an existing integrable equation.
As a byproduct, we give a new construction of complex KdV breathers in terms of a certain map, from the free particle to the complex KdV soliton.
We derive large scale asymptotics for a class of velocity-jump processes with polynomial jumps, including the fractional Laplacian as a special case.
The process is characterized by a nonlinear generator that may not possess a diffusion coefficient.

By reconstructing the characteristic method for diffusion processes with a nonlinear generator in arbitrary dimension, we show that the velocity-jump process converges to a nonlinear partial differential equation, called the generalized porous medium equation, as the jump parameter tends to zero.

In case the generator of the velocity-jump process corresponds to a uniformly elliptic operator, the generalized porous medium equation turns out to be a particular nonlinear non-local equation, referred to as the fractional porous medium equation, whose sharp interface version represents the dynamics of the fractional Laplacian.
We derive a Hamilton-Jacobi equation for the fractional porous medium equation and discuss connections of the result to a certain class of optimal stopping problems.

We present a comprehensive spectroscopic survey of stellar populations in the inner Galactic bulge, performed with the Fiber Multi-Object Spectrograph (FMOS) on the Subaru 8.2m telescope as a part of the Bulge Extinction Study (BES).
The sample includes 555 stars with extinction-corrected magnesium abundances [Mg/H] < -1.7, covering a magnitude range of 12 <
I < 17 mag.
This survey largely complements the previous works, especially the recent study by Saito et al., who targeted the redder bulge stars with [Mg/H] < -2.3.
Thanks to the large dataset, we can examine the stellar metallicity distribution in the inner bulge in detail, through construction of the MDF in several different ways.
An apparent bimodality is seen in the MDF, which reflects the well-known division of the Galactic bulge into a metal-rich component and a metal-poor component.
In addition to the metallicities, we also determined the stellar distances, the extinctions, and the rotational velocities for the sample stars.
The distances show a good correlation with the metallicities, as already seen by previous studies.

However, when divided into the metal-rich and metal-poor components, the metal-rich stars are on average closer to the Galactic center than the metal-poor stars, contrary to the naive expectation that the metal-rich stars should be more distant simply because they are younger and thus born closer to the Galactic center.
We discuss possible explanations for this phenomenon, and show that it may hint at a significant infall of gas and/or stars from outside the Galactic disk 2-3 Gyr ago.

We perform a quantitative test of general theories of the intrinsic laser linewidth, as formulated by Schawlow and Townes, and by Bergmann, to select which theory is in better agreement with experimental data.

We find that the theory by Bergmann predicts laser linewidths that are in significantly better agreement with experimental data than the theory by Schawlow and Townes, regardless of the measurement setup used.
We prove a convex version of the Pfaff-Darboux theorem of Ekeland and Nirenberg, as well as a convex version of the decomposition theorem of Lions.
As an application, we give a partial answer to a question of Crandall about higher order energy densities.
We study the pattern avoidance for set partitions, introducing a new forbidden family of patterns.

Given a set system $\{S_1,\dots,S_m\}$, we say that a partition $P$ of $[m]$ avoids the $k$-way partition pattern if there is no set system $\{T_1,\dots,T_m\}$ such that each $T_i$ is a union of at most $k$ sets from $\{S_1,\dots,S_m\}$ and $P$ is isomorphic to the partition of $[m]$ induced by $\{T_1,\dots,T_m\}$. Pattern avoidance has been previously considered for set systems.
In this setting, pattern avoidance was defined in terms of unions of consecutive sets in the given system.
Our new forbidden family generalizes the patterns considered in the previous works, while keeping the parameter $k$ fixed.
We study the pattern avoidance for set partitions `a la Klazar', introducing a new forbidden family of patterns.
It is shown that, unlike the pattern avoidance for set systems, the pattern avoidance for set partitions is not monotone.
That is, if a set system contains a pattern, then it may contain patterns of larger size.
However, we show that if a set system avoids the pattern of size $k$, then it avoids all patterns of size $k' > k$ for some specific values of $k'$.
We provide a closed-form solution to the multi-period portfolio choice problem when utility is quadratic and consumption is deterministic.
The solution is expressed in terms of the classic hyperbolic sine portfolio allocation and the problem's parameters.
When probabilities are known, the solution is identical to existing closed-form solutions to the single-period portfolio choice problem.
We show that the solution is applicable to a wide range of problems and discuss the ease with which it can be computed.
An application of the model to a hypothetical investment problem is presented in an appendix.

Abstract:
We present a new computational method for accurate and efficient simulation of fluid-structure interactions with thermal fluctuations.

The method combines the Eulerian and Lagrangian representations of the fluid and structure, respectively, and accounts for thermal fluctuations through a stochastic heat flux in the wall region of the fluid domain.
The fluid flow is governed by the stochastic Navier-Stokes equations, which are solved using a stochastic finite element method.
The structure is modeled as a set of discrete Lagrangian particles, which are treated as tracers in the fluid domain and are updated using a Lagrangian scheme.
The interaction between the fluid and the structure is achieved through a no-slip boundary condition on the surface of the particles and a drag force that acts on the particles due to the fluid flow.
We demonstrate the accuracy and robustness of the proposed method through a set of numerical experiments involving a cantilever beam and a circular cylinder.
The results show that the method is capable of capturing the dynamics of the fluid-structure system, including the effects of thermal fluctuations.
Software-defined networking (SDN) is an approach to computer networking that allows network administrators to manage network services through abstraction of higher-level functionality.
Constrained application protocols (CAP) is a family of networking protocols designed for IoT applications.
We present SCOR, a software-defined constrained optimal routing (SCOR) platform for SDN.
SCOR is designed to support CAP routing, a routing protocol for IoT. SCOR is implemented as a set of open-source software modules that can be integrated into an SDN network.

The SCOR platform includes a routing protocol module that can be used to implement CAP routing, a topology module that can be used to discover the network topology, and a forwarding module that can be used to implement the forwarding plane of the network.
We evaluated SCOR using a testbed and show that it can support CAP routing and optimize the network performance.

We investigate the effect of temperature on the topological properties of a bismuth (111) bilayer using density functional theory-based calculations.
By calculating the surface states, we determine that the bismuth (111) bilayer is a topological insulator with a Dirac cone surface state at the Γ point of the Brillouin zone.
We then investigate the stability of this topological state by performing a systematic study of the electronic structure, including the surface states, as a function of temperature.
Our results show that the topological state of the bismuth (111) bilayer is stable against a temperature increase.
The surface state retains its topological properties up to a temperature of approximately 250 K, which is significantly higher than the critical temperature of bismuth (111) bulk.
Our results provide insight into the stability of the topological state of bismuth (111) bilayer and its potential applications in electronics.
GNU epsilon is a new extensible programming language whose applications have been finding their way into various GNU software components for some time now.
In this paper, we describe the language and give a brief tour of its main features.
Notably, epsilon inherits from Lisp the ability to embed interpreted code within compiled code in a way that is both efficient and safe.
Compiled code can be written to call interpreted code, so that the interpreter can be used as a just-in-time compiler, allowing the easy addition of new functions and even new data types at runtime.
In addition, we describe a new feature for extensible static checking of type safety that we have developed as part of the GNU epsilon compiler.
We consider a model for two-phase incompressible flows of fluids with different densities, characterized by the presence of a thermo-induced Marangoni effect.
This model takes into account the dynamics of the free interface via a diffuse interface approach.
Specifically, we study a system composed of the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations coupled with the Cahn-Hilliard equation through the boundary conditions and a Marangoni type equation.
We prove that this system generates a flow governed by a velocity field and a free interface, which is a weak solution of the two-phase incompressible Navier-Stokes system.
Furthermore, we show that this solution depends continuously on the data of the problem.
We introduce a new message-passing algorithm for convex Belief Networks that decouples inference across different partitions of the graph, based on "Sigma Points" of Michael Jordan.
This algorithm has a simple, intuitive interpretation in the context of Gaussian Belief Networks, and provides an efficient approximation to maximum likelihood estimation in this setting.

Across a wide range of synthetic and real datasets, we find that the new algorithm is much faster than existing message-passing algorithms for convex Belief Networks, while providing comparable performance in terms of Mean Squared Error.
We give a simple proof of the Fourier-Mukai transform for compactified Jacobians in the case of flag varieties, and use it to prove an extension of the autoduality conjecture for these varieties.
Abstract: Cloud computing is a emerging technology that offers an array of advantages such as cost efficiency, scalability, and accessibility.
However, it also raises security concerns, especially in the area of file management.
This paper surveys the security issues in file management in cloud computing environment.
It discusses the different security threats and vulnerabilities that exist in cloud computing and how they can impact file management.
It also explores the various security measures and solutions that can be employed to mitigate these risks.
The survey includes a comprehensive analysis of the existing research and literature on the subject.
The goal of this survey is to provide a comprehensive understanding of the security issues in file management in cloud computing environment and to identify the gaps in the current research.
It is hoped that this survey will motivate further research and development in this important area.

Most organisms use chemotaxis to detect and respond to chemical gradients, but collective decision-making processes that underpin swarm behaviour often appear to rely on other cues, such as mechanical signalling or social interactions.
Here we show that collectively migrating locusts respond to odour gradients under laboratory conditions that minimise mechanical and social cues.
We found that the chemotactic response of individuals was relatively poor, yet successful migration of the group relied on odour perception.

We show that the locusts' aggregation behaviour emerges from the noise in individual responses, which is regulated by a transient amplification of responses to odour, probably caused by positive feedback between odour and behavioural states.
Our results suggest that collective odour sensing can improve detection of odour gradients and provide the basis for reliable group navigation, despite individual responses being relatively poor.

Many important multivariate algorithms can be expressed most naturally using matrices.
In many applications, however, the data are best represented as graphs, and translating graph algorithms to matrices involves significant engineering effort.
We present the GraphBLAS, a new standard for distributed memory graph algorithms.
GraphBLAS is a language based on the familiar matrix syntax, but with operations on graphs instead of matrices.
It is supported by a new reference implementation, which encapsulates state-of-the-art algorithms and data structures for sparse matrix and graph computations.
We present here seven reasons why the GraphBLAS is a good idea, drawn from our experience developing the reference implementation.
We propose and analyze a family of gridless sparse methods for line spectral estimation from random measurements under two types of missing data: missing amplitude and missing phase.

These methods rely on the solution of a particular least squares problem, whose matrix formulation exhibits desirable structure: the matrix is sparse, and (for the missing amplitude case) can be inverted via the well-known Moore-Penrose pseudo-inverse.
This latter property implies that the resulting estimation algorithm is particularly simple and computationally efficient.

We derive the Cramer-Rao bound and show that, under suitable assumptions, the gridless sparse method achieves this bound for any fixed sampling ratio, and therefore dominates the performance of the commonly used grid-based method, which is known to achieve the CRB only for a sufficiently fine grid.
We also propose an iterative method to solve the sparse linear least squares problem, for the case when the sampling ratio is relatively small.
This method is shown to achieve the CRB for any fixed sampling ratio, thus outperforming the grid-based method even in this case.
Active constrained layer (ACL) beams are a new type of smart material which are able to change their mechanical properties upon actuation.
In this paper, we study the static bending of a beam made of active constrained layer, subject to a force applied at the beam's center.
The active layer is actuated by two voltage sources applied to electrodes located on the upper and lower surfaces of the beam.
The electrostatic force induced by the voltage sources gives rise to a bending moment which tends to bend the beam.
The beam's deflection is measured by a linear variable differential transformer (LVDT).
In order to analyze the system and predict its behavior, we establish a mathematical model based on the classical lamination theory and on the electrostatic approximation.
Two different models are presented, corresponding to the cases where the magnetic effects are neglected or retained.
The obtained models are characterized by a nonlinear electrostatic equation coupled with the beam's stiffness equation.
The equilibrium equation is obtained by means of the Lagrange multiplier method and the boundary conditions are satisfied by the use of the Navier transmission conditions.
A numerical resolution scheme is developed in order to obtain the beam's deflection and investigate its behavior.
Finally, a sensitivity analysis is performed in order to determine the effect of each parameter on the beam's deflection.
Semidefinite programs (SDPs) appear in various applications, but they are challenging to solve when the dimensions are high.
One reason for this is that SDPs require inverting matrices in order to compute the KKT conditions, and this operation can become computationally expensive when the dimension is large.
In this paper, we propose a new method for reducing the dimension of SDPs using Jordan algebras.
We show that the dimension of an SDP can be reduced via Jordan algebra techniques, and we provide a condition for when this reduction is possible.
We implement our method in MATLAB and compare its performance to existing dimension reduction techniques.
Our results show that our method can significantly improve the computational efficiency of SDPs, and it is particularly useful for problems with high dimensions.
We show that the well-posedness results for semilinear stochastic wave equations with Holder continuous coefficients, obtained in the recent paper by Yang, contain an error.
We perform a quantitative measurement of the degree of squeezing of the vacuum state after degenerate parametric amplification in a birefringent fiber and verify theoretical models.

Our approach is based on measuring the second order coherence function of the field output from the fiber at two different wavelengths, corresponding to the two polarization modes of the birefringent fiber.
By varying the pump power, we observe variations of the degree of squeezing.
Our measurements are in good agreement with the theoretical model based on linearized quantum theory, including all experimentally relevant parameters.

Quantum communication and quantum computation are typically limited to distances on the order of 100 kilometers due to the degradation of quantum signals during transmission, referred to as quantum decoherence.
Reliably transmitting quantum signals between any two points on the Earth's surface, therefore, requires a network of quantum repeaters.

Here we present a recursive quantum repeater network that is capable of reliable quantum communication and computation between any pairs of points on the Earth's surface, without relying on either trusted nodes or independent classical communication between repeater nodes.
Our protocol is secure against any malicious behavior by the repeater nodes and does not require the nodes to have any synchronized clock or memory.

Our scheme enables end-to-end quantum communication and computation between the users with a negligible failure probability and does not require the users to perform any local operations, even when there are up to 30 repeater nodes in the path.
We show that the concept of multiverse, as an ensemble of structurally different Universes, can be effectively described in terms of the framework of the 'effective potential'.
We demonstrate that the set of Universes which are compatible with a given observational data can be determined by solving the corresponding differential equation for the effective potential.
This approach allows us to introduce two novel quantities: the effective mass and the effective force, which are derived from the effective potential.
In our approach, the multiverse turns out to be an ensemble of stable and unstable universes with various values of effective mass and effective force.
We apply this method to estimate the compatibility of dark energy with the multiverse.
We find that the effective force cannot be zero for any consistent dark energy model, which implies that our universe is unstable with respect to a displacement of the dark energy potential.
Finally, we suggest that the effective potential approach can be useful to evaluate the stability of any point in an arbitrary potential energy surface under small perturbations.
The paper discusses a digital project on historical directories.
It provides a concise summary of the project goals, methodology, and outcomes, including the creation of an interactive directory for Norfolk, Nebraska, based on historical data from 1899-1900.
The abstract concludes by highlighting the potential of such digital projects to enhance historical research and understanding, and encourages further exploration of this type of research.

The directory information for Norfolk, Nebraska, consists of a book of alphabetical listings of the citizens of Norfolk, Nebraska, and the head of household for each residence; the number of people in the household, and their relationships to one another.
These listings also include occupational information, as well as general information about the town, and the facilities and businesses available to residents.
This data can be mapped onto a graph, where the nodes of the graph are the individuals, and the edges are their relationships to one another.
This graph can then be used as the basis for an interactive directory for Norfolk, Nebraska.
The directory would be organized around the relationships between the individuals, and would allow users to browse the directory by these relationships, as well as by the individuals themselves.
This digital project entails significant implications for historical research and understanding.
It demonstrates the potential of digital tools to enhance the study of history, by allowing researchers to analyze and visualize historical data in new and innovative ways.

This project also highlights the importance of historical directories as sources of information about the lives of ordinary people, and the relationships between them, and encourages further exploration of this type of research.

We report on low-frequency 1/f-noise in MoS2 thin-film transistors and evaluate the impact of different device parameters on the noise behavior.
For that, a comprehensive noise parameter space has been explored by fabricating and measuring more than 800 transistors with varying channel length, thickness, and number of layers.
For all devices, 1/f-noise was observed and its dependence on frequency exhibits 1/f^3-behavior over five decades of frequency, ranging from 300 Hz to 150 kHz.
Among the different devices investigated, the thickness of the MoS2 layer and the channel length proved to have the largest impact on the 1/f-noise level.
Single-layer MoS2 transistors exhibit the lowest 1/f-noise levels, which is mainly attributed to the small thickness of a single-layer MoS2 device.
The 1/f-noise in multilayer devices exceeds the one in single-layer devices by more than two orders of magnitude.
This substantial increase in 1/f-noise can be explained by the presence of more defects and charge trapping sites in multilayer MoS2.
Additionally, we investigated the impact of dielectrics other than SiO2, since flexible substrates often require alternative dielectrics.
We found that both PMMA and PET result in an increased 1/f-noise level compared to SiO2, however, the 1/f-noise level still exceeds the one in single-layer devices by almost one order of magnitude.
Our results reveal that 1/f-noise in MoS2 TFTS is influenced by two distinct and separate noise mechanisms: structural and impurity related.

The former is attributed to the lattice of the 2D material itself and is therefore independent of the type of substrate and contact material, while the latter is mainly driven by the contact and substrate material.

Distributed statistical learning—where data are distributed across different nodes in a network, and analysis tasks must be executed in a coordinated fashion on multiple nodes—is an important but challenging problem, with applications in various domains such as sensor networks, machine learning, and data mining.

In this paper, we present an approach to distributed statistical learning based on the key observation that many learning tasks can be formulated as clustering and classification problems on a graph, where nodes represent data points and edges represent similarities between data points.
Our approach enables a variety of algorithms to be executed in a distributed fashion, allowing the task to be split across multiple nodes.

We present an implementation of our approach for the case of binary and multi-class classification problems on a set of nodes organized as a graph, and demonstrate the advantages of our approach on a real-world dataset.

We present a comprehensive overview of the landscape of superiorization and perturbation resilience, two important properties of algorithms that have received significant attention in the past few years.
We give a concise definition for each property, and survey the existing techniques for achieving them.

We also present a continuously updated bibliography of relevant papers, which is divided into sections based on the type of problem being addressed (e.g., optimization, machine learning, etc.) and the approach used (e.g., knowledge gradient, distributional robust optimization, etc.).
We hope that this overview will serve as a useful reference for researchers interested in this field.
A jet is a generalization of a vector field to higher dimensions, where instead of a rank-1 tensor field, one considers a rank-J tensor field.
In this paper, we consider the problem of distributing a constant amount of flux, defined in terms of a scalar field, over a one-dimensional domain using jets.
We propose a scheme for solving this problem using finite volume methods, and show that it is stable and second-order accurate in time.
The scheme is based on a flux-limited diffusion approach, where the diffusion is controlled by a parameter that depends on the local flux.
We show that, by choosing this parameter appropriately, the scheme is able to achieve a desired accuracy with a minimal amount of diffusion.

We demonstrate the scheme on several test problems, including a problem involving a discontinuous flux, and show that it is able to achieve second-order accuracy in both smooth and non-smooth regions.

We study the Regge trajectories of vector and axial-vector mesons in Holographic QCD.
The holographic model employed for this purpose is the 5-point function of SYM with gauge group U(N) in the presence of an infrared (IR) cutoff and a chemical potential.
The latter two are introduced in order to mimic the effects of a quark mass and a finite baryonic charge, respectively.
In the UV limit, when the IR cutoff goes to zero, the 5-point function reduces to the usual AdS soliton.

By simultaneously turning on the IR cutoff, the quark mass and the baryonic charge, we compute the masses of the vector and axial-vector mesons as functions of the IR cutoff, the quark mass and the baryonic charge.
The resulting Regge trajectories are linear, and the corresponding slopes are in agreement with the experimental data.
Furthermore, the slope of the vector Regge trajectory is slightly larger than the one of the axial-vector Regge trajectory.
The work presents a phenomenological approach to modeling structural and topological phase transitions on financial markets.
It is based on the idea of using the mean-reverting stochastic process to model the dynamics of security returns.
This process is characterized by the mean reversion of the security price, which is driven by the market forces.
The process is also characterized by the long memory of the security price, which is due to the slow adjustment of the security price to the market forces.
The approach is applied to the Warsaw Stock Exchange.
The analysis of the mean-reverting process is used to identify the structural and topological phase transitions in the exchange.
The structural phase transition is identified as the change in the exchange's structure, such as the change in the number of participants or the change in the way that the exchange is organized.

The topological phase transition is identified as the change in the exchange's topology, such as the change in the connectivity of the exchange or the change in the way that the information is flow in the exchange.
The approach is useful for understanding the dynamics of financial markets and for identifying the structural and topological phase transitions in the exchanges.
