Given a few training images, our approach learns a robust localization map that can then be used to segment new images according to whether the lesion is present or not.
We evaluate our approach on a publicly available FSMIS dataset and show that our approach performs better than the state-of-the-art approaches.
We introduce a novel unsupervised approach to adaptively register multimodal cardiac images without any initialization.

Our method utilises a variational framework where the registration parameters are learnt using a point cloud representation of the heart, and the entropic regularisation term is used to impose the registration rigidity.
We minimise the proposed entropy-minimisation objective function to find the registration parameters for a point cloud while preserving the shape and topology of the heart's boundary.

We evaluate our method on a publicly available multimodal cardiac image dataset, and the results demonstrate that our method is capable of accurately registering the heart's chambers in different modalities while maintaining a high degree of registration rigidity.
Our approach achieves robust performance even under challenging conditions such as severe noise and artefacts.
Deep learning-based techniques have shown promising results for image segmentation, but they require large amounts of labeled data for training.
This paper proposes a new deep learning-based approach for image segmentation that is both effective and efficient, and does not require any labeled data for training.

The key idea is to use a pre-trained deep convolutional neural network (DCNN) as a feature extractor, and then use a novel superpixel cut (SPC) algorithm to segment the image based on the extracted features.
The SPC algorithm is a fully unsupervised method that works by iteratively merging and splitting superpixels to optimize a cost function that measures the quality of the segmentation.
The cost function is designed to be insensitive to small changes in the segmentation, making the SPC algorithm robust to noise and small artifacts in the input image.
Furthermore, the SPC algorithm is designed to work with a fixed-size superpixel grid, making it efficient and allowing it to run in near-real time on a typical CPU.

The paper demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed approach on a variety of image datasets, and shows that it can achieve better performance than other state-of-the-art image segmentation methods.
We introduce a new evaluation metric for weakly-labeled segmentation, which we call the Weakly-Labeled Rand Index (WLRI).

In weakly-labeled segmentation, each pixel is associated with a set of candidate segment labels, and the goal of the segmentation algorithm is to produce a segment map that agrees with as many of the candidate labels as possible.
The WLRI captures the quality of segmentation by comparing the output segment map with the set of candidate labels, using an adaptation of the Rand Index.

We demonstrate the efficacy of the WLRI by comparing it to other evaluation metrics on two public weakly-labeled segmentation benchmarks, and by analyzing its ability to detect improvement in segmentation quality.
In this paper, a new approach is presented for embryo egg detection in chicken eggs based on their difference in color properties.
In our approach, we first extract the foreground from the given image using a Gaussian mixture model (GMM) based segmentation algorithm.
Then, we use the K-means segmentation algorithm based on the Lab color space to distinguish embryo eggs from non-embryo eggs.
In order to evaluate the performance of the proposed approach, we compared it to a recent approach in the literature.
The proposed approach achieved an accuracy of 94%, a precision of 95%, and a recall of 92%.
Abstract: Urban expansion is a complex process influenced by various economic, social, and environmental factors, making it challenging to predict.
This study proposes a novel approach to predict urban expansion using a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) combination.
The CNN is used to extract features from the spatial data, and the LSTM is used to capture the temporal dependencies in the sequence data.
The proposed approach was evaluated on a dataset of urban areas in the United States and achieved a high accuracy rate of 92%.
The results show that the proposed approach is effective in predicting urban expansion and can be used to support decision-making in urban planning.
Recent progress in one-shot image semantic segmentation mainly focuses on learning a per-class prototype for each category directly through annotation-driven training.
However, most existing methods treat different classes equally during the learning process, which may not be appropriate when the classes have different levels of importance.
In this paper, we argue that it is necessary to explicitly consider the semantic meanings of the classes when learning their prototypes.
Specifically, we propose a novel framework that learns class prototypes based on their semantic meanings, which are measured by an off-the-shelf pre-trained semantic embedding model.
We name our method as Semantically Meaningful Class Prototype Learning (SMCPL).
In contrast to the existing learning methods that treat all classes as a single cohort, SMCPL treats them as multiple cohorts according to their semantic meanings.
We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach through extensive experimental evaluations on three benchmark datasets for one-shot semantic segmentation.

Recent progress in computer vision has greatly improved the performance of semantic segmentation, however, most of these methods rely on a large amount of manually annotated image data, which is costly and difficult to obtain.
In this paper, we present a framework for the automatic synthesis of labeled images, or image compositing, to train a semantic segmentation model for surgical tools.
A set of labeled images are first utilized to learn a conditional generative adversarial network (CGAN).
The CGAN can then be used to synthesize training samples with surgical tools segmented.

By iteratively refining the segmentation model and the CGAN, our method can automatically generate a large and diverse set of training samples, which enables the segmentation model to learn the patterns of surgical tools effectively without any manual annotation.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in segmenting surgical tools on two public surgical datasets.
MudrockNet is a semantic segmentation deep learning model that classifies mudrock SEM images.
The model performs end-to-end training of convolutional layers using a modified Fully Convolutional Network architecture.
The model is trained on a novel dataset we created of more than 1100 manually annotated images.
We assess the model's performance on an independent test set, and analyze the effect of various factors on performance.
The model achieves a mean accuracy of 92.53% on the test set, and we present detailed analysis of model performance both on a per-class and per-pixel basis.
Code and data are available at https://github.com/ajain/MudrockNet.
We present a simple and effective data augmentation method for semi-supervised semantic segmentation.
Our method focuses on the substitution of segments in the labeled images by segmentation masks.
It generates new labeled images to boost the training process of semantic segmentation models.
We introduce a new loss function that enforces the similarity between the pixel-level labels of the original image and the pixel-level labels of its corresponding augmented image.
Furthermore, in order to obtain a good performance, we design an adaptive loss function that dynamically changes the weights of the pixel-level and segment-level losses.
We evaluate our method on the Cityscapes and CamVid datasets, and show that it consistently improves the performance of the state-of-the-art semi-supervised semantic segmentation methods.
In this paper, we propose a new method for finger vein recognition.
Our method generates code representing vein patterns of a finger captured by a camera.
The code is generated by quantizing the vein patterns into multiple levels of binary codes.
To recognize a user, we match the code of the input image with the code of a registered image.
We evaluate the performance of our method using a public finger vein database.
The result shows that our method achieves a high recognition rate with a low false acceptance rate.
Semantic segmentation of nighttime images is crucial for understanding the scene structure and extracting information from nighttime images.
However, the lack of labeled nighttime data restricts the model from effectively exploiting the domain knowledge for accurate segmentation.
In this paper, we propose a map-guided curriculum domain adaptation approach for semantic nighttime image segmentation, which effectively leverages the domain knowledge for accurate segmentation.
Specifically, we firstly formulate the semantic segmentation as a conditional generation process with an encoder-decoder architecture.
Then, we collect a large-scale dataset of daytime images and their corresponding nighttime images, where the images are captured from the same scene but under different lighting conditions.
By learning the mapping from the daytime images to the nighttime images, the model can effectively adapt to the nighttime domain.

Furthermore, to evaluate the performance of the model under uncertainty, we propose an uncertainty-aware evaluation approach, which measures the segmentation performance by considering the prediction uncertainty.
Experimental results on the Cityscapes dataset show that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance in semantic nighttime image segmentation.
RatLesNetv2 is a fully-convolutional network for segmenting rat brain lesions in MRI scans.
It employs an Atrous Spatial Pyramid Pooling module to capture multi-scale context and a weighted loss function to address class imbalance.
The network was trained on a large dataset of over 4000 images from 94 rats and evaluated on a separate test set.
Compared to the previously published RatLesNet, RatLesNetv2 achieved higher accuracy and improved reproducibility.
Further, RatLesNetv2 defines a new state-of-the-art for rodent brain lesion segmentation, outperforming other methods in terms of both F1-score and recall.
The network is implemented using the PyTorch deep learning framework and is available at https://github.com/RatLesNet/RatLesNet.
We present an approach for labeling histopathology images using unlabeled data and a semi-supervised learning framework.
We leverage the abundance of unlabeled histopathology images from the same distribution as the labeled data to improve the performance of weakly-supervised learning.

Our approach consists of two steps: generation of pseudo-labels for the unlabeled data via a conditional generative model, and bootstrapping with these pseudo-labels to refine the model's segmentation performance.
We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach on three publicly available histopathology image segmentation benchmarks, where we achieve state-of-the-art performance.
Semantic segmentation of aerial images is a fundamental task for many computer vision applications.
However, existing methods are often trained on ground-based images and fail to generalize well to aerial images due to the domain gap between the two types of images.
In this paper, we propose a simple yet effective approach for domain adaptation on semantic segmentation for aerial images.
We start by aligning the pixel distributions of the two domains using a convolutional neural network (CNN) pre-trained on ImageNet.
Then, we fine-tune the pre-trained model on a target domain using labeled data.
We finally use a cycle-consistent adversarial network (CycleGAN) to remove the domain shift and improve the performance of semantic segmentation on the target domain.
Our approach achieves promising results on the aerial image dataset and outperforms the state-of-the-art methods.
Recent works have shown that Local Self-supervised Learning (LSSL) can enhance the performance of medical image segmentation.
However, most existing LSSL methods require a large amount of labeled data for training, which is difficult to obtain in the medical field.
In this paper, we propose a new approach for LSSL called PGL (Prior-Guided Local), which only requires a small number of labeled data.
PGL utilizes a prior knowledge graph, which is learned from a large number of unlabeled data, to guide the learning process.
Our experimental results on the 3D ISLES dataset show that PGL can achieve comparable performance to state-of-the-art methods while using only a fraction of the labeled data.
We introduce DoDNet, a deep learning based approach for segmenting multiple organs and tumors from MRI.
DoDNet leverages a transformer-based architecture to jointly learn the segmentation of organs and tumors across a collection of MRI, even when these organs and tumors are not visible in all images.
We demonstrate the efficacy of DoDNet on multiple datasets, showing that it correctly segments 77% of organs and tumors with an F1 score of 89% even when trained on datasets with incomplete labeling.

Recent advances in few-shot learning have achieved promising results in image-based semi-supervised learning (SSL), but these methods tend to fail when directly applied to medical imaging due to the domain shift between image distributions of the base and novel classes.
In this work, we propose ROAM, a simple yet effective method that reduces the domain shift and improves generalization performance in medical SSL.
ROAM introduces random layer mixup to enhance the diversity of both the feature representations and the classifier predictions for base class examples during training.

Specifically, given a base class example, we randomly mix the feature representations of this example obtained from different layers of the neural network with the feature representations of a random subset of other base class examples, and then combine the corresponding classifier predictions to form a new prediction.

We show that this simple “mix and match” strategy helps the model to learn a more robust and generalized feature representation for base class examples, and thus improves the performance of SSL for medical imaging.
Our experimental results on two public medical imaging benchmarks, ISUR 2018 Medical Image Classification and 2020 MedILS, show the effectiveness of our method compared to the state-of-the-art.
Deep learning (DL) models are highly effective for medical image analysis, but their predictions are typically considered black-box and difficult to interpret.

We propose a novel framework that leverages the strengths of both DL and traditional image analysis (IA) methods to provide visually interpretable explanations for the predicted segmentation of disease features in medical images.
Our framework comprises three components: a DL model, an IA model, and a synthesis component.
The DL model is trained to perform segmentation of disease features, while the IA model is designed to estimate the statistics of the segmented features.
The synthesis component combines the predictions of the DL and IA models to produce a final output.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on the task of segmentation of lymph nodes from computed tomography (CT) scans of the chest.
Our method achieved high accuracy in the segmentation of lymph nodes, and the synthesized explanations provided meaningful visual interpretations of the predictions.
We also show that the IA model can estimate the statistics of the segmented features, such as the mean and standard deviation of the pixel intensities within the segmented regions.
Our work demonstrates the potential of combining DL and IA methods to provide interpretable and accurate predictions for medical image analysis tasks.
Medical image segmentation is important in medicine yet suffers from human error introduced during manual labeling.
A significant challenge in training deep learning models for segmentation is the amount of ground truth (GT) required, which is time-consuming and expensive to generate.
As a result, there has been increasing interest in using synthetic data for training.
However, the quality of the GT in synthetic data is typically superior to that in real data, leading to the risk of overfitting.
In this paper, we propose a novel approach to address both problems: the small amount of real GT and the error in the GT.
We first use a U-Net deep learning architecture to segment images and then use a multi-scale graph cuts algorithm to refine the segmentation results.
We then introduce an additional loss function to minimize the difference between the initial segmentation and the GT.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on three different segmentation benchmarks, where we achieve state-of-the-art performance.
We present a new evaluation criterion for cell membrane segmentation of atomic force microscopy (AFM) images based on human perception.

We show that the widely used criterion measuring the difference between the ground truth and the predicted membrane mask has the drawback of being insensitive to certain types of errors that are readily noticeable to human observers.

To address this problem, we propose a new evaluation criterion that is inspired by the observation that perception-based errors are more significant than geometric measures when evaluating segmentation quality.
Specifically, we first extract a set of image features that are relevant to human perception of segmentation quality.
We then adopt an attention mechanism that, given a segmentation mask, automatically computes the importance of each pixel by aggregating the features over a small support region around each pixel.
The proposed criterion combines the attention weights and the geometric error between the predicted and ground truth masks.
We show that our method quantitatively improves the state-of-the-art in terms of the new criterion, and importantly, the visually improved segmentation is also confirmed by human evaluators.
Recent works have shown that few-shot learning (FSL), where training datasets are significantly reduced, can generalize well when the support set has a similar distribution to the query set.

However, for medical image segmentation, creating training datasets that capture the distribution of rare diseases is often costly and time-consuming, whereby a segmentation model trained with such datasets can generalize poorly to hospital scenarios, where patients with different rare diseases need to be segmented.
In this work, we propose a self-supervision approach to train a segmentation model without requiring any annotation.
Specifically, we train the model with a sparse-coding loss that forces the model to reconstruct the original image from its segmented image.
We then enforce the consistency between the original and reconstructed image using a cycle-consistent loss, which does not require any ground-truth segmentation.
To improve the segmentation quality, we introduce superpixels to capture global structures in medical images.

Our approach significantly improves the performance of a baseline model on segmentation of rare diseases, such as COVID-19 and pulmonary embolism, with only 10 and 59 images in the training set, respectively.
Referring expression comprehension is of central importance in visual understanding.
However, most prior works focus on image regions that are explicitly mentioned in the referring expression, while it is equally important to understand regions that are not mentioned.
In this paper, we propose a novel Referring Image Segmentation via Cross-Modal Progressive Comprehension (RISE-PMC) method to comprehend both mentioned and unmentioned image regions.

Specifically, we progressively comprehend an image via a referring expression by iteratively expanding an initially sparse set of regions to form a complete segmentation that captures all regions relevant to the referring expression.
We formulate the progressive comprehension as an energy minimization problem that optimally combines the information from both the referring expression and the image.

To effectively guide the segmentation expansion, we introduce a novel cross-modal dissimilarity measure that computes the dissimilarity between regions in the referring expression and the image, by leveraging their semantic meanings.
Experiments on three benchmark referring expression datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in referring image segmentation.
Recent works in semantic image segmentation either assume access to strong, per-pixel labels or exploit image-level labels while training.
In this work, we study the security of semantic image segmentation models in the face of malicious, segment-level labeling.
Specifically, we show that a segment-level attacker can leverage untrusted labels to infer sensitive, per-pixel information, thereby breaking the privacy guarantees of segmentation models.
We formalize the security definition and present a comprehensive threat model to describe practical attacks in this setting.

Finally, we examine several defenses and show that although there is no perfect defense against inference attacks, several practical options can effectively mitigate different types of attacks depending on the segmentation model and the attacker's capabilities.
We propose a framework for finite group equivariant neural networks (FGENN) for games.
These architectures learn representations of game states that respect a given finite group action.

We show that these models can be used to unify several recent advances in the field, including group equivariant reinforcement learning, multi-agent systems, and recent work on generative models for games.
We demonstrate the applicability of our framework through a series of examples, including a cooperative multiplayer game and the game of Hex.
We introduce a class of equivariant convolutional neural networks (CNN) that we call group equivariant convolutional neural networks (GECNN).
These architectures are parameterized by a finite group and a group action on the input space, and they enforce equivariance to this action in the learned representations.
We show that GECNNs generalize standard CNNs by allowing the group action to move features across channels in a manner that does not increase the model size.
We prove that, when trained via supervised learning, GECNNs learn a convolutional neural network that is equivariant to the group action.
Finally, we introduce a new variant of GECNNs for unsupervised learning that enables the model to learn a unified feature representation for multiple equivariant group actions.
We demonstrate the applicability of the FGENN framework through a series of examples, including a cooperative multiplayer game and the game of Hex.
In the cooperative multiplayer game, we learn a unified feature representation that enables communication and coordination between agents playing the game.
In Hex, we show how FGENNs can be used for both supervised and unsupervised learning, and we demonstrate that the learned representations can be used for game-playing and analysis.
We propose a deep neural network (DNN) for 3D surface segmentation based on contour tree hierarchy (CTH).
CTH is a data structure for 3D point cloud that encapsulates the hierarchical structure of contours, which can be used for efficient surface segmentation.
Our DNN takes a point cloud and outputs a segmentation of the surface, where each point is assigned a label indicating the surface region it belongs to.

The network is trained on a large dataset of synthetic point clouds with ground truth segmentation, and we evaluate the performance on a separate dataset of real-world point clouds with ground truth segmentation.

Our results show that the DNN can accurately segment the surface of various 3D objects, and the performance is significantly better than existing methods based on traditional machine learning and contour analysis.
Our method offers several advantages over existing approaches to 3D surface segmentation.
First, it is able to handle noisy and incomplete point clouds, which are common in real-world data.
Second, it is able to segment objects with complex shapes and surfaces, which are challenging for traditional methods based on hand-crafted features and heuristics.
Third, it is efficient and can segment large point clouds in reasonable time.
Our DNN is based on a convolutional neural network (CNN) architecture, with modifications to handle the hierarchical structure of CTH.

We introduce a new layer called the "CTH layer" that operates on the hierarchical representation of the input point cloud, and we design a new loss function that combines segmentation and shape consistency errors.
We optimize the network using a stochastic gradient descent (SGD) algorithm, and we evaluate the performance on a separate validation dataset.
Semantic segmentation is a fundamental task in urban driving perception, and directly affects the performance of subsequent applications.
However, existing works usually rely on specific datasets, causing low generalization performance on new datasets.

In this paper, we present a universal semantic segmentation framework for fisheye urban driving images, named FUSION, which is trained on one dataset and can be directly applied to any other dataset with no fine-tuning.
The framework is built upon a consolidated fisheye training pipeline, where a geometric distortion module and a dataset-specific refinement module are sequentially applied.

Within the pipeline, a generic network is designed to adapt to various datasets by refining the outputs of different geometric distortion modules, which are uniquely determined by the characteristics of the datasets, such as the field-of-view and image resolution.
We evaluate our method on three standard fisheye urban driving image datasets with different image sizes and fields-of-view.
Results show that our method outperforms the state-of-the-art by a large margin, without any fine-tuning on these datasets.
Recent advances in deep learning have shown promising results in various image processing tasks.

However, directly applying deep learning models on medical image analysis tasks like nuclear segmentation in digital pathology images is challenging, mainly due to the limitations of existing datasets.
We overcome this limitation using data augmentation with sparse coding to enhance the diversity of the training data.

Given the complex structures and appearance of nuclei in pathology images, we propose to use an ensemble of decision trees to improve the model's ability to capture complex relationships between features and target variables.
Our experimental results show that our proposed method achieves state-of-the-art performance on two publicly available digital pathology image datasets for nuclear segmentation.
Furthermore, our model generalizes well to an independent dataset with significant pathologic variability and achieves the best reported F1-score on the segmenting hepatocyte nuclei (SHEN) dataset.
By aligning the distributions of source and target domains, domain adaptation has successfully alleviated the dataset bias in training data.
However, directly adapting the distribution may fail if the two domains have significant visual distribution shifts, which can be challenging to align.
To address this, we propose a co-segmentation based approach where we first find pixel-level correspondences between the source and target domains.
We name our approach Scribble-based Domain Adaptation via Co-segmentation (SDAC).
We cast domain adaptation as a co-segmentation problem where the goal is to find a scribble-like segmentation that minimizes the dissimilarity between the source and target domains.
Specifically, we minimize the Chamfer distance between the source and target domain segmentation, which is computed using scribble features.

We further improve SDAC by (1) incorporating an adaptive instance normalization to align the scribble features of different images and (2) introducing a temperature-scaled cosine distance to better handle noisy correspondences.
Lastly, we introduce a new domain adaptation benchmark with significant visual distribution shifts, i.e., the office-home domain adaptation, where SDAC significantly outperforms previous methods.
Recent advances in neuroimaging acquisition enabled large-scale recordings of neural activity in many regions across the entire human brain at increasing resolution.

While the field of connectomics aimed to map the intricate patterns of fiber connections across the entire brain, current state-of-the-art algorithms for reconstructing fiber tracts from diffusion MRI (dMRI) images are far from delivering feasible runtime performance for mapping ultra-large scale datasets, which typically consist of several thousands of images with each image requiring several minutes of computational processing.
In this paper, we present a deep learning based approach that aims to accelerate the reconstruction process of fiber connections across the human brain.

We exploit recent advances in image segmentation through structured loss functions that promote the reconstruction of anatomically meaningful segments while retaining the advantage of end-to-end differentiability.
We train our deep learning architecture on large-scale datasets of simulated as well as real dMRI images.
In contrast to related work, we provide a thorough evaluation of the algorithm's performance by comparing it to state-of-the-art methods on real datasets.

We show that our approach is not only on par with the state-of-the-art in terms of accuracy, but also offers speed advantages, making it suitable for the reconstruction of large-scale fiber connections in the human brain.
We present a globally optimal algorithm for segmenting mutually interacting surfaces in range images.
The algorithm is based on a new energy function that is derived using a supervised learning approach.
We train a deep neural network to learn the underlying segmentation model from a set of annotated range images.
The resulting energy function is a non-convex sum of a Gaussian term, a harmonic term, and a sigmoidal term that captures the interactions between surfaces.
We use a globally optimal optimization algorithm to find the globally optimal solution to the energy function.
The algorithm is evaluated on the Tanks and Temples dataset and compared to state-of-the-art algorithms.
The results show that our algorithm produces significantly better segmentation results than the baseline and the compared methods.
Our algorithm is also much faster than the compared methods that use iterative graph cuts or dynamic programming.

Urban scene segmentation is a fundamental task in urban analysis, which tends to be very challenging due to the complexity of the scene, large diversity of objects and the existence of repetitive structures.
In this paper, we aim to achieve robust urban scene segmentation with a focus on fine-grained segmentation of buildings and roads.

We introduce a new dataset, called Naive-Student, which is a large-scale dataset for urban scene segmentation consisting of 480 training videos and 192 validation videos, each of which is 20-second long.

In order to tackle the challenge of limited training data in a semi-supervised learning framework, we exploit the prior knowledge that some of the pixels in the videos can be predicted correctly based on their similarity with pixels in other videos, and thus we propose a semi-supervised learning approach, called Naive-Student, to utilize not only the labeled pixels in the current video, but also the labeled pixels in the other videos in the training set.
Specifically, we first seek the similarity between each pixel in the current video and all the pixels in the other videos based on their appearance and motion features.
Then, we exploit the prior knowledge to refine the predictions of current video pixels based on the similarity.
In experiments, we compare our approach with other state-of-the-art approaches on the validation set of Naive-Student dataset, and show that our approach can achieve competitive performance.

Autoregressive image segmentation networks have recently achieved excellent performance on various benchmarks, but training them is challenging: they typically entail optimizing a loss defined on all pixels, which leads to a very wide minima and slow training times.

In this paper, we show that, counterintuitively, it is possible to obtain state-of-the-art performance on the popular Cityscapes dataset by removing the conditional averaging conditioning, i.e., by training an autoregressive segmentation network to predict a single pixel at a time, without seeing the other pixels.

By training with SGD instead of the more widely used Adam, our method achieves a new state-of-the-art on the Cityscapes dataset without any architecture modifications, while being ~5 times faster to train.
We perform an extensive analysis to understand the reasons of this success.

Towards active learning of image segmentation, we address the setting where, given a limited budget of queries, a learner has to select the most informative pixels to query the underlying ground truth.
In this setting, uncertainty is commonly exploited as a measure of informativeness.
However, standard uncertainty estimates, e.g., entropy, are not optimal as they do not account for the cost of acquiring ground truth.
In this paper, we propose a new uncertainty measure that we refer to as cost-sensitive uncertainty.
Our proposed measure yields a higher score for pixels that are uncertain under the current labeling, but more expensive to query; and vice-versa.

We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach on three real-world image segmentation datasets, where we show that our approach yields superior segmentation performance compared to standard uncertainty measures.
In a nutshell, our approach may be summarized as "spend money to save time".
Sampling from a Gaussian mixture model (GMM) with a fixed number of components can often provide inadequate modelling of the variability observed in real-world distributions.
In many applications, including active learning and semi-supervised learning, it is therefore desirable to have a method for adding new components to a GMM in a data-driven fashion.
In this paper we propose a method for suggestive annotation of images, with the aim of guiding the process of component sampling in a gradient-driven fashion.

We apply our method to the problem of suggestive annotation of tumour regions in multi-channel MR images, and demonstrate that it can provide useful information for gradient-driven sampling, resulting in a more accurate representation of the distribution of tumour regions.
Recent advances in labelled medical image datasets have contributed to the advancement of deep learning for medical image segmentation.
However, labelled medical images are expensive to obtain, resulting in a scarcity of labelled data for many domains.
In this work, we tackle the problem of semi-supervised medical image segmentation where only a small fraction of images in a dataset are labelled.
In addition, we also address the issue of domain adaptation where the labelled images and the target domain are from different distributions.
We propose a multi-view co-training approach that leverages both labelled and unlabelled data for training.
Our method is based on the uncertainty-aware weighted sampling strategy that assigns higher weights to the data points that are more challenging to classify.
Furthermore, we introduce a new loss function that encourages the model to make predictions with higher certainty.

Our experiments on three different public datasets, including ISLES, LPBA, and MIAS, show that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance in semi-supervised medical image segmentation and domain adaptation.
Pyramidal Convolution significantly simplifies convolutional neural network design while achieving better recognition accuracy.
This is performed by properly combining ideas from human visual processing with the mathematical properties of the Laplacian pyramid.

In particular, we show that the classical receptive field arrangement of strided convolutions with pooling is extremely sub-optimal, and that the common practice of adding more layers is a patch to this sub-optimality rather than a solution.

We propose Network-in-Network (NiN) modules to replace traditional layers, which consist of a series of convolutional layers with different filters at different resolutions, followed by a concatenation of the feature maps from all resolutions into a single feature map for the next layer.
These modules can be stacked in a natural way to create networks with any number of layers.
In addition, we propose a new cost function for recognition that uses a single fully-connected layer, and show that it achieves state-of-the-art performance on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100.
When the number of classes is large, the fully-connected layer is replaced with a convolutional layer.
Recent works have shown that deep learning models can be effectively applied to medical image analysis tasks.
However, training such models requires large amounts of manually annotated images, which are expensive and difficult to obtain.

This work explores the use of multi-scale feature abstraction to learn robust representations for medical image segmentation across multiple organs, while only training on a small labeled subset of the organs in each image.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on three different organs (lung, liver, and kidney), each with only a small amount of labeled data.
Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on the MIT-BIH lung segmentation dataset and compares favorably to prior work on the LiTS liver and CK+ kidney segmentation datasets.
We survey and assess recent advances in transfer learning for medical image segmentation with FCNs.
The main focus is on semantic segmentation, but we also touch on instance segmentation.
We first provide a comprehensive overview of the field from three different perspectives: 1) What are the existing datasets and evaluation metrics for medical image segmentation?
What are the state-of-the-art methods for medical image segmentation?
3) How do existing methods perform on a common benchmark?
We then discuss the challenges and opportunities of transfer learning for medical image segmentation and list the practical guidelines for using pre-trained models.

We finally present an in-depth critical assessment of transfer learning methods for medical image segmentation, comparing their performance with state-of-the-art traditional methods on a selection of datasets.

Our results show that transfer learning methods perform on par with or even better than traditional methods on most datasets, but there is still room for improvement, especially for datasets with limited training data.
Recent advances in convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have achieved significant performance improvements in medical image segmentation.
However, these methods face challenges in calibration and out-of-distribution (OD) detection.
Calibration refers to the phenomenon where CNNs produce inconsistent predictions for the same input, and OD detection refers to the ability of a model to generalize to new, unseen data distributions.
In this paper, we propose a novel approach to improve calibration and OD detection in medical image segmentation with CNNs.
We introduce a temperature-scaling mechanism that dynamically adjusts the temperature parameter for the softmax function during inference.
By applying temperature scaling, we can control the diversity of the model's predictions and improve calibration.
We further combine the temperature-scaling mechanism with a robust OD detection technique based on the Earth Mover's Distance (EMD).

Our experimental results on multiple medical image segmentation benchmarks show that our approach achieves consistent performance improvements in calibration and OD detection, compared to state-of-the-art methods.
An index is proposed to evaluate the validity of fuzzy-possibilistic C-means (FP-C) clustering.
The index is calculated based on a similarity measure between the true data and the data classified by FP-C clustering.
The proposed index gives a measure of the quality of clustering in terms of how well the clusters are defined by the data points they contain.
The index ranges from 0 to 1, with 1 indicating perfect clustering and 0 indicating no clustering.
The validity index is compared to the fuzzy validity index (FVI) and the possibilistic validity index (PVI) for FP-C clustering.
The results show that the proposed index is a good measure for evaluating the validity of FP-C clustering.
It is a simple and effective tool for comparing the performance of different FP-C clustering algorithms and parameter settings.
It also provides a way to identify potential outliers and noisy data points that may affect the clustering results.
Compared with the FVI and PVI, the proposed index is shown to be a more effective measure for evaluating the validity of FP-C clustering.
A long-running webcam installed in 2007 at Lake Mendota, Wisconsin, has provided an opportunity to develop a time series of lake ice coverage and thaw dates.
Comparing webcam images with those from crowd-sourced volunteers using the same web interface shows that citizen scientists can provide useful data, but with considerable variability.
Guidance for volunteers on how to interpret webcam images of lake ice leads to more accurate and precise measurements, but variability in measurements persists.
Crowd-sourced data, if applied to a large region with adequate volunteer training, could provide a valuable supplement to satellite data for monitoring lake ice cover.
However, automated analysis of webcam images, as developed here, provides the most accurate and precise data.
The webcam-based time series reveals a significant shift toward later ice coverage in fall and earlier ice-out dates in spring over the 13-year record.
There is no significant trend in maximum ice extent or ice thickness.
We present a novel approach for training deep learning models for weakly supervised medical image segmentation, where only few pixels per image are annotated.
Our method utilizes an adversarial loss function that constrains the network to learn a segmentation model that is consistent with the limited annotations.
We introduce a constrained loss function that penalizes the inconsistency between the predicted segmentation and the given annotations.
To evaluate our method, we conducted extensive experiments on three different public datasets: CAMELYON, ISLES, and VIZWIDE.
Our method achieved state-of-the-art performance on all three datasets compared to other weakly-supervised methods.
Our code and models are available at: https://github.com/Radiology-Robotics-Lab/ACCL.
Recent works have shown that neural architecture search (NAS) is feasible for medical image segmentation.
However, directly applying NAS to this problem can be very time-consuming, as the search space can easily reach millions of architectures.
In this work, we present a coarse-to-fine NAS (C2FNAS) approach that significantly reduces the search space, while maintaining promising performance.

Our approach consists of two stages: a coarse search that selects a subspace of architectures that are likely to generalize well, followed by a fine search that refines the architectures within the selected subspace.
The subspace is selected such that architectures within it can use a shared backbone while still allowing customization via a lateral connection.
We apply our approach to 3D medical image segmentation, and search for architectures that can utilize a shared 3D U-Net backbone for segmentation of multiple anatomical structures.
Our approach achieves promising results, with an average increase in segmentation performance of ~5% over the original U-Net and reductions in computational resources.
Code is available at https://github.com/RameenAbdal/C2FNAS.
We introduce a new attack strategy for robustly-trained neural networks.

Our proposed method, called Mimic and Fool, is capable of performing white-box attacks on a variety of tasks, including image classification, object detection, and semantic segmentation, with no task-specific tuning.
We accomplish this by generating a new type of adversarial example that we term a meta-example.

Meta-examples are generated by first using the forward pass of the network to transform an input; subsequently, the transformed input is used to perturb the initial input via an adversarial example attack.

We find that meta-examples are more effective than standard adversarial examples when attacking robust models, and that our method is on-par with state-of-the-art attack methods in terms of both perturbation size and success rate, while providing flexibility with respect to the choice of attack algorithm.
Recent works have demonstrated success in applying flow-based models to learn coherent deformations between images.
However, such models are often brittle since they do not enforce local appearance consistency, making them sensitive to noise and fail to capture local object structure.
In this paper, we propose C-Flow, a conditional flow model that learns appearance-aware deformations between images or 3D point clouds.
C-Flow introduces a novel coupling mechanism that combines the strengths of unconditional and conditional flows.
It allows the model to capture global structural changes as well as enforce appearance consistency between the input and output domains.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on several benchmarks, including image-to-image translation, unpaired image translation, and 3D point cloud deformation.
Our code is available at https://github.com/facebookresearch/c-flow.
Recent progress in land cover classification has resulted from using machine learning algorithms on time-series of satellite imagery to identify land cover types.

A key challenge for land cover classification is the need to overcome limited training data for a specific satellite sensor, as data from one sensor typically cannot be used to train a model for another sensor due to differences in camera properties (e.g. spatial resolution, spectral bands, and noise) and environmental conditions (e.g. atmosphere, sun position, and surface characteristics).
In this paper, we investigate the problem of adapting land cover models trained on one satellite sensor so that they can be used on another sensor, enabling transfer learning across sensors.
We propose a new method for adapting land cover models using a domain adaptation approach, where the goal is to minimize the distribution difference between the source and target domains.
Specifically, we learn a domain adaptation transform that reduces the discrepancy between the source and target distributions of image patches.
We minimize a distance metric based on maximizing the geodesic distance between two distribution embeddings learned by a variation of the t-distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding algorithm.

We apply our method to the task of land cover segmentation using Sentinel-2 and Landsat-8 satellite data, and show that our method improves land cover segmentation performance compared to the state-of-the-art.
Learning to transfer labels from a pre-labeled source domain to an unlabeled target domain has recently shown promising results for few-shot medical image segmentation.
However, these approaches rely on an initial alignment of the domains, which requires a manual localization of corresponding anatomical structures in source and target.
In this work, we propose a learning-based approach for label transfer that jointly learns a reversible voxel-wise correspondence and a label transfer map, obviating the need for manual alignment.
We cast the learning of correspondence as a voxel-wise correspondence prediction task and introduce a geometrically motivated loss that enforces reversibility of the transformation.
We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach on three public abdominal CT datasets and show that our method outperforms previous state-of-the-art methods for label transfer.
We consider the problem of predicting a structured output variable y, which depends on an input x through a possibly nonlinear, parametric mapping function f(x, θ).

In many applications, such as chemoinformatics and bioinformatics, one has a very large number of samples, and an abundance of features, but only a small number of training examples for each class of interest.
For example, a dataset of 100,000 molecules may have activity data for 1000 molecules with a particular biological response, but only 10 examples for a rarer phenotype.
We propose a boosting approach which is applicable in such cases.
We handle the parametric nature of the mapping by using a Gaussian process (GP) surrogate model.
This allows us to construct a distribution over the space of possible functions, given a particular input.

We then construct a boosting algorithm where each weak learner is a classifier conditioned on the GP surrogate model, and show that our method, which we call StructBoost, induces a distribution over the space of structures, rather than just over the space of labels.
In an application to a chemoinformatics dataset, we show that our method can identify a much broader spectrum of active compounds than other approaches.
In this work, we present a novel approach for segmenting ultra-resolution fluorescent microscopy images.
Our approach is based on a meta-segmentation network that utilizes a pyramid of segmentation models to jointly segment multiple scales and resolutions.
Our network is designed to handle the specific challenges of ultra-resolution imaging, such as the presence of noise, artifacts, and complex tissue structures.
We evaluate our method on a large dataset of fluorescent microscopy images and compare it to state-of-the-art segmentation methods.
Our results show that our method is able to accurately segment ultra-resolution images while being efficient in terms of computational cost.
We present a simple approach to image segmentation based on active learning.
In contrast to related work, we use a fully-supervised classifier for segmentation, and learn the classifier's parameters using a modest amount of labeled data and a large amount of unlabeled data.
Our approach is to reinforce the classifier using labeled data only where it errs most frequently on unlabeled data.

We show that this strategy segmentates images nearly optimally in terms of a information-theoretic measure of performance, while using only a small fraction of the labeled data required by passive learning.
Our method performs competitively with a state-of-the-art algorithm that uses an order of magnitude more labeled data.

Most existing works on clustering rely on distance functions to define a metric between data points, which assumes the data lies in a low-dimensional space and fails when the data lies on a manifold of higher dimension.
In this paper, we propose a new clustering framework that does not rely on distance functions and hence is capable of clustering points on a manifold of any dimension.
In particular, given a set of n points in d-dimensional space, our method first maps these n points to a kernel feature space, where kernel functions define a similarity metric between points.
Next, we propose a spectral clustering algorithm that clusters points based on the similarity metric in the feature space.
We show that the proposed method can be used to define a data-dependent metric between points, and hence can cluster points on a manifold of high dimension.
We present experimental results on synthetic and real-world data sets, and show that the proposed method gives better clustering accuracy compared with state-of-the-art clustering methods.
Efficient 2D neuron boundary segmentation is a fundamental step in 3D reconstruction of neuron structures from confocal microscopy images.
We propose a method to exploit local topological constraints, which are inherent in neuron structures, to achieve better segmentation results.
By modeling the topological constraints with a Markov Random Field, our approach produces accurate segmentations even in challenging regions where other approaches can fail.
We evaluate our approach on a dataset of synthetic images and compare it with state-of-the-art image segmentation algorithms.
Our approach achieves significant improvements in segmentation accuracy and efficiency, with an average increase of 5% in F1-score and a speedup of 50% in runtime.
Our method is inspired by the observation that neuron boundaries are often locally connected and have a tree-like structure, with smaller branches branching off larger branches.
This local topological structure can be described by a set of constraints, which we model using a Markov Random Field (MRF).

The MRF represents the likelihood of a pixel belonging to the neuron boundary based on its local topological context, such as the presence of other pixels belonging to the boundary and the connectivity between them.
We optimize the MRF energy function using a graph cut algorithm, which iteratively updates the segmentation by minimizing the cut energy between the foreground and background regions.

To speed up the optimization process, we implement a coarse-to-fine strategy, where we start with a low-resolution segmentation and gradually increase the resolution until the desired accuracy is achieved.
We evaluate our approach on a dataset of synthetic images with varying levels of noise, texture, and curvature.

Our results show that our approach achieves significant improvements in segmentation accuracy and efficiency, with an average increase of 5% in F1-score and a speedup of 50% in runtime, compared to state-of-the-art image segmentation algorithms.
Recent advances in deep learning have achieved great performance in medical image segmentation.
However, deep learning methods usually ignore the observer variation, which may lead to inconsistent segmentation results among different observers.
In this paper, we present a new framework to achieve observer- variation aware medical image segmentation, which combines deep learning and surrogate-assisted genetic algorithms.

Given the segmented images from multiple observers, our framework learns a deep neural network in a data-driven manner to capture the common patterns for segmentation, while genetic algorithms are used to optimize the segmentation protocols to achieve better segmentation consistency across observers.
We apply our method to segment lumbar vertebrae in CT images.
Experimental results show the effectiveness of our method in improving the segmentation consistency.
Recent progresses in deep learning greatly advanced the performance of single-modal segmentation.
However, existing methods usually assume paired annotations, which are difficult to obtain, especially for medical images.
In this paper, we attempt to learn a universal multi-modal segmentation network with unpaired annotations via knowledge distillation.
Given a pair of domains A and B, we train a teacher network with ground truth annotations of domain A, and a student network with unpaired annotations of domain B.
We further introduce a domain classifier as the teacher to classify the domain of the input image.
The student network focuses on segmenting the object with the similar structure as the teacher network.
To further improve the performance, we propose a distillation loss incorporating both the segmentation loss and the domain classification loss.
We evaluate our method on four publicly available multi-modal segmentation datasets, and the experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our method against other state-of-the-art methods.
We present a simple yet effective method for segmenting building polygons from overhead imagery using deep learning.
Our approach leverages recent advances in image segmentation using deep neural networks (DNNs) through the well-known PixelLink algorithm.
We focus on the challenge where training data is limited and segmenting buildings in different countries/regions may require significant adaptations due to data imbalance and domain shifts.
To tackle these challenges, we propose a Getis-Ord Gi* pooling strategy within the deep model, which enables the model to learn more robust features for segmentation.
This feature pooling strategy can be applied to any state-of-the-art deep segmentation model such as DeepLabv3, which takes a hierarchical approach to segmenting an image.
We evaluate our approach on two public datasets (including a dataset from a third-party provider) and show the effectiveness of our approach in segmenting buildings.
Code is available at: https://github.com/microsoft/getis_ord_gi_pooling.
Deep neural networks have demonstrated impressive performance in various computer vision tasks.
However, recent studies have revealed that deep learning algorithms can be fooled by adding carefully crafted noise or adapting the input image with imperceptible perturbations.
In this paper, we investigate the vulnerability of deep neural networks to color perturbations and present a method to fool deep learning-based color constancy algorithms.
We demonstrate that deep neural networks are highly susceptible to color perturbations, which can lead to significant performance degradation.
Our proposed method, leveraging the underlying characteristics of deep neural networks, can effectively fool the network and result in substantial errors in the prediction.
We conduct extensive experiments to validate our approach and evaluate the impact of color perturbations on the performance of deep neural networks for image restoration.
The analysis suggests that deep learning-based color constancy algorithms can be fooled by exploiting their sensitivity to color changes, making them vulnerable to adversarial attacks.
Our findings highlight the need for more robust and adaptive methods in computer vision tasks, including image restoration.
We present a multi-sensor 3D object detector, named PI-RCNN, which efficiently utilizes sparse 3D point clouds and images obtained from multiple sensors.
A point-based attentive cont-conv fusion module is designed to effectively fuse the multi-sensor features for joint detection.

In this module, the point features are aggregated to global grid features via point-wise pooling, then the grid features are processed by the attentive cont-conv layers to capture the context information.
The output grid features are then converted back to point features with aggregated information.
In this way, the channel difference between point features and image features is reduced, and they could be fused efficiently.
We apply our method to multi-sensor 3D object detection for autonomous driving, and extensive experiments are conducted on the B3D dataset, which contains a variety of complex scenarios.
Compared with previous state-of-the-art methods, our method achieves much better performance in terms of both speed and accuracy.
Recent progress in 2D convolutional neural networks (CNNs) has led to state-of-the-art performance in many fields, including medical image segmentation.

However, directly applying 2D CNNs to 3D medical images is not efficient, as it requires voxel-wise predictions and extensive full-image connectivity, resulting in a large number of parameters and slow training.
In this paper, we explore the use of 2D CNNs with a spatio-temporal convolutional layer for efficient 3D medical image segmentation.
Our approach effectively reduces the number of parameters and improves training speed compared to fully 3D-convolutional networks.
We introduce a new architecture called the Thinned 3D Network (T3D), which comprises a 2D CNN with a spatio-temporal convolutional layer.
The T3D architecture significantly reduces the number of parameters and improves training speed compared to a fully 3D-convolutional network.
We evaluate the performance of the T3D on the ISBI 2017 3D Segmentation Challenge and achieve the best performance with competitive runtime.
Automatic image co-segmentation refers to the problem of simultaneously segmenting a collection of images into foreground regions and background regions.
The objective is to find consistent segmentations across the images in the collection, while minimizing the overall segmentation error.
This paper provides an overview of the state-of-the-art in automatic image co-segmentation.
We discuss the different approaches that have been proposed to solve the problem, including bottom-up and top-down methods.
We also review the performance of these methods on standard co-segmentation benchmarks, and discuss the challenges and open problems in this field.
We present a general, lightweight system for accurate 3D medical image segmentation.
Our system, called Network to Segment Them All (N2S2), is based on a single deep learning network that is capable of segmenting a wide variety of anatomical structures in 3D medical images.
The network is designed to be efficient, with a small number of parameters and a low computational cost, making it suitable for use on resource-constrained devices such as smartphones or tablets.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on a variety of 3D medical image datasets, including MRI, CT, and ultrasound images.
Our results show that N2S2 is able to achieve state-of-the-art performance on a wide range of anatomical structures, including the brain, lungs, liver, and heart.

We believe that N2S2 has the potential to revolutionize the field of medical image segmentation by providing a general and efficient solution that is capable of accurately segmenting a wide variety of anatomical structures in 3D medical images.
We hope that our work will aid in the development of more accessible and accurate medical image segmentation tools for use in clinical practice.
Recent work in deep learning has shown that training models on a large number of tasks via multi-task learning (MTL) can lead to better generalization performance on new tasks.

However, MTL suffers from two drawbacks: (1) it requires training a model for each new task, which can be computationally expensive, and (2) it assumes that the tasks are related, which may not always be the case.
In this paper, we propose a new approach to domain generalization that learns task-agnostic semantic features from multiple tasks.
Our approach is model-agnostic in the sense that it does not require training a new model for each task, and task-agnostic in the sense that it does not require the tasks to be related.
We show that our approach can lead to better generalization performance on new tasks compared to single-task learning and MTL, and that it is more efficient than MTL.
We present an encoder-decoder based convolutional neural network (CNN) and a fully connected conditional random field (CRF) for remote sensed image segmentation.
The encoder-decoder CNN extracts hierarchical representations of the image, while the fully connected CRF refines the segmentation results and regularizes the model.
We propose a novel end-to-end training approach for this hybrid model, where the CNN is trained first and then the CRF is fine-tuned.
We evaluate our method on the public VOC 2012 segmentation dataset, and achieve competitive results compared to state-of-the-art methods.
Our code and trained models are available at https://github.com/szagoruyko/remote-sensed-image-segmentation.

We present a new fully-automatic segmentation algorithm that is inspired by active contour models but incorporates a deep convolutional neural network (CNN) in an end-to-end training paradigm to learn how to propagate contours in an image.
This is particularly challenging since the contours evolve over time in a non-differentiable manner, owing to the intrinsic discrete nature of the contour representation.

We overcome this difficulty by casting the segmentation problem as a temporal labeling problem, with the CNN predicting labels for each pixel over a stack of sparse oversegmentations, obtained by partitioning the image using a regular grid.

During training, the CNN predicts labels for each pixel given the previous oversegmentation, and at test time the final segmentation is obtained by propagating labels under the guidance of the learned CNN.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on the challenging task of segmenting foreground objects in images, but our method is generic and can be applied to other segmentation tasks.
We investigate the phenomenon of overfitting in deep neural networks trained with unbalanced segmentation datasets.
We find that when the class imbalance is very severe, overfitting occurs rapidly and uniformly for all classes, even for the majority class.

We show that conventional regularization methods, such as weight decay and dropout, can actually worsen overfitting in certain scenarios and propose to replace them with a Balanced Cross-Entropy (BCE) loss, which better suppresses the false gradient for minority classes during training.
On several benchmarks, our proposed BCE loss consistently reduces the error rate of the network, especially for minority classes.
In a series of experiments, we also study the effect of label noise and the impact of different data sampling strategies on the overfitting phenomenon.
We present a novel approach for 3D cardiovascular magnetic resonance (MR) image segmentation based on neural style transfer (NST).
Given a sparse manual segmentation as the style input, our approach transfers its morphological characteristics to an otherwise unlabeled target image.
In this work, we investigate the impact of inconsistent manual annotations on the NST-based segmentation.
We observe that an inconsistent style input leads to a degraded segmentation output and analyze the reasons for this phenomenon.
To address this problem, we propose a simple yet effective approach to retrieve the true segmentation style by identifying and removing inconsistent regions in the manual style annotation.
We demonstrate the improved performance of our proposed method in comparison to the state-of-the-art on two public available MR datasets.
Our code is available at https://github.com/CristianRC/NST-Segmentation.
Image segmentation is the process of partitioning an image into multiple segments.
The main goal of image segmentation is to simplify the representation of an image so that it can be processed or analyzed by reducing the amount of data into manageable segments.
In this paper, we propose a new image segmentation technique based on a multi-threshold approach using histogram sampling.
Our method uses the histogram of an image to extract the most significant features of the image.
The proposed method is evaluated on the Berkeley Segmentation Dataset and compared to existing methods.
The experimental results show that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance in terms of segmentation accuracy.
Recent works have shown that deep learning (DL) based medical image segmentation models benefit from large amounts of annotated training data.
However, annotating medical images is a very tedious task, requiring expert knowledge, and is very time consuming and expensive.
In this paper, we investigate whether state-of-the-art DL models can be trained using only a single manually delineated scan as training data.

We show that, surprisingly, it is possible to achieve very good segmentation performance when training on a single scan, provided that the scan is manually delineated with sufficient care, with no substantial gain when more scans are used.
To demonstrate the potential of our approach, we provide in this paper extreme augmentation data and scripts used for training, and provide pre-trained models that are made publicly available.
Medical image segmentation is a fundamental preliminary step for computed tomography (CT) images towards computerized tumor diagnosis and therapy planning.
Recently, deep learning based on fully convolutional networks (FCNs) has produced significant advancements in medical image segmentation.

However, directly applying FCNs to segment CT images is challenging due to the substantial variability of tumor appearance, the presence of similar structures, and the reduced amount of manually annotated training data.
In this paper, we propose a novel mixed-supervised dual-network (MSDN) for automatic CT image segmentation.

Given the scarce amount of manually annotated data, our MSDN further utilizes a large set of automatically segmented images, which is obtained by a fully supervised deep learning algorithm, as additional weakly labeled training data.
We employ a dual-network architecture, where the prior network is trained in a fully supervised manner, and the latter network is trained with both the fully supervised and weak supervision.
Furthermore, we propose a mixed-loss function that consists of a data-consistency loss and a prior-consistency loss to enhance the segmentation performance.
The proposed method was evaluated on the public ISBI 2017 Challenge CT Segmentation dataset.
Compared to the state-of-the-art methods, our MSDN achieved a more favorable performance in terms of both the Dice similarity coefficient and the Hausdorff distance.
We present a novel method to approximate the spatial probability of inclusion for a set of points inside partial contours.
It is well known that the inclusion probabilities inside full contours can be accurately computed using the Fourier Mellin transform (FMT), but this approach fails when the contour is partial.

In this paper we propose to extend the use of the FMT to partial contours by computing the inclusion probabilities in the Fourier domain across the contour, and then extending the resulting function throughout the entire image domain.
This is achieved by fitting a suitable function in the Fourier domain that satisfies the constraints of the problem across the contour and then extrapolating it in the spatial domain.
The proposed method is evaluated on two different datasets, and compared against state-of-the-art methods using four different evaluation metrics.
The experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed approach.

Deep learning has achieved great success in learning continuous signals from input data, but most existing methods fail when the signals are geometric or relational, due to the non-differentiability of most geometric operations, such as simplex operations.

We introduce the deep differentiable simplex layer (DDSL), which enables learning with arbitrary differentiable compositions of geometric operations, and applies to a wide range of applications such as data clustering, data embedding, and relational learning.
DDSL can be seamlessly integrated into existing deep learning frameworks, as a drop-in replacement for linear layers, enabling training with backpropagation.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of DDSL on a series of benchmarks for unsupervised clustering, metric learning, and data embedding, where DDSL achieves state-of-the-art performance.
The code is available at https://github.com/autonomousvision/ddsl.

Recent advances in generative adversarial networks (GANs) have shown great potential for unconditional medical image synthesis, but most methods rely on paired or conditional datasets, which are difficult to obtain in the medical field.
In this paper, we present SkrGAN, a novel Unconditional Generative Adversarial Network (UGAN) framework for synthesizing medical images of skulls from sparse contours.
We leverage a recently proposed UGAN structure, called the rendering-based GAN (RB-GAN), which casts the image synthesis as a rendering process with a learned lighting function.
By training our UGAN on a dataset of contour labels alone, without any image examples, we can synthesize new images of skulls, conditioned on the provided contours.

We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through experiments on two public datasets of skull contours, and show that our method can synthesize high quality images of skulls, with applications to medicine and anatomy.
Recent advances in medical imaging technology have led to a vast amount of available data, which poses a great challenge for traditional supervised learning methods in medical image segmentation.
Semi-supervised learning (SSL) has shown promising results by utilizing the unlabeled data to improve the performance of supervised learning.
However, most existing SSL methods treat all unlabeled data equally, which ignores the inherent structure and domain knowledge of medical images.
In this paper, we propose a multi-task attention-based semi-supervised learning (MA-SSL) method for medical image segmentation.

Unlike existing SSL methods, MA-SSL utilizes a multi-task learning (MTL) framework, which enables the model to learn task-specific information and improve the segmentation performance for each specific task.
Additionally, we propose an attention module to weigh the importance of different unlabeled data and enhance the model's ability to focus on the most relevant information.

Experimental results on three public medical image segmentation datasets, including ISBI 2017 Brain Tumor Segmentation Challenge, abdominal organ segmentation from abdominal CT, and cell segmentation from phase-contrast microscopy, demonstrate the superiority of the proposed method compared to the state-of-the-art SSL methods.
DeepAtlas jointly learns image registration and segmentation in a semi-supervised setting, leveraging a sparse set of manually annotated correspondences and a dense dataset of unpaired images.
Our key insight is that the registration network benefits from the segmentation network as a source of implicitly annotated correspondences via cycle consistency.
Specifically, given a pair of images, we alternate between optimizing for registration and segmentation, while enforcing cycle consistency between the warped and segmented images.

We show that this framework is applicable to both fully-supervised and semi-supervised settings, and that in the latter case, the segmentation network effectively acts as an encoder for a novel semi-supervised correspondence encoder-decoder architecture.
Our experiments demonstrate that the proposed method compares favorably with the state-of-the-art on the challenging MICCAI 2012  Brain Tumor Segmentation Challenge dataset.
Recent works have shown that neural networks can learn to perform complex low-level vision tasks directly from raw sensor data, without needing intermediate 3D renderings or hand-crafted features.
We extend this approach to the domain of medical imaging, where raw data can be challenging to work with due to its sparsity and lack of a clear spatial order.
In particular, we study the task of brain tumor segmentation on multi-channel MR brain images.

Unlike images in the visual domain, the k-space data acquired by an MR scanner contains all the information about the final rendered image, but in a format that is difficult for humans to interpret and unsuitable for most existing machine learning algorithms.
We present an end-to-end differentiable network architecture that can learn to segment brain tumors in MR images acquired through compressed sensing, directly from k-space data.
Our architecture consists of a recurrent attention network that operates on sparse k-space data and learns to aggregate information across multiple channels and repetitions.
We demonstrate that our method achieves competitive performance with state-of-the-art methods that operate on fully-sampled MR images and train using 3D renderings and hand-crafted features.
Recent works in computer vision have shown that deep learning models, particularly convolutional neural networks (CNNs), can be effective in estimating the camera pose from a single image.
This paper provides an introduction to the field of camera pose estimation with deep learning.
We review the state-of-the-art algorithms and highlight the advantages and limitations of different approaches.
We discuss the challenges and opportunities in this field, and provide a comprehensive overview of the current research.
Finally, we suggest potential future research directions in camera pose estimation with deep learning.
Recent works have shown that Deep Learning (DL) models could be used for automatic segmentation of cardiac structures in Magnetic Resonance (MR) images.

However, most existing methods tend to be specialized in segmenting either the left-ventricle (LV) or the right-ventricle (RV) and optimized independently, despite the fact that both ventricles are of equal importance for clinical applications.
In this work, we present a fully automatic segmentation approach based on a Shape-Refined Multi-Task Deep Learning (SRMTDL) framework, where the LV and RV segmentation tasks are trained jointly.
Our approach incorporates shape information in the form of explicit shape-models to achieve better segmentation performance.

We evaluated our method on 320 MR images from the 2017 Cardiac MR Image Segmentation Challenge (CMISC), and achieved a Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC) of 0.8814 and 0.8610 for the LV and RV segmentation, respectively.
This establishes our method as the first approach to segment both ventricles automatically in 3D with promising performance.
We present a self-supervised learning approach to cardiac magnetic resonance (MR) image segmentation based on anatomical position prediction.
We leverage the temporal redundancy of cardiac MR sequences to learn a generic heart position prior, which can be used to segment new unseen images.
Our approach does not require any manual annotation for training, and we show that it is able to learn meaningful heart position representations from a small number of training examples.
We demonstrate the efficacy of our method on a large dataset of cardiac MR images and achieve state-of-the-art performance in terms of segmentation accuracy.
Our method can be applied to any cardiac MR image segmentation task and has the potential to reduce the amount of manual annotation required for training.
We present a novel approach for semantic image segmentation based on a supervised learning framework.
Our method is based on a regularized convolutional neural network (CNN) that is designed to preserve object boundaries and prevent over-segmentation.
The key component of our approach is a novel fully-connected layer that is added to the end of a pre-trained CNN.
This layer takes as input the output of the final convolutional layer and produces a segmentation map as output.
The fully-connected layer is designed to minimize an energy function that enforces a regularization term based on a novel boundary-preserving loss function.
This regularization term is designed to encourage the network to produce segmentation maps that accurately delineate object boundaries.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on the public VOC2012 semantic image segmentation benchmark.
Without any fine-tuning or additional training, our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on this benchmark.
Recent advances in deep learning have achieved great success in medical image segmentation.
