However, existing methods are predominantly trained and tested on the same dataset (source domain), which results in poor performance on unseen datasets (target domain).

In this work, we address the cross-modality domain adaptation (CMDA) problem, which aims to learn a universal segmentation model that is capable of adapting to any target domain with only a few labeled samples.
Specifically, we propose a synergistic image and feature adaptation approach, which combines domain adaptation for both image and feature spaces.
We first adapt the source images to match the target domain via an image adaptation module.
Then, we adapt the features space by minimizing the divergence of the feature distributions between the source and target domains.
To evaluate our approach, we conducted extensive experiments on four public datasets (MRBrain, ISLES, ADNI, and PPMI) with different modalities (T1-weighted MRI, T2-weighted MRI, Flair, and PET).
Our approach achieved superior performance compared to the state-of-the-art methods.
Learning a semantic encoder from pixel-level annotations alone is challenging due to the ambiguity of pixel-level labels, especially for blurry boundaries.
To overcome this, we propose a new training objective for a semantic encoder based on an ensemble of semantic segmentation masks, which is trained using only pixel-level annotations.
Our approach leverages the multi-scale nature of the encoder, where the layers with higher resolutions capture more fine-grained details compared to the layers with lower resolutions.

By enforcing the agreement between the encoder features and the segmentation masks at multiple scales, our approach effectively captures the underlying semantics and learns a robust encoder for blurry boundaries.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on the benchmark datasets Cityscapes and CamVid for semantic segmentation.
Our approach achieves competitive performance compared to state-of-the-art methods while using a single semantic encoder architecture for both training and testing, without any post-processing steps.
Our code is available at https://github.com/AI4Finance-Foundation/BlurryBoundaryDelineation.

Recent semi-supervised segmentation methods mostly focus on exploiting label relationships under the assumption that the available labeled data is abundant and accounts for a significant portion of the training data.
In this work, we address the scenario where the labeled images are limited and cannot afford to use many of them for training.

Therefore, we study the impact of not only using label relationships but also the budget spent on annotating the training data, i.e., the number of images used for training, on the performance of semi-supervised segmentation.
We find that the performance improves as we increase the budget, and it eventually converges.
However, the convergence point varies depending on the dataset, suggesting the existence of a budget threshold, below which the performance would not improve even if more images are annotated.

By analytically and experimentally analyzing the reasons behind this threshold, we find that it corresponds to a point where the model is already capable of capturing the underlying label relationships well enough.

Based on this observation, we propose a new training framework that first focuses on utilizing the available labeled data to its fullest, and then transitions to using label relationships, resulting in a budget-aware semi-supervised segmentation method.
Our method achieves the state-of-the-art performance on semantic and instance segmentation benchmarks.
Captions are a valuable source of information for semantic segmentation, despite most existing approaches treating them as auxiliary data or a weakly-supervised signal.
In this paper, we investigate methods for harvesting information from captions for semantic segmentation.
We propose a simple yet effective approach for utilizing captions in a weakly-supervised manner, by exploiting their temporal consistency and context information.
Our key insight is that the caption for a given frame is likely to contain information about the presence and location of objects in that frame.
We leverage this intuition to improve the performance of weakly-supervised semantic segmentation.

Our approach consists of two main components: (1) a spatial attention module that uses the caption to focus on the relevant regions of the image, and (2) a temporal attention module that uses the caption to determine the relevance of different frames in a video.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on the Cityscapes and Mapillary Vistas datasets, and show that it significantly improves over weakly-supervised approaches that do not use captions.

Towards the goal of digitizing historical urban structures for cultural heritage and virtual reality applications, we address the problem of automatically extracting walkable 3D city models from a set of panoramic historical images.

We introduce a new approach for estimating camera positions and orientations from a set of sparse 3D control points, that significantly expands the scope of input data that can be used for city model reconstruction.

Given access to a limited number of 3D control points (e.g. from laser-scan based modeling), our approach successfully estimates camera positions in challenging scenarios involving large view disparities, scene motion and significant texture variations.
In contrast to prior work, we entirely bypass the need for additional 2D-3D alignment through feature detection in multiple images.
We demonstrate our approach on a variety of panoramic image datasets of different historical cities that we have acquired over the past years.
The reconstructed city models are evaluated in terms of modeling quality and level of detail, and we show that our approach compares favorably to other state-of-the-art techniques.
Skin cancer is a major public health problem in Australia, and its incidence rate is rapidly increasing worldwide.
Early detection of skin cancer is essential for successful treatment.
However, the early detection of skin cancer mainly relies on the experience and intuition of specialist doctors, which leads to undesirable misdiagnosis or delay in treatment.
Thus, there is an urgent need for the development of computer-aided diagnosis systems to assist doctors in skin cancer diagnosis.
In this paper, we aim to develop a robust and automated skin cancer segmentation and classification method to assist in the early detection of skin cancer.
A deep learning-based approach is investigated, which utilizes a novel architecture named NABLA-N and Inception Recurrent Residual Convolutional Networks (IRRCN).
The proposed method was evaluated on a public dataset, and the experimental results show that the proposed method achieved high accuracy in skin cancer segmentation and classification.
Recent advances in computed tomography (CT) technology have enabled the acquisition of micro-CT images with very fine voxel sizes, down to 0.2 μm.
However, as the voxel size decreases, the image quality degrades, due to the increased noise and scatter.
This paper presents a super-resolution convolutional neural network (SR-CNN) model for enhancing the resolution of rock micro-CT images.
The SR-CNN model is based on a VAE-GAN architecture, which is designed to learn a mapping from low-resolution (LR) images to high-resolution (HR) images.
The model is trained on a dataset of rock micro-CT images, and is evaluated on a separate test dataset.

The results show that the SR-CNN model can effectively enhance the resolution of rock micro-CT images, improving the quality of the images and enabling the identification of features that are not visible in the original images.

The SR-CNN model has a number of potential applications, including the enhancement of micro-CT images for use in geological research, and the enhancement of medical images for use in medical diagnosis.
The model could also be used to enhance the resolution of images in other fields, such as astronomy and satellite imagery.
In general, the SR-CNN model can be used to enhance the resolution of any type of image, and could be applied to a wide range of applications in research and industry.
The paper concludes by discussing the potential of the SR-CNN model for enhancing the resolution of rock micro-CT images, and presents some future research directions in this area.
We present a cross-modal self-attention network (CMSAN) for referring image segmentation.
Given a referring expression, our goal is to assign segment labels to each pixel in the corresponding image region.

To this end, we propose to use a self-attention mechanism to capture the relationships between referring expressions and image regions, as well as the relationships between the image regions themselves.
Specifically, we generate region queries and phrase queries to represent the image regions and referring expressions, respectively.
Then, we apply self-attention to compute the weights of the region queries and phrase queries, which indicate the relevance between each region and each phrase.
Finally, we use the weighted region queries and phrase queries to predict the segment labels for the image regions.
To handle the long-tail problem in referring expressions, we propose to use a progressive attention mechanism, which gradually attends to the long-tail phrases.
In addition, to overcome the data imbalance between referring expressions and image regions, we introduce a cross-modal sampling strategy to balance the training samples.
Our experimental results on the ReferItSeg dataset show that our method outperforms the state-of-the-art approaches.
We introduce a new visual reasoning dataset, CLEVR-Ref+, that consists of referred instances of the CLEVR dataset's objects.

For example, given an image containing a number of objects and a referring expression of the form, "The small blue cylinder next to the red pyramid," our dataset provides multiple candidate referents: referring expressions ground entities in the image, and the referred instances include the entities in the image that match the description in the referring expression.
We propose a number of baseline models for referring expression comprehension (REC) that operate on different levels of image abstraction, and evaluate them on our dataset.
Our best model, a convolutional neural network that reasons about image layout, achieves an F1 score of 71.2 % on CLEVR-Ref+, a 12 % absolute improvement over the next best model.
We introduce a new dataset, host it on a new website, and make our code and data publicly available.
We present an approach to image segmentation based on active learning coupled with a geometry-inspired model.
We design an inpainting-based active learning framework, where we train a segmentation model to restore labeled regions in partially labeled images.

We couple the segmentation model with a geometric active learning strategy, which measures the uncertainty of the model in restoring labeled regions with a geodesic distance in a learned manifold of labeled pixels.
We show that this geometric active learning strategy is implicitly learned from the data during training, without using any ground truth geodesic distances.
We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach on two public benchmarks, achieving state-of-the-art performance in terms of both segmentation quality and efficiency in active learning.
Recent advances in deep learning have achieved tremendous performance in medical image classification, surpassing traditional approaches.
However, the lack of transparency in these models prevents direct usage in clinical practice.
In this work, we aim to improve the interpretability of deep learning models for cardiac pathology classification on cine magnetic resonance imaging (MRI).
We introduce an apparent flow map estimation framework that characterizes both translational and rotational motion within the cardiac chambers.
By enforcing interpretability in the learning process, our approach produces a sparse deep neural network (DNN) with a clear decision boundary.
We demonstrate that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance in cardiac pathology classification, with a controlled degree of complexity and interpretability.

Recent works have shown that deep learning models can learn meaningful and useful representations from image time series, which are composed of a sequence of images acquired over time with a certain temporal spacing.
However, existing works mainly focus on learning representations of the whole image time series, which may not be optimal for modeling the underlying temporal information.

In this paper, we propose a new approach for learning disentangled representations of satellite image time series, which are composed of images acquired over a certain period of time with a certain temporal spacing.

Our approach is based on the disentangled representation learning framework, which aims to learn representations that are disentangled in a way that they can be used to model the underlying temporal information more effectively.

We evaluate our approach on a dataset of satellite image time series and show that our approach can learn disentangled representations that are more effective for modeling the underlying temporal information compared to existing approaches.
Domain adaptation under target shift, which addresses the scenario that the target domain data distribution shifts unexpectedly in test time, has gained increasing research attention.
In this paper, we study the multi-source domain adaptation under target shift, where multiple source domains are available for adapting to the target domain.

We propose a novel Optimal Transport (OT) based method for domain adaptation under target shift with multiple sources, where a transport plan between the aggregated feature distributions of all source domains and the target domain is learned to minimize the divergence between them.

Specifically, a novel multi-source domain adaptation objective is proposed, which combines the benefits of both the Wasserstein distance and the maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) with a logarithmic barrier.
Moreover, a fast optimization algorithm based on the dual formulation of OT is developed to efficiently solve the proposed objective.

We evaluate the proposed method on three benchmark datasets for adaptive object recognition, and experimental results show the effectiveness of the proposed method compared to the state-of-the-art approaches.
Recent works have shown that contextual information plays a crucial role in medical image segmentation.

However, most existing works obtain contextual information by using fully connected layers, which hinder the performance of the model due to the spatial information loss during the flattening and spatial information inconsistency between different channels.
In this paper, we propose a simple and general framework, namely CE-Net, to incorporate the contextual information with the spatial information more effectively.

Specifically, we adopt the recently proposed Context Encoder module to capture the global contextual information for each pixel, and develop a simple yet effective spatial encoder network to encode the spatial information.
The outputs from the two encoders are then combined and fed into a segmentation decoder network.
We show via extensive experiments that our method outperforms the state-of-the-art approaches for five public 2D medical image segmentation benchmarks.
FickleNet enables semi-supervised training of deep neural networks for semantic image segmentation by generating training samples using an ensemble of stochastic segmentation networks.
Given a finite set of labelled training images, a segmentation network is trained to classify image regions.
The same network is then used to produce a stochastic labelling of unlabelled image regions, which is subsequently used to generate pseudo-labelled images.
These pseudo-labelled images are added to the training set, and the process is repeated in an iterative fashion until the network's performance converges.
Inference can be performed by a single segmentation network without any stochastic labelling.
We present a thorough evaluation of our approach on the semantic image segmentation task using the PASCAL VOC 2012 and Cityscapes datasets.
Our experimental results show that FickleNet can boost performance in semi-supervised setting compared to recent state-of-the-art methods, delivering competitive results with a large margin.
We introduce a technique for class-independent full image segmentation, using a convolutional neural network.
Our method is driven by a novel architecture, termed attention-within-segment, that is trained in an end-to-end manner on pixel-level ground truth data.
In a single forward pass, our network outputs a segmentation mask for the entire image.

A key distinction of our approach is that each pixel in the segmentation mask is assigned a "hard" segmentation class (e.g., object or background) or a "soft" attention weight, with the latter indicating the likelihood that a pixel belongs to a particular object.
During inference, the soft attention weights are thresholded using a heuristic method based on a statistical test to obtain a final segmentation.
To handle class-imbalanced datasets, we propose an extension of the attention-within-segment architecture that incorporates a loss-balancing term in the objective function.
We evaluate our method on the Cityscapes and CamVid datasets, and show that it performs favorably against other state-of-the-art segmentation methods, in terms of both precision and recall.
Fast-SCNN achieves fast inference speed and high efficiency in semantic segmentation, which is crucial for applications like autonomous driving.
We systematically study the causes of inefficiency in FCN and formulate the problem from two aspects: feature redundancy and excessive computations.
We first propose a lightweight convolutional neural network (LCNN) architecture to effectively reduce the computational cost, and then a Fast-RCNN based approach to further improve the speed.

To obtain a more compact model without sacrificing the accuracy, we propose a novel weighted channel-wise feature fusion (WCF) method to adaptively aggregate the multi-scale features in different channels, and a channel-wise prediction (CP) method to efficiently generate the final segmentation results.
Our methods lead to a highly efficient semantic segmentation network, which significantly reduces the computational cost and memory footprint, making it practical for real-time applications.
Our network achieves a speed of only ~0.23s per image on a Titan X GPU, while maintaining state-of-the-art segmentation accuracy on the VOC 2012 and Cityscapes datasets.
Recent works have shown that strong image-level supervision, in the form of pre-trained image labels, can boost performance on various computer vision tasks.
We explore the utility of these image labels for learning to segment objects in images.
We propose a simple, fully-supervised approach for learning to segment that uses image-level labels and a segmentation architecture initialized with an encoder pretrained on image-level labels.
Our approach uses at least as much supervision as previous works, but decomposes the segmentation loss into a classification loss and a regression loss.
This allows us to use all pixels for both classification and regression, and use the image-level labels to constrain the regression.
We evaluate our approach on the COCO suite of segmentation benchmarks and show that our approach is competitive with previous works in terms of performance, while being more efficient to train.
We propose a framework for the automated quality control of image segmentation outputs, which assesses both the accuracy and reproducibility of segmentations for a given imaging study.
The proposed framework utilizes a database of ground truth segmentations, which are created using a consensus of manual segmentations from individuals with advanced imaging expertise.
These ground truth segmentations are subsequently used to evaluate the accuracy and reproducibility of automated segmentations produced by commercial software packages.
We demonstrate the utility of the framework on cardiac MRI images obtained from the UK Biobank imaging study.
Abstract: Ultrasound continues to be the preferred imaging modality for prenatal care, owing to its safety and portability.
However, the size of raw ultrasound volumes presents a storage and transmission challenge, often requiring compression for efficient clinical workflow.
In this work, we present UltraCompression: a framework for high density compression of ultrasound volumes using physics modeling deep neural networks.

We highlight the limitations of conventional compression methods in handling ultrasound images and demonstrate how our approach can achieve higher compression ratios compared to state-of-the-art methods, while preserving diagnostic quality.
We show that our method achieves an average compression ratio of 127:1 with less than 1% mean squared error, making it suitable for clinical use.
We consider the problem of optimal decision-making in mixed-agent partially observable stochastic environments, where a team of agents must collaborate to maximize their cumulative reward.
We propose a novel algorithm, Augmented Q-Learning (AQL), that combines reinforcement learning with Bayesian inference to learn a cooperative policy in such settings.

AQL utilizes a hierarchical representation of the environment, with an upper level describing the high-level relationships between the agents and a lower level capturing the individual state spaces of each agent.

By iteratively updating a set of augmented Q-functions, our algorithm learns a policy that maximizes the expected cumulative reward, while accounting for the uncertainty and hidden state information in the environment.

We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in a variety of scenarios, including a mixed-initiative game and a cooperative search problem, and compare it with existing methods for multi-agent reinforcement learning.

Random pruning is a classic regularization technique that randomly selects neurons to ignore during the training of a neural network, and it has been shown to improve generalization performance and reduce overfitting in traditional feed-forward neural networks.
In this paper, we study the effect of random pruning on deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs), which have been shown to be highly successful in many image classification tasks.
We find that random pruning can indeed improve the generalization performance of CNNs, and we further analyze the effect of pruning on the representation learned by the network.
Our results show that random pruning can selectively eliminate less important features from the network, leading to a more concise and interpretable representation of the data.

We also find that the magnitude of the parameters in the network plays an important role in determining the importance of each feature, and we present a method to scale the parameters to enforce more equitable importance among the features.

Finally, we show that our method of random pruning can be used in conjunction with other regularization techniques, such as weight decay and dropout, to further improve the generalization performance of CNNs.
Recent advances in 3D medical imaging technology have generated an enormous amount of 3D medical image data.
However, the segmentation of 3D medical images remains a challenging task.
We present a fast and accurate 3D medical image segmentation method based on a data-swapping algorithm.
Our method utilizes the spatial coherence and anatomical knowledge of the medical image data to achieve accurate segmentation results.
The data-swapping algorithm is a simple and efficient approach that dynamically swaps the data points based on their similarity.
We compare our method to state-of-the-art 3D medical image segmentation methods and show that our method achieves comparable or better performance in terms of segmentation accuracy and speed.
Our method has the potential to improve the efficiency and accuracy of 3D medical image segmentation, which could benefit clinical imaging applications and image-guided surgery.
We address the problem of multiple sclerosis (MS) lesion detection from magnetic resonance (MR) images in the setting of highly limited labeled training data.

We propose an approach that combines three components: (1) an asymmetric loss function that incentivizes the model to focus on hard, labeled examples and provides robustness to noise in the form of mislabeled examples, (2) a densely connected neural network (DenseNet) that can effectively capture contextual information, and (3) a series of MS-specific modifications to both the loss function and the DenseNet architecture to handle the anisotropic and inhomogeneous characteristics of MS lesions.

We show that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on the largest available MS lesion segmentation dataset, with significantly better performance than using a symmetric loss function or a less dense architecture.
Our code and dataset are publicly available for future research.
Recent progress in 3D biomedical imaging technology has resulted in a vast amount of big data for 3D biomedical images.
However, 3D biomedical image segmentation remains a challenging task, especially when the size and complexity of the data grow.
In this paper, we propose a new ensemble learning framework, which combines multiple advanced learning algorithms, for 3D biomedical image segmentation.
It is shown that the proposed framework is very effective in segmenting 3D biomedical images, and that it is able to handle big data.
The proposed framework is evaluated on two 3D biomedical image datasets, and the results show that it achieves high segmentation accuracy compared to the state-of-the-art.
Recent progresses in deep learning have promoted the development of effective models for biomedical image segmentation.
However, most existing models treat different image scales independently without sufficient exploitation of their correlations, which may lead to the inconsistency among different scales.
In this work, we propose MDU-Net, a multi-scale densely connected U-Net, to effectively utilize the multi-scale information for precise and consistent segmentation.
Specifically, we first adopt an Atrous Spatial Pyramid (ASP) to generate multi-scale feature maps.
Then, a densely connected mechanism is introduced to exploit the correlations among the multi-scale feature maps.
Furthermore, we propose a novel gated linear unit (GLU) to enhance the feature representation power of our model.
Extensive experiments on three public datasets (e.g., ACDC, ISBI 2017 brain, and LiTS) demonstrate the superiority of our model over the state-of-the-art methods.
The source code and datasets are available at https://github.com/VITA-Group/MDU-Net.
Deep Sensor Cloning (DSC) is a new framework for replicating sensor data, such as images, with a deep neural network.
We introduce DSCnet, a convolutional neural network architecture designed to replicate lidar point clouds.
Lidar point clouds often have a large number of points, and replicating these clouds requires a network that can handle this sparsity while capturing the underlying structure.
DSCnet is designed to accomplish both of these tasks.
In order to handle large point counts, DSCnet uses a novel sparse convolutional layer that reduces the number of points to be processed while preserving the important structure of the point cloud.
We demonstrate that DSCnet can effectively replicate lidar point clouds and that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on the task of point cloud replication.

Recent works have shown that auxiliary tasks, such as modeling steering angles in autonomous driving, can improve the sample efficiency of training a main task, such as predicting the future trajectory of a vehicle.
In this work, we propose a new approach for learning steering models for autonomous driving, where the goal is to predict a steering command that can be used to control a vehicle.
Our approach is based on modeling features from heterogeneous auxiliary tasks, such as lane keeping, lane changing, and avoidance of obstacles.
We show that our approach can improve the sample efficiency of training a steering model, and we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on a real-world autonomous driving dataset.
Recent works have shown that training on synthetically-generated images can boost the performance of semantic segmentation.
However, training on synthetic data comes at an increased computational cost, and it remains unknown how much synthetic data is needed to outperform using only real-world data.

In this work, we perform an extensive experimental evaluation of the recently proposed CEREALS framework, which leverages generative models to produce virtual training data, for semantic segmentation.
We perform a comprehensive study, varying the amount of real and virtual training data, number of training epochs, and different evaluation benchmarks.

We make the following key discoveries: (1) CEREALS continues to improve in performance as more synthetic data is added, but surprisingly, using more than 30% synthetically-generated data does not yield better performance; (2) our proposed method reduces the computational cost of training by a factor of 4 (from 1.3B to 300M parameters) while achieving similar performance to the full model; (3) our method achieves better performance than the state-of-the-art on the Cityscapes benchmark, and achieves competitive results on the ACDC and CamVid datasets; (4) our method achieves a new state-of-the-art on the challenging Mapillary Vistas dataset with 51 classes; (5) surprisingly, our method trained on 100% synthetic data actually underperforms the baseline when trained on 100% real data.
Fuzzy connectivity (FC), a recently proposed measure for tissue segmentation, has shown promising results for partitioning the whole body into seven tissue segments.

However, FC suffers from two drawbacks: (i) the segmentation result is not directly interpretable in the context of body composition analysis (BCA), and (ii) the approach is not directly applicable to segmenting the brain and thighs, which require different number of segments.
In this article, we address these issues through a novel extension to FC, which we refer to as normalized fuzzy connectivity (NFC).

In contrast to FC, NFC (i) produces a fuzzy membership value that is directly interpretable in the context of BCA, and (ii) can be extended to any number of segments, making it applicable to thighs (three segments) and brain (four segments).
In this article, we demonstrate the effectiveness of NFC via comprehensive validation on a recently collected multi-site dataset, totaling 337 subjects, and including thighs, brain, and whole body.
Semantic segmentation of images has witnessed great advances thanks to deep learning.
However, existing models are typically trained under a specific scenario, resulting in suboptimal performance when tested under different conditions.
In this paper, we aim to adapt a deep segmentation model trained under clean and well-lit conditions to segmenting images in the dark, where only low-level cues are available.
We introduce Dark Model Adaptation (DMA), a simple yet effective method to adapt a deep segmentation model for nighttime conditions.
Given a source model trained on daytime images and a target dark model, DMA leverages their respective advantages to bridge the gap between the two.
It does so by first learning a latent space in which the two models can interact, and then refining the target model towards the source model in the learned space.
We show that DMA can significantly improve the segmentation quality of a state-of-the-art model when adapted to low-light conditions, even using a weakly-supervised target model.
Atrial fibrillation (AFib) is the most common sustained cardiac arrhythmia in the United States, affecting more than 2.7 million people.
Radiofrequency ablation (RFA) is an effective treatment for AFib; however, approximately 20% of patients experience postoperative recurrence.
It is critical to identify patients at high risk of recurrence after RFA for targeted medical therapy.
This study proposes a deep learning-based approach to estimate postoperative AFib recurrence using standard 12-lead electrocardiograms (ECGs).
A total of 167 patients who underwent RFA for symptomatic drug-refractory AFib between August 2016 and July 2020 were included in this study.
For each patient, the standard 12-lead ECG recorded on the first postoperative day was used for model training and validation.
Two deep learning models were developed and compared: a convolutional neural network (CNN) and a attention-based deep neural network (DNN).
The models were trained to classify ECGs into either with or without AFib recurrence.
The area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC-ROC) was used to compare the performance of the two models.
The results showed that the CNN model had an AUC-ROC of 0.80, while the DNN model had an AUC-ROC of 0.85.
The DNN model performed better than the CNN model in estimating postoperative AFib recurrence.
The DNN model may be a useful tool for estimating the risk of AFib recurrence in patients who have undergone RFA.
This study demonstrates the potential of deep learning in estimating postoperative AFib recurrence using standard 12-lead ECGs.
This approach may help identify patients at high risk of recurrence and guide targeted medical therapy.
Semantic segmentation is a fundamental task in computer vision with a wide array of applications.

However, training models for semantic segmentation is challenging: in addition to the scarcity of labeled training data, the validity of the labeled data is often hard to ascertain due to the tedious nature of pixel-level labeling.
In this paper, we present a simple and effective solution to diagnose the integrity of labeled training data for semantic segmentation.
Our approach leverages the inherent smoothness of segment boundaries by estimating the expected geodesic distance between pixels based on a collection of labeled images.
We show that discrepancies between the estimated and actual geodesic distances can reveal potentially erroneous segment labels.

We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach on the Cityscapes dataset, where we identify and quantify label errors in the widely-used pre-trained models as well as a newly collected dataset of synthetic data.
Keywords: Semantic segmentation, data validation, diagnose, smoothness, geodesic distance, Cityscapes.
We introduce Mask Editor, a novel interactive image annotation tool tailored for image segmentation tasks.

In contrast to existing annotation tools, Mask Editor leverages an intuitive UI that provides users with a direct and efficient manipulation of instance masks and an underlying neural network architecture for improved instance-level labeling.
In our interface, users can quickly create, edit, and propagate instance segmentations with a few interactions.

We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach through extensive experiments on the Cityscapes and COCO datasets, and show that our tool can be used to create high-quality ground truth data and that our neural network architecture learns effectively from the generated data.
We present an interactive binary image segmentation method that combines edge-preserving smoothing with a watershed-based segmentation approach.
The key idea is to use the smoothing as a preprocessing step to reduce noise and remove minor irregularities in the image, while preserving the overall shape of edges.
This smoothed image is then used as the basis for a watershed-style segmentation, where regions are grouped together based on pixel intensity values.
The resulting segmentation is an optimal solution in a least-squares sense, i.e., it minimizes the sum of squared differences between the segmented image and the ground truth.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on a variety of binary images, including those with noisy backgrounds and ambiguous segment boundaries.
Compared to the watershed algorithm run directly on the original image, our method produces segmentations with fewer false positives and better-preserved edges.
Our implementation of the interactive segmentation algorithm is written in Python and employs the popular scikit-image library.
We provide a user-friendly interface that allows the user to specify the desired number of segments and explore different smoothing parameters.
The final segmentation is obtained by running the watershed algorithm on the smoothed image, followed by post-processing steps to handle cases where the desired number of segments is not an integer.
The code and documentation are available at https://github.com/yzslab/interactive-binary-image-segmentation.

YouTube-VOS: Sequence-to-Sequence Video Object Segmentation

We present a simple and effective approach for video object segmentation (VOS), breaking new ground in addressing the problem in a sequence-to-sequence (S2V) fashion, i.e., forecasting masks frame by frame as a function of the previous masks.
It is trained with a combination of temporal and spatial losses, leveraging a state-of-the-art convolutional neural network architecture for still image segmentation.
The experimental results show that our approach outperforms previous state-of-the-art VOS methods without requiring any additional training data.
We release our code and models for future research.
Recent progress in sensor technology has enabled the collection of subdecimeter aerial images, with centimeters-level precision in pixel-level localization of trees.
However, the precise segmentation of trees in such images remains a challenge.
We present TreeSegNet, a deep learning based approach that is trained end-to-end to segment trees in subdecimeter aerial images.
TreeSegNet adapts Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) to align with the tree structures by a tree-structure-aware loss function.
Furthermore, it incorporates geometry information in the learning process to improve performance.
We evaluate TreeSegNet on a large dataset of subdecimeter aerial images collected over several sites in the northeastern US.
In comparison to other state-of-the-art segmentation approaches, TreeSegNet improves the F1-score on average by 12.7%.
We propose a weakly-supervised learning-based feature localization method in confocal laser endomicroscopy (CLE) glioma images.

Unlike the fully-supervised learning, which requires a large number of labeled training samples, our method only needs a few labeled samples to train a convolutional neural network (CNN) for feature localization.
By training a CNN with a small number of labeled samples, our method is able to reduce the burden on experts who manually label the samples.
Furthermore, our method can be used in many practical applications, where the number of labeled training samples is limited.
Experimental results on CLE glioma images show that our method can effectively localize the tumor regions and the performance of our method is comparable to that of fully-supervised learning methods.
Our method consists of two steps: training a CNN with weakly-supervised learning and optimizing an iterative joint label and feature learning (IJLFL) framework.
In the training step, we train a CNN with only a few labeled samples, which are produced by experts roughly drawing tumor regions on the images.
To reduce the difference between the distributions of labeled and unlabeled data, we adopt the generative adversarial network (GAN) to generate more labeled samples.

Moreover, to improve the generalization ability of the CNN, we propose a new architecture called attention-guided convolutional neural network (AG-CNN), which can focus on the most important information in the images.
In the IJLFL step, we optimize an IJLFL framework to obtain the final labeled images and feature maps.
The IJLFL framework contains two sub-networks: a label network and a feature network.
The label network takes the feature maps produced by the CNN as input and outputs the labeled images.
The feature network takes the labeled images as input and outputs the feature maps.
By iteratively optimizing the label and feature networks, the IJLFL framework can obtain the labeled images and feature maps that best describe the tumor regions.
Dilated convolutions are a key component of neural networks designed for medical image segmentation.
In this paper, we propose a novel approach for left atrial segmentation in 3D Gadolinium Enhanced-MRI using a fully convolutional neural network equipped with dilated convolutions.

Our network is designed to take advantage of the rich contextual information and large-scale context provided by dilated convolutions while being efficient in terms of parameters and computational requirements.

We evaluate our method on the publicly available MICCAI Segmentation of Left Atrium Challenge (SLAC) 2016 dataset and show that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance in terms of Dice similarity coefficient and pixel accuracy.
Our network is implemented using the PyTorch deep learning framework and trained on a single NVIDIA TITAN Xp GPU.
Semantic segmentation is an important problem in computer vision with a wide range of applications.

State-of-the-art approaches tend to rely on very deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs), but training these networks is computationally expensive and can require a large amount of labeled training data.
In this paper, we investigate the use of shallower CNNs for semantic segmentation, and show that reasonable performance can be achieved with significantly fewer parameters and less training data.
We introduce a new architecture based on the Atrous Convolution, which allows the network to utilize multi-scale information and adapt to the input image resolution.

Our experiments show that this approach is competitive with the state of the art on the Cityscapes and CamVid datasets, while reducing the number of parameters by 38% and training data by 51% compared to the current state-of-the-art.

Recent progress in GAN-based image translation models has enabled the translation of images from one domain to another, but these models produce translations that are not always semantically consistent.
To address this issue, we propose Sem-GAN, a novel GAN-based image translation model that combines an image translation GAN with a semantic consistency GAN.

The semantic consistency GAN ensures that the translated images are consistent with the semantic content of the source images, and is trained using a semantic loss function that measures the similarity between the translated image and a semantic representation of the source image.
The image translation GAN, on the other hand, is trained using a standard GAN loss function.

We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on a variety of image translation tasks, and show that our model produces translations that are more semantically consistent than state-of-the-art GAN-based image translation models.
Recent works have shown that fully convolutional networks (FCNs) trained for medical image synthesis tasks such as lesion segmentation can be utilized as effective data augmentation tools.
However, directly applying FCNs to anatomical regions-of-interest (RoIs) may result in significant structural alterations due to the lack of global anatomical context in the cropped regions.
In this paper, we present an approach to adapt FCNs for effective data augmentation without losing the overall structural integrity of the medical images.
Our key insight is that the network can be designed to learn and restore the underlying structural information of the medical images in a fully convolutional manner.
To this end, we propose a structure-preserving fully convolutional network (SynNet) architecture consisting of two modules: a structure-aware module and a synthesis module.
Given a lesion-mapped atlas, the structure-aware module precisely estimates the underlying anatomical structure in the RoI, while the synthesis module produces the final synthesized lesion map.
The proposed approach was evaluated on the 2017 ISLES challenge dataset for liver lesion segmentation.
Our method achieved the second highest augmentation accuracy and the second lowest anatomical distortion measured by the F1-score.
Deep learning has shown great success in medical image analysis but producing accurate predictions does not necessarily imply these models are interpretable or explainable.
Especially for clinical applications, it is important to understand why a model makes a certain prediction.
In this work, we focus on quantifying uncertainty in the predictions of deep learning models for medical image analysis.
We propose a novel method to compute prediction uncertainty for deep learning models using Bayesian inference.

We demonstrate the advantages of our approach compared to existing state-of-the-art methods on two public datasets, and show that our method is applicable to a variety of medical image analysis tasks.
We further illustrate the potential of our method by deploying it in a clinical environment.
CompNet is a neural network architecture for the automatic brain extraction from magnetic resonance images (MRI).
It combines a U-Net architecture with a attention module that highlights reliable regions to help the segmentation.

Our network learns complementary features by adding together the outputs of two streams: a convolutional stream that emphasizes low-level details, and a deformable convolutional stream that captures larger scale structures.
We introduce a new type of layer, the Reliability Map Layer, to provide reliable segmentation predictions in MRI extraction.
In this layer, each channel is a reliability map that highlights regions where the instance is present with a high response and vice versa.
This allows our model to put more emphasis on regions with difficult delineations, such as the corpus callosum and the dentate nucleus.

We show that our approach outperforms the state-of-the-art methods for brain extraction on the challenging 200-core MRBrainS13 dataset, and yields a promising result on the larger BraTS 2019 validation set.
Recent results in image editing with neural networks often rely on utilizing the pixel-level label of the foreground object for dense prediction tasks.
Such methods are not directly applicable to languages like English, where explicit pixel-level labels are rarely available.
We build an image editing system that operates purely in the language domain by leveraging a bilingual dictionary between natural language and pixel space.
Given a natural language instruction, our model repeatedly generates and refines a pixel-level edit sequence by conditioning on an image and the instruction in a recursive manner.
We introduce a novel recurrent attentive model that is both interpretable and capable of modeling complex edits with varying granularity.
Our model outperforms state-of-the-art image editing methods on both the COCO and PNG datasets while operating in the language domain.
Deep learning networks have achieved remarkable results in various image processing tasks.
The performance of deep learning networks for semantic segmentation of stereo-pair images is of great interest.
In this paper, we present a performance evaluation of deep learning networks for semantic segmentation of traffic stereo-pair images.
We propose a novel deep learning architecture that combines a convolutional neural network (CNN) and a recursive neural network (RNN).
The CNN is used for feature extraction, and the RNN is used for semantic segmentation.
We evaluate the performance of our proposed architecture on the CityScapes dataset and compare it with other state-of-the-art methods.
The experimental results show that our proposed architecture achieves the best performance in terms of accuracy and efficiency.
Moreover, the proposed architecture is able to generalize to unseen data and can handle large variations in the input data.
We propose a Recurrent Residual Convolutional Neural Network (R2U-Net) that leverages the strengths of both U-Net and RNNs for medical image segmentation.

R2U-Net is composed of recurrent layers and residual connections in the encoder-decoder structure to capture the temporal dependencies and improve the network's ability to learn from long-range information.
We adopt a bi-directional RNN within the U-Net framework to capture the complex and long-range dependencies in 4D medical images.
The recurrent layers enable the network to selectively incorporate relevant information from the past and future frames for accurate segmentation.
We evaluate the performance of our method on the challenging task of abdominal organ segmentation in abdominal CT volumes from the abdominal segmentation challenge 2016 (ASC16).
Our method achieves competitive results compared to state-of-the-art methods on the ASC16 dataset.
In this paper, we present a novel semi-supervised learning approach for medical image segmentation.
Our method utilizes a consensus model, which combines multiple experts to achieve improved segmentation performance.

The experts are trained using a semi-supervised learning scheme, where a small amount of labeled data is used to learn a mapping function that projects data points into a higher-dimensional feature space.
In this feature space, we apply a graph cuts algorithm to obtain the final segmentation.

We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on three different medical image segmentation tasks: lung segmentation from chest radiographs, abdominal organ segmentation from CT scans, and brain tumor segmentation from MRI.
In all cases, our method achieves state-of-the-art performance.

Introduction
Medical image segmentation is a fundamental problem in medical image analysis.
The goal of segmentation is to automatically identify and delineate anatomical structures in medical images.
This information can be used for diagnosis, treatment planning, and image-guided therapy.
Many different approaches have been proposed for medical image segmentation.
These methods can be broadly classified into two categories: supervised learning and unsupervised learning.
Supervised learning methods rely on labeled training data to learn a mapping function that projects data points into a higher-dimensional feature space.
The mapping function is then used to segment new images.
However, obtaining labeled training data for medical image segmentation can be challenging and time-consuming.
Unsupervised learning methods do not require labeled training data.
Instead, they rely on prior knowledge of the structures being segmented or on assumptions about the properties of the images.
These methods can be effective in some cases, but they may not perform well when the prior knowledge is incorrect or when the images do not satisfy the assumptions.
In this paper, we present a novel semi-supervised learning approach for medical image segmentation that combines the strengths of supervised and unsupervised learning.
Our method utilizes a consensus model, which combines multiple experts to achieve improved segmentation performance.
The experts are trained using a semi-supervised learning scheme, which overcomes the limitations of both supervised and unsupervised learning.

Many state-of-the-art approaches to facade segmentation rely on careful curation of training data, with thoroughly annotated images.
We argue that such approaches cannot scale to the variety and variability of real-world images, i.e., 'in the wild'.
In this work, we thus cast the problem of facade segmentation as a semantic segmentation problem in its raw form, where the only information provided is the class labels of buildings and facades.
To learn from this sparse information, we introduce a new architecture, Wild Facade Segmenter (WFS), that is composed of a backbone network and a transformer module.
The transformer module is designed to gather multi-level contextual information and global sentiment of the image for accurate segmentation.
We optimize the WFS to minimize the difference between the predicted and ground truth segmentation, as well as to maximize the localization accuracy of the predicted labels.

We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on the Cityscapes dataset as well as a new dataset we created from scratch, WildCity, which has no ground truth segmentation and very limited training data.
Our model outperforms the state-of-the-art on both datasets without using any annotated facade images for training.
Scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) is a powerful technique for observing nanoscale surfaces, but the segmentation of STM images into their constituent atoms and molecules remains a challenging task.
In this paper, we propose a new method for segmentation of STM images using variational methods and empirical wavelets.
Our approach combines the advantages of both variational and wavelet-based methods, and has the additional benefit of being able to handle highly irregular and noisy images commonly found in STM.

We compare our method to both variational and wavelet-based approaches on a variety of benchmark images, and show that it significantly outperforms the state-of-the-art in terms of both accuracy and efficiency.
Our method has potential applications in fields such as nanoscale imaging, material science, and computational biology.
Recent progress in 3D imaging technology has resulted in an abundance of 3D medical image data, presenting challenges for efficient and effective image analysis.
In this paper, we present an unsupervised learning framework for segmenting 3D medical images.
Our approach is based on clustering and deep representation learning.
We begin by extracting a deep representation of the input image using a pre-trained convolutional neural network (CNN).
The deep representation is then subjected to clustering, resulting in the segmentation of the image into distinct regions.
To evaluate the performance of our approach, we compared it to state-of-the-art supervised segmentation methods on two public 3D medical image datasets, and achieved competitive results.
Our framework is designed to be general and can be applied to various medical image analysis tasks.
We believe that our approach can serve as a powerful tool for unsupervised segmentation of 3D medical images.
We present an image segmentation algorithm that recursively partitions an image into foreground and background regions using a sparse subset selection approach.
Our algorithm is inspired by the observation that, in digital images, pixels belonging to different objects are usually not all connected.
Therefore, instead of relying on a dense labeling, we aim to find a sparse subset of pixels that can effectively partition the image into separate components.
To this end, we define a novel cost function that encourages spatial coherence within each segment, as well as distinguishes between foreground and background pixels.
We solve the resulting optimization problem using an efficient graph cuts algorithm, which iteratively selects a sparse subset of pixels to partition the image until convergence.
The proposed algorithm is fully automatic, parameter-free, and fast, making it suitable for many real-world applications.
We evaluate our method on a standard benchmark, and demonstrate that it compares favorably with other state-of-the-art image segmentation algorithms in terms of accuracy and efficiency.
We present a multi-layer approach to superpixel-based higher-order conditional random field (CRF) for semantic image segmentation.
In this approach, we first apply a simple yet effective superpixel segmentation method to extract a set of superpixels from the input image.

Then, we construct a higher-order CRF model based on the extracted superpixels, where each superpixel is treated as a variable node and the semantic labels of the superpixels are treated as the hidden variables.
The higher-order CRF model is learned in a supervised manner, where the semantic labels of the superpixels are predicted based on the appearance and the context information of the superpixels.
The proposed approach is evaluated on the semantic image segmentation benchmark datasets of PASCAL VOC 2012 and Cityscapes.
Experiment results show that the proposed approach achieves competitive performance compared to the state-of-the-art methods.
Recent advances in fully convolutional networks have enabled effective convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for medical image segmentation.
However, directly using these models on resource-limited devices, such as tablets or mobile phones, is still a challenge, due to their high computational complexity and large memory footprint.
In this paper, we present a cascaded 3D fully convolutional network (C3D-FCN) architecture, which significantly reduces the complexity of the network while preserving segmentation accuracy.

In our approach, a hierarchical pyramid of CNNs processes the input medical image in a coarse-to-fine fashion, where the coarser networks produce intermediate segmentations at lower resolutions, which are then used as initializations for subsequent finer networks.

In this way, our approach benefits from both bottom-up and top-down computational efficiencies, since the coarser networks effectively reduce the amount of parameters and computations in the finer networks.
We evaluate our approach on the challenging task of abdominal organ segmentation in abdominal CTs, and show that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance.

Our network has a complexity of only 1.25 MB (in terms of the number of parameters), which is 9.7 times less than that of the V-Net architecture (11.2 MB), and 22.4 times less than that of the FCN-8s architecture (28 MB).
In addition, our approach achieves a speedup of 1.5× (in terms of number of computations) compared to V-Net, and 4.4× compared to FCN-8s on a single NVIDIA Titan X GPU.
Brain image segmentation is an important topic in clinical imaging applications.
In this paper, we propose a new method for brain image segmentation based on the combination of Hidden Markov Random Field (HMRF) and conjugate gradient.
The HMRF model is used to capture the spatial dependencies and the conjugate gradient is used to optimize the segmentation results.
We compare our method with three state-of-the-art brain image segmentation methods.
The experimental results show that our method can produce more accurate and robust segmentation results.
In this paper, we present a novel method for left ventricle segmentation in cardiac MR images using a fully convolutional network.
Our network is designed to take advantage of the hierarchical structure of the cardiac MR images, and it is composed of multiple stages of convolutional layers.
We utilize a combination of atrous and regular convolutions to capture both local and global features in the images.
Furthermore, we introduce a new loss function that combines the Dice loss and the cross-entropy loss to optimize the network for accurate segmentation.
Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on the MICCAI 2012 cardiac segmentation challenge dataset, and it is able to segment the left ventricle with an accuracy of 97.6%.
Our network architecture consists of multiple stages of convolutional layers, with each stage followed by a max-pooling layer.
The first stage utilizes atrous convolutions to capture low-level features in the images, while the following stages use regular convolutions to capture mid-level and high-level features.
In order to optimize the network for accurate segmentation, we introduce a new loss function that combines the Dice loss and the cross-entropy loss.
The Dice loss measures the similarity between the predicted segmentation and the ground truth segmentation, while the cross-entropy loss measures the quality of the predicted segmentation.
By combining these two losses, we are able to optimize the network for both accuracy and quality.
Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on the MICCAI 2012 cardiac segmentation challenge dataset, which is a standard benchmark for cardiac segmentation.
Our network is able to segment the left ventricle with an accuracy of 97.6%, which is a significant improvement over the previous state-of-the-art.
In addition, our method is able to segment the left ventricle with high consistency, as measured by the coefficient of variation.
Our results show that our method is effective and reliable for left ventricle segmentation in cardiac MR images.
Improved image segmentation can be achieved by minimizing the cost of the hypothesized regions.

We propose a method for producing multiple hypotheses for image segmentation, where each hypothesis is composed of a number of regions that provide a measure of how well the hypothesis fits the image.
The cost of each region is the difference between the pixel intensity of the hypothesis and the pixel intensity of the image beneath the region.
The cost of a hypothesis is then the sum of the costs of its regions.
We propose an algorithm for minimizing the cost of a hypothesis by moving its regions.
In this way, we can improve the fit of a hypothesis to the image and obtain better image segmentation.
We present a novel approach for training a cyst detection and segmentation model using only weak, self-supervised, and automatic annotations.
Our method is based on a fully-convolutional neural network that performs detection and segmentation in a single forward pass.
We introduce a novel atrous spatial pyramid pooling (ASPP) module that performs multi-scale sampling and pooling to improve accuracy.
Our method is trained using a self-supervised annotation strategy that uses only the image itself as annotation.
We perform a grid search to optimize the hyperparameters for our method based on F1-score.
Our method achieves 95.80% sensitivity, 96.37% specificity, and 96.09% F1-score on a test set of 71 CT scans, outperforming the baseline approach by 11.40%, 6.73%, and 12.43% respectively.
Abstract - Lung cancer is the most common cancer worldwide, and computerized tomography (CT) is increasingly used for lung cancer screening.
However, the current practice of manual analysis of CT images is tedious, time-consuming, and subjective.
In this paper, we present a fully automated framework for lung tumour detection, segmentation and analysis, which is designed to assist radiologists in clinical practice.

Our framework comprises a tumour detection module based on a deep learning architecture, a segmentation module based on a multi-atlas label fusion strategy, and an analysis module that evaluates the tumour volume, mean tumour diameter and tumour-free lung volume.

To evaluate the performance of our framework, we conducted a retrospective study on 252 CT scans from 222 patients, and the results show that our framework can achieve an accuracy of 92.3%, a sensitivity of 91.5% and a specificity of 93.2% for lung tumour detection, and an accuracy of 91.5% for lung tumour segmentation.

Furthermore, our framework can assist in clinical decision making, as it achieves an accuracy of 89.5% for tumour volume measurement, 86.9% for mean tumour diameter measurement, and 91.5% for tumour-free lung volume estimation.
We believe that our framework has the potential to facilitate radiologists in lung cancer screening and clinical decision making.
We present a conditional random field (CRF) model and a deep learning-based feature learning approach for hyperspectral image (HSI) segmentation.

The CRF model is a traditional statistical model used for image segmentation tasks, where pixel-level labels are predicted based on the features of the pixels and the spatial dependencies between the pixels.
The deep learning-based feature learning approach is used to learn a low-dimensional feature representation of the hyperspectral data, which is then used as input to the CRF model.
The proposed approach was evaluated on the Indian Pines hyperspectral dataset, and achieved a segmentation accuracy of 94.4%.
The CRF model uses a probabilistic approach to capture the spatial dependencies between pixels, and is trained using a maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) approach.
The deep learning-based feature learning approach is based on a convolutional neural network (CNN), which is trained using a supervised learning approach.
The CNN is used to learn a low-dimensional feature representation of the hyperspectral data, which is then used as input to the CRF model.
The proposed approach was evaluated on the Indian Pines hyperspectral dataset, which consists of 224 spectral bands and a pixel-level labeled dataset.

The segmentation accuracy of the proposed approach was compared to the segmentation accuracy of a traditional CRF model, and a deep learning-based feature learning approach that uses a pre-trained CNN model.
The results show that the proposed approach achieved a segmentation accuracy of 94.4%, compared to 91.1% for the traditional CRF model, and 92.6% for the pre-trained CNN model.

Deep learning algorithms have demonstrated promising performance for infant brain MRI segmentation, however, there is currently no state-of-the-art method that is both fast and achieves better segmentation performance than a human rater.
We propose to address both speed and segmentation performance by combining deep neural network architecture exploration, suggestive annotation, and ensemble learning.
We find that deep encoders (shallower models with higher dimensional inputs) improve segmentation performance in all areas of the brain when compared to pure three-dimensional networks.
We propose a new suggestive annotation strategy that uses anatomical knowledge to guide the training process, and develops a strong ensemble model from a set of weak models.
This ensemble model is 1600 times faster than a human rater, while also outperforming a human rater in all regions of the brain by 2.2 percentage points.
We revisit graph construction for image segmentation.
Unlike most previous works that construct graphs based on fixed shapes or heuristics, we formulate the graph construction as a learning problem.
Given an image, we learn a graph on which the pixels are linked in a way that optimizes a cost function reflecting the similarity between pixels.
In particular, we define a new cost function that leverages the power of an external deep neural network (DNN) model for pixel similarity.
We show that our approach, which we term Dense Graph, achieves state-of-the-art performance in image segmentation.
To the best of our knowledge, our work is the first to learn a graph structure for image segmentation.
Large-scale adaptation has recently become an active area of vision research.
As more and more datasets are collected and used for training, the need for models that can adapt to new domains is increasingly important.
However, developing effective adaptation algorithms is challenging.
To advance the state of the art, we propose the Visual Domain Adaptation (VisDA) challenge.

VisDA is a new benchmark that aims to drive the research progress on visual domain adaptation by providing a collection of domains with ground-truth labels, a standardized evaluation protocol, and a common dataset interface.
We introduce the VisDA challenge track at CVPR 2020 and report the results of the first edition.
We introduce a novel approach for curve-structure segmentation of objects from depth maps.
Our method is based on a convolutional neural network (CNN) that has been specifically designed for this task.
We propose a new network architecture, namely the Curve-CNN, which is able to effectively capture curve structures in the input depth maps and generate segmentations as output.
The network is composed of several convolutional layers, followed by a concatenation layer that combines the features from different channels.
We optimize our network using a novel loss function that encourages spatial coherence and smooth curves in the output.
Our approach is evaluated on two public datasets, where we achieve state-of-the-art performance.
We also demonstrate the applicability of our method in a cultural heritage scenario, where we extract curve structures from depth maps of medieval coins.
Our method can assist in the study and understanding of such objects, by providing meaningful curve representations that highlight their cultural significance.
Random walker is commonly used for image segmentation, but its performance heavily depends on the initial label.
In this paper, we propose a feature sensitive label fusion (FSLF) method with random walker for atlas-based image segmentation.
Different from the conventional random walker, the proposed method fuses the labels of the atlas image and the initial label of the current image, and then performs random walker on the fused label.
By properly designing the fusion strategy, the proposed method can make full use of the anatomical knowledge provided by the atlas image and the local information provided by the initial label.
The proposed method is evaluated on the BRATS and Hippocampus datasets, and the results show that our method outperforms the state-of-the-art methods.
We present an improved workflow for unsupervised multiphase image segmentation based on a sparse-coding framework.
Our approach incorporates a robust initialization scheme based on an over-complete kernel dictionary learned from a significant number of manually labeled image patches.
We employ a greedy algorithm that utilizes the learned dictionary to obtain an initial segmentation result.
An iterative refinement process is then applied to the initial segmentation to optimize the representation of the image segments with respect to the learned dictionary.

The proposed approach is evaluated on the 2004 INRIA multiclass segmentation challenge database, where our method achieves state-of-the-art performance in terms of both quantitative measures and visual quality.
We also demonstrate the robustness of our approach on a difficult dataset of real clinical images.
An adaptive fuzzy segmentation approach is proposed in this article to segment texture images.
The approach is based on skew divergence (SD) adaptive affinity functions (AAFs) capable of capturing the textural information in the image to be segmented.
The AAFs are generated using SD, which is a measure of the difference between two probability distributions, and is particularly useful in handling nonlinear transformations.

The proposed method was evaluated using four well-known texture databases, and the results show that the proposed method is effective in segmenting texture images and outperforms the conventional methods in terms of segmentation quality.
Recent works have shown that training an artificial intelligence (AI) model to learn about the world from real-world data can be challenging.
In contrast, training such a model using simulated data can be easier since the simulations provide labels for every image.
We find that training an AI model using a mix of simulated and real-world data yields the best results.
When the model is trained on simulated and real images, the model performs better on real-world images than when trained on real-world images alone.
We present a new dataset, coined Real-World Affordances, containing 1.56 million images of objects in cluttered real-world scenes with affordance labels and object bounding boxes.
This new dataset, along with previous datasets, enables training and evaluating models that reason about real-world affordances.

We discover that a model pre-trained on our new dataset still performs well when tested on previous datasets, suggesting that the dataset is beneficial for training models that reason about real-world affordances.
In this paper, we propose a dynamic multiscale tree learning scheme using ensemble strong classifiers for multi-label segmentation of medical images with lesions.

In the proposed method, the tree structure is learned dynamically according to the characteristics of the input medical images, and an ensemble of strong classifiers is constructed from the learned tree structure for multi-label segmentation.
The proposed method integrates the advantages of both dynamic programming and ensemble learning.
Experimental results on real clinical data show the effectiveness of the proposed method.
Thresholding is a fundamental step in image processing, but classical methods are sensitive to noise.
In this paper, we propose a type II fuzzy entropy-based multi-level thresholding algorithm using an adaptive plant propagation (PPP) algorithm
that is applied to noise-sensitive regions.
The proposed method captures the vagueness and uncertainty of pixel intensity values in noisy images.
It improves the robustness of thresholding methods to noise and maintains the advantages of multi-level thresholding, such as good compression performance and grayscale reproduction.
The experimental results show that the proposed method outperforms the classical approaches in terms of objective metrics and visual quality.
Color image segmentation is the process of partitioning an image into multiple segments, each of which corresponds to a set of pixels sharing a common property.
It has numerous applications in various fields of science and engineering including image processing, computer vision, and pattern recognition.
Image enhancement, on the other hand, refers to the process of improving the quality of an image by increasing its contrast, brightness, or other visual properties.
In this paper, we provide a comprehensive study on the importance of image enhancement techniques in color image segmentation.

We compare the performance of various image enhancement techniques, including histogram equalization, contrast stretching, and adaptive filtering, on a set of color images and evaluate their impact on the subsequent color image segmentation process.

Our results show that image enhancement techniques have a significant impact on the accuracy and efficiency of color image segmentation and can greatly improve the overall performance of the segmentation process.
Semantic image segmentation is essential for automated image understanding.
Although recent advances in deep learning have achieved remarkable performance, these models are known to be vulnerable to adversarial attacks.

In this paper, we aim to defend deep segmentation models against universal adversarial perturbations (UAPs), which are robust against defenses and perturb the input image transgressively such that the model produces incorrect predictions onto multiple objects.
To achieve this, we propose a new UAP generation strategy that is dedicated to image segmentation, named segmentation-aware universal adversarial generation (SAUAG).

Given a reference image and its ground truth segmentation, SAUAG can generate UAPs specific to any target segmentation model such that the model misclassifies the objects in the reference image, regardless of the input image.

We perform an extensive evaluation of our method on three widely-used segmentation benchmarks (PASCAL VOC 2012, Cityscapes, and ACDC), and demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach against various state-of-the-art segmentation models as well as existing UAP defenses.
We present a general framework for doing lifted MAP inference in deterministic computer vision models, learning the weights of the model parameters from labeled training data.
Our framework is applicable to vision models with arbitrary non-linear structure, and can handle both discrete (e.g. decision trees) and continuous (e.g. neural networks) model representations.

We devise an algorithm for doing coarse-to-fine MAP inference in such models, with a logarithmic number of iterations, and experimental evidence shows that our algorithm converges to the optimal MAP assignment.
Finally, we apply our framework to the problem of recognizing rigid objects, where we learn a tree of 3D pose hypotheses, and show that our approach is able to recover the ground truth pose.
