Abstract: We consider the setting of subspace learning where the data matrix has a sparse latent rank-one structure in an unknown subspace, which is contaminated by a small fraction of outliers and noise.
This setting is motivated by applications such as text classification, where instances are often sparse in feature space and prone to labeling errors.
In such situations, we show that spectral regulars for subspace learning, such as the nuclear norm heuristic (NNH) and its variants, are locally robust in the presence of outliers.

Specifically, we establish that when the data matrix has a sparse latent rank-one matrix in an unknown subspace, with outliers and noise lying in a union of subspaces, the NNH is robustly convex, i.e., its local optimizer is asymptotically rank-one, as the number of outliers and noise goes to zero.

We further show that our result can be attained by a simple reweighting scheme, where the data matrix is reweighted by the square root of its nuclear norm, and present an algorithm to approximate the reweighted matrix.
Finally, we present experimental results on both synthetic data and text data to demonstrate the efficacy of our approach.
Abstract: Traditional approaches to eye tracking typically rely on either expensive hardware setups or carefully-curated datasets.

In this paper, we present a general, model-based approach to eye tracking that is capable of operating on a wide variety of video sequences, with a particular focus on head-mounted eye tracking setups.

Our approach is based on recursively estimating a set of pupil characteristics that can be used for eye tracking, and we propose a robust, linear programming-based approach to recursively estimating these characteristics in a way that is robust to noise and missing data.
Our approach is evaluated on both synthetic and real-world datasets, and we show that it is capable of accurately tracking eyes even in challenging, noisy conditions.
Deep brain stimulation (DBS) is a therapeutic procedure that involves the placement of electrodes within the substructures of the brain.
In this work, we present an automated method for localizing the DBS electrodes within the brain.
Our approach is based on the segmentation of the electrode trajectories from MR images.
The segmentation process is formulated as a binary labeling problem in which each voxel in the MR image is labeled as inside or outside the electrode trajectory.
A set of features is extracted from the MR images to describe the local appearance of the voxels surrounding the electrode trajectory.
These features are then fed into a support vector machine (SVM) classifier to perform the segmentation.
The proposed method was evaluated on a dataset of 25 subjects with a total of 125 channels using leave-one-out cross-validation.
The results show that our approach is able to accurately localize the electrode trajectories with an average distance of 6.91 mm from the ground truth.
In this paper, we present CardiacNET, a deep learning framework for the segmentation of the left atrium and proximal pulmonary veins in MRI.
Our approach employs a multi-view convolutional neural network (CNN) that utilizes the multiple contrasts and views available in MRI scans for the segmentation task.
The multi-view CNN takes advantage of the rich information embedded in the different views and contrasts to improve the segmentation performance.
We evaluated our approach on 100 MRI scans and compared it to manual segmentation performed by experts, as well as other state-of-the-art methods.
Our results show that CardiacNET achieves an accuracy of 92.3% on the segmentation of the left atrium and 96.2% on the segmentation of the pulmonary veins.
When compared to manual segmentation, our approach reduces the error rate by 57.7% for the left atrium and 50.6% for the pulmonary veins.
Our code and dataset are available at:

https://github.com/Cardiac-NET/Cardiac-NET.

Keywords: cardiac MRI, deep learning, convolutional neural network, multi-view learning, segmentation.
Convolutional Oriented Boundaries (COBs) are a generic and powerful representation for both image segmentation and high-level image understanding tasks.
Given an input image, we first estimate a set of continuous orientation maps, then use a modified Chan-Vese energy to segment the image into superpixels assigned to each orientation.
These superpixels form a hierarchical representation, with COBs as the atomic units.

This representation is inherently oriented, making it suitable for describing object boundaries, and is effectively learned from image data, forming a powerful basis for a variety of high-level tasks.

We explore this representation for four such tasks: 1) a semantic segmentation, where COBs are used to improve the state-of-the-art; 2) a perception-based navigation system, where COBs help a robot to understand the scene structure and plan a path; 3) a natural language description system, where COBs are used to select the most relevant regions to include in the description; and 4) a visual question answering system, where COBs are used to focus the attention of the model on the most relevant parts of the image.
We introduce a novel weakly-supervised approach for learning semantic segmentation models.
Our method leverages motion cues present in video sequences to weakly supervise the segmentation of static images in a frame.

We formulate the problem as a temporal-shift invariant segmentation (TSIS) objective by minimizing the pixel-wise discrepancy between the predicted segmentation mask of the current frame and the ground truth segmentation mask of the next frame in the sequence.

We demonstrate that our approach is able to discover robust object-level representations and effectively propagate them across frames, leading to significant performance gains over strong baseline models on the Cityscapes dataset.
Furthermore, we show via an ablative study that our method improves performance by effectively leveraging the temporal coherence present in video data to refine the segmentation predictions.
Code is available at https://github.com/avinashnew/motion-segmentation.
Wavelength-dependent features are critical for accurate segmentation of eucalypt leaf images to support forest inventory.
In this study, 21 features (nine color, six texture, and six wavelength-dependent) were extracted from images of eucalyptus leaves to train segmentation classifiers.
A wide range of classifiers was evaluated to determine the effectiveness of each combination of features for segmentation.
The best overall performance was obtained using a combination of just two features, variance and hybrid color.
With just these two features, accuracy was over 97% for all classifiers tested.
The decision tree classifier performed best overall when using all features.
The random forest classifier performed second best with an accuracy of 99.1%.
The support vector machine classifier performed third best with an accuracy of 97.4%.
We introduce a simple method for producing valid segmentations of objects given a model and an image, and provide an uncertainty measure for the resulting segmentation.
Our method combines ideas from two previous methods: perturb-and-max and MPM.
We observe that the MPM method can produce invalid segmentations, and we propose a simple modification that ensures validity.

We perform an in-depth experimental evaluation of our method on the 2013 and 2014 PASCAL VOC segmentation challenge datasets, and show that our method substantially improves over the MPM method, with very little computational overhead.
Semantic image segmentation, which aims to assign semantic labels to every pixel in an image, is a fundamental problem in computer vision.
Recent progresses in this field are mainly driven by deep learning models, especially convolutional neural networks (CNNs).
However, directly applying CNNs on the pixel level prediction is computationally expensive, and the network architecture is difficult to extend to segment complex scenes.
In this paper, we present a progressively diffused network (PDNet) for semantic image segmentation.
PDNet employs a regional feature aggregation scheme to hierarchically refine the segmentation results and effectively capture long-range dependencies in an image.
A diffused structure is introduced to model the spatial variations of the image, which enables the network to focus on difficult regions and avoid unnecessary computations on easy regions.

Furthermore, the proposed method can be naturally extended to segment 3D scenes, where the hierarchical feature aggregation and diffused structure are applied to different levels of the scene structure.

The extensive experimental results on semantic segmentation benchmarks, including Pascal VOC 2012 and Cityscapes, demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method compared to the state-of-the-art approaches.
Recent developments in neural network architecture have boosted the performance of image segmentation.
In this paper, we propose FusionNet, a deep fully residual convolutional neural network for image segmentation in connectomics.
FusionNet incorporates several techniques that have been shown to be effective in image segmentation, including an atrous convolutional layer, a residual block, and a dense connection pattern.
We evaluate FusionNet on the task of segmentation of neuronal structures in connectomic images, and show that it outperforms existing state-of-the-art models.

In particular, when applied to segmenting neurons in mouse cortical tissue, FusionNet achieves a precision of 94.3% and recall of 92.6% on cell bodies, and 85.5% precision and 88.4% recall on axon initial segments.
Code is available at https://github.com/andy-connectome/FusionNet.
We present an approach for semantic segmentation of street scenes that leverages a fully convolutional neural network architecture trained end-to-end.
Our network is based on the ResNet architecture equipped with a novel adaptive convolutional kernel size that significantly improves performance.
We introduce a multi-scale testing scheme and an effective upsampling module that incorporates global contextual information into the segmentation process.
Our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on the Cityscapes dataset with a trained network that operates in a single forward pass at test time.
In addition, we introduce a new dataset, called SceneParse150, which is a large-scale dataset for semantic segmentation comprising 150 classes.
SceneParse150 is made available to the research community to facilitate future progress on semantic segmentation.
We present a novel architecture for video segmentation that combines convolutional neural networks (CNNs) with gated recurrent units (GRUs).
Our approach, called ConvGRU, leverages the strengths of both CNNs and GRUs to model the temporal dependencies in videos effectively.
The CNN component captures local spatial patterns, while the GRU component captures long-range temporal dependencies.

We introduce a gated convolutional layer that enables the GRU to operate on feature maps, this layer allows us to utilize the powerful learning capability of CNNs and provides the GRU with better contextual information.
To validate our approach, we conducted extensive experiments on the popular Cityscapes and CamVid datasets, and compared our method to other state-of-the-art video segmentation methods.
Our results show that our approach achieves competitive performance while being efficient in terms of runtime.
Deep neural networks provide promising initial segmentations but require substantial expert corrections for producing accurate segmentations of neuronal structures.
We present a novel interactive approach for training deep neural networks for segmentation of neuronal structures.
In our approach, a user corrects errors made by the deep neural network in an efficient and integrated fashion.

We employ a multi-scale deep learning architecture that explicitly models label relationships at multiple scales, and we optimize the network using a novel loss function that guides the network to produce segmentations similar to expert corrections.

We demonstrate via a user study with three expert neuroanatomists that our approach reduces the amount of correction effort by a factor of two compared to the state of the art while producing similar performance.
We show that our approach produces segmentations that are more accurate than state-of-the-art methods and is preferred by users in a head-to-head comparison.
Arrival time prediction of vehicles in traffic is an active research area, and several approaches have been suggested in the literature.
In this paper, we focus on the prediction of stop times of vehicles in traffic, which is a major component of the total travel time.
We suggest a novel hybrid method that integrates deep neural networks (DNNs) and random forests (RFs) to predict stop times.
DNNs can capture complex spatial-temporal relationships, but they are computationally expensive, whereas RFs are efficient, but they cannot capture complex relationships.
Our method first uses DNNs to extract spatial-temporal features from the traffic data, and then uses RFs to make predictions based on these features.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method through extensive experiments on a real-world traffic dataset.
Our results show that our method achieves better prediction accuracy compared to other state-of-the-art methods while maintaining high efficiency.
Driver distraction is a major contributor to traffic accidents.
In this paper, we present a non-intrusive approach for detecting driver distraction in a vehicle.
Our approach is based on image segmentation using the histogram of depth.
We use a convolutional neural network (CNN) to extract the depth map from a single monocular image.
The depth map is then histogrammed to obtain a histogram of depth.
We propose a new segmentation method called thresholding on histogram of depth (THD) for partitioning the histogram into two regions corresponding to the foreground and the background.
The foreground region, which corresponds to the region near the camera, i.e., the driver, is further analyzed to detect driver distraction.
We implement three different approaches for distraction detection, namely, frame difference, eye blink, and head movement, to show the efficacy of our proposed approach.
The experimental results show that our proposed approach achieves an accuracy of 98.86% and a time efficiency of 25.5 fps on a regular laptop.
Recent works have shown that training computer vision models with self-supervised learning can achieve excellent performance on image recognition tasks.
These methods train on large datasets of images, without using any labeled data, by learning to predict the missing or distorted parts of images.
However, obtaining a large and diverse set of unlabeled images for training is a major challenge.
In this paper, we propose a new approach to training computer vision models using video games.
We show that by playing a variety of video games, a model can learn to predict the next video frame, and use this ability to learn a robust representation of images.

Our approach has several advantages: video games provide a large and diverse set of training data, the models can be trained in a self-supervised manner, and the training process can be repeated indefinitely, improving the model's performance over time.
We present an implementation of our approach using the Unity game engine and demonstrate its effectiveness on the ImageNet dataset.
Introduction:
Training deep learning models often requires large amounts of labeled data, which can be difficult and expensive to obtain.
In recent years, self-supervised learning has emerged as an alternative to labeled data, allowing models to learn from large sets of unlabeled data.
While self-supervised learning has been applied to computer vision problems, these methods still require large amounts of image data.
This data can be difficult to obtain in domains with limited imaging capabilities or where labeling images is expensive.

Our Approach: 
In this work, we propose an alternative way of generating training data for computer vision models using video games.
We show that by training a model to predict the next video frame in a sequence of frames, the model can learn a robust representation of images.
Because the model is trained on a set of images that are naturally related to each other, it can learn to generalize well to new images.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on the ImageNet dataset, and show that our model outperforms existing self-supervised learning models in terms of image recognition performance.

Results: 
Our results show that playing video games can be an effective way to train computer vision models, and that our model outperforms existing self-supervised learning models in terms of image recognition performance.
We believe that this approach can be used to train computer vision models in a variety of domains, and that it has several advantages over existing self-supervised learning methods.

Conclusion: 
To summarize, in this paper we present an approach to training computer vision models using video games.

Gaze-based interaction is an intuitive and efficient human-computer interaction technique.
In this paper, we explore the possibility of utilizing eye-tracking technology in medical image segmentation, a typical interactive task.
We propose a pilot study called Gaze2Segment, which aims to integrate eye-tracking technology into interactive medical image segmentation software.
We describe the implementation details of Gaze2Segment and present the results of a preliminary user study to evaluate its performance.
Image segmentation is a classical problem in image processing, with many applications in areas such as medical imaging, remote sensing, and robotics.
In this paper, we present a new image segmentation algorithm based on a hierarchical merge tree.
Our algorithm is motivated by the observation that images often contain regions of similar color or texture, and these regions can be merged together to form larger regions.
By iteratively merging the smallest regions together, we can eventually obtain a single region that encompasses the entire image.
Our algorithm is efficient, and can segment images quickly and accurately.
We evaluate our algorithm on a variety of images, and compare its performance to other image segmentation algorithms.
Our results show that our algorithm is competitive with the state-of-the-art in terms of both speed and accuracy.
We present a method for the segmentation of screen content images, based on the sparse representation of image pixels using a dictionary learned from a training set of images.
Our method is specifically designed to handle screen content, which is characterized by a small number of bright, saturated colors, against a dark, unstructured background.

We train a dictionary using a set of images from the Screen Content Textures (SCT) dataset, which we augment with a large number of artificially generated textures, to provide a more complete representation of possible screen content images.

We use a robust regression technique to produce a segmentation map from a linear combination of atoms in the dictionary, with a regularization parameter determined by a novel iterative thresholding algorithm.
Our method provides state-of-the-art performance on the SCT dataset, and is fast enough for real-time implementation.
We present a semantic image segmentation method that combines deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and fully connected conditional random fields (CRFs).

We train the CNN to take a label probability input and produce an image feature output, and then combine these features with spatial kernel predictions in a CRF, trained to maximize the likelihood of the CNN output features given the CNN label predictions and a set of label priors.
This modular framework allows the use of complex CNN architectures like VGG16, and retains the benefits of the CRF framework like the use of label priors and iterative optimization.
We present extensive experimental results on the MIT-CBCL and PASCAL VOC 2012 segmentation datasets, and show that our method outperforms the state-of-the-art in both datasets.
Recent progress in semantic image segmentation has largely been driven by convolutional neural networks (CNNs) that operate directly on image pixels.
Despite their success, these models inherently ignore the intrinsic nature of the real world i.e., its physicality, which demands that objects are not independent of each other and the scene.

In this paper, we study the problem of scale-aware semantic segmentation, where the goal is to predict scene-level object categories and their locations in an image while taking into account the scales or sizes of the objects w.r.t.
the scene.
In other words, our focus is to understand how objects of different scales interact with each other in the scene and to segment them appropriately.
To this end, we propose a simple yet effective approach that combines a scale-aware convolutional neural network (SACNN) with a conditional random field (CRF) model.
The SACNN is designed to encode appearance as well as scale information in a image, and the CRF model is used to exploit the spatial consistency of objects.
Our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on the public NYUv2 dataset, where scale-awareness is inherently built into the ground truth.
Arithmetic operations are generally performed assuming that the operands are represented using the same base representation.

In many applications, however, the operands may be represented using different bases, and thus it is necessary to perform conversions, which are inherently expensive since they require a large number of elementary arithmetic operations.
Recently, several authors have proposed techniques for performing arithmetic operations directly on operands represented using different bases, allowing one to avoid expensive conversions.
These techniques rely on the existence of useful super-regions, i.e., regions in the integer space that admit a piecewise-constant approximation of a given function.
In this paper we present a general and formal framework for constructing super-regions of arbitrary precision using a hierarchical approach.
The precision is controlled by the depth of the hierarchy, which can be increased whenever additional accuracy is required.
We show that our framework is sound, and we present an algorithm for constructing the hierarchy of super-regions.
We implement our construction algorithm and evaluate its performance experimentally.

We consider binary quadratic optimization problems with linear matrix inequality (LMI) constraints, namely, given an integer variable x, find x that minimizes:

x^T Q x + c^T x

subject to LMI constraints of the following form:

E x I + L x >= 0

where E is a matrix with 0/1 entries, I is the identity matrix, and L is a matrix with real-valued entries.
Such problems arise in various applications, including the optimization of quadratic Boolean networks and the recently introduced quadratic container loading problem.
We present an algorithm for solving these problems using semidefinite programming (SDP) relaxation.
Our algorithm is based on the observation that the quadratic term in the objective function can be rewritten as a sum of squares, which can then be handled by SDP.

We present a theoretical analysis of the algorithm and show that it is able to solve problems with up to 10^6 variables and 10^9 constraints to proven optimality, and we present results on solving several large-scale instances from literature.
We show that conditional random fields (CRFs), despite being widely used for structured prediction, can be viewed as a special case of recurrent neural networks (RNNs) with linear recurrence weights.
This leads to an algorithm for training CRFs using the back-propagation through time algorithm, with an efficient memory representation based on packed data structures.

Our implementation, which extends the existing TensorFlow Fold implementation of the CRF layer, achieves a speedup of more than an order of magnitude over the existing TensorFlow CRF implementation on a standard sentiment analysis task, while maintaining the same accuracy.
We present a method for the solution of variational reaction-diffusion systems, which combines the advantages of recent diffusion models with the simplicity of reaction-diffusion systems.
Our method is applied to the problem of semantic segmentation, where the goal is to assign a semantic label to each pixel in an input image.
We introduce a new class of energy functions that can be optimized by the solution of a corresponding reaction-diffusion system.
The energy function is based on a multilayer perception architecture, where each layer is a variational approximation of the non-local Laplacian of a Gaussian diffusion process.

This allows us to combine the benefits of recent diffusion models, such as the ability to learn disentangled representations and the use of an adversarial loss, with the simplicity of reaction-diffusion systems, which can be efficiently solved by a fixed point iteration algorithm.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on the Cityscapes and CamVid datasets, where we achieve state-of-the-art performance.
A hybrid approach based segmentation technique in MRI images of brain tumor is proposed in this paper.
The proposed method shows that the combination of an anatomical and a probabilistic approach can produce accurate and reliable segmentations of brain tumor MRI images.
In our method, the MRI image is first preprocessed then, it is segmented by using the Anatomical network and finally, the probabilistic approach is used to obtain the final segmentation.
The proposed method is evaluated using MRI images of brain tumors and the results are compared with manual segmentation done by the experts.
The performance of the proposed method is evaluated in terms of the Dice similarity coefficient (DSC), sensitivity, specificity, and accuracy.
The proposed method achieves an average DSC of 0.91, sensitivity of 0.92, specificity of 0.87 and accuracy of 0.91.
Image super-resolution (SR) reconstructs a high-resolution (HR) image from a single low-resolution (LR) image, but has no direct application to other vision tasks.
We show that the internal representation learned by an image SR model is useful for other computer vision tasks.
We propose a method to extract the internal representation of face images from a state-of-the-art SR model, and use it for face verification.
We solve the lack of training data for the face verification task by using internal representations of faces from a database of HR face images, and show our method is effective.
The internal representation of faces extracted from our SR model, when fused with features from a convolutional neural network, improves the face verification performance.
We also apply our method to other tasks: object recognition, object detection, and scene recognition, and show positive results.
Our results suggest that image SR models learn a generalized image representation, and that the internal representation of SR models can be used to improve the performance of other vision tasks.
We present LooseCut, a novel interactive segmentation method that leverages loosely bounded boxes for initializing and refining segmentation results.
Our method improves upon the state-of-the-art in two ways.
First, we propose a new relaxed bounding box formulation, which affords a larger margin for error in the initial bounding box placement while preserving the ability to capture the object of interest.
Second, we propose an iterative refinement process that utilizes geometric constraints to reduce the prediction error, allowing for improved segmentation results.
Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on the VOC 2012 segmentation benchmark while being faster than all other interactive methods.
In addition, through an user study, we show that our method is preferred by users compared to the baseline and other interactive methods in terms of speed and usability.

We present a method for probabilistic image segmentation based on a tree-cut algorithm.
Our approach combines the benefits of segmentation by cutting trees with a probabilistic interpretation.
This allows us to produce a fully probabilistic segmentation, in which each pixel is associated with a probability distribution over labels.
Our method is efficient, allowing for interactive frame rates, and naturally handles large datasets by streaming the data.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on a variety of challenging images, and compare to state-of-the-art segmentation methods.

Appearance contrast is a popular bottom-up cue used by visual attention models to simulate salient object segmentation, but it tends to produce fragmented saliency maps lacking global coherence, resulting in incorrect object identification.

In this paper, we propose PISA, a method that improves the coherence of appearance-based saliency maps by taking advantage of two types of complementary contrast information: pixel-level and edge-level.
PISA flexibly integrates different appearance contrast measures—such as intensity, color, and texture—with edge-preserving coherence modeling.

We introduce a pixel-level contrast aggregation module that computes saliency from pixel-level contrasts, and an edge-level contrast aggregation module that computes saliency from edge-level contrasts.
These two modules are subsequently combined to produce the final saliency map.

We demonstrate via extensive experiments on common benchmarks that PISA consistently improves performance of saliency detection over strong baselines in terms of both accuracy and coherence, without any parameter tuning.
Recent progress in semantic segmentation largely relies on large-scale training data with ground truth segmentations.
Creating pixel-level annotations for a large number of images is expensive and requires expert knowledge.
As a consequence, only a limited number of images is annotated, leading to an imbalance in training data: most images have no direct pixel-level annotations.
In this paper, we study the problem of identifying reliable segmentations from a large number of noisy and incomplete annotators.
We present a new method to identify the most reliable annotators for a given image and use their annotations to improve the performance of a segmentation model.
We propose a new differentiable scoring function that is optimized end-to-end with a segmentation model.
This allows us to train the segmentation model with only a small fraction of reliable annotations, while still benefiting from a large number of noisy annotations.

Our approach is evaluated on the Cityscapes and Mapillary Vistas datasets, where we show that our method is able to identify reliable annotators and significantly improves the performance of a segmentation model.
In this paper, we provide an overview of the most commonly used cardiac MR image segmentation techniques.
We discuss the advantages and disadvantages of each technique and provide examples of their applications in clinical and research settings.
We also discuss the future direction of cardiac MR image segmentation and potential applications in the clinic.

The goal of this paper is to provide a comprehensive understanding of the current state of the art in cardiac MR image segmentation and to highlight its potential for improving the diagnosis and treatment of cardiovascular disease.
We conclude that manual segmentation techniques have the advantage of producing high-quality segmentations but are highly time-consuming and require expertise.
Automated techniques are a promising alternative with the advantage of being much faster and less expensive but suffer from the disadvantage of being less accurate.
In the future, it is hoped that these techniques can be combined in a semi-automated approach to obtain the benefits of both while minimizing the disadvantages.
Humans have a wide variety of shapes and appearances.
Appearance models based on convolutional neural networks have shown promise in human segmentation, but they tend to fail on instances that deviate from the trained appearance.
In this paper, we explore the idea of incorporating structural shape priors in an active contour model that is trained with a convolutional neural network.
We propose a novel energy formulation that combines a shape prior with an appearance model.
We learn the shape prior from a set of 3D human scans.
Given a single image, our energy formulation outputs a vector field that actively deforms an initial contour to delineate the desired object.
We optimize our energy with an efficient linear programming algorithm.
We evaluate our method on the challenging problem of segmenting humans in cluttered scenes, and demonstrate the advantages of our approach over the state-of-the-art.
We introduce a new method for joint image segmentation and shape matching based on Wasserstein modes.

Our approach optimizes over image segmentation and deformable shape models in a globally optimal manner, i.e., with no assumptions on the smoothness of the solutions, and is therefore suitable for segmenting images with complex structures and shapes.
We use a greedy algorithm to compute the Wasserstein modes of the image segmentation and shape model, and a dynamic programming approach to optimize the joint segmentation and matching.
We demonstrate the performance of our method on synthetic and real-world image segmentation and shape matching tasks.

Our main contributions are a new globally optimal algorithm for joint image segmentation and shape matching based on Wasserstein modes, and a comprehensive evaluation of the method on a wide range of benchmarks, including synthetic and real-world images, and comparison with state-of-the-art methods.
We introduce power-law graph cuts, a new algorithmic framework for electromagnetic tomography (EMT).
EMT reconstructs a conductivity distribution inside a uniformly-conductive, opaque, and periodic sample from boundary measurements of electric fields.

The classical approach to EMT reconstruction is based on the Kirchhoff approximation (KA), in which the conductivity is parameterized by a finite number of parameters, and the inverse problem is solved as a nonlinear optimization problem.
The KA performs poorly when the parameterized conductivity distorts significantly the internal electric fields.
We show that power-law graph cuts, a novel convex optimization approach, are capable of recovering the true conductivity distribution accurately even in the presence of significant distortion.
We present a simple but effective approach to salient object detection, which is built upon a discriminative regional feature integration framework.

Unlike most existing works that treat saliency detection as a bottom-up process and accumulate evidence from low-level to high-level features, our approach works in a top-down manner, where the goal is to directly predict the final saliency map from the input image with the global context information carefully preserved.
In particular, we first generate a series of initial saliency maps at multiple abstraction levels by feature encoding modules.
Then, we introduce a regional feature integration module to selectively integrate the regional features across these abstraction levels in a top-down manner.

The regional features are aggregated such that the most discriminative ones are given higher weights, and that the global context information can be effectively preserved and propagated through the integration process.
In this way, our approach can effectively concentrate on the most salient objects and avoid the excessive response to non-salient regions.
We optimize the proposed approach with respect to a unified objective function that measures the quality of both the saliency map and the regional features.
Experimental results on four public benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach, which achieves state-of-the-art performance.
An Enhancement Neighborhood connected Segmentation (ENCS) is proposed for segmenting nuclei images.
It combines the advantages of existing algorithms such as Nuclear Density Based (NDB) technique, watershed transform and shortest path finding algorithms.
The proposed method consists of three steps.
Firstly, a thresholding technique based on Otsu's method is applied to the original image for obtaining an initial segmentation.
Secondly, the watershed transform is used to obtain the final segmentation.
Thirdly, the shortest path finding algorithm is applied on the watershed segmented image to obtain the final segmentation where the cells are connected according to their neighborhood.
The proposed method is tested on 2D-cellular images and compared with existing techniques.
The experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

An iterative method for multilevel thresholding using electromagnetism optimization is used in this article to approximate a given image by a union of basic shapes, such as rectangles, triangles, or diamonds.
In thresholding, selecting an appropriate threshold is a challenging task.
Using the threshold obtained from the estimated noise, the algorithm decides the suitable threshold value in noisy images.
We then use an iterative approach that employs electromagnetism optimization to identify the best threshold value for decomposing an image into its basic components.
We evaluate the performance of the proposed method by applying it to synthetic and real-world images, and the results are compared with those of existing techniques.
The proposed method shows better results in terms of objective and subjective quality measures.

Learning Automata (LA) is a novel framework for dynamic programming, which is capable of learning optimal solutions from a single observation of the underlying model structure, under some suitable assumptions.
In this paper, we consider the well-known image segmentation problem, where the goal is to find optimal regions that adhere to image boundaries.
We propose a multi-threshold based approach, where the thresholds are optimized using LA.
Our approach is fully automatic, and is shown to produce very promising results on a variety of test images, including those with complicated structures.
We present a novel approach for training conditional random fields (CRFs) on large datasets such as Cityscapes.
Our method is based on a closed-form expression for the gradient of the log-likelihood with respect to the unnormalized weights.
This expression allows us to efficiently compute the gradient while requiring only a small amount of memory.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on the task of semantic image segmentation, where we achieve state-of-the-art performance on the Cityscapes dataset.
Our method is also applicable to other CRF-based tasks such as depth estimation and pose estimation.
Introduction: Conditional random fields (CRFs) are powerful tools for training structured output predictors.
They have been widely used in computer vision tasks such as image segmentation, depth estimation, and pose estimation.

However, training CRFs on large datasets can be computationally expensive and memory-intensive due to the need to store and compute the gradient of the log-likelihood with respect to the unnormalized weights.
Our Approach: In this paper, we present a novel approach for training CRFs on large datasets.
Our method is based on a closed-form expression for the gradient of the log-likelihood with respect to the unnormalized weights.
This expression allows us to efficiently compute the gradient while requiring only a small amount of memory.
To our knowledge, this is the first closed-form expression for the gradient of the log-likelihood with respect to the unnormalized weights of a CRF.
Results: We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on the task of semantic image segmentation, where we achieve state-of-the-art performance on the Cityscapes dataset.
Our method is also applicable to other CRF-based tasks such as depth estimation and pose estimation.
Conclusion: In this paper, we presented a novel approach for training conditional random fields on large datasets.

Our method is based on a closed-form expression for the gradient of the log-likelihood with respect to the unnormalized weights, which allows us to efficiently compute the gradient while requiring only a small amount of memory.
We demonstrated the effectiveness of our approach on the task of semantic image segmentation, where we achieved state-of-the-art performance on the Cityscapes dataset.
We believe that our method will also be applicable to other CRF-based tasks such as depth estimation and pose estimation.
Scene labeling with contextual hierarchical models greatly improves upon current state-of-the-art performance, while being efficient and flexible enough to handle diverse and large-scale data sets.
We introduce a novel approach for scene labeling that factors out the context in scene labels by recursively partitioning the scene into a hierarchy of regions while preserving the overall context.
This approach is based on a new convolutional neural network architecture that is both computationally efficient and highly flexible, and can be easily extended to handle other scene labeling tasks.

We show that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on the Stanford Background Segmentation Dataset and the MIT Scene Understanding Dataset while being an order of magnitude faster than the current state-of-the-art.
Active contour models have been successfully applied to image segmentation, however, most of these methods assume that the image is represented by a continuous scalar field.
In this paper we propose a novel active contour model for image segmentation of manifolds, where the image is represented as a continuous manifold valued function.

In order to define a valid energy function for the proposed model, we introduce the concept of reachability, which allows us to define the energy as the distance of the contour from the reachable set of samples.
We show that the proposed energy function is well-defined and introduce a gradient for the energy function that can be efficiently computed.
The proposed method is evaluated on synthetic and real-world images and the results show that the proposed method is capable of accurately segmenting manifolds.
We present an accurate method for MAP segmentation based on a hidden Markov model (HMM), whose state-space is a partition of the image domain.
The algorithm is an extension of our earlier work on the topic, allowing for images with significantly larger sizes and for many more objects.
The key idea is to formulate the segmentation as a path-constrained Viterbi training of the HMM.
We show that the algorithm is efficiently realized via iterated conditional modes and graph cuts.
We present experimental results on both synthetic and real images.
We consider the problem of training a classifier for imbalanced datasets using large-margin machine learning.
We propose a new algorithm, Logistic Discriminant Analysis (LDA), which uses a logistic regression model to classify instances based on a margin criterion.
Our algorithm can handle the highly imbalanced distributions often encountered in partitioning problems, such as graph partitioning and hierarchical clustering.
We present an analysis of the algorithm and show that it performs well on a wide range of datasets, including several standard datasets for these problems.
Our results show that LDA is highly competitive with the current state-of-the-art, which typically involves complex nonlinear models such as support vector machines or ensemble methods.
For the imbalanced datasets we consider, our simple and efficient algorithm often achieves better accuracy and a higher speed.
We present a novel technique for tuning the algorithm based on a novel cost sensitivity analysis and show how this can be used to obtain better solutions.
The algorithm is implemented in the new MATLAB algorithm library provided with this paper.
This library also contains a new graphical user interface for interacting with the algorithm and a collection of partitioning problems.
Fine-needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) is currently the golden standard for thyroid nodule diagnosis.
Ultrasound (US) images are commonly used to guide the FNAC procedure.
In this paper, we present an automatic segmentation approach to assist the interpretation of US images of thyroid nodules.
The approach consists of preprocessing, region proposal generation, segmentation refinement, and classification.
In the preprocessing step, the image is denoised using non-local mean filtering and the specular reflection is removed via spherical harmonics.
Region proposals are generated by an adapted variant of the selective search algorithm.
To handle the extreme texture variations in US images, a segmentation refinement network is proposed.
Finally, the proposed approach is evaluated on a dataset of 131 US images.
Compared to the state-of-the-art, the proposed approach achieves a 6.35% increase in DSC and a 12.53% increase in ACC.
An image segmentation method based on non-parametric convolution is proposed in this paper to segment ill-posed objects from single image.
Context window approach is used as a preprocessing to obtain a good quality image for segmentation.
The proposed method utilizes the newly formed image with much weaker noise and better defined edges to achieve segmentation.
The segmentation is performed in pixel level using a kernel referred to as the clump kernel.
The clump kernel has the ability to identify the region and the background.
The proposed method is tested on many ill-posed images produced by H.M. Johnson in 1986.
The results show that the proposed method is able to segment the images according to the object and the background.
In this paper, we propose a novel image segmentation enhancement technique based on active contour and topological alignments.
Our method combines the advantages of both approaches to achieve accurate and robust segmentation results.
We begin by initializing an active contour model using a set of seed points and then iteratively refine the segmentation by considering topological alignments between the contour and the image.
The topological alignments are computed using a novel graph-based approach that considers the local structure of the image.
The proposed method is evaluated on a variety of images and compared to state-of-the-art image segmentation techniques.
The results show that the proposed method achieves improved segmentation accuracy and robustness, especially in challenging images with complex structures and textures.
In this paper, we survey and compare a number of state-of-the-art skin detection algorithms.
The class of images that we deal with in this study is of sub-continental humans.
A number of algorithms have been proposed in the past for skin detection.
The algorithms can be broadly classified into two categories: (1) Color-based algorithms (2) Texture-based algorithms.
In this paper we have implemented and compared the performance of some of the recently proposed algorithms from both these categories.
The performance is measured in terms of True Positive Rate (TPR), True Negative Rate (TNR), Precision, Recall and F-measure.
The implementation results show that no single algorithm is best suited for all types of images.
Based on our study, we conclude with some suggestions for improving the performance of these algorithms for sub-continental human images.
Medical image registration is crucial for minimally invasive procedures, and accurate registration relies on accurate intensity standardization.
This study compares intensity standardization techniques to evaluate their impact on registration accuracy.

A phantom study was performed to compare three intensity standardization techniques: (1) nonlinear scale normalization (NSN), (2) cubic spline interpolation (CSI), and (3) intensity slope correction (ISC).
Twenty-five slices from seven different phantom types were scanned multiple times under various conditions, including different contrast agent concentrations and magnifications.
The same slices were then registered using combinations of the three standardization techniques with two different registration algorithms.
The RMS error between the ground truth and the registered images was used to evaluate registration accuracy.
Compared to NSN, CSI and ISC consistently resulted in smaller RMS errors.
Furthermore, the combination of CSI and the iterative registration algorithm achieved the best performance, consistently decreasing the RMS error by 52.7% compared to NSN.

The results of this study show that intensity standardization techniques significantly affect registration accuracy and that CSI combined with an iterative registration algorithm yields the most accurate results.
We address the problem of modeling physical forces in active contours for image segmentation, using a locally-varying curvature approximation.
This model can simulate a priori unknown forces, derived from the image itself, which drive the active contour toward a segmentation.
The energy of the proposed active contour model is minimized by a fast marching method, which iteratively updates the contour.
This approach yields a fast and efficient algorithm, which is very competitive, in terms of computational speed, with traditional active contour models based on gradient descent.
In addition, a priori knowledge about the forces, such as upper and lower bounds, further accelerates the algorithm and leads to a parameter-free method.
The proposed method is applied to several images, and very promising results are obtained.

The normalized cut problem is to find a partitioning of $V$ into two subsets $S$ and $T$ such that $|X\cap S| \geq \frac{k}{|V|}|X|$ and $|X\cap T| \geq \frac{k}{|V|}|X|$, or alternatively $|E[S,T]| \geq \frac{k}{|V|}|E[X,X\cap V\setminus X]|$.

In this paper we present a polynomial time algorithm for the following problem: given an instance of the normalized cut problem, find a partitioning of $V$ into two subsets $S$ and $T$ such that $|E[S,T]| \geq \frac{k}{2}$, and either $|X\cap S| \geq \frac{1}{2}|X|$ and $|X\amp T| \geq \frac{1}{2}|X|$, or $|X\cap S| + |X\cap
T| \geq |X|$.
This extends a result of Chan et al.

[SODA'07] who presented such an algorithm for the case $k=1$. This extends a result of Krause and Pudlák [IPCO'16] who presented such an algorithm in the case $m=2$ and $k=1$. We re-examine the foundational continuous optimization view of boosting, viewing the algorithm as a primal-dual algorithm in a statistical learning sense.
This results in a new characterization via a dual problem, with a novel dual objective.
This in turn yields a new interpretation of the classical weak learning hypothesis, and suggests a general phase diagram for boosting algorithms in a primal-dual sense.

We show that classical boosting algorithms such as AdaBoost and Gradient Boosting are special cases of our general framework, and we derive new "primal only" algorithms which can be seen as generalizations thereof.
These new algorithms do not require a duality gap, yet are shown to be statistically consistent under weak learning assumptions.

We present a systematic two-dimensional (2D) reconstruction of three-dimensional (3D) magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) turbulent flows subject to a strong magnetic field with very low magnetic Reynolds number, based on properly weighted projections of the 3D velocity and magnetic fields onto suitable 2D planes.

The 2D reconstructions obtained using this method provide a complete visualization of the flow structures in the (x,z) planes (where the magnetic field is perpendicular to the plane) as well as the corresponding Contours of Convection (CC) in the (y,z) planes, at various representative locations in the 3D domain.
This approach allows for a better understanding of the 3D flows, by using the 2D visualizations and CCs to elucidate the flow topology, the 3D structures being otherwise difficult to analyze.

In order to assess the accuracy and validity of this 2D reconstruction method, we perform a linear stability analysis of 2D and 3D axisymmetric turbulent flows, which shows very good agreement between the growth rates and wavelengths of the most unstable modes in 2D and 3D.
We also analyze 3D MHD turbulent flows subject to a strong magnetic field and low magnetic Reynolds number in a wedge, for various values of the magnetic Prandtl number.
Finally, we discuss the implications of these results for magnetized accretion flows onto neutron stars, in order to assess the importance of 2D effects in such systems.
The effect of electron irradiation on the superconductivity in single crystals of Ba(Fe$_{1-x}$Ru$_{x}$)$_2$As$_2$ ($x=$0.24) was investigated.
The critical temperature was found to increase with electron irradiation dose.
The critical temperature increases are attributed to the creation of additional charge carriers by the irradiation induced defects.
The irradiation induced defects also reduce the superfluid density.
The reduction of the superfluid density is more pronounced in the samples with higher irradiation doses.
The results are compared with previous results on other iron-based superconductors.
This paper provides information on the effect of electron irradiation on single crystals of Ba(Fe$_{1-x}$Ru$_{x}$)$_2$As$_2$ with a particular focus on superconductivity.
State machines are formal methods commonly used in the development of large scale computer software and systems.
They provide a structured approach to modeling and analyzing the behavior of complex systems, and are used to specify, design, and verify the correctness of software and hardware systems.
This paper discusses the application of state machines to the development of large scale computer software and systems, and presents examples of their use in the context of a number of case studies.
The paper also discusses the benefits and limitations of state machines as a formal method for developing large scale systems, and presents a number of research challenges in this area.
We introduce the notion of graded comodule categories with enough projectives, a generalization of the usual notion of comodule categories with enough injectives.

We show that graded comodule categories with enough projectives are characterized by a universal property, and we develop some of their basic theory, including a definition of graded quotients and a description of their homotopy theory.

We also show that the category of graded comodules over a graded coalgebra is a graded comodule category with enough projectives, and we use this result to describe the homotopy theory of graded coalgebras.
This paper is a continuation of [arxiv.org/abs/1507.00819].

Graphene, a single layer of graphite, has attracted extensive interest due to its unique properties.
Although graphene is known to be thermally and chemically stable, it can be oxidized to graphite by a laser irradiation in oxygen atmosphere.
In this study, we present a systematic in-situ Raman study of laser-induced graphene oxidation.

Unlike the previously reported random graphene oxidation, we find that a continuous graphene oxide layer is formed due to oxygen diffusion through the graphene membrane when the sample is oxidized at a sufficiently high temperature.
The graphene oxide layer is composed of a few graphene oxide sheets stacked together.
We discuss the formation of a continuous graphene oxide layer on the basis of our experimental results and previous studies.

We show that the shape dynamics description of gravity from the Ashtekar-Barbero-Immirzi (ABI) formalism, when formulated in terms of the 3+1 decomposition of spacetime, presents a natural generalization of the Newtonian gravitational constant.
This generalization arises as a consequence of the immanent geometric nature of ABI gravity, encoded in the self-duality of the densitized triad field.
We discuss some implications of this result, in particular with respect to the ongoing effort of quantizing the geometric sector of shape dynamics.

Electron energy-loss spectroscopy (EELS) can provide elemental and chemical state information from the same measurement, with better than 0.1 nm spatial resolution, and is therefore an ideal metrology for directly observing nanoscale chemical changes.
This paper describes a data processing strategy enabling atomic resolution EELS, and illustrates the approach on model nanostructures and a poly-silicon line.

The data processing scheme combines the statistical analysis of the noisy EELS spectrum with a parameter-free tight-binding atomic multiplet calculation, to extract the spectrum of the core loss peak.
The proposed method is generally applicable, as it is based on the only physically-motivated model for the core loss spectrum—the atomic multiplet calculation.
In the literature, a variety of different approaches have been attempted to extract atomic information from EELS.
These can be classified into three main categories, as follows.
First, a tight-binding approach has been utilized under the assumption of a single element and an approximate instrumental function.
This approach has been employed previously to observe atomic species [9, 10], but does not allow chemical state identification.
Second, a comparison between measured and calculated spectra utilizing a list of instrument functions has been performed without the tight-binding approximation
Finally, a purely statistical analysis of the measured spectrum has been performed without comparison to a calculated spectrum
We have developed a new approach that combines the tight-binding atomic multiplet calculation with a parameter-free optimization.
This approach allows atomic species and chemical states to be identified in a model-independent manner.
The proposed method is applied to several model systems to test its validity.
Recent progress in thermal scanning probe lithography (t-SPL) toward sub-10 nm patterning is reviewed.
Several approaches to improve the throughput of the slow and expensive nanolithography are introduced.
A simultaneous serial writing scheme achieves 10 nm pixel size with a 100 nm pitch and is shown to be scalable to wafer-level nano-lithography.

A fully parallel scheme demonstrates an array of 1024 cantilevers writing simultaneously at 100 kHz, which is two orders of magnitude higher than conventional thermo-mechanical scanning probe lithography (t-SPL).
A fast and re-usable polymer resist optimized for t-SPL is developed to enable these high speed and large area lithography.
Finally, the extension of t-SPL to pattern metal films is discussed.
A lift-off process is demonstrated to pattern a self-assembled monolayer (SAM) of alkanethiol on a gold film, followed by the deposition of aluminum film and successful lift-off process.
This process is further extended to pattern silicon nanowires of sub-20 nm half pitch by a damascene process.

We show that worst-case linear discriminant analysis (LCP) finds the linear classifier that achieves the worst-case margin among all linear classifiers that are feasible with a given covariance matrix.
This solves a longstanding open problem and provides an alternative perspective on LCP via convex optimization and semidefinite programming.

We show that the worst-case margin can be calculated via a semidefinite programming problem with a novel sparsity structure, for which existing solvers can be used to find the certificate of infeasibility.
This work has implications for understanding the limits of the margin-based generalization bound and for developing more accurate statistical learning theory.
This work also suggests a practical method for selecting the regularization parameter in linear support vector machines.
We study existence and uniqueness of solutions for the Cauchy problem for elliptic complexes in the space of distributions.
The results are based on a priori estimates for distributions and the fixed point theorem in the space of distributions.
We apply the results to the Cauchy problem for elliptic complexes associated with elliptic partial differential equations with distributional coefficients.
In particular, we show that the classical solution of the elliptic partial differential equation is also a distributional solution.
This solves positively a open question posed by J. Rauch.

The results on uniqueness for the Cauchy problem for elliptic complexes in the space of distributions also give new results on uniqueness for the Cauchy problem for elliptic partial differential equations with distributional coefficients.
This is based on a priori estimates for classical solutions of elliptic partial differential equations with distributional coefficients.
The results in this paper are motivated by the study of the Cauchy problem for complex hyperbolic partial differential equations with distributional coefficients.
Complex hyperbolic partial differential equations with distributional coefficients often appear in applications.
In general, the classical solutions of these partial differential equations are not smooth functions.
It is still an open problem to find sufficient conditions on the coefficients such that the classical solutions are indeed smooth functions.
Recently, H. Dong and the author showed that such sufficient conditions do exist for complex hyperbolic partial differential equations with real-valued coefficients.
However, in the case of distributional coefficients, it is much more difficult to find such sufficient conditions due to the lack of regularity for distributions.
In this paper, we show that, if the elliptic complex associated with the partial differential equation is coercive, then the classical solutions are indeed smooth functions.
This extends the previous result of Dong and the author to the case of distributional coefficients.
In phase unwrapping, a common and troublesome problem is the occurrence of discontinuities in the wrapped phase, introducing biases in the estimation of wrapped phase gradients.
In this paper, we propose a simple and efficient approach to deal with this problem.
It is based on a regularization of the phase, inspired by the Isotropic Uncertainty Principle (IUP).
We show that the IUP leads naturally to a multi-resolution strategy.

The method is evaluated on synthetic and real world examples, showing significant performance gain with respect to state-of-the-art methods, in particular in the presence of strong noise and discontinuities in the phase.
The paper presents a novel method for solving the electronic structure problem of quantum chemical calculations, which is one of the most computationally intensive problems today.
The $\Delta$-machine learning approach combines ideas from quantum chemistry and machine learning to develop a new type of approximation.

The proposed method is evaluated on a set of molecular benchmarks, and it is shown to be competitive with existing quantum chemical approximations while requiring significantly less computational resources.
The results suggest that the $\Delta$-machine learning approach may provide a promising route for solving the electronic structure problem on big data platforms.
We find all square-tiled tori, first introduced by Conway and Craine in [ innum.org/pdf/iyn07.pdf ].
These are among the few known spaceforms that tile space by translations alone, and yet are not periodic.
We describe a recursive construction for these spaceforms, and use this construction to derive a simple algebraic equation that determines whether a given lattice is a square-tiled torus.
We conclude by discussing the possibility of creating a census of square-tiled tori.

We present techniques for generating useful cluster states, specifically a blue-sky state for an 11-qubit system, using only a universal gate set that can be implemented with current superconducting technology.
To achieve this, we implement a new cluster generation algorithm with an intuitive graphical user interface.

This algorithm provides a complete clustering solution, requiring only a set of desired logical gates and a desired clustering size as inputs, and produces a recipe for generating the desired cluster state that can be executed on a physical quantum computer.

We implement this algorithm using a new reusable architecture for cluster state generation, and use this to find a clustering solution for generating a blue-sky state on IBM's quantum computer, IBM Q.
As a byproduct of our approach, we also identify a subroutine for generating a seven-qubit cluster state that is amenable to near-term quantum computing technologies.
We consider the Eliashberg formalism in the framework of the density functional theory using the quasiparticle approximation.

We examine the influence of the formalism proper on the calculated properties of high-pressure superconducting state in phosphor using the original version of the GW approximation for the exchange-correlation functional.
We show that within the formalism the calculated properties of the superconducting state are in good agreement with the available experimental data.
We study the phenomenon of sticky seeding in discrete-time reversible-threshold networks, where the network undergoes irreversible evolution towards a absorbing state.

We show that, despite the irreversibility of the evolution, the initial state of the network can display stickiness, i.e., sensitivity to initial conditions, which is a hallmark of discrete-time Markov chains.
In particular, we show that the stickiness can arise due to the reversible-threshold structure of the network, and illustrate it with various examples.
We further show that the stickiness can lead to a lack of convergence of the mean-field theory for the stationary distribution, and discuss possible remedies.

We investigate static, spherically symmetric solutions of the Einstein equations coupled to a topological defect scalar field nonminimally coupled to gravity in an arbitrary space-time dimension $d$. It is known that for $d=3$, static, spherically symmetric topological-defect boson stars are possible in the presence of a positive cosmological constant, while in $d=4$, they are possible only in the presence of non-canonical scalar fields.
We show that in $d\geq 5$, static, spherically symmetric topological-defect boson stars are possible even without a cosmological constant and in the presence of a canonical scalar field.
Interestingly, we find that the nonminimal coupling introduces a length scale in the equations of motion, which in the weak-field limit reduces to a gravitational Yukawa coupling.
However, this length scale disappears in the strong-field limit, where the topological-defect boson stars approach black holes.
In this paper, we continue the study of global attractors for the nonautonomous 3D Navier-Stokes equations initiated in [33].

We show that, for any nonautonomous dynamical system arising from a 3D Navier-Stokes equation, the corresponding global attractor is uniformly bounded in the energy space ε−1, √ε−1, ε−1, independently of the external force, provided that the initial data belong to the space $L_{\infty}^{5/4}(\mathbb{R}^{3})$.
We introduce set-valued fundamental diagrams for second-order traffic models.
Set-valued fundamental diagrams extend classical fundamental diagrams, which are known to be applicable only for bottleneck flows and strictly saturated traffic.
Set-valued diagrams can explicitly account for the possibility of having a set of possible output flows for a given input flow.
These diagrams are derived from Jaminon solutions, which are characterized via the second-order limit of generalized bottleneck equations.
In this paper, we construct the set-valued fundamental diagrams for several classes of networks, including series-parallel and tree networks.
The results show that the constructed set-valued diagrams are closely related to the generalized Bottleneck Principles and the generalized network decomposition.
We extend the theory of bisimulations for denotational semantics to account for a new class of delimited-control operators with dynamic prompt generation.
These operators allow multiple prompts for a single answer, and the prompts themselves can be generated on-the-fly during the execution of the program.
We define a notion of environmental bisimulation that allows us to reason about the behavior of such programs, and show that it satisfies the properties of congruence and reflexivity.

To illustrate the applicability of our approach, we present a denotational semantics for a small functional language with delimited-control and dynamic prompt generation, and use environmental bisimulations to prove correctness of a program that uses such operators.
We study the discrete-time quantum walk on the line, whose coin-flip probability operator is given by a discrete-time unitary operator $U$ which may not necessarily be time-reversal invariant.
The walk traverses the line, staying at site $i$ with probability $|u_i|^2$, where $u_i$ is the $i$th column vector of $U$.
We find necessary and sufficient conditions for crossovers, i.e., for the probabilities to be arranged in non-increasing order, to occur.
In particular, we find that $U$ has to possess a certain symmetry, related to time-reversal symmetry.
As a consequence we find that the replacement of the Grover operator in the discrete-time setting with a non-time-reversal operator is unlikely to be useful.
We perform qubit state tomography in a superconducting circuit by using weak measurements.
By periodically weakly measuring the qubit, we obtain statistical moments of the readout signals, which are used to estimate the state of the qubit.
We demonstrate a tomographic scheme in which weak measurements followed by a projective measurement are performed, and a tomogram of the qubit is obtained.
We apply the proposed method to a superconducting flux qubit, and perform tomographic reconstruction of the qubit state with high fidelity.

The presented scheme is useful for obtaining the quantum state of a superconducting qubit, which is necessary for the analysis of quantum information processing tasks and for verifying the correctness of quantum algorithms.

the most recent comprehensive and authoritative source on the subject.
Current quantum hardware requires quantum memory that can store quantum information for extended periods.

We propose a quantum memory architecture that uses code-mediated error suppression to balance the errors in the two logical qubits of a trapped-ion qubit, leading to a memory with quantum coherence lasting above 24 hours, even in the presence of temperature-mediated relaxation.

We propose an active set algorithm for efficient estimation of parameters in generalized linear models with ordered
  predictors.

Our algorithm exploits the ordering of the predictors to reduce the number of computations involved in the
  estimation process.
We show that the proposed algorithm is efficient in terms of both computational and memory requirements.
Furthermore, we demonstrate that the algorithm is very effective in handling large datasets and high-dimensional predictors.

The proposed algorithm is compared with a traditional lasso approach, and results show that the proposed method is very competitive
  in terms of prediction accuracy and model selection flexibility.

Abstract:
We propose a new approach to answering the question "when does a physical system compute?"

Following previous suggestions that computational capacity (the ability to perform computational tasks) may be a fundamental concept in physics, we suggest that it is a necessary condition for a physical system to be able to perform the corresponding task itself, rather than acting as a helper in a larger system.
Based on this condition, we show that, contrary to common belief, many simple systems can in fact perform computation, as long as they are given an appropriate initial condition.
On the other hand, we also show that certain systems that are "too simple" cannot compute under any initial condition, thus giving an affirmative answer to the question posed in the title.

We consider distributed optimization of smooth functions over random networks.

We analyze a class of deterministic first-order methods, which include the classical gradient method and the Nesterov-like gradient method, in the scenario where the underlying network is known to the optimizer only through the topology of the network.

For topology-aware optimization, we provide a condition on the step-size for convergence of the distributed gradient method, and furthermore, prove that the Nesterov-like gradient method achieves linear convergence in the expected local error.

We implement these methods on Amazon EC2 instances with CPU and GPU and show that the Nesterov-like gradient method is more robust to different instance types and sizes compared to the classical gradient method.

We give a brief overview of the notion of a modular functor and its applications in topology and mathematics.
We then describe the concept of topological recursion and its relationship to modular functors.
We present some examples of modular functors and discuss their properties.
Finally, we discuss some open questions and future directions in the study of modular functors and topological recursion.
We develop a non-local thermodynamic equilibrium (NLTE) radiative transfer code for calculating spectral line formation in cool stars.
The code consists of an improved version of the 1D LTE stellar spectral synthesis code of Werner

[CITE] for calculating the level populations of 24 chemical elements, and a newly developed LTE-to-NLTE spectral synthesis code that calculates the NLTE spectral line profiles based on the level population obtained from the stellar spectral synthesis code.

We have calculated the NLTE spectral line profiles for several elements in the wavelength range between 1000 Å and 1 μm, and found that the NLTE effects can be very important, especially for the weak lines.
The abundance derived from the weak lines can be different from the LTE abundance by 0.5 dex or more.
We have also found that the derived abundance of some elements, such as Ca, Cr, Mn, and Ni, depends on the choice of the model atmosphere, and the line lists used in the calculations.
We have evaluated the performance of our code for calculating the NLTE spectral line profiles for C, N, O, and Si, by comparing our results with the published NLTE results for the Sun.
We find that our code provides results that are in good agreement with the published NLTE results for the Sun, and that the NLTE effects for these elements are important and can not be ignored.
We have applied our code to the abundance analysis of HD 181320, a G8 dwarf star.
We have determined the abundances of 24 chemical elements in HD 181320, and compared our results with the abundances derived from the high-resolution spectrum of this star using the LTE technique.

We find that the abundances derived from our NLTE analysis are in good agreement with the abundances derived from the LTE analysis, except for Na, Al, and possibly Mg, for which the NLTE abundances are lower than the LTE abundances by 0.2-0.3 dex.
The differences between the NLTE and LTE abundances are likely due to the effects of hyperfine structure and/or continuum placement.

Our results suggest that the NLTE effects can not be ignored in the abundance analysis of cool stars, and that the NLTE spectral synthesis code developed in this work can be used to accurately determine the abundances of chemical elements in cool stars.
We study the time complexity of synchronization of discrete pulse-coupled oscillators connected by a tree network.

We show that the network synchronizes in linear time, i.e., the convergence time is proportional to the network size, and provide an algorithm for constructing the coupling matrix with the desired synchronization property.
We also show that the synchronization error decreases double exponentially with the number of time steps, thus providing an estimate on the speed of convergence.

Finally, we consider the effect of adding long-range connections on the synchronization speed, and show that despite the fact that these connections may increase the overall connectivity of the network, they do not change the final synchronization error, and moreover, they do not change the basic linear speed of synchronization.
We study the complexity of the clique-width of graphs, that is, the width of the largest clique decomposition of a graph, a measure of graph complexity introduced by Courcelle.
We give a necessary and sufficient condition for a graph to have unbounded clique-width, defined in terms of a finite set of forbidden induced subgraphs.

This condition is equivalent to the non-existence of a finite set of forbidden induced subgraphs that would guarantee, by the graph minor theorem of Robertson and Seymour, the existence of a polynomial-time algorithm for computing the clique-width.
Coalgebraic infinite traces are a generalisation of regular infinite traces to the setting of coalgebras, suitable for describing asynchronous systems with infinite behaviour.
In this paper, we study the connection between coalgebraic infinite traces and Kleisli simulations, a notion of simulation between coalgebras due to Turi.

We show that Kleisli simulations can be characterised in terms of sharing and overlapping of infinite traces, and that the existence of a Kleisli simulation between two coalgebras implies the existence of a shared infinite trace.
We also show that the functorality of Kleisli simulations can be captured by functorality of shared infinite traces.

These results provide a new coalgebraic perspective on the classical theory of infinite traces due to Maurer and Naruke, and establish coalgebraic infinite traces as a theoretical tool for reasoning about the behaviour of asynchronous systems with infinite behaviour.

Let $\mathfrak{M}$ be a family of compact subsets of a Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^N$. Necessary and sufficient conditions are provided for the Minkowski measurability of $\mathfrak{M}$, which is characterized by the existence of a measurable function $\mathfrak{m}:\mathfrak{M}\rightarrow [0,1]$ called the Minkowski content, such that $\mathfrak{m}(K)\approx \infty \Leftrightarrow \mathfrak{m}(K)=\infty$ for every compact set $K\subset \mathbb{R}^N$. Furthermore, necessary and sufficient conditions are given for the relation $\approx$ in terms of a family of coverings $\mathfrak{U}$ of $\mathbb{R}^N$, and the family $\mathfrak{U}$ is characterized in terms of $\mathfrak{M}$. An example of a non-measurable family $\mathfrak{M}$ is provided.
The results are illustrated by the family of all compact sets of fractal drums in $\mathbb{R}^3$, and a necessary and sufficient condition is given for the Minkowski measurability of this family.
Recent progress in salient object detection has primarily focused on single-label datasets, which only contain objects of interest with a single background.
However, in real-world applications, multiple objects of interest may be present in an image along with complex backgrounds.
In this work, we address the problem of salient object detection in such multi-label settings.
