In this paper, we present a self-supervised approach for training a medical image segmentation model using only a few labeled images.
Our approach leverages the inherent structure and prior knowledge in medical images, specifically the organization of tissues and organs into distinct regions known as superpixels.
We propose a novel self-supervised learning framework that utilizes these superpixels as a weakly-supervised signal to guide the training process.
Our method enables the segmentation model to learn from a significantly smaller labeled dataset, making it suitable for scenarios where acquiring large amounts of annotated data is challenging.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on a public dataset of abdominal CT scans, achieving state-of-the-art performance in terms of segmentation accuracy and efficiency.

An important task in computer vision is referring image segmentation, which associates each pixel in an input image with a semantic category label, and further retrieves a referring region in the image that is most relevant to the category.

However, existing referring segmentation methods mainly rely on low-level image cues, and often encounter difficulties in comprehending contextual information and capturing long-range dependencies, which limit their performance in referring segmentation.

In this paper, we propose a cross-modal progressive comprehension approach to referring image segmentation, which leverages the power of both images and texts to overcome the limitations of previous methods.
Our approach progressively comprehends the referring information from both modalities in a mutually reinforcing manner.
Specifically, we first generate object region proposals via a coarse-to-fine strategy that integrates both image and text understanding.
Then, we develop a referring segmentation network that refines the object regions by progressively reasoning about the referring relationships between objects and their referring regions.
Finally, we employ a novel referring coherence loss to enforce the coherence of referring relationships.
The extensive experimental results on three benchmark referring image segmentation datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in comparison to the state-of-the-art.
Semantic image segmentation has received increased attention in the computer vision community in the last decade.

This paper studies a new threat model for this task: the segmentation-leak threat model, where an attacker aims to maximize the leakage of semantic information via adversarial perturbations on a pixel level.

Unlike previous work on semantic segmentation, which mainly focuses on the prediction of individual pixels, this work focuses on modeling the relationship between pixels, which requires the attacker to gain knowledge of the model's internal representations.
We first construct a membership inference attack to demonstrate the segmentation-leak threat model.

The proposed attack significantly outperforms existing perturbation-based attacks, achieving an average accuracy of 84.4% on the Cityscapes dataset, compared to 82.4% and 80.5% for the strongest versions of Boundary and Noise attacks, respectively.
We then analyze the transferability of the membership inference attack across models, and propose two defense strategies to mitigate such attacks.
Our empirical results show that the proposed defenses can effectively mitigate the attacks with negligible computation overhead.
This paper presents a framework for finite group equivariant neural networks (FGENNs), a new class of machine learning models designed for efficient learning of group-equivariant functions.
We introduce the concept of finite group equivariance and show how it can be used to improve the performance of neural networks on games.
We present a generalization of the backpropagation algorithm that allows for efficient training of FGENNs and show that it can be used to learn group-equivariant functions for a variety of games.
Finally, we present experimental results that demonstrate the effectiveness of FGENNs in improving the performance of neural networks on several games.
The paper proposes a deep neural network (DNN) for 3D surface segmentation based on a contour tree hierarchy (CTH).
The DNN takes a point cloud as input and outputs a segmentation of the surface, with each segment representing a different object in the scene.
The network is trained on a large dataset of point clouds and their corresponding segmentations, and learns to predict a segmentation based on the point cloud input.
The proposed network shows superior performance compared to other state-of-the-art methods on several benchmark datasets.
Semantic segmentation is a fundamental task in urban driving image analysis, enabling the automatic understanding of scenes.

However, existing works on semantic segmentation focus on images captured by a standard camera, while images from a fisheye camera, which has a wider field of view, contain more information and are more challenging to analyze.
In this paper, we present a universal semantic segmentation framework for fisheye urban driving images.
Our framework comprises a cascade of deep neural networks, including a fisheye encoder and two decoders for segmentation and classification.
The fisheye encoder effectively utilizes the rich information in the fisheye images, while the decoders perform segmentation and classification tasks.
We evaluate our framework on two large-scale datasets for urban driving image analysis and achieve state-of-the-art performance.
Our framework is universal and can be applied to various datasets and tasks in urban driving image analysis.

Abstract:
Traditional machine learning algorithms have shown promise for nuclear segmentation in digital pathology images, but they often struggle with the presence of complex structures, overlapping cells, and class imbalance.
In this paper, we present an improved approach using deep decision tree ensembles with sparse coding.
Our algorithm enhances accuracy by incorporating contextual information and leveraging the interpretability of decision trees.
We evaluate our method on a challenging dataset of digital pathology images and achieve state-of-the-art performance with a significant improvement in segmentation accuracy.

This work demonstrates the potential of sparse coding-driven deep decision tree ensembles for nuclear segmentation and lays the foundation for more robust and accurate techniques in digital pathology.

Below is an abstract for the academic paper titled “Scribble-based Domain Adaptation via Co-segmentation”:

Recent progress in domain adaptation (DA) has achieved remarkable performance by learning domain-invariant features from data.
However, existing methods either require a large number of training data or additional annotations, which are difficult to obtain in many real-world applications.
In this paper, we propose a scribble-based domain adaptation (SDA) method that addresses these issues.
Our approach leverages scribble data, which is easy to obtain and can be used to transfer knowledge from a source domain to a target domain with only a few images.
We formulate the DA problem as a co-segmentation task, where the goal is to segment the foreground and background of images in the target domain using scribble annotations from the source domain.
Our method is able to adapt to the target domain by learning a domain-invariant segmentation mask that can be applied to the target domain images.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on three benchmark datasets, and the results show that our method outperforms the state-of-the-art in DA.

Abstract:
Connectome reconstruction is a complex process that requires accurate segmentation of neuroimages.
In this paper, we propose a deep learning based approach for large-scale image segmentation that utilizes a structured loss function to improve accuracy.
Our approach is trained on a large dataset of images and utilizes a fully connected neural network architecture.
We evaluate our approach on a challenging dataset of brain images and compare it to state-of-the-art algorithms.
Our results show that our approach achieves comparable performance to the current state-of-the-art while being significantly faster.
Furthermore, our approach is able to handle large-scale image segmentation tasks, making it suitable for connectome reconstruction.
We believe that our approach can be used to improve the efficiency and accuracy of connectome reconstruction, making it a valuable tool for neuroscience research.

The segmentation of interacting surfaces in images is a crucial step towards understanding the spatial relationships between objects, enabling numerous applications in computer vision, augmented reality, and robotics.

However, existing methods focus on segmenting individual objects without considering the mutual interactions between them, leading to suboptimal results in scenarios featuring strongly overlapping objects.
In this paper, we address this gap by proposing a globally optimal segmentation framework that explicitly models the mutual interactions between surfaces.

Our approach leverages a deep learning architecture, termed Mutually Interacting Surfaces Segmentation (MISS), which simultaneously optimizes the segmentation of all surfaces in the image while enforcing globally optimal solutions through a novel interaction potential.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on both synthetic and real-world datasets, showing significant improvements over the state-of-the-art in interaction-aware surface segmentation.
Urban scene segmentation is a video understanding task that involves dividing an urban scene video into a plurality of pixel wise labelled object segments.
We propose a Naive-Student framework that leverages the power of semi-supervised learning in video sequences for urban scene segmentation.
Our framework takes advantage of the inherent temporal coherence in video sequences to improve the segmentation performance.
We extract a video level feature representation using a 3D Convolutional Neural Network (3D-CNN) and use a temporal convolutional network (TCN) to leverage the temporal coherence.
Furthermore, we propose a novel semi-supervised loss function that utilizes the uncertainty of the predictions of the naive Bayes classifier to regularize our network.
We evaluate our method on the Cityscapes dataset and achieve state of the art segmentation performance.
Our framework achieves a mIOU of 87.4 on the validation set, outperforming the previous state of the art method by 1.7 points.

Here is an abstract for the academic paper titled "Autoregressive Unsupervised Image Segmentation":

This paper proposes an autoregressive unsupervised image segmentation model, which is a novel approach to the problem of segmenting images without using labeled data.
The model is based on the idea of learning a hierarchy of features, where each level of the hierarchy captures more complex and abstract representations of the image.
The model is trained using a variant of the self-supervised objective, which is a combination of an autoregressive loss and a consistency loss.

The autoregressive loss encourages the model to predict the next pixel in the image given the previous pixels, while the consistency loss encourages the model to predict consistent segmentation across multiple scales.
The model is evaluated on the Cityscapes dataset, and achieves state-of-the-art performance in terms of both the mean intersection over union (mIoU) and the F1 score.
Active learning is a technique for training machine learning models with fewer labeled examples than traditional supervised learning approaches.
However, active learning algorithms often require a measure of uncertainty in the model's predictions, which can be difficult to estimate.
In this paper, we propose a new method for uncertainty estimation in active learning for image segmentation.
Our method uses a deep neural network model trained on a sparse set of labeled pixels and a dense set of unlabeled pixels.
We show that our method can accurately estimate the uncertainty of the model's predictions, and we demonstrate its effectiveness on a variety of image segmentation tasks.
We compare our method to state-of-the-art active learning approaches and show that it significantly improves the model's performance.

Below is an abstract for the academic paper titled "Suggestive Annotation of Brain Tumour Images with Gradient-guided Sampling":

Recent progress in artificial intelligence has enabled the development of computer-aided diagnosis systems that can assist doctors in the detection and classification of brain tumours in magnetic resonance imaging (MRI).
However, manually labeling a large amount of data for training these systems is time-consuming and expensive.
In this paper, we present a method for suggestive annotation of brain tumour images using a gradient-guided sampling approach.
Our method utilizes the inherent structure of the MRI data and a trained neural network to suggest probable tumour locations.
The suggested annotations can be used to train a computer-aided diagnosis system or to evaluate the performance of existing systems.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on a large dataset of MRI images and show that it can significantly reduce the amount of manual labor required for annotation.
In this paper, we present an uncertainty-aware multi-view co-training framework for semi-supervised medical image segmentation and domain adaptation.
The framework utilizes multiple views of the data, including image intensity, image-derived and tissue-specific prior knowledge, to train a deep learning model for semi-supervised segmentation.
We introduce a novel uncertainty-aware loss function that encourages the model to learn robust representations that are resistant to noise and out-of-distribution data.
Furthermore, we propose a domain adaptation module that leverages the uncertainty estimates to adapt the model to new domains while reducing the risk of overfitting.
The proposed framework was evaluated on the ISBI 2017 Challenge dataset for semi-supervised segmentation of neuronal structures in electron microscopic images.
Our method achieved competitive results compared to other state-of-the-art methods while requiring less labeled data.
An important trend in convolutional neural network (CNN) design for visual recognition is an increasing depth of the network.
Although larger models achieve better accuracy, their computational cost makes them less suitable for deployment on embedded systems or real-time applications.
In this paper, we revisit the idea of using pyramids to process multi-scale inputs, which reduces the effective depth of the network while maintaining accuracy.
We propose a general pyramid architecture that applies to a variety of CNN designs.

We then develop an efficient variant of this architecture, called PyRAMidal Convolution (PyRA), which reduces computational cost by carefully choosing the number of parameters and the optimization process.
PyRA achieves 84.9% top-5 accuracy on the ImageNet dataset with 52 million parameters, which is only 3% less than the accuracy of VGG-16 (with 138 million parameters).
When applied to ResNet, PyRA achieves 92.4% top-5 accuracy with 14.5 million parameters, which is only 1.6% less than the accuracy of ResNet-50 (with 25 million parameters).

Abstract:
Data imbalance has always been a challenging issue in medical image segmentation tasks, especially when training datasets are composed of a small fraction of labeled images.

In this paper, we focus on the task of multi-organ segmentation from whole slide images (WSIs) of histopathology, where only a few cells are manually annotated in the training data due to the immense labeling effort.
To overcome the data imbalance issue, we propose a new framework that consists of a multi-scale feature abstraction (MSFA) module and a label-efficient segmentation (LES) module.
The MSFA module effectively captures multi-scale contextual information and reduces the amount of features to be processed by the downstream segmentation modules.
The LES module, on the other hand, leverages the use of a partially labeled dataset to guide the training process and adaptively refine the segmentation results.

We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on three publicly available datasets for multi-organ segmentation, achieving state-of-the-art performance in terms of both segmentation quality and efficiency.
Here is an abstract for the academic paper titled "Critical Assessment of Transfer Learning for Medical Image Segmentation with Fully Convolutional Neural Networks":

Abstract:

Transfer learning has recently gained a lot of attention in the field of medical image segmentation.
The ability to use pre-trained models on large datasets to extract meaningful features has shown promising results on a variety of segmentation tasks.
In this work, we perform a critical assessment of transfer learning for medical image segmentation with fully convolutional neural networks.
We evaluate the performance of several state-of-the-art transfer learning models on a variety of medical image segmentation datasets, and analyze the impact of transfer learning on model performance.
Our results show that transfer learning can significantly improve the performance of medical image segmentation models, especially when the target task has a limited amount of labeled data.

However, we also find that the performance of transfer learning models can vary significantly depending on the similarity between the source and target tasks, and that fine-tuning large models can be computationally expensive.
We conclude by discussing the potential of transfer learning for medical image segmentation and suggesting future research directions.

Abstract:
Medical image segmentation plays a crucial role in the diagnosis and treatment of various diseases.
However, deep learning-based segmentation models can suffer from the issues of poor calibration and inadequate out-of-distribution (OD) detection.
In this paper, we propose a novel approach to improve calibration and OD detection in medical image segmentation with convolutional neural networks (CNNs).

Our method involves the use of a temperature-scaling-based technique to enhance the calibration of the segmentation model and a novel OD detection scheme that utilizes the spatial information of the input images.

We evaluate our approach on a public dataset for liver tumor segmentation and demonstrate that our method significantly improves the calibration and OD detection performance compared to existing techniques.
Our approach has the potential to enhance the reliability and generalization of medical image segmentation models, leading to more accurate and robust diagnoses.
This paper presents a new validity index for fuzzy-possibilistic C-means (FPCM) clustering, a data clustering technique that combines fuzzy clustering and possibilistic clustering.
The new validity index is derived using a combination of fuzzy logic and probability theory, and it is used to evaluate the quality of the resulting clusters.
The paper discusses the advantages of the new validity index over existing validity indices for FPCM clustering, and it presents a numerical example to demonstrate its use.
The new validity index is shown to be a more effective measure of cluster quality, and it is applicable to a wide range of data types and clustering tasks.

Abstract:
Lake ice is a crucial component of freshwater ecosystems and human activities.
It is an important indicator of climate change, and monitoring lake ice thickness is essential for understanding its impact on lakes and their surroundings.
We present a novel approach to monitor lake ice thickness using webcams and crowd-sourced images.
Our method uses computer vision techniques to extract pixel-level information from webcam images and crowd-sourced images of ice thickness measurements.
The extracted information is used to train a deep learning model that can estimate ice thickness from webcam images in real-time.
We evaluate our method on a dataset of images from two webcams monitoring a lake in Ontario, Canada.
